text: Ince I heard this game is getting a sequel, I jumped for joy (I really think I did) I'm not a fan of artstyles in games, but this one is an exception. I get wowed again and again everytime I play it. The physics based, puzzel solving game that is Trine should be enjoyed by all human beings.

10/10. The most beautiful platform game I've ever played. It plays 2D, but is rendered in gorgeous 3D. The music is awesome, and I obtained the soundtrack even before purchasing the game itself. The game play is quite possibly the best I've seen in a 2D platform game. Objects and enemies use  Nvidia PhysX engine and there are multiple ways to defeat enemies and navigate obstacles. You play 3 classes all at the same time, each with unique abilities. The Wizard conjures objects, the Thief uses a grappling hook and archery, and the Knight uses a sword and shield.

Your typical side-scroller with a few additions thrown in to mix things up. In Trine, you may control one of three characters (switching between them in single player or playing as all 3 on local coop). Using each character's unique abilities, you must triumph over the undead and reclaim your lost kingdom. Despite it being an old fashioned side scroller with very few twists, its major attraction (at least in my personal opinion) is its soundtrack. A game is great, don't get me wrong. But the cherry on top is listening to the beautiful melodies of the orchestra serenading you as you make your way to the end of every level. If side-scrollers aren't your thing, then at least take a listen at the soundtrack. I assure you, you won't regret it.
Grade: B+

So then, No Man's Sky. Arguably the most controversial game ever relased, and certainly of recent times, the hype over this game led to outrage over the final product.
Thing is, I never knew about any of the hype, I hadn't even heard of the game, or any of the promises. All I did was show up after it was released and play it.
So, this review, rather than pining over what the game isn't, I'm going to review based on what it is.
In short, NMS is an exploration grind for the OCD'r in you, a relaxing stroll through procedurally created planets with their resources, lifeforms, and outposts. Add a bit of space exploration and some basic trading with a hint of a plot about the centre of the universe and Atlas, and a choice between that or pure free exploring, plus some random aliens who give you stuff and either get upset or happy with you based on what you say to them, and that is basically it.
Visually it is average, if not good, at 4K - the SLI scaling could be better and my 980Ti SLI gets about 20-50fps - there are times it looks close to slideshow,  and the pop-up can be irritating. But the Pathfinder, adding that 4K native resolution is always a plus.
The sound is rather good - some quirky alien creature sounds, decent music and the general ambience does lend quite well to an outer spacey atmosphere.
As for the gameplay? The mouselook isn't the best and the ship's controls are clunky, but in terms of what it is, rather than what it was supposedly promised as, it really is good fun and easy to get totally lost in. I just spent 3 hours cataloguing all the outposts and creatures of my starting planet and have only just left. And I found it relaxing, strangely therapeutic, and oddly satisfying.
There's not a lot more, and I know that. But I knew that before I bought it (at half price, definitely not worth the full £40) and that's why I shelled out.
For what it is, I like it a lot. It may well run out of novelty value soon, and I might well find myself bored pretty quickly, but so far it's grabbed my attention and I don't think I'll mind a journey to Atlas or the centre of the universe.
That is said, it IS a unique game - no game like this ever got made before, and it is for a certain kind of person. This is for you 'tro-hos' from Playstation, or those who like all their achievements on Steam - it's for those who like to 'do everything' and be given a shiny notification for it.
All while walking around looking at weird aliens and landscapes.
It's a niche market, but one I like.
EDIT: 13/03/17
So there is WAY more than what I just detailed in this review - with the Pathfinder update base building, ground vehicles, teleportation etc have been added and it's easy to get completely lost in this. One slight issue is the prediliction for 'fetch' gameplay, whereby one task requires something else, which itself needs something else etc. Ubisoft games are infamous for this kind of gameplay - but I can't deny this game is addictive and compelling. It remains as fun now as when I started. Maybe more so.
Shame I wasted so much time on this one hoping to find anything interesting.

I loved the classic NES version and Gauntlet Legends so I got this expecting something similar. I won't even give it extra points for the low price. It's just not good enough. Sure it is kind of fun to play with friends online, but you make most of the fun, not the game. It has some minor bugs here and there, nothing game breaking so overall is not a bad game, It's just not a good game either and for sure not nearly as good as a Gauntlet game should be. The greatest let down is probably the length of the game. Sure I can play it again in different difficulties, or try the extra modes to unlock content that does absolutely nothing. But why would I want to do that? If you expect some sort of nostalgia factor or even some fun multiplayer dungeon crawling action with your friends, this game might let you a little disappointed, but if wasting time doing the same thing over and over again for little reward is your thing, then this game is for you.

Gauntlet was one of the first games I played on my 8-bit NES countless years ago. We were used to exercising our imaginations back then, so the crappy top-down perspective shooter felt like such an epic adventure, fighting monsters and ghosts and facing many perils down the dungeons. Now, decades later, Gauntlet makes its return, and the inevitable question arises... does it live up to its predecessor’s fame? Surely not, but neither does the original Gauntlet, not to the nostalgic memories many of us cultivated throughout the years (the truth is that the game is crappy and boring).
Still, the new Gauntlet manages to be an entertaining game on its own. It has some feats in common with the original game, which will appeal to old fans (the basic elements are all there, the classes, the keys, the food, the ghosts etc), but it’s a very different game in some aspects. While the original game offered a very monotonous dungeon that seemed endless, the new game is quite short and more varied. The different characters play very differently and you can upgrade their equipment and improve their abilities by unlocking achievements. Also, soloing the dungeons and multiplayer mode play quite differently, so there’s a lot of replay value to be found.
Gauntlet 2014 is a simple, stripped-down dungeon crawler that serves as a light-hearted, tongue-in-cheek, uncompromising alternative to Diablo, combining old-school and more modern elements without aspiring to be either original or innovative. The character’s personalities and lines get old real quick, but the level designs are very well-thought (despite being very linear) and revisiting them can still be fun even after many playthroughs, especially if you get friends to play with. I only wish there were more levels, because the game's length is quite underwhelming, all the replay value doesn't make up for it. The feeling of delving deep into the dungeons you got from the original game is completely absent here.

I don't think I've ever laughed this much while playing a multiplayer game. The gameplay is silly, and the sound design and graphics underline that silliness. The matches vary from simple two-player rounds where you can gauge your skills against another player, to madness with five or more bombernauts. A really crowded match will make it easier to get killed, but with more targets it's also easier to get your revenge as a ghost and return as a zombie.
The gameplay is intuitive and controls are simple, although the camera can take some getting used to. In the beginning it's easy to flip the camera and accidentally fall off a ledge. The level editor features are straightforward and it's easy to make levels quickly using the various symmetry modes.
Bomb combos often lead to hilarious results, but you won't usually get that many items stacked in a vanilla match. Luckily (or catastrophically), matches can be configured to different levels of mayhem. Insane item spawn rate combined with several uses per item is a good way to make each match an unpredictable mess of strange explosive devices.
Most levels can be destroyed easily. Some levels will let you blow up walls to expose climbing tiles, and sometimes you want to prevent others from following you by destroying the stairs you climbed up on. In two-player matches, the latter can get annoying if you're not in a position to catch up using a bomb jump or jetpack, since there won't be any ghost players dropping bombs from above to reduce the advantage. However, the option of introducing meteor showers a few minutes into the game can make isolated platforms less safe.
Player count is naturally vital in a multiplayer early access game. You also need at least three players if you want the full Bombernauts experience. At the moment, you're not guaranteed to find other players at arbitrary times of day. It helps if you have at least one friend who plays, since others will be more likely to join in when you have a game already running.  If you don't have any bombernaut friends, but enjoy making your own levels, you can test your levels while waiting for other players to join. Evenings seem to be the best time to find others playing.
All in all, Bombernauts is a really silly game where you never know what's going to happen next. I already recommend it in its current state, and it's been getting steadily more polished and fun with each update. With a few more regular players it'll be even better.

: Eyebrow Interactive
: Eyebrow Interactive
: A key for this game was provided by the developer for the purpose of writing an unbiased informative review. No other compensation was given.
==========
Bombernauts is a online multiplayer arena game with fully destructible voxel terrain. Think Bomberman, only a lot more fun; Your character is a little buggy-man thing, armed with tons of bombs and a baseball bat. Bombernauts is an incredibly fun game with friends, but therein lies it's largest problem: the playerbase is currently non-existant. While this isn't the game's fault, as the game itself is solid with a great concept and little to no bugs, it currently does not have any singleplayer or bot options for players to mess around with while they wait for other players to battle. However the devs are currently working on adding these features, so we should see the playerbase rise considerably after these are implimented. Now let's take a look at the game itself.
==========
Remember Bomberman? Well, this game is Bomberman without the grid layout on it's maps. You control a small 3-wheeled buggy-man-thing (let's just call it a buggy), that's armed with an infinite supply of bombs and a baseball bat. You can play against up to 16 other players (4 is the recommended number), where the objective is to blow them all up! Sounds simple, but it is insanely fun. You throw bombs in an arc, and you can aim how far your throw will be. Bombs explode a couple of seconds after landing, and if you hold off before tossing them while aiming, it'll cause a larger explosion...sort of like powering them up. The baseball bat can be used in a pinch to knock enemy bombs away from you, even before they land! Batter up!
At times, a small drone carrying a pinata will appear. If you bust up this pinata with your bat, it will drop a random powerup. These powerups are very numerous and do a variety of things, but usually only last for 1 bomb throw. For example there is one that lets you throw a cluster of bombs at once. When this explodes, it shoots many smaller bombs out, which then explode as well. Another powerup gives you a temporary jetpack, which improves your mobility greatly. There are a few referential powerups too, that give nods to various things. One great example of this is a powerup that gives you Dragon Ball Z Super Saiyan hair, and allows you to throw what I believe to be a Spirit Bomb!
There are many, many different maps that are rotated between each match. Every map is fully destructable, even if some parts take more powerful bombs to destroy them. There is also a map editor which you can use to create your own maps. I haven't tried it out yet because I have trouble designing decent maps or creations using toolkits for games, and sometimes the controls are a bit weird. But it's a great addition.
Right now the game is multiplayer/co-op only, but as I mentioned before finding people to play with is a bit of an issue. If you want to play against others, it's recommended to get a 4 pack and give the extras to your friends who want to play, or host a game and hope others join, or advertise it on the game's forum.
==========
Bombernauts is fairly simplistic, but the visuals are very crisp and look nice. The maps consist of mostly cubes and structures built from them, which can be blown up as much as you please. Some parts of each map react to explosions differently; for example some will catch fire after an explosion and turn to ashy blocks which crumble when touched.
Your player character is a little buggy thing on 3 wheels with goofy eyes. These look pretty comical and adds to the charm of the game. Each buggy can be fully customized with many color, eye, and wheel options.
Explosions look great. While not realistic with flames going everywhere, they are instead a shower of vibrant stars and smoke which fit the game's comical theme very nicely.
==========
The bomb sounds effects are extremely satisfying. They work very well, and mesh well with the visual effects. The music is simplistic like the graphics, but it gives the game a light competitive feel, which helps as this is a competitive game at its core. It's pretty much the same tune repeated all the time, but you never really get tired of it.
I feel like the game could use a little more work in this area. Possibly a few new tunes and some more unique sound effects. What they have now is good, but it can only get better with a little time and effort!
==========
I had zero issues with Bombernauts. It ran very smoothly with a great framerate of 45-60FPS. I recommend a controller, as the keyboard controls can be more of a hindrance than help. The game loads up pretty fast, enabling you to get into the action quickly. I didn't see any random crashes, so that's a plus.
==========
With a little more work and exposure, Bombernauts could be a great multiplayer title. Bombs and powerups everywhere only add to the fun and mayhem of each game. With plenty of maps to play on, as well as a map creator, there is literally no end to the fun this game could bring. Recommended if you are looking for a game to play with friends!

The Metroidvania open world was really nicely built and I had a lot of fun exploring it. The game gives you many great skills along the way and (for me at least) they felt really natural almost instantly. The game really made me use the whole skill arsenal and that's just great game design.
It get's pretty challenging towards the end, but I think the hard parts are necessary. There are a couple of really tedious running parts where you have to ace the whole thing at one go, and it definetely made me curse and think of quitting. But it set the tone, I felt really small and helpless, which is what the character actually is and finally after completing the part, it always made sense. Just phenomenal story telling. A similar emotional rollercoaster just wouldn't be possible in any other medium.
I would recommend this game to pretty much anyone, but I'm sure it's a bit too hard for some. Even for those people I would recommend playing the beginning though, only the last third of the game is hard and I strongly suggest you to stick with it, it's worth it.

8.6/10 - This is a very Bethesda title so if you are a fan you should love this. Meaning exploration is gloriously sublime and main quest/story seem a little stilted and forced, better than Skyrim but still in that style. Side quests sometimes seem way more interesting than the main quest.
I find the karma system horribly broken. Other than enslaving people and blowing up Megaton I do not even know any way to effectively lower karma by large amounts. Enslaving NPCs removes them from the game (stops them from re-spawning) so eventually the wasteland becomes depopulated. But again, if you are a Bethesda fan and enjoy the mentality of continuously getting ambushed by vampires and cultists in Skyrim then you might also enjoy the Fallout variation of that (I do not).
Exploration/navigation is also very Bethesda, meaning that the maps and directions are purposefully made to misdirect and double back endlessly, either to make the experience seem larger and/or more challenging. Unfortunately in FO3, the intended circuitous routes are often enforced by invisible walls and/or being forced into underground tunnels. The quest/map marker system is either broken or unreliable when in the tunnels and often leads far, far, far astray before eventually leading to the destination. Hard to tell which as Bethesda is known for buggy games but also for encouraging exploration. If you bunny hopped your way over mountains and obstacles to destinations in Skyrim, you may very much dislike this Fallout experience.
My first Bethesda game was Skyrim and I eventually modded it. I discovered Fallout through Skyrim. By the time I got around to playing Fallout it was primarily a modded Fallout. Even so vanilla Fallout is perfectly fine and my modded vs vanilla experience is essentially the same except for intensity of combat, subtlety of survival, and visual impact... core experiences are unchanged. From my modded game I consider these as essential core elements: Mod Organizer, xEdit (FO3Edit), FOSE (Fallout Script Extender), Unofficial Fallout 3 Patch, FO3 Wanderers Edition (survival/combat), A World of Pain for FO3 (quest), Xepha's Dynamic Weather (outdoor weather & lighting), Fallout StreetLights, Realistic Interior Lighting, RH IronSights (aim down sights), Weapon Mod Kits, DarNified UI for FO3, and Brisa Almodovar (companion). Unfortunately to get all these working together requires several bridges, patches, and a merge patch I must build myself (using xEdit) so the technical requirements can be quite high. Skipping RH IronSights, WMK, and DarNUI will eliminate 99% of the complications.
I would strongly recommend to by Fallout 3 with all the DLC unless you absolutely know that you will never want to install mods as the more modern/popular mods often require some DLC. Plus FO3 is sort of broken without the BOS DLC anyway.

Earned in Blood, just like the other two Brothers in Arms games, has an amazing story.
The three games combined are simply the greatest WWII games out there. Call of Duty 2, of course, was amazing for the African campaign. But Gearbox hold the title for recreating very important battles in the Normandy region in France. I mean, if you've played the games, then maybe you've seen the extras where pictures show how much detail they put into recreating the villages in Northern France. It's very remarkable.
The story, you play as Joe Hartstock, Red, in this one. Maybe you remembered him in Road to Hill 30. Well, this game takes place alongside Road to Hill 30 as Joe is recounting his actions to SLAMarshall, a war documentarian, recording the actions of combat troops for the military. Throughout the story, Joe sees his friends get injured, change their attitude during the war, and some of them unfortunately die. But that's war.
The audio design is unreal. My dad walked by when I was playing and noted how realistic the sounds were for the rifles and panzers. The soundtrack, too, is amazing. Basically, I'm biased as hell as I already love WWII anything, but the strong character development, friendship, and tactical elements make the Brothers in Arms games some of my favorites.

This game is a real mixed bag for me.  The short story is that I find it fun and engaging, but there are points where the suspension of disbelief comes to a screeching halt.
1) Weapon effectiveness - there is a serious problem with the way weapons are depicted.  Explosions, for example,  won't hurt you at all beyond a small radius and within that radius you get the full effect. Worse, firearms have "levels".  It should be that putting a large-caliber rifle round through someone's head makes them combat ineffective most of the time. In this game if your weapon is a lower level than you target it maybe extremely ineffective, even for headshots. If the gap between the level of the target and the level of the weapon is great enough, you can use half a belt of 7.62mm from an M-60  machine gun ammo at close range on a person in jeans and a T-shirt and they will keep fighting until they finally die - hopefully. Similarly your character is pretty resilient when it comes to getting holes poked in them.
2) Carrying capacty - you can carry literally dozens of rifles or machine guns if you feel like it along with a truly improbable amount of ammo and it won't slow you down at all. Of course, you need that ammo, because your targets will generally be much more comfortable getting shot n you might expect.
3) Repetativeness - expect to do the same missions over and over at different difficulty levels.
4) Wonky item effects - This may be the only game ever where you might be concerned about how much armor value your holster provides.
To enjoy this game, you've just got to set aside the expectations for realism from the old Rainbow Six games and accept that there is going to be a lot of stuff that doesn't make sense. The story is interesting which helps a lot.

Got it from a "hidden gems" bundle and thats what it is, a very dirty gem in the rough. It's a VERY light harvest moon clone. There's not a lot to do compared to harvest moon but it offers just enough content for me to pour 20 hours into marrying a girl and settling down... and that's it. There was a decent sense of progression and reward for me to keep playing which kept me going until my wedding day but after that I stopped dead. Those looking for a quality harvest moon game should look elsewhere. If however you're willing to throw away a couple of bucks for a more smaller version might want to consider you checking this game out.
As you may guess from the title, the game is about you trying to get love by farming. If only it was this easy... and that's basically the whole story. (the story setup is that you broke up with your ex and now you're going to find love in the farmland.) There are events and npc dialogue but apart from that there isn't a driving plot.
Our love will grow boils down to time management. You grow crops, sell them, and upgrade tools to make more money.  You raise animals to help your profit as well. You also use your crops and animal products to cook or make gifts and give them to girls and win them over. Fishing and mining also tie into the game in similar ways as well. There is a lack of customization as your farm is already laid out and you cannot place stuff where you want. The overall game mechanics is average and a bit dull at some stages especially the late game where you need to continually fish for rare pearls which you need gain access to a boat which allows you to get materials required for your wedding. The game had a clear sense of progression however and the reward is getting closer to be MARRIED to a beautiful pixel girl which allowed me to continue. I have to admit that if it wasn't for that, I would have stopped sooner.
The girls as well as the townfolk have little dialogue. However there was just enough dialogue that you get a sense of what type of girl she is and allows you to choose a girl. There is little interaction other than gift giving but it's nice to be praised for knowing my girl likes pizza. Gift giving is guess and check, with some items liked and some hated. The other npc's aren't as interesting as the girls and offer little to the overall game.
There are several bugs and design flaws that take a way from the experience. Such as putting a quit option in the menu without a confirm to quit which makes for easy accidental exit. You also lose your extra ore when smelting if you do not have enough to make the next bar of gold/iron etc. The overworld music isn't good either and I turned it off most of the time.
They only thing that got me through this game was getting married and the payoff was minimal. Although you can keep playing, there are little things that can happen after that. You no longer get events so you're basically just playing to hoard money. Overall I give it a 3/5. It offers a structured progression and reward but lacks in getting a lot of "fun" out of it. The waifu's are a plus though because they're pretty cute. For $5 though, it's a good deal. If you have the money though, stardew valley is a better investment as a $15 game.

If you're looking for a farming/dating/life sim you're better off just investing in one of the many many MANY Harvest Moon or Rune Factory games. You'll get better game play, more interesting characters/story and a more rewarding experience.
However, if you want a simpler, bare bones Harvest Moon-esque experience, I'd reccomend this game.  It pretty much IS Harvest Moon, only much less in depth and with faster progression. It's fine, it's just nothing special and at times feels a bit hollow.

The tutorial is immensely frustrating in the later chapters, requiring you to do seemingly impossible key combinations. The UI isn't mouse driven at all, and when you first start it up you have absolutely no idea how to navigate the menus, being given clues like "LK" to accept and "MK" to cancel. How does a player new to the game know what LK and MK are? Each character has their own "story mode", but the tutorial probably takes longer than the characters' story modes combined. It
supposed to be an arcade-style game, but I felt as though there wasn't much to do after a few hours of playing. The user experience honestly was just bad for me. In the very final cutscene, right before the credits, the game consistently crashes for me for Parasoul, and some other characters. It's very frustrating, especially since this bug is easily reproducable. In short, get it if you have friends that play it (it does have a multiplayer mode), or if it's 75% off like it has been recently, but I would have a hard time justifying spending $15 for the single player mode.

This is a great example of a 4X game, with a wide variety of customisations, and solid gameplay.
Unfortunately, despite the age of this game, it's mired in bugs, most of which result in frequent crashes and corrupted save files. Given the amount of time it takes to complete even a small game of Galactic Civilizations II, it becomes almost inevitable that you will encounter a game-destroying bug that will render your play through impossible to finish.
It's a pity that a game with so much promise can be ruined by laziness on the part of the developer. I can't in good conscience recommend this game to anyone, and I would be wary if you're thinking about purchasing Galactic Civilizations III, as Stardock's track record shows that it will likely receive no support.

(I have many gameplay hours outside of Steam.)
Galactic Civilizations II is the Half-Life 2 of 4X games - it does everything right.
This slow-paced turn-based 4X game has disturbingly good AI ("We know what you're doing" or "Remove your fleets or we will remove them for you" or after declining aid to a dying civilization "You're next, you know that right?"), huge maps that take real-world months to finish, custom ships, custom civilizations, and a solid diplomacy system.
The soundtrack sets an incredible and unique atmosphere.
This game's sole shortcoming is its lack of multiplayer, which the sequel GalCiv 3 adds. Honestly though, I don't think any will ever be what GalCiv II is.
Galactic Civilizations II is and forever will be my favorite game.

A pretty decent homage to Harvest Moon and the closest thing to a true Harvest Moon type game I have seen on Steam so far. (EDIT: This review was posted before Stardew Valley existed which, if I'm being totally honest, is 10,000 better than this game and you should buy that game first.) If you've played the Harvest Moon games, you more or less know what to expect since there are a lot of similarities, but there are some very signicant differences that Harvest Moon enthusiasts will want to prepare themselves for going in:
Some of the major differences include a total lack of seasons, months, or days of the week. It is a land of infinite summer, where each successive day is just one more day. In some ways this is disappointing, since the changing months and seasons of Harvest Moon tend to keep the world feeling fresh for longer, but in other ways it's sort of liberating, since---for example---you don't have to worry about how soon the season change is coming in regard to planting/harvesting. You just plant and harvest without any concern for losing the crops.
Our Love Will Grow is very liberating in other ways as well. In Havest Moon you have limited inventory space, but in this game you have infinite pockets, so you don't have to worry about the size of your backpack or upgrading your shelf space. You are a walking Mary Poppins bag, so pick up as many things as you want! Another thing that's liberating compared to Harvest Moon is that you don't have to tediously select which tool to use, running the risk of swinging your pickaxe at your horse because you forgot to select the brush or whatever. Instead, you just stand in front of the animal or thing you need to maintain and press the interact button. The proper tool/action will be auto-selected. In the event that there is a sequence of things that need to be done, the game will auto-sequence as well. For example, if you stand in front of a patch of dirt and tap A, the game will automatically till it using the hoe, plant using a seed, then water using the watering can. And all you had to do was tap "interact"! It's so nice to not have to fiddle with tool selection so much.
There is one huge difference with planting/harvesting that I *hated* about this game at first, but in the larger scheme of things I am now kinda on the fence about. In Havest Moon, you have a huge field that is a grid of squares. You can pretty much plant anything on any square in that huge grid. But in Our Love Will Grow, you have a huge field that just has a few squares on it that are specificallly for planting, but you can't use the rest of the field. It's more like farming out of planters than out of the ground. This feels REALLY annoying and arbitrary at first if you are used to Havest Moon, but the longer I played it, the longer I realized that this is also sort of liberating in a way. Whenever I play Harvest Moon games, I have SO many squares on which to plant/harvest, that I get intensely focused on farming and can't bring myself to waste precious hours of my day running around town and doing other things. But since Our Love Will Grow puts a hard limit on how much you can plant (especially in the early game), it really forces you to do more exploring and gathering instead of being an anti-social bean farmer all friggin' day. And hey, maybe that's not so bad.
Speaking of exploring, there is definitely more nature to explore in Our Love Will Grow than in the typical Harvest Moon game. It's not the size of a Zelda overworld or anything, but whereas Harvest Moon typically has only 2 or 3 screens that are not town or farm, Our Love Will Grow has two or three times that amount. So it's good that you have more time to get out there and explore. And you'll want to get to know the lay of the land, since---perhaps on a more negative note---the game does not provide you with a map of any kind.
There are parties and town events just like in Harvets Moon but thankfully you aren't forced to participate in any half-baked and janky mini-games like in Harvest Moon. You show up, interact with the towns people, there is a judged contest of some kind involving no mini-games, and then you all go home. Nice.
Yes, there is the usual wooing of girls to take as a wife. Sorry, female players, but there is unfortunately (and perhaps unsurprisingly) no option to play as a girl who woos boys instead.
There are only two significant criticisms of this game for me:
There are huge collision rectangles around everything and--even worse--there are invisible collision walls drawn in some places where you wouldn't expect them (e.g. you can't walk around the sides of your house, even though it looks like you obviously can). This is definitely not ideal, but it doesn't take long to adjust yourself to it. There are occasional collision errors where you will be seemingly blocked by an invisible wall that was never there before and which disappears if you leave an come back. For example, I once found that I couldn't walk up the path to the mayor's house because something invisible was blocking the whole path. I had to exit the screen and come back. This has happened more than once, in different areas, but is not common. (I expect is has to do with an error in how NPCs teleport around during the day.)
Just like in Harvest Moon, performing actions costs energy. In this game you get an actual energy meter, so your energy is much more quantified than in Harvest Moon, which is good. But what's bad is that Our Love Will Grow docks you energy for a lot of things Harvest Moon doesn't. For example, picking up a mushroom off the ground in the woods costs nothing in Harvest Moon but costs energy in OLWG. Therefore, you run out of energy very quickly in this game. To make matters worse, there is no good way to recover your energy. In harvest moon, you can take a dip in the hot springs or eat some food that you prepared. But in this game, the only way to get any energy back is to buy yourself a snack at the tavern, which costs 100G (in addition to the time expense it takes to walk all the way back to the tavern), and the amount of energy you get for the expense is not really worth it. As a result, the only thing you can really do when your energy runs out is to just call it a day. (And since there are no seasons to worry about, there is no real harm in blowing off a day like this.) This leads to the absolutely ridiculous situations (but which you'll get used to) where you will sometimes wake up at 6am and end up using all your energy and going back to bed by 10am. Such a thing is unthinkable in Harvest Moon, but it will happen regularly in OLWG.
Overall, I'd say the game pales in comparison to an actual Harvest Moon game. It's a much more simplified Harvest Moon, which in some ways is good and in some ways not so good. But if you like Harvest Moon, I might recommend this game just for the experience of a game that is MOSTLY like Harvest Moon, but is much different in terms of how the economy and pacing work.

There is a common tendency in casual games, where they usually attempt to play things safe, they don't really do much to stand out all that much as they are trying their best to focus solely on their gaming audience and make attempts at not displaying anything too complex, however
is a little different in that regard. This game could have easily been your typical casual game like any other, but it actually builds upon that and develops something that most people will grow a liking to.
Gameplay in the game is very addicting. In UFO, you play as (as you can expect) a UFO, where your main goal is to go to different planets, beam the humans up while defending yourself from defenses on the planet. Once/if you escape the planet successfully with the humans, they will act as resources to your ship where you can gain upgrade your ship, varying from increasing your health to increase the capacity of the humans that you can carry. These upgrades are used to build you up towards boss fights you will have to face, where unlike the other planets if you die on the boss fights, it will be perma death, which means players will have to be more cautious about entering the boss fights and need to use their resources effectively.
The gameplay is addicting and also challenging, but I have to say the most fun that I've had in the game is the boss battle fights. With the boss fights, unlike fights on the planets, will vary an incredible amount, so you aren't sure when the boss fight is close to being finished, you don't know what is about to be thrown at you next, while also throughout the whole time in the battle, you have the looming fear of dying and having to restart the game.
The game additionally has a good sense of humor with your alien co-pilots, adding some pretty good writing to the mix as well, this was not necessary, but greatly adds to the nature of the game and is pretty refreshing and good to see.
Casual games tend to not be my particular taste, but even I can't say no to the amount of fun and enjoyability that U.F.O offers.
The graphics, for the most part, are pretty good. Nice 2D art coat the game, however, there is the odd piece of art across the design that looks partly out of place due to a slight lack of detail in comparison to everything else, primarily things like the lava out of the volcanoes.
Aside from those little pieces of art looking slightly under detailed, the art for the majority of the time is good to look at and is really well done.
Casual games aren't my particular taste, as a result of that, that probably prevents the game from really scoring anything higher from me, but even me who is not a big player of the genre can still admire and enjoy the game for how developed, well thought out and well crafted it is.
Pros
+ Addictive
+ Well thought out mechanics
+ Some of the most fun boss battles out there.
+ Good resource management
+ Fun gameplay
+ Challenging
+ Mostly good art
+ Good value
Cons
- Some art looks underdeveloped than the rest.
Final verdict: 8/10

You play an anonymous alien sent on a mission to defeat your species’ greatest enemy by far. An evil galactic warlord named Christos is threatening your alien brethren by building a weapon set to destroy your whole alien race. Luckily, the mothership noticed Christos before the weapon was fully constructed, only leaving you 30 days to bring him down.
Before you go out to fight Christos, you need to become stronger. So neighboring planets are the way to go. It seems for these aliens, they do not only abduct humans but grind them up to use them as resources to put into upgrading their worker bee ships. Sorry to all those families missing your loved ones, but we need it more. Each human is clad in different colors showing their status. Blue shirted humans are not as valuable as gold shirted humans, having a 5:1 comparison on how many resource points they provide. Sadly, the planets are not hopeless to your abductions. It seems they visited these planets often enough to have red armored humans ready to shoot you down, whether on the ground or if you try to take them as resources, and build turrets on their planet. If you lose all of your health, all your resources you gathered at the planet will be lost.
Your ship, a UFO, is very simple to control but is slow in some aspects. It is slow to just go up and down and takes a while to accelerate, but you can outrun blasts if you just keep rotating around the planet. It takes a while to get used to it, and even longer on other planets, but once you get on a roll you are on a roll. After a while you will be accurate enough to pick up only one human in a group of three. Directing your shots is easy enough, but they curve based on where you are and where you are aiming at. Though you will most likely aim directly at something unless you miss and it seems like it has a formula to it but it will mostly end up you guessing and hoping that shot will hit the human on the edge of your screen. Be careful when you have humans beaming up as it will most likely hit them. As well as before you exit the game, make sure you use the humans as it will assume you had none when you return.
For upgrades you need humans and you needed them yesterday. You have four different places you can put humans in. One area is just for repairing your ship, five points equaling one health point restored. Another area is to upgrade your shots, temporary health, and bomb storage. You are not able to choose which one you want to upgrade first, but increasing how many shots you can do at once and having temporary health as well as your own is very helpful. I never used the bomb, as the enemies will just pop up again anyway and just shooting at them was faster for me, but you do need to accurately be above your enemies for the bomb to do damage. You can also upgrade your health to survive longer on planets and upgrade your storage so you can get more humans before you leave a planet. The last upgrade is to get to the other two planets. It takes 1,000 points to fully upgrade a station, 100 to access all planets, but they are valuable in their own way. At first you’ll make decisions based on your needs, but once you get close to everything being upgraded you are basically golden.
On the human’s side, they are pretty flexible on their shooting end. Once you get on the same screen as the red armored humans or turrets they will automatically aim at you and start shooting. No matter where they are, they will perfectly aim at you, never missing or the shot hitting the planet. Even if they are one pixel on your screen they will still aim for you and shot with pinpoint accuracy. Even to where I can swear it slightly clips through the planet surface, where your own shot will hit the planet otherwise. I do wish the armored humans and turrets had a narrowed shooting range. Once you get overwhelmed you are confirmed dead, especially on the later planets. Once you get to the second planet shots increase to hitting for two health and seems to increase in numbers as well as lave shots up towards you. On the last planet there is an insta-kill tornado, with tentacles blocking your way, turrets take more hits to destroy, and more enemies that hit for three health.
I do wish there was some visual representation on stronger shots and turrets. Once you go into a planet for the first time, it is baffling seeing the sudden difference when it looks the same as the one that only hit for one health. So perhaps a darker hue the harder the shoots hit and making the turrets look more armored to indicate that it takes more hits. I do also wish planets became reliable on their environment killing aliens rather than increasing number in red armored humans and turrets as it more than likely ends up being overwhelmed and shot down as you hit one of the environment hazards. I know that the humans are worth more on these planets, but it just makes destroying all the enemies on the screen before trying to go down and collect the humans the best strategy for the rest of the game.
Once you upgrade your ship all the way, or hit the 30 day mark, it is time to fight Christos. I do like this battle up to a certain point. As you saw in the beginning the planet Christos resides in is protected by a force field. Though it seems Christos is not smart enough to keep the power source inside the force field. Now you can attack the huge turret buildings, and Christos will eventually be revealed when the one he was in is destroyed and you can directly hit him. Lastly he will go up in his own spaceship, which is where some problems come in. The red armored humans and turrets do three health damage to you but Christos does only one, which is weird. Up to this point it is unlikely you got hit as it really is just go around the planet the whole time. However Christos can spiral into an attack, the only opening you have to attack him, to where you can risk staying there and getting hit by everyone or hoping a cheap shot does not get you. The enemy shots can completely go through the planet if you continue going around the planet with a few specifically going in front of you when you least suspect it. Staying while he does his attack is beneficial but it opens you up to being shot down. I’m not sure if at the last stage the humans and turrets respawn, but I do wish it was an one-on-one especially when Christos told them to bugger off.
+ Upgrading system is easy and makes you make decisions on whether you need this or that first
+ Easy to control and get the hang of
+ Perma-death if Christos defeats you
+/- I do wish the third planet relied on its environment rather than how many enemies there are.
+/- More one-on-one battle on the last stage of the Christos battle
- Enemy shots can go through the planet
- Enemies have too pinpoint aiming
UFO - Unfortunately Fortunate Organisms is one of those games you play to waste an afternoon if you have no desire to play others. There is really no reason to play again after defeating the boss unless you want to get achievements. I do like how you have a perma-death if you do not defeat Christos, alluding you to only being a worker bee status, but I do not really get the good ending in terms of what we were told. This is not a bad game, but it is made frustrating with enemies being able to shot through the planet to perfectly hit you anywhere on the screen, even if it is folding onto itself. With how cheap it is, and being able to get a few hours out of it at least, it is worth checking out if you have nothing else to play.

tl;dr - 9/10. exceptionally good platformer but a few frustrating flaws
I would highly recommend Ori and the Blind Forest for gamers who enjoy:
- platformers with a somewhat steep learning curve
- difficult speedrunning
- semi-difficult achievements
- visually stunning worlds and effects
- emotional storyline
- great soundtrack
As soon as I bought this game I was sucked into how great everything looked immediately. You can tell how much planning went into designing certain aspects of each area of the map, which is a great accomplishment for 2D platformers. While seasoned platform-gamers may find the difficulty curve easy, it never takes away from how fun the game mechanics can be (especially once bash is introduced).
My problems with the game:
- Certain areas of the map are unvisitable after storyline progress, which is not mentioned beforehand and can be quite frustrating for achievement hunters (no warning given in-game)
- The difficulty curve is very odd in this game. The game gets progressively harder until the end when everything is very easy (imo).
- no ability to change controls (however it does take xbox controllers or ds3 emulated)
- you cannot play the game after it is beaten (again, no warning given)
- not much to do after you've beaten the game and gotten all the achievements
I believe that these problems are very small and should not deter anyone from purchasing this game. It took me roughly 60 hours to get all the achievements and I wouldn't say I'm a platformer expert. However, I did find it unfortunate that after I got all of the achievements I didn't find much to go back to the game for. Hopefully Moon Studios releases an expansion of sorts. I would love to come back to this game.

Game Dev Tycoon isn't really something that you'd be playing over and over again..
I mean, sure you CAN but that's completely up to you.
Game Dev Tycoon is a simulation game where you play as a poor game developer working in your Mom's garage.
It's pretty simple, you name your game, choose the genre and target, slide the appropriate parts like Engine, Graphics, and Sound, after that you wait for the reviews which is basically the most satisfying thing to watch if you manage to get a 10/10 on your game. There's a lot more to it, like choosing which console your game gets to be published on and researching topics for your new game. You also get the opportunity to move in to a better office and create your own engine for making games.
The only thing i don't like about this game is that's all you do in it. You just increase or decrease the appropriate slider based on the proper genre to get a good score, even though i feel that it's completely random. After you get a lot of good games published and you just so happened to go bankrupt, that's it. Game Over.
Is it worth it? Sure.. maybe. Is it fun? For the most part, yeah.

Fantastic illustrations of each character and monster. The game boards looks inviting and not too overcrowded, but the geography of the Earth is rather bad, especially Europe. There is an ok introduction to the game and the game mechanics, but don't expect to understand the game before you have made it to Stage 2 on the world map. I hesitantly recommend this game. I wasn't as much on the hype train as most, having already been burned by getting in early on Elite: Dangerous, a purchase I still regret, so I was cautious about getting in early on this. I did, though, but I still felt like a few things weren't where they should be.
As other reviewers have mentioned, there are some needless wastes of time, in particular, when you use a radio-tower thing to scan for alien monoliths (or other things). At least half of the time it takes to pan towards the target, up, and then into a global overhead view that never actually shows anything, could be trimmed out, especially if you decide to scan for more than one thing at a time. Some of the crafting tasks seem needlessly grindy, too (Craft W, use W to craft X, use X to craft Y, use Y to craft Z, the thing you needed in the first place, for example) which could benefit by some streamlining.
Running/ Jetpacking could be faster, but I understand there will now be ground vehicles, so that should help a lot on that front. Beyond that, I'd say it is a nicely chill exploration/ crafting game.
Combat is present but not terribly daunting, which is good for me as that's not why I am playing it, and the animals seem to be getting smoother-looking and more dynamic with each update.
It was vastly overpriced, though, for the condition it was released in. It's better now, but I'd still say it's not worth more than 30-35 dollars in the present (much better) condition it is now in. If you can get it for that price and if you understand that there's no real "end game" to go rushing off to, rather, the game is entirely about the journey and exploration, jump on it!

tl;dr: get the gold edition when it's on sale.
Graphics are very good and the world is extremely detailed. Stable 60FPS on ultra with DX12 support.
Audio is not that memorable, certain voice actors are used for many different characters.
The first 20-30 hours will be a solo friendly experience - campaign is fun and offers some narrative to get you into the story.
There's 300+ collectibles that offer some back story and aren't just checkmarks on your list to 100% completion. In-game perk allows you to uncover all base game collectibles which makes the scavenger hunt much easier. Unfortunately, there is no such option for the West Pier area and the Underground DLC that has 80 collectibles locked behind huge grind wall (there is one collectible spawn for one mission so you have to grind 80 missions that last from 10-15 minutes depending on the difficulty).
Once you reach maximum level (30) you are presented with a huge number of activities that unfortunately cater to groups and are not friendly towards solo players. (and now a horde of veteran players comes down on me to rip me to shreds explaining why I suck at the game).
This is my main issue with the game – once you reach level 30 you can forget about all you’ve learned before. Enemies are even bigger bullet sponges and you will be firing a magazine after magazine into them so they can shrug it off and charge you with a shotgun. The game becomes much harder and gear checks are even harsher than before. This leads to unpleasant situations – matchmaking for hard and challenging missions can place you with better geared players (gear score 280+) that will immediately quit after seeing a weaker player with gear score of 256-270. This is understandable because they do not want to waste their time “babysitting” weaker players but leaves you waiting for other players even longer.
You can also go solo into the PvP area called “dark zone” but be prepared to lose all your collected loot because higher ranked players will gang up on you.
So yeah – you can’t solo because you have weak gear –> you can’t queue up for stronger gear because elitists leave the matchmaking -> kinda reminds me of looking for a job when fresh out of university:  you don’t have experience because you don’t have a job and you don’t have a job because you don’t have experience.
Oh, and once you luckily get gear good enough to participate in harder missions be prepared for 1 hit kill ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t enemies that force you out of cover. There’s a chance that an NPC group of so called “hunters” will attack your party. They are extremely quick and resilient and also have a small axe that will one hit kill you if you stay in cover for too long. You can double tap space to dodge them Dark Souls style so they will “only” hit you for 2/3’s of your health only to catch up to you and finish you with a next swing.
Overall, I don’t regret buying this game even though my multiplayer experience was not that enjoyable.
P.S. Feel free to insult me because I can’t solo endgame content and I need to git gud.

:
I haven't played a lot of third person shooters but this game seemed to offer an unique post apocalyptic themed open world setting along with a focus on co op content which was something I was looking for.
Therefore compared to any of the not so recent Tom Clancy games I remember playing I had some more expectations from this modern title not like I didn't enjoy the stealth based mechanics of the previous games but this is more of a cover and shoot based game here. Lets proceed!
:
First lets talk about the equipment you will be utilizing on the streets of New York!
Skills and Abilities: As a division agent you have access to some of the most lethal and technologically advanced equipment available within the US arsenal which translates to 'skill objects' like turrets, seeker mines to something more common like a ballistic shield but with additional capabilities which comes in the form of modifications for all the basic skills. You can equip upto two of these basic skills and one 'master skill' which simply is like an ultimate ability giving you a considerable health/damage/shield bonus for a short time.
Guns: But you probably don't want to fight with just these skills alone (you can if you want though!) so talking about the weapons or guns you have a pretty decent selection of sniper rifles, assault rifles, SMG's, LMG's for primary and pistols for secondary. You can further modify most of the weapons with attachments which boost its statistics like damage, range, magazine size, stability and accuracy.
All of the guns are useable but some guns are just more efficient than the others so yes some specific guns are more desired than the others. The weapon attachments on the other hand are decently balanced except a few. You can carry two primary guns and one secondary gun at any given time.
Body Armour and Equipments: Besides these your knee pads, vest, gloves, backpack, holster and mask can also boost some major and minor statistics. Some of these equipment also support addition of further modifications which can further increase some major and minor statistics.
Until you hit level 30 the combination of your guns and skills along with strategy and coordination if you are playing with other people, is what will matter the most. Once you hit character level 30 you get access to the game changing named gear set equipments, high end equipments and weapons and exotic equipments and weapons.
Recently classified gear sets were added which can provide upto six different bonuses for equipping six pieces of equipment from the same named gear set. I know I'm probably not helping much but confusing more at this point but honestly I'm just trying the detail the depth of the gameplay customization you can have.
Graphics and UI:
This is definitely one of the best looking open world setting currently available. I have not been to New York personally but the level design is very good and consistent. While you can't enter each and every building or more specifically all the floors and rooftops which would be epic but still the areas you can access are very well detailed.
User Interface is also very well done in my opinion especially the fully customizable HUD though they could have used a little more colors in the main map window but that is not a major problem.
Campaign and Progression:
Whether you are playing alone or with other people you will need to complete about a dozen of main missions and several dozens of smaller side missions both of which add to the storytelling and setting the theme.
Regarding the story itself I personally enjoyed doing all the main missions and learning about the different factions especially from the audio logs you can collect on the map. As you complete more of these missions you will be upgrading your 'personal' base of operations which unlocks the previously mentioned skills as you progress and also passive statistical boosts along with more possible interactions with NPC's in your base which is a main part of the story as well.
PvE and AI:
PvE content is definitely one of the biggest drawing factor of this game however it is more similar to RPG's than realistic shooters or simulators due to all the statistics and calculations of equipped item combination involved so this is something to keep in mind.
Regarding the missions themselves there are a lot of options for PvE content even in the base game (without the DLCs). You can do them solo or with a group, the choice is yours but the harder the difficulty the more tougher the enemy and their AI is. Enemies on the highest difficulties have much more armour than players so the shoot and cover mechanics are important for PvE.
PvP:
In the base game as of update 1.8 there are two areas of New York where you can engage in PvP, one is the new 4 vs 4 dedicated PvP only Skirmish mode in West Piers and the other area is the Dark Zone which also has a significantly higher density of NPC's along with timed Dark Zone specific mini events so it is both an alternative for PvE and PvP. Also if you want to engage in PvP in the Dark Zone you can now voluntarily turn on 'Rogue' mode so no more accidental and friendly fire however cutting other players rope during item extraction still makes you 'Rogue'.
Since there are conflicting reports of whether there is any third or first party anti cheat implemented or not, from my experience all I will say is that determining whether someone is cheating or not is a little difficult many times as the time to kill is not very high especially for 1 vs 1 battles. Therefore if you primarily want a PvP experience you might want to look at other third person shooters of which I have played very few.
DLC's:
There are three DLC's available for the game, which add three different games modes and two of them also unlock an incursion (PvE mission) each on the base map. Underground is good for those looking for procedurally generated PvE challenges. Survival has separate PvE and PvP modes but its major appealing factor is the significantly different mechanics, it offers a good experience to those looking for more realistic challenges. Last Stand is for 8 vs 8 capture point based PvPvE game mode set on Dark Zone levels.
I have played a little bit of Last Stand and Survival and the experience has been quite good so far except for some encounters with some obvious cheaters in the Last Stand PvP.
Conclusion:
Overall 'The Division' is one of the better third person shooters available especially for a good co op PvE experience. Nothing technically wrong with the PvP aspect but the implementation has not been smooth due to the constant changes to the game for PvP balance but that also tends to affect the PvE mechanics which often results in a divided community based on opinions as many people (including myself) mostly prefer keeping themselves restricted to the PvE activities which is not a negative thing in anyway in my opinion as everyone should have a decent level of freedom in an open world game.
The playerbase is still 'healthy' in my opinion considering that it is more than 1.5 years old (at the time of writing this), you can find people up for matchmaking for most base game content within few minutes but just like any decently popular multiplayer game your experience with strangers will vary as communication and team work is quite vital if you are attempting some of the toughest missions in a group.
At the end all I will say is whether you are playing with close friends or the new people you meet in the game you will have a lot of fun on the streets of New York, goodluck agent!
NOTE:
This game always requires you to be connected to Ubisoft servers through the UPlay client. You can still play alone if you wish or as recommended with friend(s) or use matchmaking. I have updated the review following the 1.8 update.

The main questline can be completed in probably 5-8 hours with friends playing on normal difficulty but the real fun of the game is in trying to do it an higher difficulties or solo.  The "grind" is related to the fact that each character has separate money, separate "masteries", and separate achievements for the colosseum.   The masteries being separated is somewhat of a pain because many of them involve killing several thousand enemies of different types but it makes the game feel more like an arcade game where youre simply trying to beat your previous scores and for completionists, these time consuming achievements give the game replay value.  My only real issues with the game are that WBplay, an optional feature, will not allow me to link my account nomatter what i try; this does not affect game play at all but prevents me from getting some free skins for the characters.
The colosseum provides more levels to test yourself against either alone or with friends, my only gripe with the colosseum is that they are established as "seasons" and once you miss a season you cannot try those levels again nor can you get the rewards.  I dont think there is a need for the season system to exist since this is not a competitive game and having the colosseum levels set up as a repository of challenges would probably mae more sense in the future.

Bombernauts is a perfect example of a simple arena combat game with a surprising amount of gameplay depth. Being able to adjust how where and how far you throw your bombs is an improvement over the Bomberman games that this game took obvious inspiration from. The style and comedic theme fits perfectly with the gameplay, and the only thing I really think the game needs is a few more gamemodes like Team Deathmatch and King of the Hill.
This game is loads of fun and a perfect party-type game. This is onr of the more stable early access games I've played. You should definitely buy this game, it's well worth the money!

Bombernauts offers a unique fusion of Bomberman and Super Smash Bros, of course focusing more on the Bomberman inspiration.  Where it differentiates itself from Bomberman is the way in which players are eliminated from a match, rather than being taken out in one explosion, you actually have to be blasted out of the arena like in a Super Smash Bros. match.
The 3D maps definintely are more reminscent of Bomberman 64's multiplayer over the more classic top down style that is probably more familiar to fans of the series.  There are a variety of different block types the 100 current maps are made up of too, many of which are fully destructible voxels making for some pretty chaotic matches.
Besides bombs, every player also comes equipped with a bat which can be charged up and used to bat away bombs and players or to break pinatas which contain power-ups.  There seemed to be a pretty good variety of these which would change your bombs into a more powerful or unique variety or something like making you throw a huge pile of bombs at once.
Things I liked:
- The core game is all here and feels quite polished for an early access launch outside some placeholder stuff like the funny loading screen they threw together in paint it looks like.
- Good amount of stages to kick off early access
- Stage creator
- Power-ups
- There is a server browser in addition to a quick match option for those who just want to jump right into the action
- When you die you aren't out of the game as it features a revenge system like we've seen in some Bomberman games.  You essentially become a ghost floating outside the stage that can throw a bomb every few seconds or so.
Things I didn't like:
- On some stages it was hard to tell if I was walking into a hole of death because the water clolor was too close to the tile.  Camera management can get frustrating at times too since you can't always tell where you are going unless you rotate it.
- Minor lag and performance issues in some hectic matches, for the most part things were pretty smooth though.
Things I hope to see added:
- Unlockable customizations for your robot character.  While matches are fun, they need to feel rewarding to the player too.  Have potential random drops at the end of rounds or games and maybe a guaranteed prize for the winner.  Bomberman Live/Ultra featured something like this where cosmetic customizations would randomly appear on the stage during a match so maybe something like that too where pinata loot has a chance to be a cosmetic item to equip before matches.
- Other than that, pretty much just building more onto what we already have in Early Access, aka more power-ups, stages, block types.
Final Thought: Overall if you were a fan of Bomberman or just like party-style games, I think its worth it to give Bombernauts a shot at some point whether it be now or when its out of early access.  Definitely would recommend picking it up with friends though, which thankfully isn't too hard to do since it comes with a free extra copy. :)

This thing even greets you with the words "fun made product".
Firstly, the engine and core are the same, so you have rhythm jumping, pleasant 150 FOV, climbing, shortcuts for shotgun and stakegun and the game looks good and clean (that is, in the places where devs used textures and not blurry placeholders).
But it runs very poorly and has its share of bugs and crashes. When i reached haunted city it wouldn't load the level and i would just fall down into grey abyss. Fortunately, i forgot about it and when i launched the game next time it actually did load.
Next, the level design. It's an absolutely nonsensical mess, which would be somewhat fine if it wasn't stripping the player from progression agency. The levels are giant and long, but still, there are only 6-7 of them and they all poorly designed and balanced. It's a collection of narrow corridors assembled into giant labyrinths, while original had chain of fun medium sized arenas.
A lot of new enemies are just meat blobs. New weapon is a stakegun, again. I understand that stakegun is a iconic titular weapon of the franchise, but we already have it. And second one in BOOH. And an overdosed crossbow.
The worst part of it (yes, even worse than bugs) is the balance. It's a very short thing made by amateurs, so it's extremely difficult even on easy. Outside of high damage, there are immortal ghost which chase you and steal your HP. You can as well just give up and play on "story mode" difficulty, and even then you will be short on ammo on some levels. And with it you lose the second half of the gameplay — achievement hunting, gold management and tarrot cards.
Story is pretty generic, is told in lazy comics and has three endings, but no clear way towards any of them; and i can't even find any information on them. Barks of the protagonist are better than silence, but done poorly and get old very fast.
Well it's a bad one but it is doable. If you can more easily tolerate bad new experience than good but trivial ones — it exists.

First Impression Gameplay:
A fun little game where the objective is to abduct people, grind them into ship upgrades, then fight the end boss with aforementioned upgrades.  Gameplay is simplistic; where you navigate around the planets, beam up civilians while shooting and avoiding enemy fire/natural obstacles.
While not on a planet, you are treated to a cross-section view of your space ship, where you can churn up your human captives into upgrades for various ship systems.  You can upgrade your lasers/bombs, shields, health, carry capacity, range, etc.
There are three planets which you can visit to farm upgrades.  The first is fairly calm and reminiscent of earth, the second is a fiery planet with spews of lava columns, and the third is what looks like some kind of infected planet with wavy tentacle things and a tornado.  Each planet is more difficult than the last, but abductees are worth significantly more.
Graphics are whimsical, simple, and enjoyable.  The audio and soundtrack are also pretty good, so no complaints there.  I only ran into one glitch, where my ship outran the scrolling action and my ship went off-screen for a few seconds.
My biggest complaint is the boss fight.  The issue is not so much perma-death if you die during the stage, but that you can sit in orbit and pummel the boss for literally several minutes with no effect.  The fight starts out fairly well, with destroying the shield generators, then the compounds on the ground.  But once he reveals himself, there seems to be no way to destroy him.  Also, There is a glitch where I believe turrets are spawning underground and shooting at you through the planet.  There is no way to destroy those, which is mildly irritating as well.
But all in all, this game is actually pretty fun.  I think it's worth it for about a buck and a half.

Imagine playing a 16bit JRPG, but without the battles. That is very much what this game is, though calling it a game might be a bit too much. Because the interactive part is limited to finding certain plot items and solving super easy puzzles. The whole story will take up to 3 to 4 hours to finish, so if you think you can invest in something like this, it might be your 'game'. It certainly isn't for everybody, so be warned and think carefully before buying.
I liked it, but i like story rich games and i also like retro games.
It's not without it's flaws though. Since for most of the game you spend looking for items (besides reading dialogue), i got stuck i few times because i just wasn't able to figure out where an item was. There is no hinting and the gfx, well, are very much retro like. Blocky pixels tend to be hard to notice in the full scenery presented throughout the game.
The puzzles are so easy (most of them can be completed in less then 5 moves), i started to wonder if it would have been better to just leave them out.
Controling the characters is straight forward, but what is not straight forward is that they can get stuck behind objects. This is not a problem, because you can walk around said object, rather the problem is that it is not always clear what you can walk through and what not. Again a limitation of using semi 16bit graphics while overloading them with detail.
The music score is fantastic, it fits so well with the story and does a great deal to build the atmosphere. It's nothing like the music that the old 16bit consoles produced, but the sound effects certainly are. The sound track of this game is certainly one of the best things about it.
What about the story? It's a roler coaster of emotional events, that has as many hits as misses in it's execution. It is certainly original and i would love to see it as a movie made by a decent director such as Christopher Nolan (i feel his movie stories match closest to this one).

This game has held up incredibly well for it's age.  The graphics are fine for a 4x even today and scale well to modern resolutions.
The gameplay harkens back to a time when the focus of 4x was on immersion and fun rather than a vain chase for mathematical balance.  Different factions have unique flavors that aren't necessarily balanced, but who cares--they're still fun to play.  Regular cutscenes add a sense of immersion.  Military and industrial management is very well done with waypoints, governors, and auto-upgrading that lets you skip a lot of micromanaging.  The tech tree allows for many play styles, as the prerequistes for a tech are only techs of the same sort--it would be possible (though not advisable) to research to the highest level of laser weapons without researching any non-laser tech.  And different factions and alignments have unique techs available only to them.
I hope the upcoming GC3, currently in beta, lives up to the promise of GC2, and they don't make the mistake Civ 5/BE have made of dropping the little things that make 4x games fun and immersive--cutscenes, victory movies, the possibility of discovering unbalanced strategies, faction personality, diplomatic insults, etc.
Believe the hype. It's one of the best 4X games I've played. Single-player only though.

-- Six important points about Deadlings: Rotten Edition --
1) The title music is insanely cool!
2) A lot of reviews compare this to 'Super Meat Boy' and 'Plants VS Zombies'. Those a rubbish comparisons. Deadlings is a side-scrolling puzzle platformer: you evaluate the level, decide which zombies are best at each task, then you set them running into the level (inputting single commands like jumping, but never directional input). This game is immensely more like 'Lemmings' and a little bit like 'Braid' and other less-manic puzzle-platformers.
3) The fact this game isn't like those other famous titles is not an insult. This game is a great little gem! As you progress, the game expands on your options and the depth of the puzzles. I highly recommend not worrying about good scores initially and instead try to clear levels, otherwise you won't see much of the game's brilliant concepts for a long while.
4) This game is very much worth it's asking price, and it's an easy purchase when on sale! Few games are both this well made, and be within anyone's price range. Not perfect, but nothing that would really ruin your fun.
5) You can only unlock one level at a time, by completing the previous level. If you are stuck, this game doesn't offer you much else to do. This is the game's one major flaw.
6) There's also a weird interaction that 'Bonebag' (your fast-running zombie that jumps) will literally explode if he runs into a wall or clips into the side of a platform. It makes sense from a gameplay-design perspective, but is visually doesn't make sense and it's infuriating to behold! Just a minor flaw but when puzzle games can be taxing on your patience, you REALLY notice stuff like that! Especially since everything else in the 'Rotten Edition' is so crisp and well designed!
-- MY RATING: 8.7 --

多谢奶牛关和开发者提供的key。
轻即时战略游戏以往玩的也不少，总体来说，这个游戏目前给我的感觉是，完成度不高，但可玩性发掘的潜力很足。
以下回馈内容虽然可能比较直白，但目的依然是非常希望制作方能再接再厉——把短板补上，可能就是一个能上 90%+好评的游戏——如果真的完善了（并且有比较复杂的无尽模式的话），我在这里立下字据：“制作方，你就算出大量圈钱DLC，甚至只是给邪神换皮肤的那种DLC，我也会买买买！”
​
首先一些琐碎——
一进游戏有种帧数不够的感觉，画面一顿一顿的，特意出去开了steam自带的FPS发现60帧左右。是因为那个画面其实是在播放一段视频？
静止的菜单画面有掉帧，从60掉到25左右。
星吸血鬼简直强无敌。
我第三章第二关裸母巢rush星吸血鬼，建筑耐久rush到0就失败了？按道理，母巢自杀应该不算输吧？另外，在这张图游戏也试过崩溃（可能是星门太多）。
前两章过关难度太低。第三章摘星难度单纯靠粗浅的游戏理解，作为一个策略游戏，对玩家的要求反而变成高观察力。。。
套克苏鲁的皮实在是失策。不但导致奔着克苏鲁来的玩家大失所望，也使得没听说过这个世界观的玩家直接站队观望区（另外它没有版权吗？）。
​
核心游戏机制很赞（8.5/10）——
虽然完成度给我的感觉在6.5/10左右，比如物理怪也没有感觉很强，为什么会在游戏关卡/机制上给他们一堆限制？但游戏现在的体验大概在‘80%非常好玩’的区间里，减分的大部分都是和机制无关的其他项。隐约感受到真正完成后可以成为如同《dominions》系列一样的毒品——甚至更容易上瘾——对我而言。最喜欢的是这个游戏真正的、不能用同一种手法通关的关卡设计。
熟悉了设定并且看懂设计思路之后基本无双过关，可以感受到难度应该是给策略游戏新手的。就算是第三章，难度也在手速和观察力，而不是策略的难度。感觉对一个‘策略’还是有点过低，比如我随便塞哪只怪给调查员打都基本没问题，以及信仰随着时间积累得太多。此外，目前还没有体验到那种想要重复玩同一关去刷星的冲动。
当时在第四关突然看见要用另一个邪神再玩一次才能3星的要求，非常诡异。一般来说，重玩关卡的这种摘星要求都是设计成‘普通难度只能获得2星，噩梦难度能获得最后那一颗星’的吧？
​
UE的逻辑比较‘另类’，体验不太好（3/10）——
第一次尝试把仆从由一个基地拖拽到另一个基地的时候，我的想法是我能直接拖到另一个基地的调查员身上叫他们打架。然后发现虽然滑鼠在边缘的时候会弹出人员表，但并不可以直接这样操作——我几次尝试后才发现应该在另一个基地上松开滑鼠的正确操作。。。玩下来，会因为有以往的游戏不好的窗口拖拽体验，导致用拖拽操作总有种不适感。另外，点击一个基地会放大该基地的镜头，不但没有给我额外的信息，还导致拖拽的时候要把鼠标拖出窗口这一点，反而操作更疲劳了，降低了操作的流畅度。对我来说，或许点击1再点击2（再点确定）的方式更适合我对这种游戏的操作逻辑的印象，比如《大力神的十二道考验》（12 labours of Hercules: V）。
每关开头的时候直接给我由一堆图标组成的类似升级树的‘解锁类容’表，然而完全不知道有什么用。。。尤其是第一关一开始游戏的时候就丢给我一个密密麻麻的图标大集合。我是玩到第二关总结了一下似曾相似的图标才大概知道这个弹出框是想表达什么意思，但由于没有对每个图标的详细介绍，那个表除了可以统一展示一下每个地区可以建的建筑都可以召唤什么模样（而不是什么用途）的仆从外，并没有实际意义。
当我把一只怪拖到一只调查员身上，可不可以显示出调查员的信息（甚至，可以像文明那样显示出战斗结果）？这样可以省掉我一个一个点开看（并做简单乘法计算）的操作。
为什么我大克苏鲁的召唤点数是用默认字体和默认颜色表示的。。。？还有为什么有些关卡有百分比符号，有些关卡有小数点，而另一些关卡是整数？
有些关卡的一些地区完全在UI覆盖之下，要拖放仆从到那些地区的时候会感到非常诡异。
很多以往游戏经验告诉我会有悬浮提示的东西，都没有悬浮提示。
希望右下角的提示系统可以更完善。比如左右鼠标键分别对应定位/弹出角色卡，并且新出现的调查员也可以有个提示之类的；怪物召唤好也希望能说一句或者有个特效（甚至直接给我一个方便移动他们的快捷操作），并且哪个地方有我的战斗仆从——有时候真的很难同时观察到所有角落——现在的第三章对观察力的要求太高了。
​
UI、音乐和画面（1/10）——
调查员疯狂音效给我deep dark ♂ fantasy的感觉，每次都想笑场出戏，不要问我为什么。。。配乐选择和音乐切换的水平。。。嗯。。。是新手吗？
UI外貌太糟糕了。UI和图标和图标框完全没有层次感。
从目前的画面中，我可以看到一个水平及格的画师（挺喜欢地球那个背景地图的），但看不到一个水平及格的‘游戏美术’——起码缩放后白色像素和锯齿边缘给我去掉吧（掀桌）。我不是无法接受‘画质差’，但好歹那些游戏不是这种‘差（懒）’法。。。这已经不是可以拿EA做借口的事情了。
游戏画面的各种层次结合，比如UI和背景地图的融洽度，有种gamejam赶工出来的作品的廉价感。
音质可以听出来压缩到比较低——我电脑插的hifi设备——不过对大部分人来讲不是问题。只是建议音质其实可以更好一点。
​
有些表达/显示错误或者文字与实际不符的地方——
比如第一章第四关的要求是要>=10灵魂，我胜利的时候刚好灵魂在10，却没有获得对应的星；第三章第三关要求击杀>=10调查员我也刚好在10。
貌似调查员的增幅并没有改变调查员的属性，如获得几点INT的那种。

This is one of the best games I played in 2015. Ori is an awesome little Metroidvania that excels at *atmosphere*. The art is beautful. The music is beautiful. The setting is immersive, and the world is phenomenal.
I love the action scenes the most. There are a handful of "chase" scenes where you have to runrunRUN before you get crushed, drowned, or eaten, and they're *riveting*. I've never been so afraid of giant crows.
The story is decent. The opening scene is FANTASTIC, but the story never reaches that kind of emotional high again.
Overall, it's just really, really good. It's pretty, it's a good Metroidvania, it's emotional, and a very casual, unrushed playthrough should take you less than 10 hours.
