I can't put my finger on what keeps pulling you back into this game, but it's like just one more match, just one more...oh crap it's hours later didn't mean to be on this long...must sleep...one more match....
LOl to get to a more serious review though:
Yes this game is fun and there's a lot more to it than first meets the eye. However, it IS A multiplayer team based (4 divers vs 2 sharks) PVP game to it's core so expect nothing else (meaning it's fast and furious team vs team gameplay).
Sharks vs Divers on an epic scale, or Divers vs Sharks how ever you perfer (mostly shark player here ;P ).
The one main and pretty much only game mode atm is Blood and Gold, but really it's all you need.
As divers collect your treasure and take it to S.T.E.V.E so he can bank it for you to use on your next respawn, that way you can upgrade your weapons and deployables, as you escort him to the end where he'll be yanked free from the jaws of those nasty sharks wanting to destroy him and you the divers.
As sharks it's your job to rid your waters of those pesky gold grabbin divers and their robotic friend S.T.E.V.E. .  As you munch down more divers you'll gain evolution points to use on your next respawn so you can be tankier, faster, stealthier, and more destructive as you grow in power.
Each shark has it's own specialized skills, for example the hammerhead perfers smashing divers into everything for the fast kill, where a thresher loves to smack the crap outta the divers with his tail lash and nasty threshing, and the tiger shark loves to go all stealth for the sneak attack.
No worries though as I said divers get a huge range of different gear to use, from a sonar buay to detect nearby sharks, to mines, to weapons upgrades and mods so you can use dual pistols or go full boar machine gun and even add bleeding or toxic to each round sent down lane at those nasty pesky sharks.
This game is unique in many ways, and ever so addicting, however it has a high skill ceiling so don't expect to just pick it up and be the best from the get go (though some do have natural talent); a lot of players have put in countless hours to be as good as they are.
The game is totally worth it, and has a good top lvl community.  Yes every bunch has it's bad apples, but most of the top players will treat you with respect and you'll find are very friendly if you do and act the same to them.
Game devs could use a little people skills, but they've put people in place to help with that.
Game gets updated often (and often includes free stuff like new maps, new diver gear, new sharks, new skin drops etc.) and has many sales that keep the community going, one of which will probably be a big one coming up that will include community skins.
If you've looked at this game and have been on the fence, just jump over it; you'll be surprised just how much there is to this game, but remember it's a multipayer team vs team kinda game so expect nothing else.

Even an across-the-map, no-scope headshot in Battlefield doesn’t tickle the same gloat centers in my brain. Thus, playing as a great white shark in Depth’s asymmetrical bloodsport was gleefully delicious.
Playing as one of the two man-eating sharks that stalk the four human divers in each match is definitely the star of the show. Navigating swiftly and silently in third-person perspective, I quickly developed a sense that these oceans were mine to lord over. The sluggish, clumsy humans huddled in groups as they inched their way from treasure stash to to treasure stash, knowing I was out there somewhere, but never sure from what direction I’d attack, or when. Regular sonar pulses showed me outlines of my prey, allowing me to keep tabs on them at great distances. It’s reminiscent of playing as the Infected in Left 4 Dead, or the Alien gameplay in the old Aliens vs Predator 2 multiplayer: speed, stealth, and a superior awareness of the environment were my primary advantages.
The humans brought numbers, hardware, and ranged weaponry to the table in response. Playing from first-person and handicapped by a deliberately-limited sight range, the intrepid landlubbers are forced to use all of these tools to survive. Starting with a basic pistol, divers unlock progressively more potent guns and utility items by gathering and turning in treasure in an interface similar to Counter-Strike’s gear market. Having net guns and fully automatic firepower is nice, but the real key to diver gameplay is making good use of items like sonar beacons and concealed mines that grant an early warning of an approaching maneater and, potentially, blow it up before it gets a chance to take a bite out of anyone’s juicy abdomen.
As the shark, I found myself in a dynamic cat-and-mouse game as the rounds progressed. Successful sharksmanship became a matter of knowing when to strike, using paranoia as a weapon, and getting the hell out of the line of fire with my supper before said supper’s friends could take revenge. As the sharks are always outnumbered and, thankfully for us dirt dwellers, still not immune to bullets, frontal assaults were almost always a one-way ticket to the Belly-Up Ball. As with any horror-movie aquatic menace, the less I was seen, the better. Performing swift passes by windows and cracks in the wall to distract the divers proved very effective, as did planning my attack vector on a straight line between two exits, with my target right in the middle.
When playing for the edible team, I had to trade in my rows of razor-sharp teeth for a SCUBA mask and a more developed prefrontal cortex, which changed the atmosphere completely. I felt slow, exposed, and under-equipped as we escorted our treasure-hauling, mechanical companion S.T.E.V.E. through the oppressive, deep-sea environments. Moving methodically, I found I often had less than a second to react between seeing the first flash of fins and meeting my crunchy demise. Awareness and teamwork were my only insurance policies, and vision-enhancing items like chemlights and tracer rounds (which can stick to a shark and allow it to be tracked at a distance) proved to be the most crucial elements in my arsenal.

Playing as a diver creates a tension that gives even most single-player horror games a run for their money. There’s something deeply unsettling about being surrounded by water, unable to see more than a few meters around me, and knowing there’s something out there faster and stronger than me that knows exactly where I am at all times. It’s the same feeling I got jumping into a lake as a kid—I couldn’t see how deep it was, or what other creatures were in there with me. My imagination became my worst enemy.
The excellent sound design enhances all of this. With a good pair of around-ear headphones, I could easily imagine myself submerged as the ambience of the deep sea swirled around me. When a shark comes within a certain radius, you’re warned by the sound of your own heartbeat starting to accelerate, making it more difficult to keep your cool and be ready for an attack.
Match to match, both sharks and divers can unlock new weapons and upgrades. These must still be purchased within each match (with gold for divers, and kills for sharks), but it gives at least some sense of persistent progression. The extra hardware and predatory adaptations I earned opened up some interesting, new gameplay styles, but each match still ultimately felt like it came down to the same sets of tactics. Each shark and each diver filled, essentially, the same role. There’s no way to represent your progress to other players, either -  visual customization is entirely absent for sharks, and is limited to a selection of three pre-set skins for divers.

The most disappointing section of the proverbial seafood menu was the lack of gameplay modes. The Team Fortress 2 Payload-style, escort-the-drone-and-collect-gold routine started to feel a little monotonous in the absence of any other options, and I couldn’t help but feel that the core mechanics aren’t being used to their broadest and most creative potential. All the variety comes from the huge tonal and tactical differences between diver and shark gameplay, and the ability to simply switch teams and feel like I was playing a different game if I needed a quick change of pace kept me deep into Depth for a bit longer.
My verdict

Depth has an ocean of tense, unique gameplay moments. The level and sound design lend themselves to smart, tactical engagements and tense periods of paranoia (or smug stalking) between them. Playing as a diver or a shark is a fast, fun, and frantic experience, and each has its own feel and set of skills. The single game mode and skimpy customization options are the weak points that make me doubt the longevity of this otherwise ship-shape game, but in the short term, the complex relationship between hunter and prey is exciting enough to keep me coming back

This game is no gem of the Painkiller Series, it is more or less one of the games that could probably rightfully be called a lemon.
Given there are some things that are good, the game itself isn't - it is a repetition of the original game just with much larger Levels - the first level is huge, as are most of the other levels, and this is causing one of the problems of this game. The loading time also is very "huge" - sometimes you wait for what seems an eternity just to start the level, reloading also takes a lot of time when you die during the level.
The graphics are as they were in the original Painkiller, but there is not much new about this episode regarding the graphics. The level design is what might also be a great drawback, you are left alone and you will fail - a lot of times just by walking off in the wrong direction or because the level was designed to make the player suffer. A good example is the spiral staircase in the cathedral, another one the chaotic layout of the valley, were you suddenly can't stop a skid and fall into your death. But there are even worse design errors - like the sparsely added new demons and monsters. Off course the huge levels are looking good, but the design errors are unforgiving and regretfully also unforgivable.
The story starts out nice, in comic style you are told why you are cast into "hell" - but then the game starts and you realize, "Oh, it still is purgatory... Bummer!". It had a lot of potential, which is regretfully left unused. I know some people who love the game as a multiplayer game - but it still is bugging around a lot, and furthermore - the loading time is taking again away a lot of fun for this game.
Graphics: 7/10 (some options have to be customized, especially on some newer cards)
Sound: 6/10 (mostly the old soundtrack, with time it becomes enervating)
Playability: 4/10 (This is representing also the loading time and the design errors which can be a mess)
Story: 5/10 (since this game isn't really making a lot out of the backdrop of the story)
Value: 3/10 (Even at 9,99 it's too expensive since it isn't living up to the potential - wait till it gets cheap, real cheap)
Overall: 5/10 (This average is a representing my own opinion, the game isn't the best in the painkiller series and as such you could decide if you require it or if you pass and try playing the other games).

We've got save game corruption bugs, falling through the map bugs, enemy AI bugs, checkpoint bugs, scripting bugs! We've even managed to add bugs to the process of selecting a tarot card!

Overdose was buggy, you say? Well yes, Overdose was a buggy, slightly unfinished seeming product, glad you noticed. We've managed to more than triple the bugs in that as well as reduce overall stability!
Remember back in the good old days of playing through Painkiller: Overdose when you'd randomly morph into demon mode and it'd boot ya to your desktop? ENJOY THAT EVERY SINGLE TIME YOU MORPH THIS GO-ROUND, FRIENDO!
And the level design is unintutive, what with checkpoints that fail to load, enemies spawning on top of each other, on top of you, and on top of a void outside the map! We've got necessary progression points hidden in corners you'd NEVER think to look here, boy howdy!

Yes, the bane of all gamers' existance, the reason nobody liked Xen, good ol' FPS platforming is back, this time in a painkiller game! To the Moon is an emotionally effecting game with a likeable retro asthetic, unique and interesting soundtrack and a storyline that admirably succeeds in tackling issues not usually explored in games such as grief and mental illness.
It's a short game that is viewed in an old school RPG way which adds a nice element of nostalgia and a hint of innocence to the story which contrasts effectively with the fairly grim storyline (which is lightened by the occassional use of humour).
The actual storyline of the game concerns your attempts to dive "Inception like" into the mind of a dying man and try to figure out what makes him tick by charting the path of a particular significant relationship. The game is very story driven and has no fail states and a minimum of puzzles which gives a satisfying element of emotional richness to the plot and eliminates grinding and fetch quests among other RPG tropes. Sometimes however, since the game requires you to progress in a very linear way this can devolve into a very formulistic "run around clicking all the buttons" type shenigans which is dissapointing.
Overall however, due to a well written and mature storyline the game succeeds in being compelling, entertaining and satisfactorily exploring themes of identity, memory and mortality.

Besides lacking multiplayer, it has addressed all of my gripes so far, and it appears that they're still pumping out updates. I think NMS has finally earned a recommendation from me.
While I still find fault with Hello Games, specifically Sean Murray, for overpromising and underdelivering at release and then radio silence for weeks after release, they've since redeemed themselves with the continued free updates that provide more depth than most other $60 titles. This game is still being developed but is due for release in March 2018.  I've been a backer of this project since 2014 and have dipped in and out of playing it since then. The level of development I've seen go into this game has been amazing and seeing one built from the ground up has helped me appreciate what goes into games like this.  The amount of involvement the community has had with building this game is fantastic.
Gameplay itself is freeflow, its sandbox and it's really up to you how you go about things. You are not spoonfed quests, you are not easily guided through so it turns into a walk and click game with a bit of fighting inbetween like so many MMORPGs these days.  You need to say the right words to the NPCs, pay attention to the clues they give you and properly look for what you need to complete quests.
Making your own armour is time consuming as you have to gather all the raw materials, make those into useable items and then craft your armour or weapons.  Much like in UO where you kill a chicken, get it's feathers cut wood for shafts then make the arrows.
It's taken me a while to learn how to play this game effectively which for me makes it a bigger investment in my time and money.  If you want a game where you can play it for hours/days/weeks and still feel there's alot left to it then this is the game for you.

First off I just wanted to say that if you have ever wanted to be a bazooka wielding skeleton with a pet dragon, then this is most definitely the game for you.
Now with that said, I love this game and I only have six hours clocked so far, but I promise you that will increase. Now keep in mind that it is still in early access so there will be bugs and at the moment there are not that many feature in place yet. But if you can deal with those two issues and you love Lego then this is the game for you.
What really grabs me though, is this games potential. There is sooooo much potential in this game. Want to build that awesome castle you tried to build as a kid but couldn't because you ran out of bricks? Yeah that's not a problem here. Or how about building an underwater city? Well with the new update right around the corner that will be possible. Or how about zipping around space and docking at a space station or lunar base? Well those are not in the game yet but I can't imagine that they would ever leave that out, it may not be coming soon, but I don't doubt that it will eventually.
What about when the add the ability to make custom vehicles!? Make that pew, pew ship you have always dreamt of. Or stomp around in a colossal mech while blasting hoards of skeletons and monster. Again not yet possible in game. But Lego has always been about the freedom you have when it comes to building and if they decide against that then they are terrible people. Now everything I have said here is of course speculation, but that is just the beginning!!
Imagine if after it's official release they begin to add dlc packs for other Lego licenses!! How about zipping around in the Millennium Falcon as Han with Gandalf at your side while Hulk and Chewie tear up an army of Storm Troopers, Orcs, and other baddies. Or how about Indiana Jones and Spider Man exploring a deep dark ruin! Or even combining Sauron and Loki together to make an uber baddie you can use to tear up your buddies newly build fortress? Hows that sound!?
Again I will say, the directions they could take this game are staggering. It already feels like I am living in my own imagination from when I was a child, but it could get even better. So, here's hoping they do Lego and all it's fan, both young and old, proud and give us a game to last years!

One of the best games I've ever played. I know a lot of people don't enjoy FPS, so an RPG that is also a FPS rubbed a lot of the original Fallout fans the wrong way... but this was my first exposure to this storyline, and I was obsessed with it for weeks.
I played most of my original hours on the 360, and even though I beat the game, I found there was still so much to do. With the PC, there are mods, and additional content as well. Things that made the game all new to me, and got me excited to play it again. My only excuse for not diving in full force again? I am a game addict, and have 200+ games... most of which I haven't played, lol. Damn those sales... they give me too many choices, and then I get distracted.
Anyway... this game is sort of like Mass Effect... if Mass Effect was more true to being an RPG... and was about three times as difficult. You have to repair your gear, upgrade many many times over your gameplay, and conserve all the ammo you have if you can. Bullets are NOT easy to come by at the start of the game... and it's easy to forget that. What's worse (and I use that word for difficulty, not for quality) is that any given location you stumble on could be for a level 15 when you're just a 2. A hard lesson you learn by being slaughtered like you're a wee child! Which is a hard, but important lesson to learn too.
On that note... "Grayditch: Those!" will kill you dead if you're not prepared for it. Stay away from fire ants if you're not at least a level 6 or higher. Fair warning. x_X

LOl to get to a more serious review though:
Yes this game is fun and there's a lot more to it than first meets the eye. However, it IS A multiplayer team based (4 divers vs 2 sharks) PVP game to it's core so expect nothing else (meaning it's fast and furious team vs team gameplay).
Sharks vs Divers on an epic scale, or Divers vs Sharks how ever you perfer (mostly shark player here ;P ).
The one main and pretty much only game mode atm is Blood and Gold, but really it's all you need.
As divers collect your treasure and take it to S.T.E.V.E so he can bank it for you to use on your next respawn, that way you can upgrade your weapons and deployables, as you escort him to the end where he'll be yanked free from the jaws of those nasty sharks wanting to destroy him and you the divers.
As sharks it's your job to rid your waters of those pesky gold grabbin divers and their robotic friend S.T.E.V.E. .  As you munch down more divers you'll gain evolution points to use on your next respawn so you can be tankier, faster, stealthier, and more destructive as you grow in power.
Each shark has it's own specialized skills, for example the hammerhead perfers smashing divers into everything for the fast kill, where a thresher loves to smack the crap outta the divers with his tail lash and nasty threshing, and the tiger shark loves to go all stealth for the sneak attack.
No worries though as I said divers get a huge range of different gear to use, from a sonar buay to detect nearby sharks, to mines, to weapons upgrades and mods so you can use dual pistols or go full boar machine gun and even add bleeding or toxic to each round sent down lane at those nasty pesky sharks.
This game is unique in many ways, and ever so addicting, however it has a high skill ceiling so don't expect to just pick it up and be the best from the get go (though some do have natural talent); a lot of players have put in countless hours to be as good as they are.
The game is totally worth it, and has a good top lvl community.  Yes every bunch has it's bad apples, but most of the top players will treat you with respect and you'll find are very friendly if you do and act the same to them.
Game devs could use a little people skills, but they've put people in place to help with that.
Game gets updated often (and often includes free stuff like new maps, new diver gear, new sharks, new skin drops etc.) and has many sales that keep the community going, one of which will probably be a big one coming up that will include community skins.
If you've looked at this game and have been on the fence, just jump over it; you'll be surprised just how much there is to this game, but remember it's a multipayer team vs team kinda game so expect nothing else.
GG-  Good Game totally worth it and I'll see you under the Sea for some more GGs'.

Even an across-the-map, no-scope headshot in Battlefield doesn’t tickle the same gloat centers in my brain. Thus, playing as a great white shark in Depth’s asymmetrical bloodsport was gleefully delicious.
Playing as one of the two man-eating sharks that stalk the four human divers in each match is definitely the star of the show. Navigating swiftly and silently in third-person perspective, I quickly developed a sense that these oceans were mine to lord over. The sluggish, clumsy humans huddled in groups as they inched their way from treasure stash to to treasure stash, knowing I was out there somewhere, but never sure from what direction I’d attack, or when. Regular sonar pulses showed me outlines of my prey, allowing me to keep tabs on them at great distances. It’s reminiscent of playing as the Infected in Left 4 Dead, or the Alien gameplay in the old Aliens vs Predator 2 multiplayer: speed, stealth, and a superior awareness of the environment were my primary advantages.
The humans brought numbers, hardware, and ranged weaponry to the table in response. Playing from first-person and handicapped by a deliberately-limited sight range, the intrepid landlubbers are forced to use all of these tools to survive. Starting with a basic pistol, divers unlock progressively more potent guns and utility items by gathering and turning in treasure in an interface similar to Counter-Strike’s gear market. Having net guns and fully automatic firepower is nice, but the real key to diver gameplay is making good use of items like sonar beacons and concealed mines that grant an early warning of an approaching maneater and, potentially, blow it up before it gets a chance to take a bite out of anyone’s juicy abdomen.
As the shark, I found myself in a dynamic cat-and-mouse game as the rounds progressed. Successful sharksmanship became a matter of knowing when to strike, using paranoia as a weapon, and getting the hell out of the line of fire with my supper before said supper’s friends could take revenge. As the sharks are always outnumbered and, thankfully for us dirt dwellers, still not immune to bullets, frontal assaults were almost always a one-way ticket to the Belly-Up Ball. As with any horror-movie aquatic menace, the less I was seen, the better. Performing swift passes by windows and cracks in the wall to distract the divers proved very effective, as did planning my attack vector on a straight line between two exits, with my target right in the middle.
When playing for the edible team, I had to trade in my rows of razor-sharp teeth for a SCUBA mask and a more developed prefrontal cortex, which changed the atmosphere completely. I felt slow, exposed, and under-equipped as we escorted our treasure-hauling, mechanical companion S.T.E.V.E. through the oppressive, deep-sea environments. Moving methodically, I found I often had less than a second to react between seeing the first flash of fins and meeting my crunchy demise. Awareness and teamwork were my only insurance policies, and vision-enhancing items like chemlights and tracer rounds (which can stick to a shark and allow it to be tracked at a distance) proved to be the most crucial elements in my arsenal.

Playing as a diver creates a tension that gives even most single-player horror games a run for their money. There’s something deeply unsettling about being surrounded by water, unable to see more than a few meters around me, and knowing there’s something out there faster and stronger than me that knows exactly where I am at all times. It’s the same feeling I got jumping into a lake as a kid—I couldn’t see how deep it was, or what other creatures were in there with me. My imagination became my worst enemy.
The excellent sound design enhances all of this. With a good pair of around-ear headphones, I could easily imagine myself submerged as the ambience of the deep sea swirled around me. When a shark comes within a certain radius, you’re warned by the sound of your own heartbeat starting to accelerate, making it more difficult to keep your cool and be ready for an attack.
Match to match, both sharks and divers can unlock new weapons and upgrades. These must still be purchased within each match (with gold for divers, and kills for sharks), but it gives at least some sense of persistent progression. The extra hardware and predatory adaptations I earned opened up some interesting, new gameplay styles, but each match still ultimately felt like it came down to the same sets of tactics. Each shark and each diver filled, essentially, the same role. There’s no way to represent your progress to other players, either -  visual customization is entirely absent for sharks, and is limited to a selection of three pre-set skins for divers.

The most disappointing section of the proverbial seafood menu was the lack of gameplay modes. The Team Fortress 2 Payload-style, escort-the-drone-and-collect-gold routine started to feel a little monotonous in the absence of any other options, and I couldn’t help but feel that the core mechanics aren’t being used to their broadest and most creative potential. All the variety comes from the huge tonal and tactical differences between diver and shark gameplay, and the ability to simply switch teams and feel like I was playing a different game if I needed a quick change of pace kept me deep into Depth for a bit longer.
My verdict

Depth has an ocean of tense, unique gameplay moments. The level and sound design lend themselves to smart, tactical engagements and tense periods of paranoia (or smug stalking) between them. Playing as a diver or a shark is a fast, fun, and frantic experience, and each has its own feel and set of skills. The single game mode and skimpy customization options are the weak points that make me doubt the longevity of this otherwise ship-shape game, but in the short term, the complex relationship between hunter and prey is exciting enough to keep me coming back

As good the first two (actually three) Painkillers were, this one is as bad. It gives the real What-How-Who-Why? feeling.
Pros:
The level design of the first (weird) and the last level (open-wide overbright depressing). Sorry but that’s all!
Cons:
Only 6 levels, but don’t think it will be a short fun thingy, not at all! I nearly played it as much time as the whole Black Edition! Why? Beacuse five of the levels are sooooooo big that there is enough space for a mediocre RPG’s whole storytaking. But they are not just big but you don’t even have a clue where to go! The compass that always helped in the previous games are mostly not working (as it seems they only function near a checkpoint), or it just shows a near health item (really, it happened to me!).
So the gameplay is: You wander aimlessly in big wide areas or ridiculously hard maze-alikes, sometimes triggering enemy spawns, fight them then toddle further without any clue what to do. The enemy spawns are randomly placed, no chance to find them all. On one of these enormous levels to earn a card you have to kill all mobs, of course i missed a quarter of them. Sometimes you find a checkpoint and you are happy thinking you have found ’The Route’, but soon realize there are more checkpoints when accidentally backtracked because of no directions given and a shortway (again thinking this is ’The Route’) just lead you back there.
Have to mention here that even if it’s a fan made product (like the mighty Overdose), the several clipping and stucking problems, incomplete areas with missing parts and walk-out-the-map-and-die things are still not acceptable!
The new enemies are ugly, some really amorphous, and extremly unbalanced. Most of them are boring easy and some are. . . ehhh: One time i walked into an open area and i’ve been presented with a new chaingun enemy, not one but like twenty. Guess who died . . . 30 times in rapid succession, until i was able to retract somehow with my remaining 4 HP and hide behind a wagon. It took me 20 minutes to clear the area by picking them one by one and of course it costed me again like 30 deaths as the guys use perfect aimbot hitscans.
Older Painkillers were famous of that the enemies were in context with the design of the levels and areas they appeared on. In here absolutely nothing. Everything seems randomly thrown into.
For the record i was able to earn only one card (first level). Yes, I’m a pretty mediocre player but seeing  how far i was to reach other cards’ requirements i say that’s a joke.
Here comes the best part: SUICIDAL ENEMIES. Let’s say this is a very unique feature of this product, as i never saw this behavior in other FPSs. It must be connected somehow with the messed up checkpoint system that sometimes (not even rarely) when you approach a new area you see a bunch of puffs meaning the mobs just vaporized themselves. Even better one of the minibosses (or boss? not sure :P) did this to me, really! I was wandered around half-crying in some Gobi Desert size crater when i found a hundred meters high door like wall. I was sure a boss is behind it, but could not open it. Hardened by the hours of playing this game I was a pro at this moment and i knew i have to find some randomly dropped checkpoints to trigger the opening. So i staggered away to hunt for the little red saviours. Periodically checked back and after a while (an hour or so), hurray! it was open. Run through it with readied heavy weaponry but i was only greeted by a big puff and a cutscene began. After it was done i gathered the fair amount of ammunitions around and started shooting at the poor enviroment to lessen my frustration.
The protagonist is an idiot for sure. As someone (J.Johnson) in an another review pointed out he (the ’hero’) „calls himself a 'world class killer' blows himself up because he can't read a bus schedule”.
The plot itself is chaotic, the conversations tells nothing besides the antipathy between the protagonist and the bosses (but there is no why). Normally i would not care but the big pile of other problems just strengthen this as well. BTW I know i did not see the real ending (again i ’only’??!! played at normal) but i have no intention to play this mess again.
2/10 - Total mess. A wandering for hours FPS.

This is my feedback of the little time I had so far with Hellblade.
I'm running a quad-core potato with a RX480 @1200p, all settings maxed and the game runs mostly solid @60fps. PC optimizations seems to have been done properly.
As said by many reviewers already, this game needs decent headphones. The voices all around you seem to be giving you tips about how to progress and they're all sounding haunting and match the atmosphere perfectly. The way that they seem to whisper in your ears is extremely well executed and helps immerse you in the experience.
Note that so far this seems far more an audio-visual art piece with heavy narrative as opposed to a combat game. Graphics are fantastic with a very trippy art style. Except from the occasional blurry texture, everything looks crisp and the character detail rivals that of games like the latest tomb raider. Impressive for such a small studio to say the least.
I'd say this game seems, so far at least, more focused on delivering a unique art style with haunting and mysterious narrative. There are some simple puzzles and the combat looks cool but (from videos I've seen) seems ultimately fairly straight forward. The games' length could also be a concern (around 6h or so I've heard). That said, if you like great sound design, trippy narrative and an audiovisual spectacle, this game seems to fit the bill. To me, it's amazing that such a small studio can deliver such a unique and all round polished experience. I'd recommend it to anyone willing to try something unique or anyone who wants to support a small independent studio.

It has tight controls, fun abilities and evokes a wonderous sense of exploration. It isn't exactly an easy game, and some parts can be a little frustrating, but never enough that I even considered quitting. One thing to keep in mind is that you CANNOT re-enter a save file after the game has been completed. Some collectables can be missed and are inaccessible later in the game.
Anyhow, it's worth every penny at full price for anyone with a remote interest in having their mind blown.

No Man's Sky did something a lot of other game companies don't do. This game may not be fun for you, but I would imagine in the coming years, this game will have a legacy all of it's own. Not only in terms of the players who truly enjoy it, but what they did for game development. I mean that strictly in terms of development, not marketing.
This is a small studio, who seemingly pushed themselves to deliver a "universe in a box", and while most avid gamers will always have an issue wrestling expectations, at least these guys are still pushing boundaries and attempting something new. I have nothing against the standard games that are being shoveled out from Ubisoft, and EA. However, all things considered, I think that's why these titles excite me. Even if they're widely considered a "failure".
It was embarassing to see to gaming community use this title as the whipping boy, whenever there are streams of titles from AAA studios who promise to over-deliver, and then ship to market a $60 product with half it's content locked away behind a DLC Pay wall.
It's all about the precedent we set for expectation, and as consumers, and how does the overall reaction go over the next time a Hello Games comes around promising the world, and "under-delivering"?
If anything, we lose one more creative studio to be filled to step in line with the content everyone else is already making.
At the end of the day, you are responsible as the consumer for your purchases, and this is one I still am happy to have purchased. The studio clearly cares enough to do something about it with the updates and patchwork, and I genuinely believe this a company who isn't just out to make a quick buck and run with the money.
The gameplay is a bit repetitive, and the environments seem to be small adjustments of the last few you've visited, but I will say it does feel like I'm in an expansive universe, and in between those moments I have had a few profound moments just taking in the majesty of space flight paired with the etheral music.
If No Man's Sky is only one thing, let it be a stepping stone into the future of adventure games with a stage as grand as a universe, and for me, it's something I'm happy and hopeful for.

This is definitely not a game for me, and definitely not one that I enjoy.
First some background on me.  I was the kind of guy that grew up with World of Warcraft - it was a Christmas present to me when I was 13.  Sure, I played some other MMOs when I was younger, but I would say that WoW had the biggest impact on me and my life.  Of course, this influenced my expectations and desires for MMO content, even to this day.  I don't really have time for MMOs these days, but when I do, I normally hop into WoW for a month or so and get my fill of MMOs for another handful of months.
Now, why would I try this game?  WoW has discovered a tried and true formula (focusing on raiding), and it has made some design choices that I don't particularly like.  I also have a friend that plays this game fairly exclusively, and he tells me how much of a good time that he has with it.  Naturally, I entertain the thought, and deside to purchase a simple bundle pack for $60 on Portalarium's website.
My initial impressions of it in 2016 was not good.  At all.  The interface felt dated, the combat felt stilted and flimsy, there was little or no guidance of what to do, the systems were difficult to undestand, and it just didn't seem to have much to offer.  I enjoy games with story, and while I do enjoy housing and crafting, those come secondary to combat and story.
Fast forward to Q4 2017, and while they have made some improvments, they don't seem to be changing the core of the issues that I have.  It's like they are putting lipstick on a pig, for the lack of a better analogy.  Let's take combat, for example, it doesn't feel any different than when I started playing in 2016.  Sure, they added more spell effects (sometimes bringing my computer to sub-60fps with a 1080 Ti@3440x1440 resolution), and make it LOOK better, but the overall feeling of it remains the same.
Who knows what this game is going to be like when / if it releases from Early Access, but I just can't recommend it in the current state. The developers seem to be quite focused on getting money from the whales by constant telethons, housing improvements (their biggest money maker) and not focusing as much on the systems that would make more people interested in it (combat, interface polish, etc.)

Read lots of positive reviews about this one, and given the high metascore, I thought I'd give it a try. However the game lost all appeal once I realized that the tech progress is completely linear. You are presented with a huge tech tree, lots of different buildings and other improvements, but they're all completely boring. It's just like, +1 armor, +2 armor, +3 armor. 1+ economy, +2 economy, and so forth. NO nonlinearities, NO interesting synergies to be seen whatsoever, but these are what makes 4X games complex and interesting! The game mechanics really lack imagination, which is a problem I see with lots of Stardock titles. With Legendary Heroes, the lack of complex R&D mechanics is mitigated by the roleplaying system which manages to keep the game interesting. In Sins of a Solar Empire, the linear mechanics are fine because it's an action- and speed-oriented RTS title. But GalCiv, that's just as dull as it gets.

This game is tediously boring.
Par for the course of these kinds of games is that you begin with a very small area and number of units, etc. and must find your way to expansion.  This is always relatively boring at first, but goes quickly since there is little to do and you can click through turns quickly.
The make or break point for this category of game is how tedious it becomes once significant expansion occurs.  Do you have to click on everything in the map to see if anything needs your attention every turn or does the game notify you whenever something important happens?  In this area, the game is mediocre.  There are notifications when significant events happen, but I still feel the need to check up on every planet periodically to know how things are going.
A huge factor for every game's enjoyability is what aspects come into focus.  Every game has good and bad parts.  The question is, do the good parts shine and the bad parts fade into the background or do the bad parts constantly nag you until you can't enjoy the good parts anymore?  Here the game is mediocre to bad.  What you consider good or bad will depend on your gaming preferences and I don't care to take the time to elaborate, but suffice to say I was not impressed with the balance (despite some quite good features).
Another big factor is the interface which is mediocre to bad depending on your adaptability and preferences.  It is never good when you spend as much time finding and clicking buttons as you do making real game changing decisions.
A significant factor that made me set this game aside was that the explanations of core game concepts was weak.  I read the manual before I played and also went through the tutorials.  Yet, as I played, I didn't really feel like I knew what was going on in many important aspects.  Some people enjoy figuring out the mystery as they go along.  I do for subtle aspects and tricks.  I most certainly don't for the basic core concepts (especially when having taken the time to read the manual...).
There are also a handful of other minor points against enjoying this game but I won't bother to elaborate since this is already a long enough review.  The important point is that with the huge number of games available for cheap today, this one just isn't worth the (extensive, tedious) time to play.
As I side note, I do not understand at all the number of positive reviews (almost all of which are little more than "YEAH!! AWESOME!! COOL!!! BEST GAME EVAH!!!!!").  I suppose it takes a certain kind of player to enjoy this title.  Make sure you are one of them before you buy it.

The quality of the story-telling is paired with that of a good novel. There are only so many changes in the direction of the narrative for you to get bored, even if you can't help but doubt the game for putting very little power in your hands throughout. And yet, no matter whether you consider To the Moon a visual novel or a game in itself, the obvious can't be denied: it will break you appart and make you think of it as a great game, not caring a single bit about how critical you are of its format.
It is not a very "playable" game, and, if that's what you're looking for, you definitely won't find it here. I consider it rather irrelevant to feel the need to label it at all, but maybe this "game" is not for everyone, and I think I should also acknowledge that. You will not have to do much for the story to reveal itself in front of you. You will not have to solve very challenging puzzles, you will not have to fight anyone around you, you will not have to make decisions, you will not have to do exploration to the point of getting exhausted. You will pretty much be the reader of a brilliant story, told in a very special way.
Packed up with an amazing soundtrack and an extremely simplistic style, To the Moon is the result of the perfect plot meeting the perfect format for it, and the armony they create together deserves every chance you may be doubting to give it.
P.S. It is also not expensive at all. Just saying!

If you don't have played every single game on the planet yet and are just looking for a game to spend time with and not be bored, then don't buy Hellblade. If you are desperately looking for new gaming experiences that you haven't experienced before, then you definitly should play Hellblade. Hellblade isn't like any game I've played before. It's not flawless though.
I think one factor that really hindered my "enjoyment" of the game is that I didn't understand a lot of things. Sometimes maybe that was intended, but especially at the ending I was left very unsatisfied and just confused. Maybe I'm stupid, maybe it's intended, maybe a little bit of both, but for me it weakened the experience.
The game consists of mainly four things: Cutscenes, Walking, Puzzles, Combat. The cutscenes are extremely well made with excellent animations, sound and camera. The Walking can become tedious, because even when running your movement speed is really slow. Sometimes you'll come across some runes or something which when activated act like audio logs that give you a little bit of lore. I found these quite boring most of the time and pointless. Sometimes I activate one of these and the person is starting to talk about things that seem completely random and I'm thinking "WHY ARE YOU TELLING ME THIS?".
The puzzles were really interesting. There were two times in the game where I got stuck. The first time I couldn't progress at all and had to look up a guide and when i saw the solution I knew I would never figure that out myself. The puzzles aren't really challenging though. Most of the time you are supposed to look for something, and if you don't find it, you don't find it. Solving the puzzles was still satisfying, because they are so different to other games. The puzzle also are heavily inspired by the stories of people with mental illness, since that is the theme of the game, so I guess the game does a good job of connecting story and gameplay
The combat is very simple, but not dull ... at least until the end. Towards the end there will be a lot of fights back to back, and some fights extremely long, which is where the combat starts to feel tedious. The game could use one or two more enemy types, maybe a ranged enemy? It is satisfying though. The moves are well animated and the enemies are really cool designed visually. Combat wasn't really challenging though.
Throughout the game it often felt like in reality they just want to tell their story but have to force a game in there somewhere, but since I don't know much about mental illness (and I still don't after playing the game), I guess I shouldn't judge that. It was worth playing. Since it's just 30€ I think it was worth the money.

Each character has their own story and every story is it's own story for that particular character. -Verdict-
6.5 Now i give it a middle score not because i think its not a good game. I think its a great game but not too outstanding aside from its artstyle and i am a sucker for beautiful detailed artwork. It's definitely unique with its universe and its certainly worth a try.

No Man's Sky started off as a $10 game that wasn't even that good. Horribly buggy, lack of variety, and grindy as hell. To add on top of this, aside from a few early patches, the Devs were completely silent about the lack of features that had been shown and promised before launch. Updates 1.1 and 1.2 seriously changed things. The ability to build bases, mark waypoints on the galactic map, and construck vehicles gave you a since of purpose and accomplishment that the game had been lacking previously.
As of August 11th, update 1.3: Atlas Rising has rolled out, and it is a huge improvement to nearly every system and mechanic in the game. The previously terrible story has been completely reworked, to have an actual plot driving you forward, rather than cryptic nonsense. Planet generation was completely reworked, and we now have crazy exotic planets closer to those that we saw in the early trailers that caused so much hype. I woke up to find that my lush, green island planet (one of many in 1.2) had become a colorful rocky wasteland with floating bubbles drifiting around, and I loved it. Not only did it look crazy and alien, but it gave me a reason to go out into the stars once more to find a new home.
Multiplayer is now present in the game, though it is a bit featureless (the patchnotes established this as the groundwork for multiplayer, which implies a more complete version will arrive in the future). Other players (up to 16 at once) will appear as floating blue orbs. Nothing they do will change anything in your game, but they can see all the same things you can. Meeting other people can happen randomly (rare), or it can be coordinated with friends by using portals, which, once activated, can take you to any set of special coordinates in the galaxy. You can use this to get to a friend's home world by entering in his location, or you can jam in some random stuff to appear halfway across the universe and hop back home again when you're done.
Overall, I'd say No Man's sky is worth $30-$40 in it's current state, a huge improvement. If you can grab it on sale, I highly reccomend it. If not, I still don't think you'd be too disappointed because of the amount of content availible, while expecting a future of sizable updates like this.

Great game for a multiplayer!
Pros:
+ Graphics are awesome considering this runs in the old Unreal Engine! The details of the ORIGINAL works tho, like the DLC items etc...those will never be forgotten now that at the time I'm writing this the game has been tarnished with workshop content that is NOT in the same quality level as the Official stuff...
+ Immersive sound and nice OST: sound even helps you while gaming since you can pin point where sharks are, what species, what kind of weapons are the divers using and what consumables deploying.
It's also quite detailed and high quality. Each gun has their own sound for example.
As for the OST, it's quite atmospheric and really gets the essence of the game as a thriller.
+ Easy gameplay: it's not hard to get used to the shark controls, much less the divers since it's basically a shooter then. What takes a LOT of time and EFFORT is getting good at it! Also there's a big difference/variety between each shark species, which means it takes effort to master them all.
+ Challenging: even bots can be a headache, but there are a lot of veteran players that can teach you some tips and tricks. Too many new players but, as expected from sales etc.
+ Amazingly balanced: Somehow, the developers have managed to create the most balanced indie game I've ever seen. Both sides have a 50/50 % win rate, and only skills tip that balance!
+ Variety everywhere: there's skins for everyone, from cringy half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥works (which thankfully aren't many...) to incredibly diverse skins. Many weapons and sharks to chose from, aswell as dozens of skins for each, without going overboard like some games tho however.
Cons:
- Toxic players: not sure why I put this here since EVERY game has it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. However, unlike most games, in here toxic behaviour is punished accordingly, so if you ever have problems with some imbecile, take screenshots and send it to the Developers, thew will take the proper actions.
- Big Learning Curve: I've played many games, but none as long to "git gud" at as this one. So this might be a deterrant to some.

This system isn't flawless but it isn't♥♥♥♥♥♥♥either: the player base is too small to be able to always put players of the same level together, so of course sometimes low levels will end up against high level players at some point.
TL;DR: Worth every little coin in full price, specially if you have friends to play with ;)

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Why this is a fantastic educational game for kids... Memorization - The Keyboard mini-game The first step, is how you approach the game with your kid. I have an old wireless keyboard I let my kid play with. We started with leaning how all the keys are arranged on the keyboard. It was pointed out to me several times that the keys were in the wrong order. Once over that little tidbit, my kid was able to locate a-z in a reasonable amount of time. This is an important exercise, as it'll decrease the screen time and frustration that could arise when trying to spell within the game. Critical Thinking This game gives a unique opportunity to peer into your child's frame of mind. With every character that needs help in the game, encourage you kid to give an answer. More often then naught, they'll be able to give you the correct answer. Reading the request and giving clues so your kid will understand are good ways to encourage an answer. I mean, what kid doesn't know what a pirate would need to be a pirate? Or someone is sick, what do they need? Medicine, of course. Geography Since we generally tried to complete 1 location with every session (about 15 - 20 minutes), we would begin the session the same way. Clicking on the global map icon, which would show us a bird eye view of the area and each of its unique locations. The locations are unlockable and grouped together with a common theme. For example, "Desert theme" would have locations: pyramids, dunes, mine shaft, etc. Being able to relate a location with the overall world, helped with the immersion, and helps diversify the gameplay. Spelling Encouraging your kid to spell out the object they are trying to create. This often resulted in the same solution for various problem (you'd be surprised how many problems can be solved with a "bat"). If a misspelling is detected, it will highlight the word red, and if submitted, it'll give a list of suggestions, much like a friendly spell check. For harder words, I'd go ahead and spell out the word and go over why the word is spelled that way. Grammar Since the game offers up both nouns and adjectives as input, this created another opportunity to practice grammar. Its one thing to describe what the differences are, its another to see them in action. It wasn't long before any animal that we'd created, would need an associated adjective to go along with it. Big purple dinosaurs were discouraged. In summary, this game is a fantastic way to teach spelling, grammar, geography, and problem solving while keeping both parent and child engaged. In fact, its probably the best edutainment game I've seen, even though it wasn't advertised as such. Music is pretty catchy too. The PC version is tied into Steam's workshop mod shop. So unofficial licensed characters such as Hulk, Captain America, or Binders of Women can be imported to your notepad.

Charming puzzle game with good humor. It doesn't fully deliver on the advertised concept, but comes close enough to be well worth $5. It also does a good job of communicating controls/game concepts without an obnoxious tutorial.
The biggest downside is the platforming and combat. Controls are clunky, and your options for dealing with enemies are very limited. The game also rates you on whether you take damage in a level as part of the 'completion percentage', sometimes this is completely at the whim of the random behavior of enemies, so completionists be prepared to restart repeatedly or give up on getting the full score.
There are many situations where skill and thinking will not help you in a fight. Bosses will often stun-lock you as you jump over them and fly you into a hazard, either instant-killing or holding you there until you run out of health. Enemies will sometimes synch up with platforming sections such that you have to suicide into them or restart from checkpoint.
Difficulty in fights is largely due to health pool and very little else. The game may have been better (although a little short) if combat had been left out entirely.
Over all the core concept makes up for it and on the balance I'd recommend it.

My review is going to focus on the mechanics of the game but let me say this game has everything:
- The story, presentation, graphics and audio create a wonderful universe.
- The interactive tutorials teach you about the characters, game systems and fighting games as a whole (mix ups, hit confirms, etc.)
- Best tools in practice mode of any fighting game I know of (I've played A LOT), including hitbox and hitstun display, slow motion, 'as reversal' dummy playback, savestates and more.
- GGPO netcode.
On to the actual fighting. Skullgirls can be played with mixed solo characters and teams of 2 or 3. Health, damage and defense are scaled so it's balanced. I prefer teams of 2 and occasionally 3, but a solo character can overwhelm a team if they get the momentum. Teams have assists and tagging similar to Marvel, though you can use any normal/special/throw attack as an assistant and all characters have unique tag in attacks.
I really like the amount you can customise your team. It definitely helps offset what some might see as a limited roster of characters.
Speaking of characters current cast of 12 (eventually to be 14) are all very unique and represent a wide variety of styles. My favourites are Big Band, the slow armour character that can actually play music (also he can parry), Cerebella, the grappler that also glides and can reflect projectiles, Valentine, because she's a ninja and can move wherever she wants and Eliza, the "stand" character. There's also a Scorpion/Angel hybrid stance character, a John Talbain pro wrestler, a dismembered cat girl with rekkas (and is also a doll character) and Fukua, the joke character that has a dragon kick so win all round.
All characters have special moves and supers, for the most part very much like Street Fighter moves. Supers use 2 buttons rather than double motions. If playing with a team you can tag mid super into the next characters super. There is however no ability to perform multiple simultaneous super moves.
Combos are largely formed out of chains, going in traditional "magic series", though there are links and plenty of unique chains. The combo system is very free form, the limiting factors are the infinite prevention system (IPS) and drama/undizzy bar. These limits are a good thing, they keep you from repeating the same thing over and over, keeping combos interesting and stopping any single combo from going on for too long. There are still high damage combos but you can't just loop something until timeout or death.
If a combo starts to loop the player getting hit can burst out for free. This means you have to either end your combo or try to reset the other player into another combo, or even bait the burst and attack after.
There are many unique character specific systems that make the game interesting and give the characters more depth. Big Band can parry attacks, Squigly can cancel normal attacks and move the screen around, Valentine can inflict 3 status effects and resurrect dead teammates, Painwheel can fly and absorb then reflect damage, and so many others.
Character diversity is definitely one of the games strong points.
So in summary, I highly recommend this game to anyone who loves 2D fighting games or would like to start playing them and to anyone who likes fighting games and appreciates the story and art. If I had to put a number on it I'd say 5/5, it's "perfect", everything it sets out to do it does beyond expected of a fighting game.

Updated for August 24th Update!
What I liked from what I played:
-It's a Lego open world sandbox, that's basically a childhood dream come true!
-The idea of exploring the world and finding stuff is improved now that you can explore underwater, and the slightly annoying mechanic that some NPCs and animals won't be added to your discoveries unless you give them a certain item from a chest, which gives more insentive to explore more than a few small areas for more chests.
-Character customization is great. It encourages you to find more people because the more people you find, the more parts you can make your character with.
-It's a really great looking game! The lighting effects are very good, and I like the little touches on the slopes to make them look like they do in real life.
What I didn't like:
-The system for brick-by-brick building isn't that improved from before. It's still very slow, and the camera is a bit iffy. Still hoping for a built-in LDD sort of thing like the old Lego Creator games did. I know you CAN import stuff from LDD, but it's not the most convient thing to switch from the game to that program.
-I should have touched on this aspect in my original review, but the menu really should be changed so I don't have to keep scrolling though a bunch of things. This problem becomes a pain when you have a ton of props or minifigure parts.
-I wish there were more ways to find the items NPCs want other than just chests, especially for thing like an apple or a bone.
OVERALL: Searching the world for stuff is more enjoyable other than the one nitpick I mentioned before, but the current in-game building system is holding this back for me to fully enjoy it.

I'll be honest with you, ever since I found the whole series, I was skeptical at first as to how they would play out. Quite surprisingly, I've fallen in love with it entirely, from the quirky antics that the group always gets themselves in, to the in-depth lore that the creator (Matt Roszak. Bless his soul) has put into.
Gameplay wise, it would play out as what you would expect from an RPG-esque like game. Statuses, buffs, debuffs, elemental weakness, spell levelling and so forth. And with four different characters to play around with, though you can only have three of them at one go, it can get kind of hectic at times. Not to mention the plethora of equipment that each of them use. Despite the numerous spells/equipment and such, you can go whatever playstyle you like. From a brute dmg build to more of a casual runthrough. Though I recommend building around enemies weaknesses and strength on the higher difficulties cos they would be hitting you really hard.
Design wise, I enjoy it. It's whacky, colourful and sets the theme of every location just nicely. The design that the creator used for the story is also very cute. The game doesn't take itself too seriously at times, given the numerous times the group would idly talk about. Heck, even the initial casts of some of the spells make it seem like they don't take things too seriously. And despite some small gripes about the group, they're all really well made.

A throwback to the classic game of the 1980s, Gauntlet does a lot of things right and a few things wrong.  On the plus side all the characters are fun and unique to play with toons such as the mage taking awhile to master.  The level designs are nice and varied and make for a fun game.  Playing with friends is also a blast as each class can balance out the weakness or another.
There are, however, a few negatives that I believe the devs could improve on down the road.  The game, overall, is very short.  On a normal difficulty and with a few friends it doesn't take long to see all the content.  There are higher difficulty levels, but you do not get to see anything new.  The game also tends to favor the ranged classes over the melee ones.  With a balanced group this is not much of an issue, but if you are playing alone or others only using melee characters the game becomes annoying on many encounters.

Gauntlet 2014 is a couch co-op action-adventure game with competitive elements. Before I start this review, I have to say that I am not a fan of the original series. Sure, I played a couple of games way back when, then I played games influenced by them, then I got this. I put the game on "Hard" because I'm a real man and played it from start to finish with two friends. All I have to say is, don't buy this game.
It's competitive aspect falls flat on it's face purely because gold is useless in this game. Players are encouraged to steal relic potions because they are scarce, steal the crown because it effectively doubles your earnings and to generally perform better than their friends in order to get a larger cut of your earnings. With gold you can upgrade your relics, except you don't have to - most of a relic's potential is already available to you from the get-go, besides, you barely get to use relics anyway. You can also spend gold on cosmetic pieces, a grand total of ten per character, excluding pre-order content, that you can barely see because you lose track of your character so often.
This game is badly optimized, a staple of Arrowhead games since Magicka, even though it's not graphically impressive. There isn't much difference between low and high settings anyway, aside for VSync and FXAA. Because of a generally drab, boring and sterile aesthetic you lose track of your character easily. It's also severely lacking in enemy variety, averaging in five enemy types per zone.
There are three zones in total, three chapters plus boss each. A chapter typically takes around twenty minutes to complete, and even that is generous. As long as you are not terrible or don't lose time quarelling, you can breeze through the game. There is a separate survival mode, Colosseum, but it's short and it's rewards, three cloaks, aren't very tempting.
As you can see, I haven't said anything positive yet, because that is of little importance. Sure, the characters were nice, the dialogue was fun, the passive mastery learning system was somewhat interesting, but having all that robbed us of actual ♥♥♥♥ing progression and strategy development. If you are looking for a Gauntlet comeback, I suggest you try Hammerwatch. If you are looking for some co-op action, I suggest you try Hammerwatch, no, I implore you to try Hammerwatch. Not this, please. It does not get better.

3/10: The controls are simple enough to learn, but the Wizards was hard not only because of a terrible tutorial that taught you the wrong way, but key binding is limited. If you are a Gauntlet Legends player, you will realize this game is nothing like it besides going into stages and levels and being a hack and slash games with the same classes you know and love. Well maybe a bit less. There is a more sophisticated combat system now and more interesting items. But it would seem legacy items like 3 way shot is gone. No potions either so you can't kill Death. Actually a stage revolves are you dodging death as you dungeon crawl. It does take a bit of skill to play it unlike the original Gauntlet Legends. All in all, it doesn't hit the nostalgic factor, but it wasn't innovative either. So it wins in no ends.

I agree with everyone else that this game has a beutiful story. But there are some factors that bother me:
1. Characters
This game has some notable characters with distinct personality and role, but there are some that are lacking both. This game jumps from one plot to another without giving us enough time to be introduced to the characters. I sometimes forgot the significance of a character. This problem even occurs with main characters. This problem also makes me less 'bonded' with the characters.
2.  The conflict
The conflict, or I should say, the important plot points seem to be stretched. This makes them giving me less impact on each of the plot points.
3. The details
There are some important details scatered around the story. All of those details supposed to help building the story. But unfortunately, this game isn't so good at 'connecting those dots'. Eventually, those details became some sort of distractions.
4. The mechanics
The controls seem to be a little floaty. And, within the game, there are mini games that are supposed to be the connectors from one plot point to another. But unfortunately those mini games felt unnecessary and distracting for me.
5. The jokes
To touch the heart through a story, one should make the player laugh and cry. This game has failed me at the laughing part.
I know there are countless positive aspect of this game. But at the end, those things above can't get out of my head. It's a little bit unfogiving, but I couldn't aprove myself to give this game a thumbs up with those things unimproved.

So, my review is that this game is not recommended. I'll say now, that some people may enjoy it, but personally I didn't. It's a time-sink, but not a particularly fun one. I'll begin with the pros.
Pros:
Good tech tree. It's interesting, useful, and well-made. It goes quickly, while still lasting quite a while.
Customization. You can build ships, create custom races, all of that. I spent most of my time simply re-inacting my books, and seeing how different races of mine would react to those of other universes.
Battle screen. If you have two fleets that are in battle, you get a more detailed video of the battle. Though not particularly useful itself, it is enjoyable to watch.
Now, for the cons. These are the reasons why I wouldn't recommend this to most people.
Cons:
Slow start. The beginning feels boring and long-running. Every game begins the same: You have your system, you colonize the one other habitable planet, then you move to the next. And even once you meet another race, you don't have diplomatic incidents to worry about. The worst you could do is sell something important to them by accident. Until you go to war, it's a very tedious and repetetive task.
Tactics are useless. Aside from wanting to attack THIS planet instead of THAT one, you don't really need to use tactics. If your ships are strong enough, you just win.
Lack of diplomacy. You can't use diplomacy at all. You can pay other races to ally with you, or to declare war on somebody, but that's it.
Finally, the game just doesn't fit the role I expected from it. Instead, I got a time sink that I probably won't play for months on end. If you want something that will bring tactics into the game, I'd recommend Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion. For those who enjoy a more basic game when it comes to fleet tactics and diplomacy, you may enjoy this. It has it's ups.

Skull Girls: Encore
Intro:
With 2D fighting hitting a slump for me in the early 2000's It was either Street Fighter, Mortal Kombat, or Guilty Gear. Original 2D Fighting Games were hard to come by. And Announced Late 2011 Skullgirls was being developed. And in Late Spring 2012 Skullgirls arrived with art from ~Oh8~ [Alex Ahad] and Street Fighter Vetran [Mike Zaimont]. With a fresh art style and a someone familiar with the pros and cons of 2D fighter of the past, I have good feels about this game.
Gameplay:
The launch in 2012 was fantastic but with Mike "Z" at the helm the game is constantly evolving. And if you're part of the Beta on Steam the power is in your hands. The infamous 6-button layout returns in the Indie Fighter with 3 punches and 3 kicks. Each button with various damage and speeds. Did you like the 3 vs 3 with the Versus series from Capcom? Think you're badass 3 vs 1? You can with this title!! With very responsive controls and easy to pick up layout you'll be mashing away with your friends until you learn those special moves. Speaking of special moves, The creators have poured there hearts and souls into their training mode. From AI controlled comupters to programable dummies. The gameplay feels wonderful and the visuals are a breath of fresh air compared to the other titles you've been juggling since 2000.
Art/Music:
As I've said before Alex Ahad brought a new style and beautiful visuals to this title. Some characters are pretty "eww" (Looking at the character Double) but the rest are eye popping with detail and so many vivid frames. And courtasy of the Fundraising campaign, the roster has been bumped from 8 to 14. Each character more interesting than the last. From Zombie Opra Singers to Pharroh's with Blood Magic. The character designs do nothing but amaze me everytime I play a round. And what's a great art style without a great soundtrack? Michiru Yamane and the music team gave a good blend of tunes that should increase the enjoyment of story mode and all the stages. Good feels from both Art and Music.
Accessability:
When folks see Mike "Z" as a seasoned vetran of Fighting Games some may be scared to try this game. I say "Nay!" Skullgirls has a tutorial mode to make even the novice of players be able to block like the pros. It may not happen overnight but the tutorial mode will tell you what to look for and it will even help you learn a character. Online gameplay is well thought out with GGPO and the players online are fierce with vigor. (Trust me I'm 0-12 still) But the story mode for each character is fun and well written. Speaking of characters, since launch Skullgirls is adding a total of 6 new characters!! Add those to the original 8 and you have 14 possible character to choose from. Each with unique animations and playstyles.
Verdict:
I like this game a lot! The User feedback, the crowd-funded characters, and the evolving gameplay! I think this game should be in any 2D Fighters library! Heck, gift it to a friend on the next steam sale. Because their lobby system involves everyone! No more boring "round robin" style lobbies! (Thank god!!) My only issues with the game is once their funding goes away, will there be a second one? Either way this title has earned its stripes with me.
Conclusion:
Thanks for reading this lame review I typed on a whim. But I hope you consider this title when and if you're looking for that NON-Mainstream title. Because I have purchase it for 2 platforms now. And I dont regret a thing!!

I simply cannot recommend this game in any capacity, I'm not even really sure what I expected in hindsight when I backed this years ago. This is, of course, years down the road. I suppose I was hoping for a multiplayer game in the spirit of the Ultima series, with today's standards.(Divinity Original Sin is, in hindsight, an example of what I had in mind - with tweaks of course IE: if it were real-time instead of turn based.) Ultimately, I can't say that this game is enjoyable, so I will give it a negative. I'll try to explain to the casual interested reader, but I can't really be brief and succeed at explaining myself.
A few quick points to understand:
They understood from the onset that the intended audience was a niche market, and that the budget would be tight, they made what I felt were 'good' decisions based on that information from the beginning.
They figured correctly they could charge extra for 'perks', so they did; other companies with similiar endless fundraising goals have followed suit, so they aren't doing anything others will not do.
I cannot say this hasn't resulted in benefits for the game, quite the contrary it has improved more than it would have originally.
But at some point in 2014 I realized it was moving in a direction that I couldn't quite understand or relate to.  The fact that I didn't register the game on Steam until much later was partly a result of this confusion. I'm staring at my screen, writing this review at the end of October of 2017, wondering just what I had backed. I watched some early backers get fed up and walk off angry, I'm not angry - just confused by my experience with it. I've backed other games that have decidedly moved in the direction this game has - but never leaving me confused like this one has in so many ways.
I am generally not at all against a developer's right to moderate their own forums and to remove harmful elements within the community. I do however feel many times this has been extremely poorly handled at best by this company; almost, at times, to the point of being angry that I backed the people behind it. Small teams are highly united, and one could hardly expect that people who feel they are being attacked sometimes rather personally should tolerate it indefinately, that I understand all too well; people who work retail also understand that reversing the situation on a customer will cost them their jobs in the majority of cases. One of my personal favorite motto's from another company on moderation: Be lovely.
About the game itself - everything about the game feels more dated than it should - from the art assets to the game design theories.
