Ohhhh, EBF. Playing this series is the best kind of nostalgia for middle school me. Flash games may be near-death nowadays, but I remember playing the second and third game in this series on Kongregate back in its heyday.
The best way to describe EBF4 is that it's a love letter old school RPG's while creating it's own unique identity. While the humor is wildly dated now, and never the drawing point in the first place, what really makes me love this gem is the intricate combat systems and heavy-tactic battles that it's nailed time and time again. There are numerous skills, elements and systems built into this game, and for someone starting out fresh it can be a bit overwhelming. Overlooking a single system, such as changing your equipment for battle or forgetting to cast debuffs at the beginning can make or break later fights. This game has no definition of "cheese;" you earn your victories from beginning to end, because it's the enemies that are overpowered. There are confrontations in this game (specifically in the steam-exclusive challenge areas) that can take upwards of an hour to defeat, with a single misstep spelling defeat. It's thrilling, and a bit draining.
While it is called the fourth one, you do not need to play the first three to enjoy this one. The original games were definitely fun, but they are rough flash games that provided the basis for this one. This is the culmination of those games in it's own charming way, and it's improved in every possible light...except for the writing. Please be aware that the humor is insanely grating, childish and mind-numbingly sexist at certain points, but that is not where the value is. It is not a perfect game, and if you are looking for an RPG with any actual story, I highly doubt this will satisfy you. While the story structure isn't inherintly bad, and the paper cut out cutscenese a treat, the characters and general dialogue are filled with outdated memes and middle school level sex jokes that gave me the worst kind of nostalgia. If this is a dealbreaker, I completely understand.
As far as a game goes, however, there is some serious meat on this beast. I'm a bit irritated that steam does not keep hour logs when playing offline, but my play count for this is easily towards the 40-50 hour range. There are so many secrets and collectibles, with a varied, intricate vania-style unlock system that there is always new equipment and abilities to find and try out. Even after beating the game, I was still finding new secrets things, although my enjoyment had waned at this point. The artstyle is surprisingly cute, and there is an insane variety of enemies and bosses. I cannot emphasize enough how gratifying the challenge areas are, as they actualize everything you have learned to that point, and can be tackled at any time without reprocussion. The concept that the enemies scale to your level means it will always be difficult, but balanced if you go in with some forethought.
All in all, this game has aged phenomenally well, aside from the elements previously mentioned. It's been almost five years and the new one is on it's way, so it was a treat to revisit. I will most definitely be trying out EBFV, but in the meantime, this game is absolutely worth playing. Keep an eye out for a sale is my best suggestion, or if you want to see if it's your cup of tea, the base version is still available to be played for free online. Hope this helped!

One of the best RPGs available on Steam. There is a wealth of content: a 20+ hour campaign; a huge number of enemy types, weapons, armour, accessories and skills that must be dynamically swapped at all times to stay on top of the enemies' weaknesses and resistances; for the first time in the series, you now control four players, allowing one to remain on the 'back bench' to be tagged in at any time, even replacing a downed ally; the story is light and full of silly references and humor - just the kind of thing we need these days, especially when a lot of other RPGs are going for the gritty, emotional stories (and you don't even need to have played previous games - though they're all free, and EBF3 is also on Steam, so you might as well); plus a save function in the menu and no random battles, so it's extremely easy to pick up and play for short--or long--amounts of time. Highly recommended - don't let the Flash graphics put you off, a LOT of work has gone into this game!

Let me preface this by saying I am in no way implying I know what it is like to live with the disease that is schizophrenia/psychosis, nor am I going to pretend to.
It is the core theme of the game, so much so that the first thing that you see when booting up the game is information about the disease.
- I wholeheartedly recommend the game be played with headphones, you will miss out on a large component of the game if you do not.
- From the onset, a few voices are constantly bombarding you, with more joining along the way. They talk over each other, while it can be frustrating when trying to listen to one voice, I believe it is the intention of the developer to do so.
- You're thrown into the deep end from the onset: no tutorial, no map, nothing. Look up the controls before you start. This is a little annoying, but there are only a few controls to memorise.
- The game is very pretty, environments and effects look great. Special mention to Senua, her mo-cap looks amazing.
- Combat is satisfying if somewhat basic, although I've only had a couple battles so far.
- There are some basic puzzles in the game, like finding patterns to open gates, these can be tricky as there is no prompting to do it.
- Did I mention these voices are hounding you the whole time? When there is silence, it feels somewhat eerie and unnerving.
- The core mechanic that adds challenge to the game: you are affected by 'the rot,' the disease within Senua that will destroy her mind once it reaches it. The kicker is that every time you die/fail, the rot extends its reach through your body. Once it reaches Senua's mind, it's GAME OVER, and you lose all progress and have to start the game from the beginning.
- It's a nice callback to games of old, a nice change of pace to the 'no fear/reload save' mentality of modern games.
- This isn't for everyone.

What to say about Ori and the Blind Forest that hasn't been said already? Well, I can certainly corroborate with everyone else that this is probably the most beautiful 2D game EVER made. A few times I was thinking "well, maybe some of the newer Rayman games are at least equally as beautiful." Nope. Ori takes the cake. It is literally better than an interactive Disney cartoon. Like, we're talking Disney at its height of artistry, circa Alladin/Tarzan/Lilo era, and the art from those films can't even hold a candle to Ori. And ya know what the most fascinating part of it all is?? The art and dev teams are TINY!! As I was watching the credits, I completely expected some insane amount of artists to have worked on this game. When I saw that it was only maybe 2, 3 artists total, my jaw dropped. Well, more like went further through the floor as it had already dropped so many times throughout this game that it kind of hurts.
The one thing I will say about Ori is that it is PUNISHINGLY difficult. Maybe it's because I was using a PS3 controller, I don't know, but there are some segments in the game which almost made me give up. The gorgeous art really kept me going, it was the only saving grace for such a ridiculously hard, frustrating, and many times unfair level of difficulty. The controls are for the most part very tight, with great platforming challenges, use of timing, clever environmental construction, and so forth. Eventually you'll gain abilities which allow Ori to more or less shoot through the air like a little rocket, which coupled with a triple jump and wall hanging make him one of the most versatile little platform critters ever. But god damn is this game hard. Word of advice: SAVE OFTEN!!!! The fact that there are hardly any in-game checkpoints means that as the player, it's your responsibility to save and protect yourself from having to redo entire areas over and over again. And there are many MANY one hit kill environmental hazards to be aware of, so I'll say it again: SAVE OFTEN!!
Overall, I do recommend Ori. As terribly difficult as it is, it's worth sticking it through to see all of the fantastic art that the game has to offer. The platforming overall is quite satisfying and rewarding, the controls work for the most part, the music is delightful, and the story is heartfelt if not somewhat typical. The subtlety of the story works well, and I could complain that it is fairly simple, but for this sort of game you just don't need a complex story with tons of characters and interweaving plotlines. What's here story-wise is nothing groundbreaking, but it works, and there are moments that pull on the emotional heartstrings.
BOTTOM LINE: Greatest art ever in a videogame (and possibly any form of media up to this point), solid gameplay, excellent Metroidvania progression, disgustingly hard difficulty at times.

Tom Clancy's The Division is one of those games that went off track so much that it was bound to get trashed by many players a every corner.
First, there was the huge downgrade from what was displayed before its release which involved more than 50% of the map displayed in previews as being removed. Then, it wasn't long before you could find cheaters in the game that were using 3rd party apps to makes them "glitchy" in game. There was also the deception from the DLCs which doesn't bring much to the game itself. (Survival is simply useless and dead because nobody is willing to waits HOURS until 4 players with good connectivity miraculously find themselves in the game.) No "group" browser makes it so that you can join others only through a random matchmaking (making you unable to find another group if you quit one) or invites.
The game can be a big pain in the butt to play with others. That's a fact and barely nothing has been done to fix it since the release.
So, why am I recommending this game? Because if you get it on sale and don't expect a Tom Clancy's game, you might find the game actually fun when things goes well. This game is basically a 3rd-person stats-based RPG set in a modern setting in New York. Think of it as the Tom Clancy's version of Borderland with bullet sponges enemies, weapon and equipments with stats, builds and skills, etc. I actually like playing it and the game still has some small-time event now and then which add a bit more to do and find. For example, they added a new zone in the city's map just recently... even if all the DLCs were released. In that zone, there are a new game mode which is Wave-Based survival.
The game isn't perfect. Far from it! But it's still a good form of entertainment. I would suggest to wait for "at least" a 50% sale before buying it.

Make no mistake: the potential is definitely there. Minecraft comparisons aside, there's something alluring about this strange cross between Minecraft and whatever game first comes to mind when you hear the phrase "farming simulator" (for me, it's Slime Rancher).
I was really sold on the idea and the demos where I saw chainsaw turrets around walls (and kind of like the idea of being able to build walls but not gates). As I played, I liked the idea of the livestock being turned into zombies, for their commodities are far more valuable than the crops on a one-to-one basis. The turrets I liked, even though no one told me the grenade turret can't shoot OVER my makeshift parapet and thus blew up both itself and the lowered wall I'd placed it near.
But, alas, this game moves like an arthritic double-amputee and it drags everything down with it. The slowness does not limit itself to the pacing. EVERYTHING in this game moves like it's wading through molasses: the zombies, the livestock, you, the crops' growth, everything. The crops I can understand, and even get why the livestock might wander around aimlessly (though that feature where everything gets blurry when I pick something up is bloody aggravating). But the zombies move slow and can take about 2 full clips of ammo from both the pistol and the uzi before they go down, making them a chore to kill. The shotgun speeds things up, but the constant need to reload (and the game doesn't let you switch weapons until your spent weapon has bullets in the chamber again) is also aggravating.
There are other things, too: the generators only provide power within a small radius, so I don't feel safe placing them near openings where the chainsaw turrets would go. There's this strange crypt on the first level which spawned a spitter every time I clicked on it, and I'm pretty sure those things can eat more bullets than their Behemoth brethren. On their own, they'd be nitpicks, but collectively each little problem adds to the irritation until it becomes duly noticeable.
Most annoying, and the one thing I refuse to forgive, is the placement mechanic. The object in question is not placed until AFTER the animation is done, and because this game tricks me into thinking it's Minecraft, I'll often place things down because daylight hours are limited and you can't build things at night for some arbitrary reason.
So, yeah, Dead Acres. Loads of potential, but the game needs to move faster and the daylight timer needs to slow down a little. I really, REALLY wish I could recommend this game, but I simply can't. The flaws are too many and too glaring, and that snail's pacing killed it for me.

Seemingly with potential, I backed this what seems like an age ago now.
Recently returned to find something I didn't expect.
I like the idea of skills levelling as you use them, and the whole classless idea gives me a warm glow, after playing Asheron's Call for many years.
Combat is poor.  RNG meant that even at point blank against something I killed easily before, I missed with arrows 15 times in a row!  RPG combat has come a long way since Asheron's Call, but this game doesn't seem to have.
Graphics are possibly due for improvement, but they feel straight out of a game 10 years ago.  Animations are very basic.
Character creation has many options to customise your face, but body is just big/small.  Even with the customisation, I struggled to settle on a face I was truely happy with.
Communicating with NPCs feels clunky with the "click on a word, answer with your name, say yes" etc.
Some little things are very frustrating too.  The mouse wheel works inconsistently, for example.
I think the problem I have with the game is that it's the core gameplay and game architecture that I'm struggling with, and I these things I feel are unlikely to change hugely this late.
In summary, I'm going to avoid this one for now, as there are better ways to get an RPG fix.  However, the developer comments encouraged me, and I'll keep checking back.

Fallout 3 is a very good RPG, with a lot of action thrown in it, and a very good story. Set in a post-apocalyptic world after a nuclear war, you'll find yourself travelling through the Capital Wasteland, which used to be Washington and its surrounding areas. Even though the world is post-apocalyptic, it still has a quite distinctive 50s feeling to it, as history in the Fallout universe is different from ours.
The story starts out somewhat simple. You live in Vault 101 with your father, but after he leaves one day, you must escape the Vault, and search for him. However, it's not as easy as it sounds, as you'll end up in the middle of a conflict for control of the Capital Wasteland.
The GOTY edition, which I'm reviewing, includes all 5 DLCs released for Fallout 3; and I'd say it's worth it getting this version over the regular edition, as they add a lot of content. From the snowy landscape of Alaska in Operation: Anchorage, to the final frontier, space, in Mothership Zeta, they all offer new quests, locations, and items; as well as enemies. Broken Steel, in particular, picks up the story from where it ends, adding three new quests after the main story.
The setting, as I mentioned, is based around the area of Washington, and there's plenty of places to discover. Even though it's not a faithful recreation (and even if you've never been to Washington), you can recognize some of its famous landmarks, like the Washington Monument, or the Lincoln Memorial.
As far as gameplay goes, it's RPG elements are quite good. Like in almost every RPG, you earn experience points and level up; each time you do, you get to distribute several skill points into the different skills, and you also get to choose a perk, which grants you extra abilities. What makes Fallout's system special, however, is, well, its SPECIAL system, in which, at the moment of creating your character, you define his seven main attributes (Strength, Perception, Endurance, Charisma, Intelligence, Agility, and Luck), which not only affect your skills, but also things like your maximum health or carrying capacity. As far as the combat goes, it's pretty much an action game, and can be played both in first and third person; however, your skills will affect how well you do in combat. Of course, being an RPG, it's not all about combat; you'll find yourself doing several quests, even outside the main storyline, helping people all around the Wasteland. There's also tons of dialogue, you can always find someone who might have some valuable information for you, or you can even avoid some combat situations simply through dialogue!
Well, in conclusion, I think this is a very good game, and I recommend it. It's a great experience, after all. I'd also add that you should check out Fallout: New Vegas as well; I haven't reviewed it yet, but it was the first Fallout game I've ever played, and it's as good as Fallout 3, if not better.

If you like franchises like Pokémon and Final Fantasy, you'll probably like this. The EBF franchise is a surprisingly deep in combat at times, and some battles on "Hard" or "Epic" difficulty can actually be fairly hard. So don't let the cute cartoon graphics fool you.
While the game can be quite hard on "Hard" or "Epic" difficulty, Easy and Normal also exist if you want a more relaxing or casual time. There's something to be had with both casuals and hardcore RPG fans.
Your party in EBF4 consists of 4 party members, and they all have various skills, equipments and weapons. Each focusing on a different stat more than the other. Example:
Matt is the sword user with the highest physical damage and physical defense.
Natalie is the mage of the group and uses a variety of healing spells and magic attack, as she has the highest magic attack out of the group.
Lance is the gun wielder who plays a support role with minor healing and Dark & Bomb skills that the others lack.
Anna is also a support, and like Lance she performs minor healing aswell, difference being she has different type of support skills and she dishes out more Earth, Poison and Wind skills.
These are just minor examples to give you an idea how each character is different.
Each biome you come across are filled with different types of enemies and sometimes mini-bosses and at the end of the biome, a boss. All of these enemies and bosses have their respective elemental weaknesses and strengths, and status infliction weaknesses and resistence too.
Each biome also have hidden secrets like various loot and treasure chests that contain new weapons and such.
Both your party members and the enemies function the same way in terms of strengths and weaknesses. Obviously you have basic stats like Evade, Attack, Accuracy, HP etc.
But depending what type of equipment you put on, including weapons, hats/helmets and outfits, you'll be giving yourself different sets of resistence or weaknesses.
Example: If you give a party member an electric type weapon, armor, pin and hat that boosts electric armor, then there's a chance your electric resistence is great depending on the percentage.
Here's how elemental resistence percentage works:
0% = Nothing special, normal damage taken.
+100% = No damage taken from said type of damage.
+Above 100% (such as 150%) = Healed from said damage type
Anything in the minus zone (-100% etc) = Weak towards it, avoid it.
Not trying to write a strategy guide here, but it IS quite in depth.

Overall Rating: 8/10
Gameplay Rating: 8/10
Accessibility Rating: 9/10
Gauntlet is a single player or co-op experience!  This tribute to the older games in its lineage reawakens the fun, top-down dungeon crawling, horde-destroying genius of the original games.
Though a bit linear and slightly redundant, Gauntlet is still entertaining in both single and co-op modes.  The Colosseum mode brings together 4 players in classic arcade fashion.
The achievements in Gauntlet come for both good and bad events, such as collecting gold or dying, and all make your character just a little better.
As a co-op game with friends, however, Gauntlet's outstanding history shines through and the game becomes fun, amusing, and challenging.
Additional replayability comes from trying to complete the game and all achievements with all of the character types.  If you're a completionist, you may enjoy trying to get this one done.  Just bring a friend!
Gauntlet has sound settings controls for master volume, music, effects, and dialogue, as well as captions (subtitles).
When you start the game, it goes straight to the main menu, so you can set captions on before any events happen.
For gamers with mobility issues, Gauntlet's primary controls are game controller, but it works with keyboard and mouse just as well.  All keys can be rebound to suit your needs.
Captions in Gauntlet are great!  Gauntlet is not a very dialogue-rich game, so most of what is said is flavor text, but it all seems to be there.
Pros:
- Captions for characters are colored according to that character's color (green for elf, for example), and captions from the evil mastermind leading the gauntlet are white.
- Captions are easy to read in large font across the bottom of the screen.
Cons:
- Captions do not indicate who is speaking by name.  Only a *minor* problem because they are colored.
Gauntlet supports in-game chat and colors text according to which character you're playing.

Right away I want to say that this game is simply stunning and honestly makes me view the game more as a piece of true art rather than just any ordinary game. There is no real hand holding tutorial telling you what button to push and yet as the game progresses you through the story, you figure things out with the voices adding a very interesting vibe to the entire experience. Those voices can really set the tone for what is coming next. So I would say that you should definately wear headphones while playing this to further immerse yourself within this world that Ninja Theory has created for us.
As for the combat system, it does seem a bit basic, but I wouldn't say by any means that it is horrible since the fighting isn't truly the main point of this game. Though I will admit that at one point I got stuck in a lovely invisible wall during a fight sequence and literally couldn't fight the monsters off properly since I couldn't move from that one lovely spot, I just figure it is because I was trying to run towards the exit of the place when a fight sequence was occuring and thus got me so happily trapped in doom.
Still, I love the little puzzles you have to go around and find using the environment which is rather fun to do. But I must admit that what I love the most is how the story plays out with Senua seeing people and hearing the voices that will give you everything you need to know, even in the mist of combat. It is artfully done and I really can't wait to see what lays deeper within this gorgeous creation given to us.

Let me preface this by saying I am in no way implying I know what it is like to live with the disease that is schizophrenia/psychosis, nor am I going to pretend to.
It is the core theme of the game, so much so that the first thing that you see when booting up the game is information about the disease.
- I wholeheartedly recommend the game be played with headphones, you will miss out on a large component of the game if you do not.
- From the onset, a few voices are constantly bombarding you, with more joining along the way. They talk over each other, while it can be frustrating when trying to listen to one voice, I believe it is the intention of the developer to do so.
- You're thrown into the deep end from the onset: no tutorial, no map, nothing. Look up the controls before you start. This is a little annoying, but there are only a few controls to memorise.
- The game is very pretty, environments and effects look great. Special mention to Senua, her mo-cap looks amazing.
- Combat is satisfying if somewhat basic, although I've only had a couple battles so far.
- There are some basic puzzles in the game, like finding patterns to open gates, these can be tricky as there is no prompting to do it.
- Did I mention these voices are hounding you the whole time? When there is silence, it feels somewhat eerie and unnerving.
- The core mechanic that adds challenge to the game: you are affected by 'the rot,' the disease within Senua that will destroy her mind once it reaches it. The kicker is that every time you die/fail, the rot extends its reach through your body. Once it reaches Senua's mind, it's GAME OVER, and you lose all progress and have to start the game from the beginning.
- It's a nice callback to games of old, a nice change of pace to the 'no fear/reload save' mentality of modern games.
- This isn't for everyone.

A number of bugged and inaccessible achievements round out my frustrations with this game.

I have been playing now for just about a full year, and have spent thousands of hours now testing, building on character development and social / community building.
Gameplay: 7/10
The world of Novia is pretty vast and is finally starting to take its final shape as every patch over the last few months has been about polishing and completing a lot of the zones.   I am actually impressed at the changes I have seen from what was once a cookie cutter zone list to unique environments.  Quests at the lower levels have been added and every month massive changes to new zones and added quests are being implemented.   Many Mob placeholders are starting to be changed over to area specific mobs with their own ai and abilities, lore and history.  Crafting, agriculture, fishing, combat, player housing, player towns, guilds, pvp, virtue system, are just a few of the things this game offers.   The new player intro and polish has made it a lot easier for new comers to follow compared to when I stared which felt like I was just dropped into a world that was crazy hard to learn.   The game itself does have a lot of elements to learn and understand and even to this day I find out new things all the time which blows my mind how complex the whole system is and where its all headed.
Combat: 6/10
The combat has come along way form the clunky feel to a more fluid system offering 2 different play styles of locked glyphs or unlocked.  (Glyphs are like playing cards of abilities and spells you have)  you have the option of only so many combat glyphs to use in a locked deck you can only have one ability in each slot.   these abilities start off simple and later upon mastering them offer the ability to charge up the attack based on its level to unleash a more powerful version.   The unlocked allows for even more abilities and draws a random glyph to each slot depending on how you setup your deck.  This gives less control but offers other abilities like combos as well reduced focus usage which is like a pool of magic you pull from.   Its hard to explain exactly how this system works in words.   The  system for each 20 level gives you basically a new card / glyph to use so that you have in an unlocked system I higher chance to pull that skill more often from your deck.  In the locked system it allows you to the that power up for each card you have.   you can however in a locked system spam your ability for each card in the deck but at a cost of heat which basically uses up a large focus cost for each use which can drain your pool very fast. ( I call it a mana burn or Oh crap spam).   Both offer plus and minus and each player will have their own opinions on which is better.  myself I'm old school and liked locked abilities to use , however I run a mix of some locked and some slots that cycle specific abilities (utility spells/traits) as well my heals.
The character development is open ended you can master everything if you take the time, but its no simple feat.  The exp required to level skills to GM is a lot and could take some a life time to accomplish.  The design uses a pool system which feeds your skills.  you can train on practice dummies or fight real enemies but once your pooled xp runs out you can't level anymore which forces all players into the world to continue to gain.   Skills require management.  In the beginning most people like myself learn new abilities and freely level everything we want only to find that at a certain point the exp draw from the pool is dropping faster then I am leveling my skills no matter what you are killing.   This forces people to maintain abilities where they can turn on leveling of an ability, off, and or unlearn.  what this does is allows you to stop the pool flow to the skills and or reduce the amount of skills learning at once so that you can balance to learn skills faster with out draining the pool.  On top of that your pool size also affects how fast you learn.  Each skills levels up x% of total pool size.  This means the smaller your pool the less that % is going to each skill.    Over all the abilities both magic and non are pretty good and still being tweaked and balanced out.  As well new abilities over time have been added and I suspect this will continue throughout the games life which will eventually force people to specialize rather than attempt to GM everything.
Graphics: 8/10
The details in the game are pretty amazing for some things and less for others.  I do find that all the new polish these last few patches as made a huge advancement in the visuals.   there is still a lot of optimizations that need to happen which is the focus the last two patches in reducing load times and to speed up frame rates.   This game will take high ends systems to its knees with everything maxed out.  last patch they added volumetric lighting which was pretty sweet.  as well the new environment weather is starting to show its face.  I understand they are going to take that to even higher levels we have seen in other games where snow will accumulate on trees etc in certain zones.   spell effects have been revamped over the last 5 patches and still new changes its seems on the horizon.   Combat side of things still has work to be done, not all weapons have animations yet but there has been a lot of improvements and added visuals to this side as well.
Housing and décor is amazing, that alone I could spend days talking about the amount of detail they put into the housing system.  It really reminds me of UO mixed with many other games where everything you collect can be placed in your house.   Armor types and weapon types are vast.  there is hundreds of different looks and new ones every month being added.   This has me excited as I am a collectors of armor and weapons for my viewing room in my Manor.  Light effects are another thing this game has done very well with.  Shadows and shaders out the wazoo.  it really makes some places at night look amazing as well the detail of the shadows and reflections are AAA.  Over all the only thing I see needing the most attention which is happening is getting that Frame rate and load time faster.   I understand the reasons for it being slow, having 1000 objects/decor in my house makes it load slower which does take the  immersion away.
Quests:
Over all the Main Story quest is very good but can take a long time to complete.   It goes from low level start and can jump into a high tier zone which can frustrate people that like smooth quest.  The design of it was to progress over time  which is why with all the new polish for early zones it leads you through several new areas and quests to fill that gap.  Most the quests are standard which what one would expect in many games, as well some puzzle types.  One hard things for new players is understanding that this system plays upon old school logic where reading is required for some quests as you have to talk to NPC's like that of the old Sierra games like that of kings quest etc.  This makes it harder for those that have no patience as sometimes one has to pay a lot of attention to what NPC's are saying.  The important stuff is always recorded in a journal but not always clear.  trying to figure out what words trigger updates becomes a game on its own.  sometimes you have to talk to multiple people to find out what to tell a specific person.
over all I think when the game releases it will be rather fun for new people.  those that have been in the game for a long time are going to have to wait for higher end content to come which I can understand some peoples frustration if they have been playing since 2013.  This is why like most I waited a while before coming into the game as I know its not complete but my expectations are that this will shape up to be what I expected and thus far has not disappointed me.
I will add more when I have time but this is where I end this.  I hope that this offers more insight then my previous :)

Not to make light on a very dark subject which Hellblade doesn't stray from in the slightest. Hellblade Senau's Sacrifice pulls no punches when it comes to delving into the darker aspects of the human mind. Atmospheric is the best word to describe Hellblade, you feel the weight of existence pressing down on Senua, her terror, & at times joy and hope.

If you're buying into this venture for the combat I wouldn't advise a purchase. While simple & lacking any progression or development it's satisfying enough to carry the story. Combat comes down to knowing the few enemy types, careful position, & good use of Senua's one ability, her focus which slows time & allows for extra strikes.

Between combat & advancing the story, the rest of the game is divided into, at times simple, yet interesting perspective puzzles. Even at times bringing feelings of portal's puzzles back.

In short...a great atmospheric well told delve into the darkness of psychosis.

I was walking to my car when I noticed my pants were on fire. I turned to my friend and said, "I think were going to need an oven and fast."
He grabbed me with his soggy fingers and said.. "Snap out of it, Man."
Then he proceeded to chant and walk in circles around me.
I looked down, My pants were still on fire, but by this time it had spread to my Uterus and three other ligaments. I was getting pretty agitated that no one seemed to care about my third degree burns, or my soon imminent death, but I went along with his plan still hoping he'd manage to save me through his voo-doo witchcraft.
After I came out of my trance from the fire I noticed that I was now in the kitchen of my grandma's house baking a cake..
I Screamed "WHAT THE F***?"
My Grandma ran in and slapped the s*** outta me for cursing.
Then she proceeded to say, "I swear if you talk like that 5 more times, I'll beat the living s*** outta you."
I was quite confused as to what was going on and what I did to deserve this true life mad lib. I just stood there in silence with a look of uttermost confusion.. and I starred at the women who had once been a kind sweet old lady, who wouldn't even kill a baby piglet, now turned into this vicious beast of a monster with veins protruding from her neck like a porcupines quills on a midsummer day.
She gasped, and then with the blink of an eye turned back into the sweet old lady I had once known.
"Would you like some cookies, dear?"
"Ummm Yes, grandma."
As she went to retrieve the cookies, I was planning my escape.. Looking around pondering what unimaginable thing would happen next if I stayed. As my grandma neared the corner with her plate of cookies, I ran to the door as fast as my burning legs would take me.
As I made my silent escape I heard grandma yell, "You forgot your cookies dear"
Little did she know I didn't give a s*** about those cookies. As I ran I thought about my previous life and how this whole day had been more interesting than my Whole entire life on earth had.. I began to ponder if this was karma kicking my a** for just sitting on the laptop all day typing short stories for little to no pay. When I decided to stop and catch my breath, I wiped the sweat from my face and looked up to see what else this new world had to offer.
Far off in the distance I could see a huge building, maybe a hotel or some sort of jail. I wasn't too sure.. but I marked that location off my list, the last thing I needed was to go to a jail and get killed by a bunch of mobsters.. I mean Hell my pants were already on Fire.
I decided to turn to my left and see what my next choice would be.
There were flying cantaloupes, rainbows and songs of happiness near by, I mean I was a little frightened by the flying fruit but I'll take this any day over Prison inmates.
I skipped closer and closer to the festivities and when I arrived I seen all my friends I had went to high school with there were holding hands and singing Kumbayah around the camp ice.. Yes It was a giant block of ice situated on three wood logs.. I felt much more comforted here than I did at my grandmas. I took a deep breath of relief and I thought Maybe, this day is getting better. I joined hands and with Germany and Tokyo and began to sing with everyone else, but as soon as I Belched out my voice changed to an annoying high pitched squeal.. Similar to ringing in your ears.
Everyone turned toward me and gave me the death stare and I knew I had screwed up once again, they all walked in slow motion towards me saying the same familiar chant I had heard earlier, before anyone could reach me I awoke in a frantic sweaty rush in my bed.. My legs were no longer on fire and I felt slightly normal again. I noticed that my mom, a preacher, and several other family members were standing around me sobbing and chanting.. I said. "What's going on?" They informed me that I had been possessed by a spirit named Robert that liked to make people crazy by making there dreams seem similar to real life, only completely insane. They told me that I had been very lucky to be through such a traumatic experience and live to tell about it, without needing to be put in a psych ward. I turned to the preacher and said.
"I think were gonna need an oven and fast."
That's when they knew I was a goner.

Dead Acres, is down as an action strategy game on Steam, but for me it is merely just another Minecraft clone.
The game play is well; almost identical to Mine Craft; if any devs are reading this, please just stop making Minecraft clones.  You are left in a field which is about the size of your back garden and you have to build your camp up from scratch. The game play is just horribly boring and has been done so many times before. What makes this title even worse is that we have another over saturated genre included…zombies. Every night you have to defend your simple plot of land against zombies. There is no challenge what so ever in this as you have a gun with unlimited ammo, so there is nothing even remotely close to becoming difficult.
There is no tutorial in the game, meaning you have to work absolutely everything out for yourself, even though there isn’t much to learn, it would have been nice to know how to farm your crops from the start instead of me destroying them by accident from using the wrong tools.
Graphically, it is actually better looking than vanilla Minecraft (no mods), the colours are bright and pleasant to look at, but that’s about all this game has to offer. The game will run at your screens native resolution, so I was surprised to see I was in the game at 4k.
I have only been playing for about half an hour now and I am done. There is nothing in this game that makes me want to even load it up again. People may think I am being too harsh given that I got this game for free, but honestly the genre has been done over and over again and there is nothing new that can be added to this type of game now.  The game is still in early access but it seriously needs a lot of work for it even to be considered a try out even for fans of this genre.  I will give the developers some credit though, they are actively updating the game, but for me it’s a definite no unfortunately.

I am going to start out by saying that this game has an amazing concept, good gameplay and fun game mechanics. And The graphics are pretty basic, but good for what they are. It still needs some streamlining, but  Overall, this game is definately worth buying, especially considering that it will be updated and improved from here.
There are some issues i would like to go over to help the developer(s?) improve the game.
First of all, very occasionally (i think it happened to me about twice in almost 4 hours of gameplay) jack will simply not appear. And while we are on the issue of bugs i found that after i used the tractor about half the time i wouldn't find all of the food in my inventory when going to trade with jack. Closing and then re-opening trade with jack seemed to fix this. I didn't check in my inventory before going to trade though.
Second of all i understand that there are tools you can buy to collect natural resources (mining rock ect.) but even with the tractor i just couldn't find the time to do this with all the improving defences and whatnot to be done.
Third of all, i had some issues with the hammer. I bought it because i made some mistakes in my defence plan but i found that it just took to long to destroy objects. Especially if you've started building with stronger materials. So rather than help improve my defences i just wasted a bunch of time and then gave up on trying. So i think that it definately needs to destroy things faster.
Lastly, i think that the whole turret system could use some streamlining. Maybe it's just me but i found i had to fiddle around with them alot. Maybe you could do something to make the whole generator thing easier?
As for ideas of things to put in the game, i think it would be cool to see something like a slime shooter that shoots a huge spray of slime that slows down any zombie it hits, and traps with a limited number of uses would be cool too. Like a pit trap, landmines, fire trap ect.
And one more thing, i didn't do alot of testing for the shotgun but i found it to be pretty useless. I also just didn't use the grenade launcher at all because i heard that was useless too but i think thats going to be fixed. So yeah.
also, just something i wanted to share with you all, i saw a guide to the game but it turned out to be a russian sausage recipe with an english translation. So, thats pretty wierd.

To the moon is an idie game that wants to tell its story. Besides finding clues like in a point + click adventure and mini games, there is not a lot of gameplay. But gameplay is not why you play this. You play it for its story. And it's so good. So beautiful. So sad.
You play as 2 scientists, going into the memory of a dying man. He wants to die remembering how he got to the moon. Why he does not know. He just feels this is right. So you have to travel deeper and deeper into his memories to find out why he never did, and to plant a trigger somewhere in his life that lets him imagine and remember what could have been...
You can play through this game in one evening. It is well worth its money (2,50€ in steam sales) for the story alone, the characters, the music, the jokes and the feels. Also, the stargazing scene hit home with me. "I won't tell you my name, people make fun of it." was way too close to personal experiences...
But even though the game is not long, it will stay with you for a long time. It is that good.

I've only played a couple hours, but I'd like to give my first impressions of The Division. I don't think it's a bad game, it looks amazing, the cover system is great, and the plot is actually sort of interesting. My problem lies in the gunplay and RPG aspects of the game. For one thing, I absolutely despise the damage system in this game. I don't understand why enemies can just take bullets like a sponge. I know it's how RPGs of this nature work, but it doesn't mean I like it. On another note character customization in this is terrible. Other notable franchises like the elder scrolls and black desert online give layers upon layers of choice in appearance. The division lets you pick from a sex, 10 ♥♥♥♥♥♥ faces, and hair color. There are tattoos and warpaint too, but they leave a lot to be desired. Sometimes little customization can work in this sort of game, like the borderlands franchise, but unlike borderlands, the limited choices aren't colorful or entertaining. I'd like to lastly talk about difficulty. Tom Clancy games have always been one of the tougher household name games, but this one doesn't feel right. The difficulty is forced by poor mechanics, not complex gameplay. I'm no stranger to difficult games, I love Darksouls, Enter the Gungeon, Dragon Age, and loads of others, but the Division feels cheap in that you just have to grind, not play better. Please, fans of the game comment if I got something wrong, but for now I stand by my words.

I went into this game with high hopes of playing an MMO that had no intention of catering to console players in the future.  I went in wanting to play a necromancer with some strong elemental backup - fireballs and chains of lightning with an undead pet, what could be better than that?
Well, the idea of playing a necromancer quickly collapsed because the necromancy skills are a serious joke - a couple really of REALLY poor lifetaps with no disease or poison spells, no damage over time spells, no slows, nothing that really says NECROMANCER.  And the pets?  Give me a break.  They're the only pet in the game the decays over a (very short) time, so you have to recast the spell over and over.  Yes, I get it.  The pet is dead so it decays, so cute.  However, what's the advantage to having a necro pet that you have to recast over and over (using costly reagents, I might add)?  They're not stronger or faster or anything particularly special.
Not that you'll see other pet caster classes running around to make you jealous of their awesome, mind you.  Everyone in this game plays an archer - PVP strategies are often "let's get 6 or seven archers..."  A tank with a sword and board?  Good luck finding one.  They're all bow-kiting and claiming to tank with their bow.  Why not tank with a perfectly nice sword or axe or something?  Because game balance is terribly broken.  There's no such thing as a pure caster since the casters don't even get root until they've leveled up a bunch of other skills first (better take the Earth tree, that's where it's at whether you want the other Earth skills or not), the damage is a joke, and you wind up stabbing stuff in the face anyway.  When you see how badly you get ganked by archers, you pick up a bow.  Then surprise, you're playing another archer... like everyone else on the server.  They like to tout the ability to customize classes, but given the skills are so badly imbalanced there IS no other option to play.  I went in wanting to play a necro, and I am basically now playing a dirge from EQ2.  It passes the time, I guess, but this isn't much of an MMO.  It's more of an archery simulator.
Also, this game very much IS pay to win.  If you don't have expensive in game housing, you can't harvest tons of basic mats and have a public vendor to gadge off of other players - you're stuck killing absolutely MILES of wolves in order to harvest a single cotton plant otherwise out in the wilderness, and then stuck with the 20% public vendor fee.  Don't even get me started on how your armor's max durability DEGRADES over time and you have to buy new armor from one of these well-heeled, landed crafters who already had miles of money already.  If you don't have housing, forget it.

I find that the comments below regarding whether this game is a "cash grab" to be exactly true.  In the recent R45 post mortem, the devs were saying that "80% of development comes with the last 20% of time" more or less, and I find that to be frightening.  There has been zero effort the last several releases to balance classes, introduce more mobs and fix mechanics, and get their quest system straightened out.  I have officially had it with SoTA, as I am stuck on a bugged quest that is core to the game and to story progression (the Path of Truth, if anyone cares.)  I am sharing a thread with other players on Shroud's forum that are having the exact same problem, and not a ghost of help or a comment from the dev team other than "gee that's weird" - no ticket number or a comment saying they will look into it.  This is a core and key quest, hopelessly bugged and with the game 20% to release!
So, Shroud of the Avatar has:
*poorly thought out skill mechanics - this is why there are some many freakin' archers
*poor class balance - and this is why there are no dedicated casters
*extremely small and repetitive zones
*huge amounts of grinding - first you must gain your XP in a pool, then use all of your skills a second time to spend the XP you gained.  Double the effort for half of the fun!  On the plus side, I know where every training dummy in the world is.  It's really a great MMO experience when I log in, auto attack a dummy, then walk away and do laundry.
*extremely punitive crafting system
*hopelessly bugged quests that give little in terms of reward
*zero choice except to run the gauntlet of the crafting system yourself, or pay $$$ to a crafter to make you something.  A crappy +5 sword with only 25 durability that you have repair constantly will run you around five grand in gold.  A low level character (say level 40) will be killing mobs that drop 12-25 gp each or so, by means of comparison.  The answer, by the way, is to farm rares and sell them to the same crafters that are ridiculously gouging you.
*Don't expect to see ANY gear drop until you are killing high level mobs, and even so that is an Extremely Rare Event.  Quests don't reward gear either, so either you run around naked, buy truly crappy vendor armor, or start saving little man...
*unless you have VERY expensive in game housing (like real money expensive) you will basically be unable to compete with other crafters, if you do choose to craft.  Here is a description of how to grow 12 THOUSAND cotton a day if you have in game housing:
How is a "vagabond Avatar" supposed to keep up with that?  Answer:  you can't.
*Semi-responsive mechanics - A lot of basic mechanics don't work, even though they appear that they should.  For example, I can stun trolls.  There is a 50% shot that they will slide across the ground with their stun animation in progress while still "running" towards and attacking other players.  This is not a stunned mob.  The other 50% of the time, the troll drops to his knees for a second before getting up and chasing the archers.  That is a stunned mob.  Some please explain this to Portalarium.
*There's no aggro management, really, since people who want to beat on things with swords cannot match the damage output even remotely of someone with a bow (casters can't, either... for some reason, a high speed sharp stick will eternally do more damage than a **lightning strike.**)  So if you can stand at range and shoot, you're in good shape.  If you want to beat on things directly, start making potions of wolf speed because you're going to be chasing aggro bounce in circles from all the kiting archers.  This is why I am so irritated by stun failing half of the time.  If this doesn't annoy you, that's great.  If you want to play a tank that dances a mob while other people kill it, you're outta luck (or a rogue type that backstabs... run, Forrest, run!)
*Aggravating and poorly conceived map layout - Most of the zones are little tiny foxholes accessed by a larger overland map.  That map is "gated" by passes that you MUST fight through, although some of the passes have a shorter "bypass route" that you only have to kill five or six things to get through.  To be fair, some of the passes also have a teleporter mage that can let you skip the whole thing - at three thousand gold pieces per round trip.
The issue with this is that in order to reach several Tier 1-4 difficulty zones, you have to go through Tier 5 passes!  Suppose you're level fifteen.  The mobs in there are level 60.  You're GOING to die - and you lose XP every time that you do, you poor sucker.  This is criminally stupid game design.
But if none of these things bother you, feel free to buy the land that your house sits on (real cash money, cheapest is 85 bucks, and easily runs THOUSANDS... and you still have to pay in game taxes) and THEN buy the house for another couple hundred bucks.  Then you can craft like a champ and dominate the game, too - but you paid to win.  I suppose that's also fine, but I can't imagine this game having any longevity for it, especially with the fundamental and serious flaws in the game's design.

So far the Pro's and Con's from a Long time UO Veteran
Crafting is a mixed bag,
- The RNG with exeptional results is good
- The Masterworking is cool
- The enchanting is decent...
- The Material need to make a piece of gear is high
- The ability to collect crafting material is rough
- Can a crafter be a true crafter with no combat skill like UO, NOPE
- NPC Item value is off which then snowballs into most crafted gear haveing little value if its not exceptional...
The Sandbox
- Beautiful
- Towns are breathtaking, huge and feel like true citys that pretty much make any city in any MMO look detailess and small....
- The Interaction with NPC's is amazing, the ability to have so many varied conversations without repeating the same answers shows alot of attention to detail...
- Loading screens galore and are a huge disappointment, what sandbox has loading screens?!?
- Running the gauntlet, the map is divided up into regions and there are always places you have too dodge extremely high level mobs to go from point a to point b, with nearly no way to avoid it!
Development effort
- Its extremely apparent on a daily basis that this Development team is working on Overdrive accomplishing alot, at a very fast pace!
- Its also apparent that they at times they seem obstinant and almost "Anti" Ultima Online, when much of the game could be dramatically improved bye simple bringing it closer to the UO experience...
Highlights!
Player Housing (Albiet very expensive and based in real world currency)
VENDORS - This one feature is what locks me into the game its so wonderful to be able to run an online business again, where your not just having to undercut or be undercut on an Auction House.
Commujnity - Havent seen an online community this good since Ultima online pre trammel...
***My Opinion***
As a UO vet, there are two must have UO features this game needs to implement, infact I think they are MUST have features that could take this game to the next level....
Rune's and Runebooks - would take this game and its economy to a new level.... mark a rune to your favorite vendor!
Treasure Hunting - This was a feature that really helped set UO above all others and this game needs it....
And Lastly!!!
While I greatly appreciate the amazing story content and effort they have put into NPC dialogues I would love too see less game emphasis on Questing. As a Sandbox player I have an imagination and Quests have always been more of a turn off then a turn on for me.... At the moment this game feels VERY QUEST heavy!!!
Infact this game feels more like a spiritual successor to what Elder Scrolls Online SHOULD have been and not but the UO Successor should be....
Overall the game is a strong 7.5 /10
- I want to play it every day
- At the same time I also know it hasnt hooked me like SWG or UO did...
- Butt its better then any other MMO I have played in YEARS....

I have one word to describe this game: ADDICTIVE!
As I write this review, I am exactly 100 minutes into the game, and this was all in one sitting. I thought I would stick around for half an hour, but i just got so involved straight away! There are so many features, and considering it is in early access I really want to see where it goes.
The main way to describe the game would probably be a first person zombie shooter farming sim tower defense. At least, that's what i've got from it so far. The game just seems to have a perfect balance, meaning you feel like you have lived through hell when you survive a night. This is a true survival game. You always seem to have just enough money to build a decent wall, only to have it torn down by some zombie that wants your brain. It requires strategy, as you need to even your budget out between replacing plants that will inevitably have been devoured and destroyed by zeds at some point in the night. It is a great game.
The art style is nice too. Like lots of games, they have gone for the blocky, Minecraft-esque aesthetic, but instead of being a carbon copy like other titles, they have created a unique environment of play. The days feel warm and bright in stark contrast to the nights which are dark and deadly. The zombies may not look intimidating from a distance, but when they are tearing at your flesh and your base is overrun, you learn to fear them pretty quick.
Overall, the game is a good challenge and very enjoyable and addictive. I can't wait to see how the developers add to it in the future.

Disappointing.
I looked at the metascore and the reviews, and I was expecting to be wowed.   I'd give it a 6, maybe 7/10.
I'll be honest, it can be easy to waste away hours in this game, but not because the game is particularly 'exciting', but because ... that's just the time the development / research tech trees.
You can strategize on what worlds to colonize and how to build them up (although it's pretty shallow), and what types of strengths you want to give your ships once you've researched far enough into the tech tree, but the core element that let me down was where you actually battled another race/ faction.   There's no input from you, as a player, as to how that battle will go.  If your ship is powerful enough, you can send a single ship to take out several, if not dozens of enemy craft.
No skill, no positioning, no planning of attacks like there might be in ROME or Age of Wonders II.   Heck, I would say that games that are over 10 years old (like RoN or AOE) are better at the battles then this game is.
Also, let's talk about diplomacy - the game tries, but the races/ characters are pretty one-dimensional.
I might play this game again every now and then, but I'm disappointed.   Dont buy this game unless it's on a sale of 75% off regular price or something.

Pros: Huge variety of customization options. AI seems to be very well balanced, and the dialogue is definitely awesome. Diplomacy is insanely well done.
Cons: If you don't do the tutorial, you will be lost, very lost, and will make a review of this game saying it's horrible after 0.3 hours played. This is the best buy I've made all year long. There's so much customization that every game you start feels new and fresh. I'm always finding something I could do better or another strategy that could be more fun to play around with that the replayability of this game just feels endless. It's addicting. You find yourself spending quite a bit of time just messing with how your ship looks before you even start popping on the components. I've made a Star Trek NCC-1701 d clone for my flagship because I could. I've also made x-wings and tie fighters just goofing around. The fact that ship building is so easy to do makes it a major point in my gameplay. The turn-based gameplay gives you a chance when you are starting off to really take your time to understand the basic mechanics of the game and start putting some forethought into every move you make.
I've played a bunch of other space sims/strategy games, Sid Mier's Civs, the older X games, AOE, etc. I love sims, space games, strategy, and turn-based combat. Galactic Civs II has thrown just about everything I love into one game. This game has been my all time favorite so far. If you get it on sale, fine. If you get it on Humble Bundle, fine. Just get this game if you like Strategy games.
You won't regret it.
Also, if the new Galactic Civs III is anything like this one, it will be my next purchase.

I have been playing Shroud since before it came onto Steam, and play it still, my played hours above are somewhat a testament to that.    I am also an early backer of the game.   The game certainly has its share of good and bad points, but as a whole, it is certainly something easily worth its price tag for the hours of enjoyment you can get out of it.
So, wall of text incoming - my honest assessment of the game after nearly 3400 hours in.
First, forget about Ultima.  This isn’t Ultima Sequel in any way shape or form.  There will be a few familiar names and places, but that’s the extent of it.   A lot of the negativity around this game is from former Ultima players who want this to be Ultima reborn.  It isn’t, and it isn’t meant to be.
Second, don’t be put off by early access.  Sure, there’s some quirks, but the game is more stable than quite a few “final product” games out there.  We’ve been persistent for nearly a year, for all practical purposes, the game is live now, new content and tweaks come every month, and the game is completely playable.   No, it doesn’t have the fantastic visuals of some of the latest and greatest 2017 titles, but it is suitably appealing.
The Bad:
Quests/Story
The Story and quest system is awkward.  Its gotten better, but its still awkward, and pick-the-keyword style npc interaction.  I wouldn’t pick this up just for the story or single player aspect, its pretty thin.   The main quest arc can be done in about 12 hours total, but you’ll need to spend a lot of time – months probably – levelling and gearing your character up to be able to do it.
Crafting/Economy
The random number generator is unnecessarily cruel, success percentages far too low at grandmaster level and the amount of materials needed to make a single suit of gear is absolutely staggering – expect 40-50 hours of mining to make a single set of middle-tier armor, with no guarantees of success (things have a chance to break crafting) and little customizability (stat bonuses are randomized).    The economy is regulated by standardized npc pricing (cash sinks), a myriad of essential cash sink items the player needs to function (food, scrolls, repair kits, reagents, crafting fuels) most of which must be bought from the ‘game’ or the materials to make them are bought from the ‘game’ in the form of cash sinks.  Raw materials sell for considerably more than crafted goods, in all cases, except perhaps labor intensive consumables.  For this reason most people make their own things, or get friends to make things in exchange for materials, and avoid the clunky “market” system.  Its “put a vendor at your house” style, or, list on a public vendor, nearly all of which are empty except the one in Owl’s Head, and you pay 20% commission to list on it, whether your item sells or not.  Don’t play this if you want a sensible economic system.  To further exacerbate this, the game embraces real-cash markets, and you can buy anything – high end gear, even pay someone to level your character – with cash.  While the game itself doesn’t sell anything “pay to win”, someone who drops a few grand is going to be leaps and bounds further along than someone who plays it properly.
The ”Risk vs. Reward” Fallacy
Everything you do in this game costs you either in-game money or time, for very little return.  Often its grinding against entropy, when spending hours killing things and selling the loot doesn’t even reimburse you for the consumables you need to travel, eat, repair your gear, cast spells, etc.   Any lucrative means of experience or cash that players find (not exploitative, just, making the best of what’s there) is quickly stamped out and Developer Chris Spears (“Atos”) has even admitted on his blog and on previous telethons that he looks to see which zones players are spending time in, and systematically nerfs them.   That being said, you feel a sense of achievement when you look at your character and see how far you’ve come.   However, then the game senselessly punishes you more, the more you play it – high level characters can lose days or even weeks of experience gain due to a single death (another brilliant Chris Spears idea).   The reality is if Shroud wants to compete in the modern market, it needs to let go of some of its cherished old school punishment systems and let players actually play the game, instead of spending all their online time grinding against the cash sinks, the property tax, the death tax, and so on.
I am hopeful that this will change, we’ve already seen the fist unclench a bit regarding convenience features (such as maps) which were intentionally left out of the game early on for realism’s sake now being integrated, and the quaint, nostalgic but frustratingly clunky UI has been slowly improved to more modern standards release after release.    I expect that in order to try and appeal to and retain a customer base they will realize that players want to make progress, and not constantly be set back or turn the game into a second job where they must constantly work just to maintain status quo.
So all of that stuff is bad.  Why the recommendation?
The Good:
First, there are a lot of features in this game.  There’s a truly unique classless skill system.    You can level anything – adventuring or tradeskill wise – with no artificial limits only the limit of your own willingness to grind out the xp for it.   You can go to any zone, even if you have no business being there.
Crafting is deep and involved, sadly, you must also be a capable adventurer if you expect to craft, it isn’t standalone, but there are hundreds upon hundreds of things you can make.  Some of the best gear is craftable, except for ‘artifacts’ which are arguably best in slot for many builds, but crafting is still important and integral to the game.  Its plagued by a random bonuses system and high breakage percentages even at grandmaster, and you’ll never make any money crafting in the game (at least, not what you’d make selling raw materials) but if you like crafting for crafting’s sake, there is crafting aplenty here.
The community is for the most part, stellar.  Community events, roleplaying, etc. are frequent, and I expect many of the friends I’ve made in Sota are friends for life.
The world is immense, and this is only a small piece of what is to come.
The bottom line is, you need to ask yourself why you play these sorts of games to decide if Shroud of the Avatar is for you.   If you want to compete against other people, and have to be the best, then …maybe it isn’t, unless you either want to spend money or you can play 20 hours a day while mainlining caffeine.   If you’re a minmaxer hardcore gamer, you will tire of Shroud fast.
If you want a living world in which to roleplay, meet new people, craft shiny things, kill things and take their stuff, be part of a community, grow crops, cook, have and decorate a house or even a town, then – yeah, give it a try.     I have played 3400 hours of this game and I expect less than a thousand of that has been in combat scenes.  I’m usually hanging around in town, writing in-game books, crafting, playing instruments with other players, decorating stuff, tending my garden, messing about taming pets, participating in community events, etc.    There is plenty to do, but this is absolutely NOT a “grind to the cap then pvp” type game, that’s not what its meant to be, and people who want it to be such will always be disappointed.  That’s not the point.  If you approach this as a living world in which to explore and make your mark, you can find plenty of enjoyment in it.

Questing is intentionally unlike that of other MMOs, in that you don't run up to an NPC with an exclamation point over his head, murder ten boars, and get a pair of pants, some gold and xp. Instead, it's more like much older rpgs (like the original wasteland), where you have a conversation with an NPC, learn a keyword, and use that keyword on another NPC. Maybe one will send you out to a swamp to reclaim an item from a monster, or recover an item from an abandoned house in a swamp. You tend to do fewer quests, with bigger rewards.
The other big difference with this game is the way experience is obtained. Your character has an "experience pool", and then skills are trained through use. If the pool has plenty of experience, your character develops skills quickly, and if the pool is empty the character develops much more slowly. There are two pools, one is for crafting (a huge component of this game) and the other is for combat (weapon/armor skills, magic etc).

This is the best platforming experience I've ever had.
There's a lot in this game that builds towards that verdict. Firstly, the controls, movement, and combat are tight. Movement is easy and intuitive. At just the right difficulty, you finish each part with a sense of accomplishment. It's not a slow platformer, you feel like you're going places and this gives you a sense of freedom that you don't get in a lot of games.
The story  is a coming of age story, there is loss of innocence. It's not complex, but it's beautiful. It's childish in some respects, but it deals with good and evil in a very mature way. You get a feeling of sadness when you play this game, but it's a good feeling that I think people should experience in games.
The visuals and audio are beyond anything I've ever played. Animations are fluid to the point where it's mesmerizing just to watch Ori hopping through the world. The backgrounds look hand painted and beautiful. The music kicks in at just the right times and the effects are sharp and spot on.
It's Super Meat Boy in its gameplay, The Legend of Zelda in its story, and it sets a new stardard when it comes to visual design and audio.
This is an experience that you should have.

No Man's Sky is a game that was tragically overhyped both by its community and its developers. It raised expectiations so high that it could never have fulfilled them all. To many it was a major disappointment, frustratingly grindy and simplistic. It is out of the question that the conduct of the developers was not okay. I assume that in their desire to keep as much of the game wrapped in mystery they ended up promising too much by simply not denying enough. And yes, there were some features promised that were not delivered, for example "meeting other players".
It is unfortunate that this is what many will remember the game for, because in actuality, it is a very special game - I would even call it a true gem. However, even now that the hype has utterly died, you should really ask yourself wheter or not this game is something that may appeal to you.
This is still difficult because trying to get reasonably objective reviews is difficult - many let their views of the game be clouded by all the disappointment, while others have still not given up on the fanboi-ism and defend the game and its flaws without critical thought. The thing is - objective reviews won't actually help you that much. Wheter or not you like this game is impossible for anyone but yourself to predict:
Wheter or not this game appeals to you probably won't depend on its graphics or sound or technology or story or gameplay, really.
I think it will appeal to you if you love exploration.
If you like to take your time,
marvel at the litte differences (because there are not many huge ones),
if you appreciate the beautiful vista in front of you RIGHT NOW,
spend a few seconds to think of a cool name for every discovery,
if you see the gameplay as a means to an end - not victory, not progress, but as a means to enable more unique experiences.
Or, to put it otherwise:
If you are a goal-driven gamer, or someone who values good gameplay, this game - at its core - will probably not be the game for you. If you play it in that way, you will be frustrated by the grind, and if you power through it, it will leave you deeply dissatisfied. You will only see the frustrating search for that one particular thing you need to progress, when really progress is pointless. Nothing ever fundamentally changes. The gameplay progression is entirely superficial, because there really is no progression in this game. Sure, your inventory becomes larger and your shields stronger, but if the point of the game is to get to the end, you dont need any of this. The game doesn't become more challenging and it doesn't reward you for playing well. It is not that type of game.
I think the point of the game is to experience it. And I do really think that a good way is to do it in a zen-like manner: Live in the moment. Appreciate that the things you see no one else has seen, and probably no one else ever will. Treat every discovery as just that, a discovery. This game is also pretty short - 12 levels total - the same 12 levels over and over. No random dungeon design. Oh look, harder skill levels - woot.
All in all I'd give this game a solid 7.5/10

The thing I am unhappy with is the fact that WB is allowed to randomly change the game whenever the ♥♥♥♥ they want. The next patch could totally break the game or make it crappy. As it stands right now the game is awesome - but who knows what the next patch will bring. If you're ok with your game just changing overnight without anywarning you'd probably like this game, but the above fact is the exact reason why I can't reccomend it. This game has quickly been climbing the ranks of my most-played Steam games, and it’s just reached 6th place.  I wouldn’t be surprised if it takes 1st, given enough time.  One of the complaints about this game is its length, and really, its length is potentially endless, considering its high replay value.  If you’re bored with the game after completing the 12 levels with one character and one difficulty setting, then yes, it’s a short game.  However, if you’re like me, and you love playing this game, then you’ll want to play the levels with each of the 4 (or 5) characters, on multiple difficulty settings.  Then you’ll want to play the coliseum challenges with all of the characters.  Then you’ll want to do it all over again with your friend, then again with your other friend, etc.  All of the characters play completely differently, so there’s definitely motivation to try them all.
I compare this game to Super Smash Bros.  The story mode is simple, linear, and short, but it’s fun to play over and over again, with different characters, and different difficulty settings, and it’s always fun to play with friends.  It never gets old.  Anytime you have a spare half-hour, you can pick up this game and have fun playing a level.  It’s a really polished game in every category (graphics, music, sound effects, voice acting, gameplay, etc.), it’s easy to pick up, and it’s fun.  What more do you want?
Keep in mind that I haven’t played the original Gauntlet, only Gauntlet: Dark Legacy.  After playing this, I have little interest in ever playing Dark Legacy again.

Reus is a nice and detailed mix of rts and life simulation, following in the footsteps of classical god games.
TL&DR: This is a great game, tons of fun, easy to learn (suitable tutorial), hard to master, and (if you are into such things) it offers a very complex system of interdependencies (WARNING: possible time sink alert).
The player takes control of four giants (water, forest, mountain, swamp), each of which has a different set of abilities that can be used to terraform the world, as well as to create and to improve resources. The latter is achieved by the application of upgradable 'aspects'. Depending on the different combinations of resources and aspects, most resource-types can be developed into new ones with different attributes.
The main feature of the game is the symbiosis system: every single resource-type provides a special synergy with specific others (e.g. res. A provides 'some bonus' - if 'next to / in range of / etc.' res. B). The proper use of these symbioses is key to progression and the development of advanced settlements.
There are some more game mechanics, adding a little more complexity.
The art (sprites etc.) is good-looking, the music is relaxing and enjoyable, although sometimes repetitive (few number of tracks).
Only negative point:
Translations for different localizations (known: Ger., rarely Eng.) contain few errors / inaccuracies that may lead to misinterpretations of requirements (e.g. for simbioses). According to the developers, this is unlikely to be fixed by an official patch.
