It's an overall excellent game. It has its quirks, but it's a very good experience and the modding community alone can be a reason to buy this game.
It's different than most other RPGs and open-world games though, you probably either like it or you don't, but it's worth a try.
I recommend you to buy the legendary edition for full experience and for full modding potential, plus you also get Skyrim SE which in itself is nothing extraordinary, but it has excellent modding potential. You can probably expect a new rush in the modding scene soon. If you don't know why you should use mods then keep reading.
The game is usually *cheap*; you can get it for €7-8. Bethesda for some reason got the price up because of the new Special Edition.
Longer stuff here:
I have been a fan of TES for a long-time. I started playing the TES series with TES IV: Oblivion. Morrowind never really got me for some reason.
However I'll try to write a review here without comparing this game to its predecessors.
PROS:
Usually cheap, you can get the legendary edition for €7-8. Look out for sales (spring, Christmas)
Mods!!!
The engine, the technology behind it.
Big open-world game.
Open-world also means that almost everything is accessible inside cities too. Basically you can visit almost every building in the game.
Almost simulation-tier mechanics regarding NPC behavior in the game. Most NPCs have their own daily routine.
Interesting lore.
Fun
Lot of quests and stuff to do.
It's a TES game which means it's unique in a way like none other.
Todd "Never Lying" Howard (Ok, this point is a joke.)
Excellent community support. Mods include bugfixes.
Unofficial Patch
Honestly you can see some points are very similar, but I did that on purpose to emphasize some stuff.
The engine, the technology behind the game receives a lot of negative opinions, but honestly it gets the job done in a way which allows for very good opportunities modding- and gameplay-wise. For example it's pretty easy after a modder made a weapon to actually have the NPCs inside the game treat it as a weapon, evaluate its stats, etc. NPCs can travel through the entire map without constraints and a modder can really easily accomplish something like that.
The modding community is awesome. Many excellent mods are made like gameplay overhauls (magic, combat, ai, etc overhauls), bugfixes, new games (yes, totally new games. see Enderal), companions with professional voice acting and all kinds of cool stuff.
One of the three essential mods I would like to mention are SKSE, SkyUI and The Unofficial Skyrim Patch (a combined one exists for the legendary edition). SkyUI gives the game a nice UI, meanwhile the unofficial patch fixes thousands of bugs!!! SKSE provides functions for mods to use and some bugfixes. There is another mod called bugfixed I would recommend which fixes some bugs inside the game engine. I recommend installing them for a proper vanilla experience.
***Generally it's recommended to familiarize yourself with the modding scene. It will keep you from having difficulties later down the road regardless whether you want bugfixes or a whole new game by applying 200 mods.***
CONS:
Modders will fix it philosophy. Bethesda can release very buggy games due to numerous reasons I won't discuss here, but this can cause problems to new players. Installing the unofficial patch is always *necessary*.
Some parts of the game; quests, guilds can be a bit shallow. However the amount of content included and overhaul mods can easily make up for it.
It's quite easy to become very powerful and "break" the game, but being very powerful can be great fun too. The game has been balanced for a more casual market. This might be a big no for some people, but mods exist to balance it in the way you want it. From hardcore overhauls like Requiem which turn it into a more classical RPG to handpicked overhaul mods working together, you can do whatever you want to do. Putting various separate overhauls (magic, combat, AI, perks, stealth, etc.) on your game each focusing on a different aspect allows you to personalize your experience in whatever way you want to.
Stupid AI. The default AI can be pretty stupid.
Mage characters are a lot weaker than warriors with the same amount of time invested.
Not that challenging depending on playstyle.
The lore in this one compared to its predecessors isn’t that dominant.
To give a clearer picture I have to say this: depending on what you do you can get pretty weak in the game. Most of the game breaking is caused by experienced players or by players who employ a more tactical playstyle. However most people sooner or later will feel that the game (combat) is weaker and they need more challenge.
Summary:
I recommend this game.
Despite its flaws this game is a very enjoyable experience and you still have things to do after 100 hours of gameplay.
The depth and possibilities in the game compare to no other games on the market, except its predecessors. It's like living a whole other life. No please don't compare it to Witcher they are quite different games for many reasons.
Mods provide bugfixes for vanilla players and interesting new stuff for players looking for something different or harder. You can even turn it into a survival simulator where you need to eat, drink, sleep and keep warm. The potential is endless. The graphics can be enhanced using ENB.

I remember playing the original Bloons Tower Defense in middle school computer classes! I've played each of the games as they've come out throughout the years, but I'll try to write this review without my nostalgia glasses on.
This game is a really cute concept about little monkeys popping balloons with darts before they reach the end of a map. There are several tower types, each with unique attributes and perk branches that leave you with dozens of strategies to try out. The main strategic aspect of this game comes from map design rather than balloon type differences by level. My main complaint with this game is that no matter what map you play on, the balloon output will be exactly the same by level. Camo balloons always comes on round 24, blimps on 46, etc. That being said, you can't just use the same strategy every time because the maps vary so much.
There is a free online flash version of this game, but this version updates more frequently and has a few features, game types, and towers unavailable elsewhere. Granted, those features aren't necessarily worth $10 in my opinion. The only feature the online version has that this one doesn't is a chat function in co-op, which I feel needs to be added. I definitely don't regret my purchase, I really enjoy this game, but I would recommend waiting until this game is on sale if you're interested in buying it.

"SotA does not stop existing at the periphery of its landmass, either. The game is being developed with active contributions from its players, and participation by the dev team in the player community. Much like the early days of Minecraft - when Notch would field questions himself and acted as a pillar of the community - "Lord British" and the surprisingly small dev team are known to make appearances.
Perhaps most importantly, it defiantly ignores the World of Warcraft mold. Those of us who have been MMO players since the term was coined will recall online worlds being less like theme parks and more like frontiers - rather than a carefully-curated series of events and vistas, we got a rough, unsettled land to explore without a tour guide. Rather than a painstakingly-balanced character progression system, we got raw fantasy fiction cut up into ability-sized chunks to swing at our enemies. There were no "duty finders" or "group finder" queues, because the biggest theme of the MMO - the most important part of the genre, in fact - was socializing."

I wanted to recommend it, but man does this game have issues...
The Good:
-If you REALLY want to know what happens next in the FEAR storyline, this is as much a FEAR story as any.
-The aesthetic is strong, and I like the better use of environmental details than from previous games.
The Bad:
-The shooting is more of a nightmare than any jump scare this game could offer. HORRIBLE aim acceleration, where when I try aiming slow, it almost doesn't move at all, and any small jerk in movement ramps the aim 1000mi an hour making it near impossible to be accurate and fluid. Absolutely abysmal..
-Stupid enemy types, like the addition of zombie-like suicide bombing hoodlems that come at you at the turn of every corner.
-Infuriating difficulty spikes. The first 2 games had managable, mostly decently balanced difficulty throughout, but in this game... One second you're blowing fools up left and right in a mech, literally 10 seconds later, I'm forced out of the mech and surrounded by 20 dudes all gunning me down before I can even activate bullet-time.
-Feels way less *scary* this time around, and far more like some sort of supernatural thriller. This isn't inherently a bad thing, but for the pace of the last few games in the series, it seems like a departure I'm not sure I think was a best fit for the game. It just doesn't fill me with any sense of dread or..............fear........ like the other games did. It's mostly just cool looking set pieces and suicide bombing gang rats...

So... yeah.  To The Moon doesn't need my positive review, really.  It's already got a ton of praise, all well-deserved.  It's essentially an interactive novel, but a very good one.  What puzzles there are, either encourage you to explore, or distract you from making certain connections too soon.  Would easily make a great movie.  Gorgeous soundtrack that is now part of my background music at work.
But here's the part I want to point out.  There are at least 5 different spots in the story that are known to make various people cry, and each spot makes you cry for a different reason. You're the type to cry at weddings?  There's a spot for that.  You only cry at tragedies?  Yup.  Chances are good that if you have a soul, at least one of the 5 will get you.
The point is, this game doesn't rely on the same emotional trick over and over to get you. It's an emotional roller coaster, if the track was designed by the inmates of an insane asylum.  It pokes and prods you until you're tender and weak, covers your head with a bag of delightful dialog, and then it beats you mercilessly with feelings.  And that's before we even get into the two DLC's.
You know what?  Just buy the thing and play it.  On sale, it's like, less than a coffee.  Start it up, screw around with it, and before you know it, you'll be marveling over that beautiful ending.

The interactions are very straight forward and logical (what did you expect in a robot world ;) ).  I would have loved a bit a free way though with exploration as this game obviously could have provided this.  As the character we play is a "scavenger" of sorts, it would have been nice to have been able to roam around the locations and find some useful parts or artifacts and have him "tinker" a bit with them in his house.
I have had one BIG pet peeve with this game though, being its controls...Yep, WASD is not for everyone (especially not on an azerty keyboard) as it is counter intuitive and I found no way to change this.    Nore did I find a way to play it with a game control pad (as it does look like it was designed for such devises). Keybinding should be a mandatory option to change in any game.
But aside from the above pet peeve and linear storyline, it's still an entertaining 7 hours of gaming.

Generally speaking, New Vegas is a better FO3 than FO3 itself.

Probably the best option is the first, so start with Fo3, enjoy a relatively short playthrough, and then dive into NV.
Enjoy!

EBF4 is a great turn based RPG for people who are into gameplay over graphics.  The game's plot and dialogue are mostly there to be humorous.  Don't expect to see some intricate story or a bunch of character development.  The game's biggest strength lies in its deep combat mechanics.  The music is also pretty good as well.
The game starts with you in the first town and in control of the new main character for this game.  You'll eventually find the 3 other characters.  The map for the game takes place on a 10x10 grid.  The game consists of 3 towns, 5 main environments, a side environment, and a bonus environment that takes place off the grid called battle mountain.  You'll spend most of the game venturing through these areas killing enemies, fighting bosses, opening chests, and getting quests.  Each of the three towns contains a weapon/armor shop, forgeable item shop, and a health/status item shop.  Main environments contain enemies (all viewable) on a main path to that environment's boss that you will have to kill to get to it.  Once killed, these enemies stay dead forever.  Enemies off the main path usually guard chests and are optional to fight and respawn upon going to a new environment.  The side environment contains an optional boss and some items.  The battle mountain is a bonus area which contains all the enemies throughout the game, upgraded versions of each of the game's main bosses, and some unique bosses.  You get no exp/gold going through this area but do get item drops and access to unique equipment/skills.  All environments contain 1 or more quick travel points, so getting around quickly usually isn't an issue.  The game autosaves on every screen transition and can be saved manually any time outside of battle.
Each of the game's 4 characters have access to their own unique set of skills.  You'll be able to upgrade these throughout the game but unlike EBF3, you'll be unable to fully upgrade every skill by the endgame unless you feel like grinding, so you need to choose wisely when upgrading.  New to this game are equipable skills.  You'll find new skills (including limit breaks) throughout the game that 2-4 of the characters will be able to learn.  Once you attach that skill to a character, only that character will be able to use it unless you choose to have that character forget the skill (wasting spent skill points).  This allows you to give characters spell types that they normally don't have access to.  Each character can equip a weapon, armor, a hat, and 3 badges.  All equipment can be leveled up by forging.  Equipment works in a unique way.  Instead of giving simple stat upgrades, such as +30 attack, they instead give bonus multipliers to a character's base stats, such as multiplying health by 1.1, attack by 1.15, etc.  Each equipment gives different multipliers to different stats as well as different elemental/status defenses, and many of them have unique abilities attached to them such as automatically casting revive or dropping mammoths on your enemies.  This means that even your starting equipment can be just as viable to have on as something you find towards the end of the game.  What you want to equip will be based on what elements enemies are weak against, what elements/statuses you want to buff yourself against, what stats you want to buff, and what special abilities you like.  Badges are useful in covering weaknesses that your normal equipment didn't cover.  They do things such as give elemental/status resistances, special abilities, or buff stats.
The game has 4 difficulty settings that you're free to switch between throughout the game without any penalty.  I only played on epic difficulty (the hardest one) and I found the game to be very fair on it.  There was no point throughout the game where I had to grind levels at all to continue on, though I did have to skip 2 of the optional minibosses and come back to fight them later.  Combat with the regular enemies feels just right and the bosses are incredibly satisfying to beat, especially the more difficult upgraded versions on battle mountain and the final boss.  I got my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me several times, but changing up my equipment/strategy/tactics was enough to overcome any failures.  The only time I might recommend switching difficulties is when fighting the regular enemies on battle mountain.  These fights usually come in waves of 8-10 whereas normal battles are usually 1-3 waves.  I stayed on Epic throughout and some of those regular battles on battle mountain can take anywhere from 20-40 minutes to complete.  If you ever do feel a need to grind, you can always switch the difficulty to easy as enemies give the same XP no matter which difficulty you play on.
As for combat, there are plenty of enemies types and plenty of variations on those types, each feeling pretty different.  There are 10 elemental types and 12 status effects, so you can never cover everything.  Status effects and buffs/debuffs matter alot.  Bosses require both tactical and strategic planning.  You'll often find yourself in situations where you have to make meaningful decisions rather than just spamming the same moves over and over every round.  Combat animations are quick, so outside of limit breaks, you're not sitting around for 10 seconds watching characters cast spells or watching enemies dance around for no reason.  Characters can be swapped in/out during combat.  Only 3 of your 4 characters can fight at once.  I  wasn't sure I was going to like this as I thought it meant someone was going to get left out, but I grew to enjoy it.  All the characters are useful, so you will switch characters in and out based on various things.
I really don't have much of anything to complain about.  My biggest issues were occasional slowdown in some battles and I had the game freeze up twice, once halfway through the final boss which was real lemon timing.  Also, the spacesuit armor is pretty good but its special power can be annoying.  It calls in 'Scanbot' to scan enemies during battle and can activate multiple times over the course of a battle.  Once you've scanned an enemy, you retain its info permanently, so when it does it multiple times it's just wasting your time.
A great RPG, wish more of them were like this.

I am a long time Ultima Fan.  I played and finished all of the Ultima games.  My favorite Ultima was Ultima 5, 6 and 8.  I played Ultima Online up until Richard and EA parted ways.  I have not had an MMO grab me like UO did.
I was very excited to hear Richard Garriot was making a new Ultima type game.  This game has a lot of Ultima 9 characteristics.  It does feel like an Ultima. I am going to talk about the stuff I like about it first.
#1 The setting is absolutely great. It feels like an ultima game.
#2 The music reminds me a lot of Ultima 7.
#3 I love the classless system.
Here are the things I do not like.
#1 The combat system is beyond dull in my opinion.  I do not like the deck system.  I am told you can go without it.  I haven't tried doing that
#2 The graphic fidelity doesn't match AAA studios, but it doesn't have an AAA budget.
#3 The game is prerelease.  There are a lot of bugs and such. I am writing this only because I am very excited to play the final build.
You might be asking why I posted a recommend.  I did because the game is in great condition for being pre release.  There is a lot of content.  I love how I can make the character I want.  If you are looking for a graphically rough RPG you can play online with your friends, give this game a shot.

Worth a shot if you willing to wait patiently for the engine optimizations (Unity must do much better than that about performance and visuals,lots of popular mobile games using it, as example FF Mobius ), big fixes and more.

EDIT: 07-16-2017
I had to totally rewrite this review after playing longer and this may be subject to change again...  This is based on Single Player and Online.
Shroud of the Avatar is an awesome RPG game IMO!  It's an Ultima game, but feels somewhat different since it is totally 3D.  What makes this so fun to me, is the leveling system.  It's a lot like Oblivion.  You use gold to unlock skills from trainers, but after that the more you use a skill the more it levels up. It's great! My character gets more powerful by the minute!
Originally I thought you had to hold the right mouse button to look around, but that can be changed in the control options to make it feel like any other 3rd person game.  You can zoom in and way out, plus the camera is very intelligent. It never gets caught or hung up behind objects both inside of buildings and the great outdoors.  It's always behind your character.
Combat is automatic which IMO is a great feature.  It let's you concentrate on casting spells and movement.  I use a bow and once the enemy is targeted, I backup as the enemies advance. They usually die before I take much damage. You can save your game in multiple save slots anywhere at anytime.  I advise you to do so before large battles. You can run from the enemies and eventually they will give up chase and return to their original areas.  Enemies also respawn once you leave the area, so you can milk them for experience!  Great feature again IMO!
There seems to be a trainer in each town to unlock skills with gold.  Some trainers cannot train you in some skills, so other trainers need to be searched out in different towns. I haven't checked other character classes, but I think all skills are available, but it's up to you how you spend your gold and unlock the HUGE skill tree! So far all quests work great and have waypoints to follow, so it's not hard to complete them.  Quests are varied and so far very fun!
The game world is large so far, but the areas are not open-world huge like Skyrim.  Some areas are larger than others and some are empty waiting for game content. You will transverse from one area to another via gates.  There is a larger overview of the map and you choose where you want to go by walking there, then it will load that area. I'm sure this is done for online multiplayer games.
Although the graphics engine is a tad old, it still looks great and should run on a lot of older computers. Some areas look fabulous and night time with the lighting is very atmospheric! The graphics and animations for the creatures & characters are done well.  Some have complained about their looks, but understand this is an online game and some sacrifices need to be made.  I think everything looks great IMO.
Sound is fabulous in all areas!  Great music as always from the Ultima games.  I am having a blast right now and this ranks up there with most great RPG's in this genre.  Just don't expect Skyrim and you'll be okay! lol
NOTE: Your single player and online character's are different.  Would have been nice to play one character in both game modes.  Online gameplay needs to be optimized better as other online characters and enemies jump around sometimes...  Still a fun game!!!

Ori and the Blind Forrest.
This is a must try game, hopefully you will fall in love with the art style and story as I did.
Pros and Cons:
+ Amazing visuals and animation quality
+ Great Soundtrack
+ A story that will take you on an emotional ride (yes, I want my games to be emotional)
+ Reletable Characters
+ Good Difficulty (Not too Easy, not too hard, I did die many times on specific parts)
+ Creative puzzles and level design.
- If you want to explore everything and find all the secrets you must do that before you finish the game.
Story: (10/10)
I won't spoil the story (for obvious reasons) but I will give you an idéa.
You are Ori, a spirit of the great spirit tree who is found by a creature named Naru. She adopts you and they live a happy life with each other until a cataclysmic event makes the forest and its food supply wither and it is up to you, to return balance to the forest.
Gameplay: (9/10)
Ori and the Blind Forest is set as a 2D open world platform game. You control Ori, a guardian spirit through his quest to return balance to the forest.
The controls are easy to learn and precise, which makes it easy and fun to travel around the open world.
During the game you'll learn different abilities (for example: shooting spirit flames and doing a ground stomp),
you'll need these powers to interact with the environment  and to solve the different puzzles throughout the game.
The game has save points scattered around the map (that heals you when you save at their location) but you can also save at any time in the game by creating a "soul link" but these can only be created using energy cells collected during gameplay.
The cost of creating a ''soul link'' is not too high, but it forces you to create them only when necessary, at least early in the game. You also use these ''soul links'' to buy various perks and upgrades for Ori, such as underwater breathing and increase the spirit fire damage. Each skill must be bought in sequential order from one of three trees to allow the next, more expensive skill to be accessible.
Level Design: (10/10)
The levels in this game are beautiful and creative and in my opinion the best looking 2D game I've ever played.
They are filled with secrets you can find, some secrets will be out of reach only to be accessible when you have learned the required ability giving you a reason to return to already explored areas.
Visuals: (10/10)
To be honest, the visuals were the main reason I bought this game. I loved the art style from the moment I saw the first screenshot and I regret nothing. This game is an aesthetic masterpiece and is the best looking 2D game I've ever played.
* The Levels are beautiful and varied.
* The backgrounds are stunning.
* The visuals has a cartoony feel, but still have realistic undertone.
* The characters are nicely drawn and animated (and ADORABLE).
* The lighting adds that little extra making the environments look and feel more alive.
So it doesn't matter if you are an artist like myself or not. I can almost guarantee you will love the visuals of the game :)
The Soundtrack: (10/10)
Soundtracks for me are important in games, it has the job to enhance the story and events within the game and Ori and the blind forest really succeeded on that part.
The music is so intertwined with the story and does a really good job in setting the scene, whenever it is calm, sad or intense the music will hit you on the right spot and make you emotionally invested in the game and its story.
So what is my verdict?
I loved this game, the gameplay was solid, the story amazing, the music and the visuals godlike.
I had a blast playing through this game and I will do so again, so I will give this game a 10/10!!!!!
If you haven't bought this game yet, I highly recommend you doing so. It's a well made game and a joy to play through. I don't think you will be disappointed :)

Scribblenauts Unlimited is not a bad game. It's just not as good as I was hoping it would be. It's put together well, the artstyle is good, the soundtrack is good (I can still hear some of the game's music playing in my head,) and the voice acting (what little of it there is) is good. So where does it fall short, then? A few places actually. Let's start with the big one: the gameplay.
The idea is to solve puzzles by conjuring up an object, or by adding an adjective to an existing one. Sounds intriguing, but really you just wind up solving puzzles with the most basic of objects. The whole idea of being able to add adjectives to objects is neat, but it's not really put into play all that much. There are a few instances where you must scare Person X away from Object/Person Y. So you just apply the adjective "Scary" to Object/Person Y. Or perhaps something needs wings, so you give it the adjective "Flying." Makes sense. But there's only a few puzzles that really make use of adjectives. The large majority of the puzzles can be solved with basic objects, and it just kinda starts to feel as though you're grinding through the game rather than really "solving" anything. It just gets rather tedious after a while.
Then there's the Steam Workshop. Probably the main reason that the game is called Scribblenauts
the way the Workshop works is you can use and in-game Object Editor to create your own objects and submit them to the workshop for the rest of the world to use. Likewise, you can download other people's creations. Now, I personally took one look at the Object Editor and said "No thanks." But I'm sure those of you out there who have the blood of Michelangelo or Vincent van Gogh coursing through your veins can imagine and create masterpieces with it. I just didn't feel like taking the time to get used to it.
Now as for the Workshop itself. It's kind of...meh. There are some really well made and detailed things in there with their own creative and useful functions...surrounded by Five Nights at Freddy's characters. Don't get me wrong, I don't dislike Five Nights at Freddy's. I just dislike seeing it in
However, you can play and enjoy the game without even looking at the Workshop, so I won't base my judgement of the whole game on it too much.
Finally,considering the game's content and how many hours you'll likely get out of the game even if you go to the trouble of 100%ing it, that $20 price tag is WAY too much. To put it in perspective, you can purchase Terraria on Steam right now for $10. That's a game that you can potentially get hundreds of  hours out of. The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth is a similar story: $15 for potentially hundreds of hours. Scribblenauts Unlimited meanwhile is $20 for around 12 hours if you feel so inclined to get all of the achivements. But to be fair, Terraria and The Binding of Isaac are COMPLETELY different than Scribblenauts. Scribblenauts isn't the type of game that you dedicate hundreds of your hours into. It's the kind of game that you finish, and then move on to something else. But even still...$20? In my opinion, if you truly feel so compelled to purchase the title, you're gonna want to wait until the next big sale.

Collecting loot, leveling up, and setting up character builds are two things you won't be doing in Gauntlet, it is a bare bones dungeon crawler. The game allows you to play one of five different classes. The classes are all very different from one another, but within each class there is very little room for customization and different playstyles.
Instead of setting a button layout for the game and fitting each character's abilties into that layout the game opts to give each character a unique feel in addition to skillset. The warrior for example is your standard light hit mapped to one button, hard hit mapped to another, and special skill, and each of those can be stringed into combos. The elf uses a bow and arrow and plays like most top down shooters where you use the right thumbstick to shoot arrows in the direction you aim the stick. Among all the classes the most fun I found to play was the wizard. The wizard has access to 9 spells and they're all done with a different combination of three buttons, it actually ends up being a pretty elegant system for spells as opposed to a spell bar, but it does take a little getting used to.
The character customization seems like an afterthought. Each character can have two relics that they can equip. The relics aren't found, they can only be bought with gold collected throughout the levels. They'll allow you to do things like move faster, freeze enemies around you, put a trail of fire where you walk, and heal the party. There are not very many relics available, only about 9 or so, and they don't really change the game much. To use relics you need to obtain magic bottles so in addition to there not being very many you also won't be using them very often.
There is hardly a story to the game, there's a big bad guy and you have to go kill him, that's about it. In some games this may be a negative, but I don't think most people would really expect a Gauntlet game to be about the story. I'm only stating this as information for those that might expect it to be a primary focus, it's not, and I don't count it against the game.
The game has jump in and jump out of game co-op where everyone has to play one of the five classes, there is no doubling up on classes. It is fun to group up and work through a dungeon together, and on the hardest difficulty it can be hard so everyone has to be on their game to get through. One of the primary aspects of the original Gauntlet games that were important to the experience was competition with your teammates. Who can get through the level with the most gold? Kill the most enemies? This version of Gauntlet doesn't seem to have that aspect for some reason. I think a few factors contribute to this: 1) not much gold to go around, 2) some classes are obviously more powerful than others and will always lead in kills. By making the classes so different they sort of ruined the competitive aspect because of balance problems. What ends up happening is the game is turned into a normal dungeon crawler where the objective is just to survive and beat the level. I think it might have been more fun to include some other competitive aspect in some way with certain types of drops or something.
Gauntlet is a fun game if what you expect out of it is realistic. You aren't going to be getting a high end dungeon crawler loot fest. It is a simplistic, watered down dungeon crawler that should be played with multiple people. I think the $20 asking price is a bit too much for what you get, but this is a great buy for at least 50% off on a sale.

Though Gauntlet may be short in its length, what it does have to offer is a polished gem that captures the spirit of its predecessor. The game is best played in multiplayer, so grab a friend and start slaying the forces of evil.

Skullgirls is a game full of things to love, which can all be appreciated on their own, which all come together to make a unique experience.
First, the visuals:
Skullgirls is easily one of the most visually impressive games you'll ever play. Every single animation is drawn in incredible detail, everything looking extremely smooth and natural. It is worth playing almost for the visuals alone.
Next, the controls: Keyboard controls are done well, but a controller is highly recommended for anyone who wants to fully explore this game, and the abundant movelists, combos, and other features. The tutorials are also far better suited for preparing a player using a controller, rather than a keyboard.
If you're a veteran at fighting games, you'll be pleased at how 'technically' impressive Skullgirls is, allowing for a ton of ways to chain attacks, get massive combos and feel in control. Players who are newer to fighters don't have to worry, there is a tutorial covering a massive amount of game mechanics, and the movelists are easy to understand. As always with fighter games, it can be quite relentless to try and get to high skill levels and pull off every move and mechanic with ease, it does take a lot of practice.
For casual players and veterans alike, there's a ton to enjoy. Story mode covers a pretty cool plot, each character's story really helps to flesh them out and make them feel a bit more alive. You fight your way through a series of matches, a few adding a bit to the story through pre-fight dialog, until you reach a pretty challening final boss where you conclude that character's story. There is a variety of difficulty options available, making it accessible to both beginner and hardcore players.
The character roster is relatively limited, with 8 Fighters being available in the base game, and 4 added DLC fighters (and a Hidden one) available through DLC. It is worth mentioning that if you own the base game upon a DLC's release, it is available for free for a significantly long time. Otherwise, you have to buy the DLCs separately. This can be quite a turn-off for some players, but given the depth of each character it is more than enough to get a ton of enjoyment out of Skullgirls.
Gameplay wise, every character has a variety of moves. There are light, medium and heavy punches and kicks (varying in range, damage, speed, etc on each character) as well as specials, crouched attacks, jumping attacks, and all the other things common to all fighters. Every character has varying difficulties, making them better or worse for less skilled players. A newcomer can likely buttonmash their way through a few PVP matches or the story mode, but on higher difficulties or vs someone who is skilled at fighters will be a brick wall to that strategy.
For many players, the multiplayer is the most important part. From a technical standpoint, the multiplayer was done well and can provide a lag-free environment to anyone who wants to get into it. The community isn't HUGE, but there's always players to face, but as a word of warning, most players you encounter online are very skilled. It can be near impossible to get into as a newcomer to fighters or to Skullgirls. For this reason I do recommend playing this game locally if possible.
Every moment is enjoyable with the beautiful animation and artstyle, there's a challenge to be found if you're looking for one, and there's a casual, enjoyable experience for those who just want to appreciate the art, voice acting and story.
And for those reaons I'm giving this game a recommendation!

Gameplay: use towers to pop balloons. The main difficulties are when the balloons rush you and the bloons that take many hits to get. There are also camofloged balloons, steel balloons, regrowing balloons, etc. You have a limited amount of 'cash' per round that you get popping bloons or via towers and then use to buy towers. There is 50+ tracks at 4 difficulties, 250 random missions, and more. The regular gameplay gets a bit boring after a while, but the random missions make up for it by requiring the use of specific towers or changing up the types of balloons on a specific track. There are also special agents you can 'buy' with money money. There is a co-op mode that some people like, altough I prefer to play individually so I can't say much about it.
I own this game on Kindle fire. That said, I would definitely recommend this version over the free version on the Kindle. When using the Kindle, I had quite a bit of problems with lag. Some towers fire too many bolts and some they added unneccesary decoration like the moving flames on the apprentice tower full upgrade. Also, in this version you can 'buy' certain upgrades with monkey money instead of real cash.
As for the cons of this game, the achievements are fairly badly done. I like comparing my progress to everyone else, but that doesn't really work in this game. Some, like fully upgrade starting cash, have gotten much more difficult to obtain due to updates. They also have an achievement for every track on co-op and regular mode, which makes the acheivements a bit arbitrary as some people will by change complete one track before another. There are way too many achievements too.

Pros:
* Like the previous game, you can create all kinds of equipment setups to strategically defeat enemies. Characters also get three accessory slots this time, some of which have interesting effects like replacing weapon status effects.
* Some of the medals are more lenient this time around, especially the treasure hunting medals.
* Battle Mountain is a good way to test one's skills against equally leveled opponents.
* The skill system allows more element variety for the characters. For example, Matt can now learn thunder skills to take advantage of his Golden Dragon sword.
* The summon system adds more depth to the battle system, since it costs SP that's obtained from killing enemies.
Mixed:
* Like the previous games, the dialogue and story is funny, but not particularly deep. That said, the main antagonist of this game is more interesting than the previous one due to their motives.
Cons:
* There's currently a memory leak due to leftover status icons. The game has to be restarted every now and then to avoid crashes.
* No explanation is given for the party's level reset this time. Though Matt (the character) did mention that he didn't work out enough recently, which implies the old party is rusty.
Some features that would have been nice:
* Level scaled versions of the final boss and glitch boss.
* Resolutions that match Youtube's preferred pixel height.
* A backlog that records recent dialogue.
* A way to disable automatic attacks and counterattacks.
Tips:
* Finish Battle Mountain before fighting the final boss. Without the Battle Mountain equipment, the final boss is about as hard as the fourth boss rush. With that equipment, the final boss will be a lot easier to defend against.
* Take advantage of the tired and weaken statuses against bosses, since most of them have 50% resistance to normal stat lowering effects.
* Don't neglect stat items, since enemies gain more per level than the player otherwise. This is especially important in Battle Mountain, where enemies scale.
* For normal boss rush, beat the boss while they still have weak minions on the field. This will give you an opportunity to reequip and buff.
* Use the developer's kongregate guide to find treasures and secrets easily.
* When fighting the
, never take your eyes off the screen while a battle animation occurs. You need to keep an eye out for their limit break indication so you can be ready to defend with Ancient Monolith. On that note, never end your phase with an attack on them, since you could trigger their limit break before you can defend.
* You can't buy chilli sauce like with other rare items.

Day 1
This game is far from finished and has been in development for years.
I have played this for most of the day today and have found my experience frustrating to say the least.
Transitioning between areas/instances is hit and miss. But for the most part takes far to long to load or just crashes entirely.
On first entering the game (after creating your toon) it does not give you much in the way of direction. So you are left wondering around trying to figure out what to do or where to go , when you do find the tutorial quest it takes you to another area far to quickly for my liking. Information is not forthcoming and it took me awhile to find where I needed to head on the main travel/map area.
I ended up having to travel to Solace Bridge at which point there is meant to be a boat under the bridge to take you to your next area, sadly the boat simply is not there. Considering these are meant to be the tutorial quest’s. The fact that the boat is not there just shows how undeveloped this game is.
I found that there is very little in the way of skill progression information in the game and very little in the way of information on how to repair items or what items are used in/for.
Basic recipes start at 250 gold each, considering that I spent most of the day playing and only managed to build up around 1500 gold It would appear to me that you will need to be making some real world purchases of in game gold in order to become proficient in any crafting skills.
I found no NPC vendors that sell any basic armor items or any information on what sort of armor would best suit my toon (a mage). It may be that I was just looking in the wrong place. I did find some player owned vendors selling armor but again the cost was way above what I could afford thus far. All the npc’s in the areas I visited never once dropped any items of armor .
You are equipped with a fishing rod when you first start in the game but there is no information in game on how to use it, a search online seems to indicate that you need to buy/train this skill from a trainer. As yet I have not come across the trainer that sells/trains this skill. You would have thought this would have been readily available.
There is as far as I can tell no way of seeing what a recipe actually needs to make it or the items value once you have made it until you have bought the recipe. With things like food this is frustrating as you really want to know the effects of the crafted item, before you buy the recipe.
It would be nice if the map would show you where you have active quests to complete or even more detail on where to go in your journal would be nice. Also some sort of highlighting of npc’s that have quests to offer you.
I paid £15 for the access to the early game in the steam 50% off sale and to be honest I’m questioning if the game was worth that. I can see it ending up being an expensive pay to win game If it ever makes it to a launch date.
This is of course all my own opinion and everybody’s experience will be different, I will continue to play for a few weeks to see if my in game experience improves with age, updates and a hell of a lot of polish needed from the dev’s. But if the game continues to frustrate as it has today, or simply becomes pay to win then I think it will soon find its way to the back of the steam shelf.
I can see that there is some promise in the game but boy do they need to get their fingers out and bring some flow to the game play in the beginning stages of your character development, skill progression and crafting skills.

I've played the game off and on since it launched with about 700 hours invested. The ride to get to where we are right now has been incredibly bumpy but Massive, Red Storm and Reflections have done an amazing job fixing the issues with the game and adding content. There is an incredible balance between builds at the moment with a ton of end-game content to experience after leveling. The leveling process has always been great. I highly recommend that anyone that has ever had interest in playing the game get it and do so now; it's never been better.
The game won't be for everyone. It's a 3rd person shooter, but it is also an RPG and a looter at it's core. Think Diablo 3, but with guns in New York instead of magic on Sanctum. So there is a gear grind, and character builds to experiment and plan for. For those that like the genre, it's a fantastic game.
Also, because I've seen it mentioned: It's an online game, so sometimes there are cheaters. I can count on one hand the number of ACTUAL cheaters I've encountered in the nearly 700 hours I've played the game and I am not alone in this assertion. The Dark Zone (where most of the cheating would be witnessed) is a multiplayer, online, competitive environment and people will often look for ways to exploit this. I feel that Massive and company have done a great job at stopping it whenever they can.

Epic Battle Fantasy 4 was a surprsingly and unexpectedly fun game. I went into the game expecting a higher tier RPG maker like game, but it was so much better than those.
Epic Battle Fantasy 4 is basically a grid movement based game with a JRPG combat style that follows from the events of Epic Battle Fantasy 3. That doesn't sound incredibly interesting from the description (which is what I thought as well), but the gameplay, progression, and secrets make it so fun. Oh and don't forget about the witty 4th wall breaking humor. The enemy difficulty scales up perfectly, and often times you will be challenged or have to rethink your fights as you go along (assuming you didn't grind). You can always turn down the difficulty as well if you are feeling too pressured, especially for some of the boss fights.
EBF4 actually has an incredible amount of things to do, stats, and items. There are 8 different elements, and 8 different kind of status effects (if I recall correctly) that you will learn to deal with. Each region has a different main enemy type. Once you scan an enemy, you can attack or use spells according to their weaknesses. Not only that, but there are a bountiful amount spells and abilities to learn amongst your four playable characters (of which only three will ever be fighting at once). Aside from that, debatabely the best part is how the designed the levels and layouts. Certain parts of the grid cannot be accessed until you get a tool, like the hammer to destroy rocks. Even in the very first area you are in, there are things you can do once you progress further into the story. Basically, you can go back and visit your earlier regions and get some good treasures! The game has strategical warp points as well making it not much of a hassle to get from part of the map to another part. As for the visual and audio side, the game has excellent music, good sounds, great fight animations, and nice but childish looking character and landscaping.
The one flaw of this game that I found extremely annoying was that when I ran it in fullscreen mode on my laptop (4k res), it lagged like hell and crashed often. The game has a really weird fullscreen mode (at least it did for me), and I wish they added better support to higher resolutions.
Overall, a really fun game that I would recommend. I might even go through a second playthrough because there is still some stuff that I missed in my first one.

I got this game earlier this year, and never got around to writing a review until now.
I don't normally play Tycoon games, but I really enjoy this game alot. I'll admit i was a little uncertain at first as to whether to buy this game, as it isn't what I normally play, but what finally convinced me to get it was actually the developer's tale of how they released a cracked version on a torrent site at the same time as the initial full release, and planted a pirate trap in the cracked version by having your company die by unavoidably hemmorage money from piracy.  Not only is it a great story, the fact that they did that to prove a point moved me so much that I wanted to support them.
Now the game itself:
For starters, it is a very impressive first release for a small developer. They took great care and put alot of work into this and it really shows.  Everything basically works. I've encountered no bugs or crashes that i could observe, so there is no techical issue to report. The steam achievements are quite amusing and satisfying as well (and kudos to the Half Life and Portal easter egg achievements :) )
As the title suggests, you basically manage a video game developer. You give your company a name, your character a name, and a little customization, and then you are off!
I won't go into detail on how to play, as it is actually pretty easy to pick up, it is mastering it that is the challenge, and the tutorial screens are pretty helpful and informative.
You start in your garage working on your own in the 1980s. The game does not specify which year, just using a dating system of Year (Y) 1, Month (M) 1, Week (W) 1, but given the technology you have to work with (and the Deloran parked in the garage) clearly indicates sometime in the 1980s.  A week goes by pretty quickly in real time, so a decent size play session can see you move over a decade.
You progress through the history of video games up through the present day (at the game's 2013 release), even to the point where the cycle of different consoles and platforms are released and phased out (with amusing parody names like mBox, Gameling, Dream Vast and Game Sphere). If you can't tell by the names, the images are clearly meant to be Xbox, Gameboy, Dreamcast and Gamecube.
One negative quirk I will point out is that, to me, there doesn't seem to be much incentive for investing money to get the licesnces to make games for any of the platforms other than PC. The changes in PCs over the years are reflected passively, so it won't cost you any additional money when the PCs get better.
All the other platforms other than PC change over time, and PC is always the cheapest platform to develop for, so I don't see much reason to take major financial risks to develop for any of the consoles or handhelds. One way they could have done this, I think, is to have it where if your games get popular, some of the console devs could approach you with a discounted or free licesnce to develop games for their platform.
Maybe this is reflective of the fact that the PC has bascially always been there and is the constant in the shifting history of game platforms.
Throughout the game you also research new topics and other features and designs pieces to make your games better and to make your own game engines. One thing I don't like in this regard is that you have to get to research and unlock Sequels. That is the one feature I think you should have by default, once you release your first game.  If you can make a game, you can make a sequel, It may be a piece of crap, but it is still a sequel.
I think there should also be a sort of passive method of helping you catch up with technology. For example. In my current company's life, it didn't get the first level of 3D graphics until the original Xbox (sorry mBox), was off the market, because i was constrained by high research point costs and wanting to improve in other areas. I agree with needing to research new tech, but perhaps at a certain point in the timeline, the reearch point cost for certain things could go down as the tech is more commonplace.
Finally, I think it should be easier to research topics. You are given a few at the start, and must spend research points to get more, but you get new topics for research at random. Topics cost 10 research points. I think they should be cheaper, or give us all possible topics researchable at the outset. Maybe I want my company to focus on military games, but i start with the topics Zombies, School, City, and Fantasy. And it may take a long time before I unlock "Military" as a topic.
My constructive criticisms aside, I still love this game, and would really recommend it to anyone.

This is a rather hidden gem, I must say. For a game that's going completely under the radar, The Uncertain has a really decent setting, story, characters, and an excellent presentation with both visuals, music, and voice acting.
The story follows a robot called RT who accidentally comes across something rather top secret and unsettling that instantly makes him wanted by the robot police. All this happening in a somewhat post-apocalyptic setting with robots ruling the world after humans have destroyed themselves in wars. Now robots are trying very hard to rebuild. There is a lot of charm to the robot characters in the game and the way they interact not only with each other, but also with the environment, like all the comments RT makes on human inventions and why a certain invention is useful or doesn't make any logical sense at all.
The gameplay is your typical point and click with puzzles. You complete tasks in each area to get the plot moving along and then head to the next area. The puzzles are all very intuitive and logical. I was never really stuck on any or needed to use a walkthrough. Some puzzles took form of some kind of a fun mini-game, such as hacking a safe, matching icons, or some other interesting mechanics. There is also a driving section where you manoeuvre through a forest on a hover car and get chased a couple of times, which was a nice change of pace.
Only a few minor gripes. Sometimes pathfinding can bug out. Like you click to approach a certain object, and on a rare occasion your character gets stuck and is unable to approach it, so you have to manually go around and approach it from another side. Static camera angles in a few places can also get a little annoying when exploring the bigger areas, particularly later in the game. Though these aren't huge issues or anything.
I did think though that the game ended way too soon. I know it's just the first episode, but the ending kind of came in very abruptly and out of the blue and I wished there was more. But I guess we'll just wait for Episode 2 and hope that it will be a little longer. Since it's only about 3-4 hours at most, perhaps it's better to get it on sale, though the game is overall very well made. Don't be put off by the fact that it's been made in Unity. It's got a lot of attention to detail and is rather well polished.

I really want to like Gauntlet. You'd be hard-pressed to find someone who found Legends and Dark Legacy more compelling. It has the hallmarks and a vague understanding of what made the series great in the first place, but just seems to miss its mark in every place. Gauntlet nails it in one and only one place, which is the true diversification of the class playstyles rather than keeping every character a twin-stick shooter. That's good! It's great, even! In the game it's in, though, it *just isn't enough.*
If it was just that there isn't meat here, it might not be so bad. I might still boot it up for some random slaughter. Gauntlet, though, doesn't really want you to like it. Arrowhead built this game - and by their own word, no less - to make you feel unfairly treated when you play it, and to cause you to get into fights with your friends. A game that should be more fun with friends is instead much less, because you're rewarded for ♥♥♥♥ing your team over. It saps the good qualities of this game completely away and leaves it drier and emptier than where its dearth of content started.
Even if 35 hours of playtime sounds like a good deal for five dollars, it really wasn't. It was a frustrating, mediocre 35 hours that I don't plan on reliving. Skip this game and leave the message that only a more faithful version of Gauntlet is worth our time.

Very addicting game with deeper gameplay than initially seems.
So I started this game out and thought it was almost like a limited version of Diablo. Arcade style. Well it's actually nothing like Diablo and not trying to be in any way. What I thought were limited abilities and simple gameplay concepts actually turn each class into a very unique class when you play on Unfair mode with other skilled players. You can actually tell who is skilled and whose not by the way the player can move around the map and use his skills and chain them in ways that allow him to survive a lot longer than the average player.
This brings me into the games key component. Multiplayer. I didn't immediately jump into it, in fact my first few hours with the game were solo. Little did I know the real phone lies in the multiplayer component and actually makes the game a lot more rewarding. You will learn how to play your class a lot better when you watch how others control that class during your sessions on hard or Unfair difficulty.
A class I had no interest in at the beginning turned out to be my favorite, The Valkyrie. What seems as a limited basic class turned into a heck of a lot of fun. Toss your shield as it seeks and decapitates enemies is a very satisfying feeling when your overwhelmed by Orcs. Timing your shield after a toss so that your in a defensive shell shows the difference between a rookie and the veterans. Knowing which direction to use your impale ability so that you aren't expose and vulnerable at the end of it can be your defeat or skillful exit from being trapped.
With that said, I haven't played too many other classes as deeply except maybe the Elf. The Wizard I haven't delved too much into yet because I'm just not big on all the different combinations you have to mix to be effective but I see the skillful players using that class no doubt.
The maps can get repetitive but with different players in the mix, it's always fun. The Colosseum mode is a nice welcome to keep things fresh with the different season changes, and above all, playing on Unfair makes the game a lot more fun since you have to pay attention to everything going on and not make mistakes.
Graphically the game looks great and runs perfect. A recent patch enlarged the cursor so it's a bit more easier to find when all hell is breaking loose.
I hope they can add more classes because the necromancer doesn't really appeal to me as of yet but I do intend to get that class unlocked eventually.
I definitely recommend the game if you have time to dig into it's deeper gameplay mechanics than what it initially seems.

Disclosure
I was originally going to wait until the game was officially launched to write a review in order to be as fair as possible to the dev team, however with persistence going on over a full year now, Early Access extended yet again to the end of 2017 Q1 or 2 of 2018, and the devs still referring to the game as a “pre-alpha stage” in discussions and in the starting screen of the game itself, my patience has worn out.
First off, since I will be discussing the devs and the community they have built around themselves, let me give you a brief history of my participation in that community.
I backed this game on Kickstarter at the Knight Marshall level ($1200) and played the early releases very regularly, as well as following and participating in the official forum community from the start. I have had Dev+ access that whole time, have never been banned (though in the last year as I’ve become more critical I have been threatened with it a few times), and have participated in many discussions and given a lot of feedback, reported bugs, had private chats with moderators and devs, etc.
The deck combat system was implemented around release 8 or 9, despite overwhelmingly negative feedback about the concept, and then overwhelmingly negative feedback about the system after it was implemented. We were told by the devs that if the system wasn't fun, it could easily be changed back to a more traditional hotbar system and a new design worked on. After several releases it became clear that not only was the system not fun, but that the devs had no intention of giving up on it regardless of the feedback and alternatives presented to them. I became tired of the devs not listening to anyone but certain high backers and sold my founder account around release 19 or 20. I had a second base account in order to check in on the game over the following 10 releases or so.
As the releases crept into the high 20's and persistence was looming, I had several friends begin playing the game and enjoying the crafting system and decorating that was in place. I decided I could tolerate the combat as it was (several tweaks had been made allowing mixed hotbars of locked and random cards) in order to play with my guild, and I increased my base account back up to a Knight level ($800).  I played from release 30 up through the launch of persistence, the land rush, and through the last year of persistence to the current release 45 as of this writing, and the guild which I started was and remains one of the largest guilds in the game, though I gave up leadership a long time ago.
Clearly, I know what the game was pitched as, I know how it evolved, I've followed it from the start, and I understand exactly what Early Access means in the context of this game. I have participated in several other games of various genres that were crowdfunded on Kickstarter and I had/have alpha access through all of them as well. My guild and I have participated in several games where we had direct lines to the developers as part of their core testing group and in many cases my group or I would be directly responsible for certain mechanics or changes implemented into some of these games. I know how development works, I know how alphas and betas typically work, and I know how Early Access works.

Inspired by Final Fantasy,
is an RPG game with simple battle mechanics, yet complex strategy.  Elemental damage/resistances, status effects, buffs, and equips all play a major part in how your party performs in battle.  Each player gets one action every turn.  An action is using a skill (attack, buff, defend, etc), changing equipment, or using an item.  Enemies follow the same mechanic on their turn, except they don't switch equipment or use items.  In a nutshell, you hit the enemy until it dies.
has a large map consisting of areas and tiles, which can be traversed using point-and-click pathfinding, or using a keyboard.  Areas are big sections of tiles which make up larger sections of the map.  Areas are inter-connected, and walking off the edge of one brings you to the corresponding area.  There's also map-based puzzles, such as pushing blocks (sounds boring, right?) until they clear a path to a chest, which can then be looted.
has a storyline.  'nuff said (I'd rather not spoil anything).  There are also side-stories in which characters make jokes, and just talk in general.
I would give
at least a
.  It has more than 60 weapons and 60 armor pieces, not to mention about 60 flairs (a special equipment type that any character can use).  There's four different difficulties and 'Battle Mountain', a place outside of the storyline where you can push the challenges to the limits.  Endless battles, foe rushes, boss rushes, new optional bosses, etc.
Newgame+ is a feature that allows you to continue your profile with all your stuff, but enemies are higher levels to accomodate for you being a higher level.  Sadly, this caps at level 50 (but Battle Mountain scales with your character level, so it doesn't).  My current profile has almost 100 hours.

The AI is outright trash and then really solid all at the same time. It's the strangest AI i've ever seen. You can be 300 feet away nobody even sees you. You toss a turret sideways 30 feet away and before it even sets up you run 30 feet further back behind cover and instantly before the turret even fires all of the enemies just bum rush straight too you. They hardly even interact with the turret and just rush straight on you. I've tested this at least 10 times and it's straight up broken AI.
On the other side of things the AI can be really great at times, they will work together and try to flank you. Snipers stay in the back while the rushers / mid range units work cover to cover and try to move in. Sometimes they end up in odd spots in the open just standing still like they got stuck for a couple of seconds. The combat is far more enjoyable with at least 1 other person. It doesn't allow the AI cheating to be as noticeable and you can work with your teammate to flank them as well.
I wish there was more room for a stealthier approach at times. The game has silencers and I use them on every weapon, but there is one huge issue, silencers do not seem to do jack. Sure they don't sound as loud, they still sound pretty damn loud, but not nearly as loud as w/o. The big issue is they don't seem to make it possible to kill anyone without alerting the rest. You can have 1 enemy 100+ feet away from anyone else and 1 shot him in the head from another 100+ feet away so now 200+ feet between you and the next enemy, but they others will hear and attack. It's the same situation as with the turret example above. Without a single AI having spotted you they will instantly shoot on your location and charge in. Not sure what went wrong here, but it seems lazily done. I have not seen anyone scenario where I can quickly kill 1 enemy w/o alerting the others, even when they are giant gaps between them and using a 1 shot kill silenced headshot. It's something not so much of an issue in multiplayer, but very noticeable in SP.
A smaller issue that just kills me is the game has no crouch or prone. I can deal with no prone, but it really needs a crouch option. It's tedious having to use cover from such further distances to move in when crouch makes more sense. There are no fire mode toggles as well despite weapons that have this in real life. In game the M4 is only a full auto weapon, but in reality can be put on semi automatic. A weapon is either semi, pump or automatic and no weapon has more than 1 type. This completely takes away from trying to get immersed in the game. How does a 3rd person shooter that takes place in the near future and has tons of weapon customization options not include the ability to toggle between firing modes? It's shocking to me how this makes it past testing , it's such a basic thing that any game along these lines should automatically have it.
Gameplay is really solid and cover is smooth, but sometimes it can make you exit on accident or your crosshairs are too low with no way to move up some more. The keybinds are great with 2 options per bind. There does not appear to be regional servers so you are tossed with people from all over.  I have a block list of 50 people simply so I can read chat because of so much non English chatter. Finding decent groups in game simply won't happen, but there is a good community on steam forums, very helpful. I've met a couple people with already who I have been playing with.
Another huge issue is that they totally fd up audio communication in this game. I play tons of games and what i'm about to describe works in every game I can remember. I have the games sound come thru my main surround sound speaker system and then I use my headset only over 1 ear for speaking and listening to other players. I speak thru my headset mic with a push to talk key and then when others speak to me I do not hear them thru my surround sound system. I only hear them thru my headset.. It does not work this way in The Division.
Players will ALWAYS come thru your main speaker system. There is an option to select the which microphone to use and I select my headset, it's all set up right as in every other game, but the audio only comes thru the speaker system. I've been on the forums with this and also with friends, this is how it is. I have to turn my game volume down to 40% and adjust from there so that players will always be louder than everything else so that I can, you know, actually hear them because they are coming thru the speakers with everything else. It's not as huge of an issue with friends because I just switch to discord and bypass it, but it's another example of how poorly developed this game was. This is such a basic thing, there is no reason to have this issue in a modern AAA game that has VOIP and P2T settings. How are some of these smaller issues going on over a year since release?
I doubt the game will get updates to the fire mode and other issues being that it has been out a while. If they pay attention to key issues in The Division and fix them along with reworking the AI it's very possible The Division 2 could become one of the greatest games ever. This game has so much damn potential

Hey! tl;dr I couldn't recommend this game any less if you're new. Pay to win is one element of this 'recommendation', but it's not even the worst part - being at the mercy of other players is.
Easily the #1 reason to not install this game is the sheer punishment for new players: You will be an easy target for experienced players for months after you begin because of the time required to build castles or amass faith points to interdict yourself.
- Did you join a faction & house to deter enemies? Too bad, you'll be targeted first in a war and your villages will be captured.
- Did you stay neutral to avoid inter-house wars? Too bad, when war breaks out, the local ruling house will raze your villages because you're an easy 'target for rogues'. If you can dodge this, the invaders will raze your villages because 'your liege lord is our enemy'.
Spending money on the game will not save you from these; only time sunk will.
- Did you start playing on a new world, where everyone starts from scratch? Too bad, experienced players have 'cards' - bonuses that can be transferred from other worlds, so that they quickly jump out, and stay, ahead of you.
Luckily, I have mostly avoided these (and similar) experiences, but I've seen them happen too frequently to others. Save yourself the time and move along to a more rewarding game.
Other cons: Sluggish refreshing, clunky UI, primitive combat system.
Pros: Classic Stronghold resource management, unique gameplay concept, meaningful research, ability to stay ahead if you can get ahead.

Ridiculously old school graphics. Ridiculously addictive. Seriously, this game makes me feel like I'm back in 2002 playing Civilization III, but in an alternate reality where Civ III was an MMO.
I really do love this game. Even with the developers' painfully sluggish pace at which they update the game in any major ways (ex. despite having graphics tailor-made for a mobile game—or Windows 98—the mobile version was only released this year in 2017), this game is still incredibly engaging at its core.
And, as most engaging games are, it is incredibly frustrating. Like, scream-and-shake-your-monitor frustrating. Every time you start out on a new server without any faction connections, and you spend three weeks building yourself up and some [EXPLETIVE] demolishes your hard-earned village(s), you'll basically lose your mind with rage. And then you'll immediately start a new village, bloodthirsty and hellbent on revenge.
That's what will keep you coming back to this seemingly simple and almost awkwardly outdated-looking game. Even if you don't care for the rather nostalgic graphics and game mechanics (personally, I love that unique aspect of it, as far as MMOs go), you still might get hooked on the deeply rooted "warring tribes" part of the gameplay, which can vastly enhance—or ruin—your experience, depending on the friends you make and the factions you join. There really is a sort of Game of Thrones political aspect to this game, involving other actual players and no AIs whatsoever (aside from randomly spawning "Kill Me!" targets).
It's not like Civilization, and it's not just a tower defense game, either. It's its own funky, old school RTS that somehow became a bizarrely functional MMO that is as engaging as it is time-consuming.
One day, you're the king of the castle, and the next, you're back to square one.

I was very pleasantly surprised by the FEAR trilogy. All three games were excellent, and I am not generally a FPS fan. This one is especially interesting, as it has multiplayer, but it isn't tacked on (necessarily).
Gameplay is somewhat varied, but still standard FPS. BIggest change is you can play through the game a second time as the partner character from the first playthrough. This is surprisingly different, and effective. First playthrough you have slow motion, which is supremely satisfying, and second playthrough you have the ability to suspend enemies, and even control them. It was very refreshing, and I went through and completed a second playthrough immediately after the first, and they were quite different.
Story is so-so, but it is at least engaging for those that completed the first two game, as all 4 main characters are there (2 playable, 1 from each game, 2 not). It was weird enough to keep me interested, but don't expect anything fantastic.
Scoring system was really interesting. Seemed out of place for a so-called scary game (it really isn't), but was very fun to try and rack up kills in different ways, using different weapons. Also provided progression, so that you naturally powered up as you play the game, but you can focus on certain tasks to get stronger more quickly.
Overall a very enjoyable game, and worth a play just for the satisfying slow-motion gunplay.

I own this game on both PS4 and Steam. I mainly play on PS4, but what I say about it is still relevant. I was one of the unfortunate souls who pre-ordered the game originally. I too was severely upset with what I received. But, for some reason, I never refunded the game. It just sat in my PS4 library... until the updates started coming.
The first update, dubbed Foundation, drastically changed the planet generation and added base building, purchasable freighters, and much more stuff. It was nice, but still didn't add a focus to the game.
The second, Pathfinder, added land vehicles (3 of them to be exact) and heavily improved the visuals, building mechanics, and introduced a quest system.
The third, most recent update, Atlas Rises, is the true game changer. It's officially called No Man's Sky 1.3, but it honestly should be called 2.0. This is what the developers wanted the game to be before launch, this is the game we all wanted. They added 30+ hours of very well written story campaign, an extremely overhauled quest and mission system, completely redesigned visuals, incredible planet generation (including new planet types like Metal planets!), new animals, new ships, new building items, Star System Economies, true faction-based gameplay trading and combat, faster load times, and truly much, much more. Including the first implmentation of multiplayer! (although rather primitive right now. Players appear as "glitched" orbs like in Fable, and can voice chat based on proximity. I don't believe there's trading with other players yet, and the interactions are fairly limited, but they have confirmed that this is only the beginning of Multiplayer implementation. This update makes the game almost exactly what we all wanted it to be.
This game is rapidly increasing in value and replayability. In my honest opinion, it is now worth the $59.99 price tag. If not now, then it certainly will be in the coming updates. I suggest you grab it, especially if it's on sale!

I was one of the original backers for SotA, and a long time fan of the Ultima series and Richard Garriot (Even an Ultima Dragon, Wildwood Dragon).  I hate to have to say it, but the entire experience has been a massive disappointment.  While I can certainly work around EA expectations, and even some shortcomings if a game experience is good enough, I just can't here.  The UI in SotA is clunky and poorly designed beyond reason. Memory usage to get it looking even halfway decent is off the chart, and is still often looks like a game made 15 years ago. and the titular shroud must be woven from load screens.  I timed them and got numbers anywhere from 2:45 to over 5:00.  That's simply unacceptable.  On top of that, combat is poorly conceived, and generally unexciting, and you'll likely die on an extreemly regular basis, as there is no indication of how difficult an enemy is.  You may take a MOB in one area with ease, then find one that looks identicle in another zone, and be one-shotted due to invisible level differences.
Something has gone extreemly wrong in the development of this game, and with respect to Garriot and the rest of the team, they need to do some serious reworking on their systems.  Stop all content for a long while and completely rethink the UI while streamlinig the engine.  It pains me to say it, but this game is quickly becoming a sinking ship.  It needs to be pulled back into drydock for a full overhaul, or we're all just going to watch it sink.
