This game is... rubish.
Most of the hours are AFK, as it usually is with this sort of genre.
-Summary
The military gameplay is boring, economy-play is isolated from players, and the political side gives few rewards outside the meta glory race
-Payment Model
First of all, It's free to play. You know that means micro transactions, which are purchased through "Crowns". These crowns can either be used to buy Premium time, or bloody boosterpacks! Yes, boosterpacks in a strategy game! You open boosterpacks up for cards for random affects, like find a small bag of gold, merchants move faster, resource production rates increase 5 fold for 6 hours, and some cards give you an army instantly ready to attack or defend. That escalates quickly doesn't it?
Since it's a booster pack, It's entirely random which card you get. You do get cards for playing, based on an achivement system, but you're yet going to have to pay money yet again if you want random free cards on a clock. You have to make an in game purchase twice, if you want free cards as fast as possible. Smooth moves, there.
Not to mention the fact that it rewards players for inviting their friends, needless to say that it wishes to use its predatory payment models to get peopel to buy cards and premium time. There are cards for everything in this game, without exageration. I literally do mean, everything.
-Military
The unit variety is dreadful. There are 5 types of units you can recruit. They are the Peasant, Archers, Pikemen, Swordsmen, and Catapults. Theres the Captains as well, however they don't do fighting, all they do is be alive and issue orders, so you can capture villages, raze them, or you can send them out to village charters which are pre-placed on the map in order to settle them for new villages.
The problem with this, is that only the Archers, Pikemen, and Catapults have any real value. Each soldier takes up 1 population in your army, meaning that the benfiets of having a weak swarming unit like peasents don't exist, because you can field the same amount of pikemen. Archers are the best offensive unit, as they attack from range and can kill most other units with ease. They struggle with walls obviously enough, so you have catapults which destroy them.
And that leaves Swordsmen, versus Pikemen. Pikemen have more health, while Swordsmen deal more melee damage, making them absolutely useless, since both Archers and Catapults do their job better. And with how sieging works, you only need one unit to make it into their keep to win instantly. Meaning that a peasent at 1% health will capture a castle and count just as much, as a captain at full HP.
And to no ones surpise, in any real fortifications those are the only 3 units you see. Capatults excluded, since they're a unit purely for attacking, you can't use them for defense. You can construct specialist towers such as Balista's which do lots of damage, but they're not catapults.
Oh, and you can't field armies versus armies, It's purely siege battles. Siege battles with castles featuring mostly the same lay out, with slight variations to make sure you can't use the same formation over and over again, forcing the oponent to have up-to-date information with scouts for your layouts of the castles, or guess which side is the least defended. Something that wont matter if they send armies from multiple cities back to back, since a fortress can only be so defended, while armies can attack as long as they have the troops to send at you. An enemy can throw the armies of 5 towns agaisnt 1 town, and no matter how much late game tech that town is, It's as good as ereased off the map, because 1 pikeman will make it to your keep, and then, the raze option will PERMENANTLY DESTROY your village. Game over, buy another village.
This lack of permenancy of villages, functionally same layouts of castles almost literally every player has if they can afford it, mechanics of 1 soldier winning the entire siege by making it to the middle of the castle, makes for a very land grabbing, village changing hands frequently type of game. While some players might not mind that gameplay, I very much do, I like naming my villages, giving them unique and fun layouts as well as cherishing the many AFK hours of work I do put into them count.
-Economy
Is non-existant.
The most a player can do is trade at the various markets, in the Parish which villages surround. The parish is a special village that plays into the politics of the game, but that's for later. The Market simply buys and sells goods you bring to with through Merhcants using gold from what are presumably NPCs that conjoure the gold from no-where. There are no player made economies, It's whatever you can generate through taxes, and the economy, which serves very few functions outside of building your army of Archers, Pikemen and Catapults. While it is true the players can sell bows they have crafted through special buildings, and another player can buy those bows in the same Parish, no transaction happened between those two players. It was all through the NPC market. This created a rather isolated feeling for me, who generally apprciates a more economic strategy of creating materials I don't need but are in high demand, to buy materials I do need that are in high supply.
In fact, the only interactions are in the games political system.
-Politics
Is perhaps one of the only things I find interesting about the game. As I mentioned before, there are Parish's, who is owned by the person who is voted into the position of the Parish. The more villages you have in the influence of the Parish, the more votes you have, which leaves the possibility of people absolutely owning multiple villages in a parish dominating and solidifying their influence. However, it gets annoying when a person owned 5 villages, and there are 3 people who each own 1 village.
After Parish's, there is anothe voting system to who owns the County, for the person who owns the town that controls said County. Eligible people is literally anyone who owns a Parish.
Then, there is another position of power, who those people vote on, in a similar system. People vote for who owns the major city to control the Province, out of those who own County's.
And lastly, the very few people who own Provinces, vote on the person who owns the Captial, and is the Monarch of the Country.
These grand and royal titles grant you the power to own the chain of super towns! These super towns, house a bigger army, and only house a bigger army! And maybe get bonus points for the Glory Race of the 20 Houses you can choose from, within those Houses are player factions. Which, simply proclaims whichever house is the winner, wins and continues with the next Glory Race until the Age ends, and new rulesets for the new Age commences, which is usually just faster gathering and production. Some worlds are in their 5th Age, others in their first Age as the servers were just recently created.
Except for the Parish's, which can build specialist buildings giving bonuses to villages in their influence. Meaning the lower level parish's are more interesting to manage.
Such an interesting system, absolutely ruined. It fails to deliver on any monarchical expirence a player may wish to have, in a flipping game about being a medieval ruler! Theres no passing laws, theres nothing to do other than having a larger army capacity. There is very little to manage, and in fact the only way to grow, is to attack other Parishs to claim their flags which allow you to build buildings in these super villages. Of course, theres a card for that as well, the super rare one as well!
In the end, It's really simply a goal to pursue for the sake of pursing it, if you want in the glory race.
Which is most of this game, since there is very little to do, and it preys upon schmucks like me who payed for the premium time. There is very little this game has to offer, and I advise strongly for you to not to play it.
Too much pay to win in a game that could be fun if you didn't get such a large advantage because you pay to have access to research and construction queues.

Cons:

You could leave for 2 weeks but come back as normal as you were before you left, unless other players attacked you of course, but that was the purpose of the game. The developers in Clash of clans made it that way so that you could play more, and if you were off for too long, well, there's a chance that people attack you, and you loose stuff. (WARNING, ESSAY BELOW)
Ori and the Blind Forest is one of the best games I have ever played, and certainly the most beautiful.                The gameplay is like your standard MetroidVania, with tight 2D platforming, lots of spikes and enemies, and occasional puzzles. The main focus in gameplay seems to be movement, as most of the upgrades add more mobility to an already somewhat floaty game. Neither the platforming or puzzles are too difficult for a beginner, but there are lots of secret spots and hidden pickups for a more experienced player of the genre. Gameplay gets 8/10 from me.
But even if the gameplay was awful, which it is not, it would be made up ENTIRELY by the presentation. This is, without a doubt, the most beautiful and emotional game I have ever played. The music is superb. It's played on a wide selection of instruments and ambient sounds, and I would probably pay the game's price just for the soundtrack alone. There's a different song for every section, and they blend smoothly between. Some songs are evocative and uplifting, some are laid-back and content, some are slow, timid, and melancholy, a few are hollow and ambient, and the boss music is exciting and extremely adrenaline-provoking. Most of the songs take one of a few main themes and add variation to fit that area, so you'll often notice a snatch of song that you heard in another, or that the boss music and the normal music of one area have the same melody. The songs blend beautifully with art, creating an incredibly immersive experience.
The art is just as good. You can tell somebody spent hours with an actual paintbrush (or maybe a drawing tablet), painstakingly add every small detail as they craft the world. Many of the art assets are used only once, and the background isn't tiled or reused throughout the entire game; every section of the background is individual and unique. The gameplay is 2D, but most of the game looks like it's at least partially 3D models.
There are only a few things that I didn't like about this game. The background and foreground blended together sometimes, which looked very nice, but made it hard to tell where you could or couldn't jump. I wasn't really a big fan of the boss levels either. Unless you have extremely fast reflexes and are very lucky with the timings, you have to do them over and over by trial and error. If you mess up once you restart the whole thing. By the end it can get very frustrating. More of a minor complaint, but my last problem with this game is you can't go back to certain sections. It doesn't make a whole lot of difference to most people, but if you want to 100% the map or you missed a valuable pickup, it can be very frustrating. But other than those things, this is a near-perfect game.
Ori and the Blind Forest was very good. There were a few gameplay issues that were a bit frustrating, but the art and music were the best I have ever seen/heard in a game, let alone in a platformer. But you can't really call this game just another platformer.
I'm going to miss playing this game now that I've finished it. I highly recommend that you buy it, whether you generally like this type of game or not.

I was told this game had an interesting story and it does. You play as RT, a robot, who lives in the woods as an inventor after an apocalyptic event killed all the humans. All robots that had been built by mankind were left behind in a functional state and there were quite a few who had fully developed cognitive functions.
All robots, RT included are required by the USS a not so fully explained organization of robots to have a job for the now newly founded robot society or they do not get provided electricity. So RT, a robot who doesn't know what he was built for but walk around and do a pathetic robots version of a human sigh builds small items and solves problems. Ahh a thinker! This game will surely be a myst like right?
Not really. For starters you engage in conversations with other characters in the game and their are a few action sequences.
So i thought this game started with an easy set of tutorial style mine game like puzzles in order to introduce players who are not familiar with this style of puzzle solving an introduction for what they were in for. I was confused when the majority of the games puzzles were comprised on this. Thinking back the hardest puzzle i found was the piano puzzle and that was easily solved when i found the blazingly clear to find hint.
2/3rds of the way through the game you will suddenly find yourself in a awful driving game through a forest. Soon after dodging trees, you suddenly find yourself being chased with the camera aimed facing the back of your car. I think the devs thought this would aid the player in dodging the bullets being shot at the player's car. Really this just makes it annoying to dodge the trees in front of you.
Your forced through this sequence twice with little explanation as to why it is happening other than its old technology and that you're in some real trouble if it happens again since you don't have a weapon. THEN INVENT ONE YOUR DOLT.
After these driving sequences the game suddenly changes the way the camera has been working for 90% of the game to follow behind you. You suddenly lose the ability to turn left and right easily as if your character got shot in spin while they were robot vietnam. I thought the game was suddenly trying to limp its way into a 3D adventure game but the running was laughable and there was no jumping. In about 10 minutes i suddenly found myself in the resident evil style camera controls the game was playing with. So not only does this robot not know who he is, the game doesn't seem to know what it is.
This game feels like the developer wanted to make all their favorite games into one game. But they decided to skip the polishing stage before going onto the next style. There is potential from this game. I hope the developer has it all worked out before the next game. The story is a bit compelling.

The planets are extremely unimaginative and the "procedural generation" comes up with things that are 90% similar with only minor differences. A child has more imagination than what you'll find playing this game for dozens of hours.
I've never seen a game that doesn't have a button to quit the game when you open the program. You have to actually load into a saved game, which can take 30 seconds or more, in order to exit the program. This is the most infuriating, basic design flaw that only a complete moron would overlook.

Now that I have over 100 hours in, I can give a pretty experienced review.
I have followed this game before it initially sold, through the monster wave of hype, then the just as large crash of expectations being burned up n flames, and finally the multiple expansions and the continued negative reviews/attacks.
As with any game (or product), previous hype can kill the views of anything sold as greater than it really is.  The creators/company definitely over hyped multiple things, but, they also described/showed spot on what real game play was like.
Going by the initial release, expansions, blogs, press releases/etc., I would have to place a rough estimate of 10% hype, 90% reality.  Yes, it doesn't have multiplayer, and many planets 'were' less inhabited than initial videos showed.
But, they delivered, and continued to deliver, a very well looking, playing game.  There are planets almost void of any animals, while others are overflowing with them (<--Dave pushes aside some of the annoying spikey little critters).
I have explored water planets (just beautiful), deserts, snowy ones, rocky, flat, deep, hot, cold, etc.  A very wide range of planets you could expect to find in the realy galaxy (if it were as beautiful and full of life as we might hope).
Many of the negative attacks seems to revolve around these key points:
- hyped beyond reality of the game, like multiplayer
- $60 being too much for what many consider an unfinished game (because of the hyped parts missing)
- redundancy in how planets/beings/etc. respond/show
My thoughts on these negatives:
As I said before, the hype was about 10% unreal, but, 90% was provided.
The $60 price tag is about the going rate for many games of this size (and a lot smaller).
On the redundancy of gameplay, many big hit/loved games, like Minecraft, PacMan, Call Of Duty, revolve around the same set of tasks/possibilities.  In Minecraft you build/destroy things and meet a small number of possible monsters.  In PacMan, well... you eat/run.  And FPS like COD, you run/shoot/throw grenades.
Going by the amount of things you can do, and I have done, in this game, I would have to say the possibilities are much larger, and the variet wayyy beyond any of those.
If you are looking for a deep story line with histories of aliens and stuff, like Assassins Creed, then this is not the game for you, it is shallow in depth of details.
But, if you love Minecraft, exploring, flying, driving, swimming, coming across a huge amound of variety in scenery, animals, ships, planets, etc. then you will most definitely enjoy this game.
For those who dislike for whatever reasons, I think you must be focusing on that 10% and blocking out the 90% that make this a great game.  As I cannot see (have read a lot) other reasons.  Maybe if you change what you 'expect' you can see how nice a game it is.
For those who like, I'm with you and see the same great achievements and enjoyment as you.  As I plan on doing so for a long time.
For those who have targeted Hello Games, posted 'hate' messages, and make attempts to give a fair review, I feel sorry for you.  I would love to see these same people create something this massive, beautiful, varied, etc. and if you do, and a large number of people who get mad because you didn't provide the 10%, see if you have the same courage and respect of your customers to continue developing, even while being slammed around/attacked/etc.  They made a fortune off this game already and could call it quits at anytime.   Compare your reactions to when you are confronted by massive negativity and let us see how well you respond.
On a last note, I am sure those with hostile 'negative' reviews will continue and probably attack this positive review.  Again, I feel sorry for you and decide not to receive your bad gifts.
For the rest, hope this review helps and I hope you enjoy your exploring.
*kudos to Hello Games, and to the reviewers (both those who like or dislike) who give honest/objective reviews without the need for attacking*

A game with a nifty core concept -as a living planet, nurture your surface and its people through the actions of your avatars, a quartette of diverse and interesting giants. Granted, it's a little Black & White-ish, but that might be mostly coincidence.
Where the game falls short for me is in the execution of that concept: You are given the giants, a quick tutorial explaining how things work in the game, and then you're off to play 30-to-120-minute sessions of cultivating life, settlements, projects and the gradual unlocking of your various giants' powers. Sound intuitive enough? ...Yeah... it could have been.
But here's the thing: it isn't.
For starters, you've got your plants, minerals and animals to keep track of, with two types of each, in two out of three cases distributed between different giants. Depending on what terrain you place something on, it will create a different base object: Blueberries from creating a fruit plant in grassland, elderberries if you use the same ability in a swamp.
Then you've got the 'aspects', such as the fruit aspect and leaf aspect, which are used to both increase the output of a resource (or some other characteristic) and to allow you to evolve it into a completely different, though usually more powerful thing of roughly the same purpose: A strawberry plant from a blueberry plant, for instance. These aspects come in different potency levels, and to ensure you get a strong enough aspect for the mid-range evolutions, you need to first use the forest or ocean giants' fertility-boosting abilities. To ensure a strong enough aspect for the really neat stuff, you additionally need to specialize your giants to the point where even in the fairly late stages of the game, you won't have access to all of their abilities, which can become problematic if you suddenly find yourself in dire need of the thing you didn't pick. This happens a lot.
From each base plant, mineral and animal, you usually have two options of what to evolve it into; more rarely, one. Which you pick usually depends on what you need: For a village to grant you an ambassador with which to upgrade your giants, you need to help them build increasingly demanding projects by providing them with resources. Again, this sounds fairly intuitive, but quickly becomes convoluted, especially later on; you have a limited number of tiles claimed by the village, and the sheer amount of food, gold or technology (the three main 'resources' humans use) needed for the final tier of village projects is frankly ridiculous. There is no doubt an ideal way to produce the right mix of resources for each endeavor, but you will need to be so mind-numbingly efficient about the exact placement of each and every resource that it sucks the fun right out of the game. Some of the evolutions are incredibly arbitrary; for instance, you might be able to evolve the same advanced fish from either a basic 'exotic' (gold-yielding) fish or 'livestock' (food-yielding) fish, based on which aspect you give them. Not only that, but to get the same fish out of different fish, they must be given different aspects, which means the fish you started with affects which aspect the evolved fish will have locked into it. This sort of thing only further tangles some evolutionary trees that are already very convoluted, and turns resource-management strategy into a sort of chess game where you have to play seventeen moves ahead in your mind...
Add to this the very large number of mineral, plant and animal tracks there are to keep track of, and how random some of their synergy properties are (which, as you may guess, are not optional to exploit to the maximum possible)... and we have a memorizing-random-trivia simulator topped with a hefty dollop of obsessive micromanagement, masquerading as a god game about a planet and its giants.
I could go on to mention how if you do too well at providing the villages with resources for their projects, they'll get greedy and start attacking each other and eventually your giants, potentially ruining a great deal of progress and/or ending your game early the moment a giant is killed. I could mention how there are two additional 'resources', danger and awe, whose only real purpose apart from triggering or supporting a few oddball synergies is to suppress the aforementioned buildup of greed, generally rather inefficiently. I could go on to say that it's generally not even worth bothering with those, as dangerous animals tend to be hunted down and wiped out by the village, whereupon they will resume their greed buildup, and awe is so ridiculously hard to accumulate significant amounts of that you may as well not bother, especially as you're constantly on the timer to gather enough resources for the next project before you lose a chance at the next ambassador to upgrade your giants with. I could mention that the projects themselves provide bonuses, that there are many projects, and that each project and upgrade stage of a project has its own little selection of potential bonuses; you can never tell just by looking and seeing that there is a market, that the market is providing a given bonus; you have to click on it and read the tiny text to find out what it's selling in this particular instance. And I suppose I have mentioned all of those things... for better or worse.
All in all, Reus is a game that could have been fun, cozy, casual, relaxing. As it stands, it is very little of any of those things. Instead it is a confusing mess that I can only recommend to people who are extremely confident in their ability to retain obscene amounts of arbitrary information in their short-term memory, and who find enjoyment in showing off their ability to do so. For those like myself who prefer more intuitive and consistent gameplay patterns where you can just learn some basics, refine your skills and make up your own style of gameplay as you go along, this is sadly not the game you're looking for.

Reus is a game with a little promise, but unfortunately only a little to show for it.
Reus sees you command four giants who roam the planet, giving it resources to transform a barren rock into a flourishing human society. Resources may yield Food, Tech, Wealth and/or Awe, and combining the right resources in the right way will give you extra bonuses on their yields. To help humans develop, you should ensure they complete their chosen projects by fulfilling the yield requirements. This will increase the village's yields and give your giants extra powers. A village which grows too fast will become Greedy, and you can only stop them attacking other human settlements by increasing their Awe.
But there is no clear goal in Reus. Everything you do seems to be pointing towards increasing the sum yield of the villages (called Prosperity), which is recorded in a big infographic in the top-left of the screen. So this should be the goal, right? Well, it doesn't seem like it was meant that way. There are no leaderboards recording your best score, or enabling you to compete with friends or online. Instead you are told to get as many achievements as possible to progress to the next "level". This is problematic in three ways. Firstly, it contradicts everything else in the game which is shouting at you to increase Prosperity as much as possible; especially, but not only, when getting an achievement would involve restricting your growth in Prosperity. Secondly, there are far too many achievements and far too many you need to get in one game for you to easily say, "right, I'm going to go for
one" - the game becomes as much about
your "goals" as actually achieving them. And thirdly, the "level-up" implies that each game is
a game, but only a stage in the wider game. So the game is not a game, instead the "game" is. It's confusing and offputting.
In addition, there is really not a great deal of depth. You put resources in a certain place, their yields will maximise - pretty simple. The only thing not allowing you to do that is the fact that resource upgrade trees and special bonuses are hidden from you until you actually place and upgrade the resources. There is no in-game encylopaedia. This means you are making sub-optimal moves not because of your lack of judgement, but because knowledge about the rules of the game - knowledge you ought to possess before the game even
- is obscured to you. If there are interesting decisions to be made in this game, I have failed to encounter any - after 3 hours of play, ie. 6 games - because I can't memorise an upgrade tree for at least 20 different kinds of resource. This unfairly raises the barrier to entry and makes whatever value the game actually has difficult to access.
I know I sound harsh. That's because I
harsh. But, sadly, Reus ultimately fails to make a game with genuine effective depth. If you want a protector-god-sim, maybe you would enjoy this. But if you want to make interesting strategic decisions, this game is best avoided.

It is a mix of a strategy game and a puzzle game. You can play in free play and do whatever you want, but a lot of stuff is locked and to unlock it you have to beat several challenges, such as develop a village a certain way or raise the overall prosperity of the world above a certain value. These have to be completed on a limited time game, where you have 30, 60 or 120 minutes to develop the world from scratch as much as you can (though you can pause to issue orders). I think this works for this game and is really fun.
To develop the world you have to increase the access of resources to villages that spawn. To do so you can place natural resources on patches of land, such as stone quarries or blueberry bushes. These interact with one another to produce stronger effects, and this is where the puzzle elements come in as you have to think how to combine these resources in order to maximize their benefits. You can also upgrade them and change them into other, more advanced resources, but to do that you have to upgrade your giants, and this is where the strategy elements come in.
To upgrade your giants you have to help villages complete projects. When they complete them, by acquiring the necessary resources and fulfilling certain conditions, they give you an "ambassador". These unlock or upgrade abilities in your giants. There are 3 different kinds, one for each type of village, and each giant receives different abilities from each one. You can choose which giant to give them to, but you have to think ahead and formulate a general world improvement strategy in order to put these upgrades to use rather than waste them, since they don't come very easily. You also have to think about how to allocate your time in order to be able to do as much as possible on the limited time you have.
Overall I was surprised on how good this game is, and recommend it to anyone who likes strategy and puzzles.

Look up the definition of "awesome" in the dictionary. When you get to the word, you should see "Galacitc Civilization II: Ultimate Edition" in the 'definition' space, because that's exactly what this game is. I have played space games/simulators/strategy since I could touch a keyboard + mouse, and I can safely say that very little in my experience has come close to the stunning gameplay that GCII has to offer. The only other space game(s) that I feel have a chance of competing against this beast are Sins of a Solar Empire (if you prefer real-time and epic space battles) and Endless Space (if you're wanting a simplified version of GC).
The graphics aren't next-gen due to the age of this sequel; but then again, one doesn't play this game for its graphical quality as GCII will prove to you in the long course/progression of a custom match.
The economic system is by far the best I've seen in any strategy game I have played (and I play most macro-scale strategy games). You have to carefully learn how to balance the taxation of your population with their overall approval of your empire, as well as how much you spend on the different budget groups (Social, Military, and Research). Sliders and percentages make this easy to understand the moment you open up your Domestic Panel (another great aspect of GCII). Keep in mind however that the more money you might place into a specific sector of your empire will yield different results, which all have their benefits and drawbacks (for example, focusing fiscal policies will return you with superior profit, some average research progression, but little military  unless you're spending your profit on fleets instead of further economic upgrades). Overall, the financial situation presented to the player in GCII is simply stunning in its conception as each choice you make will have an effect on your empire.
The Research is kind of standard, depending on how many 4X or macro strategy games you've played (various techs lead into specific tech trees, etc). But the gem of the Research aspect is how it differs between each races (which there are many of by the way) and how there are so many options depending on a number of factors (your race tech tree selection, your research spending, etc). Pretty typical of a strategy game, but your decision on even some of the smaller techs still make big differences (think ahead based upon your current empire trajectory and how the galaxy is progressing!).
The combat is cool at first when you get to see your first ships/fleets in action, but can quickly become tedious and boring (luckily there is a fast forward and end button to wrap up the combat in a timely fashion). It basically plays out like a rock/paper/scissors match based upon your ship configurations (which is reviewed below), your research into armor/sheilds/anti-missile defenses and your weaponry (beam, missile, mass driver). Obviously the superior number in various attacks and defenses compared to your enemies or vice versa will more than likely result in victory or defeat, but other factors are involved (such as hit points and some other minor military research equipment). You do not gain control in the real-time combat, but are able to view it from a multitude of vantage points while the game takes over the battle, which can become pretty epic once the fleet sizes grow to large capital ships. Other than that, nothing to report on combat (obviously planetary invasions are of an equally similar experience with much the same factors involved).
The customization is the crux of GCII, and it shows to great extent what it is capable of. Customizing the very size and decor of individual ship types can sap hours of your time if you have specific designs in mind. It truly is fun to incorporate custom designs into an automated availability system for your fleets (i.e. based on what you craft for a ship type it will become available after the required research has been met without a lot of questions as to whether you wish to use said ship type in games or not).  Micro-management of planets and planet tiles can become aggravating, only because you'll find that sometimes there just aren't enough tiles or there are too many tiles, and deciding whether to balance or focus on a particular output can cause brain tumors (but then that's the fun, in my opinion, of being the supreme ruler over every little choice in your empire).
The AI is extraordinarily intelligent, and by far some of the best in my gaming experience. Diplomacy in GCII is of the utmost importance. Creating trade routes, establishing areas of influence (which you'll learn through playing), and attending galactic council meetings/voting sessions can be some of the more exhilarating aspects of the game (United Planets council once voted against me to place an inter-galactic prisoner base on one of my best planets, doubling its production for the duration of the base, but causing a breakout of prisoners who seized ships and formed pirate fleets behind my lines, which I had to divert forces from my main front in order to crush). The muliple random events (which I recommend leaving at a high frequency) makes the game that much more interesting as well. Choices seem easy in the beginning, but later on may force you to think for a few minutes on each one as good and evil start making an appearance (Paragon and Renegade for your Mass Effect players), with each decision having either short term or long term effects (whether they be empire boosts or differences in the way you are viewed by the United Planet's empires/races).
In the end, Galactic Civilizations II easily obtains a 9/10 on my gaming scoresheet. With tons of replayability and a campaign to create a mood, for any Civ gamers or 4X lovers this is a MUST BUY.

Challenges can be fun. And Gauntlet has the fundamentals of a great challenge: interesting tools for split-second decision making, and difficult encounters that demand you play your very best.
Unfortunately, there are some awful design decisions and sloppy glitches that spoil what would otherwise have been a classic action game.
First, the pacing: Gauntlet has historically been a very fast-paced game. But the obstacles in this Gauntlet are often extremely tedious. Monster spawners take ages to destroy, and you'll have to do it over and over again. Once you've found the right strategy, you'll just be repeating that approach every time, while hoping that one of the game's many glitches doesn't ruin your attempt.
Among these bugs: Enemies will get stuck, invincibly, inside walls; the player character will get stuck in the world; collision detection screws up frequently; attacks will miss enemies directly in front of you; small elevation changes will render abilities useless (God help you if you try to fight on stairs); your defensive skills will sometimes fail to work; and relics can cause your character to lock up.
Any of these glitches can lead to a cheap death, and that often means losing 20+ minutes worth of progress, since the game's rewards are gated behind challenges like "complete three levels in a row on the hardest difficulty without dying once," while your character dies in a split second if you screw up, or the game does.
While Gauntlet seems suited for a quick jump-in, jump-out pace, the level structure actually requires completing several very lengthy levels in a row, which gets very tiring, especially when they consist of the same obstacles over and over. The level design itself is poor, with lots of boring, winding paths, thoughtless blob-shaped rooms, and cheap traps. In one of the randomly-selected sections, there's a room that can trap your character by requiring a key to exit yet not including a key anywhere in the room, or any way to backtrack, forcing a restart.
There are fun elements here, but it's a sloppy product.

I found the gameplay enjoyable for the most part, though it seemed to be incredibly repetitive. Even between the three major areas, most of the monsters were just reskinned versions of one another. It was the same gameplan all the way through, kill the spawners while fending off the minions.
Though I enjoyed the incremental improvements you could gain for your class by fulfilling a series of requirements (kill X number of enemies with ability Y), the highest tier of each requirement for each class was far too high. For example, having played through the game with one class, I still have a lot of grinding to go to complete the class-specific requirements, though I'm at least accruing progress toward the general requirements that are still locked (kill X of each enemy type, etc.).
Lastly, I'm a little annoyed that the fifth class is locked behind a $5 paywall despite having achievements associated with it and no way to unlock it through gameplay. I'd be fine with offering an alternative unlock for $5 if someone doesn't want to put in some time, but it should be unlockable by beating the game with the four base classes or something.
Overall I found it a nice diversion if I wanted some mindless and easy hack-and-slash gameplay. It was free of bugs and could be played fairly well alone despite offering content for multiple players. Thanks for reading.

Overview: (TL;DR:)
This game had a rough launch; many people who bought it were originally disapointed. However, more than a year and a half later, I can say with confidence that this game is 100% worth buying, and an absolute blast, even if you play it solo. I have just a few gripes with the game, but over all I would rate it a 9/10. Additionally, the game is almost always on sale, so while I would recommend buying it at $50.00; this game is a steal at its discounted price ($20.00)
(more indepth review)
Starting with some basic things this game does great:
-Stunning graphics
-A meticulously detailed map of new york, with so much to explore and immerse yourself in you can spend hours just walking around the map. While the map is a bit small, the devs went for quality over quantity, and the map is so densely packed that you never feel like the world is too confining.
-Enough endgame content to entertain you and your friends for weeks
The aspect of this game that is so unique is the endgame. I will admit that the first part of the game, grinding to level 30 and then ascending the world tiers, is a bit boring, especially if you are alone. However, it is all worth it when you reach the endgame, as it almost becomes an entirely new game. The endgame PvE missions are challenging and fun, and require you to strategize with your teammates, creating builds that compliment each other, and devising new plans on how to attempt missions. One example of this are the endgame incursions, which are 45-60 minute long strikes, that are extremely difficult, but unbelievably rewarding. The two main incursions, Clear Sky and Falcon Lost, took my friends and I hours upon hours of attempts, learning from our mistakes and trying over and over until we eventually pulled through.
Additionally, the endgame PvP scene is equally as challening, and even more rewarding. I will admit that there are a few problems with the PvP in this game, but they are very small (more on that later). Exploring the Dark Zone is an adrenaline-pumping experience, especially since the best gear is there, along with the most dangerous enemies (included enemy players with devastating min-maxed builds). And for those who seek balanced PvP, the recently added Skirmish mode is an absolute blast, pitting 2 teams of 4 players against each other, and balancing all stats so that some players don't dominate (it still happens, but at least it's a little more fair)
Now, on to some of the problems the game has.
Let's start with the story. If you are looking for a game with a captivating, polished storyline, you won't find that here, unfortunately. The story doesn't make much sense and the characters are completely forgettable, but the missions themselves are fun. Also the writing is so abysmal that one of the highlights of the story missions is laughing at the dialogue between characters.
My other gripe with the game is that in endgame PvP, it is nearly impossible to win against someone who has a better build than you. And for the most part, this was ok, because most of the best gear isn't very rare, and only takes a little bit of grinding. But then they added classified gear sets, which are unbelievably overpowered and rare builds. I have seen people take on a team of 4 by themselves using these builds, and after hours upon hours upon hours of grinding, I have not come across enough classified gear to make a build out of it. If the developers made classified gear a little bit less rare (currently they are rarer/as rare as Exotic gear), then the disparity between players in PvP could be smaller, which would make the endgame PvP more accessable to all players.
However, these problems barely take away from the game, and I truly believe this game is sure to be worth a buy, especially when it's on sale.

I backed away and went to the starter town and tried out the sewers there.... I was killed in the sewer within about 4 hits. Bad design to put hard hitting mobs in the starter town.
- I wanted to check out crafting in this latest patch but I couldn't find out what I was supposed to do. Talking to the craft master opened a skill window with various skills which again is over complicated. I still don't know what the crafting is like.

Quick note, I bought this game on Kickstarter for $60 back during the initial campaign.
If the idea of the game appeals to you, then I definitely recommend it.  All I can say is that the team behind the game has made astounding progress.  A year ago I thought the game might be a lost cause because graphically it was pretty bad, mechanics were not very fun and overall it felt like the direction was misguided.  I am a huge fan of the U6 and U7 era of Ultima games.  I never got into UO, but my impression is that this game is trying to cater to both types of fans, which may be offputting to some of the more extreme fans of either of those era's in Origin's history.  My personal biases led me to being highly critical of the percieved pay to have fun issues within the game.
Fast forward to today and the graphics in theis game are getting better with each release.  I would not call them great, but the progress really give me confidence they will reach a piont that I'm satisfied with.  The scope of the game is really turning out to be quite large, which was an initial concern of mine due to the way the game instances areas.  I'm still not sure about the "pay to have fun" issues yet.  Housing seems to be the most egregious issue, but the team has addressed that in a number of ways.  I'm not sure they help the casual player yet, but I'm going to be open minded moving forward.
In the end, it's not where I think it's a good final product, but I am very confident that the team will get it there based on their current rate of progress.  If you have a capped internet connection, then you definitely need to consider that this game is updated frequently and the updates can be huge.  It's not uncommon for two major updates to happen during one of their scheduled releases.  The team is dedicated to having a stable game each release, so this is a side effect of that.

This is proof and evidence that state-of-the-art graphics and even cutting edge gameplay doesn't always make a great game.
This top-down, RPG style puzzle adventure had a very rich, powerful, and almost life-changing story. This game made me rethink what I should do with my life before it's too late.
The soundtrack was stellar. It was very fitting with what was going on in the story. Tense moments would have an alarm sound, like what you would hear in a space station (this game is called "To the Moon", afterall!), and scenery scenes (yes, I did that) had amazing violins and a beautiful piano.
The story itself wasn't too hard to follow, either. I, personally, have a hard time following with time travel/in-depth adventure stories/movies, including Back to the Future. But this game has made their story crystal clear and I was able to follow along with ease.
The general setting is you are two Doctors/Scientists who travel back into a man's memories to fufill his one, life-long wish in an artificial environment before his real life death. Play the game, and you'll know what I mean.
As mentioned earlier, graphics aren't the best. I would actually say they were decent for a pixelated top-down indie. I wasn't too much of a fan of the gameplay, but the story itself got me hooked and forced me to continue till the end with tears. What made this game even better was the comic relief. At moments when something was going down, there were giggle moments to release that tension.
Pros:
+Amazing, tear jerking, easy-to-follow storyline
+Spectacular soundtrack
+Comic relief before/during/after tension
+Unexpected references
Cons:
-Mediocre graphics
-Decent, but not great gameplay/controls
-You haven't bought this game yet
Verdict:
The pros outrule the cons 10/1. You do not need the best graphics to make a great game (take Terraria and Minecraft for example). For this game, the story and the soundtrack made it spectacular, despite mediocre graphics and somewhat "meh" gameplay.
10/10

Based on this first episode alone, I'd give it a 6.5/10.
It definitely shows promise, but also shows that its developers are still learning their way.  That's not necessarily a bad thing, but it needs saying.
Pros:
* Decent (not awesome, but not wince-worthy) voice acting.
* Good graphics
* Most puzzles make sense.
Cons:
* Several of its puzzles required doing something, running to another area and doing one thing, running back to the 1st area and doing one more thing, etc, etc, back and forth, to look for the new hotspot, despite it being obvious that it would be needed earlier.
* The character sometimes gets stuck walking in a direction, until you *reverse* course or let go of the keys.  (eg: hold D to go right, then after a few seconds tap W to make yourself turn left... only you don't)
* Unable to talk about all topics w/ a character - you can only ever pick one topic, then never again.
TL;DR: It's good, but not mind-blowing.  If you're on the fence, maybe wait for reviews based on Episode 2.

I feel like this game has so much potential, but it just didn't quite hit the nail on the head. It has a great concept and storyline potential, set in a post-apocalyptic world where humans are extinct and AI inhabit the world, which totally had be engaged throughout. It's got some really nice graphics/artwork too which is always great.
However, I find that a few elements really let it down. It's a pretty slow game throughout, which isn't necessarily a bad thing if you just want something chilled to play for a bit, but it also generally seems pretty buggy and unpolished. I'm a mac user, so by no means am I on a powerful gaming pc, but I've still managed to play every other steam game without any problems. I found the response time for keys and cursor movement to be very slow even when all graphic options have been reduced to the lowest. A few other little things can be a bit irritating, like running through an area with a camera angle change and suddenly finding you're running backwards on yourself.
I think they really missed a trick by not playing up the scavenger aspect of the main character. There isn't that many items you can carry in your inventory/utilise, and you can't pick a lot of items up until specific points in the quest which is quite annoying if you've already been in that area and found it once before. It was also quite short, and seemed to end quite abruptly, but I was disappointed when it did end so I guess that's a good sign.
If you can get it on sale I would definitely recommend it, but wouldn't really say it's worth the full price of £10.99 as there's only a few hours of gameplay.

Now that I have over 100 hours in, I can give a pretty experienced review.
I have followed this game before it initially sold, through the monster wave of hype, then the just as large crash of expectations being burned up n flames, and finally the multiple expansions and the continued negative reviews/attacks.
As with any game (or product), previous hype can kill the views of anything sold as greater than it really is.  The creators/company definitely over hyped multiple things, but, they also described/showed spot on what real game play was like.
Going by the initial release, expansions, blogs, press releases/etc., I would have to place a rough estimate of 10% hype, 90% reality.  Yes, it doesn't have multiplayer, and many planets 'were' less inhabited than initial videos showed.
But, they delivered, and continued to deliver, a very well looking, playing game.  There are planets almost void of any animals, while others are overflowing with them (<--Dave pushes aside some of the annoying spikey little critters).
I have explored water planets (just beautiful), deserts, snowy ones, rocky, flat, deep, hot, cold, etc.  A very wide range of planets you could expect to find in the realy galaxy (if it were as beautiful and full of life as we might hope).
Many of the negative attacks seems to revolve around these key points:
- hyped beyond reality of the game, like multiplayer
- $60 being too much for what many consider an unfinished game (because of the hyped parts missing)
- redundancy in how planets/beings/etc. respond/show
My thoughts on these negatives:
As I said before, the hype was about 10% unreal, but, 90% was provided.
The $60 price tag is about the going rate for many games of this size (and a lot smaller).
On the redundancy of gameplay, many big hit/loved games, like Minecraft, PacMan, Call Of Duty, revolve around the same set of tasks/possibilities.  In Minecraft you build/destroy things and meet a small number of possible monsters.  In PacMan, well... you eat/run.  And FPS like COD, you run/shoot/throw grenades.
Going by the amount of things you can do, and I have done, in this game, I would have to say the possibilities are much larger, and the variet wayyy beyond any of those.
If you are looking for a deep story line with histories of aliens and stuff, like Assassins Creed, then this is not the game for you, it is shallow in depth of details.
But, if you love Minecraft, exploring, flying, driving, swimming, coming across a huge amound of variety in scenery, animals, ships, planets, etc. then you will most definitely enjoy this game.
For those who dislike for whatever reasons, I think you must be focusing on that 10% and blocking out the 90% that make this a great game.  As I cannot see (have read a lot) other reasons.  Maybe if you change what you 'expect' you can see how nice a game it is.
For those who like, I'm with you and see the same great achievements and enjoyment as you.  As I plan on doing so for a long time.
For those who have targeted Hello Games, posted 'hate' messages, and make attempts to give a fair review, I feel sorry for you.  I would love to see these same people create something this massive, beautiful, varied, etc. and if you do, and a large number of people who get mad because you didn't provide the 10%, see if you have the same courage and respect of your customers to continue developing, even while being slammed around/attacked/etc.  They made a fortune off this game already and could call it quits at anytime.   Compare your reactions to when you are confronted by massive negativity and let us see how well you respond.
On a last note, I am sure those with hostile 'negative' reviews will continue and probably attack this positive review.  Again, I feel sorry for you and decide not to receive your bad gifts.
For the rest, hope this review helps and I hope you enjoy your exploring.
*kudos to Hello Games, and to the reviewers (both those who like or dislike) who give honest/objective reviews without the need for attacking*

Relaxing simulation about elemental gods building civilization and environments on a mini-planet.
The gameplay is unique. You only control the 4 gods which can carve out deserts, mountains, and oceans. You plant herbs, fruits, minerals, and cattle to attract villagers.  The goal is to nurture a prosperous village, which is achieved through the strategetic planting of natural resources. It's simple at first but gets complex.
Should I plan the cattle next to the planets or minerals? Do I want to create more standard minerals or advanced? The game mechanics remind me more of a puzzle than a simulation, as strategic placement of cattle/herbs/fruits/minerals is the KEY to success.
If you want a relaxing and unique simulation gameplay and don't care about the story (which doesn't exist), you should check it out. It's a smart indie game and can be played in chunks.

I am going to give this a tentative recommendation. This is not a great game. It's not even a good game. It's a game that caters to a particular niche of god-game lovers: those being the people who like to set up a world for people to live in and only affect it enough to watch them grow. For the people that like such a game, this one, while simplistic, will fulfill that craving. For those of us who prefer a more hands-on approach, this game will quickly become mind-numbingly boring.
First, the game involves the player controling four primordial gods. They are Mountain, Sea, Forest, and Swamp. But just like the dollar store Avatar knockoffs they're named after, they really don't do much. You set up the world how you want it, wait for people to spawn, then use the gods to help them grow by planting flowers, animals, and minerals around their town. Most of the time, I had them looming over the villages without doing anything. The use of ambassadors from the different types of settlements as ways to buff each god is interesting but really just adds false complexity. The powers you get morph already existing plants and animals into different plants and animals, which can further improve the resources of the towns. All good. Except that the novelty of that wears off after forest ambassador number five is spawned and you have nowhere to put him.
And that's the entire game. Lay the groundwork for the settlements to improve by creating plants and animals, watch the town grow and complete projects, so you can get ambassadors, so you can plant more plants and magic more animals, so they can complete projects, so... well, you can see where this is going. I did enjoy myself for a few hours, and I managed to snag it during a sale, so I can at least say I got enough fun out of it to be worth the money. Though I believe the eight hour play time speaks for itself.

I'm a backer that hoped for a spiritual successor of Ultima Online which I grew up on. I hope that SotA some day will be worthy of that title but as it is I cannot with clear conscience recommend it in its current state.
The core issues with SotA right now are:
* Combat system needs to be completely redone ( the "card deck" system is too distracting and taking away control from the players)
* Why oh why do we have level system underpinning the skill based system?
* Loading times need to be drastically reduced (waiting for a "scene" to load for a minute+ is killing the game)
* Crafting is not a viable role to play on its own, which is a huge shame
* Everyone and their dog needs to essentially be at least to some degree a crafter
* More and bigger locations... which brings me to my next issue:
* The overmap... it makes me cringe everytime I think about it... SotA needs to be huge open world without loading screens, it is technically doable, many other games are out there to prove it so why not SotA?
* The multiplayer options (solo, friends only or multiplayer) need to go away... shared session all the way please... Other modes seem like a crude workaround to small and limited number of locations in game which leads to people crowding areas.
I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys adventure games. I have really high hopes for this game.

I purchased this game in pre-alpha because it looked like a very promising Adventure MMO. While there is quite the learning curve in its current state (something that is being made easier with the developers focus on the  New User Experience), it is very rewarding to those who invest the time to learn the games mechanics. It is one of the few games since I was a child that has given me a real sense of exploration and adventuring. Often times I play in a small group of friends, with each of us filling different roles. The games combat uses a deck based system that was initially confusing. After learning how exactly it works, it is a refreshing take on the typical hot bar approach to combat that is both intuitive, intriguing, and satisfying. Even more so if you're familiar with games such as "Magic, The Gathering". The Game also features a robust and complex crafting system that feels rewarding.
The way that Quests are handled where you actually have free form dialogues with the NPCs to advance your quests is outlandishly gratifying. For example: In one of the earlier quests I couldn't find the person I needed to talk to, who was the guard captain of a city. On a hunch, I simply asked a guard where I could find her and e told me exactly where she could be found. The ability to do something such as this blew my mind. Some of the stories told through the quests are also quite gripping, and at times can even be morally dark.
Typically, I don't care for housing in games, however one of the most interesting aspects of the game is the Player Owned Town system that offers players the ability to stake out their own place in the world, and (quite literally) put themselves on the map. I've not played long enough to experience housing, but it is something that I look forward to.
While the game does not hold your hand, or clearly explain some of the more advanced features (again, something that is being improved) the support and willingness to help from the community to aid new players is astounding. Usually I can find how to do something with a quick search on Google, which will yield a video tutorial or an incredibly detailed forum post on exactly what I'm looking for.
While there are some bugs I've not encountered anything that has made the game unplayable. Though some of the load times are a bit long, certain areas will have a low frame rate, and the game has crashed (only once), these issues get better with each update. I still highly recommend this game for players who are looking to immerse themselves in a world that is both wildly entertaining and meticulously detailed.

TLDR: Originally super disappointed with how this game was shaping up. Now, super excited, they are constantly making improvements. This game is genuinely fun and enjoyable and inspires a true sense of adventure. The Shroud team is crushing it.
A little background; I was into Ultima Online up until the Second Age and have dabbled in the other expansions since. I'm a huge fan of the open world and skill progression style games. Ultima is really one of my fondest memories of an online multiplayer game world.
I backed Shroud on day one, because I think the team behind the game shows true heart and really wants to build a world that their fans and they themselves will enjoy.
When the game came out for testing, it was too early for me to tell if I would like it, but I stuck with it. This became a pattern. Every update that would release, I'd still be like "eh, not yet."
This eventually culminated to a point where I said, "I'm not sure this game will ever be for me." With that, I kind of wrote the game off, wishing them well, because I knew it would be something special to those that wanted what they were building.
I always kept checking in through the newsletters and checking the Steam Store page.
Recently I re-installed the game again and gave it a shot.
I've been pleasantly surprised. The team has made HUGE bounds on this game, and as someone running the game with a 1070 video card, the game is beautiful.
I love the overland map, it gives me an old school Final Fantasy feel and really makes the world feel huge and detailed.
The combat has come a long way, and is starting to really feel polished and fluid.
I tried out the hotbar system, which is pretty much what you'd expect. But what's really neat is the Deck system. I will admit I gave that system some harsh criticism when I started, I just didn't think you needed to re-invent the wheel.
But I take that back now, the Deck system is really enjoyable and brings something unique and fun to the game. Being able to combo different abilities together, or being able to stack like abilities together to make more powerful variations really lends for some interesting tactics/scenarios.
The quest are well written and some are really dark. And the NPC cities/dungeons/content are designed really well and just awesome. Love it.
My main complaints thus far are that the UI needs more polish, it just is a LOT of info to have to manage. Spells/attacks need more detailed or just better visuals. NPC/ambient sounds need a polish, some areas have some really annoying repetitive sounds that trigger. A good deal of the player towns I’ve encountered are barren/not thought out well and just kind of boring.
A lot of the issues I just posted are being addressed, like they are doing a UI pass to clean things up, which is awesome. They are still actively adding VFX to abilities.

I was casually going through some old news posts from various different news sites on the internet. After a few hours of searching around I found this one article that really blew my mind. The article goes "Richmond police found two men dead in a vehicle Sunday afternoon in the Czech Crown Lands Court public housing complex in the West End. Victims names are found to be "Pat Cykánes" and "Mat Jebânek". Officers were called to the 3300 block of Bunchë Place shortly after 1 p.m. for a report of a “person down,” said police spokeswoman Lucie Myslikova."
This really made my stomach crawl. I felt like I missed something that was very important on me growing up. I started having these awful spasms of pain within me as I was thinking of everything that Pat & Mat had awaken in me since I was a little jit.
If you don't know what Pat & Mat is, it is basically a Czechoslovak stop-motion animated series created by Lubomír Beneš and Vladimír Jiránek, which first appeared in 1976. The main characters of the series are two handymen, Pat and Mat, who are inventive but extremely clumsy. As of 2015, 91 episodes of the show have been produced, and it has been syndicated in a large number of countries due to its lack of dialogue. For me, Pat & Mat is everything. I own alot of fan products, but the most "questioned" one is a custom made 45cm high, 9cm thick♥♥♥♥♥♥♥that has the textures of Pat on it. I usually combine it with a Mat buttplug.
I felt lost, and went immediately back to google to search anything that would help me to fight my ongoing constant panic attacks. I tried everything; Overdosing on Antidepressants, Opiates, Hallucinogens, Amphetamines, Inhalants and alot of other medical drugs. I tried Overdosing, Inhaling carbon monoxide, Drowning, Electrocution, Jumping in front of a train and much more. Everytime I tried, I just couldn't continue. I had this feeling of wanting to end the pain and disorder I had in me, but I just couldn't. I had something I wanted to fix, that even a suicide couldn't fix.
After weeks of constant alcohol and drug abuse, I finally found it. It was the craving feeling of emptiness caused by the missing of Pat & Mat in my life. I finally got it! Realizing it got me getting up from my kitchen table, running to the computer and opening Steam. I typed "Mat & Pat" on the search bar. Many tries of trying to type it right with my shaky hands and blur vision I got it right once and for all. I saw that the game was on sale for 1€. It felt like it was a gift from the gods. A sign. The saviour of my life, Jesus, had given me this opportunity to save myself from the depths of death.
All I had in my bank account was 1.01€, which was just enough to buy the game to my steam account. I downloaded the game and felt the rush of adrenaline running through me as I waited for the game to download. 10%, 20%, 30%... A few minutes of downloading the game felt like forever, as I tried to prepare myself for what was coming to me.
Once the game had downloaded on my computer, I opened the game as fast as I could and the first sign of my missing buddies got warmth on my heart. Pieces moved to their places. I felt... happy. I felt better than I had ever felt before. I had this constant erection that really was the first one I had since the "Breakdown" of me from a few weeks back. I had erectional disfunction that got cured just now. Now, everytime I see something Pat & Mat related, I get this huge erection, that lasts for as long as I play the game.
From that day on, I have been playing this game on every single place where I could just open my laptop and launch the game. I got kicked out of my job, lost connections to my family and friends, but it is okay. I am happy and that is what matters to me. I feel complete.
Pat & Mat were a massive part of my childhood. I was seriously addicted on the show. Every morning, 6 a.m., I woke up just to watch Pat & Mat on the television. They were the ones that motivated me on living my life. There would be nothing in my life, if it was not for Pat & Mat.
Thank you for reading my Review. Hopefully you buy this game, since it has saved mine and many others' lives. 10/10.

I usually don't write reviews.  And by usually I mean, this is my first one.
I found this game because someone had it on a top-50 best game storylines list.  I decided that that was at least enough to warrant spending $1.99.
The game is short, no doubt about it.  I finished it in about 4 hours.  I am a very fast reader and the words barely get on the screen before I ready to move on.  That being said, there is plenty of storyline to be had.  The ending is a little abrupt gameplay wise ... I expected that I was about to be given a plot twist but the story was actually over.
The music is fantastic.  I'm usually pretty harsh on music, but even at its most simplistic, it was all perfect for the part of the story it accompanies.  I still can't get the main theme out of my head at this moment.  The inclusion of the soundtrack was just gravy.
As far as a "game" goes, there is very little gameplay to be had.  It is 2 steps up from being an interactive novel.  Very quickly I found that I didn't care at all, and the few gameplay elements that were included could have been thrown out for all I cared about them.
I wish we had learned a little more about the female protaganist because her story seemed to have been really deeply thought out but then not all able to fit into the storyline.
I thought that the main playable characters were a little too wacky for the rest of the story.  I understand that they were sort of like the "comedic outlet" for a very somber story, but sometimes it detracted too much.
All in all, I thought this was a very fresh idea and I enjoyed it very much.  I will think about this story quite a bit in the next couple weeks.  It seems like it could be a movie, but I think that screenwriters would screw it up big time.  Somehow, the simple pixel graphics held this game together by making you get engrossed in the music and the story.

While this game has high production values with nice graphics and effects, I do not think it came together well.
The controls never felt right to me - the mouse & kb felt clunky and poor for character movement, while the gamepad felt floaty and way too imprecise when trying to select objects or manipulate puzzles.  I also encountered two places where the game forces you to mash on a button that is the same one that skips dialog, causing you to immediately skip the next line of dialog when the mashing is completed (in one instance you skip the player character saying a line that helps guide you to what you will need to do next).  That's pretty frustrating.
The writing is decent (though very predictable) but the voice acting is slow and just not enjoyable to listen to - while I understand that it is an artistic choice, I wish game designers would try something new for robot characters versus just having their voice actors do a deadpan monotone and draw out each and every line of dialog to such a degree that the player just wants to skip though it.
The puzzle design is not that great, nor is it all that engaging.  Don't expect to reason out a puzzle and do any clever inventory manipulation - in nearly every case, the character just says what they want to do, and you as the player just carry it out.  There are also several instances where there are items in the world your character will either not interact with, refuses to pick up, or do not even show up in the world as an object you can select or examine, until you discover one thing the game designer set up for you to find.  It's just A to B every single time.
There is also a really out-of-place and clunky set of action sequences in the mid-game that just feel half-baked; as well as some not-quite instadeath turret avoidance in the late game.  The controls may trip you up here again - they don't feel good or responsive enough for these sequences.
I am very torn as to whether I'll try episode 2.  The regular price being asked for each episode does not feel at all appropriate, so I can only recommend you test these Uncertain waters if you get to do so at a substantial discount.  Even at sale prices, it's not a game I can recommend without all the troubles I've outlined above.

I have been playing Tiger Woods '08 PC on a regular basis since it came out back in 2007. No modern game has come close. That is until this game was released.
The graphics are top notch and very realistic. The addition of trees and bushes since last year improved the visuals a great deal. The graphic improvements will no doubt continue in the future with the possible addition of 3D blades of grass using Nvidia’s graphics technology.
Online play is great with turn based multiplayer and the ability to play with up to 8 players. You can stop and resume your round at a later time. There are loads of different play modes available. If tournaments are your thing you can participate in many online. The game also has a cool replay feature that allows you to watch the last round from a number of different angles. Your opponent(s) can see the replays as well.
Another big plus for the game is the freecam mode. Take a virtual tour of the entire game from every conceivable angle and soak in the wonderful immersion that this game provides.
This game has lived up to its potential. Every update over the last year has shown improvement, especially the most recent update from last month. This community driven game will only get better in the months and years to come. Be sure to give it a try and you won't be disappointed.

I'm posting this review as positie out of sympathy. I like where the updates are going, but have a few suggestions. I think that these couple of ideas might turn this game back to what it was intended to be:
1. The space station
1a. The station has bars, you should be able to get drinks with different effects
1b. More layouts. You should be excited to explore the station, not avoid visiting it
1c. Put that procedural generation system to work. You sould be able to pick up quests from different people you                       meet. They should also not be just fetch quests (gather 100 plutonium) but have other values, like joining a faction, saving a stuck ship, and just be fun like watchdogs 2 and the fallout series' side quests.
2. Planets
2a. More intelligent species. Think back to the movie avatar. There should be primitive, but intelligent life, that you can decifer the language of and participate in the culture of (since they are primitive, thy will be restricted to one planet). The book out of the silent planet by C.S. Lewis is an example of this. He is on Malacandra and finds an otter like species. He hangs out and learns the culture and eventually gets to participate in a large fish hunt.
2b. Some planets with no settlements. Every planet you land on has pre established bases, greatly detracting from the exploration aspect of the game
2c. More vegetation. Every planet I've been on has been a worthless ball of uninteresting clay. Seriously. I have heard talk of ungle planets, but havent seen a single one.
2d. This is essential. I like this game, but you guys showed and promised that what you saw in space you would see on the planet, but this is never true. Ever. You guys need to fix this.
3. Mechanics
3a. Online multiplayer, as promised, is essential.
3b. The nemesis system, harking from the middle earth games, would make the game much funner. There should be procedurally generated explorers and pirates that you can befriend or betray (or they can betray you). They should feel like you know them or strongly hate them. The player should also have a reputation that other players can track others down in a bounty system.
3c. Multi crew ships. As in star citizen, another game with a huge hype train, multicrew ships are very fun. To be able to walk in a ship you can fly is a life changing experience. I loved it in AC 4 and rogue and even loved watching it in star citizen early access videos. While other players are extremely rare, you should be able to hire NPC's. Which brings me to my next point...
3d. In depth dialogue like in torment tides of numeria and wasteland 3 (as seen in demos). Dont make the npx's machines.
3e. PLEASE OVERHAUL COMBAT
3f. You should be able to see your character
4. Space going races
4a. Meaningful racial combat. They should have procedurally generated wars with procedurally generated reasons.
4b. Government. There should be worlds with vast cities and massive farms. You can procedurally generate the interiors. There should be a military for the different races (advanced inteligent races) that you can participate in and just become a member of their society. You should even be able to participate in government.
I know this seems like a lot, but if you follow this guide, you will get back to your 200000 player count quite quick. I have faith in you Hello Games!

I have played my fair share of Gauntlet games in my day. Originally in the arcades, every death meant I had to pump more quarters into the machine. Now, with the series hitting multiple consoles spanning different generations, Gauntlet is back after a rather long hiatus. Is it back to the feelings we all know and love, or was that really just me looking back with rose-tinted glasses? After playing this, I may be going with the latter.
In a very arcadey fashion, Gauntlet puts players in the role of one of four classes. In a top-down view, they will hack and slash (or shoot arrows and fireballs depending on the class) at hoards of enemies while they try to make it through the dungeons while gathering as much gold as they can. Don’t forget getting chased by death himself in some of the more frantic levels.
Progression is done not through leveling up, but through masteries. There are even death masteries that will allow characters to not take as much damage from certain traps if they die enough from them. Basically, doing normal stuff throughout the game will allow players to get better at that certain skill. It’s not groundbreaking in any way, but it at least let me improve my characters.
The classic classes are all back, and each plays very differently from one another. The Warrior is a brutal melee fighter, the Valkyrie utilizes her shield to both block and attack from afar, the Elf uses bows and bombs and the Wizard combines elements to fire off magical attacks. Each has their own play style and really changes up how the player will handle situations, but in the end, most of it is pretty mindless.
The standout here is the co-op play. Online multiplayer with three other people was a frantic, hack n slash mess, but in a good way. Since it didn’t take much thought to play, we ended up have a fun time just hacking away at enemies while talking. Also, fighting for the crown when someone would get hit quickly became the meta-game of it all, even though the crown does nothing except increase points at the end of the level.
The story is minimal at best, but the voice acting that is there, along with the comedic overtones are well done and even made me laugh a few times. Sure, there is no “Sexy pants!” being screamed like in Sacred 3, but the dialog that is there never takes itself seriously and gives off a bit of charm that I enjoyed.
Gauntlet isn’t much of a thinking man’s game. Find a class you like and have at it. The Wizard will be the one most people avoid, but even then, with a few other buddies along for the ride, it can be a rather fun time. Single player can get a bit more monotonous, but it is the same for the multiplayer; just having some others to share in the mindless action helps out a lot.
For $20, players get a rather fun game. Yeah, I still feel more love for the older versions of the game, but I think that’s just the nostalgia in me. Even in single player, I didn’t mind taking on the hoards of enemies with my shield throwing Valkyrie. Jumping online is where the game gets hectic, but way more fun, and the tongue-in-cheek nature of the dialog and story offer up a few laughs at times. I would say pick it up, but if you do, try to at least convince one or two friends to pick it up with you. You’ll all have a more enjoyable time together.
