Apparently I'm not saying anything new about this, since it's so highly rated and regarded already, it seems, but nonethless:
A game that I have played, stopped playing, and come back to playing again many times over the years. I've enjoyed it a lot, and for some reason a big title or two will come out and I'll eventually forget about galactic civ. for a while, and then eventually  I'll stumble upon it... always surprised by how much I enjoy playing it, time and again.
It lacks some of the graphical 'bells and whistles' of a Civ-type of turn-based strategy game, but as any player of ck2 knows, what a game lacks in polish can be very much made up for in actual game content and replayability. The depth of galactic civ (and ck2, for that matter) makes civilization look like simplistic child's play (unplayable to me, as a by-product) in comparison.
Distinctive differences/cool elements of the game:
- Skill trees are actually unique to every race.
- fully customizable ships (designing ships became one of my favorite elements of the game early, to my surprise).
- plot/narrative elements that differ game-to-game, making it very replayable.
- Races themselves are fully customizable, adding another layer of replayability and depth to the game's customization.
On the downside, it has many layers of things to control and 'develop,' so to someone coming to this from civ or simpler games of that nature, galactic civ could be daunting, by all means, even overly so. This is a game for a real turn-based strategy-lover, who wants to have a depth of 'control' that might be beyond the average gamer, whoever or whatever that even means...?
I'd say for a strategy-lover (someone who likes games like ck2, europa universalis, etc.) it's a must have regardless of price (I don't think it's more than $20, this far from publication). If you're a civilization/spore lover and you're worried this might go a little too deep and not have the 'sheen' you look for in a game, wait for it to go on sale, as it does every so often, and get it for $5, and give it a shot; Who knows? The developers clearly labored over it with love, and put in a lot of good work in making a very fine game (as I see it).

My disappointment is sadly turning me away from this game. The combat might be solid, but I simply can't see any charm in the lore or the people within it. Dialogue is surprisingly bland, the environments (although diverse) are stagnant and uninteresting. When it comes to RPGs for me, the characters in party and in the world around you need to be interesting in order for me to be immersed in the game I'm playing. Unfortunately, I don't find the protagonist interesting (she might become more interesting as time goes on, but she initially feels like a girl that doesn't care about anything), and the NPCs in the world are even worse.
My problem with the interaction of the world might have been better if I had known that this was a lore that was already set and that the characters are already set-in-stone. I simply didn't see the charm of the game, and it's a shame because the combat is great, and the gameplay is nice, but I simply don't have and excitement for the game when I find the characters and lore this boring. I understand the positive reviews, and more power to them, but I honestly think this franchise might not be my cup of tea.

I like the game... However, this is not a casual friendly, play by myself type of game.  It's a free-roaming game (sandbox)... so not a lot of in depth quest lines.  It's a game all about the community.
Best gear is player-made.. so yea you can twink, power-level, etc.   So you have two options... join a great guild.... or grind.  I'd recommend joining a guild.
Combat deck-based system is new to me "think Yugioh" and is okay, but not something I enjoy heavily as a twitch, skill-based player.  There is none of this in this game.   The skill for combat is building an optimized deck.  Not a super-fun system, but not a throw away either... around patch R33 it was horrible... now heading into patch R40 it is better, but still VAST room for improvement (cycle targetting is horrible, but you can double-click, but I cycle... so meh.)
Crafting is fun and robust (or if you hate that type of stuff... annoying as hell), but I really like it in this game.  Although, the day-one guys will try to gouge you on just about everything.  Joining a guild should help offset that.
Housing is cool... getting property though is likely going to cost you real world money from the day-oners...  There are raffles... that anyone can participate in, but the day-oners have all the gold.  So if you want property... GRIND for gold or spend real cash.  Good thing is... owning property gives you NO advantage at all... so there is that.
I've seen some people saythat the game is P2W... not the case... everything that costs money is comestic.  No advantage.
The biggest problem is... if you don't want to join a guild... DO NOT even PVP until you can hold your own in a level 5 skull area.  No skill caps... day-oners right now can level FOREVER... thus making them PVP gods!  So attack enmasse or DIE!  That is THE major problem with this game right now.
But overall it's a cool game... a timeline to final release would make this game easier to say yes or no too... but without that it's tough.  Overall though.. I would recommend... still better than 90% of the crap out there.

I'm not one for writing reviews, and this is my first on a game. That said, To The Moon is an outstanding game. Let me go over the pros and cons.
Cons:
-The Controls are awful. Absolutely awful. Many people can deal with them just fine, but I often find myself frustrated with them.
Thats it. That's the only problem I have with this game.
Pros:
-The story is so unique and beautiful, nothing I've played has come close. This game makes you look at life a little bit different. I'm not going to give away much, but To The Moon has, hands down, the best story in a video game in my opinion.
-The music is stunning. I often sit in front of my computer, game paused, just listening. As a composer and musician, I applaud To The Moon and the music it offers. I recommend buying the soundtrack along with the game. I'd also like to add that the music isn't just good, it fits the game perfectly.
-The game is a very emotional and moving, but it's not like that all the time. The light-hearted humor and cultural references really keep things fresh and funny.
-Everything from characters to visuals is perfect.
To sum everything up, this game is mind blowingly good. Its ONLY downside is the controls, which I can overlook for the music and story in a heartbeat. To The Moon is EASILY one of the best games I've played to date.

This installment is a vast improvement over the second. It should be noted though that this is still a console title that was ported to pc much like the second title. It both looks and plays much better with reintroduced cover mechanics that for some reason were omitted from the second title.
The cover mechanics in this game however feel too simplified compared to the origonal game. I this title you feel quite vulnerable sometimes when being shot at when trying to make use of these mechanics and I have found it is much easier to simply forgo them altogether and try and play it as you would any other fps.
The immersion is overall quite well done however it is broken regularly by a type of award system that is intended for a multiplayer campaign where two players will rush to complete given objectives for points to win the overall campaign. The basic concept of this is interesting however but I simply wish there was a way to turn off all the notifications for it as they remain even in single player and it does break the immersion. If not for that I would give the asthetics top marks.
The controls are both improve and worsen over the second installment, there is a more realistic range for sensitivity however there is no option to remap the controls.
Although the multiplayer side of things seems to be dead I will simply say that some of the game modes do seem quite interesting and inventive especially when compared with the usual fps game modes that are offered. I wouldnt buy it for the multiplayer obviously unless however you have enough friends who play it/who are also interested in it and you can then host locally.
I also thik one of the bigger aspects and in this case downfall of this title is that the AI are not as intelligent as in the origonal. A simple example of this is that if an enemy is pinned behind cover they wont always peak the same angle or if they do they may crouch if that option is there in addition to the AI squad mates using suppression fire and trying to flank you.
Over all this is not a bad game however I honestly feel that the origonal was by far the better single player experience with substantially better AI, more immersive environments and a bette all round feel to it.
So while the game is good for a bit of funI would not get it outside of a very good sale, I got it on steam in a fear collection pack at 75% off and in all honesty I would not buy it full price

The first F.E.A.R. is a genre-straddling classic, combining intense and engaging firefights with some jarring scares. The second F.E.A.R. tried to follow that act with more refined graphics and gameplay but lost something in the translation, managing only to be a competent shooter with incompetent spooks. Following that downward trajectory you will find F.E.A.R. 3, an even stranger mish-mash of concepts than its predecessors. It makes a surprising attempt at keeping true to the lore of the series while further refining the gameplay into something almost unidentifiable as a F.E.A.R. title. While not terrible on its own, this discordant mess proves hilariously stupid to play through until it stops being hilarious.
If you’re willing to put time into F.E.A.R. 3 then I’m going to trust you’re already done with 1 and 2, because we’re taking a crashing helicopter ride into Spoilertown. Alma’s psycho-nuclear emergence at the end of the first game has left a lasting mark on the city of Fairport, turning the skies red, the residents mad, and the ghosts angry. She’s also in the family way, if you remember the insane ending of the second game, and her labor pains are literally tearing the city apart. In the middle of all this appears The Point Man from the first game, along with his dead ghost brother Paxton Fettel, to do… something?
F.E.A.R. 3 has a lot of problems but one that drives me crazy is how pointless the whole game feels in terms of narrative. It opens with Fettel helping Point Man break out of an Armacham-run asylum and escape through the favelas of… somewhere just to return to Fairport to watch Alma go horror-monal on the city. Point Man seems to want to stop her, Fettel just wants to hang out with Mom, but there’s nothing that really drives the plot anywhere. Your useless teammate Jin from the first game shows up and Point Man is very strong and silently concerned about her, and SHE wants you to stop Alma, so… okay? These dudes are her sons so at this point I’m really unsure why any of Alma’s zombies or demons or hellspawn-things want to eat their faces anyway.
Beyond that though, it’s quite a spectacle to see how insane the series has gone from it’s origin. In a perfect world we could have kept the moody halls and sudden scares of the first game, but there’s a certain mad appeal to fighting techno-magical soldiers through a disintegrating, blood-soaked city to stop an apocalyptic ghost baby from being born. I’m not kidding about the soldiers, either. Armacham’s still got the powered armor and high-tech weapons from before but added phase casters, field commanders who can open portals for themselves and other troops. It feels like a bridge too far for the already-strained credibility of the series, and honestly they’re annoying as ♥♥♥♥ to fight, too.
Firefights should be the strong part of any F.E.A.R. game, and while they’re more dynamic here than in the second game there are new factors that can often make them more frustrating. F.E.A.R. 3 loves to chuck you into arena situations with enemies spawning in all around you, rather than giving you squads to ambush or defined battles to weigh in on. Some of these enemies fall more on the aggravating side than interesting, like the crazed citizens who take tons of hits to drop and love strapping bombs to themselves to show you how much they care. Phase casters can drag fights out far beyond what is reasonably fun, and new riot shield enemies seem to exist just to take the enjoyment out of going melee on hapless soldiers.
Your weapons have again been remixed, and again they’re more interesting than the bland F.E.A.R. 2 versions but feature new limitations. The assault rifle, for example, is way more powerful here but fires in three-round bursts. You can get dual uzis for wasting large groups of runners but they drain ammo way too fast. And the shotgun is back to 1-or-2-shotting foes but suffers an appalling redesign that makes it look like a gas station sushi display. You’re not even going to get to play with some of these much because your ammo reserves cap out at absurdly low levels and you lose all your weapons at the end of each level, which is going to be agonizing unless you’re the kind of person who pistol-starts every map of DOOM.
All of this pales in comparison to the major changes in the gameplay, though. Gone are medkits and health bars, replaced with regenerating health. I’m not a hard-liner against regenerating health by any means but it’s a knife through the heart of any game with horror leanings, removing any and all tension from monster attacks and big brawls. There’s also a cover system that gave the developers cause to fill levels with chest-high walls and place enemies far outside normal engagement range, further limiting slo-mo melee shenanigans. Biggest of all, though, is the rating system that constantly pops up accolades for killing X enemies with Y weapon, or staying in slo-mo for Z seconds. This system earns you points to level up and unlock new bonuses like more health or holding more clips or other quality-of-life elements that should have been in from the start.
You may have realized this by now, but the compartmentalized levels and limited weapons and regenerating health and rating system all combine to make a score attack game set in the F.E.A.R. universe, instead of whatever you’re imagining F.E.A.R. 3 should be. These elements put the emphasis on gamey mechanics that detract entirely from the ham-fisted attempts at horror that the developers still tried to include. On top of that, you can play the entire game co-op with one player as deadly ghost guy Fettel (or you can play him solo after beating a level as Point Man) who possesses and explodes enemies with reckless abandon. There are also multiplayer modes where you battle waves of enemies or outrun death clouds or perform other random tasks to score points.
None of this is actually bad, mind you. The shooting still works in a Call of Duty way and the monsters add some variety and the backdrop is absolutely wild Akira-style apocalypse stuff. But it’s so far from what F.E.A.R. and even F.E.A.R. 2 are that it’s almost shocking they share the name. I know the effort was put into linking the stories but that hardly matters if you’ve jettisoned even the most basic levels of tension from the game design. It’s fun in a goofy, mindless way but not in the ways you’re probably here for. Also I lied a little before, there are some seriously bad parts near the end of the campaign with some awful bosses and forced arena fights.
The graphics are very fitting for what this game is, sharp and colorful but with a certain cleanness that makes it all feel like a knock-off of what it’s supposed to be. Sound design is fine as well, and they got the actor for Fettel back to do some terribly out-of-character quips at the player, but if you’ve made it this far that’s the least of your concerns. Don’t go into F.E.A.R. 3 expecting horror or tension or brilliant gunplay or anything that made F.E.A.R. F.E.A.R., really. If you’re going to show up at all, come either for the score attack aspect of the game, the completely bug♥♥♥♥ story spiraling off the others, or just some competent shooting. Maybe they were aiming for something more with this one, but I tell you now that competent is as high as they got.

Although I enjoy PnC puzzle games and The Uncertain looks liked a fresh blood to the genre, I could not get myself to like this game. First of all, the decision to add movement with "WASD" keys do not work, unfortunately. All it does is add clunkiness to gameplay. It would be better off with the simple "click-to-move" method. Most of the time the camera is at an off angle so you can't even move straight.
Puzzles weren't satisfactory either. They were so simple that instead of testing your wits, they test your patience. Some are "pair the couple" games, some are "slide the shapes until they match up" games that simply take long trial and error phases instead of actually working your brain.
The gameplay also restricts your approach to the puzzles. For example, some puzzles or challenges are so apparent, you can see them before you even take one step forward. However, although the correct method is out there and easily noticable, you can not do it because the game forces you to try the wrong method first or does not let you try anything at all until you go past a certain point. This is shameful and does not reward actual sharp wit at all.
My biggest disappointment was the story and how the developers handled the story. I will try not to give spoilers, so don't worry. Basically, the story could be processed in such a way that could give interesting and intimate analysis and criticize the human mind and humanity in general. However, what we get is the basic, "oh humanity is so self destructive but also so unique in its own way" kind of approach. This heavily milked "nature vs. culture" clash is getting really old, really quickly.
Lately, although it's not important for a point and click type of slow paced games, optimization is horrible. One scene gives you up to 80 frames per second, yet the next can net you a 25 at most. Again, it's not an issue at all but some people are very sensitive when it comes to performance so I wanted to put it out here.

I've played my fair share of 2D side-scroller point-and-click games such as Gemini Rue, Primordia, and Resonance but this is the first 3D point-and-click I've actually played and I've found it to be quite enjoyable.
I was actually surprised to find out this was made with the Unity Engine because the environment, characters, and objects look like something out of the Unreal 3 Engine but much like Amplitude Studios with Endless Space, the developers of Uncertain have managed to push the limits of the engine and polish the game content so it looks and feels semi-realistic.
Storyline wise its pretty much yet another game involving humans going extinct yet robots and AI coming out of the woodwork to build their own society but with a sudden twist near the beginning of the game. There are also audio devices, text files, and notes littered around various parts of the game which gives us peeks of what society was like before the apocalypse. There is also the fact the main character doesn't understand the functions of certain objects and/or concepts such as swing sets, alcohol, and propaganda which adds a bit of realism in regards to sapient/sentient Artificial Intelligence.
All in all I think this is actually a good start in an eventual series of games and I'd love to see the future episodes sooner rather than later.
8/10

This game is a beautiful, carefully crafted piece of software I really enjoyed playing. The music is nice and fitting, the english voice actor sounds professional and pleasant to the ear and the translation is high-quality, without severe grammar issues like other indie games often suffer from.
I can't complain about the controls - not worse than any other point&click game, same level as Telltale. There are many fun small mini-games like hacking a system or flying an aerocar. The riddles are not too challenging and thus don't interrupt the "fluency" and pace of the game, which I liked. The visuals are beautiful and the story itself very interesting, especially if you are into robots.
The only thing I didn't like is the limited dialogue - you have several questions to choose from, but you can only pick one and then the dialogue ends. That's not a wise decision because it shortens the overall playtime and takes away story info. It would also have been great to be able to give your robot more of a "personality" - during the first conversation you could choose to be calm, aggressive etc., but that option sadly got lost very quickly.
The developers (a very small indie team) stated the game isn't abandoned yet and I really, really hope for a second episode. Devs, take your time to ensure high quality, but please don't abandon this gem.
: Beautiful graphics, nice voice-acting, good translation, fun mini-games, great sound effects and music and a cool story. Sadly, not enough dialogue/choices. The first episode is rather short (3-4 hours) and episode 2 is due yet, but I really think it's worth supporting these indie devs.

Great arcade-style hack n' slash game. I tried playing it single player and local co-op, and it's WAY better with someone else. It certainly has an old-school arcade vibe to it (4 buttons to mash, racing against the clock, fighting through swarms of baddies...), which is great, but is also a tad frustrating for a casual gamer. There are no saves, so if you die (or if you don't have hours on end to play in a row), you have to keep restarting from the beginning. And since you only have limited 'tokens' to revive, if one player is weaker than the other, you end up restarting the same level over and over again (in our case, we sometimes had to restart the same level 5 or 6 times to get through it on medium difficulty. We eventually downgraded to easy difficulty). The achievements are also a bit of a stretch, so there's not a whole lot of replay value. I still have it the thumbs up because it's worth the buck for a good night of fun with friends.

my favourite part about this book was when a random event took five planets from me and i couldn't get them back though the means i'd availed myself to
my second favourite part was the bewildering amount of stats with no clear in-game explanation or tooltips; i suppose "+30% Courage" is good, but why is it good? what is the difference between +16 Industry and +16 Production? why is there one?
my third favourite part is the constant sheet of gauzy, miserable fog of war blanketing your view like a cancerous malaise of boredom that constantly begged the question of why i was still playing it
i can see the possibility for Possibly Ever Enjoying myself while playing this game, but Civ IV, Civ V, Sins, and possibly any other 4X turn-based strategy game are much better 4X games in my opinion. chances are they'll have clearer design, better conveyance, and be more approachable. in GalCiv, everything is grey and bleary and in the fog of war and terrible, and while i adore turn-based strategy games of practically any species, there is just something less than enjoyable about a view of nothing but greyed-over bland iconography interspersed with increasingly-disinterested jammings of the "end turn" button.
i'm aware the game has tutorials, but i'm not terribly fond of the idea that playing a tutorial is absolutely mandatory to enjoy a game. i've picked up and played and had fun with other 4X games over the course of my fat obstreperous gaming career while ignoring tutorials, and had yet to find one obtuse enough to impede fun until trying my hand at this game.
with that in mind, the game's just not for me. maybe it's for you - no judgement if it is. there are just more and better games that scratch this particular itch, and while Sins is technically a 4Xoid RTS rather than a "proper" 4X game, if i want to feel like the Supreme Hivequeen of Space, i'll play that instead.

- A taste of gamedev life
- It gives some thrill to do a best seller or a perfect 10

Ok, so I'd recommend you to play 1 time this game before reading the following, but if you really want to know, here we go !
So in this game, you don't play against a simulated market, or some precomputed values, you play only against yourself !
This means you get good scores and good sales only if your new game is better than your previous games. Which means if for some reason you get a big increase in your game quality, then the next games will have a much harder time to get good scores. This is the opposite of real life where taking the lead assures good sales for a while.
Moreover, doing sequels is a very easy way to rack super high sales, as a sequel might be compared more to its ancestor than your recent previous games, which means after you have done several games, it feels like you should do only sequels of older games.
When I was playing the game, I felt something was off, but the illusion kinda held till the end of my playthrough. I won't do another one though as I think it's dumb to have to play for a steady but contained growth in the quality of my games to maximize my success.

When I first saw this game, I thought it looked extremely one-note. Four players are divers, two are sharks, sharks have to kill divers and divers have to survive. Sounds like fun for a couple matches before it gets old. As it turns out, Digital Confectioners have put a lot of love and care into such a simple concept.
First off, the gameplay. As mentioned before, Depth pits four divers against two sharks. The divers essentially play a sort of extended escort mission, guarding their robot companion as he tools around the map, busting open treasure chests and safes and other sunken loot containers. Typically this escort will be split into two alternating stages: When the robot swims between containers, this typically forces the divers to cross open water - a prime chance for the sharks to swoop in snatch someone before vanishing into the darkness. When the robot reaches a safe, it will stop for a few minutes to cut it open. Typically, these containers are in enclosed structures, which put the divers at an advantage. The sharks have to plan their kills carefully to avoid being trapped in small rooms full of bullets. Thankfully, most of these structures have hidden entryways that the sharks can break through, opening the area up.
My one big qualm with the gameplay is bots - specifically diver bots. The diver bots have damn near perfect aim, which is a REALLY big deal when sharks rely on being fast and hard to see. Having a bot on your team more or less guarantees a victory.
Moving on, the atmosphere created by the gameplay is perfect. As a diver, you're either sacred ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ crossing open water, or watching three or four different doorways (or more) for a shark to mosey on in. As a shark, you feel extremely powerful, carefully picking out which little diver you want to eat next. By the end of a match, the tables are typically somewhat turned, as divers begin to pick up bigger and better weapons, forcing the sharks to strategize all the more. Generally speaking, the game seems fairly balanced. Without much of a skill difference between teams, divers seem to have a sliiiight advantage.
Speaking of atmosphere, Depth is gorgeous. In total, there are 12 maps as of this review, most of which have very unique flavours. One map takes place in a flooded mine, forcing players to navigate through claustrophobic mine shafts and tunnels. Another takes place on a sunken oil rig, hanging over the abyss. Of course, there's also a map that takes you through a bunch of sunken pirate ships, because not having a pirate ship map would be illegal. There's also an Olmec city/temple complex, a medieval castle and many more.
Thankfully, you can filter out maps you don't like, or I would have never known there were maps other than Olmec because IT'S THE ONLY ♥♥♥♥ING MAP I GET WHEN I LEAVE IT ON.
But Depth needs replayability to keep your interested, and replayability it has. More or less. Sharks can pick from six different species, each of which has different stats and a unique ability. You could play a tanky Great White, a speedy Mako, a stealthy Tiger shark, or one of the more off-beat species like a Hammerhead, which has low damage but can smash players into walls for quick and easy kills.
Divers, on the other hand, can pick from a handful of weapons and consumables. There aren't many weapons, but each one can be upgraded in a number of ways. The consumables typically provide support effects, like the ubiqituous medpacks and ammo packs, flares and sonar which reveal nearby sharks, shark shield that hide divers in the radius from the shark's vision, and mines. Which explode. And make everyone have a good time.
And I guess there's skins and junk that you can get, but only a handful of shark skins are even noticeable. Most of the time, if divers are close enough to get a good look at your skin, both of you are doing something very wrong.
Ultimately, I think Depth has juuuust enough content to justify a buy at full price if you like underwater atmospheric games. If you see it on sale (like it is right now), don't think. Just buy.

I have had tremendous fun playing this game. It is a true throwback MMO with housing, player driven economy and some interesting questing. I have been satisfied the last several patches as content has been added, quests expanded, bugs removed and functions polished. It's a hard game, no doubt so watching "early impression" vids I can understand some of the frustration because the combat system is fairly unique. There is no minimap and no visible quest breadcrumbs.
Yet, I have found as I improve skills and continue to unlock new ones my "combat deck" has expanded to where I now have a really enjoyable bag of tricks to take down mobs.
I found advancing some quest lines sometimes requires obscure references to NPCs. It's not perfect, requires a serious commitment to literacy, and is not quite polished for some people.
However, if you are looking for a throwback with some nice graphics, depth, and large open world I sincerely recommend SOTA!

I was playing SOTA long before persistence and was one of the first 100k people to back it. Although there has been some variance in their game design, they've followed their product road map fairly well and the game has improved by leaps and bounds. While I already find this game to be very enjoyable, I really have no doubts that it will be one of the best games I've ever played once it's released (it's already kind of there for me). If you liked Ultima Online, I highly recommend this game. If you were more of a single player Ultima fan, you'll probably still enjoy the game but don't get your hopes up on the story line, yet.
Edit: The storyline for episode 1 is complete. I'm not a big lover of quests but they're mostly worth doing for the rewards. Someone that enjoys quests would probably like about 75% of the quests currently available. Some of them were buggy or boring (I can forgive the bugs since they get fixed pretty fast)
They've done a good job on keeping new content rolling in while squashing bugs, improving and completing existing systems, and optimizing the server as well as the client. Load times are very improved for older zones because of the last several optimization passes. Newer zones still need optimization. All in all, I have to say I'm still enjoying the game.

I've played Ultima 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, Underworld 1 and 2. Never really got into UO but from what I understand it isn't really comparable.
I bought this game when it was a kickstarter dream, because I figured some Ultima is better than no Ultima.
There's no feel of series continuity to this game. ESO provides way better world continuity than this, and it looks better too.
This game just doesn't have the "feel" of the Ultima world. I've heard arguments that the old systems were outdated, the combat is more adaptive, the leveling is more intuitive.
But it doesn't feel like Ultima. It feels like some fanboys medieval recreation MMO sim. Guess what, plenty of them out there, with better packaging.
The biggest thing this game is lacking? Storyline and plot. You know, the things that actually drew you into the originals, and let you suspend reality even with Windows 98 graphics (or older!).
I know it's an MMO, but WoW managed to do it in vanilla, with a fraction of the source material.
I would not recommend this game to an Ultima fan. Pray to the Shrines of the Virtues, especially Honesty, Honor, and Valor, that Underworld Ascendant somehow manages to revive the spirit of these games.
I also wouldn't recommend it as an MMO. It's far behind any other modern MMO in almost any measurable sense. The only reason I would put up with it is the Ultima universe, and it does not deliver there.

Most all of the negative reviews of this game ignore one MAJOR point: this is "early access."
What does that mean? These players aren't getting (from the start) a completely polished game. When World of Warcraft began opening its doors to the public for beta, it had already been in production for four YEARS. There were bugs, sure, but most had been squashed.
A lot of these negative reviews are outdated, and thusly, the game is posting as "mixed."
To be fair, the game has a learning curve.
To be fair again, this game is not easy like World of Warcraft, but it is rewarding to press through obstacles and get the skills and items you're after. Crafting is woven into every facet of the game, so it is necessary. For example, unless you wish to run everywhere, you're going to need to pick up a basic understanding of alchemy to create teleportation scrolls.
This IS the spiritual successor of Ultima Online. I played UO forever as a kid back in '97. I played until shortly after they introduced Trammel (a friendly world without PvP).
Please understand that this game IS in early access, and thus, we are exposed to all the wonkiness and bugs as they are revealed. However, the game is also now in persistence, meaning that before it is "released" publicly, you'll already have a head start on home placement, getting the name you want, and beginning leveling/acquiring skills.
The community is also amazing and is willing to help new adventurers. Please know that though there is the aforementioned learning curve, there is also an awesome community behind you who are more than willing to help you learn, understand, and grow.

I feel like most of these reviews underrate The Uncertain for what it is. I fell in love with this game and the story after only 5 hours of gameplay and I wish there was more to play already. It's not flawless, but the few mishaps hardly take away from the experience. This will probably be long but just bear with me. *No spoilers of the story but maybe of some of the gameplay.*
+ The mechanics aren't as bad as they are made out to be and the character movement isn't much of a problem once you get the hang of it. I also think the speed at which you move is appropriate considering you're a robot and it compliments the movement style and camera angles.
- I do wish that you could talk more with the other characters rather than being cut off after only one choice because it felt like you were missing chunks of the story.
+ I loved the puzzles. They were easy enough that you could get through them and go on with the story but hard enough to actually take some effort. That being said you don't need to be a rocket scientist to figure them out. I'd rather the puzzles be easy enough to solve on your own rather than so hard that you get frustrated and need to look up a walkthrough.
- The little car chase sequence was really unexpected, short, and awkward. Avoiding the obstacles was fun but as there was no way to fight back or really avoid the drone's fire, it seemed almost useless for it to be there.
+ The story is so intriging and I love RT's little comments on the human things you find. I took the time to look at everything you could and to listen to what was said and it helped build onto the current reality. All the little details that were put into the game just make it all that more endearing.
+ The dialogue was as you would expect, monotone and robot like, which isn't bad at all. For it to be anything else would seem out of character. If anything the little recordings of human voices that you could find were more odd to me.
- It's a slow pace game, and you just have to get used to the movements of the character and the type of game it is to appreciate it.
+ I played with the graphics on high and it was beautiful, and the story is amazing. However, these aren't the only good things about the game unless you look at it at face value.

I have serious problems with this game
The puzzles waiver between average to just lazy.  There were spots I thought there was going to be a puzzle and there wasn't, or wasn't much of one, and I just feel dissappointed.
The movement controls are really clumsy and it would have been better to just make the game point-and-click, rather than force you to use directional controls in relation to awkward camera angles.
The story is kind of intriguing and I am curious to see where they go with it, but this game completely relies on its story. Which would be fine, unfortunately a story entirely told with robot voices does lack the punchy urgency that this sort needs to feel, but I can't think of how they could help with that.
The dialogue itself feels odd at times, especially with the limited conversation trees.  Almost feels like some of the conversations are cut off, without a proper conclusion.
The dialogue, controls and all this creates a serious drag with the pacing, it takes longer to move from point to point (plot and location-wise) than it takes to solve the puzzles, so it just gets laborious after a while.
Worst of all was the driving.  It's a short section and it is kind of hard to actually lose, but it was so annoying and weird.  It doesn't really feel like your actions have any appreciable effect on you success.  I was so glad when they were over and equally happy when another one wasn't put in when he had to 'overload' his engines to get to the next location urgently.
What is really sad is I can see some serious love put into this.  So much effort has been put in for the location and character designs and back stories.  I loved the unique look of each robot.  I love some of the social ideas they have.  But they're lost in a game that just isn't that fun to play.

The idea of Scribblenauts Unlimited really appealed to me. Using your own creativity to solve the hundreds and hundreds of puzzles without any limits. Unfortunately once i played a bit i started noticing more and more Scribblenauts isn't as unlimited as it claims to be. Now don't get me wrong Scribblenauts Unlimited is a very fun game and has some nice and creative locations you travel to! It runs really smooth and has almost no loading times at all. But the game is just really limited, often i tried solving puzzles in fun and creative ways and ended up on google asking myself why nothing works, with the dissapointing news you could only choose from a set of solutions the developers already choose. This way the game starts to feel like a chore after a while, just solving the puzzles with the most basic solutions because those are the only ones that work most of the time.
Now this wouldn't be that bad if the puzzles would actually be challenging, but since this game is aimed more towards kids the puzzles are often so easy they're just boring. However Scribblenauts has some really nice and fun points aswell, you can costumize your own character and all of the different NPC's. And although the puzzles aren't as free as the game claims them to be, there are still quite a few items in the game to mess around with and you can create literally everything you can think of. The artstyle is unique and fits the game perfectly and the music is really catchy.
Yes this game can be fun, especially for kids. And even i enjoyed this game, just not till the end cause it got way to repetitive after a while. Don't buy this and expect to get creative by solving the puzzles, buy this if you like solving basic and easy puzzles, don't mind a bit of repetitivty and enjoy messing around to create fun and original stuff.

This is a game to sit down and play with friends.  Online matchmaking works, but the quality decreases by how much you get along with the others, and whether the other players took a character you enjoy playing.  What seems to work best for casual play is having a group of 3.
Replay value is no Skyrim.  But if you enjoy dungeon runner franchises - even in board games - you'll enjoy this game.  This game would earn a 10 in replayability if they add a dungeon creator.  Small incentives and bonuses are earned by playing.  These include temporary invincibility after respawn, extra gold earned, slightly increased damage and reduced cooldown, etc.  There ARE multiple difficulties, so if you enjoy upping the ante and getting real serious about completing dungeons with organized groups of friends, you will have a good time.
If you intend to get 100 hours out of this game, you will most likely have to rely on the devs releasing new content.
This game is currently being updated with new content - some paid DLC, others free.  I personally find it is a great balance.  I purchased a DLC character that I enjoy the concept of and it adds a fresh feeling to the game.
Graphics are great for the top-down view.  Enough to look fine, and enough not to overload older PC's.  Sound and atmosphere are fine.  Character dialogue, dungeon master announcements.  You will feel glued to the screen when you see a giant horde of enemies and you're discussing with your friends on the best ways of dealing with them.
Some characters are better than others.  Does this mean that a Barbarian player won't do better than a Wizard player?  No.  Dungeons are situational.  Some characters are better in certain scenarios.  Corner a Wizard in a small room and he is more likely to die than a Valkyrie or a Barbarian.  But the Wizard and the Valkyrie do seem to be the two most common - and overpowered picks.  So if you like to join games, get used to all the characters and don't make a fuss if your favorite is taken.
In co-op matches, you compete by score.  Gold earned, kills, and the player who finishes the level holding the bonus crown on their head.  This changes up how players "co-operate" in a game.  It's not just about completing the dungeon, it's about earning more than the others.  Sure, this takes away from the value as a purist co-op game, but it adds to its replay value in some ways.  You can sit down with some friends and all agree to purist co-op if you wish - and that's where I personally find the game plays best.  Playing with friends in the same room, on the same screen.  Of course playing with four steam friends over voip is nice, too.  But if you want that classic arcade Gauntlet feel, have your friends get some controllers and come over to your place for a round of Gauntlet.

So this review is about a game i havent played for long yet but i can only say that it already is very good.
Now about the game i can say that i had to turn down some of my settings for a good fps but after i did that it was solid. My PC is decent but not a high end gaming PC and most of the games on my Library were played on this PC without problems so you can see that it isnt that bad of a PC after all. Back to the point. The game runs good on my settings and i have no fps drops so far.
The main controlls, those were an issue for me in blockland, are easy as in every other Lego Game that we know. You use WASD to move around. F to interact with things. Q and E to change the size of your brush and space and controll to ascend or descend.
The Controlls about going up and down and resizing mainly play a role when you fly with a helicopter or when you build something. While flying in a helicopter you use mainly WASD to move around but you use space and controll to move up and down. While in buildmode though you also use Q and E to resize your brush so you can use it on a bigger or tinier area.
As of for the main game there is currently not much to do. The reason for that is that the game is currently in early acces and having the game itself and the engine done is for me good enough. This of course is only my opinion. But from what we have here right now it is more a game you explore instead of you building big ♥♥♥ Castles and such. But updates will come and add even more blocks.
So would i recommend the game? - Yes
But i also would say that if you arent a fan of exploring: Dont buy it yet
The game is still in development and updates can come whenever. But since there is not much to do at the moment it might be boring for some people what is understandable.
If you dont care though and still want to try out building i recommend watching the tutorial by paulsoaresjr about how to Build and Import your own custom Models into the World of Lego. Since there is a program people can use to make certain structures this might help you out a bit.
And that it is. I have gotten Blockland and Lego Worlds. Both games are similar from the Idea. But only after playing a tiny bit, even without a tutorial, i can already say that Lego Worlds is the better one. Now people might disagree but hey that is how life is.

LEGO Worlds has potential to be a great return to the creative side of LEGO gaming. While in the past few years LEGO games have been more based on platforming through various movie franchises, LEGO Worlds focuses more on building and exploring while still keeping the fun and memorable aesthetic that has become a staple of the LEGO franchise games intact. Great animation combined with a variety of LEGO bricks makes LEGO Worlds a great base game to start building onto. The current build of the game is very basic; with no real objectives implemented you may struggle to find fun in the current iteration of this game if you do not enjoy exploration and using the LEGO building tool. While I don’t think that this game will be right for everyone in its current state, I recommend anyone interested in the LEGO universe keeping an eye on it as it progresses through the early access stage of development.

When I first saw this game, I thought it looked extremely one-note. Four players are divers, two are sharks, sharks have to kill divers and divers have to survive. Sounds like fun for a couple matches before it gets old. As it turns out, Digital Confectioners have put a lot of love and care into such a simple concept.
First off, the gameplay. As mentioned before, Depth pits four divers against two sharks. The divers essentially play a sort of extended escort mission, guarding their robot companion as he tools around the map, busting open treasure chests and safes and other sunken loot containers. Typically this escort will be split into two alternating stages: When the robot swims between containers, this typically forces the divers to cross open water - a prime chance for the sharks to swoop in snatch someone before vanishing into the darkness. When the robot reaches a safe, it will stop for a few minutes to cut it open. Typically, these containers are in enclosed structures, which put the divers at an advantage. The sharks have to plan their kills carefully to avoid being trapped in small rooms full of bullets. Thankfully, most of these structures have hidden entryways that the sharks can break through, opening the area up.
My one big qualm with the gameplay is bots - specifically diver bots. The diver bots have damn near perfect aim, which is a REALLY big deal when sharks rely on being fast and hard to see. Having a bot on your team more or less guarantees a victory.
Moving on, the atmosphere created by the gameplay is perfect. As a diver, you're either sacred ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ crossing open water, or watching three or four different doorways (or more) for a shark to mosey on in. As a shark, you feel extremely powerful, carefully picking out which little diver you want to eat next. By the end of a match, the tables are typically somewhat turned, as divers begin to pick up bigger and better weapons, forcing the sharks to strategize all the more. Generally speaking, the game seems fairly balanced. Without much of a skill difference between teams, divers seem to have a sliiiight advantage.
Speaking of atmosphere, Depth is gorgeous. In total, there are 12 maps as of this review, most of which have very unique flavours. One map takes place in a flooded mine, forcing players to navigate through claustrophobic mine shafts and tunnels. Another takes place on a sunken oil rig, hanging over the abyss. Of course, there's also a map that takes you through a bunch of sunken pirate ships, because not having a pirate ship map would be illegal. There's also an Olmec city/temple complex, a medieval castle and many more.
Thankfully, you can filter out maps you don't like, or I would have never known there were maps other than Olmec because IT'S THE ONLY ♥♥♥♥ING MAP I GET WHEN I LEAVE IT ON.
But Depth needs replayability to keep your interested, and replayability it has. More or less. Sharks can pick from six different species, each of which has different stats and a unique ability. You could play a tanky Great White, a speedy Mako, a stealthy Tiger shark, or one of the more off-beat species like a Hammerhead, which has low damage but can smash players into walls for quick and easy kills.
Divers, on the other hand, can pick from a handful of weapons and consumables. There aren't many weapons, but each one can be upgraded in a number of ways. The consumables typically provide support effects, like the ubiqituous medpacks and ammo packs, flares and sonar which reveal nearby sharks, shark shield that hide divers in the radius from the shark's vision, and mines. Which explode. And make everyone have a good time.
And I guess there's skins and junk that you can get, but only a handful of shark skins are even noticeable. Most of the time, if divers are close enough to get a good look at your skin, both of you are doing something very wrong.
Ultimately, I think Depth has juuuust enough content to justify a buy at full price if you like underwater atmospheric games. If you see it on sale (like it is right now), don't think. Just buy.

If you want an introduction to fighting game mechanics, this game should be considered as your gateway game. Although Street Fighter IV is one of the major games, the tutorial in Skullgirls will teach players about many fundamentals that exist in various fighting games like air dashing, canceling, and other "advanced" techniques. With a ratio mechanic to choose between 1, 2, or 3 character teams, beginners and fighting game vets can play this game within their comfort zone. The ability to choose and customize your assists for multi-character teams brings an added freshness to those who play assisted fighting games like the Marvel vs Capcom series. This game also incorporates an anti-infiinite system, which people who play MvC and get caught in a Doom TAC loop would kind of want. This system activates to prevent long, extended, periodic combos, causing players to know how to vary their combos in order to get the most of a situation.

This game was one that I wanted to purchase for a very long time, and even though I payed full price, I'd say it was worth it. I'm very happy with the game, it features great art and anitmations, the style, soundtrack and the atmosphere are awesome, game play is fun yet challenging and the stories interplay in an ineresting way. (Look down to see my review on different aspects of the game or to see the TLDR)
DLC:
The game comes with a lot of DLC characters, and new ones are being added frequently. Each one adds something to the game and I recommend investing in some of the characters available outside of the main 8 (9 wink wonk). Plus steam will often offer the most recent DLC characters for free for a period of time so make sure to keep an eye out! The Eliza DLC was amazing, I was lucky enough to get her for free, but she is definitely kick♥♥♥♥♥as all hell. Her story (which is the longest of them so far) and move set were so worth it. (worth buying)
MULTIPLAYER:
Multiplayer is always fun with a friend, and when in training mode (multi), you can literally beat the crap out of eachother endlessly without taking damage, it's a good way to train and familiarize yourself with some of the more challenging combos.
GAMEPLAY:
Combos are life in this game, and because of the fightstick style controls, there is fairly hefty variety of combos for each character. There are basic combos that each character will share controls wise, and there are also some combos/blockbusters unique to individual characters. Blocking is definitely recommended however, while there is no guard break in this game, the damage you take is simply taken down to almost nothing. So basically you will still lose some stamina but its like the equivalent of 1 health per hit, even with epic combos. Speaking of epic blockbusters, some of the tougher ones are inSANE. Super cool attacks.
ART AND CHARACTERS:
The arts and animations, aside from the fan service, in this game are amazing, and very intricate. Plus yknow fanservice. Every characters design is unique and each one's move set and play style is different. For instance Parasol and Peacock have more ranged based moves, while Cerebella and Filia are more suitable for close ranged combat. The combo's tend to follow a similar pattern for the most part, but each characters "epic" blockbusters/combos are pretty different, some are harder to work out than others. It's always interesting to work with a different character and find out how to use them the most effectively. There is an in game tutorial mode that will basically walk you through each character and different techniques in the game, easy to learn, tough to master. Tutorial 10/10
STORY:
Every story has it's unique qualities, and most of them eventually tie together. There will be fights where they may seem random and out of context, but never the less, they are honestly just put there to give you more game time. The option is available to skip dialogue and get straight to the action, just in case you are replaying a story or honestly don't care or want to read it all. I loved the backstory for each character, and with every added character more depth is also added to the scheme of things. Each story isn't heavily reliant on each other, so each one is able to stand on it's own, even if it refers to other characters (so you don't have to feel obligated to get the DLC to progress the story, though I recommend it anyway).
THINGS TO THINK ABOUT:
SAVING:
One thing I'd have to note is that when you get the game, the stories are great, but each one is fairly short (30 min), and because of this there is no save feature when in story mode. It will save after you beat the boss in each story so that's not an issue. I personally wish the stories were longer just because they are pretty interesting and entertaining, but it would most likely mess with the game set up. Just something to be aware of.
CONTROLS:
The concept behind the controls for the game were based on the fightstick arcade style. This means joystick and LMH kick and punch buttons. One thing about the game is that it doesn't give clear directions on which buttons to press for which result, with the exception of the tutorials (kinda, not really). Yes these are a little awkward to get used to, especially when using a controller (which I still recommend, it gets easier I promise). The keyboard controls are also easy to get used to and makes remembering the position of kick and punch buttons easy, but a lot of the combos require the rotational movement of a joystick (which are still achievable with the keyboard, no worries), and navagating the menus is a tad odd with the keyboard, which is why I recommend using a controller. If you need help figuring out what each button is, play through the tutorials. The bottom will show which key/button you pressed to get a result in relation to the fightstick setup. You'll see, trust me.
DIFFICULTY CURVE:
A lot of people talk about the difficulty curve being too high. The truth is it is a tad more challenging than most fighters, button mashing may get you through most of the normal fights, but when you get to the boss, you may need to have a little strategy. There are 6 different difficulty settings, which I believe are; Sleepwalk, Easy, Normal, Hard, Extreme and Nightmare. If you want to breeze through the game and simply play for fun or the story, you want to keep the setting on Normal and below (at least at the start). If you want to try for a more challenging game, go for Hard and above. Like I said, this game is a tad harder than most normal fighting games, even Normal may present a bit of a challenge to a newcomer. This being said there are two lower settings so don't hurt yourself if you can't get through the stories on the first go. On the flip side if you are really good and want to put your skills to the test, there are levels that WILL freaking final exam the crap out of your 2d fighting abilities.
TLDR;
All in all I'd recommend this to anyone who loves fighters, wants a challenge or just to have fun and can appreciate the amazing asthetics and back stories (however short they are). It's one of my favorite fighters, and frankly one of my favorite games in my library. There is so much replay value in this game, I love it and would recommend it (and have) to any and all of my friends. (yes it's even worth full price). You get used to the fightstick style, plus its definitely worth getting the DLC <3

This is kind of a mixed recommendation. There's a good core here that they are building up and with some more time and love, Shroud will become something that will be a 100% recommendation. As of now, it's still lacking in content and not very newbie friendly. Once you get past that, however, the game does have an endearing quality. (There are many newbie friendly guilds you can join!)
The game doesn't hold your hand. It wont tell you where to go for quests nor will it tell you how to build your character. While this is a flaw to some degree as it leaves newbies completely stranded, the core systems provide a lot of freedom in how you want to craft your gameplay. Understanding the skill system, exp pool and when to stop training certain skills, you can master the system pretty easily. With only having a single character (sorry, no rerolling unless you want to completely wipe your progress) the game does make it easy to "respec" to some degree, though you don't really waste experience or time as most skills are useful and exp can be reclaimed.
A lot of people may complain about the hotbar/skill system though it really comes down to a lack of understanding how to properly use decks. Once you learn how to quicky combine or discard glyphs as they come up, the deck system is actually *really* powerful and engaging. You can get skills off way faster than you would have been able to had you locked down everything to a hotbar slot waiting for reset timers. With the ability to combo glyphs together to produce different results, you have a much wider variety of abilities at your disposal than you would otherwise. Arguably it almost plays like an action game, or at least more-so than other traditional MMOs.
Now there isn't a lot to explore or kill in the game right now. Quite a few of the "scenes" or zones are duplicates of other zones with higher level enemies replacing the other ones. There's only a few major quest lines for the different virtues and only a few npcs that provide quests. Every release, however, there is a new zone and a good amount of content added to the game every month. If anything, the team is *extremely* dedicated to this game.
If you don't want to check it out now, check it out in a few months and see if it catches your eye. With no more character wipes and no monthly fee, it's an easy game to pick up, drop and come back to months down the line.

The Uncertain is an episodic sci-fi adventure game developed and published by ComonGames. While this is their first release on Steam, the company has promised a further two episodes in addition to Episode 1 - The Last Quiet Day, which released in late September of 2016. By taking a look at the ComonGames website and social media accounts, it's easy to see that they're deep into the construction of Episode 2, but a release date has yet to be announced thus far.
In this post-apocalyptic adventure, humanity has been long extinct. What are currently modern conveniences to us are severely outdated, rustic, and worn down from the sands of time in this title. You will take control of an engineering robot known as RT-217NP, who is simply going about his daily rituals when a ship crash-lands near the house that he has taken residence in. While investigating the ship, RT comes across a robot pilot that was fatally wounded in the wreck, and he also discovers something that throws the entire plot line for a loop. The story is told very well, through various cutscenes, a few notes, and some dialogue options here and there, although this Episode does end on a cliffhanger.
If you've played any recent TellTale game, you will be familiar with the core mechanics of The Uncertain; you walk around, examining objects, picking them up, touching them, using them, etc. There are a lot of objects to interact with, and quite a few semi-hidden movie and game related Easter Eggs that I won't reveal here. One problem is that RT ends up getting stuck on objects while he's walking toward a destination, which could be fixed easily if the developers would introduce a set walking path to these locations. As well, the controls are a bit clunky when it comes to maneuvering RT, as he will continue to walk/run in the same direction, despite having switched directions many seconds prior.
Progressing through the game means solving numerous puzzles, or finding the appropriate objects to repair certain gizmos. While the object hunting can be tedious, since you need to examine some items in order to trigger another item's usefulness which leads to a lot of backtracking, the puzzles are actually fun. They're not very complex, but they're unique enough to be entertaining, and all of them fit the futuristic time period of the game very well. There are also a couple hover-car driving sections, where you will have to outwit a pursuant.
It's going to seem like a no-brainer to say this, but the graphics in The Uncertain are exceptional, and the title itself is very photogenic. The same can be said for the very atmospheric, sci-fi inspired soundtrack that helps tie everything together. While the graphics are reminiscent of The Talos Principle, and the gameplay is taken straight from TellTale Games, there is a distinct Primordia inspiration that shines through the robot characters. RT is genuinely curious about the human race, and through interacting with a vast majority of objects it's clear to see that his AI does not allow him to understand the functions or necessity of older items, such as bicycles and paintings. It's interesting how the developers were able to give even moderately deep life to the robots within this story.
The Uncertain: Episode 1 - The Last Quiet Day is a decent puzzle-driven atmospheric sci-fi adventure game that clocks in at around 2-3 hours of play time. Unlike many other episodic indie projects, it doesn't appear that this game will be abandoned any time soon, and ComonGames are currently working on the second episode, with three planned all together. However, there is a problem when it comes down to the price, as the regular tag on this release is $16.99 CAD; bare in mind, that doesn't include the next two episodes. In comparison, The Walking Dead games sell for $27.99 CAD for all 5 guaranteed episodes; that breaks down into roughly $5.60 per episode. Here, you get one episode for the price of 4 of the aforementioned episodes. It's best to grab this one on sale, or wait until the entire season has been released.

I wouldn't recommend this game, but if the second episode is good then you would obviously want to play this first.

F.E.A.R. 3 is the third installment to the F.E.A.R. franchise and I have plenty of reasons to downvote it, with few reasons to upvote it.
Cons:
If you're looking for a clear, concise, story follow-up to the ending of the second game, don't bother. The timeline has absolutely no mention of its relation to the other 2 games (9 months post F.E.A.R 1 and 2 events; had to Google), and the storyline it offers feels out of place.
F.E.A.R. 3 doesn't give the same creepy, sometimes scary, and unsettling atmosphere and gameplay as the other two titles. In fact, I spent more time running through rooms without a care in the world then I did cowering in a corner as I await the horrors of the unknown.
As was wondefully present with the first game (and in a lot of instances, the second), the enemy AI doesn't feel as fluid and intelligent as they once did. Instead of attempting to silently flank you or respond on a dime, the AI decides to camp a spot and pop out of cover predictably.
In F.E.A.R. 3, they decided to add this horrid, terribly out of place and ludicrous ranking and point gathering system. Urging to dash down a corridor and sweep that soldier off his feet in the first mission? Well, you can't unlock that till rank 2.
The playtime as compared to the previous 2 titles is ridiculous. It took me roughly 4 hours to complete the entire game.
If you're expecting to be able to gather medpacks and eagerly search every little area for a reflex booster, they also added regenerative health and a reflex boost on certain level rankings.
Pros:
If you're looking for a pretty decent FPS that bumps shoulders with Call of Duty, I'd certainly recommend F.E.A.R. 3.

Is "Shroud of the Avatar" an adventure game with a very large social component, or is it a social interaction game with a very large adventuring component?  I think its both.  This is an early access game, created by some experienced, dedicated MMO developers, who keep us "early backers" of the game fully informed as to what's going on, development-wise, on an almost daily basis.  The game is being developed with constant player feedback, for better or worse.
The game harkens back to "classic" RPG type play, so the term "old school" could certainly be applied to it.  However, there's such a level of detail, and such a sense of time and place within the game, that it's easy to get fully enveloped by the atmosphere and the story that happening around your character, or Avatar.  This is a game where simply "wandering around" is a viable alternative to constant combat; where crafting is encouraged (and actually fun!); where logging in to the game is merely Step 1 -- then YOU get to decide what you'd like to do within the Shroud world today.
As a general rule, I don't like fantasy games.  However, Shroud has completely charmed me over the past 16 months that I've played.  I've gotten to meet many of the developers of the game in person (!) and been amazed by how forthcoming and enthusiastic they are with where they're going and how we're all (players included) going to progress the game forward.
One thing to note: There's a steep learning curve the first few hours you play (the Tutorial needs a LOT of work), so be prepared to have a lot of information thrown at you at once.  Don't worry about it; don't let it get you frustrated; it'll all become clear with a little time and effort.  Once you get acclimated to the game, all the fiddly parts of it will start to make more sense.

Pros:
- decently large open world

- I like the VATS system, bringing at least a little rpg to the table
- perks! they're hilarious and awesome

Cons:
- can get borderline silly
- relatively easy
- too often it feels like a FPS than a RPG

Verdict:
Fallout 3 is a well produced FPS/RPG hybrid with a dominant FPS trait. shedding the deep immersion of it's more tactical prequels, it manages to pair fast paced combat with open world scavenging/exploring while delivering one of gamings more hilarious postapocalyptic settings.

At full price, it's way too short.

For starters, I wanna say that I really enjoyed this game.
*The graphics are amazing although they seem to use more GPU power than necessary for what is actuallly displayed on the screen.  My 1070 will hit 100% usage and the scene looks good but not that special.
*The story is also really good, although sentient robots living on earth after human extinction is a little overplayed these days.
*The music, environment sound,  and voice acting were also good.  I was sad to notice that the game doesn't use 5.1 sound at all, I'm pretty sure its just stereo. I'm not sure what is with game engines these days but I used to get 4 speaker surround sound with my monster3d sound card back in 1996.
*The game is short, I mean, like 3.5 hours short.  I like short games, when they cover the whole story.  I know this is just episode 1, but it doesn't cover much at all.  This short of an ep1 works in stuff like the Tell Tale model, where you know you are getting ep2 a month later.  I hope I still remember what this game is about by the time ep2 comes around.
*The control choice of movement keys and then mousing for interaction isn't terrible.  It is a lot like Grim Fandango's tank controls that I loved, although many people hated the tank controls and so the remake lets you choose all point and click as an option. This game kinda plays better on gamepad, but even then the controls feel a little disjoint.  You have to use your right thumb to look around, but then take your thub off to click anything (should have used sholder buttons devs).  Some of the puzzles require quick precice clicking though, so you kinda have to switch to mouse for those. I would also like to complain about how slow the RT robot moves, and how the game probably wouldn't even take 3 hours if you have full point and click controls with double click "fast move" you get from most adventure games. There are a couple of places in the game where the environment is bigger and the movement keys seem to make sence, like the woods near the lab. I'm not sure it is worth it though.
*Puzzles. The puzzles were varied from use X here at X, and then some interactive minigame like puzzles.  Also, there were even action puzzles like flying a hovercar and doging things, that was fun. I would say the puzzles were on the plus side of average, only real downfall was there wasn't anything even remotely hard or complex.  I usually play these things for the story anyway.
I spend more time keeping up with good point and clicker games than probably any other game genre. That said, I feel genre has really raised the bar lately with games like "Technobabylon", "Primordia", "Gemini Rue", "The Fall", the "Blackwell" series. Most of these games use pixel graphics, and therefore have much more develoment resources going into story, puzzels, script, etc.  You can tell that more than half of the development effort has gone into graphics in this game.  They didn't drop the ball on the rest, its still a good game. I just think that the game would have been better with more focus on gameplay etc.
*More small complaints:  The path finding algorithm almost never works.  You click on a thing to interact with an object, and most often the robot gets stuck on the path to the object.  Another weird thing is that the game has wonderful graphics, but then doesn't bother to animate then your robot pickes up an object.  Robot walks over, puts his had on an object, then gets stuck there for a littlebit, then he glitches back standing and the object is in your inventory. Kind of a total let down.
*Final thoughts: I enjoyed the game and it has me hooked to see where the ep2 takes us. I recommend the game but would like to suggest finding it on sale, or when there are more epsodes for the same price. I would also see the controls worked out.

An adventure game with a futuristic Sci-fi theme, that takes the shape of a point & click visual novel, the first episode of The Uncertain provides a story line and drama to keep your attention.
I experienced no problems with performance or lagging, and the game has only mid-range loading screens. The overall visual quality is quite nice. The artists found enough beautiful nature scenes to counter-balance the “decaying world” look of the old rusty buildings that were part of the story line. I think that is important, because some games, like Deus Ex: Mankind Divided just seem to have such ugly environments almost all the way through the game. Here, you see the contrast.
The music is at times intensely on the edge of your seat mysterious. At other times its haunting and spellbinding. The soundtrack is provided as free dlc, which is definitely a plus for the highish price range for shorter games like this. There is no replayability whatsoever. I missed 3 achievies in one playthrough so had to re-do half the first chapter for those in almost no time. I really took my time too, so I would imagine you could easily finish this game in just 3 hours if you wanted. I don’t know when more episodes will be released, or if they are included in the price. So, all that would need to be taken into consideration with the price. Just saying.
The story is where The Uncertain gives you your entertainment. Normally, I like to start with the positives and work my way down in game reviews. But, I really felt the need to be up front about the negatives this time, since I’m still recommending the game. Here is why. The story fills some deep need to exist. It is not only of high quality writing, and in a genre I love, but the story begs to be told. It’s cutting edge interest in the world around us. We all have this love/hate relationship with technology. The story is respectful of both humanity and tech. I won’t spoil the actual story itself, but I really like where it is going. If you want to know more than that, try the game yourself.
I highly suggest you play this game with both keyboard/mouse controls and a controller. You need the mouse for finding the point and click elements. But, walking and running are much easier in certain tasks with a controller… especially when trying to avoid the turrets. The mechanics of the puzzles are all generally speaking creative and unique, rather than the cookie cutter style of many games. Most of them are in the form of mini-games. Some seemed easy… too easy. One or two were a challenge. But, all seemed fail-proof. I really enjoyed driving the aerocar in the chase scenes, but again… it felt fail-proof, almost scripted.
*Excellent writing for a narrative that carries the game
*Great work on the art & soundtrack
*High quality game production & graphic design
*Somewhat overpriced for the time in game/ lack of replay value
*Scripted elements feel heavy
*Not as challenging as it could have been

I was an original backer and didnt initially put this game to launch through steam so not all my hours were recorded. What I can say is quite a few of the key features I wanted to check out about this game are either locked behind hours of grind or not what I was hoping for.
Taming - You MUST be a gatherer and crafter to be able to tame effectively, and its not just that easy, you must get up to the level of being about to kill level 30+ creatures and have the mining skill to be able to mine the silver then have an alchemy skill high enough to make collars to ensure you can tame a level 3 wolf. Convoluted enough for you? I remember (this game being a "spiritual" successor) in Ultima where you didnt need anyhting to tame between 1-3 creatures at level 1. They weren't very strong but you could ride the horse you tamed without a saddle etc. How do you make a games system so much worse being a spiritual successor?
Spell System and Leveling - It sounded like a great concept. Pooled exp you get from doing quests and killing mobs allows you to allocate said exp into the skills you want to level. It's a great concept except that sometimes you have to level skills you wont even use just to get the skills you want. I would rather a skill just has an exp requirement at level 1 to learn and once you reach it you can dump it in. To add to that, once you've learned a skill you have to use it to dump the exp in. Logically it makes sense except for the fact the level of creature you fight determines how much exp goes in as well as the amount of exp you have pooled and how much exp you have going into other skills. How much more convoluted can you get.....?
Questing and Talking - This was innovative, they wanted to go back to the base level of RPGS where you had to be an individual who actually read what was going on in order to actually do quests and get information. Great idea except that with a mediocre story at best its not engaging even when reading it. It bored me to tears at some points and was mildly engrossing at others so I just stopped doing quests and went out to farm.
Overall leveling and Exp gain- Again great concept with the pooled exp, but it seemed more like skill points you couldnt allocate until you got X, X being the money for the skill, or finding a high enough mob to practice the skill on so you could actually allocate exp. Also, originally they had an "Adventurer level" that you could see and guage where you were at in terms of progression. Well due to the reason of "You should just be playing the game" they took it away and now there is no real way to guage where you should be going or doing based on level you are simply supposed to feel that this is no longer a challenge and find a different place to hunt.  Fine, intuition but its a game and i'd like to measure my progress somehow....
Monetization - The Obsidian coins you can buy with real money are interesting to say the least. Some give buffs and some repair gear depending, this may have changed a bit but thats the basic in game concept of why they sell on the market for in game gold. So all now you bought some in game currency and can now buy a tamed pet off the auction house! Good work with that credit card! Oh wait you dont have the skill to summon that creature out of the whistle because it requires a "whistling" i.e. summoning skill of 10 to summon! Oh too bad so go ahead and get a lower level one. Good job! Now summon it! Great you gained level 2 from one summon, so now dismiss your pet. Now theres a 15 minute cooldown on your next summong! HUH?????????
Avoid this game, great concepts poor execution.
