"Stay a while and listen" (blizzy pls don't sue me, k, thx, bai!) ... or in this case, read a wall of text  :P
What I first noticed about the game is its menu, it's simple, clear, all a menu should be.
Then the game started with the tutorial, forcing me to play it. I did not see a "skip tutorial" button (my bad if there was but pretty sure there wasn't).
Not nice forcing people to do something they don't want to, give them the option to choose.
And if you are going to argue that they had to do that the way they did so people would learn about the characters and their mechanics then i say to you: "I'm sorry but I do not agree!"
There are better ways to introduce important stuff then forcing it on people, hide it like Portal and Portal 2 did - almost the whole game is a tutorial preparing the player for what is to come, but we are not here to talk about Portal, Gauntlet time.
The tutorial on its own was put together nicely, introducing the characters and their mechanics through gameplay rather then through text, which is always nice.
The characters are ok-ish defined.
The Warrior being a warrior can take damage as well as dish out damage of his own.
The Elf uses range attacks to defeat his enemies, although his range isn't that great. I expected more from an elf ranger.
The Valkyrie is a nice mix of the two (i particularly liked the Captain America like shield throw).
These three characters are pretty straightforward, but the Wizard is a bit more complicated.
Having 9 spells to choose from, the Wizard can access his spells with a certain button combination. The desired spell is then ready to use, assuming its not on cooldown.
Not too intuitive, and a bit confusing at first but fiddle around with the spell combinations and you will get the hang of it.
I must point out that the ice spells were not as useful to me as the other two types of spells (fire and lightning) and i ended up playing mostly with fire and lightning spells, and even here with not all of them.
The Fire Bomb is useless if you are near a doorway or a low ceiling-ish area it will hit the ceiling and explode dealing no damage to the monsters below it or it won't end up exploding where you expected it to cause it ended up hitting something you did not thought possible (could be a bug or just bad design).
Also Lightning Discharge was of no use to me, if i wanted to knock someone back I can use my Storm Barrier, so I ended up using it only when I incorrectly combined buttons to get a spell.
The RPG elements are kind of wierd in concept and implementation.
If you buy armour and weapons you only get a cosmetic change. But you can also buy relics to give you buffs to your speed, damage, attack speed or the ability to summon illusions or a demonic gargoyle to fight by your side.
However you can only have 2 relics and can not use any without potions. These potions you can not buy, they can only be found throughout the levels, as well as food which restores hit points.
Instead of gaining traditional levels for each character, you can only improve your stats by performing achievement-like actions called Masteries. For example killing 10,000 monsters grants a 10 % damage bonus.
First time around, the structure of the game is interesting and the level design is a mix of pre-made and randomly generated environment.
Some levels are more complex than others, tasking you or the group to push blocks, insert statues into spots, or fill a lava pool to raise a bridge and then finally an okay-ish boss battle.
The campaign is broken up into three acts, with four stages, four repetitive stages.
Each set of those stages unfolds in the same way:
First you start with a standard level, then you move on to a shorter level with a frustrating twist like being chased by death which btw is bad at its job and its not so hard to outrun (just frustrating) or a dark cave eating away at your nerves as you try to hold back the urge to pluck out your hair and then (as i already mentioned) a boss fight.
Higher difficulty only makes enemies more resistant to damage and drop more gold.
Once the campaign is finished there’s not much incentive to revisit and replay the game.
The A.I. is not to bright either. Getting stuck frequently on each other, corners, doorways and other stuff lying around the level.
After some time you notice how they move and can kite them around the level making them easy targets. Easier than they would have been on their own.
And a one last thing, the camera, oh boy ...
The view is zoomed out far enough to cover an area, but not far enough for a four player co-op play through. The camera does not follow any player controlled characters but hovers above an area of the level and its easy to lose sight of your character.
Additionally if any teammate goes idle you can't move on without them cause the camera will stand still in an area and try to cover all players.
I am sure that Arrowhead did their best but they neither went full retro nor did they break from the past.
As i see this game, its like they tried to stay close to the original (Gauntlet from 1985) but not to close cause people my not like it today and tried to make it an appealing 2014 role-play, dungeon crawl, hack and slash game but actually got stuck in the middle of it all resulting in a not so good game.
In short its repetitive and overly simplistic, awkward camera, an uninteresting upgrade system and too little substance or variety to satisfy players.
However, with four committed players the co-op works well, and it’s certainly not the worst Gauntlet revamp there’s ever been.
All in all IMHO this game is a 5.5 / 10, nice try but u failed, sry and i do not recommend this game.

Fear 3 takes the consolization that Fear 2 introduced to the extreme. Regenerating hit points, check; start each level with a pistol no matter how the last level ends (literally walking out of a building from level 3 to 4), check; lots and lots of cut scenes, check; goofy point system that upgrades how much ammo you can hold in your weapons, check. The game throws any logic to the world out of the window. The game totally screws up the mech portions as others have mentioned that were a lot of fun in Fear 2. How about an AI so dumb that enemies lose track of you when you are coming out of a door in a house if they don't see you for a while and there is no where else you can go but out of the door? Each game after Fear seems to have less slo-mo time than the last, Fear 3 feeling like hardly any time at all.
Also, you can only carry two weapons at a time (not that there were many to choose from anyway), and you can't pick a weapon by key, only switch between the two. Pretty much you stick with the assualt rifle and shotgun or penetrator later, using the sniper rifle and rocket launcher when given for a specific threat. Pistol is worthless, SMG only good in the beginning or when there is lots of ammo for it, the dual SMGs for the blue guys, and the laser for guys holding riot shields or blue guys.
Most of the game is okay as a generic shooter with the exception of level 6 in the mech and the last level which was garbage. But if you played the first two games, don't expect anything remotely like a Fear game.
Finally, I guess Fear 3 ignored Jin Sun-Kwon's fate in Fear: Extraction Point. That annoyed me since this game tries to continue the story from the other Fear games, including the fate of Point Man at the end of Extraction Point.

I bought this game from the Overwhelmingly Positive Humble Bundle for 1€.
I can't believe i'm writing a review of this game on Steam after playing EBF2 on Newgrounds in 2009. Time flies.
What is this game about? How the description on the store page says, this is a turn based rpg with cute graphics and stupid humor, how i like it. At first the gameplay seems simple but the game tells you from the first battle to scan every enemies because elemental weakness and resistances are the core of this game.
The game gives you a lot of equipment because to succeed you need to change your gear before starting an encounter or between waves to not be overwhelmed by your opponents. This is a good layer of strategy alongside the usual buff your party and debuff your enemies.
This brings another point i liked of this game, the forging. It's quite simple here, you need to have the materials acquired by slaying enemies or bought by stores to increase the atrritubutes of your gear and some also have passives like random chance to summon a belly flopping mammoth on an enemy each turn, auto cast buffs on your party or a damaging spell after attacking. So try equip and upgrade different piece of gear for some nice combos, don't focus on what looks the best!
The plot is quite simple and funnily enough it serves just as a background for our "heroes" to adventure on the map and acquire gear while doing stupid stuff. That's the charm of this series, the party is a bunch of goofballs with barely working brains. As Anna said: "I have no idea how they survived this long with no survival skills". Quite a different tone from your usual RPG.
Finally, the soundtrack, which is free by the way, is really good. It set up the pace perfectly with happy tunes while exploring the grass areas or fighting the early enemies, to dark tones in the toughest fights. The composer is really good and she made EBF3 music too, check that out!
Now, after praising basically everything, i will nitpick a couple of complains. First of all, some fights will drag a lot, expecially on higher difficulties, where the stats of enemies are increased, and when i saw an encounter was composed of 7 waves i was already rolling my eyes after finishing another long wave or a boss fight. I don't think it's boring, but i tended to overthink my strategy and equip for each wave and probably my brain was melting.
Second problem is that the game offers 4 characters, but unfortunatly it's best to focus on 3 and two slots are occupied by Matt (warrior) and Nat (Mage) for their highly specialized stats so the third slot is contested by Lance (Gunner) and Anna (Archer) that overlap a bit on their utility but many guides and myself went with Anna in the end since she is the newcomer and brings a bit more on the table than Lance (cough, evasion buff).
To conclude my fanboy review, i say this game gave me more than 30 hours of enjoyment for just 1€, and i plan to play   new game+ on Epic difficulty, but i can say that i should have bought this earlier, even at full price (11€.... not a lot) because it's a bargain for someone that enjoyed in his youth Final Fantasy and other turn based rpgs in the PSX era. Just don't let the "anime" graphic, "childish" humor and flash coding influence your opinion on this game.
If you aren't sure, you can play this for free on Kongregate or Newgrounds, the only thing you will miss is Battle Mountain, another end game with extra loot, but unrelated to the main quest, so you aren't missing any plot by not playing it. So you also have a demo, what more do you want?! :D
Now, i'm waiting for EBF5, currently in development, and this time i will get it as soon as possible.
TL. DR. game is good!

Lets just say it is a Semi-thumbs-up for The Uncertain.
It is a nice little game(for a first episode), but has its flaws in some parts.
The Idea of this game is good. Its a simple and somehow possible scenario for the future. And you come to the conclusion that a robot with AI and suddenly no purpose will possibly act like the robots in the game.
I can understand some of the negative reviews. Maybe its the motionless vioces of the robots, but it feels exactly like playing a robot. Simple is that. There is no emotion and no thrill to the story. But even though it is a average good indie game. disclosure:

in terms of gameplay, 'the uncertain' follows closely behind the footsteps of telltale games such as 'the walking dead' series and 'the wolf among us'. for those arguing that telltale games gave you different routes, and that this is fairly linear i will say this:
i don't think having the choice between 'npc x' dying or 'npc y' dying in your playthrough makes a great game. i love non-linear roleplaying games as much as the next dork, but to argue a game has no replayability because it's the same story on each playthrough is the same as saying there's no reason to rewatch a movie you enjoyed.
i've seen some complaints about the visuals, translation and controls so i want to address those.
in my opinion the graphics are fine, not as cel-shaded as games like 'borderlands' or the aforementioned 'the wolf among us', but on that side of cartoon-ish 'realism'. it works with the story just fine. nothing seems out of place. the lighting and the colours are great. it's not breaking any new ground, but i didn't purchase this game expecting cutting edge graphics and photo-realism.
i've seen nothing wrong with the translation so far and those who dislike the voices are arguing about subjective tastes. the voice acting isn't as painful as 'mars: war logs', for example. the protagonist's voice reminds me of tao lin, or an unaffected midwestern accent along the lines of a cyborg david foster wallace. in fact, some of the dialogue (both the script and delivery) has made me laugh -
- and the sound engineering in general is fantastic. there are beautiful echo effects in small spaces which give life to the environments. the soundtrack is quite nice, too.
the controls are what you'd expect of a game in this genre - fixed camera angles, simple motion controls and basic interaction from the mouse button.
i felt compelled to write this - and recommend this game - because it's what i wanted from telltale. an original, thoughtful and enjoyable story with gameplay that allows that story to be told. as much as i enjoy telltale games, it's nice to have a new environment, universe and characters to explore rather than following the same formula and slapping a 'batman', 'guardians of the galaxy' or 'borderlands' face on it.
i picked this game up on sale, but i buy most of my games on sale. i don't like getting into the "i paid this much money and only got this many hours of content!" discussion so i won't.
as an aside, i've been let down by episodic games before. that's another argument i don't want to rehash. 'd4: dark dreams don't die' was a fantastic game which i loved, but there won't be any more of it.  the developer of 'blues and bullets' has all but disappeared after two episodes - it doesn't mean i didn't enjoy what i got to play. i'm happy to support developers who create things like this, because these are the games i want more of.
tl;dr: if you've ever enjoyed a telltale game, wanted an original, creative and well-written story, and enjoy supporting independent developers go ahead and play this game.

There is literally no redeeming quality to this game - it's not scary, it's forgettable, the story sucks, every single previous feature has been neutered (you can only hold 2 guns, you have to UNLOCK the hand-to-hand abilities from the previous game, and the enemies are somehow more lackluster and devoid of character than freaking CLONES). And, there's a so-called progression system that does nothing (or, at least it seems that way). Bottom line, do not buy this game. Hell, don't even pirate it. I intend to beat this game eventually because I still for some reason want to finish the series, but I already know I'm gonna be wishing for my 2 hours back. I'm gonna be a sucker and attempt to get my money's worth out of this steaming pile of game. Sigh. The first game was really freaking good. How did we get here....

It's either 'where it all went wrong' or 'where it all went right' with Fallout 3.
I reckon it's a little bit of both, as this quasi reboot of the franchise has a lot in store.
Pros:
- decently large open world
- setting. Washington, DC is a great wasteland to roam around.
- open world. it truly is. you decide where to go, who to fight (everyone, duh) or help. There's plenty of places to discover and tons of quests to do
- neat graphics
- I like the VATS system, bringing at least a little rpg to the table
- perks! they're hilarious and awesome
- it's a sad but funny world
Cons:
- can get borderline silly
- relatively easy
- too often it feels like a FPS than a RPG
- it gets boring and repetitive. I found that only a few quests really are enjoyable (stealing the declaration of independence or blowing up megaton)
Verdict:
Fallout 3 is a well produced FPS/RPG hybrid with a dominant FPS trait. shedding the deep immersion of it's more tactical prequels, it manages to pair fast paced combat with open world scavenging/exploring while delivering one of gamings more hilarious postapocalyptic settings.

shroud of the avatar is a different game, i'd say its the first "old style new age" mmo. What i mean by that is , you gonna find all the core elements of old mmos, the hardcore pvp, very deep crafting system, exploration and more. Casual players won't enjoy this game, the game is based in the classics ultima, runescape and tibia system in which what you have to do isn't very clear. The lack of map and quest pointer is turn off for many but it's amazing for me. That's what a quest suppose to be, you need to explore the cities and talk to people (real talk, not only hi, quest, yes, bye) to gather clues to know where you suppose to go. When you finally understand the basics of crafting, skills, scenes you notice that this game, if polished and optimized, is the last mmo i will be playing for a very long time and probably the closest experience you can get of the old typing rpgs and table top rpg nowdays. My down points are little but there are some. Poor tutorial, confusing skill system, maybe, just maybe, too much needed recipes for one dishe and the travelling system. Do Not Buy This Game
First, this game really is early access, yet it has launched.  It is not complete, major systems are broken, reworked, or even added every patch yet it launched July 2016.  That is when it went persistant and you could build your character, claim your house, start playing the game.  I may change my review when Port declares it done but at this point it is not worth even the $40 minimum.  You truly are beta testing the game in a world where all the mistakes along the way leave lasting imacts.
Shall we start with combat?  That is most of the game after all.
There are 10 action slots that can be filled with abilities. Potions and count as abilities.
You build a 'deck' which is drawn into those slots.  You can specify which slot cards go into so at least the same ability will be on the same button but there is no guarantee that the ability will be available when you need it.  This adds a distinct random quality to combat.
So buffs, healing, combat attacks, anything except swinging your sword and moving is a random ability.  Keep the decks small and it is workable but not exactly a good system for real time combat.
EDIT:  There was a second non-combat button bar all along.  That was hidden durng combat but is now always acessible so potions do not take up an action slot.  Improvement but the deck randomness still remains.
EDIT: Cover was also added some some bit of combat positioning can matter.  Reviews on this show it being rather buggy with small terrain featires providing unreasonable cover.  Tuning needed but a good start.
EDIT:  A new parallel system to allow non-random decks ot be competitve is being developed.  'Heat' where locked abilities cost more focus to use if they were recently used should allow for burst or sustained use fomr fixed abilities.  This is a second parallel combat system that will need tuning when the primary deck based system has never been well balanced.  Again, a good start but much more work needed.
Move on to loot. A reason for the combat.
There is none.  Not implemented.
At this point you fight for the exp or to go mining.  The only way to get gear is to craft it.  Sure this will change eventually but right now the same mobs drop the same rusty daggers in the tutorial and in the highest dungeons.
EDIT:  Some loot, Artifacts (very rare drops) were added.  You can not just pick up the armor & weapons off your various fallen foes to use as you progress.  You'll have a rusty weapon and no armor if you try.
Speaking of which, the mobs.
Very little variety in the creatures you fight.  Same 10 models are reused everywhere.  Spiders have root attacks, some creatures cast very annoying confusion spells but that about fills out the list of special abilities.  There is no 'don't stand in the fire' positioning when fighting anything.
Character development and EXP, the other reason for the combat.
Killing things builds exp into a pool.  Using skills moves exp out of the pool into the skill.  Straightforward enough except...
The spending exp on skills happens much faster than the filling through kills so the pool is rushes to empty.  What you must do is turn off raising skills except the one you want to raise.
The amount of exp that flows from pool to skill is proportional to the size of the pool.  A big pool will push more exp requiring fewer uses of the skill to raise it.  So you might want ot just turn off all skills and go kill 300 wolves to fill the pool.
Crafting works the same way except the pool is filled by harvesting.  Actual crafting does add some to the pool but not enough to raise a skill.  Make sure to skin everything to fill the crafting pool then just dump the hides.
There is no cap on EXP.  You can raise every skill to 100 (grandmaster) and beyond if you want to spend enough time killing.
Death will take some exp from the pool and if it is empty will drain it from skills.  The amount death takes is proportional to the total amount you have spent on skills.  This makes the exp cap the level where death sucks as much exp as can be farmed between deaths.
Oh yes, Whoever gets the killing blow gets all the exp.  Killstealing is back.
Lets talk about the world.
The world is an overland map and little zones that can be entered at various places.  Some places like mines have entrances inside other zones but most everything is off the world map.  The world map is broken into regions by control points you must fight through to get to the other side.  That is the overworld.  Nothing to do there except move from point A to point B.  Move along the roads only or you move much slower, don't explore.
The zones are for the most part small simple rings or walled forests.  Under development, to be finished, many are repeated.  There are some very pretty ones but most at this point are bland.
There are load screens when passing between zones, average ~1min right now.
There are multiple modes of play.
Multiplayer online.  Pretty obvious, standard MMO.
Friends Online.  This sounds like it should show your friends and possibly guildmates but it only shows your party members.  There is still guild chat.
Single player online.  Sounds obvious but is the same as Friends online.
Single player OFFLINE.  Obvious.
Given the state of optimization Multiplayer online may not be playable for you.  All resources and mobs are shared and killstealable so you directly complete with other players in multiplayer.  Not really a problem if the zones were large and numerous but they are not.  So, you switch to friends only and never see a single other person in the world.  The huge world and towns are empty.
There is no good solution to that at this time.  The world is either too small and crowded or empty with no middle bear.
Crafting...
Crafting takes resources, of course.  Crafting taking insane amounts of resources is no so obvious.
Walk around the towns and you'll see massive cotton fields, care to guess why?  It is not to sell, it is to make the one or two good pieces the RNG will give you.
Metal armor is the same way except you can only get it in mines.  There are half dozen mines around the world total with 30-40 spawns in each.  If you do metal crafting you will spend days, literally 48+ hours, in those mines to raise your skill and make armor.  You will do this alone in single player mode.
Wood...  Oh the poor carpenters.  Running around forests past all the trees to the one you can actually cut down.  They are available in more zones but not in any great quantity so again you'll be running around in single player.  For the record it takes 8 trees to make a bow.
Improving items beyond base or adding enchantments takes silver and gold so get back in those mines.
And that is just the gathering part.
The actual crafting is heavily RNG based with the downside being powerful items made out of glass.  Durability ends up being very low on the more powerful created items and only the very lucky result is usable for long.
For the record I spent a little over $600 on this game because I knew damn well that without a house you'd have half the game.  (before row houses)  Keep that in mind, if you do not own property you get half the game or less.  Gardening is essential if you cook or craft cloth, requiring a house.  I expect farming to be required for alchemy before 'release'.  I've put 180 hours into the game trying to find the fun parts and have failed.
I have not even touched on the PTW portions but have focused on the actual mechanics and gameplay.  There is no good reason to play this game and actually are more downsides not touched on in this already long review.
TLDR
The result of all this is a never ending grind.  Grind mobs for exp, grind mines for material, there is nothing else to the game at this point.  Of course if you don't start grinding now and instead buy the game at 'release' you will be a year behind the curve with no cap to level things out.
No need for more words than "forsaken virtues" here.

Imagine with me, if you will.  You are leader of a small but prosperous empire, controlling roughly two dozen small star systems.  You and your allies have been at war with the most powerful civilization for years, and you've managed to gain the upper hand.  A long and costly war has cost you several star systems and most of your fleet.  Finally, they agree to peace.  You sign the papers, and begin to focus on internal affairs.
As you check your intelligence briefings, you notice that another empire has been building up their military.  Significantly.  As it stands, the Yor have four to five times as much firepower as the rest of the nations put together, as well as a much larger population.  They begin to greedily prey upon the weaker nations, demanding tribute or conquering them.
You halt all social and military production, and begin pouring all of your resources into your R&D projects, developing weapons and shields specialized to counter the growing threat.  One by one, your allied nations fall to swarms of powerful Yor ships.
After the research had advanced sufficiently, you empty your coffers and upgrade your small fleet, and purchase some additional cruisers.  You position your fleet on the Terran-Yor border and wait.
Its time.  Your destroyers flash across the border, seeking out the numerically superior Yor fleets and engaging them.  Terran ships begin to explode, but the Yor are technologically inferior, and they explode faster.  War erupts across the galaxy as civilizations pick their sides.  A galactic conflagration begins.
Behind your destroyers, fleets of heavily-escorted troop carriers descend onto Yor worlds, crammed with billions of troops.  Tens, then hundreds, of billions die as your begin to inch your way towards the Yor homeworlds.  Your war machine keeps turning, producing dozens of sophisticated warships.
Eventually, Icos itself falls.  You survey your vast empire, won with the blood of countless billions.  Your huge fleet dwarfs all others.  Your allies are afraid of you.  You've positioned fleets on all of your borders, backed up with troop ships.
Then you realize: you've become what you set out to destroy.
This is Galactic Civilizations.

I would acredit this game for getting me into indie games in the first place. It is a narrative based game, that is less about gameplay and more about progressing through a story. Call it an interactive novel if you will. In this game, you walk around to gather clues and information and solve several puzzles. These aspects are not too involved in the game as its primary focus.
Don't let the apparant lack of gameplay get in the way of a heart-tugging story. This game was meant for casual players who desire a story they can follow. Travel back in time through the computer simulation of the memories of Johnny, an old man, dying on his deathbed. Discover key moments in his life, both happy and most deffinetly sad as you gather information from Johnny's memories and give him the dying memory that he desires, to go to the moon.
The game's aesthetics reflects that of an old 4th gen. RPG. What was most impressive about the game, aesthetically, was the soundtrack. Especially listen to tracks like "For River","Everything's Alright", "Lament of a Stranger" and even "Beta-B".
Some will say that this game isn't a proper game, because it doesn't have enough gameplay to it. I could respect that perspective. Just keep in mind that this is a game that leans heavily on narrative, over gameplay and aesthetics. This game isn't meant to please every gamer, but it disserves recognition by every gamer.

Reus is a god game where you cultivate a planet and help the indigenous tribes to build and improve their villages. You control the four giants, which can create water, mountain, forest and swamp areas. Into these areas, they can put animals, plants and minerals. These resources differ depending on their surrounding area type. Furthermore, you can bless and improve these tiles to get boni from interactions between tiles. And on top of that settles a tribe that tells you what it needs and that offers you challenges to get unique boni (i.e. "reach 50 wealth"). By doing that, you unlock ambassadors, which can be placed on your giants to unlock new or better abilities. You can pause the game anytime and look around to plan ahead. It's really easy to start and understand, but as it carries on, the game offers a suprising depth by showering you with so many combinations!
You can do everything just with your mouse if you feel like snacking etc., but you can also use the keyboard to make the whole affair much more efficient.
You get exactly what you see in the videos and pictures above. The graphics are cute and the planet seems vivid due to its inhabitants derping around and doing stuff. The game is underlayed with soft background music, which was very soothing.
If I recall correctly, you first have to unlock different modi. Then you can chose between 30, 60 and 120 minute era games, free play, or to start in the 1st, 2nd or 3rd era. I'd say for me, one hour was the average sitting at first, and then I started to try to reach higher challenge goals. In my 14h of total playtime, I unlocked roughly 43% of the challenges (achievements), which offer you a nice to keep playing and improving your skills or rather your knowlegde.
A very enjoyable game if you're into the genre. I'd say it's also beginner friendly, as you don't have to learn much early on in order to be succesful. I liked the aspect that you're not fully in control of the people, which makes for a greater challenge. And if a village settles in the "wrong" zone, you can always snuff them out with the rock giant's handy earthquake ability. =P
Great for achievement hunters and worth the full price, so definitely get it when it's on sale!

Epic Battle Fantasy 4 (EBF4 for short) is the fourth installment of popular jRPG-esque series
that originated as web browser games. The series is basically a parody of famous Japanese RPG games (mostly Final Fantasy). If you want some more preview on the older games, I suggest you read my review on previous game, EBF3 (which is also on Steam), if you haven't already.
But to keep things short, I'll just give you a small preludium:
the series started as free browser games that were made for fun and played to kill some free time, and even EBF4 itself can be played via your browser, but there's also an expanded, paid version (AKA the one I'm reviewing now), and it's not exactly cheap, 11,99 USD. Some professional games cost as much, and thus, the game will be judged like one.
So, first, what's the premise?
As a rather typical jRPG like game, you can expect the usual: explore the world, find treasures, both hidden and not, talk to stupid NPCs so they can give you their stupid quests, upgrade your skills and fight the enemies ( and there's lot of those).
The creator approched the matter with a safe and proven method:
the world itself is open, but it's filled with various obstacles and road blockers (such as rocks or trees, but also more absurd ones, like floating clouds) that make your road linear at first, but with time you acquire means of bypassing them, one by one. This not only allows you to progress, but also lets you find hidden treasures, enemies, and other content, so you will definitely be coming back to old places through your entire playthrough.
As I've said, it's a safe method that was used in countless titles. And it's not a bad thing really. Experimenting is good if you know what you're doing, but if something just works, I see no reason not to use it.
The world itself will charm you with its simple graphics (which are still a major improvement over the previous one) and varied environment, as well as subtle themes to be found, such as various references to other media and clever comments spoken by your team members.
Overall it may not be masterfully crafted, but it's full of its own unique charm.
Combat has always been
core element of these games, and as such I'm very happy to say it spectacularly failed to disappoint me.
Not only it's great on its own, it also improved on everything from the previous games without changing the basis even slightly.
Aside from the usual stuff like attacking, healing and using your Limit Breaks, there's 12 different status effect, 10 elements and over 100 unique skills which can be used BY you, or AGAINST you. Add shiploads of unique pieces of equipment and you've got EBF4.
That means a vast array of different strategies that you can use to defeat your enemies, and believe me, if you play on Epic (the hardest difficulty), you will want to spend some time thinking about them.
Want to debuff your enemies to such point they can barely scratch you? Sure.
Want to go full offense and counter your lack of defense by making your enemies unable to move? Guess that will work too.
Naturally enemies have their strengths and weaknesses, and there's a whole lot of them (147, to give you the idea), so you will have to use everything at your disposal thorough the game.
Overall it's just what a good turn-based jRPG should look like. Give the players freedom in their playstyle and let them experiment. I have absolutely no reason to complain.
Each game has its pros and cons, and I've already explored the pros.
Now, the story was never the main focus of these games, but it still deserves some attention. I can't really say much without spoiling it (as the story is partially revealed thorough the game). I'll just say that if you're enjoying the game itself, then the story will keep you interested, but if the game doesn't turn out to be your type, you won't stay just for the story.
The quests are just what they were in the previous game - that is, fetch quests. You are told to get some items, and you either get them from defeating monsters (or buying them from shop), or from some treasure chests, or from other quests. Simple as that. I can't say I expected more, but it certainly would be nice to see a more expanded and developed quest from time to time. Say, a bunch or chain of quests that all give you key items that together allow you to challenge some hidden boss or whatever.
The game is moderately long, with plenty of additional content (most notably a fully optional location featuring lots of optional bosses and extremely long and challenging enemy waves, full of unique treasure), and fun gameplay will make sure you will play more than one time.
If you're an old-school fan of the jRPG genre (I'm not, personally), it's a must have.
If you're new to jRPGs or RPGs in general, you should at least give this game a try. If you're not sure about spending money on it, go ahead and try the browser version (or previous games whatsoever). If you happen to enjoy them, then definitely buy it, as it's only better than all that came before.
I give it a solid 9/10

I hired out Gaunlet many times years ago on Xbox. It was a little different to this version but everything I loved is still here. 4 player same screen co-op! TONNES of enemies! No overpowered characters. And best of all, veteran level difficulty; My friend and I took about 6 tries to get past the very first level on Normal difficulty!! (Partly because of the retro style levels containing no checkpoints - which can be annoying but it's a damn fun kind of annoying!)

I have fond memories of the original Gauntlet. I remember playing the Amstrad CPC version for a whole day, only taking breaks for food. I also had the Gauntlet Legacy games which I thought were ok but too different from the original game. This latest incarnation of Gauntlet does not disappoint. It retains aspects of the original: 4p co-op, overwhelming numbers of enemies and a good dose of humour. It's a great homage to the original with many elements that have been updated to modern standards.
This game surpasses the original in my opinion which is no mean feat. Each character plays very differently. My favourite is the wizard who is tricky to use at first but when mastered can be very powerful.
I've seen some reviews which accuse the game of being repetitive. There is some truth in that, especially when you have to restart a level from the beginning. The action is so fun that I don't mind repeating the same level again and it also allows you to gain more gold and level up your character.

I've not played the original arcade Gaunlet very long, mostly seen youtube videos of it. This game thankfully isn't that level of hard but with varying difficulties you can probably get it right up there. You get 4 characters and they cannot be picked by more than one player (this has some people miffed for some reason).
The game is fun, each character feels unique to a degree and you slaughter (or try to) tons of enemies and spawners as you traverse the game. You can unlock useless vanity items as your characters are super tiny when actually playing and you can't zoom in so that hardly has an effect.
While it's fun, the game is VERY short, I'm not sure how long 1 playthrough was but I was surprised when it was over. I expected there to be another whole part or something but nope. Maybe that's a good thing to some, swing in for a sort play and back to work or something. That said the $20 dollar price tag is just a bit much to ask for with this, $10? Sure. But it feels like it needs more.

Old-school feel I was looking for was there, but it was very short-lived..  in comparison to previous Gauntlet titles, there just isn't enough content. There's only 3 zones, and 4 characters to choose from.. (5 with DLC).

Graphics are good enough, and the game plays out smooth. It is a very linear story that you follow though, so have that in mind.
A minor drawback is controls, wich cannot be customized, so that can be an issue if you have a left-handed setup or is used to use a controller with inverted axis, either or both of them, since no customization at all is available. It's WASD to move if you use the keyboard, only alternative is a controller. Controls are easy though, and there's seldom a rush for anything, so it really don't have that much of an impact. Other minor issue is that some moments and minigames probably could've been cut without that bothering anyone.
All in all, I consider this a good game, but I do not recommend it, and this comes down completely to the price. I don't know if following episodes are included, but if they aren't, I'm going to have a real problem with the pricing of this game.

As good as this game is, I'm having a hard time accepting a price of nearly €15 for it. My one real complaint: length. This game can be beaten in one sitting. No kidding. If you have a day to kill you can run through the whole game. Yeah, there are still things to level up and what not but you will have played every level. The original Gauntlet games had an insane number of levels, moving exits, random events or rules on each level, exits that warped to further levels instead of going in a linear fashion. None of that is here. You get three areas. Each area has four levels. Each level has three floors except for the last level which is a boss fight. Not nearly long enough to be a real Gauntlet game. There's a lot to like about The Uncertain's first episode--the story and world-building are interesting, the graphics are polished, the voice acting is strong, and it has a great atmosphere. Unfortunately, the stylistic elements aren't supported by the actual mechanics of the game. First of all, the interface and controls are awkward and draggy, especially if you insist on high resolution. I agree with a lot of other users on here that the game likely would've benefited from a first-person POV. No matter how immersive the atmosphere is, you can't get lost in a game when you're bogged down by clunky navigation and distracting camera angle switches.
Finally, the actual gameplay itself is more focused on puzzles than adventuring or mystery-solving. Which would be fine, except that the puzzles are hilariously easy. At one point, while I was supposed to be maneuvering my little ship evasively, I decided to experiment by not touching the keyboard at all and letting it coast. Guess what? The bad guys still didn't catch me, and I didn't crash. The visual puzzles and logic puzzles (which constitute the majority of the game's challenges) are no better, so easily solvable that you feel like you're missing something, like there must be more to it. I finished this episode in four hours, and even that was a little longer than necessary. I took my sweet time, clicking on just about everything and getting up to grab a snack while I waited for sections to load. Luckily, I got the game on sale for under $5, so it's not like I lost much. Still, it's a shame that an episode that looks and sounds so well-produced falters when it comes to the actual gameplay experience.
For a worthwhile follow-up, the devs will have to improve the controls drastically and add in some more challenging puzzles. Barring that, I'm not sure I'd be willing to shell out even the sale price to find out how the (admittedly fun) story ends. I'd probably just go watch Battlestar Galactica instead.

An underwhelmingly inconsequential end to an overwhelmingly consequential series, F.E.A.R. 3 leaves a bad taste in literally everyone's mouth; it is also my favorite bad video game.

- Modernized the control scheme for the first time in the series (before, Shift was ADS and Left-Click was Melee, with ALT being used for sprinting in F.E.A.R. 2; Shift is now Sprint, Left-Click is ADS and Middle Mouse Button is Melee), meaning players didn't have to rebind basic controls from the menu.
- To its credit, F.E.A.R. 3 does its best to continue and bring to fruition the series' clearly drawn-out story of Alma and her sons.
- Adds a new playable character class (the Phantom/Paxton Fettel), a treat for the hardcore fan.
- Introduction of a Co-Op mode, which is actually pretty cool.
- Offers the opportunity to take control of an
mech, something the previous games had not offered (F.E.A.R. 2 allows for the control of a basic mech, but not the larger, "enhanced" variant).
- The AI isn't entirely inept, and offer a challenge at higher difficulties.
- Uses Steamworks for Multiplayer and Achievements, so was unaffected by the GameSpy shutdown that helped to bring down the multiplayer aspects of the previous games.
- Uses true 7.1 audio output (F.E.A.R. 1 only supported it with EAX hardware installed, and F.E.A.R. 2 was 5.1).
- Introduces DirectX 11 for improved performance on higher-end videocards.
- Right away, series' veterans will notice that the graphics in F.E.A.R. 3 look
, especally in comparison to its predecessor F.E.A.R. 2.  And despite this, F.E.A.R. 3 will still perform worse than both its predecessors on lower end hardware even at its lowest settings and with DirectX 9 forced on.
- While the developers clearly did what they could to salvage a thinning story, they still managed to completely muck-up several key plotholes that even casual fans of the series would be highly irritated with (The Harlan Wade factor, the disregard for F.E.A.R. 2 Reborn, an inpromptu transition from the end of Extraction Point to F.E.A.R. 3, the wanton disposal of Michael Beckett as a series' character, the list goes on...).

- Gunplay

a watered down Call of Duty; the guns do not sound realistic even by CoD standards, the guns are not balanced -- several were clearly intended not to be used except in specific situations -- and the ai, while manageable, just doesn't have the teamwork capabilities of its predecessors (especially F.E.A.R. 1).
As I stated at the beginning of this review, F.E.A.R. 3 leaves a bad taste in everyone's mouth; the series' fans hate it for the evident lack of quality control and damage to the storyline, while casual players are turned off by a generic CoD gunplay clone and what they perceive to be a bland, confusing storyline where the final turn off is when they realize that, yes,
.
That being said, I call F.E.A.R. 3 my favorite bad game for a few reasons: bias, pity and self-loathing.  Bias, in that I'm a fan of the previous titles.  Pity, in that I'm aware of the very limited timeframe the developers had forced upon them by Warner Brothers.  And self-loathing, in that I don't know any better than to hold on to only a handful of franchises I like no matter how underground or deteriorated they become.
And, yes, it can also just be a stupid-fun game.

If you loved the gameplay of old-school JRPGs, then Epic Battle Fantasy 4 is right up your alley. It's one of the few examples of a Flash game that's actually good. The story is silly and almost nonexistant, but the gameplay is satisfying and scratches that JRPG itch. The game is well-balanced almost all the way through, with almost no points that feel badly-designed. If you do pick up EBF4 do yourself a favor and start on the highest difficulty (Epic), as I feel that's the way it's meant to be played. You can always switch to a lower difficulty if it ends up being too much, which is nice.
The biggest flaw I can find with EBF4 is the 3-character party. There are 4 playable characters, but because there are permanent stat-boosting consumable items, the optimal way to play is to choose your party and completely ignore the 4th character for the whole game, because any stat-boosters would be wasted on them.
Other than that, EBF4 is a great game that, while it may not be a masterpiece, is still a lot of fun and an homage to a genre that the game industry has long since forgotten.
Uniquely styled JRPG, it's ok.

A turn-based RPG with a somewhat unique take on the genre, at least in terms of the usual story vs. gameplay argument. I've never subcscribed to the idea that an RPG needs to have a massive, epic, complex story, and this game seems to agree with me. The story of this game is basically an RPG story template that hasn't really been filled in or built onto, though the details that are there are at least charming and lend a little bit of an identity.
Instead, this game really seems to lean on its gameplay and its combat system. The weapons and armor that you equip can have a huge impact on your stats, and require different tactics to capitilize on their various perks and bonuses. There's a pretty good amount of enemy variety, and encounters are scripted instead of random encounters, leading to some battles that are created specifically to encourage you to take advantage of different armor and weapon sets.
Defeating enemies gives you ability points, which you can spend to learn new skills or upgrade ones you already have. You've got a lot more control over the tools available to you than some other games give you, and I really appreciated that. However, the fact that better versions of skills are added on top of the weaker ones instead of replacing them, and the fact that some skills give you little to no reason to use them mean that the skill pool is smaller than it looks like it is.
Playing on Normal difficulty, I never found myself having to grind for experience or ability points to be able to move forward, but some enemies reappear when you leave and come back, so it's possible to save up some more EXP or AP if you think you need a bit more of an edge. Even when playing on the hardest difficulty, the boss fights never really pushed me too hard, though some of them did take a long time to beat. Worst case scenario: one of tne of the post-game bosses in the Battle Mountain area took me 47 minutes to beat, but I still managed it on my first try.
Beating the game adds a New Game+ mode, scaling up the enemy levels and letting you replay the game starting with all of your endgame equipment. This opens up strategies you may not have had the first time through, and gave me a reason to play the game again. Beating New Game+ gives you New Game++, which just scales up enemies even more. it's basically just New Game+ again, so there's no real reason to play a third time unless you want all the achievments.
The game just endlessly repeats there. You can keep playing New Game++ over and over, and continue getting more stat-boosting items (whose effects carry over as well), leading to some absolutely ridiculous stat levels, and even the highest difficulty fails to provide any meaningful challenge after a while. The game kinda ends on an anti-climax, but the path there is definitely interesting, and given the price tag, it's worth a look, even for people who aren't super into RPGs, since the combat system is so well-refined and easy to get into.
Oh, and the music is just, amazing. Especially that final boss theme.

Although there will always be some who are resistant to Kupo's monetary direction with the Epic Battle Fantasy franchise, I for one am glad that I can finally support this indie developer who is beloved by his fanbase, not only for the plethra of content he's put out for free online, but for the continued, friendly support he's shown across the board on his games and site.
With that said, EBF4 is a light-hearted take on the RPG genre that takes the best out of its traditional norms and combines them into new, fun, and creative systems. Gone is the abnormally intense grind to level your characters beyond all reason, as enemies and bosses scale to player level, and can be brought down using a variety of strategies based on equips, attacks, and status effects, all of which you continually obtain more of to keep the battle system fresh and flexible to differing playstyles. The story is limited but enjoyable, requiring no previous experience with the series to appreciate fully. And while the map progression is a little linear at first, various secrets and puzzles still make exploration rewarding, not to mention the lack of random battles means you can set your own pace with the game, choosing the order of battles at your leisure.
The addition of Battle Mountain to the Steam version was a welcome change to returning fans, and a great place to accquire game-changing gear to boost your battle tactics throughout the story and beyond. Not to mention, by the endgame, quite a challenge to clear all the boss rushes, making the last dozen or so achievements quite satisfying to get. All-in-all, a must-have for any RPG and/or Flash enthusiasts; the port from Newgrounds/Kongregate was masterfully done, with no noticeable performance issues on my end, as Kupo was thorough in addressing them into and well after release.
If the price tag is a little too steep for you, pin it on your wishlist for a while, Kupo's never modest about putting EBF4 for generous sales throughout seasonal events and not. Or check out his other titles first, here or elsewhere: EBF3 is up on Steam for free, and is a good demo of what you'll be seeing in this one.

Even though the plot is basic, a more complex story has been announced back in January or 2017! So I look forward to see what Comon Games has in store for their player base. I am also noting they stated to have listened to our feedback's on this project and will be including more puzzles and even more story driven episodes. They will be hiring writers as well to make the next episode longer and more complex in its story. How exciting!
Onto my review:
Sure the controls were sticky and the puzzles were basic; However! They set up a creative world with interesting mechanics, a great story plot, and useful characters that may provide deep backgrounds in the future. This was a point and click adventure that acted as an interactive movie more than a video game. Unfortunately this means that there is no chance for replay-ability and different outcomes. The ending was a bit cliche' but it does make you wonder where the story will be going in the future. I also found the change in perspective very refreshing. Usually in this genre you play a survivor or a lone wolf who is a human. It was nice to see the concept of this world played out in the eyes of a artificial intelligent machine rather than a human.
If I was to rate this game I would give it a 4 out of 10 because of its delivery or price. It appeared that the project was rushed, making the ideas and the mechanics very simplified. This left little room to explore any of the characters background stories that would have added depth and more time in the universe. My second issue with this game is the amount of content you get for the price. $15 is a usual price you pay for a movie or an anticipated indie game. Even though this game could be considered an interactive movie in some regards, its not worth the price. In conclusion I am looking forward to the future changes to this episode and episode 2 so I'll keep it around for now.
Because Comon Games has stated very bold acclaims about adjusting their content for future episodes I will leave a positive rating for now. However if that changes so does my review. I still recommend avoiding this game unless you believe the price is worth 2 to 3 hours of gameplay.
It was fun but the story gets chopped off becuase its only the first episode. With an independent developer will eps 2 ever appear?

I think I picked up this game for just under $6 USD. For that price, it was worth it.
The controls are very tight. The graphics are very well done. Multiplayer 'just works'. There aren't a ton of people playing, but enough to find most game types at any hour of the day.
There is a bit of a grind...when you beat levels you get to keep the gold you picked up. This also drives competitive gold stealing between players which, surprisingly, adds to the game instead of makes it more frustrating.
With your gold you can buy and upgrade a few basic items. Those items do not do anything other than some special power which can only be used if you have potions -- which only exist for the stage you collect them on (stages consist of several levels, four stages to each major act, three major acts make up the entire story of the game). For that reason, the items are very useful -- but not everyone even needs them. One guy with a highly upgraded lute can use all the potions you find as effectively as splitting it up between the players.
There are also some 'level ups' you get which seem more like achievements than levels. They are different for each of the five characters. They consist of things like, kill x number of creatures with a certain attack, die x number of times, lose x amount of health, collect x gold, etc. They grant that specific character special passive abilities such as doing more damage, having shorter cooldowns, etc. However -- the benefits are slight...2% here 5% there...what makes a player able to handle the hardest difficulty mode is more to do with player skill than anything else.
All said and done, the game feels much shorter and less grindy than previous Gauntlet titles -- but the controls are WAY nicer and the graphics and animations are of a much higher quality than any prior gauntlet I've ever played.
It makes for a fun 'pick up and play' casual arcade game that is fun for shorter periods of time. It has more replayability than I expected for having so few levels, but even so, there really are very few levels.
Thankfully, the replayability comes from trying to perfect your handling of your character. And each of the five characters do seem to play rather differently and are pretty well balanced.
The Elf is good at sniping, bombing large groups of mobs and roll dodging.
The Valkyrie has a powerful shield and some dash and shield throw abilities that make her good at quick skirmish attacks.
The Barbarian is able to charge and do some larger AOE attacks and kick more butt with melee.
The Wizard is challenging, as you have to memorize 9 different key combinations to switch to the appropriate spell at any given moment. If you screw up, he can die very quickly as he doesn't have a 'basic attack.' That being said, he's incredibly powerful if played correctly.
And Lilith (some kind of necromancer) can only be played if you bought the expansion which costs about as much as the base game. She seems to have some fantastic abilities that seem poached from the other 4 classes along with the ability to summon a bunch of undead as meat shields.
One tactic I found very useful is with Lilith and the Wizard. Lilith gets into a corner near a monster spawner and summons undead. The mage teleports behind the undead wall and then casts frost beam at the spawner. Frost beam does more damage the longer it is active and since you won't have to run away because you've got a nice meat shield you knock down spawners very quickly.
For ~$6 this game is worth it. The lack of levels and content is a big negative. No user created levels was a mistake as Gauntlet is supposed to have a billion levels...and this would have been a way to do it. This is a shame because the graphics, and fluid controls of the game means it has a very solid base to build from.

Alright.  So, I basically bought this game because I enjoyed it a lot when I tried it on a friend's PS4, and was looking forwards to the much faster loading times and easier to aim part from using a PC.  So far I've most played just the vanilla game (not much into the underground/resistance/other), and done some... "wandering" in the dark zone.  And from what I can see/have experienced, it's more or less just a decent shooter with good graphics.
Pros:
- HUGE weapon variety (seriously, there's something like 50 different weapons you can use in game)
- Decent cover system
- Decent skill variety (however this is also a con, I'll go into that later)
- Very realistic environments
- Large mod variety (on both weapons and armor)
- Weapons are relatively realistic
- No microtransactions that truly affect gameplay (majority are purely cosmetic)
Cons:
- Out of that massive weapon variety, only a few are anywhere near decent at end game
- Out of the decent skill variety, only a few are any good in PvP, the rest are just PvE gimicks
- PvP is horrible.  You can literally be just doing your own thing in the Dark Zone (where you should be on your toes regardless) just to have someone come up to you, and then out of the blue switch to rogue and gun you down with a shotgun.  No warning.  Was better when they didn't have rogue protocol, so at least you would be more on your toes when someone was around.
- Once you get to level 30, and after you've exhausted all the intel, the only real way to get good gear is the Dark Zone.
- There are only a few viable builds at end game
- Enemies after a point are just huge HP sinks, and your character is comparatively incredibly squishy.
- Missions are repetitive, and can sometimes just be obscene for single players because of enemy tankiness
Mixed:
- Weapon stats are relatively clean and simple in concept, but can be misleading on how they actually perform in game
- Game stability is usually good, but when it's bad, it's really REALLY bad
- Open world means you have all of Manhattan to explore, but since there are no vehicles, you have to walk everywhere.  Character sprint is unimpressive.  However your character never gets tired, so you can move faster more or less forever.
- Parkour mode makes travelling very easy, since your character will automatically vault over objects, go up ladders, go down ladders, etc etc, HOWEVER it means you have to pay attention since it glitches on ropes, and your character (when on auto run, which makes the huge map tolerable) can sometimes get stuck on a tiny♥♥♥♥♥rock in the middle of the street (sort of like fallout)
- Dark zone inventory is tiny.  Good because means you lose fewer things when your extraction gets hijacked, bad because it means you can't carry around as much decent stuff to extract in the first place
Overall, I'd have to give this game a thumbs up, mostly because it really is very very fun.  I would however only recommend buying this game when it's on sale, since let's face it, $60 is harsh, and at most this game will give you maybe 100 hours of gameplay before you die of boredom.

Reus is an enjoyable and unique strategy game. It combines the all-mighty power of 'Gods' with the endless problems of 'the people', providing for a fun and challenging game.
Every move in the game is governed by the four possible Giants of the world. By their actions, you may guide human inhabitants into settling, growing, and thriving, or into struggling, agitating, and invading. Human behavior cannot be directly influenced--you have to plan ahead and use your Giants wisely. And while the game is decidedly simple in concept, the execution is brilliant and provides for a complex range of strategies.
For game play, there is a nice assortment of achievements and difficulties, and players can customize game play for all sorts of goals and styles. As someone who takes a bit of time to 'grasp' the right strategy for a game, I appreciated being able to figure things out through playing, and being able to take on more aggressive challenges as my skill grew. The bright style of the game also drew me in visually.
Pros:
-Well executed strategy
-Fun balance of God Powers with Human Problems
-Simple or Complex Play
-Super customizable set-ups
Cons:
-They had bugs for a while that limited play on some systems
-Lack of add-ons (though base game is pretty fun)

The story is silly and funny. It's full of little intenet speech and memes references.
The big thing that has me recommend this game though is the combat system. It is hands down one of the single best turn based combat systems I have EVER played. I have been playing RPGs for over 20 years, hundreds of them completed. This not small praise. It's an excellent system.
Unlike many RPGs, elemental effects actually matter. Ever single enemy has elemental weaknesses to take advantage of. All your weapons (bar a few non-elemental ones) have elements that deal damage of its type and buff spells of its type.
The game actively encourages you to swap equipment mid-combat to take advantage of the situation. Giving yourself over 100% resistance to an element will allow you to be HEALED by that element! More than once I've had all my team with close to, if not over, 100% resistance and the normally very strong enemy deals pathetic amounts of damage.
I cannot recommend this enough if you love RPGs and especially love good combat systems.

Scribblenauts Unlimited is truly Unlimited.
Want to throw an exploding potato at a defensive man to have the man get angry and explode when he eats it? You can do that.
Want to make a tiny purple kazoo that will sing whenever you use it? You can do that.
Want to throw strong evil babies at old men? Yes, you can even do that.
I'd never think any of this would be possible in a video game, but it is.
Sure, there are certain words you can't make such as drugs and copyrighted stuff like Harry Potter, but now that we have the object editor, we can have those things come true... if you're good at making stuff in the object editor, that is.
I really wish there were multiple save files for this game, since I don't want to lose all my data just to replay the game. I also wish there was a level editor, like in the previous games. But it's still an enjoyable game.
Truly, a great experience.

For a lot of FEAR fans, this game is terrible, but to me, it's great. I wasn't impressed with the FEAR games that preceded it, and this one finally did something fun: it added asymmetrical co-op! By that, I mean one player is the lead protagonist, who slides, kicks, shoots guns, can initiate bullet time, etc., and the other player is a telekinetic ghost/wraith that blasts everything with ghostly energy that doesn't do a ton of damage but is infinite ammo, and you can
for a limited time per enemy. It's fantastic.
I love playing as the wraith character, jumping into an enemy's body and gunning down his friends while my partner is shooting up the rest of the room. While I've possessed a body, I can do anything my partner can do other than bullet time, and it's pretty great.
The story is fairly okay, and the ending isn't all that good, but I play this game for the gameplay, which I really liked. Maybe this is the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ization of FEAR, but I didn't hold FEAR in a lofty position beforehand, so I welcomed and really liked this game. Ah, GalCiv2... Memories...
I sank so, so many hours into this game. I owned it on CD before losing them and having to buy it again on Steam. And then sank in some more hours, for good measure.
So, what makes this game awesome? It's often compared to Civilization, but in space. Yeah, that sounds about right... but it's not totally true either. See, GalCiv has many things Civilization does not. Unique tech trees for every race: check. Unique gameplay for every race: check. Being able to customize every single ship: check. That's right, no Warrior vs Warrior here. You can build your ships however you like with the ship builder and put whatever weapons, armour, modules and engines you damn well like.
The political system is also well tought-out and doesn't feel out of place. Want a bigger economic bonus? Go Star Democracy! But what's that? Oh yeah, we're a democracy now, I can't just declare war on a whim... Alright then, let's ask what the parliament thinks. They approve? Oh yeah, let's kick some alien butt, baby! (If your approval is too low, good luck getting your people to follow you into war. They have other priorities you know.)
Okay, enough talk. You're a strategy fan? Need another 4x game to sink time into? Get this game and thank me later!

An all around great game.
The AI actually understands its own game well enough to play without breaking its rules. It's certainly not a genius, but if you turn the AI's ability all the way up, it will make deals that don't involve the player quite often and build armies designed to counter whatever they're fighting is using. They also use spies properly and generally play the game.
It's easy to customize. Got a 256x256 and a 430x280 png of something. Drop it in the right file and attach it to a custom civ. Want to make your custom civ have the same bonus stats as an initial civ or increase everyone's stats, open an XML editor and the notation will practically tell you how. Then there's the ship editor atop that, which is easy to work and works even out to the map. Want to build a giant robot or a mecha space scorpion, you can do it, and watch it advance on enemies.
It has some of the best macroing of 4x games. You can easily create a few templates, then drop the templates on worlds as you get them, and the game will auto-assign improvements to the tiles that would give them bonuses. Then you can assign ship building and rally points with a few more clicks without ever touching any of your planets. Or you can do it all by hand.

I keep replaying this game every so often trying to figure out why I do not like it. With 1.8, I decided I would give it another go and start a new character.
Played through the story again and I figured now I would write a review.
There are many things that I don’ enjoy about this game and we will get to those in a moment. First let’s go over what is good.
Pros:
•	This game has a solid environment. NY in winter during the fall of the city looks amazing. Little details make this environment feel true. They really put some work in everything in this city works together to tell a story of desolation and distress. The day and night cycle is beautiful. And as much weather as there is in the game does wonders. That surreal feeling of running through with snow flurries limiting your visibility during a firefight is great.
•	The main narrative is all right. However, what I really enjoyed was the little pieces of the story scattered around the city. The echoes, the cellphones, and the laptops do a better job of informing you of the breakdown of the city than the main story does itself. There were times I would abandon the main narrative to chase down cellphones for a while because they were more interesting to me.
•	The firearm selection is fairly solid, and the mods are a nice touch.
•	Co-op, anytime you can play with friends is nice.
•	The audio is great. Little detail, the echo of a firefight, the ringing in the ears after a bomb goes off, the hum of electricity and lights. It adds a great amount of depth and helps the immersion.
•	The particle systems are excellent.
•	Just so many details. Shoot through safety glass and it chips to pieces, Shoot a tire and it blows out. Shoot an extinguisher it puffs into a cloud of fire retardant.
•	The dark zone is a cool concept.
Cons:
•	Core gameplay mechanic. Are you ready to grind to extend gameplay? That’s what this game is built around. You are going to grind until you get good enough guns to feel comfortable and then end up needing to grind some more.
•	End game feels empty. I mean once you are at the top what the point is. It is there only to push you towards the multiplayer.
•	The dark zone multiplayer is boring. If you have better gear than the other person, you spray bullets at them until they’re dead. If they have better gear, they spray bullets at you until your dead. If you are evenly equipped, you hope you interrupt them before they interrupt you and you both spray bullets at each other until one dies or the other does. In teams there is a bit more to it than that, timing skills and all that but really that is it.
•	Nothing ruins fun than just sitting there dumping two 55 round magazines into a person to see that they have only lost 1/6th of their health. In addition, it is only fun for so long to have people dump magazine after magazine into you while you just mow them down and regen health on kills. It gets boring fast.
Tl:dr
So, The Division is a game with all sorts of cool and interesting ideas and details that are buried beneath boring combat and a level grinding loot system.
Do I recommend the game? No, unless you can ignore the negative aspects of the gameplay. If you can do that there is a great enviroment and a fairly interesting story.

As a direct sequel to Epic Battle Fantasy 3, this games improves on pretty much every aspect of the previous entry in the series. You liked the previous one and want more ? You'll like this one.
If you haven't, you can start by playing the others but it is by no mean necessary. Epic Battle Fantasy 4 is a basic Rpg made by one man and although it sometimes shows, the game is worth playing if you can get past a few things. Those things will change depending on the player. I, for instance, had to get over the graphics that feel extremely simple, the humor that can be plain or corny sometimes, and maybe the length of the fights toward the end. But once again, those might be assets to some peolpe.
What else is there ? The game is quite long ( about 25-30 hours ), it's got some depth to it that goes beyond enemy weaknesses / resistances, and overall you have fun most of the time you spend in the game if you get hooked. It's honestly still quite impressive for a one-man-game. Plus there's post-game content !
For the price it's at, if you like the rpg genre, and if you have nothing better at the moment, this will definitely be worth your time as a filler while you wait for another release.

Actually more fun than you might think at first, as there's something oddly relaxing about watching and hearing those little blips stack up as you get better and better at what you do. It might not look like I have much time in it, but 7 hours is about how long it will take to get from beginning to end, plus a little in the post game.
I only have a couple gripes with the game, but they aren't nearly big enough for me not to recommend the game. Firstly, if you know the course the Western games market has taken since the 80's, you will essentially never run the risk of dying out as long as you find some good game idea combinations.
I wish there was some level of dynamic history in this, like a world where Atari stays as the top dog until the modern day or PC never takes off as a gaming platform. As it stands, I know that doing things like staying with the Nintendo consoles until the PS1 comes out or jumping ship to multi-platform is always better than brand loyalty are the keys to success, and always will be.
My other gripe, also pretty small potatoes, is about how the world accepts your games. My company had started producing a line of moderately successful RPGs, becoming the equivalent of the Final Fantasy series where my iterations ended up in the double digits, including two MMO's, one of which eventually bankrupted me in the postgame. However, as well as these games sold, nothing ever compared in terms of reviews or sales as my Truck Simulator. Needless to say, if this had been the track a real company took, and I were the lead developer, I would be pretty disappointed.
Overall, I still recommend the game, but I got it on sale and so should you.

Before I start this review off, I want to say that I do believe that video games are a form of art.  Because of this, they will be interpreted differently by every individual that plays them.
So, while I do recommend this game, there's just a few things you need to know to determine if it's going to be an enjoyable experience for you.
Initially you may find it hard to become attached to the characters being developed in the story line.  Stick with it though, as you unravel the journey and continue, you start to learn more.
The two main characters certainly have their quirks.  There's a few (seemingly) out of place "pop culture" references that maybe could have been excluded.
Overall, the characters are developed well enough for you to empathize with them, but still leave you enough to fill in gaps or use your own imagination to create the story how you desire.
The actual story, once you see it as a full picture, meaning start to finish, is very touching.  This plot will pull you up and down from elation, to scratching your head, to pure sadness.
I felt choked up at a few points.  Perhaps the most emotion I felt was after completing the game and then doing something else.  I found my mind wandering back to the story and the characters.  I started thinking about how I really felt about what happened and then started reading what others thought.
This is a story that you most likely will have some sort of emotional connection towards, I can almost assure you of that.  I can't say much more, other than it's a definite thinker and I loved it.
I don't need to say much here.  It was created in RPG Maker, so you can already tell what you're dealing with graphically.  I often relate these types of games (graphically) to games like Final Fantasy VII.  Perhaps that's because I played that game extensively when I was growing up.  However, the graphics should never, never have and never will take away from a game's ability to tell an amazing story.
If you need amazing graphics to enjoy your gaming experience, then you might want to skip over this title.  I WILL say that you'd be missing out on an awesome and captivating experience though.
I mentioned above the way it looks graphically, so you kind of know what you're getting into.  It's an RPG Maker game, so it's essentially direct the character to this point, interact with this sprite or asset, and continue on.
At times, it can be annoying, slow, and confusing.  However, the game does lead you in the right direction (most times) if you're observant enough.
There are points where I personally felt that the actual interactivity was taking away from the story, but that was just me.  I got over it very quickly when I saw the next gap in the story line being unfolded for me.
As a whole, the gameplay isn't bad.  It's a little frustrating at times, but not so much to make me dislike the game.  Because really, every game has it's quirks.
At the bottom of this review, I've included a link to the "guide" that I used so I wasn't fiddling around trying to find things and I could just enjoy the story.  NOTE: The guide does not share any spoilers AT ALL.
First off, the controls are definitely a little bit clunky.  At times they make even annoy you or put you off from enjoying the entirety of the game.  I'm here to encourage you to just let those things slide.  You'll get through the parts that require you to take control of the characters.
I used a game pad to control the characters, and then my mouse / keyboard for the puzzles and there's one section towards the end that my gamepad was useless for.  I suggest you do the same, but again, you'll quickly figure out what works for you.
Do I recommend this game?  Absolutely - 100%.  I bought it on sale, and the story alone (gameplay and the fact that it's a game aside) made it more than worth it.
I am definitely considering going back and playing through the game a second time now that I know what happens.  Perhaps digging a little deeper at some of the items you can explore.  Talking to more characters, etc.  I don't think I missed much, but if and when I'm ready for an "interactive" emotional rollercoaster - you can bet thet "To The Moon" will be getting some more gameplay from me.
Thanks for reading!  Happy gaming!
