It's a generic, bland FPS with the F.E.A.R logo on it. It's like the devs started out making a Call of Duty clone, then halfway through development they remembered it was supposed to be a horror game, so they put in some arbitrary jumpscares and zombies and called it a day. There's no atmosphere, the game isn't scary at all, and it's not even that good as an action game either; all the shooting sections feel the same, the enemies might have above average AI capabilities but it really doesn't work well in the envirionments: all the environments are set up to be typical cover-based shooter galleries, where you slowly advance by hiding behind barricades and poking your head out, shooting at enemies that are doing the exact same thing for wave after wave until you hit the kill count that magically opens a door and lets you progress to the next area to do the same thing all over again. Everything is heavily scripted and predictable. The story is barely coherent and isn't interesting, everything seems really arbitrary and nothing is explained, the entire time you'll be asking "Why am I even here? What am I doing and why?"
tl;dr if you liked the original F.E.A.R then don't bother with this one, the devs just removed everything that made the original F.E.A.R good. Playing this really feels more like you're playing a Call of Duty clone.

F3AR is like that uncle that shows up at your house uninvited.
You play as either the Pointman or Paxton Fettel, one being able to slow down time and the other being able to possess enemy soldiers. Paxton and Pointguy team up in order to escape “The Creep”, a horrible monster formed unintentionally by the memories of Harlan Wade.
Oh yeah and Alma is having A BABY! Time for baby showers and free food for me to gorge on!
Anyway, don't play this one.
FEAR 3 is the first game (I think) in the series not developed by Monolith productions but instead is developed by Day 1 studios. Who apparently didn't get the note about “Make stylish shooter with spooky stuff splattered in between.”
Spookems 3 is more of a by the books shooter. Instead of having to contend with squads of crafty super soldiers who do their best to trick, ambush, suppress, or flank you. You now just kind of go into new areas and then fight off waves of enemies until the game decides that you've killed enough and you can move on. They also have a tendency of finding one piece of cover and then sticking to it, removing that element of power struggles the first two games had.
There's also this big focus on taking cover, even though enemies can still hit you while you're in cover. And reflex mode for Pointman is just kind of useless now since the enemy will still fill you with holes anyway even if you are slowing down time. Paxton has a neat gimmick where you can possess the enemy, but it's not enough to save the game.
Also for some reason they made the Pointman this quiet grumpy guy instead of a silent self insert. He's not really likable, and I don't really see Fear 3's Pointman going down on anyone's top 10 favorite character list.
The entire game can be played Coop. Which I did, and now we have a suicide pact together. It's not that bad, I'm kidding. But♥♥♥♥♥♥ it's close.
Anyway, don't play this one. It's not fun, and the other games are much spookier. Which is saying something because they weren't really all that scary to begin with. Just play Fear 1 and 2 and pretend the series got canceled after those two.
Is it the worst game ever made? No, not even close. But is it just a complete cluster fudge of mismanagement and idiot decision making? You bet your sweet butt it is.
Oh yeah, and it's like, 4 hours long. This retailed at full price when it came out.

I first bought GalCivs II when it was new and after a bit of a learning curve (Having never played a Turn Based Strategy Game at that time) I figured out just how amazing the game actually was.  The ability to customize your faction in almost every aspect, plus continue to develop it down the path you see fit, provides an excellent replayablity and immersion.  The ship designer even allows you to recreate designs from some of your favorite Sci-Fi tales, or develop your own line to help crush the galaxy.  The ability to watch fleet battles was a huge plus, and the game's soundtrack is exceptionally easy to modify if one wants to mix it up after hours of playing.
Once I saw a chance to pick up the Ultimate Edition for 75% off, I bought it in a heartbeat and put in another full game or two.  I've had a number of games in the past taking months to complete on the largest map settings, so the increase in maximum size and depth of the factions only made things better.  The option to customize your enemies ships and faction name sets the stage to truly create your own sci-fi epic, for those you find themselves essentially role-playing such immersive games.
In short, I can't reccomend this game enough, as it is a brilliant buy and at an affordable cost.  Even better, one doesn't necessarily need a high-end computer to run the game, despite its high entertainment value!

Full Video review -
You are RT-217NP, and your curiosity about the human race takes you on the beginning on an adventure, potentially unravelling a conspiracy within the perfect society that currently inhabits the earth.
-Presentation-
What else is there to say about the presentation of this game other than it was built on Unity. Well… just by saying that, it immediately opens the flood gates for a great deal more to be said. IT’S A GOOD ENGINE! But, there is always the risk of games looking the same as each other when using a commonly used game engine. With some projects you can really see some conscious effort to leave a mark through art direction and delivery. This is one of those projects. Now, I’m not going to sit here and say that it looks amazing, because it doesn’t. In some places the artwork looks a little “primitive” like on aero cars for example, but you can see that most of the work has been done where it really matters and I would personally take a stylized approach over an “amazing” approach everytime.
The character models for example are very individual and polished, regardless of how small a part they may play in the experience. Most of the environments are really well done too with a diverse array of artwork and colour schemes that contribute very much to the wide array of looks and feels you come across. There are certainly clear inspirations from the likes of Portal and numerous Tell-Tale IPs.
The in game camera is also very well utilised. Throughout the game there are fixed camera angles, 3rd person, 1st person and dynamic cameras. I have to say that each of these different cameras worked really well for the event or scene going on at the time.
The soundtrack relays just as many diverse feelings and atmospheres as the visuals of the game from the get go. From solemn piano pieces to the integration of a sort of “synth ambience” as well as some general rock vibes mixed in there for good measure. The soundtrack speaks in a number of ways, adding addition colour to the visual aspects of the experience.
The voice work on the other hand is average. Individually, each of the characters stands solid, really well delivered actually. But, putting them together in a conversation is where the quality of the voice cast and voice direction start to show in a bad way. It’s almost as if the cast each had a vision how “quirky” a robot would probably be, which is creatively beneficial… but none of these visions really matched each other, or the game’s setting sometime. It’s either “near monotone robot voice” or “real person stuck in a robot body.” It can often lead to disjointed sounding conversations, even by robot standards. The many cases “recording alone in a booth” awkwardness in the tone delivery shows just how badly this voice cast needs voice direction.
-Gameplay/Mechanics-
Anyone who has ever played a tell-tale game will feel right at home with The Uncertain as there are clear signs of inspiration being taken from their games. In order to work your way through the rather intriguing narrative you do a lot of walking, a lot of NPC and object interaction, conversation trees and some puzzles, which vary in difficulty and style. Nothing that we haven’t seen before and thankfully, executed just as well. Excluding the puzzles, the UI for everything isn’t too different from titles in the Tell-tale lineup. Whether it be in conversation or interacting with an object, you just hover over a point of interest, which expands into a secondary UI with a choice of applicable options relevant to the context of the interaction.
The conversation element of the game, while providing plenty of options for replying to those around you, didn’t seem to play a very big part in the outcome of this episode. This IS episode 1 in a series though, so I’d like to think that the decisions and interactions that were made here may influence events and plot developments in the future episodes. I guess we will have to wait and see…
-Overall thoughts-
We are in a time in history right now where automation, AI and robotics are quite common conversation topics. There are many sides to these conversations, but it usually boils down to whether or not the development and embracing of such technologies is a good thing or bad. There are those who believe that we are doomed to be exterminated once AI is advanced so far, and there are others who propose that human beings can stay in control these creations and have them assisting us.
This game presents an alternative. Human beings killed themselves through their own actions… and robots are left to fend for themselves. Would robots miss us? Would they be as curious about us and our civilization to the point that we are about say… the Mayans? Despite their efficiency and rational nature, would they be as fallible as those who created them and inherit our flaws as they evolve, perhaps causing division as they evolve as individuals leading to conflict and their OWN extinction? Would they really be any different from us?
As for the game itself, my adventure with The Uncertain so far has been laid back and pleasant. It's pretty, the dialogue although poorly executed is quite well written and despite The Uncertain being nothing “new” per se, it has taken the right inspiration from the right projects to create a unique feeling addition to the “tell-tale” genre. Episode 1 has set a nice foundation that discusses a controversial topic from a few of different angles. What is lacked in “drama” it made up for in building a solid foundation to build on. We have been left questions left in our minds of the relevance of the characters, their roles and events that hopefully episode 2 will elaborate on.

This is a graphically modern version of the old point-and-click adventure games from the likes of LucasArts, Infocom, and Sierra Online that were popular in the late 1980s and 1990s.
Character controls are similar to the old point-and-click games - WASD controls forward, backward, left and right movement. SHIFT allows a "run" mode - but to be honest, the difference is between a very slow walk, and a slightly faster walk. You can't roll, dodge, crouch, or jump. You can't fight or shoot. Interaction involves scanning the scene with the mouse until hot spots show up, which allow options such as examine, use, take, talk to, etc.
Each scene is viewed from a fixed camera position. You can walk your character about the scene, but you can't move the camera. As you move from scene to scene, the camera view will change. Movement directions are tied to the camera, not the character. So you can walk your character forwards from one scene into another, and find that your character is now walking backwards, because the camera view has changed. I found this super annoying.
The majority of the gameplay involves exploring your environment, discovering and examining objects, and interacting with other characters. Some objects must be picked up and used elsewhere. There are also puzzles to solve. As you complete these tasks, a story unfolds, but I'll try not to give too much of that away.
Overall, I enjoyed the game. But, for me, it had some problems. I'll break it down into Likes and Dislikes.
Likes
The graphics are very well done. Characters and scenery are nicely rendered in 3D. Animation is smooth, fluid, and realistic. There is some real talent here.
The English voice acting is pretty fair. The main character is very well done, most others OK, and a few less so, but not unacceptably. For a small Russian indie team to achieve this is quite a task. It's hard to be convincing in a language that's not your own.
There is a deep story to this game, and I suspect much of it is allegorical. The central theme is that the majority of the population have been brainwashed into hating and destroying another group. It's no surprise that such a theme should come from creative Russians - although nowadays it could equally apply to Trump's America.
The game works. I was able to play from the start, right through to the end, without major bugs or glitches. There's not many AAA developers who can claim that for their initial release version.
Dislikes
One crucial puzzle can't be solved unless you're a musician with perfect pitch. Seriously. Re-think this one, developers - you're excluding 95% of the population.
There are a couple of sections that require you to rapidly mash the "F" key. I'm not sure why. It doesn't achieve anything. It's so obscure that the game even has to tell you "now mash the "F" key". So you do, and the sequence completes. Why bother?
There are a couple of airborne chase sequences, which, for me, because of the poor controls and unpredictable response, ended up as an exercise in crashing into trees and the landscape. At one point your viewpoint changes, so you can only see behind you. You're still flying forwards at breakneck speed, still (now inevitably - you can't see) crashing into obstacles. I've no idea what you're supposed to do in this sequence, but after a few tries I survived it. Crazy stuff.
Despite the clunky, unresponsive, and inaccurate controls of a point-and-click game, despite the fixed camera that means you can't see most of the room, they introduced a stealth sequence. I can't believe it, but they did. It was awful.
Overall
As I said earlier, by and large, I enjoyed the game. The point-and-click sections work well. The controls and interface are NOT suited to an action or stealth game. In the future, such sections should either be hugely improved, or removed altogether. My score - 7/10

Imagining a world like something out of an Isaac Asimov novel isn't such a leap of logic here. Unfortunately the story and gameplay don't hold up well under scrutiny.
While the game has excellent visuals (if a bit bland), my GTX980Ti GPU still (seemed to) struggle with max settings - the game displayed some minor load times, jittery / shaking in some areas with a large field-of-view. But it might just be the game engine.
Gameplay revolves around some minor puzzles (honestly, most Hidden Object games have better puzzles... if you want good puzzles and a robot I'd recommend Talos Principle) and it becomes more of a point-and-click experience than anything else, searching for items to use on devices and advance the plot.
Exploration is limited. Your walk and run speed is limited. To my surprise, the protagonist can't even jump. Now this is simply absurd. What kind of futuristic robot can't even jump, for pity's sake. I hope I don't sound brutal here, but I've seen toddlers run faster than this robot too.
Speaking of speed, the whole game seems a plod-fest. The whole story, the pacing, the protagonist's pithy motorized legs - I haven't even glanced on the plethora of repetitious dialogue - just drags the whole game down. Heaven forbid they release more episodes of this coma-inducing snooze-a-thon.
On that dialogue though. If the little note in the top left corner isn't enough to tell you what to do, or the fact that there really isn't anything much to pick up and use in the first place (I'd for sure grab one of the police guns... if I could) and if you haven't turned into a pillar of salt from all the sleep grit in your eyes then you can always have a conversation. About the only thing the protagonist has going for him is he sounds like a robot more than all the other robots - a proper flat, emotionless tone, as we would expect. Too bad he doesn't stop blathering on to himself. There is at least one instance of a character literally repeating itself.
Part of the game's blurb is "make fateful decisions". To this I say: balls! The story will be identical for everyone that plays it. There are some dialogue options, true, but it's essentially a linear game. Oh, you can choose poorly and get destroyed, or you can not get destroyed. Some choice huh. Makes you wonder if all the awards are legit.
That's the truth as I see it. Very restrictive on exploration, tedious chatterboxes, overly simplistic puzzles (even running past defence turrets is a cakewalk), no meaningful choices (as they themselves said there would be), and everything just feels slow, sluggish and drawn out. Maybe deliberately so to make the game episodic? I don't care at any rate, I won't be getting it.

I have to say, I was not expecting The Uncertain to be as good as it is. Created by the small studio, ComonGames, The Uncertain is clearly inspired by the modern TellTale games but frankly, it does a number of things better than its inspirations.
Set in a post-human world, you play as the nondescript robot RT-217NP, or RT for short. While the post-apocalyptic world is way overdone at this point, The Uncertain takes it in an interesting and unexplored (to my knowledge) point. Without any spoilers, the story is presented from a perspective and lens that I have not seen in a sci-fi story before, which is quite refreshing. Planned as a three episode arc, the first episode presents an interesting world and gives just enough history of what has happened for there to be a great sense of mystery and uneasiness about the world. The characterization of the robots is done pretty successfully and are presented as calculating, logical robots should be.
Playing the games will obviously illicit comparisons to the TellTale games but I was surprised at how well ComonGames executed their vision. For starters, The Uncertain looks better than anything that TellTale has done and runs ten times better. That alone should be noteworthy for Uncertain and damning for TellTale as their engine has been poorly optimized for a while now. The Uncertain looks great and often times puts you in environments much larger than any of its counterparts would. This leads to some actual exploration when it comes to puzzle solving, which the game does quite well. I found the puzzles to be pretty intuitive and there were a handful of minigames (think hacking) that were a nice change of pace. There’s even a driving sequence thrown in for good measure and the QTE’s are only given one appearance.
I’m genuinely surprised and impressed by the level of polish that The Uncertain has. For the first game from the studio, this is quite the effort. A minor complaint I would have is that the walking speed is on the slow side, a run option would have been nice. The foundation for The Uncertain is a strong one and I hope that it sells well enough so that all three episodes can make it out. There’s a unique story being told here that I would love to see the ending of. I think that The Uncertain is absolutely worth your time and money.

Well that was an interesting two hours. I'm Dayvis2 and today I will be reviewing LEGO Worlds!
OK, so, LEGO Worlds is one of the latest games in the popular LEGO franchiase. Being a LEGO lover and having done a few reviews on them beforehand, I knew that I should buy the next game while it was fairly cheap on Early Access. As the game loaded up, an epic fanfare began, and a LEGO minifigure of an old explorer was waving at me beside a LEGO model of the world I would be playing in. I named the world, then found the same minifigure skydiving down into a Minecraft like world made of blocks. I landed with a thud, then saw that I was in a forest. Soon I was riding horses, meeting a Dinosaur expert and even battling the undead. Having played Minecraft since Feburary 2013, it was strange to see the same kind of gameplay in LEGO style. Like Minecraft, LEGO Worlds has biomes like forests, mesas, oceans and even some based off LEGO sets. For instance, after about fourty five minutes of play I was exploring a " Spooky Woods" biome that seemed to be based off the Monster Hunters LEGO brand. In the woods I met a Minotaur and tried to unlock it as a buyable character by killing it ( as anything you kill, ride, break or enter becomes available to be bought with studs that you get for destroying, as like the other LEGO games), but during the battle I accidentally hit an unsuspecting vampire that then chased after me. Minotaurs are easy to kill, but vampires are quicker and deadly, so I ran. I quickly scaled a tree by walking up to it, then used the smooth camera rotation to check on the vampire and Minotaur's progress. They were still at the bottom of the tree, but soon skeletons, werewolves and dragon wizards had me surrounded. In a break for freedom, I summoned by trusted steed, Edmund, a horse I had bought from the store, jumped onto his back and made him leap from the top of the tree while I clung on. Edmund was much faster than the monsters, and I escaped as the sun rose and the creatures were forced to go into hiding until night. Later, after performing a few tricks by riding a motorcycle around a valley and making it fly into the sky, I met a dragon master, who told me of a volcano that had a  dragon at the centre of it. I quickly discarded my motorcycle for good old fashioned Edmund, and followed the map over to the volcano. There I found the dragon, but before I slayed it I decided to fly around on it for a bit. As I flew, I saw a group of minifigures stood on the ground far below me - the figures were the dragon masters, and they had staffs that were shooting spells at the dragon. Now I was trapped high in the sky on a dragon that was being shot at by dark wizards. Then I realised - the dragon was innocent, it was the wizards that were evil. I let the dragon go full Smaug style, and it flew down towards the figures. I held on for dear life as the dragon shot fire from its mouth. The wizards scattered, and the dragon only killed one of them, but by the looks of things they wouldn't be harming the dragon anymore. I jumped off the dragon, and was surprised to see I had unlocked it without having to kill it. I left it in peace. I also built a huge castle and accidently created a hill by spamming a button. Anyway, LEGO Worlds has been good so far, and it hasn't been glitchy ( like LEGO Jurassic World, still♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥about that!) I may update this log, so check back for more soon, but don't just wait until then, buy the game and have your own epic adventures!
-Dayvis2, signing out, 26/7/15, or 7/26/15 if you're American.

To the Moon really blew me away. That's not to say I didn't already have high expectations after all the positive things I'd heard, but it's just something that you have to experience for yourself before you can truly understand.
This game is all about the story, but that's not to say that there isn't any gameplay there. You play as two characters who are working to fulfill the wish of their dying client. His wish is to go to the moon. While their goal isn't to actually send him to the moon, it is to make him believe that he did by entering his memories and watching his life unfold backwards. The further back these memories go, the more this emotional roller coaster will grip you and not let go.
To say any more about the story would ruin it, so let's talk gameplay. As you jump through these memories, you explore the environments to uncover more about the client, and you must examine items throughout the areas that kind of act as 'keys' to allow you to progress. None of them are ever overly complicated, and the pacing is just right to give you a little break from reading to look around and stretch your digital legs before hopping back into the narrative. Between memory jumps, you solve simple puzzles that stand in your way of proceeding. These also aren't very difficult, though there were a couple that I had to stop and think on.
While I don't find graphics important, I did find this game to be beautiful. It really had the feel of a good looking old school RPG like Chrono Trigger or Final Fantasy VI, with all of the settings and colors really setting the mood well. Some of the areas almost made me feel nostalgic.
The music was great as well, tunes always coming into scenes like they owned them. The same piece of music served to make me feel happy at one point in the story, and sad in another. You can tell that the score was very important to them when making this game, it honestly shows.
To the Moon is a fantastic indie game that might take you around 3-5 hour to beat depending on your level of exploration. It's full of references to popular culture, and will pull your emotions back and forth as you play through. I bought it on sale, but would wholeheartedly recommend paying full price for it after actually experiencing it. After all, games like this don't come around often.

I'm not the longest running fallout fan, in fact Fallout 3 was the first title I played and oh my god I don't regret it. Set in apocalyptic 23rd century Washington, you are a vault dweller from vault 101 who at the age of 19 is forced out of the vault and into the capital wasteland in search of your lost father. Since this fallout title came out in 2008 I myelf have played through all of this game and the next two sequels, 2010's Fallout New Vegas and most recently 2015's Fallout 4. All three of these mostly great games have shown how the rpg has changed and evolved to bring us a new and fresh idea to entertain players of all types.
Positives
-The story presented here in my opinion is better then Fallout New Vegas, FNV was longer and had more distinct endings but it basically came down to who owned this casino chip which didn't give me enough personal involvement to care much. Here however the story is very personal for your character as it revolves mostly around finding your father who has left your vault and has gone missing. Liam Neeson kills it as the voice of your dad and you can really see in his performance that he cares and is not just phoning it in like some other voice actors (Peter Dinklage, Destiny). As the story plays out you come across a range of great and depthful characters and factions that all have a motive to either work with you or kill you. The variety in weapons only help combat the wastleland's darkest creatures and help yourself in succeeding. Some moments in this game will sure tug on your heart as certain events unfold and difficult choices have to be made. The story in Fallout 3 is definitely going for the personal approach and it thus makes the game more engaging and enjoyable.
-Variety in weapons, even most of the legendary weapons are a completely different design which means you won't keep seeing the same weapon with a different name too often, even tho it does occur to an extent.
-The leveling system here, for the time, was rather new and refreshing as it has been copied countless times over the years. It's still to this day is deep and you can loose hours just in searching through all the different skills, perks and advantages they supply the player with.
Negatives
-Trust me when I say I love this game, but the stories length is a joke. If you just look at the story alone it only clocks in at about 15 hours or less if you know what your doing. The shortest Fallout game I've ever played as Fallout New Vegas was around 30 hours and same with Fallout 4. I say short is sweet, and it is pretty sweet, but come on as a Fallout game, and rpg and a title from the legendary Bethesda it could've been a little longer.
-The crafting in Fallout 3 is down right bad, the worst part of the game for sure. Very little amount of things to craft when comparing the past Bethesda titles, but still on it's own it is not anything special. The thing that kills it for me is the UI, on both console and pc it is jumbled and messing and different to navigate.
-Graphics, even for the time it looks ugly. Not that the textures are bad for 2008 but the wasteland is just colourless and lifeless and to be honest, very hard to look at.
Final Thoughts
-Just like every game, it's not perfect. But the game in it's story, characters, rpg elements, quantity and quality shines above and beyond the negatives making it one of my favourite games of all time. In conclusion I give Fallout 3 an 8/10 because unlike some games, it sticks with me for the better.

Scribblenauts Unlimited tests your creativity by giving you relatively open-ended situations, and the ability to create any object.  Add on customizable avatars, and Workshop support, and you have a true sandbox game.  That is why you should pick up Scribblenauts Unlimited.
Developed by 5th Cell Media and published by WB Games, Scribblenauts is a series of sandbox games that started on the Nintendo DS as a follow-up to Drawn-to-Life (Think Scribblenauts, but drawing specific objects rather than creating them).  The next release, Super Scribblenauts, added the ability to use adjectives for further customization.  This game has all of the features introduced in the franchise thus far: nouns, adjectives, the works.
The game is simple enough for anyone to pick up.  A few mouse clicks here, some typing there, and that\'s about it.  This works to the game\'s advantage because it doesn\'t burden the player with a confusing control scheme.
Of all the hard work that went into this game, I have to give major props to the art team.  They created every object, background, and emotion in the game.  The team basically sat down with a dictionary and drew every noun.  THAT is dedication.
While the game is a sandbox, there is a plot.  It\'s completely unobtrusive, and basic enough to allow for a ton of creative freedom on the part of the player.  tl;dr: Your sister is cursed, and you need to get Starites to save her.  Enough said.
If you want to create something, and it doesn\'t exist in the game proper, worry not!  This game is fully integrated with the Steam Workshop.  In the workshop, you can find just about anything.  If the thing you want simply doesn\'t exist at all, you can use the built-in object editor to make it, so the only limit is your imagination.
Scribblenauts Unlimited is the definative Scribblenauts game.  While Unmasked is newer, it doesn\'t have that same freedom that Unlimited has simply because it\'s a brand-deal game.  Unmasked is specifically DC, while Unlimited stands on it\'s own.  That\'s why I recommend Unlimited over Unmasked.  This game gets my Seal of Recommendation.

Finally got around to finishing this game a few days ago and I definitely recommend it.  It's easily one of the best Metroidvania games out there, and it's fairly unique; it doesn't borrow too heavily from the other games in the genre.  There is notably a greater emphasis placed on the platforming mechanics in this game than the combat, though both are solid and very engaging.  As you gain power-ups, both by traversing the world and by spending ability points, you are handed more and more creative ways to approach certain obstacles or enemies.  This makes backtracking much more enjoyable, which is necessary since there is no fast-travel in this game.  There are three "dungeons" in the game, but instead of boss battles at the end you will go through these high-adrenaline chase sequences.  These can be difficult, but not so difficult that you won't get the hang of it before you lose your patience, and you will feel a huge sense of accomplishment when you make it through one.
The graphics are beautiful throughout the whole game world, to the point where you will be mesmerized by staring at the scenery while you run through the forest.  The music is very atmospheric and perfectly fits whatever situation you're in.  The story is simple, but still keeps you hooked.  Definitely buy this game if you haven't already.

1 – GENERAL
The Division is a 3rd person shooter with RPG elements. We play in a post apocalyptical Manhattan that was caught by a human engineered disease that wiped almost the entire population. I've always asked myself why this sort of stuff always happens in Manhattan. Poor people...
The graphics are quite impressive, I must say. I do not know the city, but all stuff that I've seen seemed quite close to what I imagine. It seems real. It's not common for me to get this kind of feeling. Buildings, streets, cars, people, animals... I quite like how all those elements were mixed to create this world.
All the sounds set together create an immersive environment to walk around. NPCs have a proper amount of voicelines, and sometimes we pass by them and they are making a proper dialogue. We are quite able to sense desperation. When we see someone in need and we are able to help him, it's quite rewarding, at least it was to me.
The only sound I do not like a lot was the one from the guns. It can be quite accurate, but it seems quite "short" like it was a paintball gun. Despite that, I guess I just had low tier weapons, and maybe that's not the case in the better ones.
2 – GAMEPLAY
The gunplay is based on a cover mechanism, that I usually do not like. Most time it reminded me of Spec Ops: The Line, a game that I've loved, and probably that's the reason it gets me playing more at first. Glad I did it since the mechanics are very well balanced. We can do missions in co-op, up to 4 players, and it was quite easy to find players from my level to join me in any mission. With proper tactics, the game becomes quite fun and engaging. When 4 players are able to work together some very interesting moves can be done, and sometimes we get a great sensation of accomplishment when we are able to defeat some stronger boss. NPCs are some sort of bullet sponges. Probably it would be possible to make them harder to beat without using that, but I admit is not the best system in the world... it's ok.
Unfortunately, we spend tons of time walking around, and that gets quite annoying after a while.
Main missions are balanced and exciting, but you will spend most of your time doing side missions to find loot, gear and level up your character. That's not optional. You have to do those or you will not be able to progress in the main plot since the NPCs get stronger way faster than you. For me, both of these aspects are the worst part of the game.
I got stuck in the main plot quite fast, and I was forced to start doing all the side missions suited to my character level... ohhh, and those are standalone missions... all to spend some time doing the main missions with 3 other guys.
I'm not entirely sure about the replay value of the singleplayer. I suppose that after you beat the game, and since you are forced to do so many side missions, there's not much interest in playing again, except if you are a completionist.
3 – CONCLUSION
This is just a first impressions video. I've not tested many things, like multiplayer. I was not very tempted to try it also, I think the risk is bigger than the reward, and I wanted to give my best at the main mission.
I loved the way they have implemented the co-op. It's quick and easy to find someone to play with us.
People that have played with me was friendly, but the community on Reddit was not very talkative. Maybe since the game is mostly singleplayer, I do not know.
Without a sale, the price is quite high, but with a sale, the game is totally worth it just for the singleplayer alone. I think most of the initial bugs are now gone. It may not be the best game in the world, but I think most of the criticism is not deserved at this point.

Visually, this game is excellent. But the writing and gameplay  aren't holding my interest.
* Most of the puzzles boil down to finding the right thing in the environment to click on. It's usually either too easy or too frustrating, depending on how easily you can find whatever it is you need to trigger progress. This issue is exacerbated by RT's refusal to pick up any item that has no immediate use for.
* RT keeps talking about whatever his immediate objective is, as if the player needs a reminder every few minutes. Being told what you already know you need to do repeatedly is tiresome.
* Whenever you're in a dialogue, you only get to pick one choice. This can be frustrating when you're in a conversation and you'd like to ask questions about multiple topics, but you only get one before being cut off. This also makes parts of the story feel incomplete, because if you ask the wrong question then you don't get a complete understanding of what is going on.

Set on a post-apocalyptic Earth
is a point and click adventure game that tells the story of what happens when mankind has seemingly been wiped out by their own wars and now robots roam freely. This is the first episode in what will hopefully be a series and thus doesn’t tell the full story. In this part you play the role of a simple engineering robot whose life becomes complicated when he finds out some truths that the government is trying to hide. Dive into this unique story accompanied by lovely graphics, memorable music and puzzles to solve as you try to find out what happened to humanity.
In this episode you control RT-217NP, a robot just minding its own business and building things for other robots. This all changes when a shuttle crashes and RT learns a well hidden truth; humans are still alive. Upon learning this the police arrive set to destroy him for finding this out but he is saved by an underground resistance. After this RT really has no choice on what to do so he helps the resistance out in trying to save humanity. Since this is only the first episode most details aren’t developed too deeply so don’t expect many answers to the questions and situations brought up. The story isn’t unique but it’s still interesting and well-told, though RT has a habit of being heavy-handed with his speeches about how humans ruined the Earth or made stupid choices. My biggest issue with the story is that this game is told in episodes, so the first episode opened a can of worms and now players have to wait and wait to find out more. What makes it worse is that the game ends right when things are getting exciting. The pacing is very slow, RT is just going through the motions and laying ground work for whatever is going to happen later in the story.
On the subject of being slow, RT moves very slowly. While the game can be played using a keyboard and mouse combination or a controller and mouse combination, I found the latter to be best for controlling the main character but even still he moved very slowly. I used the controller because it was easier to make RT sprint and for some things, like a certain car chase scene, I couldn’t imagine trying it with a keyboard. While I can select things with the other joystick on my controller (I used an X-Box 360 Controller), sometimes I needed the fine motor skills of a mouse, especially for certain mini games. Whichever method you choose be ready to point and click a lot of things, RT has unique dialogue for every item and explains thing through his robotic perspective. The game mainly has puzzles that require logic, like getting the lights working again in a lab or fixing the internet somewhere. Some puzzles, however, are outright mini games. These were very easy for the most part, and I wish there were more of them.
Aside from the story, I would say the graphics in the game are its biggest strong point. The animation is fluid and the cutscenes are also well done. There is plenty of natural world scenery to contrast most of the darker and more robotic elements in the game though since the story is linear you won’t be exploring much. The game has full voice acting in either English or Russian. I stuck with English though I did switch to Russian to see what it sounded like, I found both versions to be well done. All of the actors did a good job of conveying the emotionlessness of a robot, there are also old audio clips laying around from the days of humanity which are also well done as well. The game has a great soundtrack, which comes free with your purchase, that really helps make this an immersive experience.
I enjoyed playing
and while I would recommend this game to others, I suggest buying it on sale. It took about three hours to finish this episode and in my personal opinion that is too short for the steep price tag, especially since any future released episodes will also have to be bought separately. Also, if you don’t mind a bit of a wait I also say wait until all of the episodes are released, but that is purely my personal preference as I do not like episodic games. The game has Steam trading cards and achievements for those into them. Overall, this was a fun experience for me. It’s a bit slow and certain things seemed to have been added just to drag on play time, an example would be having to press buttons to climb up a ladder which could have easily been a simple cut scene. Also, fair warning the download size of this game is a bit large. However, I see promise in this story and look forward to future episodes and where things go from here.

An adventure game with a futuristic Sci-fi theme, that takes the shape of a point & click visual novel, the first episode of The Uncertain provides a story line and drama to keep your attention.
I experienced no problems with performance or lagging, and the game has only mid-range loading screens. The overall visual quality is quite nice. The artists found enough beautiful nature scenes to counter-balance the “decaying world” look of the old rusty buildings that were part of the story line. I think that is important, because some games, like Deus Ex: Mankind Divided just seem to have such ugly environments almost all the way through the game. Here, you see the contrast.
The music is at times intensely on the edge of your seat mysterious. At other times its haunting and spellbinding. The soundtrack is provided as free dlc, which is definitely a plus for the highish price range for shorter games like this. There is no replayability whatsoever. I missed 3 achievies in one playthrough so had to re-do half the first chapter for those in almost no time. I really took my time too, so I would imagine you could easily finish this game in just 3 hours if you wanted. I don’t know when more episodes will be released, or if they are included in the price. So, all that would need to be taken into consideration with the price. Just saying.
The story is where The Uncertain gives you your entertainment. Normally, I like to start with the positives and work my way down in game reviews. But, I really felt the need to be up front about the negatives this time, since I’m still recommending the game. Here is why. The story fills some deep need to exist. It is not only of high quality writing, and in a genre I love, but the story begs to be told. It’s cutting edge interest in the world around us. One or two were a challenge. But, all seemed fail-proof. I really enjoyed driving the aerocar in the chase scenes, but again… it felt fail-proof, almost scripted.

It was a shame on my side that I did not hear about this game before. I bought it in Summer Sale 2017 when I saw the attractive deal, and decided to give it a go. Although I still follow gaming industry, buy games regularly and play games from time to time (most of my games were never even opened once though) I am not captivated in most games like I was before.
This game was something different. It blended one of my childhood dreams (becoming a game developer, or animation expert, or an author. A storyteller in general) with one of my hobbies (gaming) in one of my favorite game genres. I litterally did not expect much from the game, but when I started I just played for hours.
The game provides a great journey from the very start to today in the history of computer gaming, letting you drown through memories, remember some of your favorite games in the past, and having the urge to recreate them.
In general, the process is really good defined, some very nice details, exciting surprises and hidden easter eggs are to be found. Graphics are okay in an indie game level, music is too much repeating and to be turned off after a while, but gaming experience is something special.
A few constructive feedbacks for a possible sequel: the game goes too fast, maybe a slower timeflow and sometimes pause and review option would be great. The game combinations are great, but sometimes (for example Call of Duty series have in general great story and single player experience, but here action games have to lack story to get great scores. Similarly another example: Skyrim - RPG - Game Engine mods etc.). A bit more detailed adjustments, and more options in game development would add much more to the game. Secondarily more detailed interviews, having the option to look into the gaming industry and opponents (opponent games, genres, positioning in cons etc.) would increase the game experience dramatically.
In short with the game's own words: "Great game", "Played it for days", "More please", "Can't wait for a sequel" and "shows potential". Well "shows potential" is a low grades, actually shows an incredible potential.

As a huge fan of the original Gauntlet, the throwback references in this game are awesome. The game has been totally revitalized and the result is something super addictive and new, but still has that classic hack and slash feeling. This is what Diablo III should have been. Kill, kill, kill.

The Quick Review
A very short and a not too awfully fun game. If it's on sale for about 80% percent off, then I might recommend it if you have some friends that would want to crank up the difficulty and have a few beers a couple of nights.
Some quick negatives:
- it is extremely short
- not much character selection
- you can't unlock the "hidden" character, you have to buy him with real money....
- extremely repetitive. Levels were made with much copy and paste
The Report
My wife is a huge Gauntlet fan. The old school Gauntlet on Nintendo 64 was once of her favorite games, so naturally we grabbed this as soon as it went on sale. As soon as I loaded the game and was looking at the few choices presented for character selection,  I noticed at the bottom of the list the Necromancer character with a lock over his name. My first thought was "cool, you probably get him after beating the game or something."
That's what I had hoped anyway. Then the more seasoned side of my brain said "wait a minute, this is 2014. I bet you have to buy it." Quick Google search later and yes, you have to pay to unlock the "hidden" character. For me, this was an instant down vote with very little hope of being saved.
Then we started playing... The only character that is really worth anything is the Valkyrie. She has everything:
- A ranged move, which is throwing her shield. Small cool down
- A shield to defend with
- Sword for up close quick attacks that deal good damage
- A spear she can use to charge through hordes with. Insta-killing most
So what does the warrior get? An axe and a low IQ, which is humorous at times but gets old rather quickly. He can swing … and swing. No defense whatsoever. You do get some perks to help later, but still, it's very annoying to just be able to run in with no defense options.
The archer? A bow that does little to no damage, and a bomb. The bomb is useful, but your friends will probably kill everything before it goes off anyway.
The wizard? Believe it or not he's not bad. He can mix and match up to nine spells, which does make playing him pretty entertaining. But there is something about him that just doesn't make you want to keep using him. The spells get a little boring after a while, and a couple of them could really use some tweaking.
Keep in mind the above mention of the wizard is just my opinion. He can be a good character to use if you adjust yourself to his playstyle. The warrior and archer, however, are seriously lacking some needed adjustments.
All that  being said, you'd expect to find everybody running around with either a Valkyrie or Wizard, right? Well, two people can't play the same character, so two of your friends are going to soon not be your friends.
As for the rest of the game? Short and repetitive. It's really sad how short this game is considering how many times they just copy and pasted when making the levels. Even some of the bosses are duplicates, just with different models. The first set of levels is alright, but once you've done those four, you've seen all this game has to offer. There were honestly moments when we were playing that I thought I had picked the same level again, or we had messed up and it was making us redo a floor for some reason. They were that similar.
My final opinion of this game:
Just another cheap rip off that was crapped out by another gaming company that is no longer interested in making a good game. They too have fallen into the get rich quick schemes and make more for less. Finished product? Better chop it up and sell some off as DLC.
Remember:
It’s wise not to pay full price for a game in today’s market. Also, NEVER pre-order a game, pay to be a beta tester, or support DLC. Maybe once upon a time those things were alright, but the video game market is exploiting it now, taking away your hard earned money and giving you nothing in return.

Let's get the important thing out of the way first. I love the original and would I recommend this game as a remake? Yes. Yes I would.
The play style is challenging and rewarding in its own way, just as the original was. It's not as fast paced as the original, but that's ok because the graphical improvements and mechanics match so overall you get a very similar feel playing it.
The character mechanics implememnted match the original feel of what you'd expect, and they've done it seamlessly in this new visage. Each of the different classes now even feel more specialized and unique than they used to, which isn't hard considering the advances made in technology, but it truly holds the Gauntlet Essence.
This is not going to be a "This game is perfect, buy it" review though, far from it. There are some key elements that are missing that draw from the overall appeal of the game.
Firstly, is how linear the levels are. I know, how can a dungeon crawler not be linear? The original Gauntlet did it. Even in something as simple as finding the right path through all the locked doors and getting the most from the environment was a challenge. Go through the wrong door and you're stuck, start again. There is not that element of trapping yourself here. You might find 3 or four rooms the entire game that you won't have the keys to open, but you can't really trap yourself on a level. It throuws you essentially down a corridor. Follow it, and you'll beat the level. Very, VERY basic.
Secondly is the distinct lack of playable areas. There are 3 dungeons, broken into 4 parts. 3 of the 4 parts have three levels. An introductory level, the dungeon specific special level, and a survival level. The fourth stage is a boss fight. That is it. As every dungeon takes less than an hour to defeat on hard, one would argue quite validly that this game is not worth more than $5. There's less than 4 hours of gameplay here, you aren't going to find any more secrets, ways to beat it, or in fact HOW to beat it by playing the game more, only Unlocking a more powerful and well dressed character. The same tedious ... i've forgotten the word so I'll just use nonsense, that every MMORPG has for their endgame. GIMMICK! That's the word. Gimmick.
With that last point in mind, with the clothing at least, there are not alot of options. Sure, you can play through the game at a harder level, and unlock ONE more equipment set, but it doesn't effect the damage you take, the damage you do, or anything more than cosmentic. And the variety of cosmetic appearances aren't that great. On that note, it needs ALOT more depth since they decided to implement it, they might as well make it worthwhile.
As for the character strength unlocks, they're just do this X amount of times. Some of the unlocks are just stupid as well. Instead of a crown dropper achievement, how about a crown wearer achievement? Something that rewards you for being good, not something that rewards you for being stupid.
I know all those negatives scream, "how can you recommend this game after all that negativity?" Simple. I never beat the original Gauntlet. I loved it to death. I played it for years. I could never beat it. This, I beat in an afternoon and not on Easy. I can now finally say "I've beaten Gauntlet!" MUAHAHAHAHA and I think there's alot of people who would like to say the same and might even be why they made it in the first place...
Ideally this game is suited for someone who wants to play it for 20 minutes to an hour at a time, then move on to something else. It desperately needs more dungeons with more levels and more challenging levels. It needs something else cosmetically whether it be a boon or just sheer volume for those elitists out there, and it needs more depth within it as a whole. But if you're only looking at playing for an hour with friends or by yourself then go onto something else, it is a hell of alot of fun :)
But, if you're looking for a game that's all that and more, this isn't it. It feels like they've spent 90% of production getting the character concepts right, getting the gameplay down, and then realized they have a week left and threw the rest of the game together. another 6 months before release and this could have been brilliant, but three months after release all they've done is make a new character that costs $5 and implement another gimmicky online mode for some capes... Hopefully soon we'll see some good dungeons come after them.
I've just realized that I can't recommend it, so I've changed it. I really apprectiate and commend getting the original feel of gauntlet as far as the way it plays and characters right, but everything else is just so cheap and rushed I can't condone it. It's still really REALLY fun for 20 minutes to an hour though, the rest is just gimmicky.

If you are a fan of the single player Ultima series then you might want to reconsider looking into Shroud of the Avatar, at least for the time being.
The gameplay mechanics and economy seem to favour MMO mode to single player mode.
After 3-4 years of heavy development, the devs have ignored single player relevant questions...almost completely- instead bringing the focus upon MMO-centric content.
The combat system is not Ultimaesque, rather its a bizarre blend of randomly generated cards or locked cards with annoying penalties. No, I'm not kidding. I wish I was.
I would describe the project as 'floundering' and 'favoring big $$ spending' from the add-on store where prices are insanely high
Whilst the game does possess some of the freedom or charm that made the Ultima series great, there is no open world- but this is still ok- its just different.
PvP? Full loot is sadly not on the radar at this time
Currentlt, the game is one for mmo enthusiasts or the who enjoy decorating houses etc.
Direct from Shrouds kickstarter page:
Shroud of the Avatar is the “spiritual successor” to Richard’s previous work in the FRP genre. Our primary objectives are to tell a story even more compelling than Ultimas IV-VII, create a virtual world more interactive than Ultima VII, develop deep rich multi-player capabilities beyond combat akin to Ultima Online, and offer a bold new approach to integrate them with “Selective Multi-Player”.
Shroud of the Avatar is infused with rich storylines, deeply integrated into game play,
Players will adventure in an interactive world where their choices have consequences, ethical paradoxes give them pause, and they play a vital part in weaving their own story into the immersive world and lore surrounding them.
Shroud of the Avatar is a Selective Multiplayer game, allowing players to choose how they want to play! Whether in Single-Player Offline mode or any of three online modes, the main quest line will provide greater than 40 hours of focused, story driven content.
Shroud of the Avatar can be played as an offline DRM free solo experience or online,

Set in apocalyptic 23rd century Washington, you are a vault dweller from vault 101 who at the age of 19 is forced out of the vault and into the capital wasteland in search of your lost father. Since this fallout title came out in 2008 I myelf have played through all of this game and the next two sequels, 2010's Fallout New Vegas and most recently 2015's Fallout 4. All three of these mostly great games have shown how the rpg has changed and evolved to bring us a new and fresh idea to entertain players of all types.
Positives
-The story presented here in my opinion is better then Fallout New Vegas, FNV was longer and had more distinct endings but it basically came down to who owned this casino chip which didn't give me enough personal involvement to care much. Here however the story is very personal for your character as it revolves mostly around finding your father who has left your vault and has gone missing. Liam Neeson kills it as the voice of your dad and you can really see in his performance that he cares and is not just phoning it in like some other voice actors (Peter Dinklage, Destiny). As the story plays out you come across a range of great and depthful characters and factions that all have a motive to either work with you or kill you. The variety in weapons only help combat the wastleland's darkest creatures and help yourself in succeeding. Some moments in this game will sure tug on your heart as certain events unfold and difficult choices have to be made. The story in Fallout 3 is definitely going for the personal approach and it thus makes the game more engaging and enjoyable.
-Variety in weapons, even most of the legendary weapons are a completely different design which means you won't keep seeing the same weapon with a different name too often, even tho it does occur to an extent.
-The leveling system here, for the time, was rather new and refreshing as it has been copied countless times over the years. It's still to this day is deep and you can loose hours just in searching through all the different skills, perks and advantages they supply the player with.
Negatives
-Trust me when I say I love this game, but the stories length is a joke. If you just look at the story alone it only clocks in at about 15 hours or less if you know what your doing. The shortest Fallout game I've ever played as Fallout New Vegas was around 30 hours and same with Fallout 4. I say short is sweet, and it is pretty sweet, but come on as a Fallout game, and rpg and a title from the legendary Bethesda it could've been a little longer.
-The crafting in Fallout 3 is down right bad, the worst part of the game for sure. Very little amount of things to craft when comparing the past Bethesda titles, but still on it's own it is not anything special. The thing that kills it for me is the UI, on both console and pc it is jumbled and messing and different to navigate.
-Graphics, even for the time it looks ugly. Not that the textures are bad for 2008 but the wasteland is just colourless and lifeless and to be honest, very hard to look at.
Final Thoughts
-Just like every game, it's not perfect. But the game in it's story, characters, rpg elements, quantity and quality shines above and beyond the negatives making it one of my favourite games of all time. In conclusion I give Fallout 3 an 8/10 because unlike some games, it sticks with me for the better.

Due to the fact that I played Fallout 3 after New Vegas and Skyrim, I was really afraid of what I would experience in the game that's 7 years old and commonly hated in the Fallout fandom. As with all other games, I decided to play it COMPLETELY unmodded, in order to experience the very game Bethesda wanted us to play.
I played New Vegas and simply loved it. Also, I played Skyrim and even today I consider it to be the best game I have ever played. Hyping myself for Fallout's 4th installment, I decided to buy Fallout 3 and ultimately decided whether it's so bad as many people say. Surprise, surprise - it's not!
The beginning is very slow-paced, but it gives a nice touch to the whole story. But right after entering Megaton - boy, was I impressed. That was the very moment when I felt the "Bethesda spirit", because of which I love their games so much. Interesting backstory of the location, quite nice backstories of each character in the "city", a lot of interesting loot, nice dialogues and the big introduction to the essence of the game - BE GOOD OR BE BAD.
The morality/consequence system in the game is based on extremities - there are just a few moments when you can stay neutral with your decision. Therefore, most time you decide whether you want to be good or bad. However, sometimes your seemingly good/bad choices can result in the opposite of your intention - that is why a player has to THINK while deciding - it pays off and it's really cool.
Due to the common belief that F:NV is a better game than F3, I'd like to contribute a few words to the discussion. As a whole, I consider F:NV to be the better one, but my F3 playthrough was twice longer than any on my F:NV playthroughs. Draw some conclusions. Also, Washington in F3 seems to be much more affected by the atomic explosions than Las Vegas in F:NV. The whole world of F3 seems also to be more miserable and hopeless in contrary to the one of F:NV, which seemingly make it more suitable to the postapocalyptic vision, but I guess it's a matter of taste - personally, I still like more the atmosphere of New Vegas, but I completely understand why some people prefer the one from Fallout 3.
The gameplay is rewarding and satisfying - every kill, succesful attempt of persuasion/lockpick/etc. results in earned exp, which just HAS to make you feel good - and it does. You can have your own home that you can upgrade with some Fallout lore technology, you can capture people to make them slaves, you can hunt slavers, you can help or kill almost any person that has his/her's own personality and habits. Oh, btw - habits. I love the habit system, as it makes the world feel ALIVE, and the immersion is the first thing that I'm looking for in RPG games. NPCs have their break-times, eat breakfast/dinner, sleep and have random conversations between each other. So, if you suffer lack of funds, why not steal from the cash register of some folk? You walk into the shop, but he observes your every move. Solution? Just break into the shop during the night time - he will be sleeping, so as long as you maintain to be silent, you're good to go. AWESOME.
Now, some bad things. Unlike developers wanted me to, I completed all of the available DLCs BEFORE ending the main story. As for the DLCs - they are mediocre at their least. Some of them are even worse. Somehow, I regret my decision to play them instead of discovering the locations from the main map. Most of the DLCs are linear ("Point Lookout" is the only exception) and - let's face it - just boring. Playing them wasn't a very good idea also because of one more reason - with little more than half of the game's locations discovered, I hit the 30lvl cap and the game became a dull chore - the character progression just stopped - no more perks, no more skills. Therefore, I was forced to install a mod which allowed me to raise the level cap. After 62hrs of gameplay, I raised almost all of my skills to 100 and raised all of my S.P.E.C.I.A.L. stats to 9/10. I know that there are some mods that actually fix this problem, but I wanted to play the game itself, not its modded counterpart. Now, the only thing left is to discover the rest of the locations (20-30, maybe) and to finish the Broken Steel DLC (which is available only after finishing the main questline). Now, I probably need a short break before I complete the game in 100%.
Also, the optimisation! It's... bad. Skyrim runs much more fluently on my laptop, and it's a game that is 3 years younger. And much bigger. And prettier. At the very start, the game was unplayable with its constant freezes and crashes. This solution fixed it for me, both on my desktop PC (i5, GTX 970) and laptop (i7, GT650M SLI):
"Open up the fallout.ini file in: My Documents\My Games\Fallout3
Find the line:
bUseThreadedAI=0
change it to:
bUseThreadedAI=1
Add another line after it and insert:
iNumHWThreads=2
This will limit the game to 2 cores and prevent the engine bug from causing the game to freeze."
Hope that you find it helpful!

If you like Civ IV/Civ V, epic, long games, and space, then GCII is definitely for you. It strikes an incredible balance between providing large-scale epicness and surprisingly robust micromanager's playgrounds.
**While micromanager's playgrounds are not uncommon in modern games, it's exceedingly uncommon for a game to include them sporadically enough that they don't become tedious obligations and yet give them enough weight to make them worthwhile and rewarding. You can go an entire game without ever creating your own ship if that's not your cup of tea--but boy is it ever satisfying to wreck other civilizations with ships you designed.**
GCII is such a vast, epic game it'd be a bargain at twice the price. It's got a bit of a learning curve, but dive right in with a custom scenario and learn by doing until you master the incredible depth and number of facets to it--it's way easier than doing the tutorials. Then, like Civ games, sit in stunned silence when you look up and realize that you've been playing for 13 straight hours. It's that good.

Have you gotten tired of Fighting Games with fifty or so characetrs, and every character just plays like a slightly-different version of the other? Well then try Skullgirls, the pool of characters is small in comparrison to other fights (such as Street Fight, Marvel Vs Capcom, or Brawl), but the characters all actually feel totally different!  This small pool of varied and balanced characters also avoids the problem other Fighters have where there are 40 characters, but then you see the 4 most top-tier in every other match.
Have you gotten tired of Fighting Games where it's always best to select one character with another, simply because they have THE BEST assist for your rushdown game, or your keepaway? Skullgirls lets you set custom assists, meaning that ANY move a character has (aside from Blockbuster moves) can be used as an assist. Almost every character has moves that will work to cover any other character. This means you won't be stuck in situations like in Marvel Vs Capcom, where you have to learn a character you don't like because they have a godlike assist.
Have you gotten tired of stupid infinite combos? Skullgirls has an infinite combo prevention system, which works in such a way that infinite combos are actually impossible. This also adds another layer to high-level mindgames. You can do an infinite combo to bait out someone's Infinite Combo breaker, leaving them open to a follow up.
But, let's say that you're not into Fighting Games super hardcore. You don't care about mindgames, delayed wake-up, and all that other stuff. You might go online every now and again, but you expect you'll get beat down REALLY hard. What does Skullgirls offer for you, then?
Firstly, the art is fantastic. Just look at the screenshots and videos above -- the game is a joy to watch in motion. This is further helped by the art team's fantastic palette system, which allowed them to make over 20 palette swaps for every single character! And many of them have more details than you might expect out of normal palette swaps (such as adding symbols to character's clothes, or making their skin constantly change color, for example). If you're a fan of video games, or anime, there's a ton of references in the palette swaps that you're going to get a kick out of (including, but not limited to, Jojo's Bizarre Adventure palettes, Puella Magi Madoka palettes, Adventure time palettes, and a whole bunch of original color swaps as well!)
Every character has a Story mode. How good the story modes are range wildly from character to character. In general, most of the original cast's story modes are subpar at worst, and interesting at best. Not too great, not too bad. However, with the DLC characters, Lab Zero really stepped up their game. One of the story mode's in particular is especially heart-breaking, and most people I know who played it got teary-eyed at least. Some actually cried. The story modes can be THAT good.
The game can be seen, in a way, as an investment. Every character that's getting added to the game as a result of their Indiegogo campaign is free for the first few months. I've gotten $15 worth of DLC characters for free just for owning the game, soon to be $20. Buying it now ensures you don't have to pay for DLC characters later down the road, so the sooner you buy it, the more money you save.
As far as other gamemodes go, there's an Arcade mode which puts you through a randomly generated challenge (as opposed to Story mode, where the characters you fight are always the same). There are five difficulties you can play at, for both Arcade and Story mode. It's worth noting that there is no "Endless" gamemode in Skullgirls. If you want to fight endlessly, you'll have to go online.
Speaking of gamemodes for fighting other players -- there is a versus mode to fight people locally, a tournament mode for setting up local tournies, a quick match option to be quickly put into a versus match against someone, and a lobby mode so you can play in a lobby of up to 8 people again and again. Lobby names can also be changed to say that you're new, or you want help learning, if you want to get into playing the game online.
Also speaking of "getting into" the game, Skullgirls has the deepest tutorial system of any Fighting Game I've ever played. Don't know what a Mix-up is? Skullgirls will teach you. Not sure what meter-managment is? Skullgirls will teach you. There are very few high level concepts that Skullgirls tutorial mode doesn't teach you! The best part is that there is a tutorial for every character, so you can learn how to play them before hopping into online or story mode, and it's all optional. If you don't want the tutorial, you don't have to play it, the game will not force you through it.
So, what's bad about the game? I've spent a while singing its praise, but what should you be careful about?
While the character designs are all very good, there are a couple characters (Namely Filia, Valentine, and Cerebella) who are very fan-servicey. If you're worried thaat someone might walk by you and judge you because of some risque character designs, then your cast of characters might be limited.
If you're new, there's no easy-operation mode. And the character specific tutorials don't actually teach you any bread and butter combos for that character. There isn't even a challenge mode to teach you combos, like how other games such as KoF have. Being new and going into online usually consists of hitting a 5-10 hit combo with the character of your choice, whereas your opponent retaliates with a 20-40 hit combo, depending upon their character. If you want to get good combos, be prepared to go research them on Fighting Game forums, or put a lot of time into training mode.
In short, the problems Skullgirls has are mostly only problems for newer players. Some might call this a staple of the fighting game genre, but it's still worth considering if you're not into fighters. If you want to get good at Skullgirls, you can't just play storymode. You'll have to research your character's combos, get beaten up in match-ups to learn them, learn about proper spacing and so many other high level strategies the game doesn't teach you. It takes a while to learn the game at a high level, but that's a problem ALL fighters have.
TL;DR
-You can't be hit by infinite combos
-Instead of having 50 characters that all play mostly the same, Skullgirls has a small cast of characters that play in hugely different ways
-Has a great tutorial system, so if you're new to fighting games, Skullgirls is probably the best way to get started. But don't expect the tutorials and story mode to carry you into EVO levels of play -- you need to do research and put in the time if you wanna "git gud"
-Amazing art and animation, with a ton of palettes for every single character. This combined with the custom assist system makes it feel like you're really creating your own, personal, custom team.
-Lacks a few modes you might expect, like challenge mode or endless mode.
Overall, I believe Skullgirls is well worth the price for any hardcore fighting game fan, and anyone who wants to get into Fighting Games. I would heartily recommend the game to anyone who has even a passing interest in fighters.

is a game I've wanted to play for a long time but now that I've gotten to know it better, I can't help but be disappointed.
You see, the planet awoke from its sleep and saw that everything on its surface was dead. So it sent the Giants to make it habitable, and not long after, little creatures called men appeared. The Giants tried hard to help humanity develop, but the harder they tried, the greedier the people became. And so it went until the mission timer run out and the planet went to sleep again.
In
, you control the four Giants, your avatars in this world. Through them, you terraform the earth, place different resources to attract the humans, and then make sure that they have everything they need. The last part involves upgrading resources and placing them in such a way as to make use of their special properties and synergies. In return for your help, humans will offer "ambassadors", who grant your Giants new powers. But if you let any village grow too fast, it will accumulate greed. Greedy villages will start waging war on other humans, and eventually will even turn on the Giants. Then, assuming they haven't grown too powerful yet, you need to punish or even completely destroy them.
This all probably sounds great. In particular, the idea of having to maintain a balance between growth and peace is fairly interesting. Unfortunately, the game is actually rather shallow. Terraforming, for instance, is limited to making a mountain (which will, in turn, create a desert) or a sea (which will create a "wet wasteland" that you can turn into a forest or swamp area). Notice I said "a" mountain... You don't really get the ability to freely change the shape of the planet; instead, your actions are sort of symbolic.
Even the "balance" idea is not really as fleshed out as I wished. Essentially, you can only grow any given village in little steps. If you add too many minerals at once, for instance, or ones that are too "powerful", the greed will start accumulating. You can combat this in a couple ways, and it's not a terrible mechanic (though it is somewhat annoying at times), but it doesn't really reach the potential I thought it would; for instance, interactions between the villages matter little, there's also no "civilization vs nature" conflict you might expect. Perhaps I hyped myself too much.
The worst example of the game's shallowness is actually the most core of its gameplay mechanics — exploiting the many different resources. In order to efficiently use resources, you need to place them in certain ways: for example, placing an animal next to some particular mine will give a bonus to that mine. But the animal itself may want a plant next to it. Of course, you will quickly find out that basic resources are really weak and so you will start "transmuting" them. Unfortunately, you don't know what the new type will do, other than from a very short description in-game — or your memory — and the effects and interactions are not really that intuitive.
It turns out that rather than strategy, what
requires is trivia knowledge. Pretty soon you'll be checking the wiki to get a quick reference or plan your moves — in fact, the game links to its wiki from the main menu. But if your core gameplay revolves around something that can or even should be done through referencing a wiki, and there's little thinking otherwise, then something's wrong.
That's not to say that because
is shallow, it doesn't have a lot of content or good ideas. It does actually allow you to use different strategies or playing styles, mostly through deciding what you want your Giants to specialize in. Do you want to focus on animals or plants? Of course, getting the animals specialization may require a swamp village... And so on.
There is a lot of different resources to use, too, with complicated "evolution paths" to get them. Most will be locked at the start of the game and will require fulfilling "developments" to get, which are essentially in-game achievements. (If the name "developments" seems somewhat awkward, well, the whole game is sort of like this, full of typos and weird turns of phrase.) I know some people dislike achievements in general but in this case, their use is great. In fact, I would say that their lack would pretty much break the game — I, personally, feel like I'd spend just a couple hours exploring the mechanics and quickly get bored. "Developments" provide you with goals to fulfill and different ideas for playthroughs, to motivate you to continue playing.
The playthroughs themselves are interesting because of the limited time you have. You can actually specify whether you want a 30, 60 or 120-minute long "match". I felt this worked fantastically in the beginning, as I could have a quick, half-an-hour game whenever I felt like it. But eventually, you start needing that extra time to further develop your villages and fulfill more difficult "developments". It all starts to slug down then.
It's hard for me to rate
in terms of "buy it"/"don't buy it". I spent some considerable time playing it and don't really regret it. At the same time, it was underwhelming. The premise is great, yet the execution very shallow. It has good music but the graphics I didn't really like, and overall the game feels and looks kind of like a Flash game. Perhaps it could have been made better through the inclusion of some co-op multiplayer mode — it really feels like it should be there. But as long as the gameplay relies on you remembering odd transmutations, it doesn't really offer the sort of depth I was expecting.
In the end, I can't really recommend you get
unless you feel that the mechanics I described here are something you'd really enjoy. But to be fair, if there was a neutral grade for Steam reviews, that's what
would get. It's not bad, just underwhelming.
