I've always heard that FEAR 3 was a really weak game but I never actually played it. Rectified that recently, hence this review. Overall, it was a disservice and a poor end to the series.
FEAR 1 and its expansion packs were solid games that made even people like me who are adverse to horror/suspense feel thoroughly spooked yet interested. FEAR 2 was a decent revision in the gameplay department with interesting combat mechanics and more weapons, but a lot of the horror gave way to sci-fi and alienated those who liked the horror/suspense aspects more than the shooting. The AI for FEAR 1 is considered legendary, to the point of having its own academic papers. FEAR 2 was less impressive in this regard, but was a little more varied in terms of combat environments and gunplay: the player is no longer just crawling through stairwells and basements in FEAR 2, and the weaponry gets a little more exotic.
FEAR 3 does none of these things. In fact, FEAR 3 regresses in comparison to even FEAR 2:
If one looks at FEAR 3 objectively, it isn't bad in the sense that it's a functioning game, isn't prone to crashing, appeals to a certain audience (casuals, people who never played the previous FEAR games), and has an interesting score-based co-op mechanic. FEAR 3 carries on the story that began in the previous FEAR games but you dont have to have played the previous games to like and/or enjoy this one. As far as game play goes, FEAR 3, like the previous FEAR games is a horror themed FPS.  Take away the "horror" theme and FEAR 3 still works really great as an FPS all on its own.   Using cover and taking your time, its difficult to die on normal difficulty setting but despite this, the enemies/enemy AI still make for a solid challenge.  The enemies move around a lot, use cover well and come at you from just about every direction.  They will even persue you if you refuse to go to them.  Enemies are also thrown at you in great enough numbers that you, yourself are always seeking the best cover/fighting positions.  Playing as the combat guy, you get to slow time and have a fair number of range weapons to choose from.  Playing as the dead brother, you get to possess people and use mostly melee skills.  This game can be played multiplayer but I dont bother much with multiplayer in any game so I cant tell you much about that.
Bottom line;  FEAR 3 is a great FPS with a fun and refreshing horror atmosphere.  The story is even fairly interesting if you have all the installments of the game and can follow it along.  Dont go into FEAR games expecting to be frightened out of your witts though.  I dont think the FEAR games were ever supposed to frighten you(except for a few jump scares here and there).  I think the idea of the horror theme was simply to give a warn out FPS genre a new flavor.  As far as Im concerned, it worked.  Despite having come out in 2011, FEAR 3 can still easily compete with more recent FPS games.

Finally got around to finishing this game a few days ago and I definitely recommend it.  It's easily one of the best Metroidvania games out there, and it's fairly unique; it doesn't borrow too heavily from the other games in the genre.  There is notably a greater emphasis placed on the platforming mechanics in this game than the combat, though both are solid and very engaging.  As you gain power-ups, both by traversing the world and by spending ability points, you are handed more and more creative ways to approach certain obstacles or enemies.  This makes backtracking much more enjoyable, which is necessary since there is no fast-travel in this game.  There are three "dungeons" in the game, but instead of boss battles at the end you will go through these high-adrenaline chase sequences.  These can be difficult, but not so difficult that you won't get the hang of it before you lose your patience, and you will feel a huge sense of accomplishment when you make it through one.
The graphics are beautiful throughout the whole game world, to the point where you will be mesmerized by staring at the scenery while you run through the forest.  The music is very atmospheric and perfectly fits whatever situation you're in.  The story is simple, but still keeps you hooked.  Definitely buy this game if you haven't already.

How the Circumference of Earth Was Accurately Estimated 2000 Years Ago
Born around 276 B.C. in Cyrene, Libya, Eratosthenes soon became one of the most famous mathematicians of his time. He is best known for making the first recorded measurement of the Earth's circumference, which was also remarkably accurate. (And, yes, people at that point had known for some time that the world wasn't flat, contrary to popular belief.)
Eratosthenes was able to accomplish this in part because of his education in Athens. There, he became known for his achievements in many different fields, including poetry, astronomy, and scientific writing. His activities became so talked about, in fact, that Ptolemy III of Egypt decided to invite him to Alexandria to tutor his son. Later, he would become the head librarian of the Library of Alexandria.
The mathematician must have been thrilled to have this opportunity. The Library of Alexandria was a hub of learning at the time, attracting scholars from across the known world. Eratosthenes was able to rub shoulders with the likes of Archimedes while continuing his own learning.
It was probably in the Library of Alexandria that he read about a curious event that took place in Syene (now Aswan, Egypt) at the summer solstice. Syene sat to the south of Alexandria. At high noon, the sun would shine directly overhead and there would be no shadows stemming from the columns. However, Eratosthenes realized that at the same moment in Alexandria, columns clearly did have shadows. Being a good mathematician, he decided to use this knowledge to do a few calculations to figure out the circumference of the Earth.
To do this, Eratosthenes measured the shadow of an obelisk on June 21 at noon. He discovered that the sun was about 7°14' from being directly overhead. He realized that, because the Earth is curved, the greater the curve, the longer the shadows would be.
Based on his observations, he hypothesized that Syene must lie 7°14' along a curve from Alexandria. Furthermore, he knew that a circle contained 360°, which meant that his calculation—7°14'—was roughly one fiftieth of a circle. Therefore, Eratosthenes thought, if he multiplied the distance between Syene and Alexandria by 50, he would have the circumference of the Earth.
The missing information was simply how far away Syene was from Alexandria. He measured the distance in stadia. There isn't an exact modern day conversion to stadia, and it isn't perfectly clear which version of the stadia Eratosthenes was using, but regardless, from what is known, his estimation was remarkably accurate.
There are two theories as to how Eratosthenes figured out the distance: first, that he hired a man to walk there and count the steps. Second, that he heard a camel could travel 100 stadia a day, and it took a camel about 50 days to travel to Syene. Whatever the case, he estimated the distance between Syene and Alexandria was 5,000 stadia. If that was the case, then using his formula, the earth was 250,000stadia around.
Due to the uncertain distance that stadia represents (and particularly which stadia he was using), historians believe that Eratosthenes' conclusion was between .5% and 17% off the mark. Even if the latter case was true, it was astoundingly accurate given the limited technology he was dealing with at the time. But many scholars think it likely that he was using the Egyptian stadia (157.5 m), being in Egypt at the time. This would make his estimate only about 1% too small.
There had been previous attempts at discovering the Earth's circumference (which don't count as "first recorded" because their methods didn't survive, though we have references to them) which resulted in a 400,000 stadia figure, 150,000 more than Eratosthenes'—obviously far from accurate.
While finding the approximate circumference of the Earth was probably Eratosthenes' largest contribution to scholarship at the time, it was by no means the only one. Eratosthenes is also credited with coming up with a way to map out the known world by drawing lines north-south and east-west—early latitude and longitude lines. However, these lines were irregular and often drawn through known places, meaning they weren't entirely accurate. Nevertheless, it provided a precursor for maps we know today.
He is also remembered for the Sieve of Eratosthenes, a simple algorithm that makes it easy to find all prime numbers up to a certain limit. Though none of Eratosthenes' personal work on the sieve survives, he was credited with the creation of the algorithm by Nicomedes in his Introduction to Arithmetic.
Not only that, but Eratosthenes estimated the distance to both the sun and the moon, and measured the tilt of the Earth's axis all with amazing accuracy.
He also wrote the poem Hermes, correctly sketched the route of the Nile, and even gave a more-or-less accurate account of why the Nile flooded, something that had baffled scholars for centuries. He worked on a calendar that included leap years and he also estimated and corrected the dates of various historical events beginning with the Siege of Troy.
Despite these accomplishments and many more like them, Eratosthenes was often nicknamed "Beta." Beta is the second letter in the Greek alphabet and referred to Eratosthenes being second-best in everything he did.
Eratosthenes died around 194 B.C. and is thought to have starved himself to death. It is believed that he started going blind in his later years and, unable to continue his work, he simply stopped eating.

I bought a Desura copy of the game in a bundle a while ago and was provided with a steam key by the dev free of charge. Like other reviewers I was also approached by the dev via email who asked me to write a review of the game in exchange for several more keys -- an offer which I declined. I will, however, still leave a review so feel free to skip the rest if you think I am biased because of the above.
With that said, StarFence is a simple turrent defence game in which you place turrets (manually-controlled) to shoot down incoming ships to protect a space station. Progressing through missions unlocks more difficult enemies and other turrents and/or defences to use. The basic turrents all aim towards the mouse cursor and can be placed anywhere on the screen to plan out lines of fire. Turrets can be destroyed however, and enemies target them just as happily as the space station so some thought should be put into their placement.
There seems to be a decent variety of defences and power-ups available -- automated laser turrets, friendly ships, mines, asteroids (walls), fire rate boosts, double fire, station shield, etc. Each turret can also be upgraded for arbitrary 'upgrade points' which are gained during each stage and persist across the campaign stages -- e.g. with rotation speed upgrade since by default turrets rotate sooooo slow.
Speaking of the campaign -- things start off really slow. In fact I was not sure if I could be bothered to finish the first few levels, but the game picked up the speed a few stages down the line. It gets more frentic and challenging with each campaign mission, though I have yet to get to the end so can't say just what the end game looks like. There's no story to the campaign past a simple 'you're under attack, defend yourself with these'.
Game also offers a survival mode that pits a wave after wave of enemies against the defences and I can see this being a decent pastime for fans of arcade games.
In terms of presentation it's a simple 2D top-down game with static sprites moving across the screen or rotating. Laser-based projectiles look like glow-sticks hurtling through space and rockets resemble javelins with their long exhaust trails. It's not bad though, simple but agreeable and not too harsh on the eyes.
Would I recommend it? Yeah, kinda. I'd say it's a 'for fans of genre only' kinda game. If you like the sound of an arcadey turret defence game and need something to now and then offer distraction from other games then yeah, this might be worth the while at $5.

Two scientists are contracted to fulfill a dying man's dream to go to the moon. Their work involves the use of a machine that allows them to explore and manipulate memories.
It's a wacky premise, but one that's presented with more charm and emotion than you'd expect from such a simple game. The writing is fresh and sprinkled with pop culture references, the back-and-forth between the two protagonists is always entertaining, and the story intrigues you more and more as the memory manipulators begin to encounter complications.
The game clocks in at about 3-4 hours for the average playthrough, with the free DLC offering another hour or so. But be warned: while the game proper is on the whole a bittersweet experience (which isn't a spoiler - you know from the outset your client is on his deathbed), the DLC (the second one in particular) takes on a more sinister and creepy vibe.
That said, I don't hesitate to recommend this short game to anyone looking for a unique tale. It'll certainly leave you thinking.

I purchased Depth a few days ago and have enjoyed the game immensely.  In this review, I will go through several key aspects of the game that I found to be great.
The premise of the main game mode, Blood and Gold, seems fun.  I have not played the other two game modes yet, but the majority of the game focus is placed on B&G.  The objective of this game mode is for the divers to escort the robot, STEVE, through a set route on one of many maps.  STEVE will stop several times in relatively safe rooms where the divers can fortify against attack.  Transitioning from one safe room to another often requires the divers to traverse relatively open areas where sharks gain a short advantage.  It is really fun and I have had a good time playing this, and I really enjoy the STEVE escort concept the game is based around.  It keeps the game focus moving around the map and works well.
The game is quite well balanced.  None of the abilities, talents, or items in the game feel unfair or too overpowered, and both the divers and the shark sides seem to be equally matched in terms of tactics and gameplay they can do to try and win.  There is also a whole lot of skill to this game and I'm already hooked on trying to improve my game.  Nothing really feels unfair, and there's a way to fight everything by improving and learning and becoming better at the game.  Depth's community has some very strong players that have inspired me, showing what's possible when you really know how to play.
Depth has graphics that I find to be both good and not a huge strain on my computer.  I have no issues running the game with my 980M NVIDIA card and the game looks really well put together graphically.
I have not had a whole lot of direct interaction yet amongst the community of the game, but it seems good so far.  The devs seem to care about the game and announce they regularly add content such as skins and maps and seem polite to the playerbase.
I recommend buying this game, and if you do definitely buy it with some friends.  It is a lot of fun to play with other friends you know.

Alright, this is my first Steam review, but I'm used to doing this on other sites. Let me start by saying that Skullgirls is quite easily the greatest fighting game I have ever played, and that it ranks as #3 on my list of all-time favorite games, behind Team Fortress 2 and Final Fantasy X.
Now that my fanboy session is over, let's get to the review. I will not say that Skullgirls is a perfect game. While I love it, just like loving a person, it's not perfect. Close, but no cigar. Other than a few unnecessarily difficult commands, the only thing I can legitimately say that I have a problem with is the painful amount of lag during online play. I have fairly decent hardware, so the game runs perfectly on my computer, but the first time I tried to play online with one of my friends, we both ended up with lag to the point that the timer would lower by a second after three seconds in reality. Honestly, this kind of pains me to say, but it is something that I do truly hate about Skullgirls. Otherwise, I hold this little slice of gaming heaven not just close to my heart, but against it. With my own prejudice set aside, I give Skullgirls a heartily thought-over 9.7 out of 10. Anytime somebody asks me for a game that I recommend to them, I have two immediate thoughts: Skullgirls, and Five Nights at Freddy's.
And to you, wonderful developers, you probably won't end up seeing this, but I thank you, for giving us this unbelievably amazing game, and I hope that, in the future, we can help to Keep Skullgirls Growing.
With heartfelt regards,
Arrick Pearson

Another round of moderation and silencing of any and all criticisms of the game.
"We do have the addon store to help fund the game, as all of you are well aware. What seems to be missed is the many times more items that are added in the game that are craftable and support the lifeblood of the in-game community."
Yes, sure, we were well aware of that AFTER the KS. We had no choice, we were FORCED into the cash shop. How many of those many items added in game, were just added in game for the pure reason to make re-skinned cash shop items?
"We need your help here to post constructive feedback and ideas on how to bring in more players, and to start creating your own fan sites. Posting "the game is going to fail unless we do away with x, y, z" is not going to help."
Once again, silencing criticism. The only "constructive feedback" they want to hear are positive ones. They don't care to hear about things gone wrong or they need to fix. They don't care to hear the reality of how the outside world sees this game outside of their safe haven bubble of a forum. As long as a very niche minority of players continue to keep handing money over to Portalarium the players that WOULD be interested in this game can continue to ignore it. Perception matters, and the perception of this game are whales, cash shop, and shouting down and moderation of any criticism.
Same thing goes to fan sites. Only POSITIVE fan sites without critism is what they want. Anything with any form or hint of any criticism will be shouted down and ignored, and any users that use such sites with any critism will be ridiculed and ignored as second class citizens that no longer matter as soon as they voice their concerns about the direction of this game.
Oh, and not to mention that asking for only positive things and fan sites reminds me when a dev specifically begged for positive Steam reviews. And how well did that work for Portalarium before it very quickly backfired on them? How soon after that backfire did they have to delete that forum post and thread, to cover their collective butts?
How far does this moderation and shouting down of criticism go? Not only does it come from Portalarium themselves, it comes from the strongest backers of the game. So much so, that even in a Hospitaller meeting (that group, that is made up of volunteers, to help new people and such) when one Hospitaller dare give any criticism to the game, she was quickly "shouted" down and "moderated". Enough so that she stormed out of the meeting in frustration, because how dare ANYONE have any critique of this game, right?
So where is my review of the actual game itself? When the company and the white knights go hand in hand to shout down and moderate criticism, there is no reason to even attempt the game. If the game was able to stand on its own, it would not have this much criticism. It would not have such a bad perception and reputation outside of their collective thought bubble.
There is hope, but as long as Portalarium and the whales keep going in the path they are headed, there is no hope for either the short term enjoyment of the game or the long term longevity of even the company itself. Final Fantasy XIV was able to listen to the harsh and constant criticism of version 1.0. They re-grouped and released 2.0 and guess what? It was a success. But I don't see that happening here with Portalarium. They would have to allow criticism first. And before it was quickly swept under the rug they would have to actually listen to it. And there is no hope of either of those happening.

I have a little bit of time on this game and I think I'm ready to write my first review ever.
I'm going to compare this game to the In-Browser version for you to determine if it is worth the $5 it is on sale.
Pro's of Steam Game
1. Very Fluid and there will be little to no lag ever. For me, lag usually started around round 60 In-Browser, in this version, it does not start occuring to maybe the 100+ levels, and that is with plenty of towers out and darts flying everywhere.
2. More Turrets to add some more variety. These include Engineer, Helicopter, Shredder. The helicopter is my personal favorite and these new turrets add some new dynamics to work with.
3. There are maps after maps after maps. I mean just maps galore. It will be awhile before you finish all of them on all difficulties.
4. Monkey Cash just flows in while playing the Steam version. It seems as though you always have cash handy which allows you to actually buy the agents without thinking that you are wasting money and that you would actually have to spend real money to do microtransactions.
Now  there is a negative that occurs in this game though, which all surrounds the Co-op.
1. There is no chat. Like none. You cannot communicate with your teamates on Co-op and it is really hard to do hard levels without this, which will make you just have to play them with a friend you have and just hop in a Discord call or something.
2. There are glitches that occur with Co-op all the time. You can usually play one game through with a friend, but lets say that you fail and want to retry, 9/10 times, it will glitch up and your friend will never join the next match. So you have to leave and make a new lobby and re-invite. Not horrible, it just gets really annoying after a while. Also, if you go into a quickmatch, expect 50% of the time, you will get disconnected from your team mate.
3. Invisible Bloons. While playing with my friend, I have noticed that sometimes i will be able to see some bloons and my parter won't. This has cost us countless matches because he legitimately can't see the bloons that I can.
4. Banana glitch. In Co-op, if your friend puts down a banana farm, the bananas will pop up on your screen as well. They have no impact to you and they don't give anyone money, but they will still pop up on your screen. The only way to have a temporary fix is to have your friend put down the banana farmer agent. He will keep the bananas off your screen.
Overall I really like this game. Co-op can be a little bit of a hassle and annoying; however, if you can get a game going with a friend, it can be very enjoyable. I would rate this game a 8/10 with the 2 off being Co-op.

There is A LOT that can be said about "The Division". Much has beed already written so I write what continues to stand out during my playtime.
The Story ...
is repetitive, you have to make your own story in this game ... if you can´t - you just run after a carrot someone holds in front of your face. There is potential but Massive was not able to string this into a cohesive and interesting storyline. Result: Clutter everywhere or more carrots to run after.
Positive
Not such a bad Coop-Loot-Shooter. The Atmosphere has something to give away. The Soundscape is ok and fits to the content. Voiceover is mostly okay but varies.
Edit: The Combat can have it´s moments ( once you learn to avoid to get stuck ...). Manual crouching or even going prone would be a nice addition ( soft-cover ). The Game reminds me a little of Assassins Creed Unity ( many Interiors, Rooftops, Passages, Undergound areas ). This Game has potential, if you would be allowed to use it ... this would be great.
Things you should be aware off:
NO OFFLINE MODE. ( Fact is: It´s badly needed - explained below )
The Game needs an over-exessive Server connection even in Singleplayer which is BAD. No way to change the Server in Singleplayer ( Why ? ) to reduce LAG that creates unplayable situations. ( In which the AI bugs out pretty bad ) Example: Invincible Enemies, AI freezes in T-pose, AI is warping allover the place, AI wallhacking - lets them shoot through everything, AI spawns into the ground and so on.
Login queues can tick me off ...
Loading times in "Fast Travel" ... not always
Graphic glitches in Weapon modification page
No possiblity to flag yourself as PvE only.
More Graphic issues around "town" ... requires to restart the game
No option to "host" your own Singleplayer session
Ah, yes. There is the "Darkzone" which I avoid, because of above mentioned Server issues which can result in glitches - some players exploit this - aside from that, it can get YOU banned as well. ( Good Job Massive ... )
It could be a really good game. Stealth could be an interesting addiition to the game (PvE only) so could additonal evasion animations (moves) as well as some more melee attack options/possibilities/moves. Sadly the decisions made by Massive limit the fun you can have in this game.
Still, with a friend or friends an interesting 3rd Person COOP Game in which you can waste sometime. The above mentioned issues should be addressed, have a feeling this will never happen.

I have had this game since the day it was released so I don't know why I haven't decided to review it until now.
Basically, if I was going to choose a GOTY, this would be in my Top 3. The art style is absolutely gorgeous and the guys at 'Moon Studios' should be highly praised for the visuals this game presents, everything looks perfect such as the bloom on the bright neon plants for example.
The soundtrack is amazing and sets the atmosphere of the game really well, I constantly found the music giving me goosebumps throughout the entire story, I hugely recommend listening to the OST even if you do not buy the game.
Even within the first 20 minutes, the plot of the game provokes emotion from you without the need of voices or text.
The platforming itself is also presented very well, it's solid and doesn't feel floaty at all which is expected within this game since it can get pretty hard in the latter half and will challenge even experienced platforming gamers. The new abilities which Ori gains throughout the game all serve a purpose and the delay between each ones makes it feel like a real reward, even when you only get the double jump ability.
It's a shame that indie games with as much care and effort put into them such as Ori and the Blind Forest don't sell well because the majority of gamers are drones who only want to play adrenaline pumped action games which are just a cheap thrill.
TL:DR
I'd give Ori and the Blind Forest a 10/10 and recommend it to anybody who is just curious about purchasing the game or anyone who wants a game that they will remember for years to come.

Okay... a more nuanced review...
I really enjoyed the first three or so hours of Ori.  The art style is really good, the controls are adequate (once you get used to them being "floaty") and the story is surreal/engaging.  The game is difficult in some places, but balanced.  I died many times, but eventually got the hang of saving at strategic locations.  I wasn't frustrated, but definitely challenged.
Then, I hit the cliff of stupidity shown in the video.  After beating my head against this section.  I found the video and saw that I had made my way most of the way through.  But had no desire to try to make it to the top of the Gonzo Tree.
This section of the game is ridiculous because it suddenly introduces a timed component.  The only way to proceed is by memorizing timed jumps.  And if you miss one of those timed jumps, you're swallowed by the bile of the Gishna tree.  It's like I was playing Outland and was suddenly transported to Super Meat Boy (either of which are better platformers).  I was totally frustrated and it completely changed my opinion of the game.
Could I spend another 30 minutes memorizing jump patterns?  Sure, but why? Life is too short to make it to the top of the Gitmo tree.

The story starts off with two scientist-type fellows known as Dr. Neil Watts and Dr. Eva Rosalene, employees of a mysterious corporation known as Sigmund Corp. They are specifically tasked with providing the elderly and sick with fulfilling lives before they die, by using the means of a certain memory-altering dream machine that allows them to rewrite their client's memory to fit their ordered specifications. Their client, an old, withering man known only by the name Johnny, has enlisted the help of these two scientists. His request, to become an astronaut and fly high into the sky, to reach the outer edge of the world and engage in a long-awaited rendezvous with the moon. Things go routine for a good while, until it appears that something is very wrong with Johnny's memory. Segmented and heavily disjointed, the mind of the elderly man seems to only connect via a single thread, memories of his deceased wife, River. You'll find along the way that she holds major significance to Johnny, much more than could be originally thought, but I'll leave the satisfaction to you.
Surely no game is great without some equally complementing gameplay. Whilst travelling through this cavalcade of emotions and memories, you'll have to deal with searching the man's memories and finding items that can link each piece together, like a grand cranium jigsaw puzzle. Mementos will be scattered about for you to interact and find, and engaging in absorbing the story from each memory is a must if you are to succeed. You'll have to go through some light puzzle elements in order to gain access to the linking power of the mementos, but it's nothing a little brain power can't fix. And even with all this brainiac gameplay, there are indeed moments of action. Remember that squirrel you narrowly dodged on the road? Well, I won't say much, but I can say that you surely haven't seen the last of him. You'll need to have a fighter's spirit, but keeping a shoe handy is about the same.
The game holds with it not only what you can gather from surface value, but it also carries underneath it a plethora of teachings and meanings. Now nothing I say here is set in stone, as you take what you will from the experience, but what I've collected from the game is as follows: One of the hardest things to do is to do nothing at all, that sometimes love will find us no matter where we are, and that strangers we meet can be the most interesting people we will ever get to know. These certainly aren't the only lessons to be drawn from this wonderful game, interpretation is a most beautiful thing. I leave the gorgeously complex teachings of this game to you to find, as making your own connections is supremely satisfying, and I'd be nobody to deny you the pleasure.
This game is definitely worth the priced listed. A fine game with charming graphics, a beautiful story, and a heart-rending conclusion that will leave you fully satisfied with your purchase. With the characters very fleshed out and unique, alongside the "worlds" you'd be visiting, not to mention the beautiful OST that'll be accompanying you, I'd give it a most well-deserved 9/10. Buy this game, love this game, remember this game.

Game Dev Tycoon is a glorified flash game, not a tycoon game of old. It offers an interesting premise and enjoyable gameplay, but lacks the depth and variety to last much longer than a few hours. That isn't necessarily a bad thing - the first few hours are old-fashioned fun - but I went in expecting more.
If you're like me, you'll have about five hours of gameplay before you get bored, though mods can draw that out a bit longer. Though I can't recommend this game at its full price, you should definitely check it out during a sale.
In Game Dev Tycoon, you play as a dudebro from the early 80s. You only have your computer, your garage and your desire to become a game development giant. Is the journey from zero to hero as exciting as it sounds? Well, yes and no.
GDT provides you with a lot of interesting mechanics, but does not bother to give them the depth they deserve. For example, you can steer development by adjusting a side of nine sliders. A strategy game will benefit from putting a lot of emphasis on artificial intelligence, but doing the same with a rhythm game doesn't make much sense. GDT rewards logical choices with high sales and punishes games that are less well thought out with commercial failure. Unfortunately, the system doesn't leave much room for experimenting; any formula that hasn't proven its worth in real life is bound to fail. Discovering which formulas are successful and which aren't is fun at first, but racking in the money becomes deceptively easy once you've figured out the rules. Matters are not helped by the game's console timeline, which is static and does not change between playthroughs. At first, it's entertaining to anticipate the launch of the Ninvento Gameling (Nintendo Gameboy) or Vena DreamVast (Sega DreamCast), but the timeline's scripted nature makes for very poor replay value. Your first time playing GDT will be exciting, the others not so much.
In our world, sales are dependent on more factors than game quality alone; the renown of the developer, the brand strength of the franchise and the size of the marketing budget are all equally important. GDT partially acknowledges this by implementing fans, sequels and a rudimentary marketing system. Like most of GDT's mechanics, however, these systems are incredibly oversimplified. Did you look forward to bribing reviewers and recruiting a team of shrewd marketeers? Walk past GDT, because you aren't going to find anything of the sort here. R&D allows you to create a console and even your very own Steam-clone, but is similarly dumbed down.
A final point of criticism is the game's interface. While it is visually appealing and easy to use, it provides you with almost no information. The game has no statistics, tables or graphs of any kind, making it hard to ascertain your financial situation or monitor its development. For example, you're billed operating costs every month, but you can't break them down into their individual components. For a tycoon game, GDT is severely lacking in the financial department.
Of course, not everything about GDT is bad. The art style is appealing, the soundtrack unremarkable but good. The game also deserves praise for its almost non-existent learning curve, which is rarely seen in the genre.
Staff management works well, too. You're able to overwork your staff members to hell and back, but doing so eventually results in a burn-out and a spectacular drop in their efficiency, forcing you to send them on a holiday. You can subject your staff to a wide variety of education programs to improve their skill and more experienced staff members will even demand a higher pay grade. It's definitely one of GDT's better executed systems, but still suffers from the game's tendency of omitting as much complexity as possible. You can't negotiate about salary and severely abused staff members won't quit. In addition, you can never grow your team larger than a dozen or so employees and develop projects of a truly massive scale. Still, the system does its job well enough to be functional.
All in all, Game Dev Tycoon is more a proof of concept than a full game - it succeeds in demonstrating the potential of its niche, but mostly fails to live up to it. If you're just looking for a few hours of fun, go ahead and buy it. People who expect this to live up to its illustrious name, however, should probably this one over. One thing is certain: Greenheart Games definitely has me excited for a sequel.

This game is currently the target of an on-going review bombing campaign (On both sides). Legitimate positive reviews and crappy negative reviews are being downvoted or upvoted, respectively. There are legitimate negative reviews that should be taken into account, but don't trust when a rating is "helpful." Even if it's a positive review with a high helpful rating.
TL:DR - This game is very much targetting a niche crowd. Odds are, you are not in that crowd and this is not the game for you. So why does this game have a positive review if I don't recommend it for the average player? This game offers a type of gameplay experience that is unique, and the niche players it caters to can't find it anywhere else.
This game was toted as the next Ultima Online. However, it's a far cry from UO. It's closer to second life in that you can own your own property and land, but likely only through the use of RMT (Real Money Trading). The developers have giving the green light to trade your in-game gold(IGG) and other items for cash, which you can then utilize to purchase property. There is a means of acquiring property in game, but it is through a raffle system is will be taxable, costing IGG upkeep. Over time you will have enough coin saved up to buy a tax-free property and upgrade from there, but it will take significant time to reach that point.
The skilling system is based off of XP gained when gathering / killing enemies (and occasionally from completing quests). This XP can then be moved into other skills to define your own class. Currently there is little balance and meta builds are far more powerful than other builds. If you've played Diablo 3 with your own, non-meta build and watched other meta builds faceroll enemies 10 times faster than you, it feels a lot like that. However, the next few releases (monthly updates) should, hopefully, fix this as system implementation is taking dev priority over balance currently.
This game is all about the community. If you're looking to be a solo player, you won't have as much fun. Find a guild early and try to become active. It will assist your experience a lot. The community is small enough to earn a name for yourself in a certain field, such as crafting. On the topic:
SotA is punishing to crafters with high chance of full item destruction when enchanting / masterworking and is RNG heavy. Despite this, good crafters can make a name for themselves and their vendors will become the go-to vendor when looking for equipment. Equipment degrades over time, but can be repairs with an ever-increasing cost of RMT currency. Eventually, you will need to find a new weapon / armour and will need to revisit those crafters.
The UI is dated, but they have been (very) slowly updating it. Performance is currently wanting, but I have seem major strides in this field in the past three months (having gone from 19 frames to 60 in the main city), though load times are still somewhat long. If you want to play this game with high graphics on, you will probably need a high-end rig.
If you've made it this far in the review, you might wonder why the hell I'm still giving it a positive review. It's because I've played this game for two years now. I've seen the leaps and bounds of improvement and I do, in fact, have faith that the team will continue to improve the product. And, despite the negatives, this game can be enjoyed in it's current form as long as you understand what to expect from the game.

This is a management game that is simple on the surface but quite complex when playing for the achievments or playing longer rounds.  You control 4 demigods that then control different biomes. From there you build up settlements by laying down ground layers of different biomes then planting various resources that accompany the demigods.  Each resource reacts differently with different biomes.  As settlements build you will be presented with requirements of various resources to upgrade the city.  Upgrade too fast and the settlement will become greedy and attack nearby settlements.  Upgrade too slow and you will lose the opportunity to achieve that upgrade and will have to wait some time for a new set of requirements.
Through these mechanics you can play relaxing games of 30 minutes that will have little chance of greedy settlements killing each other, or you can play much longer games on bigger maps that will require a greater level of skill to beat.
This is why I would recommend Reus.  It is entirely viable to be played as a casual game, but it also has a pretty high skill cap and level of depth.
Not to say it doesn't have its flaws though.  It can be frustrating at times, and slow.  You will feel like you don't have any control, but control is something you will achieve with practice if you desire.  Also if you are going to play a longer game a fair amount of planning can be involved.  You will be surprised how fast the time goes by when you are actually trying to achieve something specific.

Where do I even start with this? Day 1 Studios took everything about the F.E.A.R. games that made them so good and either threw them out the window or ruined them beyond all recognition. Even the parts of the series that weren't as good were somehow messed up too.
- Mildly dark lighting, and then a barrage of a dozen mediocre jumpscares at once with no sense of pacing, as opposed to setting an atmosphere that leaves you on edge through dark lighting and silence and then delivering a single jumpscare. How is a falling object scary after seeing the same jumpscare redone multiple times in the last 15 seconds?
- Reflex time, the staple of the series, is almost useless now
- Levels are badly designed and feel "gamey," unlike the levels in the first 2 games. Environmental detail is lacking, and it's hard to tell where you're supposed to go
- The guns don't feel responsive, recoil is near nonexistent, and the weapon designs look stupid (shotgun and assault rifle come to mind)
- Health kits and armor are gone, with regenerating health in its place
- It's a cover shooter now, but the cover system is half-baked.
- Some of the enemy design is straight up stupid in this context. Suicide bombing cultists, Hellhounds, and a soldier covered in an energy shield that can teleport new enemies in are a few examples
- The story is a joke. The pointman joins forces with the main antagonists of the series, Paxton Fettel and Alma. Why? Who knows, perhaps the pointman has a death wish and wants to see the end of the world. Instead, the antagonist is a monster that's a psychic manifestation of the memories of
, who you feel you should be rooting for since it wants to destroy Alma.
If you played the first two games and loved them, and you want to complete the series, don't. If you're a newcomer to the series, forget this game ever existed and play the F.E.A.R. 1 or 2, preferably 1. This game isn't worth your time or money.

F.E.A.R.? Awesome game and an instant cult classic.
F.E.A.R. 2? Lame ending but still very cool game with terrific features.
F.E.A.R. 3? RUINED.
What were they thinking? The game plays more like an arcade shooter. You literally get 'points' when killing an enemy and get extra for headshots. This series was always about the story and the creepy factor with awesome gameplay as an added extra. This particular game, caps the series off with a ridiculous display of awful.
The only good thing is that the shooting mechanics are very good. This is actually the best in the series as far as point and shoot, mouse movement and controls. It is just unfortunate the story is so lame.
Is it worth playing at least once to finish off the story? I would argue no. The story was pretty much ruined at the end of F.E.A.R. 2 anyway so just play the first two and pass on this one.

F.E.A.R 3 was developed by Day 1 Studios instead of Monolith Productions and is published by WB Interactive Entertainment. As development house changed, so did F.E.A.R as it became like Call of Duty rip-off. Most people hated this, but to be honest. This game isn't awful and if you look at previous game (F.E.A.R 2: Project Origin), Day 1 Studios actually improved some aspects but unfortunately made some things worse, which is why we never got another F.E.A.R after the third installment.
I should mention that it has been a long time since i've played co-op in this game and I haven't tried Fettel playthrough, but I've gathered some information about it, so I know what it offers. I haven't played any multiplayer matches but even if I would've, there most likely wouldn't be any matches.
So here are my thoughts:
+ F.E.A.R 2 had worse A.I than in F.E.A.R but in F.E.A.R 3 A.I acts pretty similar compared to the first game, though it is hard to say if they are better or worse. Most people would've praised this aspect if only maps were more open.
+ Fettel playthrough: You can possess enemies and use their equipment, including tougher enemy variants and also use some sort of blast that knocks your enemies down. It offers some replay value if you want to play more.
+ Some story and gameplay ideas are actually interesting. I could go into detail in comments if you want to know more.
+ Melee is actually viable option unlike in other games where you sometimes strangely miss melee strikes.
+ Guns feel great, espcially in bullet time.
+ Sound design
+ Pretty stable and loading times are quick.
* The game takes weapons away from you multiple times but atleast it happens everytime interval ends so it is expected.
* Co-op missions:
* Pretty boring level system, but it's functional and achieving challenges is useful and somewhat enjoyable.
* Health regen is another thing from other shooters but due to it there doesn't seem to be any unfair moments. You know like, melee strikes and going to cover and all. If you disagree, it's fine.
- Very bland look. The game also hasn't dated well in graphics department.
- Lack of dark areas and lighting effects are dissapointing.
- Two weapon limit. This would be fine if previous games didn't allow to carry three weapons (four in F.E.A.R 2)
- Lack of weapons. There could've been more.
- No ability to blind fire from cover despite the fact that enemies can do this.
- Why reveal Point Man's face. First game didn't reveal it, because Point Man was YOU instead of some random generic white guy.
-
- Alma screams. They are not scary, but annoying.
- Level design: I don't know if it was Day 1 Studios or WB's idea but I wish game publishers would avoid COD style levels. They are limited and offer no exploration value. They also make artificial barrier, which include invisible walls, unrealistically blocked off areas and prevents you from backtracking by locking doors behind you.
- Hallucination and forced walking-sequences. ♥♥♥♥ them, they are not immersive and makes you feel like game controls your character instead of you controlling it.
- This game is FEAR, but it's not scary at all. Maybe one or two times I got spooked but thats it.
I've put this game into non-recommended status, because I think whether it is worth your time is up to you. I do think that this game is slightly better than F.E.A.R 2: Project Origin. Devs made changes that are a lot worse but for some reason, I enjoyed this more than 2. A lot of negatives and positives. I guess 5/10 would be pretty accurate rating for this game. Offers some fun (especially in Co-op) but as F.E.A.R game, it's really bad.
If you like F.E.A.R (2005) and F.E.A.R 2: Project Origin, I honestly don't know if you are going to like this or not. Some people like F.E.A.R 2: Project Origin more and some people like F.E.A.R 3 more. I'll leave this entirely up to you. If I missed something or you want me to add something important to my review, leave some feedback in the comment section below.

The story starts off with two scientist-type fellows known as Dr. Neil Watts and Dr. Eva Rosalene, employees of a mysterious corporation known as Sigmund Corp. They are specifically tasked with providing the elderly and sick with fulfilling lives before they die, by using the means of a certain memory-altering dream machine that allows them to rewrite their client's memory to fit their ordered specifications. Their client, an old, withering man known only by the name Johnny, has enlisted the help of these two scientists. His request, to become an astronaut and fly high into the sky, to reach the outer edge of the world and engage in a long-awaited rendezvous with the moon. Things go routine for a good while, until it appears that something is very wrong with Johnny's memory. Segmented and heavily disjointed, the mind of the elderly man seems to only connect via a single thread, memories of his deceased wife, River. You'll find along the way that she holds major significance to Johnny, much more than could be originally thought, but I'll leave the satisfaction to you.
Surely no game is great without some equally complementing gameplay. Whilst travelling through this cavalcade of emotions and memories, you'll have to deal with searching the man's memories and finding items that can link each piece together, like a grand cranium jigsaw puzzle. Mementos will be scattered about for you to interact and find, and engaging in absorbing the story from each memory is a must if you are to succeed. You'll have to go through some light puzzle elements in order to gain access to the linking power of the mementos, but it's nothing a little brain power can't fix. And even with all this brainiac gameplay, there are indeed moments of action. Remember that squirrel you narrowly dodged on the road? Well, I won't say much, but I can say that you surely haven't seen the last of him. You'll need to have a fighter's spirit, but keeping a shoe handy is about the same.
The game holds with it not only what you can gather from surface value, but it also carries underneath it a plethora of teachings and meanings. Now nothing I say here is set in stone, as you take what you will from the experience, but what I've collected from the game is as follows: One of the hardest things to do is to do nothing at all, that sometimes love will find us no matter where we are, and that strangers we meet can be the most interesting people we will ever get to know. These certainly aren't the only lessons to be drawn from this wonderful game, interpretation is a most beautiful thing. I leave the gorgeously complex teachings of this game to you to find, as making your own connections is supremely satisfying, and I'd be nobody to deny you the pleasure.
This game is definitely worth the priced listed. A fine game with charming graphics, a beautiful story, and a heart-rending conclusion that will leave you fully satisfied with your purchase. With the characters very fleshed out and unique, alongside the "worlds" you'd be visiting, not to mention the beautiful OST that'll be accompanying you, I'd give it a most well-deserved 9/10. Buy this game, love this game, remember this game.

Fallout 3 is an Open World, Post-apocalyptic, FPS RPG that I love to bits. Some may argue that Fallout 4 is better than this, but I have to disagree. I enjoyed this game more than I did Fallout 4, mostly because this game feels more like the RPG that the Fallout franchise is supposed to be, rather than something more alnog the lines of a Fallout setting, but a game that feels like a Borderlands game.
In Fallout 3, you escape from a vault, a nuke shelter. But, not any vault; this is Vault 101. You are out to find your dad, who went missing without reason, in a wasteland once called Earth. It is a great setting, and great story. However, my only complaint about this game is it's lack of color. The game is mostly gray, with vauge hints of colors here and there, but the game was just a little too pale. Well, that is a bit of a lie, for there are some colors that are clearly visible all through out the game, but compared to Fallout 4, this game is a bit pale. But, beside that, Fallout 3 has some great features, and is a long game, with hours of content.  one of my favorite features in Fallout 3 is VATS, which is where you can target certain enemies, in certain places, for more damage.The main story doesn't take that long; it took me 10 hours to beat the main story line. But, there are a LOT of side quests, that actually have a backstory, unlike games like Skyrim.
This game contains all the DLC for $15 less, so you already know that this is a good deal. The DLC themselves only activate after you beat the game. Well, that too is a lie. Only the Broken Steel DLC is activated after you beat the game. They are basically add-ons to the main story of the Fallout 3. And, the are really fun. but, they are also REALLY difficult. For example, one DLC mission has you go into a sewer, and that sewer is crawling with Deathclaws. And when I say crawling, I mean CRAWLING! Some DLC add on to the main plot of the story, and others are just plain fun to play. For example, one sends you into space to fight aliens, and another one sends you back in time. But, for Fallout 3 fans, this game definitly is the one to get over Fallout 3, mostly because you can save money by getting this one, rather than buying all the DLC's and vanilla Fallout 3. There are soo many new armors, weapons, and places featured in the DLC's, that make the game soo replay able. And if the replay ablity isn't enough for you guys, there are five DLC to play, each one unique from the rest. And they add sooo much more gameplay and hours spent playing the game, than just playing though the main story line, like I did. And if all the above don't sell you, in the DLC, you can controll a Deathclaw. Need I say more?
Overall, I REALLY like Fallout 3. It is my favorite game, even surpassing Skyrim. And, yes, I would recommend this over Fallout 4, for this game is better than the 4th, in my opinion. It just feels more like an RPG, which is what the Fallout franchise  is supposed to be. I recommend this game to everybody, whose parents will let them play it. Because war... War never changes.

The Uncertain: Episode 1 is a very unique game with beautiful level design, great music, interesting plot and immersive story. The amount of gameplay is somewhat short (maybe around 3-4 hours), but well worth the ride and the experience. The game does a great job of putting you in the shoes of the main character and making you really want to delve into this mystery that you're presented with. It really challenges you to think and explore in order to move forward. Most puzzles are pretty simple but are well varied and fairly fun to do. Dialogue options are mainly there to provide some backstory and give you relavent info rather than to affect the story with your choices. You do get some here and there, but for the most part the story feels unchanged regardless of your decisions. Whether these decisions will affect episode 2, I'm not sure. But I wouldn't be disappointed if they didn't. As some of us have seen with Telltale and other similar games, too many choices and variables makes the devs have to kill off characters and blend together plot in order to keep it going. Soundtrack and artbook are included free, so bonus points if you're into that sort of thing.
There are a few negative things about this game, but they're all very mild considering. Things like some spelling errors in subtitles, a couple cases of dialogue not entirely matching subtitles, some puzzles that require hearing (not a good thing for the deaf, hard of hearing or those simply without audio) to be able to do with no option to skip that I found, and some cases of slightly bad or oddly spoken english that can either be chalked up to robot-speak or, more likely, lost in translation with the voice actors. The game also has what feels like some poorly written sections of dialogue, some odd camera angles and controls and a lack of action sequences (even the ones it does have feel very calm). However, it seems the developers seem to really care about all the feedback from players and are addressing many of these issues in the next episode, which, while it's still a long ways away, is refreshing to hear.
I bought this game on sale but highly recommend it for the unique experience, great visuals and immersive story and interaction.

This is a short game (3h tops) that is more akin to Telltale's interactive stories than adventures (episodic nature included). Though the production quality is a level lower:
1. Level boundaries are, in many cases, are not disguised at all. You simply hit an invisible wall without any explanation whatsoever
2. "Puzzles" are overly simplistic, but tedious - in many cases you will need to go back and forth between locations just because your alter-ago in contrast to ordinary adventure rules will refuse to gather certain items until he knows what they are for (but he does it anyway in other cases). Other than walking around and searching for stuff there is no complexity - you do not even need to match objects in your inventory. Unlike telltale games there is not enough action to compensate that.
3. Controls are clusmy and, in many cases, are not well-though or play tested. Who though it would be a nice idea to ride a car through a forest with the camera pointing backwards? Controls are relative to the camera and you cannot control the camera, so it somewhat makes it even worse
Story is somewhat poorly written, but still intriguing, but it is way too early to tell, because there is not much of it to judge. But so far the good potential of the story and setting is somewhat underimplemented - performance is lacking, story "twists" are predictible, overall chain of events is predictible too. The whole concept of robotic world is rather underdeveloped (I think Primordia and The Fall are much better in exploring various parts of the topic, with Primordia obviously much closer to what they are trying to achieve, while being much more well-though and atmospheric).
TL;DR: Good potential, sloppy execution. I would suggest waiting for a few more episodes to come. If the developer will not raise production quality or improve writing, this is not worth it. Only recommending them because there is no "neutral" option

Turns out it's a really enjoyable and addictive game that runs great on my non-gaming work laptop. Sure there is a fair learning curve and you need to invest some time on YouTube to get your head around the games ebb and flow but there is a lot of depth to the game - the tech tree is enormous.

Stardock have announced Galactic Civilizations III, due for release some time in 2014 so I'm looking forward to checking that out while I play GC2.

Despite being classical, this is still one of the best turn-based 4X space strategy, developed by Stardock known for established reputation of developing great strategy games.
There're no other games with the same variety of strategic options as this game has.
You choose your race from 10 preset ones or create your own custom race, pick your political party with various bonuses and aim for victory on randomly generated galaxy through negotiations or wars with other races, you can also choose which victory condition so it's replayability is quite high!
There're so many options you can choose while playing, such as alignment of your civilization (good, neutral, evil), form of your government, and you can adjust your tax rate, the ratio of your government spending and its distribution to 3 categories : ship, building, research.
The most fun part is ship design, this allows you to create your own ship by combining various components!
You can also choose what type and how many of weapons or shields or engines to mount on your ship.
This game needs many requirements to declare war compared to other 4x games, which makes the game progress slower than other 4X titles, crush of civilizations begin around 100th turn.
The range your ship can travel from your friendly planets is determined by the amount and efficiency of life-support modules on your ship, which means you need to research better ones to colonize or invade further planets.
Turning citizens to colonists or soldiers for invasion means less workers and tax payers on your planet so you need enough population and your people's approval which affects planet's population growth rate for maintaining your economy.
Espiionage is also important to know which type of weapons and shields your enemies use.
Yes, interplanetary warfare costs so many resources including manpower...
The only annoying drawback is that it needs a Stardock account before activation...its old menu, interface and graphic aren't much concern for playing.
This is definitely a great strategy worthy playing.
Thanks to its tutorial and many players' guide, getting the rule isn't difficult.

This game is a highly in-depth. gritty, and realistic insight into the world of balloon warfare. Some claim that the bright colors and cartoony style give this game an air of nonsensical fun, but the fact of the matter is balloons, (or "bloons," as this game dumbs down for us) are remorseless killing machines that have not been stomped out quite yet.
It's easy to make fun of something like this when the balloon wars of 1956 are a thing of the past, but I, for one, still remember the days of terror, of uncertainty.
Those were days when you hid in your bunkers, not just to be safe from a rogue rainbow, but from the A.C.Es' (Aerial Combat Experts) wayward flying darts, or the explosions of mortar and missiles alike splattering the ground with half melted rubber.
Those were days when you were lucky to get anything to eat that wasn't your daily half-banana ration, as they needed the rest for the "war effort."
Those were days when the most common activity during free time was listening for that low drone over the sounds of explosions and plasma firing that heeded the approaching blimps.
I still remember Charlie, who sacraficed his own life to take down a rogue red balloon that had snuck past our "army"'s single 0-0 tack tower.
So this game is not some silly pastime, and it is not a joke. It is a look into the lives of not just soldiers, but civilians during one of our nation's greatest crises, and I for one, applaud this game for it. It doesn't hold back the grim truths of the balloon wars, and chooses instead to teach us our past mistakes, so we may never make them again.

The Good:
--- satisfying economic progression within villages
--- opportunities to build in-game communities
--- diplomacy as deep as you want it to be
The Bad:
--- absurdly imbalanced pay to win elements
--- game environment stacked heavily against less powerful players (e.g. frequent AI assaults that scale with the average power of players in an area and therefore demolish the least powerful players, repeatedly)
--- arbitrary caps on in-game communities that ensure most players remain irrelevant forever
--- high player turnover
--- flavorless combat
The Ugly:
--- instantaneous combat that creates a dogpiling META (i.e. sending coordinated simultaneous attacks with thousands of troops that all crash against the walls in a single realtime second) and gives zero opportunity for the defender to respond
--- lose days/weeks/months of work in the blink of an eye, probably while you're asleep
This game might appeal to you if:
--- you join with friends
--- you (very quickly) find an in-game community that you enjoy being a part of (for reasons other than simply as a means of staying alive)
--- you have more money than you know what to do with and enjoy throwing it at pixels on a screen
Since this won't apply to most people, I can't recommend this game.  That being said, I'm going to continue playing it, because I'm an idiot.

Skullgirls is a team-based fighting game set in its rather original world full of colourful characters, dark stories and general weirdness.
Using general premise of games like MvC, SG has rather conservative (in terms of numbers, at least) roster of rather diverse characters with quite a bit of options. Development team constantly works on the game, regularly patching bugs and other issues and - what's, perhaps, the most important part - constantly experimenting with existing characters in BETA build every SG player has access to. New characters are added every now and then and as of now, at least two are yet to be released in addition to a dozen of existing ones. If you have the game when those are released, you'll have them for free btw.
The game can be fast and complex enough for FG veterans to feel at home, while keeping basic inputs as simple as possible. Combined with very decent tutorials, it makes SG pretty welcoming to new players, including those not very familliar with competitive fighting games (even if it's probably not the simpliest FG to become average or better at, but it's understandable given it's premise). It can be pretty fun to play casually too, and it helps that visual style, while possibly repulsive at first glance to some people, is pretty creative and occasionally funny, can be pretty decent party game.
Basic idea (teams) of the game can be describled somewhat like this:
- You pick a team of 1-3 different characters, smaller team has more HP and damage per character;
- You control one of them while you can call others to assist you or to replace your "point character";
- Assist move is chosen before the game starts, it can be any of normal or special moves available to the character, plus every character has one move that is used specifically when she's called to make an entrance and stay.
- Fight until only one team has someone left standing.
It's simple, but can lead to rather deep gameplay - if you choose to go there, of course!
Would definitely recommend for gameplay, artstyle and for the fact that this game has developers' support that every fighting game should have in my humble opinion.

Alright, I think I've waited long enough. Time to get this off my chest. To put it short: this game is my new favorite game *gasp* Yeah, I know, kinda surprising after I gushed out all of my love for Dust an Elysian Tail, but honestly, it's true in this case. Ori is better than Dust.
Now, with the gist of it out of the way, let's dive into what makes this game great. I first heard about this game back during the first months of the Xbox One release, as I believe it was a launch title for the system. At the time, I thought it was a generic platformer or puzzle game with a spiritual, avatar-esque fantasy world setting, so I paid no attention to it. It was a couple weeks ago that I noticed it on Steam, and actually saw that it was a metroidvania. Metroidvanias, for the ill-informed, are subgenres in which the player starts out weak, but gradually gains new abilities, which can both aid the player in combat AND promote further exploration in large, semi-open landscapes (I say semi because you are still set to one path from point A to point B), good examples of which are, as the title says, Metroid and Castlevania. Ever since I played Dust, I have been on quite a Metroidvania marathon. I have so far played the likes of Quacamelee, Wings of Vi, Shantae and the Pirate's Curse, among others, all of which I have enjoyed. Anyway, given my adoration of Metroidvanias, I decided to buy the game and give it a go.
I certainly don't regret that.
I honestly do not want to give the full story. Every moment of it is either really sad or really memorable. To put it in the most spoiler-free way possible, you play as Ori, a drop of light in the shape of a lemur-like creature, who is called by the Spirit tree to restore the light lost to a large owl named Kuro. To do this, you must restore power to three elemental stones throughout the land, gaining new abilities passed down by deceased light forms. This is as much of the story as I can say without giving anything major away. It's best seen for yourself how it progresses.
A good story doesn't matter if a game doesn't play well. Thankfully, Ori has good gameplay in spades. The gameplay consists of platforming and fighting mechanics, along with a few puzzles sprinkled in. Defeating enemies drops EXP that, when filled up, will turn into an ability point. Ability points can be spent at restore points (that you make yourself, BTW), to upgrade certain attributes, such as the potency of health and mana drops, attack power, as well as the ability to see certain things on your map. You are able to go through the game without spending them (which is an achievement), though the upgrades you can get in the long run can prove useful when combined with powers you get in the game. Speaking of the powers, they incredibly fun to use. You have your basics, like a wall jump, a double jump, and a ground slam, but you also get some really kickass ones like a super jump, a catapult power that let's you fling yourself off of enemies and most projectiles, and the ability to run on walls, which really helps in many parts of the game. Exploration is also fun. While the map does seem large, you can get to places fairly quickly once you know your way around and when you have the right abilities. It becomes extremely satisfying when you find a hidden area that leads to a health or mana increase, or even an extra ability point that lets you power up faster. It's just as satisfying to complete difficult puzzles or get past hard battles thanks to the powers you gain.
The only complaints I have are the lack of boss battles and inability to continue upon completion. When you complete the story of the game, you are sent back to the menu, and are locked out of that save file, meaning anything you forgot to collect before entering the final dungeon (which is a point of no return), becomes impossible to get unless you play the game again. This is quite a kick in the groin if it's your first playthrough, since you think you can just go back in and collect what you missed. I understand in the case of how the saving system works, but I'm sure there was another way of doing that. As for boss battles, there isn't any in the entire game. While there are a few tough enemies to fight along the way, there are no large bosses, not even one of Kuro, the main antagonist. However, the game does make up for it with the exciting escape sequences when you complete a dungeon, as they do a good job of testing your skill with the abilities you gain on your adventure.
One last thing, the music. Is there really anything to say other than I have the soundtrack that I legally purchased playing in the background as I type this? The soundtrack is awesome! Easily topping my favorite OSTs. Each track is played at just the right moment, and with just the right mood to go with the scenery. If there is anything I recommend buying, it's the soundtrack, if not the game itself.
Overall, Ori and the Blind Forest can now be classified as the best game I've played. Great story, awesome gameplay, amazing soundtrack, everything blends into one grand package that any metroidvania or platformer fan can enjoy. I highly recommend it.
Rating: 9.5/10

Ori excels in places that go beyond the medium of videogames with it's soundtrack and amazing art style. As a game, it simply deserves a place as one of the greatest games of all time.
The characters, the environments, the setting and sounds portray a wonderful story, although somewhat simplistic, that works perfectly with the design of the game. Each character conveys an archetype that works both as a narrative element, but also as a mechanic element for gameplay purposes. Which leads to the fact that Ori's top notch fine tuning controls makes it a blast to play through the game. Unfortunately completionists might get frustrated by the fact that some secret pickups are tied to the story and might not be reachable after some point. and there's no way to revisit the file of a game that has been completed.
But, even so, anyone who plays and enjoys any platformer game, especially in the realm of metroidvanias, needs to know Ori and The Blind Forest, as it is one of the greatest games of all time.

A game about making games by a studio who made this as there first game.
Damn...that's seriously meta.
You play (player name here), an indie developer and designer who is making games out of his garage. You also appear to own a DMC DeLorean with a Mr. Fusion strapped to the back. Your job is basically to mix an dmatch different genres, topics, and platforms to make successful games. As you go you research more additions you can make to your games, such as multiplayer support or voice acting.
The game is quirky, but good ;) It feels like the developer is not only trying to make a wonderful tycoon game, but also write a narritive on how hard it is to work in the game industry. One or two bad games can absolutely bankrupt you, even with a massive back catalogue of popular games, especially when you get your first office.
While the platforms are released in their respective months and years compared to their real world counterparts, I think that the arbitrary way you unlock more researchables for game design is a fault. I personally would have preferred to unlock them through research, not by developing games. Each researched item leading to a few others, like a research tree immediately so that you don't have to release games without features that should clearly be available to a specific platform simply because you haven't released a game or done a game report.
All in all, I adore this little gem, and for anyone who likes tycoon games and wants to live along side the evolution of gaming platforms, or live out their dreams of being a game dev super star, I cannot suggest this game enough.

Alright, for my first review :P
Bethesda did a pretty good job in transporting Interplay's Fallout series to the 3D age with Fallout 3. I bought the Game of the Year Edition which includes Fallout 3 plus all of it's DLCs but in the end I only played the main quests (Broken Steel included), Point Lookout and Operation Anchorage and then moved to Fallout NV.
The Fallout 3 main game got me entertained for almost a whole month. It presents the player with a ''lore-rich'' post-apocalyptic world with countless possibilities for character development and creation. The main quests are entertaining, sure, but the side quests were what made my eyes freeze on the screen to find out more about the story of the Capital Wasteland. Galaxy News Radio's music gets quite dull after you've heard it for the millionth time but Bethesda makes up for that with a good spirited DJ who hell knows what a disk is.
Broken Steel adds to that story (AND HAS A HUGE AMERICAN ROBOT WHICH SHOOTS LASERS AT FICTIONAL COMMUNIST SCUM, HOW COOL IS THAT???) and is certainly a DLC worth buying.
Point Lookout presents the player with a whole new region for him/her to explore with new mutants and a nice main quest, although once again, it was the side quests that caught my attention. Definitely a DLC worth buying.
Molly, Operation Anchorage was the DLC whose main quest I most wanted to play AND was the one which I most hated during and after I played it. It's Bethesda ♥♥♥♥♥♥ attempt at making a Call of Doody style shooter. It did feel like a whole new game to me, one that made me slam my head to my keyboard twice in disgust over the half made story and enraging gameplay. SoTA is much better than some of these very emotive reviews suggest. It's not there yet by some distance, but in recent patches it has started to shape up and you can now begin to see what the Devs are after and it should be a solid and very deep story driven game in the long run with plenty of moody ambience.
The Dev's took a huge risk releasing a pre-Alpha product (that's Alpha not Beta), and I guess it was optomistic in these times of instant gratification to expect folks to grasp that SoTA isn't actually a fully playable game, but rather a 'Proof of Concept' against which you can consider investing your money and time if you like the vibe and if you do invest, you are encouraged to contribute towards its development.
I think also some folks are having a bit of an issue with their expectations. SoTA is intentionally fairly unforgiving by the standards of mass produced MMOs these days and somewhat old school in that there is very little hand holding. You are expected to work things out for yourself, which when you do is gratifying. After several months I myself have just worked out how to grind experience properly(!) and so now I'm having a much more satisfying time preparing my Avatar for the main quest lines.
The Devs have been honest. There is plenty of information warning and informing people about what theyre getting into if they buy. People don't seem to be reading before they commit and the subsequent ranting and indignation  is sadly missrepresenting the product in some of these early access reviews.
If you are at all intrigued by SoTA, I would recomend you dig a little deeper into both the reviews and background info on the product. Ive ticked the recommend box, but its a very personal choice and not cut and dried. This is no cut and paste MMO for the masses. You have to put effort in to get reward out, but as is often the case in such situations, the reward is sweeter.

This is a very well done puzzle solving platformer, and it also has metroidvania aspects where you get new powers and can go to places you couldnt go to before. The platforming is superb, you move quickly and have fluidly. I would compare this game mostly to the new Rayman game, having similar artsyles and nearly identical movement. The only flaws i can see so far is that all the projectiles in the game have no indication of them being projectiles, and blend in with pickups like health and experience, and i often time get hit by something i didnt even see. Another thing i didn't quite enjoy is that alot of the traps in the game are instant death. When you die you respawn instantly to the last waypoint you set, and you can set enough of them to save after every puzzle or challenge. The only problem is, i usually dont save everytime i enter a room, and run forward to hit an unskippable cutscene, to be instantly killed 2 seconds later and now i am all the way back to where i began. The cutscene plays every time, and some of the instant kill traps are very hard to dodge. Some instant kill traps didn't even look like a trap, and i ended up running into it and dieing after clearing a frustrating challenge only to go back and redo it. The only solution is to get good which is not a bad thing at all. The story is nothing to write home about, but its enough to get the job done. Its hard to get a good story where isn't a focus on speech, but there is one nonetheless, and it is not a bad one at that.
TLDR
Pros:
-Quick, fluid, easy to learn movement and platforming
-Amazing art
-Orchestrated Soundtrack (although alot of it is ambient)
-Challenging Gameplay
Cons (very minor nitpicks):
