The 1980’s Gauntlet characters return in this new era of gaming: Thor the warrior, Thyra the valkyrie, Merlin the wizard and Questor the elf. Each one having their own progression called masteries. As you chop down, skewering, obliterating or sniping foes, the character becomes stronger overtime, even awarded in death too! Relics, a new feature, activated by potions, have different effects on oneself or enemies. Having it on the right the character can make all the difference in heat of battle. The voice acting is a neat touch and nicely done for the characters to feel more lively, especially Questor’s having a Scottish accent.
Unfortunately, the biggest letdown of the game is the length… it’s short. Finished roughly about five hours on the second hardest difficulty. After completing the game, the repetitiveness is harsh because you’ll be playing the same dungeons again, again and again. At that point, you’ll be increasing the character’s masteries. Still, it declines interest and the replay value quite fast.
The developers no less stuck true to the 1980’s Gauntlet feel. With its amount of content and shortness of the game, it’s going to be hard to love the game. I still recommend the game if your looking for some good old hack ‘n’ slash cooperative fun.
And remember… don’t destroy the food.

Prepare to die.  Often.  Very, very often.  Even on "Easy".
And, (SPOILERS) in the second level, you get to run from Death Incarnate while roaming a labyrinth that changes every time you retry the level.
You can't grind for XP or levels, but every hit or destruction or manner of death is progress toward various achievements, some of which are reflected on Steam.  The in-game achievements earn you bonuses and assistances, which eases some frustrations if you manage to unlock them.
While the Warrior, Valkyrie, and Elf all get four attacks, the Wizard, my usual favorite Gauntlet class, is stuck with a Magicka-style element combo magic system.
Unlike other Gauntlet games, you can't throw or activate potions for various effects against enemies.  The only potions you get are boosts for relics -- which are not attainable early in the game.  You do have keys to unlock progress, food to replenish health, enemy generators to destroy, and things to interact with.
Worse, while Gauntlet is optimized for gamepads, it only recognizes certain advanced ones with XInput, and not my older but very serviceable Logitech Dual Action gamepad.  I prefer not to use the keyboard, especially for movement purposes.   While I can map the keyboard commands to the gamepad, I am then stuck with the mouse target cursor.
Oh, and the opening tutorial forces you to go through all four classes and successfully kill with their moves.
Good things:
It looks good.  Characters and enemies are a bit tiny compared to other 3D dungeon crawlers.
Voice acting and writing are good, with nice bits of humor.
My verdict:  If you think you can handle the insanity, great.  Otherwise, stay away.

It's not what people thought it would be, but knowing what it really was before I started playing it, I had a different set of expectations. Here's what it's not:
- It is not a game based on the sheer wonder of exploring worlds that are varied and unique and all of them look interesting.
- It is not a game that has a deep story and lore
- It is not a game that gets everything right (inventory is a giant mess)
Here's what this game IS:
- It's a mostly relaxing game that you probably won't play for hours on end, but it does scratch a very unique itch when you're in the mood for it.  Even people that seem to talk the most amount of crap about this game will still occasionally be seen logging on to play it.  If it's really that bad, you wouldn't return to it.
- It's a game that has frustrating combat, annoying inventory, and a lot of things not going well, but for a small independent studio, this is an incredibly ambitious game that does get alot of things right as well.  It's fun to poke fun of the flaws, it's easy comedy.
Bottom line... if your expectations are low and you just want a moderatly fun space game with some decent freedom and atmosphere, No Man's Sky is a great time killer that certainly justifies the price if it's on sale for $30 or less.  Is it worth the stubborn $60 price tag it still demands?  Absolutely not.  In a game this "big", there's really not enough there to justify the price tag when there are games out there that deserve that price point for both quality and sheer number of hours of enjoyment to be had.
In all honesty, this game is a decent game. I don't think it is worth the $60 but it definitely will be, we just have to give the devs time to add more things to make this game more complete.

This game follows two /or perhaps just one) inmate in a post-Sovjet Russian mental asylum. Patryev and Matovsky, their real names unknown, are completely, 100% clinically insane. Schizofrenic to the brain-stem; they believe that they are in fact handymen in the Czech countryside, helping what is only vague after-images of people they once knew.
That is the story, as far as I know, as anything else goes unmentioned in the game itself.
Now, if that doesn't draw you in, there are three more things I'll take a look on: Gameplay, Audio, and Video. Oxford comma for added effect. And readability.
They claim that "...gamers will enjoy original approaches and non-typical puzzle solving." I guess that is enjoyable. If it is true. The only way the puzzle-solving is intuitive in the matter they claim, is by being completely nutjob insane. An example; in the first puzzle, that I'll samelessly inform you I didn't manage to solve, due to reasons I'll come back to later, one of the two (I don't know which, they never tell) punctures his car-tyre, while driving to gods-know-where. They then decide to follow some weird plan they found on the ground, and saw their own fence in half with some chainsaw just lying on the ground, most likely rusted to the very core, and turn a tree into a non-functional crane with the planks. I won't spoil too much, and I can't spoil either, since I haven't played much further, but apparently there is some kind of DYI minigolf-course later on, as well as dressup-minigames. Cool!
Either way, my game bugged out, and one of the two stood still, lifting and putting down a brick floating two metres behind him, and in the end the level ended up unfinishable. By that point I was on the verge of passing out (from laughing), so I quit. The humor is there.
The audio in the game consists solely of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ sounds for the chainsaws and cars and murder-weapons and whatnot, as well as the worlds most anoying ever-looping jazz-pop soundtrack. That's to say, they leave about twenty seconds of nothing in between the overly cheerful tunes, possibly only to spite. It's absolutely horrible to listen to in the long run, and I'll confess that it's likely one of the major reasons for my forthcoming suicide.
Finally, the visuals. I have to say, this is probably the best part of the whole game (You hear that, CoD-boys‽). That, sadly, doesn't say overly much in the game's favour. Now, I have never seen "...the popular TV series..." that is "...well known in many countries all over the world." (The Czech Republic) I have quite simply never had the chance; I have never heard of it before. Therefore, I can't tell if the game features "The very same Pat and Mat you know from your TV."
However, after some quick Google'ing, I can tell you that the Czech in the game is way of, and that the visuals are as well.
Overall, I recommend this game to everyone who can't decide if they want to kill themselves, as well as "Casual players..." who "...will like the humor and easy-to-use controls..." (That's a lie, by the way.
Seriously, though, ♥♥♥♥ this game.

This is a very fun indie RPG.  It's light hearted, cheeky dialogue and enemies are very memorable and endearing.  I've played it through 4 full times and haven't gotten sick of it yet.
Pros:
- The music is unbelievably good.  Phyrnna (the composer) is up there with the best in the business.  While the game is great, the single most impressive aspect is the music.
- The underlying battle system is very well balanced and expansive.  Tons of skills, summons, items, weapons, variety and it also works well.  You don't find yourself having to rely on the same tactic over and over.  Different enemies require different tactics.
- The dialogue is really enjoyable.  Many, many hilarious lines in this game.
- Nice variety of achievements to add replay value.
- Characters have strong personalities and are very unique.  Quite memorable.
- Puzzles are fun, not too common and well designed.
- The game itself is nicely designed and does a good job of rewarding you for searching for secrets (hidden treasures and stuff, nothing super important)
Cons:
- Can feel a bit grindy at times especially when you get to the battles that have 3 waves.  Fortunately amazing music is there to take the edge off.
- Not enough reason to utilize your 4th character.  It's too easy to just park Lance in the back up slot and never use him.  He's a fun character, but Anna is the better support character since she has access to the party defense up and reflex up buffs.  Lance just can't keep up with her and thus gets overlooked for important battles.
Overall:
This is unquestionably a fun, well made game.  The game knows what it is trying to be and pulls it off extraordinarily well.  Kupo Games is a one man, independent studio who puts out high quality games at good prices.  For the price, this game is a no brainer.  I couldn't recommend it more strongly!

Worst game I've played in three years(around 120 games completed in between).
I played the first Fear game when it launched and had a mixed opinion. Replaying it a couple of years ago didn't do any good and I felt that although the gameplay was still quite nice, the actual game didn't offer much original content to me to waste any more time with it. The expansion packs were a lot worse, but the second game somewhat uplifted the series. Yet comparing this game to the other parts of the series or just any other FPS, this is by far one of the most disgusting pieces of gaming you could do on your own.
I must say in the games defence, that I felt that this could've been a tad better with co-op. It feels like it's more or less designed to be played as co-op rather than single player. Nevertheless, the game offers single player and I'm reviewing that part of the game.
Short synapsis of the game. The protagonist is now again the same from the first game, the anonymous and mute 'Pointman'. Not very interesting character to begin with and there's not much progress in his story here. Apparently he and his brother, the antagonist from first game Paxton Fettel, are on a mission. Their mission is to kill the protagonist, Becket, from the second game, who was♥♥♥♥♥♥♥by their mother, Alma. They also want to kill their offspring or their mother, not sure what was their primary plan. His brother is some sort of wraith or the like, who can occasionally do stuff in cut-scenes but doesn't actually appear in game. The game ends on a rather hilarious scene where the game counts your score and compares it to Fettels score and then you win. No surprise that the character who only appeared in cut-scenes didn't rank up many points. Makes sense in Co-op, not much in single player.
The game is divided into 8 intervals, lasting from 10 minutes to 30, so the game's lenght is a tad under 4 hours solo. Rather short but most likely the main reason I completed this.
The intervals are not very connected, the character just pops into another totally different looking section of the city. The level design is yet again beyond boring. If you need any reference, just think of any Counter Strike clone, and add some candles and blood just about everywhere. That's about it. The Environment is very static, the levels are very crammed and really short. I'm not sure who though that overexcessive spattering of blood and hundreds of candles are scary or in any way related to the contents of the game.
The lackluster level design is not helped by the enemies that most of the time keep spawning from thin air or from behind closed doors. You mostly encounter (yet again) masked enemies, robots and zombies. Boring enemies were a problem in the first game but in this game they feel even more dull. This is not helped by the fact that most of the time you have to listen to this nonsense military radio chatter: "Whiskey tango actual, bing bong order, ding dong negative". Though they never reveal how or why you listen to this, but I think the contemporary success of 'modern warfare' games had something to do with it.
Although the game works quite well, it also has some bugs that prevented going forward and I had to reload the most recent checkpoint.
In the end the game is just weird shooting lane. You go forward / Fetter mumbles something about destiny and power/ military mumbo jumbo on radio / go through 10 rooms with excessive amount of candles and text written vertically with blood / Alma appears behind a window / more military mumbo jumbo and boring enemies appear out of thin air, cut scene and mission over. On to the next.
Don't waste your time, not to mention money.

The first game is without a doubt a classic shooter, with great intense action and really creepy levels. The second was not quite as great as the first, adding a new protagonist and taking away a few of the scares, but still felt like a worthy sequel. What I dislike most about the third installment is that is does not bring the horror that I liked from the first and second game. At one point you have a shoot out in broad daylight in a brazilian favela, it just did not feel right.
The controllable armoured power suits or mechs from the second game return and again just take away from the horror/thiller experience I don't want to feel like a bad a$$ in F.E.A.R I want to feel vunerable and scared.
Overall though, putting aside the fact its basically a military shooter with some light horror elements F.E.A.R 3 is a fun shooter, you can't deny that and I appreciate that we got to revisit some of the original characters again and get a decent ending... sort of. I would not really reccommend it unless you are a massive fan of the first two.

The camera is the most frustrating thing about this game. The camera is more deadly than any of the mobs. In a game where there are ranged heroes and melee heroes, your ranged heroes are obviously going to want to stay a good distance away from danger, So what does this do for anyone playing a melee hero? It literally forces them to not be able to see anything. Wizard/elf will want to keep distance, but you can't keep distance, but you can't get close because you can't see a ♥♥♥♥ing thing. Another issue is when the camera moves because someone is pressing along the side of the screen, any aiming devices are instantly pushed in the direction of the camera, making skillshots hard to land.
The second problem is depth. The last gauntlet I truly remember had more depth. You got gold via the levels which were spend on a variety of stats. There were secrets that lead to unlocking new characters. There were combination attacks, specials that ran on a turbo meter, so what do you get in the new Gauntlet? Relics, which cost money and have several tiers of upgrades. Now this sounds like it could be cool, but it's not. Like in lord of the rings, there is one to rule them all, and it's super fancy ability is healing and forcing the mobs to ignore you. The biggest problem with the relics though, is how they're implemented. You don't do damage to build a meter to use them or anything of the sort, you find potions that are always in the same place every level and are scripted into the levels. That's all you have to spend gold on. Oh wait, there's items? They don't do anything, they change how you look, and by the time you unlock them you'll be bored. The only other way to increase the power of your character is done through grinding. And some of the objectives are utterly mind-boggling. Want to take 35% less damage from spikes? Well let them kill you of course! Want to have a lower freeze duration? Well die when you're frozen! Nothing that I've seen so far indicates that any of the bonuses are rewarding, they're just grinding. Want to heal a bit more from food? Eat lots of it. God forbid something along the lines of clearing an act without eating a single piece of food could of been used, give the game a little replayability. Most of the upgrades are utterly inconsequential in any case. 1% damage boost, still 1 hitting everything with a power attack or two hitting with a weak attack, it makes no difference.
Level variety:
This is the big issue with the game. Everything looks the same, even the levels follow the same pattern. Random level -> Level with death -> fight a large group of spawners. Everything kind of looks the same too, the monsters feel the same, the special monsters are just repeated over and over. The first real boss is kind of interesting, it tries to incorporate a 'don't stand in the fire' mmo mechanic, but it's so sparsely used it basically feels like the rest of the previous levels. Kill the spawners, you'll be killing a lot of spawners, and they'll have little to no variety in what they spawn.
On to the smaller problems:
Gold. I'm repeating myself a bit, but the issue above was more about how little character customization there was. This is just about the gold. You want to collect it. But after you get a maxed relic it serves no purpose at all. And the ability to hold two relics is utterly pointless since A. Situationally you will always want to use the one which makes things ignore you since the only thing dangerous in the game is trying to kill spawners without being swarmed. B. And more importantly, relic use is capped by how many potions you have, and potions are capped to the level you're on. If a turbo system was used where dealing damage charged your relics, this would be different, but you'll always without any fail want to use the song.
Graphics. They look nice, but they're bland. Repetitive. Much like the design of the game, so I guess it fits. It's also very easy to get lost on the screen because the colors look, I don't know, washed out? There isn't enough pronounciation of the colors around your characters. Even worse is losing your cursor in the storm of things spawning, spells casting, ascerbated by a good wizard who floods the screen with alternating fireballs/chain lightnings/slow fields. If you're ranged it's not a big deal, but any melee character will find themself using abilities off key which can be dangerous.
The positives:
The feel. It felt like a gauntlet game, albeit a step backwards from previous versions I've played(namely in the gamecube/ps2/xbox era), which is a disappointment. A few changes to the gameplay and how the game functions would make this a 5/5 game for me and my friends.
The jokes. Specifically the little random quips characters will say about things and the taunts when someone dies, the first time you hear them they're pretty entertaining.
In conclusion, I give it a 2/5. It's boring and repetitive, a big step back from the gauntlet games I played in my childhood, and a disappointment from a developement standpoint. The biggest issue is the camera. We're not all sitting around the same screen, let us have our own screen, it would instantly push this game up a whole point from my perspective.

I found out about this game in August of 2016, the week before the (actual) release. Therefore my review isn't influenced by all the hype and anticipation, and thus all the disappointment, from the launch.
I clicked "Yes" that I do recommend it, but I kind of need a neutral. I don't recommend paying $60 for it, but I have recommended the game. It's worth more like $20 in the current state.
There are a lot of bugs: ships falling through launch pads, whenever I teleport back to base I have to restart the game. There are a lot of balance issues: I can't find some resources that I need, but I keep finding traders selling things that are far more rare. And there are interface issues: I can't see below the ship to know where to land, the interface is really clunky and it's easier to press a key to switch inventory views than it is to click and hold for the right amount of time. There's just a lot of things that don't seem to be well-thought.
But with that being said, I continue to play it and I like it. I don't play first person shooters, my game of choice is Minecraft. Of course that makes my opinion less valuable to a lot of gamers, and I'm ok with that. But for what it is, space exploration, time wasting, wander around procedurally generated planets (and my graphics card is not good enough so I had to lower the quality, it's still pretty) ... it's just enjoyable. In normal mode there's some difficulty without having to really try very hard. That's what I prefer out of a game.
So I recommend it, but only if you just want to goof around and only if you get it on sale.

I've waited a while to post a review for this.  Wanted to collect my thoughts on it.  After having watched the drama of this game's release unfold, I'm convinced that there are in fact,
No Man's Skys.
1. The game 'the hype' promised- and never delivered
2. The game that fifty-thousand raging neckbeards can't seem to stop despising
As I wasn't on the hype train (I bought the game shortly after the Foundation Update), and I'm not especially prone to groupthink or fits of unreasoning rage either, I'll try to address that third game- because I
think gaming journalism is messed up.
I just happen to
think that the primary dysfunction has essentially become a difference of extremes.
Which is another way of saying:
Not- mind you- that I don't think that what happened with 'the hype' isn't reprehensible.  It is.
On the other hand I also think it's unfortunate in the sense that there
an audience for a game like this.  It's probably a far smaller one than the hype generated, but it's also probably larger than the wave of hate that followed it's release (that
to follow the release) allows for.
So what is that third game?  Well, it's an atmospheric exploration game with crafting and some survival elements.
It has some action, but it's not an action-oriented game.
It has some survival elements- but this isn't "hardcore"in that regard and I don't see it ever being.
It's got some crafting elements- but the list ins't tremendously expansive and the flow isn't necessarily... optimized.
It's set in space- replete with different races, lore for those races, factions and so on- but it's not a free-form Mass Effect, no.
What it does well is it's sense of ambience and atmosphere, while giving you a little of all of the above things.  Some might find this boring (and even I tire of it from time to time), but I don't think that the mere fact that you can be bored with a game necessarily makes it a bad game.
This isn't a game for everyone- as I think I said above.  But if you think you might find the idea of exploring a vast-
universe for a bit, while occupying yourself with gathering and cataloguing things, you might enjoy playing this game.
I know I have.
One thing I will absolutely agree with most of this game's detractors on is the price (at least the $60 one used at release).

That puts it in a similar category with a lot of other games like it.
So, if you do get it, wait for a sale- definately.  But again, keep in mind  that there's a lot of nonsense surrounding the game's release.  It's easy to avoid the over-hyping of the game nowadays since it's out and we've got plenty of it's features catalogued and we know what the game is and isn't.
But it's still easy to fall victim to the rage train still following the game.  Make your own decision.  Don't let anyone else (including me) tell you what to buy.
It's space exploration.

This review is coming at a time when most people who would play To The Moon have already done so. So what can I say that would convince somebody to buy this game? That's not the purpose of this review.
To The Moon is a rare production. With graphics and interface that would, by today's "next gen" standards, be considered far outdated or perhaps even backward, To The Moon still manages to break through the hearts of so many of its players. You could say that To The Moon is also not a challenging or difficult game. But it IS challenging and difficult, in its way. I'll explain later.
For now, the basics. The basic premise is that you play, interchangably, a pair of doctors who work for a company whose speciality is traversing the memories of its clients at the point at which they are dying, so that they can then rewrite those memories in order to have their clients fulfill a dying wish. To The Moon is really easy to grasp gameplay wise. Made in RPG Maker, the game uses a standard "isometric" viewpoint popularized by RPG's in the 1990's. Gameplay elements are limited to an object-hunt across the memory your characters are traversing, plus an additional picture puzzle that follows a traditional "flip square to complete" format.
The visual art of the game is crisp and at times quite beautiful, but not spellbinding in any sense. You can tell the developers worked hard on the pixel art, though. Nothing stands out as terribly constructed.
But we have to dispense with these elements of presentation. Well, that is to say, presentation wise, the game is "good." It WORKS, knowing what it is and its limitations, it does its best to present the world it wants to create and the story it wants to tell, and it genuinely succeeds in that endevour.
But then, it's the story where this game takes its place in the halls of, honestly, one of the best games ever created. Using this pixel art and limited, yet consequential, gameplay, To The Moon gets at the heart of so many sublime questions. What is the nature of truth? What is the nature of memory...of love? of memories of those whom we love? What matters the most in our brief existence in this life? How does memory function in the construction of the real?
To The Moon is perfectly paced and impeccably constructed on a narrative level. The writing AND gameplay are done in such a way that connect you intimately to the characters in the story. At the close of the game, you legitimately love all of them. And it's a rare experience that can deliver that to you.
The music? Oh my god, the music. Kan Gao, the main developer of this game, is also the composer of most of the music. And, in a way, the music is a character of its own. Gao's talent is apparent from the very beginning, as the menu opens with what will become an iconic theme throughout the game. There is so much care and love in the music of this game. There are no throwaway themes or repetitive, ear-worm tracks. You find yourself emersed in the musical experience as much as the gameplay and narrative experience.
Is this game "challenging" and "difficult?" Not in the way you may think. The game will challenge your perceptions of reality, your thoughts about love and loss, your idea of what is true and worthwhile. Is it "difficult?" The game will leave you shattered, emotionally. There are times in the game that are honestly "difficult" to sit through. There are times when you become so overwhelmed that you actually forget that you are NOT part of this story.
To The Moon is a work of art that will live in the annals of gaming for...well, for as long as gaming remains a form of artistic interaction. There are not enough things to say about this game that will live up to the impact it will render on the generations of gaming to come.
If you haven't played this game, anyone who is an enthusiast of this medium will, in 10 years time, ask you why the hell you haven't.

"The Uncertain: Episode 1 - The Last Quiet Day" is an episodic adventure game set in a post-apocalyptic world.
You are playing as engineer robot, which is very curious about humans and their life. He will be drawn into dangerous mission which have a really deep plot.
Graphics are really good, music and sounds are amazing and the story is very addictive.
To be honest I just couldn't stop playing. I didn't care how long this episode will take, I just needed to know what will happen next.
I can't wait for more episodes and I recommend to buy this game :)
interesting story. looking forwards next episode.

Bottom Line: Buy it for the story and art, know that you will be enduring the gameplay, hope that the next episodes will learn from this episode's mistakes.
You are on a quest as a robot who has stumbled upon a mystery the involves all of mechanical kind! With every 'level' you meet new robots, explore what's left of human remnants, and solve puzzles to achieve objectives. There are many different types of gameplay in this episode from fixed camera movement to driving along a fixed path while avoiding obstacles, to a 3rd person 'swivel camera' that allows you explore your environment freely.
WARNING: STARTING CRITIQUE RANT -
What the game does right is the art, story, and attention to detail. I can tell that the dev team put all eggs into the design and concept basket. The reason I say this is the environment looks expansive, detailed, and movie-like BUT there are invisible walls everywhere.
Wanna cross the street? You cant
Wanna see what's further down the way? nope
Finally, during 'solve puzzle by fetching item' quests you may (or may not) see an item that stands out. However, unlike similar games where you can pick up the item and use later, your character makes a comment about how he doesn't need it right now. Typically this item is on another floor, forcing you to travel distances to reach that particular item ONLY when you need it. This was unnecessary and felt like game completion time buffering.
Hopefully the next episode will make less of these mistakes and I look forward to what the story will hold!

I made it into the slum area before asking myself the touchstone question: "am I enjoying myself"? Answer was a big fat "no", and it all just felt like a chore. When a game feels like hard work it's time to cut your losses.
It's worth saying that I only play single player mode.
The shortfalls of the 3rd instalment have been documented comprehensively elsewhere, but for me the killers were:
* Can't turn off head bob (= motion sickness)
* Waves of quite hard-to-kill opponents. In FEAR 1 & 2, you knew you had 3 or 4 in each squad to tackle.
* 2 weapons only
* Pointless "psychic links". Why am I collecting these? For co-op I think.
* Poor, blurry environments.
I normally take "save your money" advice as a challenge and prefer to make my own mind up, but I think in this case : "save your money".

Great little game, it's got a ridiculous amount of adjectives. You can spawn an evil version of yourself that randomly creates things to see how advanced it is, you'll see things like "noctophilic haystack" or "serendipitous pho." They use lots of playtesters to see what solutions people would come up with so that combined with lots of items fitting into similar categories means that most puzzles have an incredible amount of solutions. Spawn a pregnant man and a midwife and you'll get a thin man and a baby man, for example. I don't know how that helps solve puzzles, but there's a lot of dynamic events that pop up. It's worth a look and you can buy it, get a feel for it and return it within 2 hours if you don't like it. That's more than enough time to see what the game is like and whether you want to keep playing, after the opening cutscene and tutorial, you're essentially thrown into the game and have all your abilities. The only downside is the Steam Workshop, which is really cool. Lots of... interesting things there but the only way I've found it to work is that you have to subscribe to things from the game itself, that's the only way it would load what you want. I would've also liked to be able to use downloaded models for the character selector but I suppose the detailed character creator is a more configurable tool. Still, it's nigh impossible to pick Jango Fett or Samus as your character unless you know what you're doing.

I'm a long time Ultima Online player and when this game was announced, I did back the game through Kickstarter.  Knowing that this game was being developed by many of those that brought us Ultima Online, I was expecting a new game but hoping for a lot of mechanics (housing, crafting, etc) that I was introduced to in UO.
This game is NOT Ultima Online.  It is different but you get the sense of UO in it.
That being said, I knew from day one (3/8/16) that housing was important.  House size and location is very important if you want to make and sell things.  This is why I backed the project.  To be honest, logged in two or three times over the past three years but didn't play heavily.  Once they announced persistence, I logged in and went about the world and started to play.
I've been on since late August 2016 and I've logged over 400 hours now in the game.  In the beginning it is very hard to start out.  It took a bit to understand the mechanics and once that was learned, understanding the leveling system and what to do took some effort.
You cannot play this game successfully right now, it is Alpha, unless you use these resources:
1. Discord - this is the prominent chat system between players.  If you have friends in the game or are in a guild, then group chat is viable.
2.
- This site has the most complete map of the lands and you will abuse it until you know your way around.
3.
- This site isn't perfect but it has a lot of the information and answers to your questions.
4.
- If you are crafting then you need this site.  The crafting system is complex and you need to understand how resources are refined and then used crafting.
The hardest part I found with crafting so far is that you need so much stuff.  If you want to make a bow then you have to do the following:
1. Chop trees to get wood (need an Axe).
2. Create Timber from the wood (need Creosote to make Timber).
3. Need bow staves from the timber.
4. Need to make a bowstring (Need cotton or leather and wax).
5. Need to assemble the bow and craft it.
All of that takes time and takes gold.  Don't have gold?  Need to hunt, salvage items and sell loot.  This is difficult in the beginning.  Lot's of time and effort to gain a few hundred gold pieces.
But here is the deal, if you stick it out and figure out how to approach it, you will find yourself as a mid-level character and it's easy to generate gold and resources.  For example, I can now spend an houri in a mine and generate ore for ingots and make a couple of 1000 gold as well.  Each time your character advances you can do more and more.  It's not grinding for grinding sake; you are progressing your character so you can live and survive in the world.
People complain about people like me who have housing deeds and stuff that gives us a leg up.  Yes, I do have that but I paid for that.  Let me explicit, I paid money to Portalarium and I'm funding this project and effort.  Anyone was able to do that and even today you can still do that by:
1. Buying house deeds in the store.
2. Buying homes and decorations in the store.
3. Buying Prosperity Tools in the store.  (These tools don't decay or wear out).
Do you have to "buy" stuff?  No.  If you don't then you will spend time and gold in the game to earn those items.  For example, they had a Property Lot Deed raffle going on right now.  For 5k or 10k gold, you can purchase a raffle ticket and have a chance to get a Property Lot Deed.  You need those to own land and place a house.  I bought (1) ticket in the first raffle and was fortunate to win a 2nd property deed with only one entry.  You can do the same and have the same chance.
There is a lot of content in the game right now and each month they introduce new content and put out patches during the month to address mechanics and balance the game.  All of the reviews I have been reading seem to be judging this game as a final release; it is not.  It has a lot but there is a lot more coming.
In the past 1.5 months I have immersed myself in the community and took the time to learn how to play this game.  This game isn't pick it up and you are lead down the rosey path of the game.  You have to approach almost like real life.  Set goals and work toward them.
For example, the first goal I had to make a chest so I could put it in my house and store stuff.  I figured out what the recipe was and what I needed.  I spent my first two or three days working to do that and succeeded.  After that I decided I wanted to make my own Bow and did the same.  Then I decided I wanted to make my own arrows and did the same.  Today I sit with a full set of enhanced Bronzed armor, an enhanced bow and all of it I made myself.
This game isn't for everyone.  It is involved and it takes time and effort.  That doesn't make it a "bad" game.  For some, especially the UO type of players, it makes a lot more sense.  For others, well it doesn't.  But all the complaints about it being slanted towards "backers" is just noise.  You can still back and support the game.  You can still buy items if you want to.  But it is up to you.
If you get stuck in the game then ask someone for help.  I do it all the time on discord.  If you want, friend me in the game and I will answer/help as I can.  My in game name is "Elaina Strongbow".  Good luck, happy adventuring and safe travels!

You can gradually watch your games improve and see how the gaming world evolves around you. It's also a lovely way to reminisce on gaming history.
On the other hand, the game has a few negative points too. For example, the reviewing algorithms are very predictable; you can follow the same formula game after game and get high ratings every time. On top of that, the game kind of runs out of content at the end, but that is made up by the fact that you can control a big portion of the gaming market, including the production of consoles and the organisation of events.
So in conclusion, if you've got a couple euros laying around, Game Dev Tycoon is more than worth your time.

I found out about this game in August of 2016, the week before the (actual) release. Therefore my review isn't influenced by all the hype and anticipation, and thus all the disappointment, from the launch.
I clicked "Yes" that I do recommend it, but I kind of need a neutral. I don't recommend paying $60 for it, but I have recommended the game. It's worth more like $20 in the current state.
There are a lot of bugs: ships falling through launch pads, whenever I teleport back to base I have to restart the game. There are a lot of balance issues: I can't find some resources that I need, but I keep finding traders selling things that are far more rare. And there are interface issues: I can't see below the ship to know where to land, the interface is really clunky and it's easier to press a key to switch inventory views than it is to click and hold for the right amount of time. There's just a lot of things that don't seem to be well-thought.
But with that being said, I continue to play it and I like it. I don't play first person shooters, my game of choice is Minecraft. Of course that makes my opinion less valuable to a lot of gamers, and I'm ok with that. But for what it is, space exploration, time wasting, wander around procedurally generated planets (and my graphics card is not good enough so I had to lower the quality, it's still pretty) ... it's just enjoyable. In normal mode there's some difficulty without having to really try very hard. That's what I prefer out of a game.
So I recommend it, but only if you just want to goof around and only if you get it on sale.

I've waited a while to post a review for this.  Wanted to collect my thoughts on it.  After having watched the drama of this game's release unfold, I'm convinced that there are in fact,
No Man's Skys.
1. The game 'the hype' promised- and never delivered
2. The game that fifty-thousand raging neckbeards can't seem to stop despising
As I wasn't on the hype train (I bought the game shortly after the Foundation Update), and I'm not especially prone to groupthink or fits of unreasoning rage either, I'll try to address that third game- because I
think gaming journalism is messed up.
I just happen to
think that the primary dysfunction has essentially become a difference of extremes.
Which is another way of saying:
Not- mind you- that I don't think that what happened with 'the hype' isn't reprehensible.  It is.
On the other hand I also think it's unfortunate in the sense that there
an audience for a game like this.  It's probably a far smaller one than the hype generated, but it's also probably larger than the wave of hate that followed it's release (that
to follow the release) allows for.
So what is that third game?  Well, it's an atmospheric exploration game with crafting and some survival elements.
It has some action, but it's not an action-oriented game.
It has some survival elements- but this isn't "hardcore"in that regard and I don't see it ever being.
It's got some crafting elements- but the list ins't tremendously expansive and the flow isn't necessarily... optimized.
It's set in space- replete with different races, lore for those races, factions and so on- but it's not a free-form Mass Effect, no.
What it does well is it's sense of ambience and atmosphere, while giving you a little of all of the above things.  Some might find this boring (and even I tire of it from time to time), but I don't think that the mere fact that you can be bored with a game necessarily makes it a bad game.
This isn't a game for everyone- as I think I said above.  But if you think you might find the idea of exploring a vast-
universe for a bit, while occupying yourself with gathering and cataloguing things, you might enjoy playing this game.
I know I have.
One thing I will absolutely agree with most of this game's detractors on is the price (at least the $60 one used at release).

That puts it in a similar category with a lot of other games like it.
So, if you do get it, wait for a sale- definately.  But again, keep in mind  that there's a lot of nonsense surrounding the game's release.  It's easy to avoid the over-hyping of the game nowadays since it's out and we've got plenty of it's features catalogued and we know what the game is and isn't.
But it's still easy to fall victim to the rage train still following the game.  Make your own decision.  Don't let anyone else (including me) tell you what to buy.
It's space exploration.

This review is coming at a time when most people who would play To The Moon have already done so. So what can I say that would convince somebody to buy this game? That's not the purpose of this review.
To The Moon is a rare production. With graphics and interface that would, by today's "next gen" standards, be considered far outdated or perhaps even backward, To The Moon still manages to break through the hearts of so many of its players. You could say that To The Moon is also not a challenging or difficult game. But it IS challenging and difficult, in its way. I'll explain later.
For now, the basics. The basic premise is that you play, interchangably, a pair of doctors who work for a company whose speciality is traversing the memories of its clients at the point at which they are dying, so that they can then rewrite those memories in order to have their clients fulfill a dying wish. To The Moon is really easy to grasp gameplay wise. Made in RPG Maker, the game uses a standard "isometric" viewpoint popularized by RPG's in the 1990's. Gameplay elements are limited to an object-hunt across the memory your characters are traversing, plus an additional picture puzzle that follows a traditional "flip square to complete" format.
The visual art of the game is crisp and at times quite beautiful, but not spellbinding in any sense. You can tell the developers worked hard on the pixel art, though. Nothing stands out as terribly constructed.
But we have to dispense with these elements of presentation. Well, that is to say, presentation wise, the game is "good." It WORKS, knowing what it is and its limitations, it does its best to present the world it wants to create and the story it wants to tell, and it genuinely succeeds in that endevour.
But then, it's the story where this game takes its place in the halls of, honestly, one of the best games ever created. Using this pixel art and limited, yet consequential, gameplay, To The Moon gets at the heart of so many sublime questions. What is the nature of truth? What is the nature of memory...of love? of memories of those whom we love? What matters the most in our brief existence in this life? How does memory function in the construction of the real?
To The Moon is perfectly paced and impeccably constructed on a narrative level. The writing AND gameplay are done in such a way that connect you intimately to the characters in the story. At the close of the game, you legitimately love all of them. And it's a rare experience that can deliver that to you.
The music? Oh my god, the music. Kan Gao, the main developer of this game, is also the composer of most of the music. And, in a way, the music is a character of its own. Gao's talent is apparent from the very beginning, as the menu opens with what will become an iconic theme throughout the game. There is so much care and love in the music of this game. There are no throwaway themes or repetitive, ear-worm tracks. You find yourself emersed in the musical experience as much as the gameplay and narrative experience.
Is this game "challenging" and "difficult?" Not in the way you may think. The game will challenge your perceptions of reality, your thoughts about love and loss, your idea of what is true and worthwhile. Is it "difficult?" The game will leave you shattered, emotionally. There are times in the game that are honestly "difficult" to sit through. There are times when you become so overwhelmed that you actually forget that you are NOT part of this story.
To The Moon is a work of art that will live in the annals of gaming for...well, for as long as gaming remains a form of artistic interaction. There are not enough things to say about this game that will live up to the impact it will render on the generations of gaming to come.
If you haven't played this game, anyone who is an enthusiast of this medium will, in 10 years time, ask you why the hell you haven't.

THE DOWNFALL: Instead of fixing the game, Ubisoft released DLC packs and added microtransactions to try to squeeze money out of the remaining players.  However, because of this the game fell even further down the hole that is lined with other Ubisoft games (RIP Ghost Recon: Future Soldier) and pushed even more players away.  People dubbed the game as "Dead" and wouldn't recommend it to anyone. The game was on the brink
RISE FROM THE ASHES: In recent months, Ubisoft has made a one-eighty and has started listening to people who purchase their games.  It started with the announcement that Rainbow Six Siege would be worked on and all the bugs that made the game unplayable were either acknowledged and fixed, or have been outright removed for gameplay sake.  The announcement that they wouldn't be pumping out a yearly Assassin's Creed and spreading themselves thin so they can focus on the games that are already out instead of worrying about what's next.  This brings me back to The Divison, a good amount of bugs (not all of them) have been fixed, hackers have been caught and banned, and there are supposedly more free updates to come out that would bring more content to the game.

The load times are flat out unacceptable though. 12 seconds to load into a town or a random battle is absolutely ridiculous.
I suppose if I were to say anything, the game is average. In that regard it's tough to recommend unless you're a gung-ho Ultima fan dead set on making sure you have fun.

A MMORPG lives and dies by its community.
Unfortunately Shroud has two very vocal groups within its community which are causing irreparable damage to the game.
These vocal groups have access to the developers through a constant presence in Discord developer area and through direct communication at some of the higher 'backer levels'. One of the things they are the most protective of is their access to the developers so that the 'lesser players' don't influence the developers or the game.
This group of players are mainly concerned with protecting any perceived entitlements that they have such as developer access, the only world chat (Noble chat, majority of players don't have access to any world/general chat), restrictions on decorative purchases from earlier in early access (remember the game still claims to not be 'released' yet). Many in this group seek to profit or protect their profits from their privileged positions.
Closely related to the Entitlement group are the Immersives, often the worst of the players belong to both or use the excuse of immersiveness to protect their entitlements. Through the claims of immersiveness we see many restrictions on the game such as no global/world or even a proper regional chat. Players in this group often like to claim that things ruin their roleplaying experience in order to make the game less fun to play or restrict access to certain game features.
Finally the game itself has some very real problems:
Very small players base (Peak Steam numbers list the population at around 300, with information from other sources including the developers showing that 50% or more of the population is on Steam. This means that at most 700 people are playing the game at any one time (including both steam and direct at the same time).

The feeling of a dead world also exists due to some poor design decisions that see most players playing in either singleplayer or friends only mode so it's rare to see other players. Coupled this with no global/world chat means that new players quickly feel isolated and leave the game. The immersive crowd push to maintain this isolation via arguing against a global/world chat and also against auto multiplayer mode in places like the overworld map (where there is no combat) and NPC cities (which likewise are entirely safe from either monsters or pvp).
The game is still in development and lacks a large amount of content, the game is funded through sales of items and player housing through the 'addon store' - due to the low playerbase and the problems brought about by the Entitlement and Immersive Crowds the game is unlikely to grow and the funding that has been sustaining the game to this point is likely to dry up over the next 12 months.
Shroud also has been built on the unity engine, and the flaws with that engine for mmorpg design are apparent with a large amount of loading screens being needed. Animation are poor and the graphics are so-so.
A robust crafting system could also help to save shroud, but again it has been sabotaged by poor decisions such as having better items being available through the add-on store rather than being crafted. (For example home decorations etc).
In summary, avoid this game.
Updated 24/11/2016 : Recent patches show that the developers have continued to listern to the vocal clique - results are a continued drop in playernumbers.

Reus is just another Indie game. This game will give you a planet with four giants (Forest, Desert, Swamp, and Water) to create life on it. The giants help human to build their village and resources, like fruits, herbs, mine, and animals. Nomad will move to your village as soon as more resources are available. You as a "God" of the planet should take care of them. The villager can be greedy because they want more than expected.
You are limited to 30 minutes to play the game for the first time. Then, the playing time changes to 60 minutes and 120 minutes. You will be given a challenge for each playing session. When a challenge is completed, the achievement will be unlocked. Some challenges are easy but others are not. Anyway, you can also play tutorial.
Speaking of game features, this game has nice 2D graphic that you can zoom in-out to see the details. I like their art styles. Keyboard and mouse are supported. I recommend to use both when you're playing the game because there is keyboard shortcut. Keyboard shortcut helps you to choose a giant easily. By the way, Reus is available on Linux. If you are a Linux gamer, this game may be your next wishlist.
So, I would recommend this game.
Note: the store page of this game doesn't tell if the game is available on Linux. I have played this game for more than 40 hours. It runs flawlessly on Linux.

I look up from the screen and am perplexed to find it is very dark out, I'm briefly concerned thinking a particularly big storm had moved in, but a glance at a clock confirmed that no, that was not the case. WARNING: PRODUCT MAY CAUSE INCREMENTAL TIME TRAVEL

Galactic Civilizations II (or GalCiv, as it's affectionately called) is the overall best space 4X available.  There are others which do individual pieces better, but none which match the whole polished package provided by Stardock.  One thing Stardock does particularly well - at least as well as Firaxis with CIV and CiV - is their expansions - and you should play GalCiv with all of them enabled for the full experience.  (All the expansions are available in the Ultimate Edition.)
Make sure to spend some time in the ship designer - the stock designs are very pretty, but nothing compares to fielding a fleet of dreadnoughts that you designed literally from the keel up, using an intuitive system of stock pieces with various connection points, a sort of intersteller LEGO.  You can also download ship sets made by others and import them into your game; designs based on popular SciFi universes abound.

Definitely a good game worth playing if you like a focus on the story. If you're instead after something challenging with lots of gameplay elements, this is not for you.

Great, super fun game!  The underwater aspects are a refreshing change to normal shooter mechanics, although the game feels very familiar and is very easy to jump right into.  The main game mode is very similar to a round of Payload in TF2, and the humans vs. sharks dynamic is similar to lot of other games I love like Dino D-Day.  Aside from that, it also feels like Call of Duty, Battlefield, and Left 4 Dead at different times, effectively capturing the feeling of a scene from "Jaws" or a shark-related horror movie.  It's TERRIFYING playing as a diver and suddenly having your buddy snatched out by a rapid shark lunge!  And on top of all this, the game has some of THE BEST matchmaking mechanics I've seen!  You can actively choose beforehand whether you want to be a diver or shark, choose which of the 12 maps you'd like to play on, and even easily form a party with your friends!  The only drawbacks I see are the seemingly low amount of players (can take about 2 minutes to find a game in matchmaking) and just how graphically demanding the game seems to be.  I have to run the game in a SUPER low resolution just for it to work decently, but I'm far from having a good computer.  Still, HIGHLY recommend!

This is an inoffensive point and click adventure, albeit in a 3D environment rather than 2D. Get item A, take to location B etc. A few quick time-events, some puzzles, and the odd 'arcade' driving sequence thrown in for good measure. They do mesh together quite well, but are sometimes poorly executed.
The plot and setting is nothing new. Post-apocalyptic romp where robots have replaced humans as the dominant 'species'. To be fair there's a little more to it than that. It has a film noire vibe, robot factions, some character development and ... spoilers ... and this is only Part One after all.

Expect to complete in around 3-5 hours. The puzzles and point and click elements are logical, but with simple and obvious solutions. The arcade events are terrribly easy. These all seem to be there simply to help immerse you in the experience, rather than challenge you. And that's okay. Just don't expect otherwise.
The English translation and spoken dialogue is a bit off from time to time. Some words dropped into conversations at an odd point in the sentence, or mispronounced, or words that carry the wrong stress or emphasis etc. Mostly it's fine, but noticable to a native English speaker. This might break the immersion a little.
Graphics and animation are okay. At PS4 level. Sound and music is okay. Nothing amazing, but it's appropriate and it fits. And a shed load of Easter Eggs and references to popular culture - if you like that sort of thing.
I don't think I'll be buying Part 2. This was enough to keep me engaged for an evening, but no more. So I'm not sure I can recommend on that basis alone, especially given the clunky implementation of the game camera and controls, and the occasionally awkward Russian to English translations.
Buy when it's on sale, or spend your £'s watching a Sci-Fi film instead.

This is a great game. I'd say it's more of a Telltale-ish narrative story than a point & click since there's a set course that your character must follow during the story. The graphics are incredible - it's hard to imagine better graphics and designs for this game. The story was also interesting and kept a decent pacing. The attention to detail with some of the UI/interfaces which your character interacts with during the story were always enjoyable. I'm on Windows 10 / GTX1080 and it ran perfectly for me without any performance issues or hiccups.
The main complaints that I've seen about this game involved the movement and speed of the main character. Personally, the speed wasn't an issue for me at all - in fact for indoor running I found it to be the perfect pace. Also, I rarely found myself ever needing to walk long distances in the game. The only time it bugged me was one brief scene outside but that was only for a few seconds until I realized which direction I needed to go. The movement of the character was a little weird I'll admit since there's a few milliseconds delays in start/stopping to walk/run, which coupled with the changing of camera angles going between rooms, did cause me to bump into things now and then - but after 20min of playing the game, I didn't even notice it anymore. The only thing that annoyed me a bit were the invisible walls that kept you on a relatively straight course in the storyline. There were some areas where I hit an invisible wall even though there was plenty of space for my robot body.
Will definitely be buying the next episodes which hopefully are on schedule.

Reus is fun for the first 2-3 hours. By then you've seen everything the game has to offer and realize it isn't worth continuing just to nab all those elusive steam achievements.  The game seems pretty well-made but it is ultimately just a casual god-sim severely lacking in excitement.
You control four giants that can terraform a barren planet, adding oceans, forests, mountains, and swamps, as well as plants, animals, and minerals to each.  Your job is to make the planet habitable and provide human settlers with whatever resource they need from food, tech, and wealth.  You have 30 minutes to make the humans as prosperous and happy as possible. Or you could kill them if you think they're becoming too greedy.  The choice is yours and yours alone!
Helping the humans complete projects (i.e. acquire a certain amount of food, tech, and wealth in a limited time span) provides an Ambassador for one of your giants.  Picking up the ambassador provides minor power-ups to the abilities you already possess.  The game has 13 different tech trees for you to attempt to understand.  Each possible tech tree is tied to a biome (ocean, forest, mountain, swamp) and resource (animal, plant, mineral).  You cannot unlock all abilities in a single play session, so you'll need to pick and choose how to use your ambassadors to best affect.  I really like this concept, but in practice it is poorly implemented.  The in-game prompts for how Ambassadors affect each giant and how each upgraded ability affects the different resources is incredibly confusing to understand.
The game attempts to offer replayability by providing a number of conflicting objectives (steam achievements), forcing you to play a ridiculous number of times in order to complete all the objectives. Forsaken virtues is right - forsake your virtues with your credit cards.
It is like the majority of the features implemented in this game were done to destroy the typical QoL aspects of most games today. Immersive roleplaying is paramount here, your frustration breaking-point is not. Do you like to know where you are in the world and where you are going? No! No map! Do you like to be able to stash your insane number of items in the closest bank to where you are adventuring? No! No linked banks! I could go on, but it isn't necessary to do so; you get the picture.
Imagine, if you will, coordinating with your brother to spend enough money to buy a plot of land and a house in a game that is in 'Alpha'. You log in and are immediately disgusted by the character visuals in the creator. I've seen better character models in Paper Mario. After playing Witcher 3, it's like I went back in time. A previous review mentioned Maple Story - Funny - even those graphics are better.
Once my brother and I slugged through the tutorial, my impression on the graphics improved a bit. The characters are still vomitous but the environment and landscaping is pretty impressive. We spent hours traversing through towns of this infantile game to discover that any land plots we were dreaming of had been taken. Well if that isn't circa UO-97/98, I don't know what is.
After hours of searching we eventually placed our house. Fantastic! Another couple of hours were spent decorating our new home with rewards we had received for our pledges. I even went to the cash shop to buy some trees. You know, you can never have too much green. Plus I wanted to cover up the ughly town-house exterior of pleasantville with a little bit of uniqueness. This was only to discover that 2 of the trees in the package wouldnt even fit on the lot.
Then we logged out and went about our busy lives for a couple of days; you know, looked after our kids, worked at a job, paid our property taxes. When we logged back in we were shocked - we owed property taxes for our home in-game!! Woah, talk about immersive!! Well, I guess we better go farm up some cash!
We ventured out with our newly created characters and our 5,000 gp debt. We killed 1...2...5....10...20....50 skeletons. Surely, after 50 monster kills we must be nearing our debt oweing! Well, apparently 50 skeletons x 10 gp = 500; I guess we have 450 monsters to go. Hopefully we can kill these things faster than our debt increases. Good thing they haven't implemented interest yet. I wonder where we can find loan sharks?
Clearly killing monsters for money to cover property taxes is not feasable for a new player. Lets go try crafting! That mine in Owl's Head looked promising. One vein equated to one ore. After 4 hours of mining, we were shocked to discover the following formula:
1 Plate Chest Piece = 10 metal(i'll use iron) sheets, 1 coal, 1 metal binding
10 iron sheets =  30 iron ingots, 10 coal, 1 sheet mold
1 metal binding = 1 iron ingot, 1 coal
31 iron ingot = 124 iron ore, 31 coal, 1 ingot mold
That's right, to make a chest piece you will need to hit up at least 124 iron veins. In the meantime our tax debt is increasing. It's a good thing that to get out of the mine, (to get back to our local bank on the other side of the planet) instead of needing to run accross two huge zones, loading
(since there are no maps) to find out where the hell we are going and zoning twice, we can just log out then log back in and click "start on world map".
I don't have the patience for this game. Call me an impatient child if you will. The reality of the matter is that I am 35 years old with two kids. I do not have the free time to spend 4 hours mining, 20 minutes running back to my town and another 15 minutes at the crafting station to make 1 chest piece (which doesn't even sell for the equivalent of the materials that went into it btw). If you do, all the power to you. Ultima Online successor - pheh. I found more enjoyment sitting around town playing random ABC songs on my lute to absolutely no one in the largest, yet barren, town the game has.

Two thumbs-up. Really good start on a good Tycoon concept, for a first release. The user interface needs work, as it currently is MODAL (meaning that dialogue boxes pop up and stop time until you press 'Ok'). Modeal interfaces are never good in Tycoon games. Time should progress unless the user presses pause. There is also no way to speed up or slow down time progression.
It seems that there is no way to actually save a game for replay later. The game seems to save itself occasionally, but when you use the menu to "save", there is no way to name a file and it seems that there is no indication if the game actually was written to disk or not.
There are certain visual icons that have no fly-by text. This is difficult because you don't know what these mean until you try it, so you're not sure if they are something you want to use. For example, the turbo-lightenin bolt.
The game seems to end prematurely, after 30 years of game time. It would be better to build in additional story lines to allow the game to be played far into the future, for example , futuristic devices or technologies.
Getting back to the modality, news dialog boxes should not pop up. A news ticker would be a better implementation of informing the player when a new device comes to market or is withdrawn from the market. When releasing a game, its painful to watch the reviews role in , again , this should be non-modal and non-blocking.
The human resource pool is over-simplified. Where are the QA testers ? The people you hire with the video preview skill should produce actual demo videos of the gam ein development, reviewable periodically.
The tech tree is fairly deep, but you cannot get to all the tech you need within the 30 years of game time. Also, you should be able to create your own tech, for example, a proprietary video format, or a proprietary AI algorithm, with unique features that present a competitive differentiator to your consumer audience.
Love the Back-to-the-Future Delorean in the garage, nice throw-back !
There needs to be more levels. More building space to move to. The developers need to be seen playing foos-ball or Nintendo.
More finite control needs to be given over the employee salaries and benefits. Need to be able to hire an HR person, or outsource to Administaff.
Hope these suggestions spur some more creativity for continued development of the game. Its a great start and would be an awesome game if you could smooth out some of the wrinkles.
Best of luck and please work on 2.0.

That said it certainly made me tear up at points, so I won't fault it for trying. Another thing that annoys the heck out of me is the controls, using the mouse is maddening at times. To the Moon is an original and very creative work that I find a little hard to refer to as a game, due to the relatively few critical interactions available and the complete linearity of the plot. However, unlike A Bird Story, which I thought would have been better as a non-interactive 'movie' using the game engine, To the Moon had enough interactivity to keep it interesting, even if the player was unable to make any choices that really changed the game experience in any way, I guess I think of it as an 'experience' similar to a very easy adventure game.
The story is alternately beautiful, funny, corny, and tongue-in-cheek. The setting is enjoyable, and the main plot device is very imaginative and well thought through. The writing itself is simple, but excellent, and in terms of grammar is much better than most AAA games available today.
The music is delightful, if a bit repetetive (a fact that does not go unnoticed by some of the game's characters). And even though by the end one knows exactly where the story is going, it is still heartwarming -- and also sad -- enough to bring a tear to the eye, while the occasional jokes and unexpectedly offbeat situations were funny enough to elicit a least a few genuine laughs from me, and quite a number of chuckles.
As with A Bird Story, but even more so here, the pixel graphics are brilliant. There's a wide range of settings throughout the story, each with a unique feel, but I did find myself becoming a bit sick of some of the repeated areas, even though they were required for the plot.
To the Moon even has some minigames to break up the flow, which works well. I didn't enjoy them enough to replay more than was required to advance the plot, but they were a great addition to spice things up a bit.
The regular price of To the Moon is a little higher than many other games, for the number of hours of enjoyment you'll get out of it, but even had I paid full price, rather than picking it up on sale, I would not have regretted the purchase.  To the Moon is most definitely recommended for anyone who isn't turned off by extremely well-done pixel graphics and a cheesy, but completely enjoyable story.
To top it off I just noticed after I finished To the Moon tonight that there are two free DLCs available for free. What a great bonus to an already fantastic experience!
I was a bit disappointed with A Bird Story, Freebird's short 'game' released sometime after To the Moon, but having played To the Moon now I am very much looking forward to other productions from Freebird.

I took aim and fired at the tiger shark to no avail, and watched horrified as it charged towards me with its black, lifeless eyes.  Before I could react, the shark was upon me and had locked its steel jaws around my arm. Depth is a very enjoyable multiplayer game in which 4 people play as divers searching for gold and protecting S.T.E.V.E. a safe opening, chest busting robot gold-digger, while 2 other players play as sharks with the sole aim to eat the divers and stop them from escaping with their plunder. Each team has 30 respawn ‘tickets’ which, after one team runs out, the other team wins. Unless the divers escape with their plunder before one team has run out of lives.
This game is one of the best multiplayer games I have ever played. From my first game I played on the free weekend, I couldn’t stop playing it. It was as if I was being drawn to it. Even now, whenever I think of playing something for 10 minutes, my attention isn’t directed at Rocket League or Team Fortress 2, but Depth. In both Rocket League and TF2, it’s quick action with constant stress until the end when you either win or lose. In Depth, it’s something very different. The feeling of playing as a diver as your heartbeat in game begins to beat faster and faster, the tension growing as you can only see a couple of feet in front of you when all of a sudden your screen is filled with that of a shark. You mash your mouse button as your diver desperately slashes and stabs at the shark’s nose to no avail. ‘CRUNCH’ your body spasms as you are left sometimes limbless, sometimes in half, until the menu pops up in front of you. ‘Respawn’.
As a shark, having the feeling of being the predator, hunting your weary prey as you swim elegantly between rock formations and pieces of rusted, crumbling sunken ships. Your screen becoming increasingly red as you get closer and closer to the divers. Your primordial growl as you are but mere feet from your prey. You swoop in with the power of your tail to thrust you, you snatch a diver before his teammates have even noticed, and by the time they get to where they last heard the screams, there is nothing left but bubbles. Depth is a fantastic game but, like everything in this world apart from your wife/girlfriend, it isn’t without its flaws.
Depth, although extremely enjoyable, has a very small player base (around 4000 people on a free weekend but after the free weekend stops, it’s between 1200 and 1800 players). For a game like no other, it suffers from a lack of people willing to buy/play it. I, personally, have had no issues with this as all of my games I have played (around 15-20 at the time of writing this) have connected within 30 seconds and people dropping out of the game is very rare. The player base is fine and is one of the less toxic communities that I have had the good fortune to experience. Many people even willing to help new players like myself.
Although I said people dropping out of the game is rare, when they do, the game fills their position with a bot that is seldom filled by a real player for the rest of the game. This puts a strain on the divers as bots tend to hang around outside and quickly get snatched by a shark. Although fun to watch as the red mist clears and the muffled screams die down only to reveal a mangled torso, it slowly brings down your teams respawn tickets and makes it much easier for team shark. The same with team shark but, because team shark only have 2 players, winning as team shark after a player has bailed is difficult, nay impossible. A bot shark will enter a room full of divers and do nothing for a couple of seconds in which time the divers have turned it into a shark-shaped pin cushion as it sinks elegantly to the bottom of the ocean like something out of a David Attenborough documentary.
Other issues I have found with this game is that, if you are playing as a shark and you are up against a team of ex-Navy Seals (AKA very good players who work well as a team), you stand no chance as S.T.E.V.E. only stops to open safes/chests etc. in closed off rooms and, although you can smash through some walls/doors to make more entrances/exits as a shark, these points are quite obvious and you have to hit them multiple times to break through which, of course, makes a lot of noise which alerts the divers. Expect a storm of bullets to come your way when employing this tactic. The issue with this is, as a shark, you need to kill divers to get evolution points. 1 diver = 10 Evolution points. Evolution points are used to give your shark perks and the edge you need to defeat the divers. From quicker movements to an increased resilience to bullets, evolution points do all sorts of things with the top level of evolution costing 50 evolution points. So do the math. The best skills cost 5 divers in your stomach. Divers do not evolve, but with the more gold they get and return to S.T.E.V.E., the better weapons they can buy, which can kill the sharks quicker. Because of this, if you cannot kill enough divers early on as a shark, you are unlikely to pull victory as later weapons are very powerful.
I found while playing a diver, if you can collect $4500, you can buy the harpoon which in 90% of cases is a one hit kill on a shark, which seems a bit OP as divers don’t need to kill sharks to get better guns, but sharks need to kill divers to unlock better skills. At this point the game is basically in the divers favour.  So sharks need to keep on their toes, or should I say fins?
The only other game mode is Divers VS Megalodon. In this game mode, as a diver you collect gold to get better weapons (as you pick the gold up you automatically get a better gun, unlike sharks and gold game mode ((the one I have just been talking about)) which you save up and get to choose). Then you kill the Megalodon and take its place. You then kill as many divers for points as you can until you are killed and other diver takes your place. The diver/Megalodon with the most points at the end wins. A very enjoyable game mode that I have enjoyed as much as Sharks and Gold.
Overall, Depth is a fantastic game with a well-deserved place in anyone’s steam library. You will have many an enjoyable game in this brilliant yet different approach to multiplayer gameplay.

I went into this game expecting nothing, since I heard it didn't hold up against FEAR 1.  Truth is it doesn't, but that didn't stop me from having a great time anyway!
FEAR 3 is a pretty standard corridor shooter, at least if you play it as a single player game like I did.  The sound design is great, guns and explosions feels satifyingly punchy.  In one part of the campaign had your character go temporarily deaf due to an explosion for about 5 minutes, at first I thought it was a bug but it works great for the scene, very memorable.  The music is great as well, it really enhances some of the spooky bits.
Some of the environments are downright inspired, level 2 where you're fighting cultists in a costco TV electronics section that looks like a hall of mirrors is a standout moment.  Making your way through crashed train cars on a collapsing bridge was another great scene.  The level where you're fighting your way through cultist martial law suburbia is like a dark take on Modern Warefare 2's levels in the same setting.  Whoever put the shower jumpscare in the game, congrats, that one got me good.
The difficulty is definitely skewed for consoles, play on the hardest difficulty and it's fun.    Didn't run into any bugs on my playthrough, although a few sections were next to impossible to complete without abusing the AI.  The enemies are dumb cannon fodder in this game, nothing like FEAR 1.  Playthrough took maybe 7-8 hours.
In short, it's a fairly standard shooter with some brilliant environments.  I'd give it a shot if you enjoy single player fps games and can get it for cheap.

So I've spent over 500 hours with No Man's Sky on the PS4 and just recently started playing on PC.  First off, this game is not for everyone.  If you are looking for a story driven game or one with lots of action then this probably isn't the game for you.  One of the reasons that I love NMS is that I love open world/giant sandbox type games.  In the past, I've played such games as Red Dead Redemption, GTA, Fallout 4 and Skyrim. I found myself just wandering around these open worlds and taking everything in, the missions became secondary to exploration.
No Man's Sky is a very chill, meditative, tranquil experience that is ALL about exploration with some aspects of space combat. The visuals are stunning and the soundtrack is amazing. The game definitely does not hold your hand and while there is no storyline, no missions, no cinematic cutscenes, there is a very in-depth backstory/lore to the game.  This often gets overlooked but if you take the time to read the interactions with the Atlas Interface, Alien Monoliths and Plaques, you can piece together the history of the Alien Races and it's a pretty interesting story.
There is a new Survival Mode which is a very nice addition and at times, feels like it's how the game is meant to be played.  They have also added base building, freighters, side quests and will continue to provide more free content updates which will improve NMS over time.
** Post Path Finder Update **
Just wanted to drop my two cents on the latest free content update.  A bunch of new features have been added including the addition of land vehicles (on home planet), owning multiple starships and storing on your freighter, visiting other players bases, create a race mode (haven't played this yet) and an amazing upgraded photo mode.  And many other in game features.
My recommendation has only been strengthened by the latest update and really looking forward to what they have in store for the next one.
