Original review below.
===========================================
The game needed persistence to increase the engagement with players. Sadly the game was not ready for persistence with broken combat skills, economic turmoil and not variety within systems like combat, crafting or gathering. This would not result in a negative review, if it were not also for the way they handle the challenges that come with a highly monetised persistent Pre-Alpha, or however they wish to term it now.
Early Access is very true here, but with a live game, the developers do not know how to handle game balance on a 'live server' and swing widly and often with drastic changes to gold gain, taming and mining. No one disputes adjustments were needed but taming was made a dead skill tree, not 'balanced'.
Gold gain reduction has me in a place where I must grind easy mobs for gold for 2 hours a week to keep rent payments up to date or my $80 add on sits in a bank, worthless. This grind is considered an example of 'Risk versus Reward'. The risk beinbg falling asleep while spending hours ferrying loot for handfuls of gold. The only real risk is spending hours playing the game and not getting anywhere because of repair and reagents because you do not wiki search for the 'best loot grinds'.
A proposed solution to the above when this feedback was provided was to buy premium currency at a rate of $1 per week to skip the in game gold grind.
This same currency (Gold Crowns of the Obsidian) can be sold to players for gold to avoid the nerfed gold grind even more so. A way to keep up with the repair costs, the magic reagent cost and purchase the raffle tickets to get the Lot Deeds being 'reffled off' by Portalarium
Game direction takes queues from players well invested in the game, at the expense of lowere pledge players, let alone new purchasers. See the cave from giving everyone a free raffle ticket to win land to place a house. A result from being under pressure by those with lots of ingame gold buying into a 'raffle' and assuming the odds were favorable as gold is hard to earn without a great deal of ingame experience.  A raffle should not reward such expectations. They should have had NPCs buyback Lot Deeds from players who were now unable to 'game' the system, rather then further make it harder for new players to own any land. But it is a timely example of how the game is directed.
Housing is nice and enjoybale. But crafting items to furnish require hundreds of trees and ore. One table is 4 wooden boards. 2 Wooden boards is 1 Piece of Timber. One timber is six wood. Do the math and you need 12 pieces of wood for a table which, unless you have very high lumberjacking or tools purchased on the add opn store for RMT, you are chopping down on Average 12 trees for the wood to make one tbale.
And you still need 2 Wooden Poles, which are another 4 timber and another 24 trees to make the legs for the table.
36 trees to make one table, now it's time to make the chairs.
Each step is a gold sink using non farmable fuels as well, feeding into the economic drain. Equipment is much worse then this as well with components being far more intense in use of materials and fuel.
You can buy tools and gathering items that are indestruictable in the store. These are not small transactions, but cost over $100 if you wanted a full set. They also only sell them in predefined sets so you can;t just buy what you prefer.
Kickstarter backers are selling pledge items for both ingame items and real money. Comission free vendoprs (Think Auctiuon House Listing with no taz) are selling for about $140. Lot deeds are being sold, rewards for testing releases are for sale, everything is monetised whether by players or developers.
Quests are currently limited and lack depth. Most being fetch quests, fedex quests or kill quests. None of it changes the world and even bandits you 'help' don;lt change their attitude towards you. *Early development*.
Combat is unbalanced but it's early access. Wait until they refine it if that's important to you.
The map has inbvisible walls and unexpected paths through mountain cliffs and so on.
I don;t want to go on, but that's the state the game is in as far as I wish to represent it.
There is potential, but I feel it requires the development to shift focus to longevity and access of new players when this is in opposition of 'old money' protecting their status.
If that doesn't change, there is no reason for new players to join

Kingdoms is fundamentally flawed - it is more efficient for established players to 'conquer' new players, and take their village(s) after allowing the new players to develop the village for them.  As a new player you will lose your village to an unstoppable force from an established player every 3 to 4 weeks of playing. Any premium tokens or card packs that you bought to help develop your village only benefit the conquering player as you must start a new village over. Rinse and repeat.
I would suggest to anybody considering Stronghold Kingdoms to steer clear and instead pick up the original 2001 Stronghold game during a sale, which is by far the best of the bunch from this franchise. Alternatively, have a look for other, more popular real-time building MMOs -there are many to choose from, without the same lose-everything-you-paid-for-to-an-established-player design that Stronghold Kingdoms has.

On occasions the game gets tedious as you dowse the entirety of the map for the next object to take you to the next area. Raquel woke up and got out of bed. She could barely walk and she moved very slowly. She looked outside to see where she was, and to her dismay she was no longer in a Spanish-speaking country. She turned on the television and found out that all the channels were in English, except for Univision. She also saw American flags outside. Raquel was in the United States, but she wasn't living in Los Angeles; she was in a rural area.
Was it all a dream? It must have been, because she didn't speak a word of Spanish. She didn't have any family in Mexico, either. As a matter of fact, she had no immediate family; they were all dead.
She looked in a mirror and noticed that there was a contrast between her real face and what she looked like in her dreams. Raquel was not a young lady, but a geriatric woman rotting away on a farm with her feline companions. She never found love in her real life; Arturo was just the man of her dreams, and she could no longer live without having him by her side. She said, "I'd rather burn on Hades' grill than live another minute without my beloved Arturo!" These were her last words before she fell into an eternal sleep due to her overdose on Lortab.

I have to agree with some of the other reviews I've read here since playing the game. The FEAR series started off as a game that was truly it's own genre; paranormal FPS. It stood proudly amongst it's predecessors like DOOM and Castle Wolfenstien.  The scare element was in the fact that you had all the firepower in the world, but it amounted to nothing to what was truly terrfying; a psychic ghost that is Alma, who seems hellbent on either scaring you to death, or burning you, whichever comes first. The first game really playing into lighting, textures and sound; right at the cusp of when the gaming world was really experimenting and playing with those elements. The enviroment was great, the gameplay was pretty smooth for its time. The combat was fun (slow-mo done right), the story was intriguing with just the right touch of spooky mystery, and the scare moments were downright terrifying. Had more than a few moments where I had to save and quit simply because my overly beating heart couldn't take anymore. Overall a very solid horror game that was quite a few years ahead of it's time. 9/10
FEAR 2 brought in more of a balance between the combat and the scare moments. The combat was much much smoother compared to FEAR, and the graphics were amazing compared to other games of it's time. You still played a silent protaginist, which was odd considering that you don't officially play as Pointman, but overall the story was very tight and the scare moments were still pretty scary and fairly unpredictable. Overall an improvement in some subtle ways, but there were a few moments where it seemed a little TOO combat heavy. A for effort though, and I have to say I enjoyed playing it across the board. 7/10
And then FEAR 3...changed developers, which can be either really good or really bad for a game mid/end series, and right during the COD craze being at it's peak. And by God did it show. Restricted to 2 weapons, majority of the weapons vanilla and mediocre. Over half the special weapons gone, and the really fun ones (Nail gun and laser gun I'm looking at you two) were only given sparcely during the end and really had next to no screen time. The scare moments were also next to non-existent, despite a few gems of those moments being hidden here and there, and the combat was so heavy and pointless it felt like I was playing more of a crappy, cheap horror rendition of a Call of Duty game than a horror FPS. And since a lot of the expansions from the first two games was rendered non-canon, the story had a ton of plot holes and the ending was just crap with it being so open ended. I was vastly disappointed with how a wonderful game series that I had grown to love had crashed and burned so horribly. If you're looking to simply finish the story, if you can even call it that it's so bad, from the previous games that is virtually the only semi-good reason to buy this game. Otherwise, I wouldn't recommend it at all. 2-3/10

This game is a great mix of single player and co-op gameplay in a pretty large and very detailed open world map with a ton of tactical and visual customisation for your character and weapons.
You can enjoy the game alone or by teaming up with other players. It's obvious they created this game with co-op in mind and I do hope they will manage to keep the community alive by introducing content more often.
The weatherin this game is amazing, probably the most realistic and beautiful ingame weather created the past years, and by far, this game makes the most out of volumetric effects (lights, smoke, fog) and combines them all together like no other game. Often I like to stop and look around how the snowflakes are falling near light lighting poles in a foggy night.
Not sure how the game runs on other PCs but I enjoy it max details, without performance issues and rarely drops under 80fps.
Another great aspect of the game is the cover system, combined with great animations, it doesn't get boring easily.
There is a huge ammount of weapons, from old bolt-action rifles (russian m44) to modern SMGs (vector) and also a large variety of attachments (suppressors, grips, magazines, scopes).
Also, there are many visual items to collect for your character (hats, coats, boots, vests, etc) and skins for the weapons.
The weapons you find/buy/steal have varying stats, no weapon is the same. While progressing through the game, you find better and better weapons with increase stats, allowing you to fight through more difficult regions of the city.
I personally don't have bad things to say about the game, it's the modern-era RPG I wished for (not a big fan of medieval-era inspired games), but there are some things you need to know, that you might not enjoy):
•Except for a short intro, the game does not have cutscenes, it does not tell the story in a classic way, you are mostly briefed through your audio device (whatever that is) and most of the story unfolds through found items, phones, documents, videos and in some cases by just watching the visual clues of the world around and asking yourself what went wrong there.
•You might find the game repetitive, there are multiple types of missions but, except for the main missions, they are mostly the same in each region of the map: defend supplies, save hostages, repair antennas, offer support to your allies and so on. What makes them different is the way you approach them, your choices for weapons, attachments, skills, tallents.

I'm a huge fan of empire building and 4X genre (such as Galactic Civilizations II, Endless Space, etc) and despite owning several titles, I've never really got around to playing any of them... until now.
With that in mind I have no real base of comparison with other games in the 4X genre, which in case you were wondering stands for 'explore, expand, exploit, and exterminate'. However, I enjoyed this one.
For whatever reason the game was kind on me. All settings were on random and it generated a fairly good sized galaxy, with 3 Civilizations on it, so there wasn't a mad war from the off. Getting to grips with the game, and realising that while on the surface it looks simple as you start to look and prod there is much more to the game.
I somehow managed to corner the market on diplomatic translators, which meant no other Civilization could make them - so only I could make and trade them! Nice! Then I discovered the Ship Creator tool in the Shipyard, which allows you to design your own ships. Oh man.
The trading and diplomacy looked fairly straight forward, then I was invited to the UP for a Galactic Council vote, which I thought was a nice addition.
I think what gives this game a mark of 'good' for me is that I had played for 2 hours and not realised it. Going in a thought it would be a 'time sink' game, and it is, yet it's fun to play. IF I do manage to 'win' at this game, I'll keep it installed and play it again. I have a feeling there's a decent mod community out there, and can imagine that there are plenty of community designed races and ships to use.
If you enjoy empire building games, don't mind time sink games, and think you can lead your own alien race to glory... this game is for you.

I backed this game just after the Kickstarter finished, and occasionally popped in to see the progress and see some of the scenes as they were being developed. While not overly impressed with the progress at the start, I could see the visuals, depth of the game and the community developing very well. I started playing properly as soon as I heard persitence was starting, and I'm having so much fun exploring the world, learning the skill system, crafting system and being in an MMORPG again.
It's the real deal as an adventure games goes, so much to discover and it doesn't hold your hand too much, but the community is awesome, and you have to deal with real people sometimes to figure stuff out.
You can also go to single player online mode and get away from the crowds to explore, grind some materials or level up. But you can still be in contact with your guild and friends if you need to switch back to multiplayer online mode to join up with them for a party! I really like how they've designed this multi/single player online system.
It's a great game already, and it's still in Alpha with so much more to be added. Of course there's a multitude of bugs and polishing to be done, just don't expect it to run perfectly either, as much optimisation still needs to be done.
The game is good value at the moment, but expect a steep learning curve, and a gameplay style which is only made up by what you want to do, and the goals you set yourself. Highly Recommended if you can stomach it being in Alpha at the moment.

After playing Pat and Mat for as little as half an hour, I found myself able to appreciate the lesser things in life. The things we usually take for granted. Our protagonists 'Pat & Mat' live a rather simplistic existence as handymen in an unnamed Czechoslovakian city (easily mistaken, by the uninformed, for a rustic hamlet) where life plods along at a snails pace. Indeed, the setting is incredibly tranquil and as one might imagine, this placidity is reflected in both Pat & Mat's temperament. To say that the duo are relaxed in any way, would be a massive understatement, yet they are no strangers to a little bit of hard work. Even their simple life style comes with the odd challenge (ones that some players may not appreciate, due to their urban locale) yet they never falter in the face of in surmountable odds and always pull through in the end, even if their schemes are ill thought out at the best of times. Whether they player can appreciate their twisted logic will determine how much they get out of the game.
Indeed, even when it comes to something as simple, as say, the construction of a mini golf course, their own unique ingenuity shines through, who else would thing to cover a course in sand after all? Let alone the construction of several courses over a sizeable body of water, whilst neglecting either any standing area for the player or mounting platforms to make reaching aformentioned courses possible.
How they managed to construct these, despite professing to be mere handymen, is beyond my knowledge (presumably they are lying to me, after all, Pat (or perhaps Mat?) claimed to have taken 17 hours to finish a single course, when really, it was possible to do so after only three, perhaps they merely did not wish to hurt my pride? I would not put it past them, the cheeky scamps) but regardless, it is presumably for that same reason that they later found themselves short of supplies to construct the remaining courses.
The knowledge of this left me a little hurt, as I had expected a little more, especially since mini golf was one of only four games on the main menu and in total only had a play time of roughly ten hours. For 39p, I could hardly complain. I will privately shake a first in the twins direction but nothing more, they are not deserving of my ire, not today.
In short, if you are wondering, is this game for me? Then ask yourself how much you enjoy taxing puzzles. If you are a self professed puzzle fanatic (like myself) and felt a little bit let down by the linearity of the new Thief game, then look no further, this is the challenge you have been waiting for, though the overarching plot is nowhere near as forboding, the characters still retain a certain amount of charm that will invariably win you over, with time, should you allow them into your heart. All I can say, is to be patient with this one; invest yourself in its charming narrative and with time, you will surely reap what ye sow.

Continues the story of Pointman, Alma's son, and in some ways is the strongest of the Trilogy and expansions, and in some ways is the weakest.
I played FEAR 2 and 3 back to back, and FEAR 3 has the better sound, graphics, and cutscenes, the AI is slightly improved over the previous games and the variety of enemies had increased.
On the downside, the biggest strength of FEAR 2 is that the story telling was something that was incorporated into the gameplay and you learned the background as you played through which was a huge improvement over the original game. You wanted collectibles because they advanced the story. In FEAR 3, there are collectibles, but they only really exist to improve your score .... yes, each level gives you score, you play for numbers, rather than story. These collectibles are dead bodies you can psychic link with, and Alma dolls! which only function to give you a better score at the level's conclusion which breaks the immersion. The story is brought to it's conclusion (or is it?) and while it was the least interesting of the games (for me), it really wasn't enough to give it a thumbs down. Try to pick it up on discount.

I think Reus is a very elegant god-game simplified down to a very fun level. Some people like the ability to actually influence specific citizens or creatures, I prefer the Reus approach where the little factors all are automatic and you just make big decisions. Some people also prefer an open-ended game, while I prefer the goal oriented design of Reus. You can play for as long as you want even after the era ends so I'm not sure why some people complain about it.
I am rather confused on why many reviews call it a puzzle game. Yes, you have certain objectives meaning you need to structure your cities in a certain way, but it doesn't pigeon-hole you into a puzzle by any stretch. For instance lets say you need 100 food to make a farm - you could plant some bushes, or you could make your grassland an ocean and make fish, or you could put chickens by your bushes, etc. Or you can choose to destroy the farm and make something else. The tech tree is quite substantial and there are countless ways to build each city. This is no more a puzzle than making a research centric city in Civilization. You build the things that boost that one aspect and reduce the others. Perhaps you need to make more trade-offs in Reus and people don't like that?
The only criticism I have is that after you unlock everything the game is kind of boring.

Reus is an indie god game that often plays more like a puzzle game. Instead of single god, you actually control four different giants who shape the land and place down various resources. Soon enough villages start popping up and begin demanding various things. As is usual in a god game, you only control the four giants and have no direct control over the villagers.
On the surface Reus might look like a fairly casual game. There's a decent amount of complexity under the surface, however. The villagers will demand various resources for their projects and these demands will get harder and harder to fulfill. You also need to be careful when improving your villages. With rapid growth the villagers get greedy and can start attacking the neighboring villages.
The core gameplay consists of placing the right natural resources on the right tiles on the map. This is also the part that makes Reus feel more like a puzzle game than a typical god game. Optimal placement is rather crucial as the resources boost each other in numerous ways based on a complex symbiosis/transmutation system. Personally I found this part of the game quite fiddly and rather unintuitive. The game could definitely have used a better in-game help system for all these bonuses.
Each game has a fixed time limit (only 30 minute game is available early on, later you unlock 60 and 120 minute games). To unlock longer games and other features you need to complete as many developments as possible. The developments are goals that require you to grow your villages in specific ways. As the game length is limited, you can typically only complete a few new ones in each game.
I wasn't a big fan of the slow pace of the game either. You need to play a lot of games to complete the various developments, always starting with the same empty world with only the basic giant skills available. For me this got repetitive fairly quickly. After a while I decided I don't have the time or patience to continue playing and just gave up. Perhaps a more traditional campaign would have helped to keep things more interesting.
While Reus does some things quite well, I wasn't a big fan of the fiddly resource micromanagement or the slow pace. I'd recommend this game only if you don't mind these issues or if are a big fan of the genre. Everyone else is better off waiting for a sale or a bundle.
The good:
- Nice and clear art
- Good difficulty progression with more and more things unlocking as you keep playing
The bad:
- Game is rather slow-paced and there's no way to fast-forward time
- Gets repetitive and you need to finish a lot of games to complete the various developments
- Resource placement and the symbiosis/transmutation system is rather fiddly and not very intuitive
The ugly:
- A few minor UI issues like wrong font size and an empty dialog window

1- GENERAL
Reus is a strategy God game where your control and coordinate 4 different giants (oceans, forests, rocks and swamps) to provide to a planet conditions to humans to settle and prosper. From where do the humans arrive? Who knows, but they came in a donkey.
You start in an empty planet when the giants awake, and then you have to coordinate them and all of the available abilities to sustain life and unlock new stuff during the predefined amounts of gameplay time. Yes, you are not able to choose how many time your gamewill last...

2- GAMEPLAY
You start from playing 3 different tutorial, and they are very good to be honest, and then you start your slow paced journey through eras. Having no fast forward option surely helps giving the slowish feeling to this game.
Placing minerals, plants in animals in the correct spots to boost production to the max is the secret. This resources will allow us to finish projects that will give us ambassadors, that unlock new abilities, that will allow us to upgrade the resources, to allow new projects to get new ambassadors, to unlock... you understand the point. In top of that you are not able to select projects, and people sometimes are bumb and select projects impossible to finish. Some upgrades are worse than the previous version of the resource, and I do not know that previously to the upgrade. That's not normal.
If you give a lot of resources at a time, people will start to become greedy and will start wars against other villages or even against the giants, and then you'll have to just finish them off. That is fun, but some achievements depends in having war, and you need villages to have those. Bummer!
It's not hard to unlock all content, but you can get bored quite easily with the lack of content of the game.

3- CONCLUSION
This is a small and fun game, but with not much to offer. The general mechanics of the game is very good, but I was a bit disappointed with it. It seemed different when I saw some gameplay. Do not get me wrong, the game is fun and entertaining, but it lacks some must have stuff of this kind of games.
At the moment only costs €9,99 and I think this is a fair price for what the game offers.

A god game whose whole purposes is about frantically rearranging resource buffs in an optimization puzzle to satisfy the peoples' demands.
Met demands give you gods more abilities to improve your resources further, and this usually involves changing everything, because each resource synergizes differently, and makes you make significance changes to adjacent resources, then the ones adjacent to those, etc.
There's meta-progression as well - each world only lasts a fairly limited amount of time so you will need to start fresh on new worlds. Earn achievements, unlock more stuff that can make you more productive the next play through to help you earn more achievements.
Again, this is a resource placement optimization game. If that interests you, this game should interest you. Otherwise, not so much. $10 I feel is a reasonable asking price for the game, if still a tad high for my tastes. Sale purchase recommended.

TL;DR: This is a nice god-themed puzzle game, with nice graphics, innovative design and fun gameplay. But it has its shortcomings.
In a nutshell, in this game you play as four Titans, each one with unique powers, and by laying out biomes and sources (animals, plants and minerals) and upgrading them with your Titans' abilities, you can make suitable environments for humans to settle down into villages. Your villages will then request random Projects from time to time, and by fulfilling them, you get either Ambassadors that upgrade your Titans' abilities and structures that provide your villages with resources. As you complete goals (achievements), which usually requires your villages getting a certain amount of resources, you unlock further sources, which can be used to complete more difficult goals.
To fulfill your villages' Projects, you will need to combine sources and structures that sinergize well. For instance, the Apple Tree will provide extra food and tech if you place it near an animal. The Granary will provide extra food if next to plants.
By using the resulting Ambassadors you get, you can unlock better Aspects, which in turn you can use to upgrade your sources or turn them into completely different ones, which you'll then use to fulfill more demanding Projects.
And you must do it all while managing your time (you're on a timer), the different interactions between your sources, and also your villages' Greed, a game mechanic that prevents you from building things too fast, or your villages start wars against one another (or against your own Titans).
All in all, these mechanics make up a very nice game. However, you may expect that:
1. It will require a lot of brainpower to get all the important achievements. Considering how they are necessary to unlock all the sources, it can get frustrating at times if you plan (as I did and failed) to get everything this game has to offer.
2. You're on an undelayble timer; you can't upgrade every Titan ability to its fullest potential (you only get a certain number of ambassadors per world, which are not enough to upgrade everything); the projects you villages start are very random and sometimes too demanding; the different Aspect tiers required to unlock different sources are very difficult to get; the sources interactions are very complex, and usually replacing one requires replacing several others as to maximize their sinergy effects.
3. Sometimes, you'll feel lost. You'll need several different villages, usually at least one of every biome, and you need to tender to their needs often. Sometimes you'll need several complex sinergies between your sources, and that will require very careful planning of sources layouts. Sometimes, a very useful source will be out of your reach because you've chosen to upgrade the Aspect of one Titan over another; sometimes, you won't be able to give a Titan the Aspect you want, because doing so would jeopardize your plans. Sometimes, your villages will start dumb projects that go against your plans. And very often, replacing a source or getting a new Project requires replacing several other sources, so as to maximize their sinergy.
4. In order to get the most difficult achievements, you'll fall short of having to plan the entire world layout and Titan upgrade path beforehand. If you wander just a little from your plans, you may not achieve the goal you want.
5. It may get repetitive after a while, and the worlds you create are not persistent.
6. You will check the game online wiki frequently. Do you remember the innovative Civilopedia, the one in-game encyclopedia that every complex game should have? It doesn't exist here. And several critical pieces of information (like upgrade paths) are not available in-game.
Despite these shortcomings, if you like complex puzzle games, you'll really enjoy this game. Just beware that this is not truly a god game, despite what the Steam tags would make you believe.

All in all I would say a 7/10 with room for improvements and I am a little biased as I am a massive sci-fi fan, so keep that in mind for you own decissions.

There's a reason why so many people end up not playing this game even after putting countless hours into it. It's completely reliant on having a group of friends to play or the game will just end up being tedious and completely boring to play. Matchmaking with other randoms is never fun since most of them play as if they're playing alone and they basically look at you as if you were the JTF AI friendlies (who are useless). This game is balanced around playing co-op and there is no balance at all for people who are playing solo. I tested how much health increase or spawn rate for enemies and it doesn't seem to change at all if you increase the amount of players in a party. So basically this game is only fun if you have friends who are committed to playing with you or you are so patient that you would look up solo builds and crawl (oh there's no crouch or crawl button) through missions very very slowly.
I know this game is completely an RPG and is not meant to be a tactical shooter but at least implement ai (for both allies and enemies) that don't involve braindead men with guns who either stand still and shoot at you, take cover randomly, lob grenades that have a range of an entire street or rush your position just because they have a ridiculous amount of health and know they can kill you in 2 seconds or less. I know the bullet-sponge enemies are meant to be a thing but come on the ai is clearly aware of this as the enemies with less hp such as the snipers will run away like little pusses when you come for them.
There's just no fun to be had unless you have friends who actually play this game. The graphics look great. It runs with little to no frame drops (even on my craptop). The shooting is decent for an rpg. The customization is okay (you can collect the same cosmetic over and over with a different colour. I collected 5 beanies in a row with different shades of blue.) You can't really say it's pay to win either but it's pay to unlock more content for the game (after paying $60 for the base game). The matchmaking system is absolute garbage. Leveling up only unlocks higher level gear and occasionally a slot for passive skills. Unlocking abilities require farming for 3 types of supplies (medical, technology and security) and then using the supplies to build parts of that facility (your "ultimate" ability from which there are three choose from is also unlocked here). Looting feels pointless because you only loot for consumables which don't really turn the tide of a fight (only useful consumables are the explosive and incendiary ammo which gives you extra damage for a set period of time and the consumable that lets you do more damage to the "elite" enemies because they have so much damn health).  You can only hold 2 of each of consumable which is a terrible limit. Maybe at least 5 because they have a global cooldown. In terms of gaming, the Ultima VII games, which I spent tonnes of time playing as a teenager, are in my top 5 favourites of all time.
I started backing SotA off the back of my love for the Ulima series, and off of Richard Garriot's notariety and reputation, in the belief that his involvement with the project would result in a product that illustrates the same affection for the genre as so many of those earlier games did.
Having been following the development, and playing the game on and off for over 2 years now, I've now resigned to the fact that this game is and will always be only *barely* playable.
Everything about it, from changing the resolution to exploring the dungeons to crafting is unfulfilling, frustrating and unpolished. The beautifully-crafted landscapes and artowrk are obscured by relentless perfomance issues and countless bugs that are being blamed on the Unity engine (which.. the game devs conciously chose and chose to stick with despite all of these problems). There is non-existant customer support. The documentation and world map archives are massive, and both services are maintained by 3rd-party volunteers. You find yourself spending more time looking at the 3rd-party documentation trying to figure out how/what you need to do and where to go than you actually spend trying to play the game, let alone actually spending your valuable time enjoying the experience of playing.
Games should be intuitive, engaging and fun, and SotA is none of those; don't waste your money.

If you like turn-based strategy games and scheming, then buy this game. You probably won't thank me directly because you'll be too busy playing it for ten-hour stretches and resenting that your meat machine body can't supply the endurance that your addicted mind demads.
Details: This game feels pretty bottomless; it's very complex and that in itself is a huge bonus to replayability and also very rewarding. At the heart of it is its AI and the game's tech tree.
AI is (at least seemingly) more complex than one is used to, playing favourites and scheming alongside you. They have a general "like" factor toward everyone that affects how they react to events, and how aggressive they are. In the most recent game I had, #1 position started to attack me (in #2), so everyone floated me ships to fight back and it worked; not because they liked me, but only because it was better for them for me to assume all the risk in fighting.
The tech tree is massive and you will not research it all (unless you really make a point of doing it). The technologies range from implements on planets (improvements), to political systems, to weapons and support modules for ships.
Trade between civs is vital, and balancing taxes with social/military/research spending and espionage spending is a game in itself.
The units (ships) have modules that are unlocked by your technology. You can use the vanilla computer-designed ships, or you can put together your own purpose-built fighters/support/scout ships (by means of clicking on items and attaching them to the hull). Engines, life support (range), sensors (view radius), weapons, and defenses are all up to you. There are three weapon types and three defense types specialising in protecting for a specific weapon type.
Meta-managing your civilization plays a role in this game too. You get to adopt political systems and depending on the system, you will be subject to an occasional vote (to see if your desired party bonus remains), and may receive bonuses if certain criteria are met. You must keep your subjects happy. Though you can do some unsavory things like set up some "special police" that keep the happiness high.
There are number of victory conditions to compete for in this game. In my most recent game, I ended up being cast into a pretty terrible corner of the galaxy. I aggressively spread through some far systems and started to work my way into 2nd place. I started whoring myself out technologically (selling tech) and monetarily (you can pay for the stuff you "buy to complete now" choosing from a few types of loans with increasingly-lower amounts of money down and higher weekly payments). The game worked itself up to a head-to-head between just me and #1 (who I couldn't attack by my choice because of their alliances). I fought fiercely and managed to usurp their military power; but they were close to winning through ascension  (~50 turns and falling). I spent the better part of a couple hours combing through the map for a  base to blow up, trying ot turn the tides of war. I thought I had found it, only to see my work result in an extra 30 turns or so before I lost. I was madly racing to keep afloat, selling the least harmless and more-valuable tech off to last-place civs in an attempt to keep my army and civilization with a positive figure in the vault. With 4 turns left, I used a purpose-built scout to find what I was looking for, blew it up, and I was then on a level playing field. I haven't been that engaged in a strategy game for a long time. Right now, our civilizations are evenly-matched in power, and I fear that as soon as I bring my opponent to their knees, the rest of the galaxy will seize the opportunity and all be on my♥♥♥♥♥at once.
Highly recommend if you hunger for complexity, involvement, and strategy... hahaha

One of the best, if not THE best, fighting game I've ever played.
Yes, the learning curve throws people off. Thankfully the tutorial is super-comphrehensive; I've not yet played a fighting game with a better tutorial.
The gameplay is really fluid. Since Skullgirls is so lenient with its inputs relative to other fighters, it's easier for a newcomer to get down the inputs for a basic bread n' butter combo. This leads to players exploring the mechanics of the game and how to use them to their advantage, with a minimal amount of time fumbling over buttons. The netplay is really good too, compared to other fighters thanks to GGPO.
The general artistic direction of the game is great too. Instead of pixel art or 3D models, the sprites for each of the characters is hand-drawn and animated, with a custom-made lighting engine to add a last bit of polish. The soundtrack and stages all are consistent with regards to the game's "Dark Deco" art style and, like the sprites, are beautiful (Maplecrest and Under the Bridge being my favorites in both regards).
The game is generally bug-free, and the only thing that I think people wouldn't like about it are the skill curve (which all fighting games have) and the amount of boobies and panty shots in the game (which not all fighting games have).
Overall, it feels like everyone who worked on this tried their hardest on this and treated it like their baby, and it shows.

What caught my intrest with this game was the story behind it. Set in a Post-Apocalyptic world where robots now try to rebuild what the humans have destroyed. The story revolves around the fact that all humans have not gone extinct and the robot government is trying to hide their existence by killing any humans they find left alive. To me this was a great back story, and if executed right could be a masterpiece.
The game itself does not look bad at all. The movement of the grass and trees look amazing, and the gameplay in the city really does a great job of setting a mood. Graphics aside, the camera placement of some areas do get annoying. For example, if you hold "w" while transitioning into another area, you can get stuck in a loop of going back and forth between camera angles. But all in all this wasn't a big deal to me.
The voice acting in this game is on par when you realize the fact that robots aren't really supposed to have emotion when speaking. The thing that doesn't work out with the voice acting is the lines that are spoken. THE GAME FEELS RUSHED. Throughout the whole game, the context doesn't feel as if it is telling a story. It feels more like, "This is your next puzzle, please find out a way to beat it to help the humans." Even when you do beat a puzzle, the new found story doesn't feel as if it was a suprise. You kind of see it coming. I hope they make the game more engaging to the story and less predictable in the upcoming episodes.
I really enjoyed playing this first episode and I plan on finishing the rest. But as of right now, I'm not really intrigued with the story. I will not give this game a thumbs down only because I feel like the game an story hasn't really had a chance to form fully yet.

A rushed cliche' scifi which doesn't know the type of game it wants to be.
The Uncertain is a point and click adventure with wonderful aesthetics, huge potential but is extremely shallow under the surface. The underlying story has potential to be really deep but often flounders with little to no context or character progression. Considering this is the first episode I expected a hook, a reason to want the rest of this story but I was left empty, a little confused and barely enticed.

While this is mostly a point and click adventure and puzzle game a few times it steps out of this genre and adds things like evasive driving which is completely unnecessary and a quite frustrating.
Camera angles and lack of camera controls rival early resident evil games and though the puzzles and fetch quests are simple enough they can be blindingly obvious but require 'future information' to be interacted with.

Credit given where credit is due, this game does have pretty decent voice acting. The main character however sounds extremely depressed and I was hoping this would tie into the story line some how but so far no.
There is one point where a character doesn't have voice lines at all during a conversation which was a little odd and could be a sign of rushed production.
There are also quite a few spelling mistakes in the subtitles and at one part the subtitle says the complete opposite of the voice line, considering this is from a Russian developer one can assume there were some errors in translation. This was an interesting title to get into. I've clocked well over a hundred hours on the DRM free version, so I am speaking from more experience than I appear to be with this one.
A long long time ago I used to really love Populous for the Sega Genesis console. It was a really interesting isometric strategy game where randomly generated maps created a landscape over which I ruled as a god. I could foster my followers, or show no mercy and destroy with natural disasters.
Reus takes this a big step further.
Control elemental giants that can create and destroy, settle the world and watch villages grow and prosper, or destroy. There is a lot going on and this game can get really deep really fast. The tutorials made it easy to figure out the basics.
The game controls really well, and a simple stage can last for hours. Performing tasks such as evolving plant, mineral, or animal types unlocks different other plants, minerals, animals, and so on. This opens up all kinds of possibilities.
Managing villages is fun, and pretty simple at first. Inevitably they make tougher more complex demands. Which can grow tense as timers running for each task count down. I would liken it to spinning plates; try keeping too many going and you might lose track of of one or two of them and not realize you've missed something until it's too late. Other tasks might include fostering a great village only to see them become greedy and destructive toward others. And yet other tasks, or requests, could be sacrificing one village for another to meet shrine requirements.
There's not much I can tell you that you can't read elsewhere and better. I can tell you I enjoy this game immensely, and will probably clock another hundred hours on my steam copy as well. This game is a lot of fun, and a great way to chill for a few hours.
Honestly, I had fun, but if someone had described this to me before I'd played it wouldn't have understood the game. It get's my recommendation though.
This game won't win everyone over, but as a former Populous fan, I'm hooked!

A very sad near-complete waste of potential. Should have been great. Comes close to being great. Ends up mediocre and frustrating.
So, you think this is a god game, right? Well, not so much. It's more of a puzzle game. The gameplay is based on villages that can use a few tiles around them, and you have to use your giants to put resources on those tiles and improve them. Pretty much all the resources have interaction bonuses, so you have to place the right combination of resources in the right order so as to get maximum progress for a village. It's not as fun as it sounds.
The first annoyance is that there's no in-game guide to what the upgraded resources do. You can see what the current level's possible upgrades can do, but for the levels after that, you have to alt-tab into the wiki. And since different level resources have wildly varying effects, this is important. The same applies for placing a basic resource - what you get depends on the terrain, but there's no tooltip for it, so either you have to memorize it or alt-tab into the wiki. Or just place something to find out. But that's not a good idea, because the giants' abilities are on cooldowns.
And speaking of cooldowns, you'll be annoyed at those a lot. See, you can't just freely place resources to solve the maximum efficiency puzzle. No, there's a cooldown on the resource-placing ability, and a cooldown on the upgrade-boosting ability. The latter is very important, because without it there's a 67% chance of getting the bad version of the "aspect" that you need to place in a resource to upgrade it. And you'll be dealing with this multiple times, because the game goes something like this:
- Place initial basic resources
- Complete projects for villages to get more powers for your giants
- Use those powers to upgrade the resources
- Rearrange resources because higher level resources have different combination effects
- Use resources to complete more projects for villages
- Get second level resource planting abilities
- Re-plant, re-boost, re-imbue and re-upgrade EVERYTHING!
- Use resources to complete MORE projects for villages
- Get second level "aspect"-imbuing abilities
- Re-plant, re-boost, re-imbue and re-upgrade EVERYTHING!
- Dunno what's next. I got too bored to continue. According to the wiki, there's a third level to the abilities, so extrapolate that into more re-doing everything.
Add to that the fact that village projects take up tiles and wipe whatever you had placed there upon spawning, casuing you to potentially have to rearrange everything in the area, and you get a lot of frustration.
Now, all this on its own wouldn't be too terrible. What makes it inexcusable is that the main game mode has an arbitrary time limit. A limit of 30, 60 or 120 minutes, your choice. After you unlock the longer options, of course.
Yes. You read that right. A god game, a management strategy game, has an arbitrary time limit before it wipes your progress and you get to start the next session on a barren planet. I'm not joking.
It doesn't need to be said that one of the major appeals of this type of game is the opportunity to craft a working city/region/ecosystem/whatever and have it sitting there for you to admire. This game goes in the opposite direction. You get a short time frame to set up a few villages before the session ends and reports what achievements you've gotten and what upgrades they've unlocked. Then you start over, using the upgrades to get more achievements.
There exists a free play mode, but it feels hollow, as you're locked out of the progression system. And you'd have to cheat first to get the unlocks, because free play only lets you use what you've unlocked in time-limited mode.
Another thing that needs to be mentioned is how disappointingly simplistic the humans are. The store page description promises virtues and vices, and your giants praising and punishing them. In reality, a Greed stat is all there is. It goes up when the village still hasn't begun using all the resources you've made available, and it goes down when the village catches up. That's it. It's a pretty transparent way to implement an arbitrary limit on the speed of village growth, and this in a game with arbitrary time limits on game sessions. I don't get it.
A predictable aggression mechanic is shoehorned in - at about half greed, the village will start attacking other villages, and at full greed it will start attacking your giants. If the latter happens, you have to destroy 3 armies and it will become peaceful and go down to 0 greed. This mechanic tends to be quite annoying, because there are achievements (and associated unlocks) tied to villages winning a number of wars, but they stop attacking other villages if they get too greedy (and turn on your giants), so you have to keep providing a surplus of one type of resource, waiting for the greed to go up until the village catches up, waiting for the greed to go down somewhat, then replacing the tiles with another type of resource, waiting for the greed to go up until the village catches up, etc.
All that said, the game is still close to being great. If it was based on unlimited play, with unlocks becoming available as they're achieved, not at the end of a session, and with village projects being built on the tiles already taken up by the village instead of on resource tiles, those 2 changes alone would be enough to turn me into a fan.
Gameplay aside, the game is at least quite visually appealing.

Considering this is not only a (loving) parody of JRPGs, but was also originally a Flash game, this game is somehow really amazing.
The turn-based battles are pretty simple, but the summoning system and being able to swap in a backup character - even when the one you're swapping out is dead- is a nice change. And the variety of weapons, armor, and accessories give a ton of options to tackling enemies. Then there's the fact that they can all be upgraded to be even more useful.
The art style is simple too, but also pretty clean and nice to look at. Basically, it won't turn any heads, but this game is technically several years old from the time of Kongregate. The characters all look really nice and have a lot of charm, especially in their idle animations that love to add in a few fun references. And the characters themselves also have some fun personalities and banter. I really only wish that there was a little more development involved in it.
Next up is the music, which is very fun-sounding and doesn't get tiring to listen to. And considering the soundtrack is free, its definitely worthwhile. The only real complaint I have is that the tracks themselves don't seamlessly loop like you would expect, so it's pretty obvious when they do.
One of the biggest differences from the original browser version is the addition of Battle Mountain, a side world with extra-tough battles. And grinding isn't an option since levels scale (but try to come back later with more skills). It's a nice addition that will keep you coming back for a challenge, in addition to the game's already solid level of content.
This game is overall a fun experience, that while a bit dated, can still bring some chuckles and enjoyment. So play it if you like simple turn-based RPGs.

I've been playing this game since it came out on Armor Games and Kongregate. EBF4 is the latest entry in the Epic Battle Fantasy Franchise, an RPG series inspired by franchises like Final Fantasy and Pokémon.
It has an unique and recognisable artstyle and a quirky sense of humor. There is some story to be enjoyed here, but unlike some other RPGs, you will be playing this for the gameplay. You will be surprised by the lenght and depth of this game. One thing to note though, is that this is in fact a flash game, which means the game does require a mid-grade computer despite the games' simplicity and the steam overlay/keeping multiple tabs open doesn't work as well as usual.
Even so, grabbing it for either a sale or the full price is a steal in my opinion.
Pros:
-Quirky cast with the same tone of humor
-Decent Story
-Unique and colorful artstyle
-Good Game Lenght
-No random encounters
-The ability to save anywhere outside of battle
-Surprisingly deep and fun gameplay, while still being very a accessible RPG
-A small party of well balanced characters
-Tons of videogame and other references
-Decent game config options
-A good amount of saves and a autosave feature
-4 difficulties to choose from, providing a good challenge for everyone
-Side quests and Challenging extra content to get even more stuff and replayability
-Good character progression/equipment system (you should find this out for yourself, discovering what I'm talking about    here is part of the fun!)
Cons:
-Only on pc (although there are ways to get around this, including the web version)
-Somewhat low frame cap (although it really doesn't matter for an RPG like this. Trust me, you won't even be bothered by this unless the game lags for you.)
-No Shift + Tab Steam Overlay or F12 Steam Screenshots
-Responds somewhat slowly when switching tabs
Other things to note:
-Good pieces of music, although there isn't that much music in comparison to the size of the game, which means it might get a bit repetitive at times when you've played the game this much.
-There is some puzzle solving involved, although I personally think the puzzles add to the game rather than taking away from it. These won't change according to difficulty, but you don't need to be Einstein for this stuff.
-The humor can get a bit weird sometimes (boobjokes, for example), which you will either love or hate about this game.

-Completing the game 100% requires a lot of time and mastery of the game. A lot. This might be annoying to some, but does provide a good challenge.
I recommend this game to anyone who is open to games with semi-serious story. You don't need to be a hardcore RPG fan to enjoy this game at all, and you get a lot of bang for your buck. It happens pretty often that the ones playing these games become dedicated fans of the series.
Epic Battle Fantasy 5 is currently in development and is shaping up to become even better. Epic Battle Fantasy 3 is also available for free on Steam if you want to get a good taste of the series first. Be sure to check those out if you're interested.

This game is a basic dungeon crawler meant for quick play sessions. If you know that getting into it, you'll be fine. If you're expecting something like Diablo 3 that you can sink a grand total of 50+ hours into it, look elsewhere. This is a party game, it's something you play with friends or to just relax and have fun after a long day.
First of all, multiple people can play on one screen (which more PC games need to do!). I have an Xbox 360 remote and I can give that to a friend next to me and I can use the keyboard and mouse to play. It can also be played online. The controls are not what you'd expect from a top-down dungeon crawler, but they work. WADS moves, mouse attacks. With older Gauntlet games (Arcade, N64), each class would have ranged abilities. Even the warrior threw axes. This Gauntlet, melee classes are melee classes, ranged classes are ranged classes. Warrior and Valkyrie use swords as melee weapons, the mage and archer use their ranged powers. This seems like it was done for two reasons: One, to compete with Diablo 3 and two, to stay on par with modern games. The typical gamer is not going to buy a dungeon crawler where every class is ranged.
I played the first act entirely, hoping it would change. It did not. The entire first act is a tomb. When I got to act 2, it was a cave. If act 1 was any example, all of an act is the same as the first level. Don't come here expecting to explore a vast mountain range or anything from the classic games, it's all in the most literal sense... a dungeon crawler. Now, that is kind of a let down, but the dungeons themselves are fine. There are traps to avoid, keys you must collect. It's all very straightforward and doesn't B.S. you. What you see is what you get. The sounds are very awesome, they harken to the classics. Arcadey dings and so forth. Makes picking up items more satisfying. However...
The combat is overtuned. I get that they wanted to stay in line with the old games, but it's too much sometimes. I played on normal and in 4 hits, my shield wielding valkyrie was dead. You cannot carry potions, so if you find yourself locked in a difficult boss battle with one sliver of health left, you are probably screwed. You have to find food to replenish your health and it does so on the spot, which is fine. But because of the difficulty, you will find yourself running mobs in circles behind you as you sloooowly pick them off with your special abilities like shield toss instead of engaging in normal combat just to avoid dying. The two bosses I fought did not properly telegraph their moves. The green ghost would fire a laser and I'd have a half second to do anything to avoid it. The mummy boss would stomp me and in the blink of an eye, before his foot hit the ground, I was shot across the room and had 1/3 of my health destroyed.
On the subject of that boss, I did not understand what I had to do for 10 minutes. (spoiler) There are two circles on the ground on the sides of a larger one in the middle. They turn the larger circle when you stand on them. I was supposed to make the boss stand on the larger middle circle while I turned it by standing myself on the smaller ones, but this was never shown to me or hinted at in any way. When I used them correctly, it took a very, very long time to notice any change happening to indicate I was doing it the right way, so it took me a lot longer and I was under the impression I was doing it wrong.
The mobs hitting so hard on normal is disheartening, especially if I want to do it on harder difficulties, of which there are two more above that and an easy below normal. If I die in four hits on normal, then surely the difficulty above that is a nightmare. It might appeal to the sadist in some of you, but your average gamer is just going to find frustration. So, it's a toss really. It kind of also seems a little lazy how almost every room is just you killing mobs that spawn out of these spawner towers that you have to destroy. Most rooms are just you breaking the spawner, clearing the remaining mobs and moving on to do it again. If you're okay with that, it's still fun. Just don't expect complex battles. It's monster mashing in its most basic form.
There are four classes. Warrior, Valkyrie, Wizard and Elf. There's a fifth DLC class - Necromancer. I have played three, the valkyrie the most. Valkyrie tosses her shield and uses a sword at melee range. She also has a dash with a polearm that leaves you open to attack so it's situational. The shield toss is a lot of fun and gratifying. Tossing it as it goes through mobs on its own then returns is great. She can also raise her shield and deflect attacks. I find her the easiest to use. The warrior uses melee weapons, the wizard uses magic only. Now, the wizard I found to be difficult for no reason. You have to switch magic by using two button combos. You can create combinations like fire+shield = something I forget, and so forth. Most of the spells have long cooldowns except for the more basic ones and it's hard to remember them all. But, when you get used to it, it's a pretty awesome and interesting take on the spell caster class.
Every other level, though, I had to run from Death himself. He would show up, chase me for maybe 20 seconds, disappear, wait another minute maybe, then repeat. He chases you the entire level and it happened every other map. It got old, fast. It should not be so frequent. He only does it on certain levels, but it's a bit lame and forces you to run through some of the rooms and not get any of the gold or food. The items you have to pick up are only food, gold and potions. Potions give you a use of special items like tornados or speed boosts and the food is self-explanatory. But... you can break the items with your attacks. This is annoying. If I toss my valkyrie shield, it seeks the food out if it's near enemies and breaks it. If I'm trying to break boxes in front of an item so I can get it, I will 9 times out of 10 break the item by accident. It's an unnecessary aspect of the game and ONLY serves to frustrate. If it wasn't so easy to break the items, I'd let that one go and say that it's to make you be more careful. With all the chaos going on, it's difficult to be that meticulous.
The announcer was neat at first, but he nonstop reminds you of things like not to destroy items or that you're close to death if your health is low. I do not need constant repeat reminders that I am going to die if my health is low. His frequency is too high.
There is also a shop outside of acts you can use to buy items but they are largely useless. Armor upgrades are locked until you clear higher acts on higher difficulties, which I'm most likely not going to care about because, if I'm past halfway through the game, I'm not going to care about gearing up unless it becomes necessary. The armor should be something you can buy and use earlier in the game so that we have more time to enjoy it. The other items are utility items like speed boosts and freezes. Maybe they can be useful in a pinch. I can see some people enjoying them. But, this means you have to pick up potions to use which you are going to accidentally break half the time. Still, I did enjoy the tornado. It was a lot of fun using it and watching tons of mobs get sucked up into it and flung about. The freezes can be useful if you find yourself getting cornered.
The game is good, I do recommend it. Just know what you're getting into. It's a basic, quick-session monster slaying dungeon crawler. It is not complex but it isn't meant to be. If you're okay with that or looking for some fun to have with a friend, get it. It's on sale for 10 bucks right now and, at that price, if you're a gamer, there's no excuse not to get this. If you can ignore the minor issues this game has, it'll be a great buy. I suppose with a bigger game like Diablo 3 or Dungeon Siege 2, the issues I mentioned would matter more. But here, it's excusable.

3) Is exploration something you like or not?
If you answered yes give it a go, if you answered no then dont. Shroud of the Avatar is the spiritual successor to the Ultima series of games.
The game is a throwback to how games used to be.  It features an overhead map where you load into various scenes, similar to the early Ultima and Final Fantasy games, a quest and dialog system that does not hold your hand (no ! floating over people's heads here$, and a skill based approach to leveling your skills.  Want to be a plate mail wearing Fire Mage?  Go for it!  Your armor may cause you to fizzle a few spells but your build is still viable.  Want to be a renowned carpenter creating furniture, bows, or arrows for other players?  You can do that too!  And with the same character!
The most positive aspect of this game however is the community.  Hop on over to the official forums to get a feel for the types of events that players are putting on.  There are plays, gladiator tournaments, poetry readings, astronomy sessions, taming seminars, happy hours, and musicians putting on live shows.
This game brings back the concept of what it means to be in a sandbox.  It's a lot of fun.
Now, onto the negatives and please do remember that this game is still in early access.  The games engine is not the most pretty and load times moving in and out of scenes can seem excessive although they are more manageable with a SSD.  The graphics can appear dated although there have been times when I've stopped to take screenshots because everything came together so well that I had to capture the moment.  The interface is clunky, the quest system may be difficult for people used to being led around by the hand, and there are times when you will feel lost (as the stories and questlines are not finished).
But, with that being said the game is a blast and I hope to see you in game.

First, I will address the question most people are considering when reading a review. Is it worth the money at the moment? For me, $15 for 2-3 hours of gameplay is fine. It is comparable to a movie with the benefit of direct interaction. You decide if that is enough game for your money.
As someone who has played a lot of point-and-click adventures, I would not put this on the level of old school LucasArts classics like Monkey Island, Full Throttle, The Dig, etc (primarily due to length). However, it is a notable step above anything Pendulo. I was not frustrated with the experience, but I came away from it unsure if I would buy the subsequent chapters.
The story is compelling enough. The player is afforded the opportunity to experience the protaganist's struggle with his perception of humanity, technology and education.
All characters feel a bit too one dimensional. I would like to see them have a slightly broader range of emotion.

The environments are varied and visually appealing within the framework of the story.
The music is good when it exists. There are many transition moments where the protagonist moves to a new environment, and the game just goes silent. It feels extremely anti-climactic. This makes the game feel more hollow than I believe the developers are trying to convey, and for me, it took away any sense of accomplishment in clearing the area.
Movement is a significant downside of the game. The protagonist moves too slowly in larger environments. I suspect this is intended to give the player more time to examine surroundings, but it feels like the game is gradually slowing down.
The puzzles that are not fetch-quests are pretty good. I would like to see more actual puzzles and less running back and forth in the upcoming episodes.
The dialogue trees and interaction readings are okay, but the pause after every line feels like an eternity. Also, I hated being locked into hearing something because of an accidental button press or forgetting I had previously interacted with an object. As a personal pet peeve, if I play the next chapter and hear the protagonist call something "useless", then I will immediately turn off the game and request a refund. If the character thinks it is useless, then why would it stand out as something the character should interact with in the first place? That is so illogical that I wish the game allowed you to kill the main character for the sake of catharsis. I do not think that is how the developers want me to think of the main character.
Ultimately, I say Yes to a recommendation for this chapter. I will probably read reviews and developer comments before buying the next chapter though. The Uncertain flirts with some much needed new ideas for this genre, but it needs to be a more immersive experience (music/movement) in the next chapter.
EDIT: I nearly forgot about something that is more of a note for the developers. There is an ability to skip ahead to a specific item pickup while in the last environment of the game. I will provide more details if the developers are unaware of this.

The Uncertain: Episode 1 - The Last Quiet Day is an atmospheric and story driven adventure in a post-apocalyptic world inhabited by robots, and driven by logic.
The majority of the game feels pretty laid back, but there were a few brief moments of excitement during the playthrough. A lot of the game play is walking around, exploring areas, and clicking on everything to learn more. At first I thought it would be a point and click adventure, but you do actually move and control your character using the keyboard.
Like many other adventure games, you have to follow the exact sequence of events, and I would have liked a little bit of flexibility. (For example, I had to go on the charging platform, and I knew I would need to power it up first. I couldn’t power it up though, and I had to click on the charging platform first for the game to tell me that the power wasn’t on.)
The game took me about 2.5-3 hours. Given how great the game looks and sounds, part of me can’t help but think that if the game had been a first person experience, it could have been even more immersive, and even more enjoyable. I still liked the game though, but the first episode has a lot of buildup, and is very slow paced. It ends right where the action feels like it’s about to begin. It’s certainly a game worth checking out if you enjoy games with a similar feel to other story rich point and click adventures. However, you may want to wait for more episodes to be available or a sale price.

So sad to not recommend this. But the thing is, it's just not fun to play.
When I saw the art and the idea and the trailers I was hooked. I thought it was brilliant. I got it and was even making plans to buy a copy for my 10yo niece so she'd have some fun and learn a bit about how nature works, how it interacts with humans, how symbiosis works, those kinds of things. Did I have too high expectations? Maybe.
When you get to the gameplay, problems start to arise. Let me try to list a few:
1) The planet is super small. As far as I could find there's only one size, that's it.
2) Then you go through the tutorials. Which is a nice thing of course. Except that you can't save. And the gameplay is a bit boring so I wanted to play for a few minutes, save, and come back later. Nope, can't do that. Gotta endure the whole thing at once.
3) There are three tutorials (eras). Every time you advance to a new one it starts from scratch. Oh, come on. I just spent some time building and caring for my planet and first thing you do is take it away from me and make me start again. And then again. And then again. Really?
4) My misunderstanding but I thought gameplay would be a bit more... natural and less calculative. Everything is numbers calculation, there doesn't seem to be any space for a more natural and organig development, for luck/chance, nothing. That's not how nature works! That kind of mechanics might cater for some but it's not for me.
5) The main gameplay seems to share that major flaw with the tutorials: You won't care for "your planet". Because you'll play for 30 min. and ditch it, then for 60 min. and ditch. What? :(    I don't know but I love tycoon games and one of the things I like is how attached I grow to "my city", "my prison", "my civilization". In Reus you seem to be just starting over all the time.
Anyway. I could go on but these were the first/main things that struck me. To be honest I couldn't wait to just close the game and go play Banished or Prison Architect or Civ V or Cities: Skylines or
that may have a resemblance to this one. They are all just... better and more fun.
The art is beautiful and the idea is amazing but the gameplay falls short. It's repetitive, boring, calculative, and just not engaging or entertaining enough. A real shame as my expectations were high and I
wanted to like it so much.

tl;dr its gud.
The game draws deep influences from old time metroidvanias such as Super Metroid and Castlevania: Symphony of the Night, and mixes them with some newer games with more palpable gameplay elements for lesser complexity. Aquaria is probably another huge influence on this game, both artistically and gameplay-wise.
Everything related to the gameplay mechanics is pretty solid within the game, the player is easily able to grasp what is supposed to be a puzzle or not, and it's easy to notice if you are able to solve it at the time, or if you need a newer power to solve it later. The game is pretty solid, with 1 big world map, the player has a lot to explore, and the powers the player gets have great influence over the world itself. You feel more powerful as you get more upgrades for your character. And also, nothing feels too easy or too hard, everything is suited for a balanced overall experience. The only flaw within the game is the combat system, it is not as solid as the whole platforming, level design and doesn't help the fluidity of the game sometimes, with some burdening and annoying enemies that halt your progress for some seconds if you don't deal with them, and dealing with them doesn't feel interactive.
The soundtrack and sound effects are superb, similar to Child of Light's soundtrack most of the time, but still unique, helping ambients in the game feel different, and apart from each other, each with its own theme, and each cutscene with its own music, sound cues help the player many times, and none of them are too awkward or annoying.
The art direction is amazing, the level art is incredible, with unique aspects and props for  each level and part of the world making it easy to tell apart one place from another. The character design is excellent.
The story. The story is exceedingly good, overwhelming, so many unexpected plot twists, it is something that picks the game from others, the story is unique, and very well written, its pace is rock solid, easy to understand, out of this world. The main characters are also very significant to the whole story, none feels wasted, and you can feel the life within the forest.
Overall, it is a huge piece, an instant classic with all of the elements deeply connected into each other, the game is rock solid and if you don't enjoy it, then there's something wrong with you.
