This review is intended, first and foremost, to be helpful for people browsing and considering whether to buy. Like most reviews ostensibly are. This is all written by and geared towards a new player, and thus written in layman's terms and not game lingo. I have something like 86 hours on record as of this writing, so I'm not really qualified to comment on high-level, end-game content. And obviously I like the game, so don't pin me for not including or glossing over some aspect that makes you or your favorite Youtuber upset. I'm a casual.
My bottom line up front is: if you're reading reviews, try to acheive balance in the information you abosorb. See the negative, see the positive, but identify things that you think you'll like about the game and how it does thsoe things. If you've done that and are still on the fence, buy it. With my 86 hours I've not completed the main story with either of my two characters, and am still enjoying it. Most developers can't dream of how to keep a player base past 40 hours, much less twice that. There are players with thousands of hours into this game and the most recent patch (1.8) rolled out a ton of new stuff for them to do.  If there's one thing all these updates say about Massive, it's that they CARE to retain players.
Ok, so to be a little organized:
Main Story:
Fantastic. Very well written, somewhat believable, and usually fun missions. The voice acting for the named characters is typically quite good, and the presentation of missions is clear. The issue I have is that there's not a lot of depth to the characters, good or evil. On that, there's essentially zero morally grey options. Everyone in the game is either a green health bar or a red one. Take that for what it is. You also will not be making any choices, really. You do have some autonomy in how you move around the city, sure, but the districts are level-locked. That is, the enemies in the area always spawn at Level 19 if it's a level 19 zone. Nothing stopping you from going in as a level 3, but the design is such that you won't much feel like it. You won't be able to complete the missions if the enemies are much higher than you unless you're insanely skilled (new players, like me, are probably not).
All that said, if you accept the game's structure like that and go block by block it definitely contributes to the feeling you're "taking the city back." However the pacing is insane. You'll take a baddie hideout and send virus samples to the lab, which will be analyzed, tested, and turned into a report in about... 6 seconds. You'll jump ten levels in a few hours, accomplish a bajillion side missions and encounters in the span of 24 hours. Doesn't feel too realistic. This pacing will be talked about a bit later.
Gameplay:
I think it's solid as hell. To me the controls feel fluid and in tense moments it's rare that I can't run, climb, duck, or dodge in the direction I desire. The gun mechanics are generally solid and very satisfying. Each weapon class has a distinct feel that makes learning each class a bit different. Once you get comfortable with how LMGs handle, you feel a sense of pride and putting more rounds on target. Headshots with your sniper rifles are extremely satisfying, and enemies  are aware enough in most cases to flank you, forcing you to switch to your secondary on most engagements. But the biggest thing about the gameplay, and potentially the most unique aspect of The Division, are the talents- basically powers.
The powers unlock early and often, as long as you're running the main story's PVE content. It gives you the choice of what to unlock and when and how to use it. The number of combos is pretty high, and unlimited. Want to use a sticky bomb and health station? Sure. Want to pair upgraded cover with an enemy-finding pulse? Great idea. Want to mod your sticky bomb into a sticky flashbang and throw a flamethrower turret down beside it? ENJOY the barbecue, fella. This openness, this freedom in HOW you play is where the game comes into its own. There are also a dizzying array of options that come with your gear which enhance your abilities, giving you buffs to your guns skill or more HP. It gets VERY deep, VERY fast, and you will happily spend hours just going through your gear and guns and talents making sure you're maxing out your particular, unique playstyle. It works very very well.
Dark Zone:
Uh oh. Yep. It's available to lower level players, but that doesn't mean MY DZ experience is anything like the higher level dark zones. Here's what I've observed. During the early hours, everyone is curious about the Dark Zone. You go in, sneak around, come up against an NPC mob who folds you in freakin half, then you run away screaming. You don't even see another player. You go back to PVE and story content, but that urge to return to the DZ is there eating at you. So you gain a few levels then go back. This time you're stronger, you join up--officially or not-- with some other players and take down the mobs together, exhilirated by the fact that you're DZ rank is increasing. (DZ rank is totally separate from your real world, ie story mode rank. Though your damage output and other stats inside the DZ are all based on your story world rank)
So the first time you enter the DZ is a truly unique experience. The transition from "safe" world to DZ is one of the coolest transitions I've seen in a game, and it's utterly seamless. Same with extractions. Unique experience in gaming for me. Such a sense of accomplishment and teamwork.
So you keep doing this until you get sick of meeting the same NPCs, doing the same blockade, etc. Then you just start going rogue for the hell of it, and it's addicting. Grouped up or alone, it's a blast. Yes there's a gear gap, but at the lower levels it seems much less pronounced. You will have all kinds of players in there and the skill gap is VERY obvious with your level that low, dealing such small amount of damage with so little HP. If you get the drop on someone and hit them in the head with a full mag, you'll probably win that fight. If you get the drop, miss your shots, srcrew up the timing of your medkits, and he lays into you with a full clip of machine gun ammo, you'll lose, like you should. Fights have the ability to drag out, and going back to your build, it feels a lot more like EVE online than COD.
In EVE, your build is very very important, but it's not going to save you if you don't know how to fly your ship, pop your skills and use the game's systems to your advantage. Same in the Division. The fighting and looting and crafting, tweaking your gear and your guns, it's all the preliminary work. It's not going to win the fight for you. Don't take the Dark Zone personally, it's just the Dark Zone. It's unique in the land of gaming and the risk/reward is FAR more forgiving than in a place like EVE's nullsec.
Inconclusive Conclusion:
So again. There are lot of things this game is not. A buyer has no claim to ignorace these days.  Don't buy it expecting it to be something it's not, and expect it to magically be for you what hundreds of people have said it's not. On the things it does deliver, it delivers very well. If you're hoping for the witcher-level side quests, do not buy. If you want fallout 4 levels of crafting, do not buy. If you want character development ala The Last of Us, do not buy.
If you want a beautifully rendered open world that gets you in the fight to try out YOUR unique playstyle as often as possible, then yes. This game is all about your fighting style, and rewards you with new gear and loot to help you either get better at that style, or try something new.

This game is a blast from the past for me, and I'm very happy it's on Steam. It's a fun little Flash RPG, with silly humor and goofy battles, but with incredibly solid mechanics. The battles are fun and satisfying, and can also be pretty challenging on max difficulty. The only issues I feel are worth mentioning are the following two: the character balancing, and the graphics. It's not that the graphics are bad, I rather like the art style. But when you try to play on fullscreen, it lags like crazy, even on higher end PC's. As for character balance, it's hard to ensure all party members remain relevant throughout the game. In my experience, it's typical for people to settle on the three they like most and just roll with them the whole game. While this isn't really a bad thing, I think it would just be more interesting for each character to be built for a certain role, and perhaps to have all 4 fighting at the same time. Regardless, this game is very well made and I loved it long before it ever won any awards (which is hasn't, shamefully!), which is why I nominated it. Great work Matt, Looking forward to EBF 5!

Not as fun as I hoped for. It's a classic point-and-click adventure, which is nice to see, but lacks a lot of the refinement one may see in others.
The movement feels... so... slow. Even with running, it feels about half as fast as I would like. Even characters talking is slow! The subtitles can be read about 70% faster than the spoken lines are delivered, and the spoken parts are NOT skippable. And be careful examine any object, as you can get stuck in a monologue! It hurts me everytime. Pacing: 5/10.
The puzzles are unique, and do challenge you to think a bit. Even mundane tasks like flipping a power switch become tedious, lengthy mind games. Not really fun, but challenging for sure. Puzzles: 7/10
The graphics are quite amazing. The scenery is beautiful, the environment feels real, and the characters are all unique. The parts where it is raining are a little nauseating, as what I can only assume is water flowing down the camera lens distorts reality. Graphics: 8/10.
The story has a decent setup to it. Perhaps given a little more time to develop would have really hooked me, but I was at the very least interested. 7/10.
My largest gripe is the main character: R2-Jack-Off. Is he happy, sad, or confused? You’ll never know! His tone is monotonous, which is not surprising for a robot, but it also lacks… personality. It’s hard to understand why a character should make a decision if you can’t tell how he feels about it!
This is more disappointing when you realize his face is a screen that can change and move! It shows a battery when he is charging, a question mark when he doesn’t know something, and a diagnostics screen when he turns on! You can show an entire range of emotions with just a few facial changes!
Is he gaining new, startling information? Raise an eyebrow! Is he having to make a tough decision? Loading circle! Surprised? Big♥♥♥♥♥exclamation point! The two horizontal lines are the lightbulbs in the empty house of his mind. No one’s home. Character: 3/10
Overall, the game isn't bad, but a few more tweaks could make it quite amazing.

I've been playing this game since release, and still come back to it once in a while.
Most people compare it to Black and White or other god games, but it has its own flavour, combining god and puzzle game genres into an innovative and appealing mix, suited  for both casual and hardcore gamers (with me being hardcore one).
Pros:
1)Refined and innovative gameplay. This game is similar to none, a definite musthave for a strategy or fantasy or puzzle gamer, who have seen it all and needs something new.
2) Nice graphics. Your giants are really cute, and its interesting to observe how the population changes according to buildings they manage to finish with your help.
3)Replayability. Each game is short (30-120 min) and you can and should try different approach each time, depending on facilities your villages randomly decide to build. Just a note: this random is not infuriating...mostly)
Also, there are numerous viable approaches and plant/animal/mineral combinations, which are fun to find out, try and compare. I should also mention that there are several modes of playing.
Cons:
1)Just one. The creators of the game abandoned the development of it, leaving it with some minor bugs and typos. Bugs are mostly of such kind, where the description is slightly different from what is really happening, but it's not gamebreaking.
Nevertheless, 10/10.

1.  SOTA is simply imo, a throw-back to "text-based mud" and old school RPG/MMO games.  It will not hold your hand, or even attempt to give you directions.  It literally forces you to "think" and try to READ and figure things out on your own.  What's the bare minimum you need to enjoy this game?
1. SSD drive.  If you do NOT have a solid state drive, (aka you have a hard drive), i'm sorry, but you need to stay-away for now and wait for optimizations.  I hate to alienate players but the load times would be unbearable IMO and ruin the game.
2. A good 3-4 hours of actually sitting down and devoting yourself to understanding/grasping what to do and whats going on.  If you cant turn off your music/tv/and thoughts, then this is a wash.  Stay away because you will throw this game in the trash and walk-away.
3. An understanding that this is NOT a "twitch" game.  Its a throw-back to actual strategy/thinking while you're in combat.  It gives you time to actually counter a parry/dodge, to run behind cover and actually start healing.
4. An understanding, that I have NEVER seen a dev team pump out with this kind of accuracy Patch after Patch, EVERY WEEK ON-TIME!!!

500 + hours invested, I have played SotA since Release 15. The game has had its ups and downs during the ongoing devlopment as the dev team molds this game into what the players want ( a succesor to UO). Many backers were frustrated and there are plenty that still are not happy. However, The game has VASTLY improved as well as the number of active players.
Be warned this game is a time sink and thats just one reason why I love it! Every avatar is a creation of each players time and EFFORT. Not since playing UO have I played a game that has required so much effort on the players part to level up mold their avatar in to whatever class/skill combination they want, skills are open to all classes (there really arent "classes"). It could take a casual player several months to level up an avatar enough to fight level  3-4 skull areas (area levels are marked by the number of skulls on a stake).
This game can also be a money sink. SotA is buy to play so the dev team needs to continue to make money for ongoing development and support. There are "telethons" held approximately quarterly in an effort to raise additional funding for the game and I completely support this idea as long as progress is being made. Special rewards/rares are made avaailable to avatars donating to the telethon.
Yes it is grindy, but all the grinding is purposeful if you are playing the game correctly and using all gathered resources collectively to maximize crafting skills.
Those of us that backed the game early recieved tax free lot deeds, which to my knowledge are no longer available. Any new player is going to have to pay taxes on their lot. I actually enjoy the position based combat and having the ability to move my focus of attack by moving the reticle and positioning my avatar in a postion of advatage (If there is one, as in standing uphill). The combat is fluid and fast paced. There are a huge amount of recipes to learn for each crafting skill. There is plenty of stuff already in game to keep any avatar busy for months.
The game is still in development, there are no mounts as of yet, but I can say that I do recommend the game for players who are looking for that old school satisfaction of putting the time and effort in to a meaningful character and account that down the road if you decide to quit playing, may be worth quite a lot of real world cash ;)

Overall, I would absolutely recommend that anyone interested in concise story-driven experiences check this out. There isn't a whole lot of traditional "gaminess" in To the Moon, and it actually works slightly to the games disadvantage when it does throw in a flip puzzle every fifteen minutes or so, ostensibly for the sole purpose of adding more player interaction to the narrative. But To the Moon knows its strength and smartly focuses on them.
The story is told beautifully and the music interwoven with the narrative works wonders to convey mood against the decidedly lo-fi graphics. The characters and their interactions with one another are enjoyable and aren't lacking in dimension, which would otherwise have been a deal-breaker in an experience like this. Similarly, the length of the game felt perfectly edited - nothing seemed to run long and the punchiness of the storytelling came through at just the right moments.
That said there are a few rough edges that could have been ironed out. Playing the game with a 360 control worked, but the limited range of movement (cardinal directions) was stifling and would have been better suited to using the D-pad, though the game only works with the analog stick. Walking around with a limited range of motion was made even trickier by inconsistent collision. While they looked nice enough in most cases, there are many cases where the game's graphics do a poor job of identifying what the player can and cannot walk through, leading to a lot of awkward bumping into things like a specific patch of grass while being able to walk through another next to it. Near the end the game throws in a strange action scene with no stakes that feels completely out of place and nearly derails the pacing of the story - the tedium of this sequence was magnified by the horrible button layout it forced me to use on the 360 controller. While the storytelling was usually on point there were more than a few instances where the dialog seemed at odds with the tone of the game. Comic relief was welcome, and even worked well at times, but the game often went awkwardly far out of its way to make cheap pop culture references for seemingly no reason.
While To the Moon has few bumps in the road, none of them are enough to tarnish an otherwise fine story. A short ride that anyone can play without fear of a game over or any fear of losing with a big emotional payoff, it isn't hard to recommend this one.

I had heard of this game but really knew nothing about it, so when the free weekend popped up recently I figured I'd give it a go. I was really pleasantly surprised! It has a very Borderlands feel to it, but set in an incredibly detailed version of Manhattan. The world design is SO well done. The ambient noise and events are very immersive, the graphics are quite impressive, and the designers really did a great job of putting together a Manhattan that has been mostly abandoned on short notice. Trash is piled up, cars have been abandoned where they sat, and leftover people are everywhere struggling to survive. One thing I really appreciate is how well optimized the game is. My older rig runs it on high settings with no issues save for a few sign textures taking time to sharpen up as I got close.
The story premise is pretty good and revolves around a terrorist virus release on Black Friday. There are hundreds of collectables hidden thoughout the gigantic game world that are voiced and provide background information. The in game missions aren't bad but I felt the story wasn't told as well as I would have liked in them. I found characters were mentioned that I knew nothing about. It was a little jarring to suddenly have to deal with some new person I didn't know, though the aforementioned collectables help you learn about them all in time. The idea of The Division, a set of sleeper agents within the US to be activated when everything else has failed is a little silly but easily forgiveable.
Not unlike Borderlands, the gameplay does get a little repetetive. I never found it to be too much of an issue as I find the shoot and loot mechanic pretty fun by itself. There are a small number of special abilities that you can use and that can be customized and it allows for multiple types of character builds to suit your playstyle or different game modes.
The PvP/PvE area of the DarkZone holds a lot of promise but as I was playing solo I never really enjoyed my time there. I would sneak around and pick off NPC's to get their better than average loot, only to suddenly be swarmed by 4 human players with matching clan tags that killed me and took my stuff in a couple of seconds. Perhaps with teammates it would be more enjoyable. I have always been more of a lone wolf type player though so we'll see if that happens. I also haven't tried the dedicated PvP modes because of this.
Finally, the end game content I have played so far has been decent. There are a variety of daily and weekly missions and activities that you can grind out for various game currencies that you can use to buy gear boxes. If you are a fan of grinding for better gear or want to grind for set items to complete a gear set you are working on, you have many choices of how to go about it.
All in all I am really pleased with this game and can see myself coming back to it repeatedly over the next while. If you are a fan at all of loot collecting type games then give the 6hour/8 level trial version a shot. It will give you a very good idea of what to expect. Highly recommended!

So, so many things wrong with this game, but in short: they forgot to think while designing it, and threw out so many good, already working ideas through the windows.
We got back Point Man, the mute hero from the first game, but in F3AR we have multiple awkward third-person cutscenes where people talk to him, and he just stares angrily like a neanderthal.
The combat features "evolutionary slow-mo modes" that's apparently still revolutionary, 6 years, 2 games and 3 expansions later. Also the combat is strictly cover-based shooter with iron sights, auto-healing,  bad granade-throwing physics and bad AI, ocassionally a mech section. Also it has about 4 different types of enemy if we don't count the different weapons on them.
*edit: and a sneak peek into AI: I crossed a corridor and got hidden behind the corner, and the enemy started having radio chatter about how did I vanished, impossible, and started to repeatedly look after me in a 2m*2m room without them realizing that I can not be there.
The gameplay has close to no horror elements, just sh*tloads of gore because apparently blood paintings = horror. The game ignored the second game's story and Fettel is still just a spirit, despite him having a new body (so a gimmicky coop can work), and changed the storyline so Alma, who was multiple times stated went straight-out crazy (and murderous) around 6 YO, was actually a misunderstood child who never wanted to hurt anyone but "her demons" were drawing out the evil in her.
The whole game just... changed from dark and threatening and manipulative into teenage horror movie props and save the little girl themes... and also don't forget the levelup and xp system that makes so many xp popups on the screen during playing that it's severely distracting.
Add the abysmal looking graphics to this - it looks like someone smeared vaseline over the screen, everything is blurry that's more than 4 metres far... I can't believe that Fear 1 and 2 looks so, so much better than this game.
The only positive thing I could point out that's the coop campaign because it's really rare that it's present in games, but uninspired cookie-cutter covershooter with slapped on FEAR story and bad graphics doesn't make me want to relive the campaign ever again. It was well enough once.

Overall I would recommend this game for people who enjoy casual relaxed TD. 10€ Fairly high price indeed, but in terms of how much time you can spend playing this game, it ain't that much.

Once again, a game that has been with me since i was young. BTD was an old series thought up by Ninja-Kiwi (or taken upon by NinjaKiwi) about Tower Defence. It came around in the time when Tower Defence flash games were kicking it, and its one of the few to remain popular throughout it. BTD was about a bunch of monkeys keeping balloons from killing them, wierd huh? Well the Monkey's Tricks are spectacular. Each Tower has its own pros and cons, and can upgrade based on two paths, each one can be upgraded up to twice, but then you must choose which path the Towers upgrades finish through, Right or Left. Each one leads to a powerful new Tower that can either do MASSIVE damage to 'Bloons' or help support their fellow monkeys on the front. But, BTD was always a childerens game, hence why its art style is so. The Game has 3 forms of currency, Match currency which resets every Match, Monkey-Money which allows players to purchase elite units, and Coins which allow the player to purchase upgrades for their account to improve lives, starting cash, or Tower attack speed. Leveling is hard and tedious, and if you happen to accidently 'Delete' your save, you'll lose everything and go back to square one. BTD DOES get boring after awhile but can be revived by letting someone else try it out. If you're looking for something to kill time, play with friends, or challenge others to, Bloons Tower Defence 5 is a game for you to try (P.S. They added more towers in the purchasable version, not the free one on their website >:L)

Seems like your typical 4X game.  Fly around, meet new people, and take their stuff.  There's much more to it than that, though.  The AI is exceptional.  At higher difficulty levels it's smart, adaptive, and even cunning in a way a lot of human players aren't.  It also doesn't discriminate between player and AI since computer players are as likely to screw each other over as they are to go after you.  AI races play to their strengths and try to avoid exposing their weaknesses. - Militaristic races will hit you with powerful ships, economic races bribe others into attacking you, and diplomats form coalitions to take you down.  The game is also very customizable - It comes with its own editing utilities (though you do have to look for them) and designing your own races and ships using the ingame designer is easy but powerful.  My only complaint is that it lacks any real multiplayer capability - If it had that, it would be close to the perfect game.

Easily one of the best indie games of recent years. If not one of the best Turn-based RPGs of all time. Speaking as someone who has never played a traditional turn-based RPG prior to finding this game on Kongregate years ago (Unless Mario RPG counts, which i don't think it does.) I can therefore say that this game is a PERFECT gateway RPG. Just enough depth in it's combat system to make vetrans feel welcome, while not alienating newcomers like alot of other RPGS do (Xenoblade and Final Fantasy X come to mind)
The gameplay (once it gets rolling) consists of 3 party members (with 1 in backup).
Anna is the support class with her basic attacks not doing all to much damage but having alot of skills to debuff enemies or inflict them with bad statuses.
Matt is the physical attacker, with alot of non-elemental high power skills.
Natillie is the Magic user / Healer with most of her power revolving around her ability to deal elemental damage or heal/revive part memebers.
Lance is the glass canon with not much defence or HP, but with a ton of enemy devestating moves.
When you complete battles, you gain EXP and money (In this case, Choclate Coins) like other RPGs. You also gain AP which can be used to level up or learn new Skills or Specials
The difference between Skills and Specials is that Skills are character specific, whereas Specials consist of a pool that multiple characters can learn from. Each special can only be learnt by one party member. This makes for some intresting strategic opertunities as alot of arts are here.
This game also has Limit Breaks, which to be honest, are not that much different than in Final Fantasy 7. But for those of you unfamilliar, Limit Breaks are powerful attacks that can only be used once a character has taken enough damage. What's different here, however, is that limit breaks can be saved for later use as the attack command is still there, where as to do so in Final Fantasy 7, you would need to keep using Magic instead of attacking.
The equipment system in this game is in my opinion the best type of equipment system in any RPG. No 2 pieces of equipment are exactly the same, nor are there any that are inherently better than other pieces. They all have their own use with their own stats and resistances. I cannot think of any other RPG where i was never like "Oh, this sword does more damage than that sword with no downsides. Better sell my old sword for this upgraded one"
The music is annother shining point of this game. Phyrnna did an amazing job. Explaining it can't do it justice, so i suggest you listen to it for yourself.
Overall, 10/10. If you are looking for annother good RPG that isn't too confusing to get into, look no furher than Epic Battle Fantasy 4.

Only downside is that the game is a bit intensive. Lower end computers might want to at least chanmge the graphics to medium (still might lose some frames).
With about 10 status ailments, a ton of summons and skills, tons of equipment, a vast amont of achievments, silly dialogue, a decent story, with all of this topped off with a fourth party member, I have come to truly love this game in the EBF series. Basically you gain experiene completing quests and killing monsters, and then you level up skills by using them - but the great part is, you can't just macro it because leveling up skills draws from your experience pool.  Cast healing touch 100 times and it won't level up if you've used up your experience pool.
What I REALLY like is that I can let skills decay (this is what prevents you from getting infinite skills - though you can get a lot of skills up) and totally change your build.  Maybe you're an archer with air magic (how I started) and you transition to a fighter specializing in sword & earth magic.  Or you go pure chaos mage + fire.
Don't get me wrong, the game isn't done, and you'll see lots of reviews that dismiss the game because it's not finished (or they don't like it)- and that's pretty fair.  It's unfortunate that they didn't read the warnings in some cases - and in other cases they just won't like the game, not everyone likes every game.
Housing - this is where some people get up in arms.  Yes, there's some huge HUGE lots called castles, I think there's (30?) in the game that people got by paying a lot of money to support the game development.  But who cares?  The smallest property size which can hold a 4-story house and 5-story basement (row lot) is 85$.  And it is absolutely possible (at the time of this writing) to grind the gold and trade it for a row lot from someone.  Yeah, it'll take time, but long-term goals are good - and even at 85$ that's, what, a 6 month subscription to WOW?  The game has - NO SUBSCRIPTION - it sold property deeds/pledges instead to fund development of the game.
Pretty much anything can be accomplished in-game as even things like buying a fancy blue version of a chair (that you can craft the brown leather version in-game) can be obtained by trading with other people.
So, DO NOT PLAY - if you cannot take a game that isn't slated to be released for still another 6 months (and may only be hitting what you might call beta around that time), but if you want to get in and play with friends and can accept that there is still balancing, a few crash-bugs to fix, and a growing community (there's been 60k game copies sold, but I think that's fine for a game that is still in pre-release/early access and not launched yet).  If you have any questions feel free to look up "Lord Andernut" in the forums.
The forums do require 5$ to post publicly in, but Private Messages are free.  Buying the game also allows you to post.  (Used to be some targetted spam issues that stopped with the 5$ minimum).
Long story short, I like what I see, I'm enjoying playing and trading with people in-game, but I can't stress enough that it's not done.  So you can level up, and explore, but there's a lot of game-content and game-mechanics still to come.  I'm personally avoiding the "story" until it's finished and polished.

"Computing Machinery and Intelligence." This is the name of the paper, on the topic of artificial intelligence, in which Alan Turing proposes to the public what is now known as the Turing Test. The paper opens with the question, "Can machines think?" Ever since this question has been proposed, a grand topic in science fiction has been formed, comprising years and years of imagination, prose, novels and movies. Worlds where mankind and AI are harmonious with each other, living together in peace. Worlds where robotic prejudice is apparent, creating a dystopian divide between the ruling class and the oppressed. The Uncertain provides a different situation. One where mankind is extinct, leaving behind a war-torn society of intelligent robots. In this world, robots have overtaken humans, and years have passed. Morality is nowhere to be seen, as logic becomes the driving force behind everyday choices and major decisions. That is, until we meet RT-217NP - an engineering robot that desires to have a sense of control, strong enough that it self-deactivated all automatic software updates in order to allow itself to evolve on its own.
The Uncertain: Episode 1 - The Last Quiet Day is, in essence, a fully-voiced 3D point & click game. You control RT-217NP; a seemingly reclusive robot tending to its salvaging and fabricating business in some secluded hillside, wondering what its primary mission might be. You, RT, have been contracted by a construction robot to manufacture a plasma cutter in an effort to aid in the restoration of the city. Right after completing the task, an airship crashes next to your place of residence. That's right, an airship. I guess that's something that exists in the 22nd century. After uncovering sensitive information aboard the airship, a deep and dark secret is revealed. One that penetrates all throughout USS Robotics - the megacorporation that produces new robots, employs the entire enforcement branch of the governing body, and releases crucial software updates to the robotic public.
Forced to cooperate under threat of disintegration, RT begins to unravel the mysterious nature of USS Robotics and the story around it. In this world devoid of morality, you must don a robotic heart in order to face your fears and confront the unknown. Make fateful choices and discover what is being kept from you in The Uncertain's 1st episode: The Last Quiet Day.
RT's path is always filled with objectives that require tasks to overcome. These tasks comprise the bulk of the gameplay in The Uncertain, revolving around solving puzzles, fetching items, and using logic and observation to progress. Many veterans of HOGs or P&C adventures will find no issue tackling or confronting the challenges; however, newcomers to the genre may find certain tasks to be frustrating, obscure, or tedious. Just understand that this is the nature of P&C games in general, but overall, there shouldn’t be any major difficulties hindering progression.
Mini-game type puzzles provide very original and refreshing experiences, even though there are only a handful of them. From hacking and calibrating to rebooting and rerouting power, these puzzles are a nice reprieve from the P&C searches. Pair matching, pipe, and switch games are some of what you will find in your play through. If I had to point out a disappointing aspect of this game, it would be the lack of puzzles, but only because I find them so enjoyable.
The Uncertain masterfully weaves two crucial aspects together in harmony, successfully creating one of the most atmospheric point & click adventure games released this year. These two elements that define the core of the game's immersiveness pertains to its expansive world building, and the accompanying visual design. A plethora of minute details help expand RT's known universe and put you in the mindset of RT and its life as a robot. Some of these details include utilizing robotic amenities and accommodations such as charging stations and built-in music players, to describing RT's waterproof body model in order to disregard weather concerns. Furthermore, within the first half hour, well designed visual cues establish that robots have the ability to functionally operate similar to that of a human society.
As I said before, it takes two to Tango, and the incredible immersiveness of The Uncertain is supported by polished visual design. For example, during transitional cutscenes, the scenery will sometimes flicker or distort; something akin to waving a magnet around a CRT TV. This adds a subliminal effect of viewing the cutscene as if I am a robot myself. Various moments throughout the campaign will also let the viewer go into first-person (ahem robot) view, especially when inspecting objects or solving puzzles. Before I knew it, I became one with RT. Its troubles, its worries, and its fears.
The Uncertain's first episode managed to captivate me to the end. When I saw the final eye-opening cutscene, I had a sinking feeling that the episode was about to conclude, which it did. In a nice cliffhanger. After doing a little bit of digging, it seems that The Uncertain is designed to be spread across 3 episodes, with the 2nd episode to have an expected release approximately 3-4 months after the first episode's release (
). I don't want to spoil the ending, but I know that any game with an episodic structure will generate a specific set of questions that everyone will flock towards reviews to get answered. So here goes.
First, the game is on the shorter side, depending on your puzzle solving skills and intuition regarding point & click adventures. I definitely would have preferred it if the game lasted longer, but the variety of scenery locations helped ease the pain in hindsight. The game offers no method to replay specific chapters, or create multiple dedicated saves, so going for all of the achievements would add a lot of play time assuming you are into that. Second, this episode is not entirely self-contained. There are still a lot of things left unanswered, clearly to be addressed in the subsequent episodes. Third, I still find the first episode to be extremely enjoyable and worthwhile, especially since there is a lack of non-hidden object point & click games on the market.
Hopefully I was able to answer some of the common questions that will be asked upon release. For those that subscribe to a certain price/hour mindset, I would advise getting this game only if you are a fan of sci-fi P&C adventures games. Alternatively, you could also wait for the developers to release their season pass, containing all of the episodes in one purchase. It's possible that they may include some sort of discount. Otherwise, take solace in the fact that interesting P&C games with such depth and engagement are hard to come by, so be sure to check out The Uncertain: Episode 1 - The Last Quiet Day when you can.

Ori and the Blind Forest is an absolutely marvelous indie title that mixes Metroid-vania style gameplay with imaginative and challenging platforming. Not only is the platforming immensely creative, but it delivers a heartfelt and intelligent story that is sure to tug on your heartstrings.
The game follows the story of an orphaned spirit creature named Ori, who sets out on a journey to revive a forest who loses it's life sustaining light. It only took 10 minutes for the game to get me emotionally invested and I enjoyed every second of it thereafter. The classic Metroid-vania formula is done well here, but it's high peaks and most hectic and intense moments will put Metroid escape sequences to shame.
My only minor gripe with Ori and the Blind Forest is that, after a while, the save mechanic becomes too generous. I died 203 times during my first playthrough, but many of those deaths came from me trying to rush through some difficult sections because I could save so often. I rarely felt the need to carefully plan my next move and exercise patience when I didn't risk losing a lot of progress. Just as long as i remembered to save often, I didn't mind dying all that much, and that should never be the case.
But Ori and the Blind Forest gives you a great sense of mastery and accomplishment and the difficulty progression is done extremley well. It's an 8-10 hour experience that left me satisfied and it's a game well suited for speedruns, and I wanted to dive right back in once the credits rolled.
This is one of the most impressive Indie titles I've seen and it is a must own if you like platformers!
Score: 9/10

I have t admit to being a huge fan of the F.E.A.R. series.
I still have my origional F.E.A.R. games on the CD's I bought way back when and all the subiquent add-ons to that first game, I particualy like these because they where some of the last games made where if bought the game it was yours ... no online service required, that's another story ..
I liked F.E.A.R 2 quite a lot but missed all the different weapons we had in the origional game .. but it was OK.
This is my second time with this game, and the first time on this Steam account, I have played through it prior.
F.E.A.R. sometimes get's a bad rap, as being more of a run and gun, as opposed to a horror shooter as the first ones where. To that I have to say, maybe ... BUT ... it is still one of the most satisfying shooters ever made (my opinion) it's just plain fun blowing the enemy away in slow motion.
And I suspect many of the critics that say it has left the creepyer aspect and moved more toward a shooter have adjusted the gamma up to the point it no longer is as dark a game as intended. Let's face it when you walk into a room covered in pinkish blood vs. red blood it looses a lot of the effect.
One thing F.E.A.R. has going for it, and why I decided to get it again instead of another COD title is the fact that once you play through it, you un lock the dead evil brothers abilities. And for a quick, fun, purely satistying experience few games (for me at least) fill that bill. I would concider myself a Battlefield devotee, That is where much of my gameing time is spent online, BF4, and Hardline. When I just want to spend some time playing for fun without the pressures of playing as a team mate or against other experienced gamers I play Dead Space, and Dead Space 2.
I started thinking about this game while playing some MW2 and MW3 Speciacl ops, just having fun, and remembered just how satisfying this game was. Did they get rid of most of the puzzles, and maze's that so many game use now a days ... yep,.. and they replaced that stuf with great shooting action. (my opinion again) whats the best way to screw up a half decent Resident Evil game ??? QUICK TIME EVENTS !!! none of that crap here.
Again I will admit to being some what bias and a fan of the entire series, when I say that this game F.E.A.R.3 is a very re-playable game. You may not re-play it to "re-live" a story, but for a a good satisfying shooter for a hour or so on a rainy day, to take a break from your normal gameing persuits on BF or GTA, or what ever you are into , it does that very well, just as good as Dead Space. As with may things in life it is a personal taste ... some people like stratogy games, some like simulations ( I used to be a hard core sim guy back in the JANE's days and Falcon 4) but I now spend most of my time with shooters like BF because I really like the guns and toying with different configurations and the tactical situations that they solve. But sometimes I just want to play something fun ... and for me at least this game does just that .. it is fun, not funny like Saints Row, but just fun. The weapons sound and feel good enough to satisfy, and slow motioning the sniper rifle or shootgun is a lot of fun.
In summery .... Scarey ... ummm maybe not
Boreing, retracking where you where to figure out what to do or where to go ... nope ... not here.
Solving tedious puzzles .... nope
Doing B.S. quick time events ... nope
Fun ... yep
Just grap a gun, stay on your toes, and have some fun.
Kind of long ... but I really like this game, and wish I had remembered how much I liked it before I bought some of the other shooters I have gotten since.

Lumber Island is a horror game. The game takes place at an (almost) abandoned island, named Lumber Island. The island was full of rare wood, which was really popular for lumberjackers. The citizens of the island needed to leave their home land, because there were deposits of oil under the ground founded. When there was no more oil left, the island was left abandoned.
In the beginning you are drowned in the ocean and looking at a wooden boat. A few seconds later after the cutscene you are on an island in the middle of nowhere. Your only objective is: that you need to explore, survive and find tools to open doors or chests. The game got me good, because I was already jump-scared at the first two minutes of the game. The game is really exciting to play out until the last minute there is.
Pros and cons of the game.
Pros:
- The graphics looks nice
- The game has a controller support
- The game is not too easy and not too hard to play
- The game got the exact soundtract all horror game needs
- The game is cheap
Cons:
- Sometimes you need to restart the game, because some tools you need are glitched
- No variety in deaths
The €4,99 you pay for this game is totally worth it. I look forward to play the game on my VR and to play the sequel (if there will be one).

Here's a real review:
The majority of you shouldn't play this game. That's the truth. In this ADHD and short-attention span era we live in (which I myself have) this game has a steep learning curve, especially for somebody like me who's never played games like these before. And even with the three part tutorial (which took me about 2 hours total and which I repeated again), I'm still confused about a lot of things. I also bought Abbey Games' (the developer) other game "Renowned Explorers" which I briefly started up (and which I plan to get further into when I've become a little more comfortable with this game). That game also isn't accessible in terms of play. That's not specifically a criticism of either game or of Abbey Games. To some gamers, the sophistication of gameplay and mechanics is a draw and part of its appeal. That's why I'm not giving this game a thumbs down. That, and the fact that it is kind of fun (albeit frustrating) trying to learn how the game works.
Essentially though, you're dealing with three elements: food, wealth and technology. One of the main objectives in the game is to get efficiency from the land by trying different combinations with animals, plants and minerals which allow you to get more food, wealth and technology from the land and complete timed missions in a village. Completing one timed mission in a village allows you to get an "ambassador" which then unlocks a skill that you can use to help you in the game. The game is obviously more sophisticated than that, but that's my version of a simplified way to explain it.
Only buy it if you have a track record of fighting through (what I consider) games' steep learning curve. I'll update the review as I play more of it and hopefully unlock more developments.

Ori and the Blind Forest is an amazing example of a game which has action, puzzle and platforming elements that nearly perfectly work together, with mechanics and control that are nearly perfect and visuals more gorgeous than any game I've ever played for even a single second.
The game has a death counter like the usual rage games and REALLY hard platforming games. By the end, I had 279 deaths, 149 of them gained in the last zone and boss level. Unlike most platformers however... there's not a single problem with the game's controls. The controls are literally flawless in their execution.
The levels themselves are designed so well with the abilities in the game in mind. Each ability you get, allows you to do something new and will allow you to reach new places. They are all simple to use with very clear limits and conditions to use them. Even the beginning areas have places you need the last ability to access. The only areas you never need to go to, are areas that contain no more secrets, and they all contain secrets.
The character designs are very interesting to me, my favorite being Ori out of all of them for obvius reasons. (She's adorable, cute, agile and very glowy, also she looks like she's one of Stitch's cousins) Though the other characters are great too.
The visual style of the game and the quality of even the smallest things are stunning, every environment being made so well to fit and convey their theme, and to make you feel like you would, if you were there.
At all times, you feel small in a large world and weak. Enemies and hazards will destroy you in 3 hits usually no matter how much health you have. Some hazards straight-up kill you instantly no matter what, like Lava and Lasers.
Due to how the visuals are, I feel it's a good thing that you can't turn down setting other than V-Sync. The game would be much less effective and interesting with toned-down graphics.
The soundtrack works very well with every level and never gets old, always fitting the situation. The music itself is very well-made, all having a great quality to them, easily worth buying the soundtrack for some nice, relaxing or intense, epic music.
Many games have had this said aobut them. To my opinion, with this game it's entirely true unlike many of the others. When you die, it's because you messed up. In games such as the Souls series of From Software, unfair series of platformers from multiple devs, this is said, however there is a very clear difference.
Ori and The Blind Forest itself is crafted so well and with so much love and attention, there's nothing arbitrary in it that's just there to make it harder. There's no artificial difficulty padding unlike in the Souls series, this game is literally near perfection in literally every aspect.
There's no instant-deaths from nowhere, there's no damage that just happens because "difficulty"
You will die many times in this game. As a veteran of Mario games, I got 279 deaths. As a noob to this game, my sister got 1000+ deaths, most of it gained in the last area, which she's yet to complete. Amid this fact, you can create a checkpoint and save anyplace no enemies are, and anyplace you're not in danger of dying from going afk. All it takes is a resource called energy.
Anytime you die, time reverses back to when you last saved. You rarely gain energy from killing enemies and you also gain it from blue crystal plants in the environment, or when you save in spirit wells, but it is a very scarce resource at first.
If you are on the fence, ask yourself if you like platformers with puzzle and action elements. If the answer is even a vague "I guess" then get it.

This game is a sleeper for most gamers. It looks cheap and boring on the outside, but what lies beneath its exterior is a massively complex and brilliantly engineered game. I have looked for other games like this, such as Endless Space, Sword of Stars, Sins of a Solar Empire, and no other 4X game, not even Civ 4 or 5 come close IMO.
The AI is excellent. The developers didn't want to use artificial bonuses for AI to fill the skill gap between human players and what you typically get with most AI's skills. They actually made it so that the AI is thinking and planning while you are taking your turn, so you don't have to wait around for the AI . to perform all of these calculations, which it does. Often the AI will fight poorly when at a disadvantage however, but I always find adequate and fair challenge when I play from some of the AIs.
I haven't played multiplayer, so I don't know how that is.
The UI and game flow is smooth in spite of having a ton of complexity. Prepare for an in depth tutorial when you first play this game. Once you get the hang of it, it's wonderful.
You can wage war or play diplomatically, try to tech up fast or build a trade empire. There are many different ways to play. I have waged proxy wars where I supply another faction with weapons I designed to be effective vs our common enemy, an enemy that I didn't want to go to war with myself due to my trade routes being too close to their territory.
There are just so many situations that can happen and each time you play, there is no guarantee that the same strategy you used before will work again. You have to assess the situation and act accordingly. For example; a faction near me declared war on me, and while I had ships that could fight, they were too slow to intercept the enemy ships, so I scrambled to station them in each of my worlds to defend while I researched warp technology. Those worlds I coudn't get a ship to were lost to the enemy for the time being. After defending for a long time, I sent a small fast attack fleet to strike back eventually leading to their downfall. All the while there where huge wars going on in nearby clusters (clusters of star systems).
Some issues I have with the game are that special events can unbalance the game to the point that you may as well surrender. Like a ship with massive damage and defense emerges and and stars to obliterate all of your ships. Or half of your worlds defect and form their own faction, which is cool, but could have been implemented better. These things can be turned off however.

The Division was overrall a dissapointing game. I bought The Division about 6 months after the game dropped, so I can't say how it was initially, however, when I bought it my initial impression is meh. The dark zone was terribly unbalanced, as I would constantly group up with people and plan things out, but then fail because of being hacking, exploiting, or just having insanely overpowered loadouts. Loadouts were constantly shifting, and making older ones totally obsolete while others were insanely overpowered. Other than the Dark Zone, there was also nothing particularly interesting to do. Most things lacked the urgency, the interest, or the feeling of progress the story had. I noticed another review saying the gameplay lacked the urgency it needed to keep you in the late game, and that is absolutely the problem. The reason I liked the Dark Zone despite the horribly overpowered weapons and rampant cheaters was because of how much fun it was.
Because of how little has improved since release, and how little there is to do past the main story, I've gotta say it is not worth the money at all.

Having grown up with a classic 1985 arcade cabinet version of Gauntlet at a bar down the road from my house, I was a sucker when I first saw the news of a remake. I've played through a couple iterations of the game throughout the years, none of which really felt like the classic but were all still pleasent gaming experiences on their own. This latest remake has the same feelings of team-work or competition between players I loved about the classic, plus nostalgic game play elements such as the mob skeletons, death himself, or just hearing that "Warrior needs food BADLY!" made the 12 year old gamer trapped inside of me go wide eyed and fall in love! A common complaint about the game so far is that there is little to no replayablity, something the developers are clearly attempting to correct with the addition of 6 seasons worth of Colosseum challenges for hardened players to take on. I also fear that those who bash the game for being short played one or two characters before closing the books on the game for good. Each character plays differently in a suprisingly dramatic way, and with the latest 1.1 update we saw the introduction of a new chacter who fit into the game seamlessly. The game only sets you back $20 (a nice price these days) and that's likely to drop in the near future. So if you're on the fence about purchasing The Gauntlet let me just say that crawling through dungeons with friends or strangers is as satisfying an experience now as it was in the 80's (or 90's if you're me).

Certainly a throw back to old school Gauntlet games; this title is fast paced, thrilling, and filled with hours of fun!  I could argue this game is a backlash against the "slowness" of more recent Gauntlet games that lost a lot of those classic aspects when jumping to 3D in the 1990s.  In terms of gameplay, it is the Gauntlet-style hack and slash you've come to expect.  The environments as a mish-mash of typical fantasy motifs, common to the genre.  But, that fits the return to its roots, rather than the use of weird anachronisms and zany bits seen in newer Gauntlet games (which is something I enjoyed at the very least.)  I wouldn't say this game intends to push the envelope, but it is sure to provide a good time with up to 3 other friends.
That said, 20 might be asking a bit much.  This game is quite simply too short.  I'd personally advice waiting until the game goes for 10 dollars or less.  Much of my initial complaints with the game have been fixed (no ability to communicate with other players, servers constantly booting me off, random lag despite all computers playing being good quality, etc), so much of my initial distaste for the game is gone.  Still, it's certainly not perfect and the game will be too short and lacking customization until more DLC comes out.  If you're willing to work past this, pick it up for cheap and enjoy with friends.

would be a good game without its two major problems. I'll give a detailed explanation on both.
PROS:
-Nice online castle building game. It's really easy to learn and everything requires planning.
CONS:
-Major problem number one: This game is pay-to-win. You can unlock in-game cards by playing the game or buying them. These cards give you different bonuses and boosts. These cards can sometimes give you a huge advantage. You can for example buy lots of cards that give you knights. Then you can use those knights to attack other players' castles. I have played this game for over 450 hours and many of my castles have been destroyed by people with OP armies they bought from the store.
-Major problem number two: You need to play it every day. Anyone can attack you at any time and if you're offline during that, there's no way to stop them.
-Minor problem: The time it takes to construct buildings increases progressively. For example, if you build a house that takes 10 minutes to build, the next one may take 12. And it increases all the time so at some point you'll have houses that take hours to build.
-No.

Quite literally my favorite fighting game!

One day, a
forum regular decided he could make his own game that would be a proper successor to Marvel vs. Capcom 2. And it was good.
Seriously, Skullgirls is a labor of love from fans who also happened to be art wizards and super knowledgeable about fighting system design and balance. Then they hired the lady that did the music for Castlevania: Symphony of the Night to score it. It's fast paced, and has a combo system that's satisfying for both beginners and experts. It's got the best tutorial in a fighting game ever by miles, and actually attempts to teach you how to do things like block properly and hit-confirm instead of just making sure you know how to dash and do specials. You can play 1v3 or 2v3 if you feel like it, and the game adjusts character strength for the matchup. You can assign custom assists by simply wigging your stick and hitting a button at character select.
For praise exclusive to the PC version, it's got extensive controller support. Unlike a large number of PC fighting games, if you can get windows to recognize your stick as a gamepad, Skullgirls will probably let you map it however you like, and there's no weirdness with the 2nd player also using a pad/ stick. The PC version updates often, and will get balance changes and new characters months ahead of everyone else. It also appears to come with the beta (at least IGG backers get that, but last I heard everyone did,) which will let you preview changes and sometimes see WIP versions of characters if they're working on any.

It's pretty repetitive: find all the things in the level, go to new level, rinse, repeat. That's not really too much of an issue here. This game is more story than game (an interactive movie if you will), where player interaction exists mainly to increase immersion and aid the storytelling.
It's pretty, in a 16-bit sort of way. The only problem is the icky 4:3 resolution that freaks most PC displays out and refuses to upscale reasonably. That doesn't detract too much from this game, but it sure is annoying.
This game
story-driven. The plot is very novel and touching. It's a real tear-jerker, but this is not $5 tearjob you get behind a Sunoco station in downtown Detroit. This game costs $10, comes to your house, wears some nice lingerie, and jerks your tears real sweet-like. A really well-crafted plot with great character development and structure.
The soundtrack complements the game well, and is very good in general. If you get this game, it's probably worth getting the soundtrack bundle for what little extra it costs.
Sadly, after four hours, your $10 in-home tearjerk is over. That's it. Nothing more. No collectibles, no real achievements. You're done.
As much as this game is great, it isn't really worth ten dollars for an hour-and-a-half-long visual novel that lasts four hours because it's padded for time with a "game", whatever a "game" is. Truly, it's a wonderful story, but if this story alone is worth ten dollars, then Donnie Darko should be on display in the Louvre. So, if this is on sale, go for it. Otherwise, I can't recommend it.
While I can't recommend this game at full price, I would highly recommend it on sale for any price below $5 or $6. It would be well worth it for the story.

I bought this game when it came out, and played it through 100%.  In fact, I enjoyed it enough that I reset the in-game progress, just so I could unlock everything all over again.  Even with all the achievements unlocked, I still play the game, although obviously making my own challenges is required to keep the game fresh.  All in all, I cannot recommend this game strongly enough for anyone who wants to sit back and just make their dream planet.
For gameplay, this game is essentially an evolving puzzle where you need to find which available resources will best go in each spot to maximize the effectiveness.  The challenge results from nurturing your cities fast enough to meet their challenges, but not so fast that they declare all out war on each other.  The visuals of the game give you enough information to tell what is happening for the most part and make the world feel alive, while at the same time not stressing my computer too much (which many other modern games tend to).

This is not only a great puzzle game, it's one of the best god games I've played. I've spent hours in freeroam just messing around with my planet and it's inhabitants.
Reus is, like I said, a puzzle game wherein you wield god-like power. You control 4 Giants: Forest, Mountain, Swamp, and (Mr Krabs) Ocean. Your goal is to place down resources to help the people of the land grow their towns in different ways.

Each giant has a set of powers that allow them to change the planet in different ways. The forest giant, for example, can create fruit plants, Each giant also has the ability to add aspects to placed plants, animals, and minerals, which not only gives the resource a buff, but lets you "upgrade" it into a new kind of resource. Giving a blueberry bush a fruit aspect will a: make it produce more food, and b: let you upgrade it into a apple tree, which produces more food the more apple trees are around it.
While on this topic, different resources have "symbiosis" with other resource types, letting you combo them together to create tons food/wealth/tech. This, of course, is for the humans that live on the planet, and your goal, once again, is to make them as prosperous as possible. The humans, however, tend to be greedy, and if you give them too much to fast, they will begin to attack each other, and then you. A angry mob of peasants fighting agains mountain sized giants goes about as well as you'd expect.
There's more to it but I can't be bothered to explain the whole game. So...
TL;DR
This is a fun little puzzle title with god game elements. If that sounds like something you'd like, go read another review first because I'm bad at explaining things.

You can lock skills in a hotbar like traditional rpgs with cooldowns or you can use the deck system which will randomly deal you glyphs (skills). If you use the unlocked system you gain perks like no cooldowns and the ability to stack multiple glyphs to make the skill more powerful and cost less focus (mana/energy) to use. You can also combine two glyphs to make a new skill. For example Fire Arrow + Death Ray = Fiery Decay. This is a very unique system, that has a lot of room to grow in future updates.
You can tame most animals in the game like spiders, wolves, bears, etc. There is an entire skill tree that will allow you to increase your pet’s base stats as well as learning pet based skills like healing your pet.
You can choose to play using tab targeting with a mouse cursor like older rpgs or reticle targeting which is more common in recent rpgs like tera and black desert online.
This is a charge and active click based weapon attack system. For example, if you have a bow you can charge for around 2 secs to fire a more damaging bow attack or you can rapid click LMB for quick low damaging attacks. If you rather not actively engage in weapon attacks you can enable auto attack at a slight dps loss and concentrate purely on casting skills.
You have to actually look for gathering nodes in the game world, for me this is more immersive and I enjoy it more than staring at my mini map for node dots. For cities you need to take out a cloth map and look for landmarks, this could be positive or negative depending on your preferences.
If you flag pvp you can fight others flagged pvp and loot their bodies. You gain items like "Bob's Skull" which you can display in your home or sell to other players. Concerning gear, the defeated player has the option to buy back their gear via a ransom system, so this is not entirely full loot, but it's much closer than most mmorpgs.
Pretty realistic and straightforward; you're not forced to craft 100 useless weapons before you can make one worth using, although as you raise your skills you will have access to better modifiers. Crafted armor is the best armor in the game, this helps promote a player driven economy and makes finding a committed crafter to make your armor and weapons relevant even for end game gear. There has been a lot of change to crafting leading up to r32, so I expect it to be a focal point of polish work well into the end of the year.
The night is dark enough you need to use a skill or item to navigate it. I like dark nights and pulling out a torch to navigate adds immersion for me, I like environment mechanics that force game play choices.
You need magic reagents and arrows, it's refreshing to run out and have a reason to go back to town. Again this could easily be a con for some players.
The heavier your armor the higher your fizzle chance with be, as fizzle chance increases you're more likely to fail while trying to casting a skill, this makes balancing magic and armor interesting. If you're a min/maxer you'll probably enjoy this system.
These are playable freeform or using MML or ABC files similar to LOTRO.
SotA is instance based much like GW1 & 2. To connect all the areas the game uses an 3d scaled map where you can walk across the world, since the game has limited fast travel options this map offers a nice balance between getting places quickly and still feeling like you're actually part of the act of traveling.
This game has no monthly fee, so personally I think it's a good amount of content for the price.
If you don't have a solid state drive, you can spend a bit of time watching loading screens.
At this stage of development, combat still needs a lot of love. While it does offer a lot of flexibility in playstyles and targeting, that same flexibility can often make it feel like it lacks a solid direction. It has been getting better each release so I choose to remain positive that the direction will solidify as they shift from prototyping to polishing mechanics.
Currently there isn't a lot to do after you've Grand Mastered some skills and done beginning storyline. There are some high level areas to keep you grinding in a party, but it currently lacks complex boss fights. The dev team has been vocal that they'd like to push traps and puzzles in dungeons once they finish the main storyline.
Although you can earn lots for housing with in game currency, the amounts atm are fairly high. If you aren't planning to spend money in the cash shop, expect earning your house and lots to be a long term goal and not something you are going to have instantly. However, much of the community has extra lots and houses and the people you meet or guilds you join may gift you one much earlier than you could earn it in game.
This game is built in Unity, it's not the cry engine, but Unity 5 has had some very nice material and lighting upgrades recently. Currently the graphics and animations are passable, but it's no black desert online. Improvements are being made every release, but don't buy this expecting FFXIV level particle effects and animations. You may encounter NPC monster animations that make you cringe, but in all fairness these are areas you polish last in development and the recent custom models/animations have been much better.
Atm the chat system feels very dated and clunky, there is no world chat channel, so if you like playing mmorpgs to start random conversations in general chat you will probably find this games current chat system lacking.
Despite it's current flaws and being in early access I would still recommend this game to fans of the genre. If you crave a sandbox rpg that brings back some of the immersion lost in recent rpgs, this turns away from quest markers and general hand holding. You'll find that SotA offers plenty for a buy to play game with no monthly fee.

I've been playing on and off since about release 20. I'm a developer level backer but didn't really delve into it until last year (too many other games to play and real life stuff). Over those releases I made a few chars but never really understood what to do when getting into the game. It's not new-player friendly, but neither was Ultima Online which isn't a bad thing. It just means you need someone to help or look up what to do. At the start of this year I got back into it and played through the Solace Bridge starting scene and got to the first area which I've done several times.
For some reason in this play through I 'got it' and worked out how to interact with the NPCs, how to access my quest journal and how to read the map. The map names are in Runic text which I used to be able to read fluently when actively playing Ultima Online a decade ago, but have since totally forgotten. This was initially really annoying as there's an in-game zone map but it's very light on detail and again the names are in runic. The runic letter system started coming back to me the more I worked out the zone's actual name and then started to compare the runic letters with known letters. Anyway, long story short after finally figuring out some of the zone names, there's an option in settings to display the English name as well a runic on the map (#$%!@$%!).
Started questing with a mate and the game started to really shine. As I obtained each quest, used the unique world travel map and then played through the initial few zones, it all started making sense and it was actually really fun and engaging. I started to read everything the NPC's were saying but this gets cumbersome after a while and I then focused on the 'action words' (words underlined) which progresses the story/quest for that NPC. After a couple of weeks (of playing a couple of hours one night per week), my character was starting to get some good items and defeating challenging monsters.
That was until I got up to a certain stage of the 'love' storyline quests and came across red-flagged mobs (red coloured difficulty, like other games – ie. too hard). There seemed to be a huge step up in difficulty with this quest/zone, whereas up until then the progression was very well balanced. I put it down to the devs just haven't fleshed out the next areas/main questline arc etc. I played a bit more after that, exploring other map zones that the quests hadn't taken me to, and dying a lot as the difficulty was higher than my char. I then decided to hold off making any more chars until the upcoming final wipe.
I would recommend giving this a go, especially if you're already a backer, and also if you're a fan of Richard Garriot's previous games, namely Ultima Online. It was really exiting learning the game and progressing through the quests. It is early access and it does feel clunky at times but I knew that and accept it, so enjoyed it for what it is at the moment. The devs really do listen to the feedback, especially the developer level backers who have their own forums to discuss feedback/changes with the devs. This is evident in the multiple examples where the devs have changed direction on gameplay elements based purely on the players feedback (eg. combat re-hall a few releases back).
Definitely worth getting involved, particularly after the final wipe at the end of the month. Will do another review in a couple of months time.

Has Promise, but quest content and "things to do" severly lacking.
I have been playing SotA for ten months now, and generally I enjoy it; however, that enjoyment decreases with time.  My enjoyment has waned enough to change my view from a recommend to a not recommend at this time.
I would say the "bones" of SotA are great - an online RPG with questing and player housing.  Players in game are generally helpful and will stop and chat.  Finding quests is a step back in time with keyword usage to engage NPC characters - this is kind of nice if you want something different from the exclamation point, breadcrumb quest systems out there.  The goal of a sandbox type game with adventuring, questing, and crafting tied into a player driven economy is  nice to see.
The big question is is whether or not all of this comes together in the coming months once SotA is officially released.  This is my worry - in ten months quest systems, quest content and general content in general really haven't progressed in a meaningful way.  There are many, many dozen zones that are "cloned" and have no real content other than generic enemies.  Loot is not optimized and makes hunting very unrewarding.  Quests are not finished and use an old school text keyword system.  While there is some charm in this system and it is nice to not have the WoW and Elder Scrolls Online "!" points to guide you, it is way too old school.  Some quests are literally a pixel hunt for a book or item with very little guidance as to how you should find these items.
The saving graces right now are the housing system is the most robust I have ever seen, with in world housing, thousands of decorating items and quite good placement and design features.  Also, the community is great - player run events are fun and for the most part the players are nice, helpful and mature.
However, playing the game right now, whether crafting or hunting, just is not fun.  Grouping areas or dungeons are lacking, loot is lacking (while crafting is supposed to trump loot drops, which I support, the lack of really anything fun or helpful that a monster can drop is really boring).
I wish I had more hope that this will become more content complete, but the dev team is small, and the quest team even smaller (like 2 to 3 devs doing quest work).  It is a sandbox game without the polish or hooks to probably keep me, and in ten months the movement on those areas has been glacial.  I hope I am wrong, but I am not getting my hopes up...

I must say this game surprised me a bit, straight from the beginning. The graphics are beautiful and the story is interesting and I do recommend it, but I will discuss the two main things that bothered me the most.
You, as the player start the game with no hints as to what your goal but as you start exploring,  the story begins to unfold and you come accross an intimidating enemy whom at this point - you know nothing about.
