Lumber Island- That Special Place is an Adventure game set in a horror setting. Most of your time will be spent exploring and solving odd puzzles like getting a murderer to leave you alone by fetching him his shoes. You play as an unknown entity who you will never see. Not even it's hand is visible when holding a lighter, it just kind of floats on it's own. Starting off you awaken in a nearly abandoned island which is home of a murderous lumberjack that roams these lands. You will have to avoid him as you try to figure out a solution to escape this place. Your character has no means of defending itself and if he is spotted all he can do is flee then hide under a bed, hoping not to be seen. The lumberjack is surprisingly fast so if you spot him close by it may already be too late to flee, in which case he will jam that axe into your head. Dying means starting the area all over which is annoying, however the areas are small and knowing exactly what to do, you can get to where you were before your demise rather quickly. This game has a checkpoint system that also saves the game but you never know when you have reached one. That does make dying feel a lot more frightening though on the other hand you don't know when it is safe to shut down the game without losing any progress.
One of the first things you will notice when you are given control of your character is how sensitive the camera is. The slightest movement of your mouse will send the camera flying and there is no way to change the sensitivity levels. Camera on the gamepad is more tolerable but still far too sensitive, making it annoying to explore the ares for clues. This is made into a bigger annoyance since many of the puzzles require you to find a small object that you may easily miss and searching every nook and cranny can grow to be a pain. After the first beginning area you can take all the time in the world due to only the first level having an enemy that wanders around. That's not to say your completely safe however, there are a few cheap deaths scattered about that you have no real way of predicting. Strangely enough the first areas of the game have the hardest puzzles and after that they make a lot more sense. Being a Adventure game you have to throw some logic out of the window and remember that you can carry anything from a lever to a entire lever in your pants. There is no way to see what is in your inventory for some odd reason so it is best to play this game uninterrupted or you will more likely than not forget what you were doing.
From start to finish this game has a foreboding and creepy atmosphere that has you certain that you will be killed if you take a step further. The lumberjack feels like a very generic enemy that has a sack over his head but the rest of the monsters are very creepy and if you spot one you will not have much time to get more than a glimpse of it's grotesque features before being in serious trouble. You never get a good look at them and are the type of enemies that will surprise attack you and leave you no hope of escape if you wander into a place you shouldn't. There are no indications of what places you shouldn't go in which both makes for cheap deaths and a sense of dread as you are forced to explore to continue. The monsters animations are rather crummy though this works to the game's advantage as their unnatural janky movements add to the sense of eeriness. Your only interaction in this game is a sprint button and a button that picks things up, allowing you to throw them around to find hidden items. Whats rather nice is that you can sprint for as long as you want, unlike many other games where if your character runs more than three feet he will stop to take a rest. You have very little indication of what you are supposed to do but my advise is to look for the teddy bear.
It is a good looking game and can be rather taxing on your system. I experience occasional frame dips and a certain area near the end of the game had me down to the 30fps range due to all the books in the area that could be interacted with.  This game is dark, very dark. Your lighter draws very little light and most of my time was spent squinting at my monitor hoping to find something that would let me advance. The combination of having to find small items plus being unable to see further than two feet in front of you can be irritating. Another annoyance with the game is the music/ambient sound. It is a very short loop that plays through the entire game and quickly becomes tiresome and funny enough the few instances where it stopped the game felt much scary. In your journey to escape the island you will come across notes that either aid you with cryptic clues or adds backstory to the setting. To be perfectly honest the story completely flew over my head and I understood none of it. I'm sure there is more to it than meets the eye but I left the game more confused than when I started the it.
Lumber Island is not a long game by any means. If you are more competent at Adventure games than I am it will likely take you about an hour to complete. It is a low priced game so only you will know if that is a acceptable amount of bang for the buck. The replay value comes in the form of trying to get a grip on the story though that seems unappealing due to having to squint at my monitor some more searching for extra notes I may have missed. I would say it is worth a playthrough as the good outweighs the bad and it is a pretty creepy game. It is the kind of game that has potential but is heavily weighed down by quite a few flaws. It is an Adventure game first and a horror game second as every room seems to have something to find and figure out. None of the areas are large but they will take some brain power and sharp eyes to get through nonetheless. There is very little blood and no gore in this title. It is centered around a few disturbing monsters and psychological trickery to keep you on your guard. When all is said and done Lumber Island is a solid enough Adventure game to recommend to fans of the genre that also enjoy a horror setting.

After partying on a yacht you wake up on a dark, deserted island with no memory of how you got there: you set out to see if you can find someone or at least something that'd help you and soon realize something is very, very wrong.
Lumber Island - That Special Place is an horror adventure where you solve puzzles while trying to stay alive and discover what happened to you, it's a fairly decent title that has enough to stand out from the plethora of Slender clones and jumpscare filled games that are on the Store.
-the graphics are pretty good
-good sound design keeps you on edge and mantains a good sense of tension
-creepy,eerie atmosphere
-decent story and narrative
-some puzzles are quite obtuse and can get frustrating, this is generally due to a lack of clues or the fact they require small objects that can easily be missed or are hidden to begin with, leading you to move books, cushions etc in an effort to find what you're looking for
-one level was very dark with a blue tinge on it, this made seeing where I was going very difficult
-a few cheap deaths
-can't avoid some overdone cliches in its plot or gameplay (chase scene)
-pretty short, unless you get stuck on a puzzle you'd be done in around a hour and a half
-ending is a bit too cryptic
-still has a few glitches
Lumber Island is part of a genre that's quite overdone nowadays, in fact the game itself is pretty formulaic and does follow certain cliches to the letter: thankfully at least part of the story is decent enough to stay interesting and its narrative- that seems to be following two different stories or mindstates- is original enough to stand out.
Gameplay is pretty straightforward as you explore areas, read notes for clues and gather objects to solve puzzles: as said before certain puzzles can be too obtuse for their own good and leave you stuck, possibly dying in the process and foricng you to repeat the level. It's a shame the dev insisted on hiding certain objects or making them quite small as this detracts from the good atmosphere found in each level: thankfully if you're stuck or too frustrated you can find help in the forums or Youtube.
If you like the genre you'd do much worse than Lumber Island, the game is decent and its story is worth a playthrough at least as long as you don't expect tons of originality.

Hello! This is my review for the indie game
I usually don't make reviews for games, but this game is an exception. This game was absolutely beautiful. Ori and the Blind Forest is a staggeringly well-done combination of beatiful art, evoking music, and tough-as-nails but fair gameplay.
If you couldn't tell from the screenshots, the game has some of the best visual design seen in games. Handmade background and foreground art combined with 3d models are weaved together in a way that is much better than it probably sounds on paper. Each zone has carefully chosen colors to represent the state of the forest of Nibel and its corruption. In my experience, I often just stopped in places and just looked at the detail and the designs of the different environments found in the game's rather expansive map.
Gareth Coker must be some kind of genius, because his soundtrack for this game is fan-freakin'-tastic. Each level and scene's music is made with purpose. Some inspire endless and genuine wonder as you gaze upon the Spirit Tree of Nibel, others are a rushing anthem of triumph as you escape a torrent of water chasing after you, and some are terrifying as the great bird Kuro swoops after you, talons poised for the kill. It's beautiful, purposeful, and emotional. It's probably one of my favorite aspects of the game.
Ori and the Blind Forest is not only a marvel in regards to its artistic aspects, but it also has tight and simple controls along with just a good movement feel in general. Some parts of the game can get crazy tough with spikes, monsters, hazards, poisonous water, and even some lava. Luckily, you can make your own save points in just about any place in the game. It's gets rid of a lot of frustration in parts, as long as you remember to actually do it. Jumping around is fun and feels great. One of my favorite little touches is that if you do three jumps, Ori does a little flip. Over the course of the game, you'll acquire new abilities such as wall jumping and double jumps. As you collect these abilities new parts of the world open up to you in that classic Metroidvania style. There's a lot of secrets to be found with your growing repertiore of abilities, and you will be rewarded for your dilligence in finding them.
A good tip is that generally if you see any blue crystals (which give you energy, which is needed to make a save point) then that would probably be a suitable place to save. Now, I've seen some examples/talk of saving yourself into an unwinnable corner, but I've recently discovered that on title screen you can choose previous saves if you somehow end up doing that. I've never had it happen, but it's good that it's there in case it does.
As for the story, I don't want to say much about it. I feel like it's something that needs to be experienced. Although I will say this, I originally pirated this game, but after playing the first 20 minutes of the game I was emotionally destroyed by the game's opening enough that I closed the game and bought it right then and there, full price. It still stands as one of my favorite games ever.

Point Lookout

Mothership Zeta

I could say alot of things about this game in particular. But what makes F3AR a particularly sour note, is that it forced me to re-examine the FPS genre of that time(COD and Halo being exempt)
So, picture this. You enter a room. There are 4 enemy soldiers in that room. Thanks to FEAR's slo-mo mechanic, you drop them with relative ease. One guy suddenly comes down a ladder, and two more from a door to the left. Down they go. Just as the last guy falls, 3 more soldiers burst through a window. Once they drop, finally, a heavy breaks down far door, flanked by 3 more soldiers. After a brief 'boss; battle, all enemies are down, and you may proceed to the next area.
But, did you notice something? At no point in that encounter, were you ever fighing any more than 4 enemies at a single time. This was hidden from you through cleverly placed spawns to give you the feeling of fighting off a sizable force. But you wouldn't know it by the end, because bodies aren't persistant beyond 4 either. Almost every FPS game made around that period of time stuck to this 'rule of 4'. And on top of that, most of them had a slo-mo, or something similar to make getting kills easy. The moment you realise this, the hardest difficulties stop becoming hard once you're aware that you'll never fight any more than 4 grunts at a time.
I'm not downvoting this due to F3AR being a bad game. Because it's not. I'm downvoting because this was the game that made me realise how bland the genre of FPS was back then.

In this game you can control nature but you can't control people.
You manipulate nature through Gigants, sort of elemental semi gods. They have different abilites for terraforming and controlling natural resources. The Gigants can use their abilities in different combinations in order to increase richness and help populations grow and get more resources.
If enough resources are left on an unclaimed area, a new tribe will settle, as the villages grow, humans will start different projects and your challenge is to help them complete those projects. As a reward for helping them, they will give an ambassador for each project completed. The ambassador can join a specific Gigant, giving them new powers or improving their old ones. People will continue starting bigger and bigger projects, raising the challenge level quite fast. Each project will require different types of resources and your goal is to help them get what they need from nature. Eventually, the different settlements will start competing for space and resources, they will fight and die to each other and even attack the gigants if they are greedy enough.
The mechanics are simple. The game is easy to learn but the dificulty raises before you know it. Your decisions will profoundly affect the world so one miscalculation can mean the ruin for you and your villages.
The tutorial teaches you all you need to know (it is basically letting you play a normal game with assistance texts) You can pause the game to think and even give your gigants orders during pauses. Also you can save at any point in case you need to backtrack your steps.
An experience I definitely enjoyed and would recommend to anyone. Weather you are looking for new game styles, are into indie gems or simply want a fun way to spend your time, consider giving this one a try.

Before I go on:
The reason this game has such poor reviews is really based on three things:
1. The expectations for this game were made unrealistic by the public
2. The developers greatly contributed to these unrealistic expectations, and
3. The gameplay and content fell far short of what a triple A title should entail.
The negatives in my eyes:
This game costs far too much ($30 or even $40 would be fair) given its current state.
The gameplay is repetitive (not much of a negative though because who else here has hundreds of hundreds of hours in Minecraft or CS?)
The positives:
Regardless of the expectations, this game did something that I haven't experienced in videogames before, the concept is cool, the execution is good, and the gameplay leaves you feeling lost and alone in a universe that really doesn't care about your existence. The atmosphere is eerie yet enjoyable, and the gameplay is elegant and simple
The developers know they messed up, and have been working towards releasing additional content and improving the game.
Survival mode is painful, and a good challenge for the patient and unwavering.
I have enjoyed the experience so far, and I highly recommend buying this game when the price drops.

Lumber Island – That Special Place is an adventure horror game developed by a single man named Dean Forge using the Unity5 engine. The game was released in October 2015 on Steam.
The game is played in first person as you explore a derelict island which was once a lush forest,, hence the name Lumber Island.  The game gives no real indication on how to progress out when you begin. You are essentially left to your own devices and have to work out everything yourself. You find clues scattered around the island that point you in the right direction of where to go next or how to progress, but no real in your face objectives. Your character is only armed with a lighter or a flash light in the later levels. Thankfully this isn’t one of those games where you have to manage your batteries or fuel reserves, allowing you to light your way to your hearts content.  Each of the four or so levels have one enemy in – these enemies will kill you as soon as they come into contact with you. You can only run from them in order to escape your demise; you have no form of fighting back.  Most of the game focuses on finding keys and opening doors to the next level; this is cleverly masked by other tasks to make it not seem so dull though.
Due to the game not giving you any clear clues on how to progress at points; you do get the feel that you should be looking to progress just a little bit further than last time when you die. Yes you start right from the beginning from the level, but you can soon catch-up to where you died since you now know how you got there, so you can skip out the time wandering around trying to work out what to do. I really liked that the game gives you no aims – the way it words the clues and notes scattered around means you actually have to read them and take in the information for you to actually understand what is happening.  For those that have played Penumbra, this game has very similar traits to that in this sense.
Graphically, Lumber Island does look really good. As it is running on the Unity5 engine you would expect it to be as of a certain standard, but it does go beyond that standard. The lighting in the game could be done a little bit better; but the poor lighting also adds to the horror effects of the game. The animation of objects and characters in the game are all done well; I had no problems there. I did notice a few texture glitches in walls though, there is a faint flicker where the textures join up, only a slight issue but still can be easily resolved.
The story in this game is fairly interesting as well, it has a lot of flash back scenes which do become a bit confusing, but it adds to the story as a whole. You can really immerse yourself in the story with the amount of notes and reports around each of the levels; I would highly recommend people take the time to read them to get the most out of the plot here.
Lumber Island’s soundtrack is one of the most horrifying I have heard; it keeps you on edge constantly.  Whilst playing people actually had to leave the room because of the music playing in the background was freaking them out so much. On top of the soundtrack, the sound effects also play a huge role in horror games; there aren’t massive amounts of them, but the ones which are in, are produced very well and add to the atmosphere.
As I have said before, the game gives you no clear objectives, so this can lead to times when you are literally walking around the levels with no clue on what you need to do next. This will probably put a lot of people off straight away, but if you can look past that element, the game actually still has a bit of difficulty when it comes to the enemies you have to overcome. Some of them will rely on you being quick on your feet in order to escape them, the scene in the third level is one of the most memorable horror scenes I can think of in recent memory, and took a number of retries in order for me to actually pass it.
Lumber Island’s level design is fantastic, the first stage especially, you have so much to explore and find in the world, whilst also dealing with the main plot. Some of the areas on the map bear no importance to the main story but are still there for you to see and enjoy. A lot of care has gone into creating each of these levels to a really high standard.
I finished the game in just over three hours; this was done completely blind with no aids from walkthroughs, so I was actually quite pleased I managed to do it! The game is completely linear though, so once you finish it, there is no need for a second play through.
Technically, Lumber Island is a sound game. Yes I wasn’t able to push out 4k graphics with settings on full, but this is a really punishing game on the graphics, but I was able to get a constant 60 FPS when in 1080p on full graphics. A keyboard and mouse was used to play the game due to the first person nature, and the game is definitely best played in a dark room to add to the effect.
Lumber Island is a real hidden gem in the Steam store; you really wouldn’t think this was made by just one man, and I applaud him for creating such a great game. The price of £3,99 is absolutely perfect for this type of game. Yes it can be completed in three hours, but would you rather experience a really well done indie title, or have that foot long sub? I know which I would choose….

Little can be said about this game, it's just fantastic. Jaw-droppingly beautiful graphics (thought they might sometimes cause a bit of lag on slower machines, like mine), enthralling and powerful soundtrack, with each track fitting perfectly with each moment.
Story's a bit lacking, if I must say, as there are many unanswered questions (I won't go into much detail to avoid spoilers) like, for example, Ori's origin, but honestly that is the least of my concerns, if you play this game, it should be about the experience, it might as well be considered an art game.
Now about the game itself: It's your average metroidvania platformer (surprised not to see a "Metroidvania" tag up there) with a lot of exploration, secret hunting and, most of all, backtracking (not entirely essential to play the game, but completionists will sure do a lot of it). The controls are a bit clunky sometimes, specifically in parts that involve interacting with other moveable objects in order to progress, but as you master them you eventually look past this minor nuisance.
Combat was particulary fun for me, and even if there is somewhat of a leveling system and skill trees, you'll find that grinding is hardly 10% of what you need to unlock all of the abilities. You'll most likely end up "grinding" simply by killing the enemies in your way as you explore the vast territory of Nibel.
In an overall: Beautiful graphics and soundtrack, rather confusing story, yet pretty, when you look at the big picture, tight controls, for the most part and very fun combat. I strongly recommend this game, and I sure hope to see more work by Moon Studios in the future!

What makes To The Moon great isn't its gameplay aspects, but its narrative quality. The main story of To The Moon is touching and relatable. Seeing someone relive their life through memories, through all the good times and bad, reminds us of our own mortality and the mix of emotions that makes up the human experience. To The Mood keeps you wondering what happened with this man, John, right up to the very end. When the story does end, everything ties together nicely but still leaves you reflecting on the experience.
There were several points where I found myself a little annoyed by the relatively poor minigames, wondering why they were included in the first place. But, everything else about this game makes you quickly forgive this lacking quality. The well-paced, touching narrative, combined with an excellent soundtrack which adapts properly to the situation, and the nostalgic art style and settings make To The Moon a memorable experience. Games like To The Moon remind us that the video game medium is a powerful way to tell a story.

To start off, Gauntlet is a pretty fun game. It feels a lot like the older ones in a way but with newer visuals and soun... Now I still enjoy this game and would recomend checking it out. If you like the original feel of Gauntlet, this is for you! However, there're some problems that popped up which I had great fears of before this game even came out. This is because i was more of a fan of Gauntlet Dark Legacy.
Gauntlet is far too short. It has twelve dungeons... no more. Each dungeon (excluding the three boss levels) has three levels. There're also only three different locations you visit throughout the game that span accross all dungeons. The lack of variety in enemies and locations gets a bit dull after a while where as Gauntlet Dark Legacy had eight realms with many different locations and enemies... It also had many hidden levels, many bosses, items, and so much more.
The other problem that bugged me is the lack of character choice... Gauntlet Dark Legacy had many characters you could unlock. While Dark Legacy had its own problems with each character playing the same, this's not the case here.
in short, I do recomend people try this game out. If you liked the original Gauntlet games more, you might like  this one a lot because it plays and feels very much like those. However, if you are expecting the same amount of content as Gauntlet Dark Legacy, then this game is sadly not for you.

"Bloons Tower Defense 5."
A review by Richard Valkinsenn.
"Pop goes the bloon!"
No doubt NinjaKiwi's answer to wildly-popular titles like Plants vs. Zombies, Bloons Tower Defense 5 is the latest and finest entry in the memorable Bloons Tower Defense series. Originally starting out as a browser-based game series, the latest entry has recently seen a full release on mobile platforms like Android and the PC. And rightfully so, since Bloons TD5 is, frankly, one of the finest tower defense games on the market right now, easily stacking up against such titans as the aforementioned Plants vs. Zombies. Featuring a cute cast of memorable characters in the form of intelligent, organized monkeys, the player has to employ said characters to defend a series of widely varied and challenging tracks. The enemy: a horde of hostile, baloon-like entities collectively referred to as Bloons. If too many Bloons make it through the player's defenses, the game is over. It's a simple formula, but one that's easy to get into and spend countless hours with. In addition, there's plenty of modes to play through, including an online co-op mode, daily challenges, and special missions designed to test the player's skill. However, if there's one gripe to be had, it's that the game lacks a story-driven campaign mode, though the vast amount of content the game offers up compensates for that.
Overall, Bloons TD5 is an amazing and very enjoyable casual game that serves as a refreshing take on the tower defense genre, and should not be missed under any circumstances.
Final Verdict:
I love it.

Good for a quick romp with a friend, but sacrifices its horror for cheap thrills and explosive action. F.E.A.R. 3, I feel, suffers from a sort of identity crisis. It is built in a way that suggests it was meant to appeal to numerous crowds, resulting in a game that is a jack-of-all-trades. It isn't particularly good at anything, but isn't particularly bad either.
The campaign, suffering from a story that goes in far too many directions, shifting from tonally disturbing to joyously outrageous, is incredibly disjointed and is marred by shoddy writing and overacting. It feels like it should be campy, but I'm under the impression the game wishes to be taken quite seriously. In the beginning and end there are levels that capture the stakes quite well and have an immersive horror atmosphere, but this is broken to pieces by the Michael Bay-esque action in the middle of the story. It's difficult to determine when you should be turning your brain off and when you should be paying legitimate attention. The dynamic of the two protagonists is a very intruiging idea, but the game fails to represent its own ideas, throwing out the potential for a psychologically disturbing plot and instead diverging with bombastic action (including, no joke, mechs).
Levels are quite boring, shifting from department stores to airports, and a large majority of enemies are agents with guns. The action, in these segments, is quite good, even if there are few weapons to choose from. Both protagonists have different playstyles, so there is some value in replaying this four hour campaign.
Co-operatively there is some competition in gaining more points than the other player, along with the ability to "steal" points from the other player. It is an interesting factor, one that could lend itself well to the rivalry between brothers, but the main protagonist is a silent one. The only banter you will hear is from the secondary protagonist, the dead brother. It would be one thing if the main character expressed himself verbally in any other way, but he does not. He keeps the same angry face throughout the entire game and fails to utter a word. This, in my opinion, is the biggest mistake of the game.
TL;DR This is a really stupid game, but it could make for a fun evening with the right person. I can't recommend playing it solo, so this is best played with another person who has a sense of humor. No matter how hard the game tries, don't try to take the game seriously; you will be disappointed. Instead, enjoy it for what it is: a fragile mess of a game with a few cool tricks and a penchant for changing its tone on a dime. If you see it for under $5 and have a friend to suffer with, give it a go. Otherwise, this game is best left on the shelf.

What makes To The Moon great isn't its gameplay aspects, but its narrative quality. The main story of To The Moon is touching and relatable. To The Mood keeps you wondering what happened with this man, John, right up to the very end. When the story does end, everything ties together nicely but still leaves you reflecting on the experience.
There were several points where I found myself a little annoyed by the relatively poor minigames, wondering why they were included in the first place. But, everything else about this game makes you quickly forgive this lacking quality. The well-paced, touching narrative, combined with an excellent soundtrack which adapts properly to the situation, and the nostalgic art style and settings make To The Moon a memorable experience. Games like To The Moon remind us that the video game medium is a powerful way to tell a story.

I've got to be honest; I'm not entirely sure what the point of this game is.
Alright, alright. On the surface, Reus is a game about creating the perfect environment for a bunch of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ NPCs who get really murdery when you pamper them too much. You do this by placing down various types of tiles whose properties vary based on biome and which can be upgraded further with upgradable upgrades you get from upgrading the NPC villages, which you use to upgrade the NPC villages more. "Upgrade" totally just stopped sounding like a real word. There's not really a lot of room for personal styles in this game; things have to be placed together in very specific ways for optimum benefit, and the game runs on timed rounds so even if you did create something asthetically pleasing it'll vanish sooner rather than later anyway. Going for achievements is all there is.

This game is made for PS3 and XBox360 and it shows. You don't use the mouse at all, which is expected. The keybindings for fighting are somewhat intuitive ingame (although you have to look them up first of course), but it's hard to navigate the menu at the start because buttons like escape and enter don't necessarily do what you'd expect. Once you find the keybinding menu you'll also need some time to understand what is going on. Once you've seen a bit of the tutorial and found the "rebind all keys" button it's fine enough, though.
The largest problem for me was pressing 2 buttons at once in fights. It feels extremely clunky on keyboard and needs to be done a lot because a lot of strong moves depend on it. Most of the time it didn't register both buttons at once but recognized them as different events (example: you need to press "light kick" and "light punch" at the same time to grab, instead my character would kick and then punch). This was even the case when I did the same in training mode with no opponent that is fighting back, so it can definitely not be traced back to my inadequacy in reaction times. This is of course very important in a fighting game. You can solve some of this problem by setting up makros in your controls, which means binding one button on your keyboard to multiple buttons pressed at the same time. You have two of those available. I suggest setting at least one makro up for throws. Obvioulsy, with only two makros available, this does not solve the problem at all, and nor would more makros because you're slowly running out of keys that you can reach comfortably.
There is no mouse control in the menu, which sucks a great deal as well but seems to be a sickness of console ports in general. The same goes for move lists for your characters. When you press the down key it doesn't even scroll, it just goes down one more move, so if you have to look up stuff a lot while learning characters either get ready to hammer away on your keyboard or just load up a webpage and look it up there.
Everything else works, but this is very incomplete in my opinion.
2/10
It doesn't need a lot of options because it is a 2D fighting game. There are separate sliders available for audio, which is good. You can run it windowed, fullscreen or borderless mode. Keys are rebindable, but not separately - as far as I'm aware you always have to rebind the whole set (which is over in a breeze, though).
8/10
Except for the limitation in controls described above gameplay is very fun. There are a ton of different moves: different types of punches and kicks in different heights, combos, special moves, airborne moves and so on. Blocking also works fine, although it is bound to the "back" key, so you'll move backwards when you hit it. Most characters have moves which make them dash in some way or another. Throwing is also possible, but again as described above feels more than clunky on keyboard. You can even switch characters mid fight which results in a special move.
There's not much more to say. It's fun.
9/10
There is arcarde mode, story mode, local and online play in various forms available. The stories themselves are not long but there's one for every character, so there's a lot of content there. It pretty much has everything such a type of game needs. You can spend a lot of time learning and practicing moves, chaining them, and trying to recognize what your opponent is doing.

Bite Size Review - FEAR 3
The Good:
- The slowdown mechanic is still satisfying in this game
- A good variety of guns to play with
- The setting (horror mixed with call of duty) is still interesting
- Big robot sequences are some of my favorite parts
The Bad:
- The story is very one note (need to get to Ulma)
- Main character (Point Man) is unlikable and un-interesting
- Some of the new mechanics like the cover system are less useful than just moving from out of cover with WASD
- Less Horror levels/moments in this game, more Call of Duty
- The first game in the series still has the best enemy AI and Horror inducing levels, this game takes a step back with both of these aspects
The Verdict:
This game is a bit of a mixed bag for me. On one hand if you are looking for a cheap 6 hour romp through a semi interesting game, this is a good choice. If it is on sale and you have played the previous two games, I would recommend it. Other wise, if you want to buy a game, buy the first one, it's better than this one and the second game.

Method
Preheat the oven to 325 degrees F (165 degrees C). Grease cookie sheets or line with parchment paper.
Sift the flour and baking soda into a bowl, then add the salt and set aside.
In a bowl, mix together the melted butter, brown sugar and white sugar thoroughly.
Beat in the vanilla, egg, and egg yolk until light and creamy. Then mix in the reserved sifted ingredients until mixed.
Stir in the chocolate chips by hand using a wooden spoon.
Pour 1/4 of the cookie dough at a time onto the prepared greased sheets. The cookies should be about 3 inches apart.
Bake for 15 to 17 minutes in the preheated oven, or until the edges are lightly toasted. Cool on baking sheets for a few minutes before transferring to wire racks to cool completely.

LEGO Worlds has potential to be a great return to the creative side of LEGO gaming. While in the past few years LEGO games have been more based on platforming through various movie franchises, LEGO Worlds focuses more on building and exploring while still keeping the fun and memorable aesthetic that has become a staple of the LEGO franchise games intact. Great animation combined with a variety of LEGO bricks makes LEGO Worlds a great base game to start building onto. The current build of the game is very basic; with no real objectives implemented you may struggle to find fun in the current iteration of this game if you do not enjoy exploration and using the LEGO building tool. While I don’t think that this game will be right for everyone in its current state, I recommend anyone interested in the LEGO universe keeping an eye on it as it progresses through the early access stage of development.

I've been playing Kupo's games for years, since the very first Epic Battle Fantasy game. I've completed every single one - and most, more than once.
With all that said, allow me to attempt to explain why this game is good:
-Elemental attacks\resists system is very intuitive. Very much an old-school JRPG system.
-Multiple difficulty levels, with the easiest one being 50% enemy stats and various attacks weakened to allow the weakest players a chance to progress anyway. Meanwhile, the most difficult setting gives enemies 200% stats and allows them to use their nastiest attacks, making for a real challenge.
-Can be played for free on Kongregate for a try, if you're uncertain. The paid version not only supports the author but also includes a miniboss and boss marathon, as well as some new bosses to challenge players.
-Everything in this game is beautifully drawn and totally adorable in every way; from the legless cats to the slimes to the shrubs and even the characters.
-Jokes are well spaced out, and the game doesn't break the fourth wall too often to devalue it.
-Multiple skills and abilities allow for varied strategies.
-Good clock-time, with new game plus and new game plus plus to extend it even further for those hungry for more.
Now, the cons - for almost every game has some. They are nit-picks, though:
-The game has permanent stat boosting items, and while you have four characters only three are active at a time. This means that the most effective strategy is to dump all the stat boosts on three characters and leave the fourth as backup permanently.
-Eventually your strategy will devolve into buffing your party, debuffing the enemy party and using one big all-target skill or spell for an attempted instant kill. You will be using different skills for different elemental types, though.
-The higher difficulties don't offer increased experience\item\skill point rewards, despite taking at least four times as long (enemies have 200% health on hardest, to the 50% on easiest). This means most players will usually fight trash mobs on easiest and only fight the bosses on the hardest. Even that, only once, for the achievements.
-The game has some of the "but I might need it later" with one of it's consumables (chilli bottle, which refills the limit break bar of a character).
-The huge variety in gear does lend to some very slight inventory management, mostly just before bosses.
I absolutely love this game. 9/10.

Just to start my recorded playtime is a lie because I used FOMM to play with mods so it didn't record it. I'm of two minds with Fallout 3. It's a very, very competent and enjoyable open-world RPG. But if you *really* want to roleplay you're going to find side content extremely lacking. Like with most recent Bethesda open-world RPGs the game is designed around the concept of min-maxing with regards to the Lockpick, Science and Speech skills (despite most of your dialogue options never really capturing what it is that you want to say and instead boiling down to Good, Evil/Jerk, End Conversation options in just about every encounter).  You'll also find that many sidequests also gate your access with a Very-Hard terminal or locked door, which really helps to derail any semblance of exploration at times.
Furthermore the story, aside from having Aslan as your dad, is lacking. Everyone you encounter is on either end of a morality scale. The evil characters are cartoonishly diabolical, and the good characters are saccharine-sweet. Plus everyone you talk to are just plain whiny jerks aside from a handful of NPCs. It's jarring to have the characters you're supposed to emphathize with being irredeemably bossy, whiny or just plain unlikeable. The radio DJ Three Dog comes to mind immediately.
This game also runs like butt on 64-bit Windows 7. The game would crash to desktop almost once an hour for me.
In conclusion Fallout 3 is a solid video game with solid fundamentals but FO3 is a flawed iteration in a growing line of iterations for the Bethesda open-world template where you're the "God of Everything". All in all I prefer New Vegas as my definitive modern Fallout game, but it's unfair to rag on FO3 with that experience in mind because I played NV first and went into an earlier game in the series expecting the improvements to issues that had yet to be identified or weren't even issues at all at the time of Fallout 3's release.
7/10

THIS GAME HAS IMPROVED DRAMATICALLY!!! If you haven't played in a while I suggest loging in and check out the story elements, and the new updates. This game is more than on the right track!!!
COMBAT AND MAGIC (Dramatic Improvements here since I last played 6 months ago):
Last year I was just about fed up with the game because the combat and magic seemed like gibberish and meaningless. I was stressed out by the deck and magic had no mystic or fantasy quality it was just damage this buff that... As a pure mage that bothered me a bit.
However after taking 6 months off I am amazed at how the managed to smooth over the deck/combat system. The addition of a skill based leveling system offset by an experience pool is very well done in my genuine opinion. Schools of magic are all unique yet there are still similarities (there is usually at least 2 ways to accomplish something in Richard Garriott games). So we are not forced into any particular spell tree, and so I'm finding my character development path challenging not because I'm lacking anything but because each skill path is compelling for different reasons. As one who wants to be a pure mage, I'm discovering that there is no single mage architype that is superior but for the first time in my gaming career the best mage class is actually the skills that seem the most fun for me. I'm so relieved I don't have to min/max. I mean that! I have such a tendency to be a perfectionist that if I'm given a min max scenario I will lose sight of the fun and try to min max till I become perfect like everybody else and then get bored.
SKILL DYNAMICS:
All the spell trees are intriguing to me, and I find that I want to try something new each time. I think it is possible to be a pure mage and never attain grandmaster a single tree and still have fun and be able to play the game and have fun, and then I can imagine it would also be fun (and powerful) to grandmaster master a few skill trees if I want to spend time to do so... Without the min max looming over my head I feel free to just play without worrying about the end game of my character so much. I don't know about anybody else, but for me not having to be overly critical about stratigizing about the endgame is a totally new experience.
The new use based skill gain where we find a skill trainer to train a skill and then leveling each skill through use is fantastic. Adventuring experience (completing quests, and combat) accumulates as a skill pool from which we can gain skills. Focusing on the skills we want to gain at that time, and maintaining others. I was very skeptical about hearing stuff about skill decay, but now that I've played I don't see how skill decay is even a problem. Unless you've consumed all the skill pool, the only skills that could ever decay would be the ones you do not care about, and want to decrease.
The result is flexibility to make changes after the fact and abandon skills we discover we don't use much in favor of taking on a new skill (which levels up fast until you get to higher levels). This will also be good when new skills come around and we can easily alter our character accordingly without having to "RESPEC" like so many other games do.
**************************************
COMBAT TARGETING (New Feature):
This new targeting system annoyed me at first, however in less than a week I not only got use to it I wouldn't want to play without it. It relieves me of the burden of having to lock onto targets by using keyboard keys like tab to select next target, last target, target self etc... Now I've learned how it works and I'm able to run free focusing only on movement and planning my next action, while the targeting system feels as easy as just looking at a guy with my eyes. It is second nature for me now. Not only that It requires a player to aim at distant targets which makes archery and ranged spells more interesting because you are expected to aim at distant targets, and the system intuitive as to who you would be attacking, and who will be attacked if your weapon can hit multiple targets.
*******************************
STORYLINE IS SHAPING UP TO BE AWESOME:
The best part by far for me at this point is the discovery of the story elements they are releasing (love story line to be specific). I'm totally amazed by the interactions with the people of Ardoris in the pursuit of the virtue of love. This is a very deep and intriguing story that drew me in within about an hour of game play. This is probably the most important factor in any single player game. Yet I've played in multiplayer mode the whole time, and I'm still getting the single player experience.
This story is shaping up to be in my genuine opinion, even better than the Origional Ultimas (Ultima 4 and beyond). Ultima Online really didn't have much as far as story is concerned, but the killing and being killed, PvP, aquiring wealth, and the housing is all here if that's the stuff you like. However this game is well suited for those who want to think and be immersed in a totally open path open world experience. The ability to ask any question I want by typing is very useful to go back to topics that I discussed previously with an NPC, and I also found the ability to just click the key words useful when following up with a dialog. So NPC interaction has the benifit of both free text and click to talk.
The story is so good, I honestly had to tear myself away from it and go back to leveling and crafting. I personally want to wait till the complete story is ready and polished because it is so good I want to experience it without spoilers!!! I have lots of opinions about what is going on from where I left off, but it is so good I don't want to share them (but I really do, but I wont).
*****************************************
SINGLE PLAYER/MULTIPLAYER --- I experienced both at the same exact time (First game ever to give me this experience)
I was in multiplayer mode and interacted with two people in 10 to 20 hrs of game time only to ask questions, but for the most part I was able to go about my own business even in the full multiplayer online environment. However I also know I can get neck deep into PvP or community events on a moments notice, because I did that the last time I played over 6 months ago. In this release I plan on continuing to play in the multiplayer online mode since it neither hinders my single player experience and only serves to make the world feel more populated. Besides it may be convenient after I level and acquire more wealth to just visit a player vendor to buy some equipment.
(I've since changed my position because I have never been a crafter before, but now I discovered that I like the crafting system and the sense of completion after making a good set of gear is really awesome. So I actually want to become a crafter as well. Carpentry, or tailoring??? not sure maybe both, and maybe alchemy too. I'm actually considering doing it seriously to become good enough at at least one or two complimentary trades.)
**********************************************
HOUSING:
Also I have not once visited my home from my pledge reward since I placed it first day, and I don't plan on doing so until the final wipe this summer (I actually did, but I moved my place and checked out basments and played the piano and did eventually use a storage chest for goods once I wanted to craft a few items). Truth is I have a lot to catch up on after not playing for six months they dramatically improved this game and it feels almost like a completely different world. However, I don't see the housing being any pay to win issue for anybody except those who love the game so much that they want to be a permanent citizen of the land.

Gauntlet is a special game series to millions of people, stretching across several generations.  But this isn’t a history lesson or a trip down memory game; it’s a review of the newest incarnation of Gauntlet. Let us start off with the FACT that it is $20.00, a lot of the hate this game gets for being too small or not enough content. For the price this games give a very good amount of content and with the newest update giving us a free arena mode is just icing.
Gauntlet is made to be played with friends, and not just randoms you find when looking for an online match through match making, but with real friends, friends you can grind with, friends that are just as likely to act on their vendetta as they are to just let it go, friends you can curse at one second and give grats to 5 seconds later. If you play Gauntlet with friends you’re going to be hard pressed not to have one hell of a good time. It begs to be played like 1996 start on easy play all the dungeon’s rooms on easy and work your way up to unfair, because that’s where the fun is had.
Gauntlet is fun plain and simple... well as long as your group accepts the rolls of their chosen character because they are unbalanced as hell. It would be a complete waste to describe what the issues are as the developers are still changing things around, but it bares saying that you’re not going to complete the game on unfair without an Elf & Wizard. The Dungeon’s are fun and quirky especially the when diving around in the dark looking for treasure , dodging fireballs flung from angry volcano or just running from the grim reaper.
The games looks nice and has a clever retro option in the menu to let you crank up the nostalgia. Issues with the HUD getting in the way have been addressed in the v1.1 update. The games play is solid but the Valkyrie, Warrior & Elf play best with a controller, and the Wizard is a powerhouse monster when played on a keyboard with macros set up.
In the end Gauntlet is a grind fest and that’s okay, on unfair it will take a full cooperation of your entire party to finish the game and it’s a killer great challenging good time. And definitely worth your $20 and if you have friends go ahead and get the 4 pack. Gauntlet just don’t go paying $5.00 for the necromancer.

I've been a backer since Kickstarter, I had high hopes for this game.  Right now the best hope for this game would be if it follows the path of Starwars The Old Republic and is a complete flop at launch, at that point they may actually start making changes people actually want to see.  At this point in development I can not recommend this game, unless you really really want to participate in the pre-alpha process. Even then I would recommend waiting for it to go on sale for a deep discount, You will be disappointed if your expecting a game that is fun to play. If you don't already have money in this game, give it another year or two.
Most of the high level backers and high profile community members that were really driving the community in a good direction have sold their accounts and moved on. It feels like the game is dying while the devs are talking about how awesome it is.
Currently the game swings wildly from month to month and suffers from a lack over all design clarity.
At this current moment in time combat is clunky, and feels like trying to play a tablet app game on the PC.  Combat is a hybrid of several other combat systems with a "twist".  There is a manual swing/shoot element that requires you to click and hold to power up skills. (this can be disabled to auto swing for less damage) There is a Draw system, where combat glyps are drawn into hot bar slots, and can be manually stacked on the same glyph for a slightly better effect or with a Combo partner glyph to combine them into a new glyph. This Stacking can be done with by draging the glyphs with you mouse, or by hitting the Start combo hotkey + the hotkey for the first glyph + the hotkey for the second glyph.  On top of this, they have added a poor implementation of Reticle targeting. (Crosshairs)  Such that things that are forward and closer to the crosshair are more likely to be targetted.  If your a fan of old school tab cycle through nearest targets, your going to be disappointed. If your a fan of ultra modern FPS targeting, your also going to disappointed, at the moment we have a system that has all the flaws of both but no real benefits other than to claim its "unique".
Crafting skills are very grindy, and they are currently working on slowing down gathering even futher. It's becoming clear that Crating and gathering are going to eventurally benefit from add-on store perks to make them playable.  At this moment they are considering intoducing Permenant durability loss for equipment. Most likely this will kill off the crafted gear market, and everyone will just wear NPC vendor bought gear, because it takes several real life days of farming to gather enough resources to make a suit, that needs to be repaired often.
Fishing skills are useless and currently the bait used to fish cost more than anything you can fish up with the bait.  Their anti-bot logic is that every cast near the same spots reduces your catch chances, which means if you don't have a very long beach to run up and down with "fresh casts"  you chances to catch anything quickly desends to less than 1%.   Hopefully this will improve with an economy rebalance that has been promised for years
Argiculture takes days to grow crops and costs more in seeds and water than what you can buy the finished product from a NPC vendor.  Hopefully this will improve with an economy rebalance.
Graphics, in game graphics are basically a billboard of things for sale in the Unity Asset store, lots of copy and paste templates for towns, very little variety.  After 3 years of development, more would be expected in this department. Unfortunately everytime they get a graphic artist that really makes things look good they get hired away to other projects.
NPC story and dialog, progress is extremely slow at this point,  Their flagship feature is no quest dialogs,and NPC's that engage in "real dialogs", however at this point it's basically at matter of trying to find the right keywords to progress quests. There hasn't really been anywork in this area, just more expansive list of keywords.
Customer Service, They have several bug forums that are used to report bugs. However most reports go unanswered very few make it to the "bug entered" list or get any official reply. They provide very little feedback as to why bug reports are not entered for the majority of issues reported.
We don't want new capes... we want new maps and areas.  The whole game seems like the same 10 hallways and intersections with different graphics.

Gameplay is intense platforming that can be challenging and frustrating, but ultimately satisfying when you complete it (most of the time). You keep gaining abilities as the story progresses which gives you access to parts of the map you couldn't reach before, in a very metroid kind of style. My biggest complaints:
There's a lot of learning via repetition, forcing you to redo long sequences where you only fumble towards the end. I almost never find this enjoyable as a mechanic. A couple sequences I was happier that they were over than I was for accomplishing them. Regrettable considering they were well designed just long and unforgiving.
Even worse. There's points in this game where you can not go back!!!
- Beat the game, it's done you can't go back and grab the couple things you missed.
- Went left instead of right? A sequence might happen that locks that area forever even though you didn't get a chance to explore that tiny area to the right first. If you're the type of person who likes to strive for 100% complettion be it for achievements or otherwise... back up your save game often and take things very slowly. I wanted to explore every nook and cranny of this game, it's very pretty and fun to explore. It feels a little punishing that there's no warning these things will happen.

Excellent dungeon crawler!
Operation Babel fixes up the single biggest shortcoming of it's predecessor, Operation Abyss.  The problem with Operation Abyss was how overpowered Samurai was relative to every other class, being the only class with a skill allowing you to hit every monster in a row/group.   In Operation Babel, you can have a class and a sub-class, and gain the skills from both.  You can also equip accessories which grant specific skills.  This means you can get a samurai's multiple-hit skill either by equipping an accessory, or by having Samurai as a subclass.
If you're like me, and you enjoy relatively fast party turn-based combat, you'll probably enjoy this game.
The sequel of Operation Abyss,just like the first game Operation Babel is a fantastic dungeon crawling focused RPG with great production values.

The gameplay itself doesn't changed much from Operation Abyss, which for me is a good thing. The problem with texts was solved and they appear nice now. There is an irritating glitch with one track of BGM, which doesn't affect gameplay, but seriously annoys anyone who doesn't just skip over every text because they don't care about the story. (I hope they will fix it, and do it soon.) So, if you are one of those, then there isn't really any problem with the game.

Performance: OS: Windows 7 64-bit  CPU: AMD FX6300 , GPU: GTX970 , RAM:8GB .
The game runs fine on my PC with steady 60 fps , never encountered a crash or any other problem so it seems at least for me that it is a good port.
Pros:
- Lots of different character portraits to use ( they added more than operation abyss) . The exact number is 45 portraits if you use the basic mode unless you play classic mode which doesnt use character portraits.
- Can use 2 blood codes instead of 1 ( for example you can have a warrior combined with a knight blood code. So this helps you use skills from both blood codes and increases your stats too )
- 10 different blood codes for your squad including (Knight ,Mage, Priest , Academic ,Archer , Warrior , Samurai , Monk, Conjurer and Assassin)
- Good Mouse and Keyboard support and you can also change the keyboard bindings.
- Has endgame content.
Neutral:
- The game is difficult when you reach the final bosses and if you are not carefull or haven't leveled up before, they could kill most of your squad members with one hit.
- UI is not simple enough and it was difficult to get used to. You might like it but I got easily lost many times.
Cons:
- Some puzzles are very difficult to understand especially the ones in the beggining of the game .( I also left some MEMO if you get stuck on a puzzle they might help you)
- The tutorial could be better. Also there is a ingame manual with a lot of information which explains many things but you will get confused with so many information so just read it if you get stuck on something.
Overall the game was good for me and I can reccomend to people who like dungeon crawlers and for people who completed the first game. For me this game is one of the best dungeon crawelers we have on Steam ( Dont know about consoles)
P.S (1): When you reach Shinobazu Prison sewers just go back and save your game. Trust me.
P.S (2): If anyone is interested I recommend that at least in your squad you have a Knight(for the skill "Aegis" which protects your squad members) , Academic (can help you with hidden floors and traps) and a Healer. Without them I feel that the game would be very difficult.

Beat in the vanilla, egg, and egg yolk until light and creamy. Then mix in the reserved sifted ingredients until mixed.

Pour 1/4 of the cookie dough at a time onto the prepared greased sheets. The cookies should be about 3 inches apart.

LEGO Worlds has potential to be a great return to the creative side of LEGO gaming. While in the past few years LEGO games have been more based on platforming through various movie franchises, LEGO Worlds focuses more on building and exploring while still keeping the fun and memorable aesthetic that has become a staple of the LEGO franchise games intact. Great animation combined with a variety of LEGO bricks makes LEGO Worlds a great base game to start building onto. The current build of the game is very basic; with no real objectives implemented you may struggle to find fun in the current iteration of this game if you do not enjoy exploration and using the LEGO building tool. While I don’t think that this game will be right for everyone in its current state, I recommend anyone interested in the LEGO universe keeping an eye on it as it progresses through the early access stage of development.

Great game. It looks amazing. It sounds fantastic. The story is filled with interesting characters and the world built within the game feels very real and alive. The mechanics are great-- the guns feel good to shoot (even if the enemies are a bit bullet-spongey) and the process of acquiring gear to level up your agent is engaging throughout the game and never really feels like a grind.
So why can't I recommend this game? One word:
Uplay.
I downloaded this 27GB game in about 90 minutes. When I launched it from Steam, Uplay launched and began updating.
This 66MB update took the better part of an hour. It crashed eight times during this process (the "Uplay crash dump" error) and never topped a blistering 45kb/s download speed.
Finally it finished updating... and it asked me for a CD key to play The Division. Since this isn't 1999, I don't have a CD key. It was a digital download.
After some Googling, I found out that even though I had just endured that torturous Uplay update, that's not ACTUALLY the most-recent build of the Uplay launcher. I uninstalled that version and installed the version from the Ubi site-- and dealt with the same slow, crash-filled, hour-long process for a second time.
If you're counting at home: that's 90 minutes to download and install a 27GB game-- and 2 hours to download and install the ~60MB launcher for that game.
But it's cool because FINALLY I get to play the game! And man-oh-man, was it fun! I played for a few hours and then went to bed, eager to play again the following day.
The next day, I launched Uplay... aaaaand NOPE. Doesn't launch. The application just entirely refused to start. I found a workaround by launching the game through Steam-- which then launches the Uplay launcher. [This issue has since been resolved as it seems Uplay conflicted with my anti-virus software]
Mid-mission, I lose connection and get kicked. So I exit the game to check on my network connection and--oh what a surprise-- Uplay has crashed. Restart Uplay and I'm back in... for fifteen minutes and it does it again.
Since then, it's been more of the same: Uplay won't launch, Uplay won't connect at launch, Uplay won't recognize that I own The Division, Uplay crashed, Uplay loses connection mid-game, Uplay crashes during updates, Uplay updates at a glacial speed...
[After a post on Reddit, a Ubisoft team member reached out to me and asked for my launcher logs in an effort to suss out the problem. While this doesn't necessarily wash away the bad taste Uplay has left in my mouth, I think it's extremely cool that Ubi reached out to me like that. I'll update this review accordingly depeding on the results of this investigation.]

In a sentence: Simple, but tons of fun. It's a basic RPG in the old school turn-based style, but a well-crafted one and full of charm. Great entry point for those inexperienced in turn-based JRPGs and curious to try them out, because of it's simplicity: Everything about the game is easy to grasp and satisfying to master. The combat and customization will never get you lost and yet decisions are not entirely brainless, the exploration is rewarding and backtracking never feels like a chore, the level and grinding curve is done just right. Seasoned veterans of the RPG genre may find it too basic, and they'd be right, but even them can find something to love about this game.

If you're into RPGs that don't take themselves seriously, or if you're into pastiches of anything and everything, then this game is for you.
It plays really well. Only downside is that, as many people have complained to Matt Roszak before, you spend most of the game with a set of three characters, and leave the reserve one in the dust. Once you have a good enough skillset between three characters, there is no motivation to switching partners unless that partner's ability is ABSOLUTELY NEEDED for a particular battle.
The visuals look cute, I guess. I don't know if the cutesy style goes well with some dark bosses later on, but for the most part, it works. True to Roszak's style, the machines and mechanisms in this game are so well-designed. It's generally pleasing to the eye. The animations are fluid, and the Limits look really awesome. Also, given the certain types of characters that appear in the game, and certain types of armour and equipment you get in the game, I can presume that Roszak has at least done some research into them. So, good on that front.
The writing is class. There is no punny humour, but it still leaves you laughing mad. That's the kind of humour I thoroughly enjoy. I highly recommend players to not skip the dialogues because just reading them shows the amount of thought put into these jokes. Then of course, there are the occasional pop-culture references, so any future reviewer might say that this game is a product of its time, and a sort of mirror to what's going on at the time. There are certain things that aren't recommended for younger audiences, like panty stealing and the Pervert medal, so you'd have to be at a certain age level to be able to understand them -- but when you are, it really comes through brilliantly.
The other language I play this game in (out of curiosity, of course, and because I speak it as my second language) is French -- and the jokes by-and-large translate well, though there are a few lines that sadly, do not get translated well, or even at all. For instance, there's that one laser that's gonna SHOOP DA WHOOP if you're not careful. That line is put in, verbatim, in its English form, in the French translation of the game. And if a French-speaker doesn't understand what 'shoop da whoop' means, it's gonna be lost in translation. There are some parts where punctuation is missing. It's little bits like these that niggle at the player, and make all the difference between a well-translated game and a poorly-translated game. It's not "poor" by any stretch, but could use some work. And in the case where a direct French translation can't be found, a Bowdlerism might come in handy here.
All in all, it's a nice game. For someone who started out indie, this game has done well and managed to relate to any and all corners of society in some way, shape or form, and rightly so. If you're into RPGs, do try this out. If you're into parodies and pastiches, absolutely try this out. And if you're just browsing Steam looking for a game to try out, perhaps give this one a shot.

5th Cell have made a few very good games that I have played, and this is one of them. This game company has made a few games that can really inspire creativity, such as Drawn To Life, and Scribblenauts, though of course inspire creativity  in different ways.
Scribblenauts is a game that encourages you to come up with ways to solve moderatly easy puzzles, where there is no one solution. Because there is no one solution, it has high replay value, with you figuring out what else works, and different ways to do the same thing. At first you might start out summoning a sponge to clean a wall, later you will be using aardvarks for everything.
This game has changed a lot since it's start on the Nintendo DS, and you can even MAKE new things with parts of things from the game, and even script their behaviour! Or if you are no good at making things, you can download some from the Steam Workshop!
There are very few flaws in this game, as no game is perfect. One flaw I find is not really a flaw, but can be seen as one, you have way too much freedom in this game. Limits really work well in certain games, and with games with too much freedom you can get bored, or you see no challenge. If you get bored, there are heaps of achievements to get and there are little challenges in-game for you to solve. But if you have done everything, you can always clear the game data and start anew, and maybe even have a challenge of your own, like, for example, only using aardvarks, which is something I find myself doing a lot.
This game doesn't just stop at the limitless freedom, it also has a very heartwarming story, that premotes kindness. Which is a very nice touch on top of the rest of the game. These types of games are very hard to come across, they are very different from most games, and because they are different and very special, they are games that you must have, even if you are a gamer who plays zombie games, or plays a lot of indie games (a lot of the time they overlap) you must have this, as it is not just another generic game, it is Scribblenauts Unlimited.

It is a beautiful game. A wonderful combination of mathematics, art and coding. A game changer, challenging how we might approach and play games of the future. And that's clever. Very clever. It puts Hello Games and Sony in a unique position for its future success.
To be able to leave the surface of a full size living planet and in 'real time' fly seamlessly to any moon or planet in the sky, indeed across the universe, is an extraordinary achievement.  On the new world, visit new landscapes and life there, then choose any other star in the galaxy and fly back and forth discovering things no one else has. Follow space ships into battle in grand fantastic 'art painted' science fiction encounters on a massive scale, with superb sound design and detail.  With 18,446,744,073,709,551,616 planets to discover there is an impossible lifetime of adventures.
Accompanying the game is an astonishing sound and musical soundtrack by the award winning band 65 Days of Static, quite out of this world and full of empathy for the design.  Comparable to a mash up of artists like The Orb, Radiohead, Chemical Brothers, Orbital and Air, the band has lovingly created its own defining genre of haunting atmospheric music that mingles in the halcyon days of 90s techno and dance, one of the best of any modern video game.  Arguably worth the price tag of the game alone.
No Man's Sky despite much discussed promises (and every modern game has flaws), is way ahead of cumbersome games like Elite and Star Citizen which suck all the fun and imagination out of childhood 'B-movie Adventures in Space' leaving just a complicated, text plagued, violent, orange and grey shooters set in a shiny dull tin-can void of padded cupboards and joyless music and design. Science Fiction remember is fiction otherwise we may just as well crowd fund a space tractor simulation in zero gravity for hard core gamers to drool over.  (Yes, tractor simulations do exist).
NMS pioneering design quirks perhaps leave it suffering from letting us roam in an infinite universe where there really are no rules, asking us to question how we play games as real virtual explorers. Many things could be refined and developed and they will be.  The platform seems ideal for VR development and future improvements to real-time environmental effects would add to the already remarkable experience of setting foot onto an alien surface.  Gravity can be a little silly at times but it can be amusing landing on a tree or destroying objects and realise your starship remains stuck up in the air.  But then you realise you have a jet pack or can blast tunnels through mountains to reach your ship.
Updates have improved user controls and added an enjoyable well thought out base building and satisfying animated farming experience, without interrupting the flow of the game.  Massive freighters, silent behemoths of the skies, now dwarf planets and moons, giving the player opportunities to win control of and defend your very own Star Wars like the star destroyer, that wowed cinema goers seeing for the first time the opening scenes of A New Hope in 1977.  It’s easy to be awed by the game’s extraordinary work of art on show and forget that the No Man’s Sky universe is at its core procedurally generated by extraordinary mathematics.
The procedural challenge Hello Games are developing allows you to create your own science fiction adventure without a pre-determined choice of routes.  This is not to say goals are to be ignored in games.  That's the point of a game to take part and reach a satisfying end.  NMS has to decide if there is one goal or infinite goals that can be affected procedurally.  Imagine landing on a planet and being caught up in a war.  Flying to another and having to do search and rescue.  Crash landing and escaping from an alien virus or having to pilot a giant freighter with other players across challenging space and horizons.
The core procedural planet concept has been realised. Now procedural evolution of storytelling needs refining. It's an enormous undertaking for such a small studio. Procedural animation and emotion might be improved. Sound too, though excellent, might be developed procedurally to define a wider range of birdsong and alien life to captivate the voyager discovering a new horizon.  Animated cinematics revealing story choices might compliment the well written, if slightly obscure, text based story links. Perhaps the game needs some protagonists players call on for help? It would be fun to leave loot or clues or put out distress calls for other players. Maybe even transport alien life from one planet to the other.  The possibilities are infinite.
The first person approach borrows visual cues for its unique stylised look and procedural concept from all sorts of loved science fiction landmarks like Tron, Forbidden Planet, Hitch Hikers Galaxy, Star Trek, Time Bandits, Star Wars, Alien, Myst, Dr. Who, H.G.Wells, Isaac Asimov, Dune, Star Man, Star Gate, 2001, Moonraker, Natural History documentaries and many, many more. NMS is all the things you want science fiction to be.
The game is colourful artistic space at last, on a grand, vast scale. Who knows what has yet to be discovered finding that last rewarding creature on a planet? Space is finally fabulous to look at, like all the paperback science fiction covers enticing us to read them. It's fun and serious, it's what YOU want it to be.   With an impossible number of life sized planets to fly to and discover it could be anything you imagine and that is perhaps what challenges us as players to give up an arguably tired, traditional way of playing games that essentially follow a pegged out story mode or 'latest map release' that has become more and more violent.
Hello Games seems to have angered hard core fans for turning their perceptions of gaming upside down. The goal is discovery and serendipitous adventure. Forget the boring bits of space landing, animated starship steps, over designed sliding doors and fussy spaceships, climbing in and getting out, shopping trolley music and marvelling at what latest fashion to wear in rival space simulators.  Let's go where No Man has gone before... No Man's Sky puts the fun into space.
Small developers and artists have a passion for their games.  They wouldn't continue to create otherwise.  Hello Games has vision, talent and clearly demonstrated a love and enthusiasm for their science fiction and their artful game.  Something public relations would be wise to handle with care and not stifle.  Despite the bungled early release of the game No Man’s Sky sets a benchmark to be a science fiction dream that appeals to all generations.  Sony will be proud of it.  If not they should be.  It's a great game, flawed perhaps only by its ambition, but a beautiful game none the less set in an astonishing magnificent universe, on an impossible scale, full of ideas that continues to surprise with each update.
Look back only a few years and compare Tomb Raider for PS1 to today's PS4 franchise.  Look at defining landmark games such as ICO, the early Medal of Honour series and Medal of Honour  Frontline animations, theatre, music and sound, Grand Theft Auto, Deux X and realise how they all changed computer gaming.  There are plenty of classic games which have now become massive franchises but are they as good as when they were creative blocky digital pioneering 3d?  Not really, but great ideas will endure and change.
