Ori and the Blind Forest, is perhaps the most polished game i've played in a long time. At release I passed it by, however after being gifted it for my birthday, I tried it out. I was not dissapointed.
For a game to grip you within the first twenty minutes in my opinion is rare, or at least, none from recent memory come to mind, but Ori manages it, and with no real voice acting to speak of.
Honestly I havn't felt feels like that in a long time.
Bug wise, I havn't encountered any, however if you visit the forums there are posts where people are having issues with controllers and the game running slow, this is all down to individual experience however rather than a for sure it's going to happen to you, as I have experienced zero problems.
I'm going to parrot what people have been saying frequently about the graphics here, you could take a screenshot at any  point in this game and turn it into a picture to hang on your wall, it's that beautiful. 2D artwork at it's best, it gives the perfect impression of being 3D as the backgrounds give a good sense of depth and motion. I mean you can tell the game is going to be beautiful just from the main menu alone.
As for difficulty, i'm not the best platformer player out there, infact I don't play that many at all. The game starts easy, but there are times where the difficulty seems to spike to an unreasonable degree (I'm looking at you Ginso Tree). This is perhaps the only gripe I can think of with the actual game itself. Despite the many deaths you'll probably experience on your first playthrough, I never found it rage inducing, more the music and the story itself kept me motivated. I had to continue the story, I had to heal the forest, I had to help Ori complete his task.
There are many secret places you'll find throughout your travels, although you wont be able to get to them yet, until you access a certain ability you might unlock later in the game. If you want to find all the health and energy orbs, you're going to have to backtrack, even more so than the game already makes you do to access some of the later areas, not that this is a complaint. It's fun to revisit an earlier area and kick it's behind with new abilities and skills.
I'm going to devote a parahraph to the soundtrack now, because it is brilliant. Some of the pieces give me chills, and it gives the real sense of how fickle nature can be. It fits the mood of the game perfectly and changes fluidly along with whats happening on screen. Honestly it's well worth the price to buy, however a couple of the tracks are not included in the OST, however they can be found on Soundcloud, posted by the composer.
Ori is an amazing game, if you enjoy platformers, i'd advise you try this game out. If you enjoy a good story, i'd try this one out too. And who knows? You might fall in love with it as I did.

Easily one of the best games released this year, Ori and the Blind Forest brings the Metroidvania genre to a fantastic pinnacle. With hard-as-balls platforming, secrets to discover, incredible powers to unlock, vibrant graphics with deep colors, a decent-to-great story, and one of my favorite soundtracks this year, Ori and the Blind Forest is a game that everyone should check out, regardless of whether you like platformers, Metroidvanias, or great games period.

I have never played any Gauntlet game in my life but I knew what it was all about and when this one was announced it picked my interest immediately. It didn't disappoint.
It carries that "arcade type of game" vibe with some modern concepts to spice things up. It won't generate random maps, which is a bummer for some, but others will find amusing to memorize all the choking points, barrel bomb positions, spawners, secret rooms... Just like an arcade game of the good old days.
Gauntlet 2014 is an action game with some RPG elements. This is no Diablo. If you want to dodge an incoming attack you better get out of the way. If you want to block you better push the block button. There's no chance dictated by status here. You either do it or get hit and they hit hard. The game is quite a challenge.
The four classes are well implemented and they are completely different from each other. The animations are good and the moves are consistent to the class. The way developers managed to make they work in sinergy during multiplayer, each playing its role, is commendable and it adds a lot to the fantasy setting and fun. This game solo is quite good. Play it online and you're going to have a blast. Gauntlet 2014 is a simple/deep kind of game. You pick the basics right away but it takes some time to trully master it.
Graphically speaking its a nice game. It won't win any "best graphics of the year" prize but its not ugly at all. If you're like me, far from a high end PC, Gauntlet might be a good surprise. The same can be said about sound. The music is dynamic. Calm and enigmatc when no monster is around and tense for that moment you see a horde coming your way. Sound effects are also good. Clash of weapons, magic being cast, voices... They are all nice and add a lot to the overall experience. Talking about voice, some dialogs here are going to put a smile on your face.
I see a lot of people complaining about lack of content and most of them have played the game for less than 15 hours and rushed to the final boss. Indeed, if you're looking for a huge amount of stages and all you do is push foward you're in for a disappointment but if you like games where you must trully learn a class to reach "suck my Yoda" type of mastery look no further. The game also offers some very lite RPG elements like relics that are basically skills you can use in battle, masteries that increase your character strenght and defense the more you play and some cosmetic equips beating the game on multiple difficulties. When you're done, master another class and have fun for more 20 or 30 hours.
I'm having lotsa fun with this game but I do understand its not for everyone. If you exclusively like games that offer infinite ammount of random generated dungeons and/or deep and complex character development, stay away. This is not for you. If you're looking for a game with a gameplay thats simple and deep at the same time, addictive and most of all, fun, you can't go wrong with Gauntlet 2014.

Nice game, game about divers vs sharks.

Disclaimer. I have only played this game for 10 minutes or even less but I feel that it was enough for me to get its essence.
Pros:
- Original concept (I don't know any other 1st person underwater/diving game so this may have created a new genre which is 1st person water exploration).
- It puts you on edge if you're playing the diver role, which is good if you like horror games. It gives you a rush.
- It's a fun game to play with friends if that is what you are looking for.
Cons:
- This is a subjective thing and, as such, this may not be a con for you but this game is not oriented towards realism, simulation or immersion so if you were hoping to see dive to the depths of the ocean and experience it immersively in all its realistic detail and feeling like you were actually diving then this is not your game. This game chooses, instead, to be more a game for fun, a game to get your kicks off. I even found myself laughing histerically during some parts of it due to the rush it provides. Being a realism fan, the game is too "arcade" for my personal taste and, as such, it lacks depth (no pun intented). There is no story or realistic situation supporting it and the mechanics and details are also oriented more towards the fun department than the realism so, if you are beyond a certain age like I am, it may become monotonous and get tedious after a while, once the novelty/fun thing wears off. Of course that this is precisely what some gamers want (a fast and fun game) so this is a personal subjective thing and not necessarily a con for everyone.
Conclusion. I think it's great that this game was made because it introduces novelty as far as gaming genres go. The present game genres are good but it's always good to have more. Also, for the current price (5€ in Europe), I would say it's a very good deal if you're into a fun, (unreal-tournament-style) quick-match game with an original concept and nice graphics to play with your friends.

It can be difficult, in some cases, to decide if you like a game or not.   Scribblenauts: Unlimited, for instance, is a game where you try to solve problems.  You can stick to mundane solutions, which often work; or you can get a little playful--which sometimes doesn't work, but other times will work in hilarious ways.
I'm about halfway through the main "campaign", if you can call it as such, and while I'm occasionally stymied (what do you mean I can't conjure a lot of nontangible concepts? Boo!), the things that stymie me are the sorts of things not remotely possible in a whole lot of other games. It's not what I'd call a difficult game; or even a challenging one. Sometimes it feels like a chore list, but when it gets to feeling that way, I take a break and come back fresh in almost no time at all--it's not the game's fault my creativity runs dry.
But I suspect, to be honest, the real joy about this game is something I haven't quite tripped over. I haven't spent a lot of time just GOOFING AROUND, which, to be honest, I think is kind of the 'point' of the scribblenauts series--less constructed video game, more toy box. In fact, the toy box feeling is pretty apt.  Still, at the price it's at, I kinda get some kicks out of it.  Lacking outside context, I give this game a tenative reccomendation: It's not for everyone, but maybe it's for you.  I wouldn't buy it at full cost, out of crippling poverty, but, well--I have it! So I'm enjoying it.

In this game, you control Anna, a ranger whom ends up tracking down the team of Epic Battle fantasy 3 on the accusation of them having stolen the gem of her village. You end up going on an epic adventure with them, going through adorable settings all over. The game is beautful with hand drawn settings that have tons of love in them, making every single area feel likable, even if it's not your favorite!
You'll be playing with a total of 4 characters, having 1 of them on backup in case your main team falls, and for me that meant that the person on back-up often ended up being forgotten in regards to stat boosting items and equipment upgrades, but that's how i like to play the game. The person in back-up gets XP just like everyone else in battle, as long as they are alive at the end of the battle. Switching someone out with the back-up is smooth and seamless at the single press of the button, and if you regret it you can always switch right back. The battles move at your own pace, as the enemies cannot take their turn until you are done with yours, making the game move however you want it, wether you wanna go fast and spam your strongest move or if you carefully want to plan out the next upcoming turns.
The game thrives on it's exploration, the humor and hidden references (which unfortunately had to be partially censored at least by name in order to avoid legal issues as far as i'm aware), but most importantly the music. Oh man, the music is great! It's often high tempo, but it calms down when it needs to, and it does a fantastic job att setting the mood for the current situation, which is really the only thing you'd truly want out of music for an RPG game.
The game also features a bit of puzzle solving and NPC quests (most of which are fetching quests where you give them crafting items of different kinds) but if that's not your slice of cake, it's not a problem because the quests are entirely optional as far as i know, and the puzzle solving, while mandatory in some parts, is never so difficult that you feel like you want to take a break because the puzzle is just difficult.
Now, there is a free to play version available on the web, both on Matt's own website aswell as several different gaming websites, but there are a couple of differences. Mainly, on the premium versions on the gaming websites as well as the steam edition, you can access an area called Battle mountain, which features tons of bonus equipment, items, skills, summons and more. But most importantly, it features some very heavy challenges, ones that will have even the best of players on the edge of their seats as they lose over and over, slowly making progress towards that sweet goal, giving you a dark souls feeling of success when you finally complete the ordeal! That takes me to the difficulty of this game!
Overall, this game isn't particularily hard in many ways. The puzzles aren't extremely complex for the most part, the battles shouldn't give you that much trouble, and there's plenty of oppurtunity to heal yourself in between battles (one of which is just to stand around, as you do have natural regeneration on both MP and HP), but here's the fun part.
On the options menu, you can instantly switch between the 4 different difficulties at any point on the world map, and since the battles are all actively triggered along with fleeing being 100% reliable, you can customize the experience according to how you like to play your games!
If you want to play through the game having a chill time, you could just cruise through on easy.
If you want to play through the game having a TOUGH time, you should play on Epic, which is when the game itself becomes so incredibly difficult at some parts that you might have to end up fleeing a battle, changing your entire equipment loadout and then trying again. However, if you feel that a battle is at any point TOO difficult for you, it's always possible to simply flee and turn the difficulty down.
As for equipment, there is a ton of variation in everything from weapons to armor and accessories.
Every character has their own type of weapons, and every type of weapon comes in a varied and unique form, ranging from a gun made of marble in the shape of a fist that will smite undead foes and steal health based on how much damage you do to a bow that will inflict random status ailments on each hit to a staff that is a literal incarnation of deaths' scythe, you'll find your favorite to use pretty quickly. However, even if you find the number one weapon you prefer, almost never will weapons feel obselete as enemies come in a ton of different elements and forms, and weapons almost always carry with them a special element, so ultimately, it comes down to deciding wether you want a weapon for its stats or if you want it because of the special effects it triggers. A lot of different equipment trigger special events before your turn starts, such as a random attack triggering before you get to act, or maybe a random positive buff on your character.
The armor is divided into two groups, one with male armor and one with female armor, since there's 2 of each in the game. This is nice as upgrading one set of armor could potentially benefit both of the specified users, however i feel this is also a slight drawback as if one armor set is used by one character, the other one has to use a different once, which can lead to trouble sometimes if you are for example looking for specific elemental resistances and you only own 1 armor piece which protects against it, as you'd then have to choose which one would be allowed to equip it.
Furthermore, accessories are shared across all your characters, and they come in the form of small badges, and while the effect more often than not isn't extremely impactful, it's nice to get small additional bonuses from time to time.
Overall, this game is alot of fun, any fans of RPG games or JRPGs will most likely instantly love this game, and for people that aren't into RPG's yet but are looking for somewhere to start, this would make a great candidate!

Epic Battle Fantasy 4 despite its quirks is a reasonably well made JRPG with a solid combat system that comes with interesting itemization(optimization for fights ahoy!). Sadly I found the story rather lacking. Obviously it makes fun of many stereotypes in the genre and overal tries to make jabs at how easy our heroes mow through zones while npc's pretend like it's all ever so hard...
In the end I cannot help but feel that the lack of any kind of story to get invested into really hurts the game since it really only has the gameplay going for it. When a serious game makes a joke or two you can really appreciate them since they contrast with the serious nature of the game. Epic Battle Fantasy 4 sadly makes a joke out of everything which ends up making everything unfunny.
So is the game worth playing? I bought it for about €3,00 or so and I'd say the 25 hours I got out of it were easily worth it. Get it at a discount and you'll have fun without trying to justify the price. I enjoyed the game since it has solid combat and itemization but it's not going to be something people will talk about much since storytelling is often such a strong part of JRPG's and it simply hurts the game not having much of any.

I'm going to begin with the negatives:
-This game has practically no controller support. Unless you have the one and only special-snowflake kind of controller the game was made for, it doesn't work. Even the usual workarounds for this problem are thoroughly broken. The developers don't seem to have any plans to fix this glaring error, ever.
-The mouse+keyboard controls of this game are okay, but appear to have been designed for someone with either three hands or twelve fingers.
-This game is exceptionally laggy at times, and the cutscenes only sort of work, occasionally freezing or skipping over parts to continue playing.
-This game's story isn't very good. It suffers from an overabundance of pathos and otherwise is rock simple.
-This game commits the two major cardinal sins of overall design that any otherwise fun-to-play metroidvania could possibly commit: there are missable upgrades, and there are upgrades after a point of no return.
-This game has no bosses; instead it has sections where you have to run away from instant death walls. This was a bad decision. Why is there an awesome-looking gigantic owl monster in your game and I don't even get to fight it?
All of that being said, this is a fun game to play. Despite control issues, it has a nice, frenetic sort of platforming and fighting. It has decent puzzles and mostly non-cheap ways of hiding upgrades for the player to find them, and there are a lot of cool sections to level design. The atmosphere and graphics are good; the music is good for what it is.
Overall, if you're looking at the screenshots and think you want it, and if you can put up with the issues I've listed above for an otherwise good game, you should get it.

Ori and the Blind Forest, aka 10h of your life you will never forget.
There is little wrong that you can say about the game. It grabs your attention with beatiful and captivating music and visuals, introducing a bitter-sweet tale of a light-creature named Ori. Once there, you will find yourself presented with quite the beatiful little world to explore, populated by deadly creatures and with many secrets to uncover.
Make no mistakes, the forest of Nibel is as pretty as it is deadly, and the challenges thrown at you will make you die. A lot. Be it a new enemy, new skill or just a "simple" platforming sequence requiring great precision, there is no clowning around. Not even with full health and defensive upgrades can you laugh in the face of your adversaries, especially when they stop being a thing to kill and become just another piece in platforming dance with the death, all of it the courtesy of Dash ability.
That one gets a special shout-out for being absolutely ingenious, adding a lot of new possibilities in all areas. Exploring, combat and platforming becomes much more when you acquire it, and proper use can turn damningly hard sequences into a breeze.
With everything flowing perfectly, always feeling like a well-thought package and keeping just the right pace of introducing new elements, enemies and challenges, is there really anything negative to say about Ori? Actually, there is.
There are special areas in the game that won't be accessible after completing them, and the save gets locked once you finish the game. What it basically means is that if you slip up in exploring or completing the game, there is nothing you can do aside from starting a new save slot. It is not a terrible flaw, but stands as one thing that could've been done better, especially since you can' have more than one save of the given playthrough.
That is only a mild annoyance, however.
Play it once, and you won't be able to be mad at the game for trying to make you dive in once again.

FEAR 1 and 2 were absolutely fantastic games that were unrivaled in the fusion of Horror and FPS, and still are, to this day. Eventually FEAR 3 came along to complete the trilogy. FEAR 1 had atmosphere, difficulty, great story and great gameplay. FEAR 2 had more of the same, but with a more streamlined approach to the story, but it didn't have as many open ended levels.
FEAR 3 ditched the horror, the good writing and ended up adding COOP to follow the COOP craze. The game was not difficult, the horror elements were completely removed, and the story was so out of wack, incongruent and just horribly written. Both the first 2 FEAR games had incredible AI that provided difficulty. Here, they might as well just be standing still. The level design is horribly linear, with no options of going in a different way.

Did you like FEAR? Did you even suffer through FEAR 2? Well, that's what you get for it. I present to you FEAR 3, the worst entry in the franchise.
The good:
- Gunplay is surprisingly solid compared to FEAR 2. More like the first game.
- No almost endlessly respawning enemies like in F2
- Sprint button
- Grenades are again simply thrown and not selected. Thank you
- Graphics are kinda neat
- Fettel is still a badass. Kinda.
And that's about it...not a lot to see here
The bad:
- Gameplay is so generic it hurts.
- COVER system in an FPS...
- Regenerating health
- Silly "level up" system
- Boring weapons
- Bugs
- Glitches
- Even on easy annoyingly unfair at times
- Story is quasi non-existant
- No manual saves
- Long checkpoints
- You still do not talk...everyone else does...
- I wonder what "we" did during FEAR 2...disjointed narration
- Short, oh sooo so short, and still glad it's almost over.
- Is this supposed to be scary?
So, well, yeah, while the basic shooting mechanics are solid. Everything else just kinda falls flat on its face. The story makes little sense and is just boring. The scary or unsettling moments are almost completely gone. You have to run from checkpoint to checkpoint. Firefights are often protracted sequences with aiming out of cover. You die really fast in this game, but hey, regenerating health...yay.
There's also an "achievement" system in the game through which you "level up". For example getting a sprint melee attack, more health, more slo mo time, etc. It's completely shallow and weird though. Not to mention you restart most achievements with every new instance. There are also some glitches and game breaking bugs, which require you to restart a checkpoint (for example, an enemy somehow dropped out of the world and was thus invincible, thereby not triggering the next set of enemies that let you advance through the level). Did I mention that this game is SHORT!? I played FEAR 1 for about 8 hours (12 with DLC), Fear 2 for about 6 or 7 hours as well, but this one? No more than 4 hours spread over 8 intervals. The different settings are also not very interesting from an artistic view point.
*sigh* Just play FEAR 1 instead. It's better in every regard, except graphically.
Edit: Also terrible FOV and motion blur which cannot be changed, unless you dig through Google to find out you need to edit the settings file in a certain way. That is just ridiculous. The game literally made me sick playing it without this "fix".

I really like Guantlet. I remember cursing at the original, and couldn't resist getting this. I'm really on the fence about the thumbs up/down rating...and I'm going to give it thumbs down because some basic changes are needed to make this game what it should be.
The intro is a tutorial that cycles through each character with steps that must be completed to progress. This intro foreshadows the faults in the game to come. There is a clear lack of direction in the tutorial, and this is underscored by a madness-enducing introduction to the Wizard's controls. Don't give up; there are guides that explain Merlin...yeah...
The controls are wonky at best. The game claims to be best while played with a controller. I agree that it felt best with the controller, but I would have preferred the option to set my own keybindings. I know there are workarounds for this, but this is a basic option for PC games and when it's not there it makes games feel like a lazy port. Thankfully keybindings can be set with a keyboard/mouse, but auto-aim mucks controls up a fair amount at harder difficulties and cannot be turned off.
Merlin's controls are hilarious. I had to fight the urge to spin in my chair to change a spell as I felt I was doing everything but that. I'm sure practice makes perfect, or macros would bridge the gap...but like controller emulation...beyond what I want to do. Why, oh why, not utilize the mouse wheel to switch between spells, or lcontrol, tab, etc.? The problem is the controls are too limited. Limiting all actions to 4 keys (basic combat actions) on a keyboard really sucks.
I wish the loadout equipment was beyond cosmetic...I really do. Thankfully the relics are quite usefull, and the masteries prove to be alot more useful than regular achievments of most games. It's like a limited skill tree that I wish was a little more than kill 80, then 8000; there could be more inbetween to make the grind between mastery levels seem less arduous.
I always struggled with Guantlet and even just at the hard difficulty this game does not dissapoint. There is minor grind for gold, cosmetics (if your into that) and a decent grind for masteries...but none of those are really required. The game is fun, but the controls make the game too frustrating to endure for anything but short bouts, which wasn't the case for the original that this game hopes to compare to.

I bought this game as a 4 pack thinking my friends would enjoy it (4 of us total).   However, we all found the game more tedious and annoying than enjoyable.   The reward system in the game makes you want to gouge your eyes out with a dull spoon.   They tie the relics to potions which don't drop frequently enough to make them useful.  You end up "saving" the few you do get to the point where they become useless.   A better system would be that the potions boost the effectiveness of your relics.  The relics if not boosted, would be on some timer.  This would give you the thrill of feeling like you had some nice power to use in tight situations, but not make the game seem too easy.   Having potions to boost the effectiveness would give you the option to save the power until a very tough fight or simply clean house when you had the boost active.
The other annoying detail is the destructibility of the healing and relic powering potions.  The tight quarters force you to use your powerful aoe spells to survive.  However, those same spells blow up your only means of a) powering your relics and b) healing yourself.  I found myself driven into a frenzy of madness.  You are slivers away from death, surrounded, and forced to use your only means of defense to blow up enemies and unintentionally, your salvation.   We all gave up before we could finish it since the joy was sucked out of the game with annoying mechanics and a terrible loot / reward system.

This is modern Gauntlet. You could call it a remake, but it's not really that. It's so much better. It's a dungeon crawler and arena twin-stick shooter. It's Gauntlet on steroids, but it hasn't lost that old-school charm. Best played with others, especially when you get into Hard and above.
The biggest flaws I've seen are a lack of variation on encounters. This was a chance for the team to take Gauntlet even farther, but they stuck with something more tried and true. Granted, it's been refined so that the annoyances of a generation ago aren't still here. There's also a new relic system to give you some sense of progression other than making it through the dungeon. But at it's core, it's the same sets of encounters over and over again, and when you've seen them once, you've seen them.
My other big gripe is that the loadouts do nothing but change how your character is dressed. Certainly they could have given some other bonus, especially with some of them requiring you beat certain levels on specific difficulties. At the very least, they could have made the loadouts be more visually interesting, because right now, they're a bit boring. I'm not really interested in spending my hard-earned gold on them for such little gain.
That doesn't make the game not great though. The normal campaign will last you about 6-8 hours depending on your abilities and that's not bad. Add in additional difficulty levels and you've got a competent remake. The added charm of the announcer quipping about Warrior needing food, badly, or the food being shot by the clever wizard harken back to the game we all know and love.
The story is a bit drab and predictable, but you're not here for the story, so who gives a♥♥♥♥♥♥ The visuals are great, the sound and music fit the game perfectly, and the difficulty scales well. All-in-all, the Arrowhead team has done a great job! I look forward to Gauntlet 2.

Videogames: Artform or Entertainment? It's a debate that's been waging on since the concept of a "videogame" first came into existance, and it's only gained momentum as the medium has advanced. Some emphasize that videogames are just for juvenile entertainment, citing commercial projects such as C.O.D and G.T.A. In these respective examples, I'd tend to agree. However, those games weren't meant to be art, they were meant to be enjoyable and casual. They have storylines and plot, but only to serve the game. When I think of gaming for pleasure, those games, along with a multitude of First Person Shooters, come to mind. They're enjoyable, but they aren't art. When I think of the medium as an artform, I think of stories that can be portrayed, actively lived through, personally experienced, more so than a film or book could offer. Videogames offer the player immersion, the chance to be a part of the story, and, when done correctly, I deem this experience as etherial, personable, artful. Such is the case with Freebird Games' "To the Moon." I don't want to go into much detail, as this is a game that should be experienced as a clean slate rather than a preconceived expectation. However, I will say that this is a heavily story-driven title, so there's little gameplay aside from moving from one important piece of information to the next. There are puzzles, but they're extremely simple, serving as a break from the constant traversing you'll do. This may sound boring to some gamers, but trust me when I say that the lack of gameplay is both made up for and exceeded by the game's compelling story. As you play through, you'll find yourself laughing at Neil Watt's witty humor, as well as possibly shedding a tear or two along the journey to Johnny's childhood. I know that this all sounds vague, but to go into any more detail would risk spoiling some of the game's charm. This game is definitely worth the 9.99 you'd shell out for it, and then some. It's all of what one would enjoy in a well crafted novel as would be portrayed in a videogame, and I'd go as far as to say it's one of 2011's prime examples of the medium as an artform. I highly recommend a purchase and playthrough.

No Man's Sky as it is isn't for everyone. It is a game for people who like to walk around and look at things. That's what I've had the most fun doing. Some people might be bored by that, but there are some very nice sights to see for those willing to look.
In a sense, it is a game for people who don't like games. The token economy is arbitrary and can be essentially ignored, or  even ignored completely in creative mode. There are very few challenging elements, discounting survival mode. The "story" is vague, unfulfilling and very much up to interpretation, which is personally my favorite kind of story. The closest thing you might come to contact with another player is seeing one planet that they've been to. But, what No Man's Sky does have is an aesthetic unlike anything else. So if you're sick of mindless token economies, unsatisfying and poorly executed stories in games, failing at the same level over and over again, and even people in general, you might like No Man's Sky. After all, it is the best hiking simulator on the market.
I played a lot on ps4 and finally got a decent PC to play games on. So as a final note, mods add a whole new breath of life into the game. Three I have to recommend are Big Things, Tall Diplos and Constructs, all of which can be found on the No Man's Sky mods website.

No Man's Sky is a beautiful game based on exploration of the universe. The level of detail and variety on different planets is astounding, and there are many in-game mysteries to learn and to relate to. Crafting and base building helps to build your own little empire and helps your explorations, and the promise of future updates makes it interesting to invest in the game. BUT it requires patience and an explorative mindset. It is not an action game, nor a flight sim. It is not multiplayer, it is straight single player as of Foundation update anyway. If you are curious to explore and discover anything from star systems, to planets, to weird interstellar plants and animals and mythical alien sagas, then this game is for you. If you are looking for  game in which action/fighting or flight simulation is propelling the story forward - then this game is not for you. Basically, it's a sort of game that you either spend 100+ hours on, or just 30 minutes, depending on what you are looking for.

A somewhat new, and certainly note-worthy addition to the 2D fighting arcade genre.
Not only can you tell how much work has been put into it (I've watched some of the Lab Zero live streams and can confirm), but there's a good system set up where you can not easily abuse an infinite combo chain.
Well... unless you have no idea what you're doing or your skill does not even come close to matching up to that of your opponents.
That is my only complaint about the game.
It's a very addicting and fun arcade fighter, but I've come to a point where the CPU level is too easy even on Nightmare difficulty. When I switch over to online, you have people playing that are even more pathetically easy to beat, or they're the complete opposite and you are going against some ridiculously skilled opponent or spammer where you will not even be able to move a single bit the entire round due to being constantly attacked.
Other than that, it's fun if you enjoy a challenge, and clean looking, and I've had no problems with frame rate or anything of the sort. Also boobs, if that really seems to be a key selling point for you.
And Lab Zero still puts out DLC, so there's some great things to still look forward to.

The gameplay is like World of Warcraft, except with guns and near-future/prototype tech. Basically, enemies are bullet sponges, elite enemies and the bosses will soak lots of damage before they die even after multiple headshots. Many levels are hard to beat not because the enemies act smart, but it's just that they're hard to kill - especially those in the Dark Zone (both enemies and players alike).
Even though it has an interesting lore, the story is pretty short for an RPG, you can finish it within just 25-30 hrs. By the end of the final mission, chances are you're already level 30 - by then you are now in the 'endgame'. Quite short, really.
Nevertheless, you may engage in the Dark Zone and the newly released areas to acquire better gears and weapons (Endgame is all about Statistics not Tactics, you will meet players with better stats and no way to eliminate them [especially countering rogue agents], unless you start grinding). It's quite fun with friends (or in my case, random people).
The gameplay is pretty fun, if you're into games that are all about stat-building to overwhelm your foes then grab it. But if you're in a more tactical, realistic damage intake, swift kills, etc. then better buy something else. Lots of clothing apparel to chose from, also (quite a nice dress-up game, actually).
The game is graphically beautiful, it's well detailed - the weather is dynamic and everything just feels alive.
Is it worth full-price? I believe no, for a triple A title - the base game severly lacks content, so you'll have to buy the DLCs to expand further. That being said, it's best to grab it at discount of 50% or more. Uh, no, on second thought make that 70% off.
I actually want a sequel, hopefully by then the Devs have learnt their mistakes and I wish the gameplay would be like Wildlands.
Edit:
PVP mode (DZ, Skirmish, Last Stand) in endgame is ALL about STATS; there will  be instances where enemies will just soak damage without being killed. It's created a mentality that 'hur dur that why you got to grind dur' which basically does not justify how unecessarily complex your stats should be just to be of match to others. Wish the developers could give us a proper scaling, because the current meta feels like a poor made free2play RPG game.

If you're thinking of buying Ori, don't. There's no need to think, just buy this game.
Ori is the best single player game I've played in years. Don't let the beautiful and fairy-like graphics fool you, Ori is hard. I don't just mean a little hard, I mean really, really hard. At it's hardest it walks the perfect line between pull-your-hair-out frustrating and "I know I can do this"-hard. Each area has it's own feel and unique look. Everywhere I went felt like somewhere new. No two parts of the map are the same. You're not going to find two corridors that have the same layout, just with some decoration/mobs moved about. The rooms themselves were a treat to see for the first time, and the hundredth. Even when I was dying 50 times in the same area it never lost its beauty. The soundtrack was impressive and mood-defining, but never felt intrusive or disturbing when you needed to concentrate for a particularly hard part of the game.
Platformers will never really be the same again after playing Ori.

The artwork is beautiful and reminiscient of a children's fairy tale, but make no mistake - this is a tough game and you WILL die a lot. Certain sections of the game are extremely unforgiving, but it's all worth it in the end. Prepare to be captivated by the amazing artwork (the likes of which has never been seen in a 2d platformer before) and soundtrack. The only game of the same genre that comes even close to Ori in terms of artwork is Aquaria. Buy this game and support and reward developers who come up with gems like this.

By far and away one of the best games I've ever had the pleasure of playing. This game has the most drop-dead gorgeous artwork I've ever seen in a video game, a phenomenal soundtrack, strong core gameplay mechanics and a story that, despite very little exposition, very nearly brought me to tears many times. Tasked with essentially restoring the world's life-tree, as the plot progresses, Ori (the little guy and the main character) gains new powers which enable you to defeat new enemies and explore new environments, as well as return to hidden areas in areas you've already beaten.
It wouldn't be inaccurate to describe this as a Metroidvania-style game: you explore a variety of interconnected 2D levels and environments, defeating enemies, discovering secrets and power-ups. There are a wide variety of enemies, a few boss fights (as well as Ori's recurring nemesis, a giant eagle named Kuro), as well as challenging puzzles and well-designed, tricky platforming sections. if you add in all the secret areas and collectables, this game has a solid amount of content. As you can see it took me about 12 hours to play through, and I missed a few secret areas. There are also achievements for no-death and no-ability-point runs, as well as a three-hour speedrun.
The art is almost entirely 2D but
rendered; the artwork is simply beautiful, particularly playing at 1080p 60fps with AA. Some elements such as the game characters are rendered in a very smooth and almost unnoticeable 3D though, and it works really well. The soundtrack is absolutely astonishing as well, with wonderful ambient tracks as well as pieces that really elevate the pathos of the moment's more emotional or exhilerating moments.
Everything comes together to make for a truly special game that I think I will stay with me for a long time. I absolutely adore this game.

An incredibly fun game with incredibly fun-ruining bugs. Set your expectations accordingly.
I picked this up as a fun co-op introduction to RPGs for the GF and I. It definitely worked and got her engrossed with the great story and decent voice acting. The gameplay itself is a good mix of tactical combat and RPG lore-building and conversations. I don't really have much to say about the positive aspects of the game as they're well documented in other reviews - it looks good, has a great story, and will offer a moderate challenge if you pick the right difficulty, plus the co-op is always a major plus.
However, the bugs in this game (even the enhanced edition) are too overwhelming for me to give it a positive recommendation. Co-op (even on a LAN) causes the 'remote' person to constantly see wrong values for HP and even stats. The GF is always asking me 'am I at full hp?' because her screen shows her at half health while I see her at full. We consistently run into a bug where her dexterity will drop to 5 or 7 and her crossbow will suddenly be useless on her end, but if I swap characters (there's an in-game option for this) I can use it just fine, so it's not a debuff or other in-game explanation for it.
The most infuriating bug happened tonight. She's been permanently wet pretty much since the game started. We reached a snow zone and she became frozen instantly. Every time she's unfreeze, she'd regain the wet status and freeze solid again. This was effectively a game breaking bug since we couldn't progress. I had to spend a few hours on the forums finding hundreds of other posts about this (and no worthwhile dev responses) until I finally came across a player-made savegame editor that I used to strip her wet status.
I write this review now as I come off a ragequit following a bug where she would finish a dialogue before a fight and as soon as combat begins, I would crash. Reload the savegame and crash again. My previous save was only a few minutes prior but I shouldn't have to keep reverting to previous states to escape the garbage fire of buggy coding that is this game.

Let me say, that I have a lot more complaints than I do praise. Despite this, I generally really enjoyed this game and was sad to finish it and will totally recommend it.
-I play games on hard. I start the game on hard with a cleric/rogue combo. Get through the tutorial and decide to change it up. Got walloped with different combos in the tutorial maybe 8 times before setting game back to medium and resorting back to cleric/rogue combo.
-Beginning of the game is a real drab and I hated it at first. Basicly because you need to do non-combat quests for a while before you are high enough level to leave town and not get smashed. Story is meh, I dont give a♥♥♥♥♥♥who killed that one councellor. Typically in a party RPG like this I will leave 100's in my wake. You will accidentally dig up a skeleton in the town graveyard that will wipe your party in short order. You can run away, but then that doesnt stop combat and the skeleton will start killing importent quest people so save often. Awesome feature, you can choose how many unique normal/quick/auto saves will be written before they start overwrighting themselves.
-The game is not really 'open world'. You kind of just wander through a maze and when the enemies are too hard you know to try a different direction. There is a big difference in difficulty between enemies 1 and 2 levels higher than you. You will eventually finish the maps and the main quests will solve themselves as you go along. The side quests are not intuitive and the game does not hold your hand. If you dont get the 'talking to animals' talent there are quests you can start and not finish. You can ruin quests by not doing things in the correct order and they will be stuck in your log. The log is seldom helpful for hints.
-The puzzles can be difficult and some I didnt solve. Some can be solved multiple ways if you think about it. And the pyrimids come in super handy. I didnt realize this until later in the game. You will need a character with high perception or you will be punnishing yourself trying to do some.
-I made it to the last temple door and was not allowed in. Turns out
which I didnt catch in the quantity of dialogue so I was not allowed in and the door is basically saying 'turn back and complete more of the game before you can enter.' I was pretty annoyed by this and until this point I had thought I was going to get through the game and not needed to reference a walkthough or wiki. This is the point, at the end of the game, where I said: meh. So I start looking up wikis and doing the unsolved side quests I had when I got to the end (and believe me, you will have unsolved side quests when you finish) when I had the capability all along to enter the temple because I had found enough of the stones.
-Your characters start getting good when you get to a high level and get some Master skills. Unfortunatly it takes all game to get to that point so you dont get to enjoy it long. Nice thing is that all characters are not restricted to a class, what you choose in the beginning simply gives you a preset build, but if at 80% of completion if you want to turn your warrior into a mage you can do that.

This game isn't exactly "hard", per se. What makes it hard is coming up with the most creative solutions possible to the puzzles before you. Yeah, you could introduce, say, a bank or a post office as a fixture of a small town, but why do that when you can create a morgue? Advertise its existence with a town crier, and balloons and those wavy noodle-men spawn outside and the townspeople come running. It's interesting how the game pushes you to be creative without forcing you to be.
Unfortunately, the biggest reason I bought this game--the item creator--is a MASSIVE disappointment. Do you want to start with a male knight as your base? Too bad! Be prepared to type in the word "knight" 50 times in a row until the game decides to stop spawning a lady. Want to add a tail and make a cat person? Good luck finding the two pixels where you can actually attach the tail to their butt and not their leg! It's unwieldy, difficult to use, and frustrating. It's a miracle anyone has the patience to make anything with it.
I say I recommend this game, but I'm glad I bought it on sale. If the item creator functioned properly, this would definitely be worth full price, but as is...nah.

I give this game a tentative recommendation. Personally, I didn't find it to be as engaging as some past entries in the series. I find the open world format actually limits the puzzle solving somewhat. There are no longer puzzles that must be solved in a number of different ways, and no way to re-solve anything you've completed, so I often found myself simply taking the path of least resistance. The main plot wraps itself up several areas short of the end of the game, provided you're clearing most puzzles, which leaves those last few areas in a strange place of "not quite post-game, not quite proper game." The word puzzles found in the menu are also probably some of the weakest puzzles I've ever seen from a Scribblenauts game. Instead of presenting an engaging challenge, they simply turn into a large game of "guess what the devs were thinking." For the overworld puzzles once solved they're solved for good and with only one save slot the replayability of the game is somewhat limited unless you're willing to do a hard reset.
All that aside though, most of the puzzles are well thought-out and offer both an easy path and allow you to think outside the box. The object interactions are fun and the game is full of little easter eggs. It is a fun game, and if you've enjoyed Scribblenauts games in the past you'll probably like it and if you've never played one before this isn't a bad place to start.

A very cute and quirky turn-based JRPG. If you only have a laptop that's a few years old (like I do) you may need to turn down the settings a bit as there's a bit of lag. If you have a good computer, though, max it up. So, here's what you need to know about the game before you buy:
1. It's a turn-based JRPG. Think Final Fantasy up to FFX and you'll get a good idea about what you're getting into.
2. There is a story, though it's usually behind a lot of humor, including a bit of meta humor. If you want a game where there is a story, but with a lighthearted tone (for the most part), this should be good.
3. Depending on how you play the game can be preeetty lengthy. It depends on whether you want to grind just enough to beat the bosses or grind A LOT and look around for any treasure.
4. Lots of skills to learn and equipment to find, and all of them can change your appearance. It's a good way to mix and match the characters you get in terms of the roles you want them to have in combat.
12 dollars is an alright price for what you get here (though it'd probably be smart to wait for a sale). If you're really stringy about if you want this game, though, you can play the first three EBF games (as well as a slightly stripped version of this one) for free on most flash game websites.

Epic Battle Fantasy 4 is an adventure RPG game, developed by Matt Roszak, releasing on Steam is February 2014. This is my first foray into the Epic Battle Fantasy series and have no other previous experience with other games in the franchise.
Gameplay is a simplistic RPG style view, with turn based combat for the fights. Controls are so simple; you literally can play the whole game with just your mouse. The game has a real “Pokémon” feel to it, as you explore you will find parts of the map you can’t explore yet because you don’t have the required skill, for instance, to cut a tree down or to smash a rock. Once you learn said skills, you can backtrack quite easily to explore and find treasure hidden in the previously locked area.   The game has well over a hundred different enemies to kill, and learn their strengths and weaknesses of.  My favourite part of the game play is easily the loot and item system.  The game boasts over 170 different items for your characters to use; you can upgrade these items through using the Forging mechanic which require you to use craft-able items to make the upgrade.
The combat system is really well designed too; you have a party of four characters eventually, but you can only use three in a battle, the fourth acts as a backup in case one of your others dies. The Pokémon element theme is a key mechanic too; making sure you use the correct weapon with the right effect on the enemy is an almost absolute must most of the time.  Characters can also learn “companions” which acts as like “ultimate” attacks, and any of your characters can use them rather than having them bound to one of your party – the best and most fun by a country mile has to be the Super Nova, which just obliterates the entire screen.
Visually, EBF4 is again, simple, but that comes across very pleasantly. The in game art style looks colourful and vibrant, and has a very 3DS look to it. The narration parts of the game are done in a beautifully, almost hand drawn style of art, as if they have just been pulled out of a children’s book. I was enchanted by the visuals straight away as soon as I saw this. There is little animation in the game, given the 2D aspect, but the small amount of animation in the game is done really well, no odd movement cycles or strange looking attacks. There isn’t any voice acting; however there aren’t walls and walls of text to read through, so that can be forgiven.
EBF4’s difficulty levels can be changed on the fly, and you are almost encouraged to play on the highest difficulty until you start hitting a brick wall. I played the game on a normal difficulty and still felt sufficiently challenged by the fights. You can ramp up the difficulty to epic mode for those wanting to get extra achievements though. Once you complete the game you have the option for New Game+. Not to mention the Fire Mountain area of the game. This area scales with your characters level, allowing you to take on unique beasty bosses for extra special loot. This for me again, reminded me of the Pokémon games and the Elite Four trainers.
The world, in which you play in, is full of extra little bits to do, with roughly 20 side quests to complete, which offer no real variety but still add a bit more game play. The quests are only collection quests, so don’t expect to be getting really in depth quest lines like other RPGs. The quests will reward you with stat increasing items, or more equipment to make use of. There are also a number of NPCs scattered around the world that whilst they offer no game play advantage, they do have a bit of lore behind them though.
EBF4 took me just under 20 hours to complete. I went into this game expecting it to be over in five hours. I am absolutely amazed at how much content and how long this game actually is. What really does this game the most credit is, I wasn’t bored once whilst playing, and I wasn’t waiting for the end of the game to roll around as I was having that much fun playing. There may not be a massive amount of replay ability given the linearity of the storyline, but the New Game+ mode will definitely cater for any people that are fans of the game play.
Technically, the game runs in a much smaller resolution, whilst you can play full screen, it is a scaled up version. For some reason, I almost had a lot of stuttering during some moments in the game. This was fixed by reloading the game, but I couldn’t quite work out what was causing it. Obviously the game isn’t very taxing to run, given the 2D graphics, but still, I was dropping frames every now and again.  The game cannot be played using a controller without the use of third party software, but I would recommend people play this game with their mouse.
To sum up, I am absolutely amazed at the quality of this game. It is easily one of my favourite RPG experiences I have ever had. I remarked quite a bit in this review about the resemblances between EBF4 and Pokémon, and that comparison really does this game justice. It is an absolute masterpiece of a game that looks so simple on the outside, but is beautifully and carefully developed on the inside. The game is so perfectly priced at £8, 99 too, with hours of content and high quality content at that!

The beginning of something that is, hopefully; truly marvelous. Steam community has a bad habit of banding together to destroy a games reputation through the review system, as we all know it is a toxic wasteland of angry, poorly endowed losers who can't help themselves but to vent their frustrations with a product in the form of bad reviews.
So now that we have settled that, lets get on to the review of this tasty little RPG product shall we?
First off I would like to comment on just how professional and well managed this small team of dedicated developers really is... if you are like me and got sucked into Early Access before, you would know that despite growing budgets and fanbase these indie devs take forever to produce small amounts of mediocre content and provide almost no support for the game at all. The guys at portilarium treat Shroud with the professionalism of a AAA title while delivering the hands on player feedback in the forms of detailed updates and patch notes. Also to note, a major content publish is pushed once a month on a fairly tight and strict schedule. Making for predictable and transparant roadmapping on how the game is progressing.
The game itself is what you would expect from a 3D action rpg. Shroud of the Avatar has an MMORPG flavour but delivers itself in the form of a single player RPG experience. The world is vastly more detailed and interactive than seen in traditional mmos, objects can be picked up, containers opened, keys for doors, traps on floors. It really brings that old RPG feel into the online market, allowing players to group up and enjoy the experience, or play the game entirely solo, even offline.
Now with any game, especially in early access, SotA is not without its flaws. Bugs, unfinished content and poor performance in zones without optimization (these are usually the construction zones you see and to be honest its only certain places). These obvious ones aside, the cons are almost entirely subjective. So rather than introducing my pros/cons list I will list some of the features that pop out at me and you can decide for yourself.
1. Game uses an overworld map
'akin to JRPGs and 8 bit Ultima games. Players are expected to travel on that map and zone into points of interest. This allows the game to expand its content in a more intelligent way, rather than editing maps and zone lines as in open world games, portalarium can just put more POI on the map and create zones. So is it a Pro or Con?'
2. Skill based, No-Class system
'trying to innovate and build upon what started in Ultima Online, the game uses a 'use based' skill up on every single individual spell and skill (passives raise with the related usebased skills). This part I hate to be honest, but everyone has their opinions.'
3. Interactive Roleplay Environment
'Truly interactive world with simulated time, NPC scheduling and many sub systems to aid in the Roleplay aspect of the game. Shroud community puts an awful lot of focus on the RP side of things, which is nice when compared to the eliteist, completionist, competative and boss/loot banging nature of most MMORPGS.'
4. Non-Instanced Player Housing
'directly on the maps, in the towns and cities you visit and in player owned towns you will find the homes of Novias inhabitants. Similar to Ultima Online, and to an extent Vanguard (reminds me of EQ2 if the housing were not instanced... and cities wern't tiny). This feature to me alone makes SotA vastly superiour to any other online RPG.'
5. Crafting is Important
'Period. Player made stuff is the best, game actually has an economy to mention'
6. Active and continuous Development Cycle
'game will be treated as an MMO with no subscriptions, with updates and content added to the game over time. This wont be a 'pump and dump' product.'
The feature list is immense so I will leave it at six, and encourage you to read the negative comments and reviews so you can see how others might feel about the product. SotA has a lot to offer, but for players looking for a perfect finished product to fill all their desires it might not the the game for you. Just saying.
I do recommend though as I feel it is a great value for the cost and the game is shaping up great!

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Moon Studios has outdone themselves on this game. Every positive aspect of every Metro-vania style game that came before comes together to make this masterpiece that is Ori and the Blind Forest.
The action in this game is crazy fast, it keeps you on your toes, but the controls don't hold you back, they're super-responsive. This game strikes the perfect balance between reasonably challenging and totally brutal. If you run out of health, you die, but unlike other games where you have a significant several-second delay or even a condescending "Game Over" screen (NINTENDO!) before you can resume playing. This game doesn't give you any of that. If you die, you're sent back to your save point instantly, there's no delay, you can retry. Because of that, you sometimes have a sense of "ah, dang, I died again, but that's okay! I can just try again!". You get frustrated in this game, but you don't get discouraged by it at all, even through the several dozen/hundred times that you WILL inevitably die in this game. More the opposite, it makes you want to try again, to beat that area even more! That's the magic of the gameplay that this title has.
The visuals are absolutely stunning. If I bought a 4K monitor just to play this game on, it would be totally worth it because the artwork is the most beautiful yet unintrusive eye candy I have ever seen in a game like this. Such rich and vibrant colours, but with a really awesome atmospheric feel to the setting that I can't get enough of. If you're on a TN monitor, I feel sorry for you.
Ori and the Blind Forest's soundtrack is wonderful. I love it. It reinforces the addictive nature anti-discouragement characteristics of this game so well, and it's beautiful to listen to on its own, too. I listened to the game's music and then tried to listen to Super Mario Galaxy's famously-orchestrated music, and the difference is like night and day. SMG's sountrack is nice but next to the Ori soundtrack sounds terrible. The music in this game calms you down, gives you feelings of the area you're in, and sets your heart racing whenever it feels like it. I get adrenaline rushes from the dungeon escapes just because of the music, it's terrific.
The storyline is great. It's simple, there's not a lot to it, but that's all you need. Even though Sein is the only one who talks throughout the game, it is just enough to make you understand what is going on without pages and pages of dialogue. Sein is the Navi that Navi should have been.
If I had one wish it would be that this game was longer. Don't get me wrong - this game is a good 8-9 solid hours for the average person, if not more to complete the game entirely. Honestly, I have never played a game where you do so much and progress so far in what in retrospect does not seem to have been that much time. It's just that at the end you're left wanting more. Which is fine, I guess - replaying the game is a sweet deal!
If I had my way, this game would be heralded as a hallmark of the 2D platformer genre because of how well it has been made. It's an absolute masterpiece. I would have no problem calling Metro-vania-style games Blind Forest-style games after playing it. That's how good this game is for me. It's so good that it makes me crave more - which is really hard to do!
Glowing recommendation from me. If you like 2D platformers with fast, smooth action with the best visuals and accompanying soundtrack an indie developer can muster, this game is for you.

What follows is a critique, not a review. I really like the game, but want to discuss some of the elements and its representation of the industry.
Game Dev Tycoon (GDT) tells the story of a solo independent game developer hitting it big and creating a successful AAA game studio starting from a small studio apartment. At the time of its release, this story embodied the hopes and dreams of many new indie developers and comes across as a relatable American underdog tale. It tells this story surprisingly well and with an interesting perspective on game development, but creates a slightly reductive view of what makes a game high quality and fails to discuss the bigger issues in the gaming industry.
You pick a theme, genre, and platform (later getting to pick up to two genre and three platforms), then, in three stages, decide how much time to invest in three different aspects of the game, like level design, graphics, and story, over the course of development. The primary value of the game is determined by how well the theme (like mystery or sci fi) fits the genre (action, RPG, etc.). Just think of a real-world game that did really well and make that and you’ll almost never go wrong.
This seems against the grain of the indie movement, though, where developers have more incentive to mix different influences in order to create more unique games. GDT may say, for example, that a mystery-themed RPG doesn’t work, but does that mean that no developer could ever make such a game fun? GDT in its mechanics supports a worldview that says tried-and-true formula are good, original and innovative ideas are bad--yet its own existence as a business-themed strategy/RPG seems to contradict this.
This reflects the paradox of games as art in a commercial setting. The subjective qualities of a game makes it endearing to players, but inside a capitalist system made at a specific point in time with a specific available audience. We may think of the original Mario as an objectively great game, but if it had only been released last year, unaltered in terms of graphics or controls, its retro aesthetics and simple controls might not receive the same critical acclaim. So while games are art, we seem to have trouble viewing them as valuable as something other than commodities, comparing them to other games available at the time. The value of games as a form of expression, even if that expression is the experience of its contents, only makes sense in this lens if it has favorable objective qualities compared to the competition on the market.
Eventually, you unlock the custom game engine which becomes a secondary value indicator and reinforces the idea of games having value based on objective qualities. As the audience demands better, higher quality games, the player researches features to add to an engine, then builds a new engine incorporating these features, and games using that engine. Eventually, after 35 years, the player has researched almost all things and all platforms have been released. Since one cannot then construct better engines, the maximum value a game can achieve has already been reached so playing on becomes a fruitless endeavor. The only thing left is to tally up the high scores.
Around the midpoint, GDT introduces the concept of publishers who offer contracts with randomized demands like “make an action game for the PS2 of any theme” or “make a pirate/simulation game on any platform”. Sometimes these contracts are really bad with mismatched themes and platforms or target audiences. Unfortunately, until one grows a substantial fanbase, self publishing will lead to lower sales, regardless of the game’s quality. In this way, GDT portrays publishers as out-of-touch capitalist enterprises, encroaching on artistic freedoms, but necessary to make games sell. Still, if reasonable contracts exist then signing one seems to have little downside. Sure they collect royalties, but the increased sales can overshadow that. It makes one ask what’s the value of going independent? And after building a large fan base and self publishing, what do we use this artistic freedom to do?
Sequels. As long as each subsequent game grows in quality (game engine features), GDT does little to punish players for making the same game over and over and over again. Once unlocked, sequels become one of the smartest ways to make bank. Reviewers will praise the games for expanding on their predecessors, but never criticize their sameness. In this sense, GDT replicates the risk-averse behaviour of modern day AAA companies, again undermining the indie movement which values new ideas over tired formula.
Eventually, you’ll move into a larger office, hire and train more developers, fund an R&D department and even produce your own not-Steam online platform and game console. The sixth edition of your AAA franchise will become an MMO and you can spend the rest of the game making expansions to it until it spontaneously ends at the 35-year mark.
GDT allows players to live out fantasies of creating great games, but one could imagine a more realistic game business simulation that demonstrates the much harder problem of managing a project with different people of various skills, contracting artists and musicians to create the different elements, all participants willingly risking financial peril for something which consumers may, or may not, actually appreciate.
The irony of Game Dev Tycoon is that it feels like a simple, fun, innovative indie game where you live your dream of making great, fun, innovative games for a living, but instead end up producing Call of Duty three times a year--the kind of profit-driven behaviour that drives players to indie games in the first place. One could argue that GDT parodies the game industry, but its up-beat music and artwork and themes leave little room for asking deep questions about how the industry should behave vs. how it does and gives little ability to change it, nor does it challenge the player to do things differently. The biggest questions it asks are whether you should sue the makers of fan-based games, whether you should open source your old game engines, and things like that with very clear binary, good/evil outcomes.
In every way, even down to the way GDT evaluates the objective quality of a game--asserting that specific theme/genre matches are good, others are bad--expresses a reductive view about games as a form of expression or art and the merits of experimenting with unusual combinations. Instead, it looks at them as products, only valued for their commercial success. Again, indie games have done great in showing how to creatively blend concepts to create new ideas about interaction, but GDT doesn’t reward the application of such creativity in its representation of the industry.
At the end of the day, Game Dev Tycoon still offers a good experience for the asking price of 10$. When you fail and go bankrupt, it motivates you to get back up and try again. The gameplay is simple, but that makes it all-the-more addictive. It just doesn’t seem to fairly represent the indie community, many of the most successful of whom didn’t come from modest dwellings in hopes of running AAA companies, but rather ex-AAA employees wanting to explore different avenues. It glorifies companies like Steam that produce high-quality products consistently, even if many of them are sequels, but not companies like Double Fine which fund the development of smaller-but-experimental games consistently.
Game Dev Tycoon encourages a rationalist worldview where love and passion for games takes a backseat to profit and greed. A practical mentality that I find morbid and depressing.

I am a fan and avid player of the original Gauntlet.  Later releases of the game (especially the 3rd person view ones) just never interested me as much.
But I love this game.  It's shorter, and the mechanics are slightly different, but it's very close in both body and spirit.
Some major changes:
-Warrior and Valkyrie are now the melee classes and have no shooting attacks (well, Valkyrie has one weaker one).
-Elf is now the primary ranged class.
-Wizard has the most abilities, as he can change through 9 different spells.  (difficult to learn, but great when mastered)
-Characters each have one primary attack and 3 secondaries.
-Potions no longer trigger 'magic' attacks.  Instead, the gold from the dungeon is used to buy relics, and potions power these items.
-Death is truly unbeatable (instead of just having crazy high hp)
All in all, I love this game and it takes me back to the time I spent with the original.  It is a very good update of a classic.  :)

Each class in unique which means you can replay the game 4 times with 4 different sets of achievements and 4 different special moves. You can also obtain various pieces of armor, I'm not sure if they're just aesthetic but you unlock them by completing certain stages on certain difficulties. I never got to play the original Gauntlet from way back when, but this game definitely adds a newer idea to an older game concept. Crazy addictive and fairly unforgiving at higher difficulties, as games SHOULD be nowadays.
As most games are set, the melee are generally easier to deal with. Not here. Ranged characters like the Wizard or the Ranger are clearly more capable in dealing with large hordes a bit better than the Warrior or the Valkyrie. It makes things a bit tougher when you can't reliably hit everything unless you're swinging an axe in their face. ;D So that's a nice twist. I found Merlin was probably the best choice for mauling everything, though he's the most flimsy and probably one of the trickiest to use.
I can't really decide if the Keyboard and Mouse or the controller is more fun. I've been an avid PC gamer since I was six...so the latter is less fun for me than the PC control system. I love this game. The  5 hours I spent playing before thsi review were probably the most fun I've had in a good long while. :D Absolutely recommended for anyone who liked the older Gauntlet game or anyone who enjoys dungeon crawlers with friends.

While its fun for a few hours, the game can be completed on hard (in a party of 2) in about 5 hours. Sure there's replayability but with only 3 areas and 12 (short) levels to choose from, whats the point? Gaunlet legends -a game released on PS1- has more content than this. Perks are mostly useless, not much variety in levels or boss fights and most of the achievements are for grinding. On the plus side the characters keep you entertained at least til the end. 5/10

I give this game a tentative recommendation. Personally, I didn't find it to be as engaging as some past entries in the series. I find the open world format actually limits the puzzle solving somewhat. There are no longer puzzles that must be solved in a number of different ways, and no way to re-solve anything you've completed, so I often found myself simply taking the path of least resistance. The main plot wraps itself up several areas short of the end of the game, provided you're clearing most puzzles, which leaves those last few areas in a strange place of "not quite post-game, not quite proper game." The word puzzles found in the menu are also probably some of the weakest puzzles I've ever seen from a Scribblenauts game. Instead of presenting an engaging challenge, they simply turn into a large game of "guess what the devs were thinking." For the overworld puzzles once solved they're solved for good and with only one save slot the replayability of the game is somewhat limited unless you're willing to do a hard reset.
All that aside though, most of the puzzles are well thought-out and offer both an easy path and allow you to think outside the box. The object interactions are fun and the game is full of little easter eggs. It is a fun game, and if you've enjoyed Scribblenauts games in the past you'll probably like it and if you've never played one before this isn't a bad place to start.

You can probably tell from the extreme number of hours I've spent playing it, but I love this game.  It manages the rare and delicate balance between strategy gameplay and engaging story in such a genuinely clever way that it's honestly tough to compare it to anything else.  It's a game where cleverness counts and the mechanics of the game give you the space to play out the encounters creatively.  If you like story driven strategy RPGs, it's hard to fathom you not liking this game.  It's only faw is also its greatest strength and that is player freedom.  Given what you can get away with, it's possible to accidentally engage the second part of a story before the first which can botch up your quest log.  If you're a completionist like me, this can be a tiny bit frustrating.  I found plenty of online help to assist me through these and repeated playthroughs are definitely worth while since they give you the chance to go back and replay the story as  well as try out any cool skills you skipped the first time.
