This is actually an excellent game, if you don't mind the grind of gathering leet cards and the futility of a ladder system that has you flailing to keep up. It's the same fundamental issue I had with Hearthstone, of which this is a clear (and probably superior) successor.
If, in Hearthstone, you played actual minions (instead of cards) that moved across a battleground and fought each other before attacking the hero, you'd essentially have Minion Masters. The same issues are very obviously going to arise - mastering the meta and collecting "legendary" cards is going to trump anything else. So if you can do those things, you will win, and if not, you will lose. The game board adds a small amount of spatial variation and reactivity to the formula but it's not enough to free you from playing by formula. You don't need to buy the in-game currency but you can, if you want to speed up your chances of getting better cards, more heroes, and some aesthetic upgrades.
The "expeditions" portion of the game is fun and rewarding. Here's where I have a suggestion. I would love to see this fleshed out such that it could constitute a full single-player (or co-op) experience without the necessity of grinding ladder matches to fuel your expeditions. The AI is pretty straightforward in the expeditions; it doesn't seem like a technical challenge to build this part of the game out to suit casual gamers or people who just like to have adventures with their friends.
I don't care about being stone or wood or diamond or fish tier or whatever. I don't want to fight battles against random strangers that much. At this point in my gaming life I can see the addiction hooks immediately and I'm grizzled enough to stay away from them.
The real reason I don't recommend this game is that it's clearly designed to be addicting, and consequently to siphon money out of those without the awareness or willpower to resist. Plenty of people CAN use responsibly. If you're one of them and you'd like a well-executed CCG, go ahead, and enjoy yourself.
I can't comment on the overall balance of the game with my playtime, but I played ten or fifteen ladder matches and didn't lose any. I am pretty sure this is because I lucked out on my first spins with the "power tower" and got purple and orange cards. Maybe I just played against muppets. But if it was the cards, that's bad news for casuals.

over 25 years ago my high-school friends and I were popping quarter after quarter to the sounds of our often-starving dungeon heroes blasting & hacking away endless hordes of monsters. oh did we hate those lobbers! today, nostalgia has brought us back to this remake of the old classic arcade game, to gather the gold and the kills and the skull coins - cheaper than quarters! - to revive our fallen heroes. this Gauntlet version falls a bit short on the nostalgia front, but not always in a bad way. some of the sounds are missing, no lobbers to be seen, and the game mechanics are somewhat different. each of the four player classes - and there can only be one of each in a game - has at least three attacks or special moves, up to an impressive 9 spells for Merlin the wizard (cast with sometimes awkward key combos; presumably the game is better played with a gamepad than keyboard/mouse). gold can be used to buy vanity gear, or relics with helpful, short-lasting powers, which are triggered by using up the potions found in the dungeons. that is all the potions are good for, no "smart bomb" effect as in the original. lots of monster kills get you skull coins, an in-game currency used to bring players back from the dead. on Hard and Unfair difficulty levels, better make sure you have at least one skull coin available at all times. there is also an achievement system for each class, which slowly improves its power and survivability as you meet quotas of kills, destruction, deaths, healing, etc. funny how it rewards your failures and mistakes.

the gameplay is a lot of fun - much more so with friends - but the dungeon content is limited: three dungeon sets, each with three dungeons and a boss room. each individual dungeon has 3 or 4 floors. after a handful of long game nights we finished the whole thing on Normal and are close to done on Hard. we can only hope there is DLC coming with more dungeons and new monsters. maybe even a new class? if no DLC, there is still some replay value in trying the different classes.

if you're looking for a dungeon crawl to enjoy with friends, that is simpler than the Diablos and Torchlights, but a step above the old arcade fare, there is enough fun to be had in this Steam version of the Gauntlet.

F.E.A.R 3 Ultima Ascension of the FEAR franchise. After but 5 minutes the plot collapses in on itself and twists and turns a previous tactical shooter into a CoD clone for 10 year olds.
The Gameplay is average. Gone is still the uber shotgun from FEAR 1 and so is the enemy AI. The game is so easy on next to hardest difficulty Fearless, and the hardest one being Insane which is locked until you finish the game at least once. No effort was required of me as I blasted enemies to dust and only died when I was either stupid or engaged in honorable melee with the enemy.
The levels are boring and repetitive, and the level transition will leave you confused. At an early point in the game, you are trying to flee the city, and get shot down while doing so, and after crashing you immediately return to the city. What!?
Oh, also, Point Man crashes, explodes and falls from mortal heights and still survives, It's a cliché nowadays but it's still complete garbage to look at.
Levels consists of open areas with enemies spawning around a small map. Kill enemies, proceed through a corridor to the next big area, and repeat. It's also that annoying kind of map that won't allow you to jump over things the devs don't want you to jump over! Want to jump over this couch? Can't do that. Want to crouch under this railing? Can't do that. But you can only crouch under the only thing that will continue the on rail shooting segments. The pacing is♥♥♥♥♥♥as well, there is no time for you to breath out between battles, no puzzles of any kind exists other then, press button, open door kind. Not like you'll ever get worked up playing this PoS since the scary/creepy parts are all but gone. If this game didn't have FEAR in the name I would never have associated it with the series att all.
Story collapsed in on itself after about 5 minutes. Why answer questions like: Where are we? Why am I here? What am I suppose to do? Point Man apparently has character now, which is funny since he's a silent MP, so It's stupid. Also Fettel now apparently thinks family is super important and now wants to help you/you help him to get you to mother. Why is he there? Is another question I asked myself since you did put a bullet in his head in the first game. And now he is ghost, or, something, but still needs to walk through doors. I don't care anymore, why should I when the devs didn't care either. Also dead characters are alive as well that died in FEAR Extraction Point expansion for the first game but I guess, RETCON! Didn't happen, character is alive now, hurray! Or the expansion simply weren't canon, but FEAR 2's dlc was! Cuz Fettel.

I bought this game when it came out, but only made it a bit into the first town. I was extremely bored, and kind of lost as to what the game was expecting of me. It left a bad taste in my mouth, and I put the game down for a bit.
When Divinity Original Sin 2 was released, my friend urged me to give it a try. It was awesome, the pacing and balance was much better. I only played a few hours in, co-op, before I realized I needed to give the original another try.
I returned to try the game again, solo, and was determined to make it past where I had before.
When reviews say "you just have to make it past the first xx! And then it really opens up!" I roll my eyes. I shouldn't have to suffer through garbage for some hope at something really great. But I really can't put into words how true this does ring for this particular title. There is just a load of talking to people in a town, and if your any sort of complettionist and dont want to rush through and cheapen the Main Quest, it can really drag on and get old.
The thing that draws me to this game is the combat, hands down. Its extremely tactical, rewarding, and I found myself reloading even after successful battles, just to see if I could do it better somehow. The game does so much with simple RPG abilities we have all seen and known for years. I wish there was even more things to fight, but honestly the game is very well balanced in terms of Role Playing, Combat, Dungeon Diving, and Choice Making. The difficulty is so perfectly tuned, it amazes me from a Game Developer standpoint. (Although it did get a little easy towards the end, but I had some pretty solid character builds)
I am very excited to hop back into DOS:2, and can't wait to see what that game has in store.
If you are any fan of games like:
XCOM
Final Fantasy Tactics
Dragon Age
Icewind Dale
Baldurs Gate
etc...
Than you really need to look no further than a game that truly respects the art of the Turn Based Adventure RPG.

A game that doesn't look great but is rated 98% on Steam, uh..? Okay, let's try the Flash version... Ah, the agony, you have to point and click to move the character around, they're moving on a grid and you get ugly icons everywhere you point at... My, my. The character designs aren't exactly good... Okay, since these are both one-man projects, I'll at least say that it looks much better than Undertale. It also beats it in terms of laughs and overall complexity.
Really. It's absolutely hilarious, and also excrutiatingly overwhelming at the beginning of the game. Ah, those crafting materials...!
After an hour I decided to buy the Steam version, and couldn't stop playing it ever since. This is nothing like a RPG Maker game, it seems to use its very own engine (which, amusingly, is quite slow even on a high-end PC... Thankfully it's still playable). This has a lot of advantages.
It pays respects to its elders but never tries to be lazy about anything. My main complaint? It's a very difficult game... If you want to 100% it, you'll suffer. A lot. Be prepared to spend tens of hours on it. I'll just be happy with at least two thirds of the achievements. If you don't mind not getting everything, then... I get it's doable. But you'll still need to grind a lot, or use a money cheat to buy all of the items you need.
And this was my 42nd Steam review, a milestone for any self-respecting geek. Not my finest hour, though!

I want to start off by saying that I love this game, on the Playstation 3. I was hoping by playing it on the PC I wouldn't start having late game issues like one would have on the console because the PC is capable of handling more. But in this PC port I found a rather annoying bug called the "glide bug." If you stop moving while your mouse is in motion then your character will slide a good 4-5 feet more forward. This only happens on the PC version and it also happens in New Vegas. Contacted cutomer support and they acted like nothing like that has ever been reported but apparently it is on every PC port.
Although this is not a game breaker for some, it is for me when I'm trying to sneak up to a person or deactivate a trap and I completely over shoot it because my character slips like he's on ice. Throws stealth and accuracy completely out the window in a game where accuracy with weapons is already an issue. Very disappointing and an embarrassment to this games reputation.

SotA is probably one of the worst purchases I've ever made in my life - be it in a game or the other forms of entertainment I've spent money on. The fact I was an original backer for this sorry excuse of a game during its Kickstarter only serves to drive in the knife of regret even deeper. This game is a disappointment in every sense of the word, and the product that it's become is barely a shadow of what the original Kickstarter pitch proposed, which was a heavy story-driven game in which the player's choices had meaningful consequences. For more details on that, look up the original pitch and be disgusted with what you have now.
The developers are notoriously bad at engaging the community and are completely out of touch with reality. If you really want to know how bad they are, look up BrightLocker, another project the developers are involved in. If you think the debacle over Battlefront 2's lootboxes are bad, you have no idea what BrightLocker intends to bring to gaming (fortunately it's very unlikely the project will get funded).
SotA doesn't even have a release date yet. The developers keep changing established definitions to suit their needs (Early Access, beta, pre-alpha, launch and (L)aunch).... When you launch the game it says it's in Pre-Alpha; Steam says it's in Early Access; developers say it's "story ready" but not (L)aunched yet (whatever that means); the game has been persistent for one and a half years, has an active cash shop and RMT with an official RMT, yet they won't concede that the game's been released, which it has been, for all purposes and intents...
SotA is the culmination of greedy developers and blind fan boys. SotA is the epitome of form over substance. There is NOTHING in this game that is good or sets it apart from any other game out there. F2P games are better and more balanced than this P2W crapfest. The dwindly population of barely 200 players (over half of which are alts of each other) is a testament to that. SotA will go down in history as one of the worst KS projects ever. Keep up the good work, Port and the SotA community!

Then all the players that sink a ton of money into the game come in and stomp all over it, even if you're playing it peacefully, not attacking others, only AI, and if someone attacks you and they explain that they have a perfectly good reason for it other than "just for the resources" or "for the fun of it", you just forgive them and never hold it against them. Well the Pay to Win players just attack for the fun of it, or to keep you from even getting up to where they are. The big dogs only see us small pups and the people that play this to have a good time and experience a new type of gameplay as a threat from the day we even drop into the server, and the game's PVP attack immunity doesn't even help, becuase the moment that goes away and they've had your eye on you from day 1, then nothing is stopping them from marching straight to your village, with 100+ troops, destroying the beautiful and incredible castle you worked so hard on. And once they destroy your castle, next thing you know, they already sent another army to clean up what the 1st one couldn't, then they kick you to the ground, spit on your face, and end your entire game there. Not even trying again will help you because then this entire process will start all over again.
The only way to win is to give the devs money, that's it. Real world money is what drives this entire game, not skill, not tactics, not teamwork of other F2P players like you that actually want to see what this game has to offer. Without giving money, these devs just throw you to the wolves, that's it, they don't care about all the higher up breaking the rules, as long as they keep giving money to stay ahead, then anything goes. I hate to see that a game this unique is completely ruined by money and people who stay on for literally months, that's right, MONTHS, on end and never even shut down the game just so they can watch over the little guy and plan on how to end them the very second they get.
This game would be great if the rich people and the higher ups didn't stomp on everyone who can't afford even the smallest in-game item like me. It would be better if it was better controlled, alt accounts are against game rules, but they don't have a way to enforce it, so you got 1 person, with a ton of money, creating 10+ accounts, ruling a huge chunk of land, sinking tons of money into those accounts, collecting all the resources they can get, just to hammer down all of the players that just want to explore the game.
This game needs to be better moderated, give the F2P players a fighting chance, and even out the balance of power, becuase all those are the reason I do not recommend this game.

Skullgirls is a fast, hyper-fighter type of fighting game. Attacks are quick, flow nicely into other attacks, and combos can reach unbelievable numbers of hits. It is not the most beginner friendly game, as while promoting a very lengthy tutorial service, playing against veterans of the game can be very infuriating to newcomers. Thankfully, the PC version has a matchmaking system, with lobbies designated towards the scrublords of new and old.
I adore Skullgirls. While gitting gud can be difficult, the outcome is a fighting game that I feel no other can top. Fun as hell, and brutal too, Skullgirls is a game old fans and newcomers to the fighting game genre should enjoy.
(If anyone else can recommend fighting games similar or just as much fun as Skullgirls, please feel free to put them in the comments. I'm trying to branch out as a fan, and ideas are very much welcome!)

I have this and Game Corp DX, both are good games. Game Dev Tycoon is better, longer, and more realistic, however. This game takes a LOT of consideration into making a game, and later allows you to mix different genres, choosing from dozens of topics, and even multi-platform.
PROS:
-There are plenty of options to make almost any game. Wide range of topics from Werewolf to Fashion.
-Training and cultivating employees into specialists is fun.
- Unlike Game Corp, you don't do any "furniture management" which is a big bonus. Employee maintenance is sending them on vacation periodically.
- Lots of late game perks and reasons to keep playing past the "end".
CONS:
- OH MY GOD. PLEASE STOP INTERRUPTING MY GAME EVERY 5 SECONDS WITH RANDOM CONSOLE ANNOUNCEMENTS AND OTHER BS. This is really, TRULY annoying after your first playthrough when you know what everything says. This is made even more annoying because the entire left-hand side of the screen is dead space the WHOLE GAME. Put announcements there!!!!
- The "hints" you earn don't guarantee you even a passable game. There are a ton of influences on a game's success that aren't mentioned or explained in detail.
All around a good game with a major design flaw that has me cursing at the screen, especially when I'm trying to do time-sensitive stuff and keep getting interrupted.

4 people play as divers to get their DPV to the very end, and 2 players will play as sharks to stop them. Each team has a collected 30 lives and once those are up then you lose. There's quite a few sharks you can choose from, and divers get a plethora of weapons to use, so each match will be different from the next. It's much better than a lot of AAA games that have come out in these recent years.

So in my opinion this game is heavily influenced by the modern style of games. What do I mean by that?
It feels like a mobile/tablet game as it rewards you a lot for playing, especially at the beginning when you are still new to the game you can unlock a lot of achievements and new objects just by playing it once. Of course later, these "easy" ones are gone and you have to focus on a few achievements to unlock them in a game but then you have more experience so it balances out again. On the other hand you have these very specified time lengths for your games. I found myself mostly playing the 30 minute mode up to now but you can decide yourself and also go for 1-hour-games for example.
The graphic is really cute and good in my opinion and it fits this game perfectly. The rounds you play will be always a bit different from before even though you always start with an empty planet of a certain size. But because of the possible achievements and your own preferences you can change it into different planets every time but the bigger the planet and the more cities you have, the more you are running around with your giants and sometimes you might lose track of one village because you concentrate so much on the other side of the map.
Overall I really like this game and I think it fits the newer gamer generation very well with the short but rewarding round-style. But if you like build-up games you can have lots of fun with this game.

I picked up this game in extreme early access, because of the legendary accomplishments of its maker, Richard Garriot. While it's been a long road, I can say that this game is a mountain of fun to play at this point.
Aside from a mind-breaking large map, with many layers to it, and three potential game plot lines, there are a host of wonderful and often novel features to the game. As an example, online mode (MMORPG), offline mode, and friends-only online mode (basically pulling a Borderlands). Players can have an extreme impact on the shape of the map.
Early on, there was a bothersome limitation on the number of monsters available, but that time has passed. Combat has exploded in detail. The conversation system is reminiscent of the unique style used in the original Ultima games. Crafting? Crafting is off the hook.
It is, technically, still early access and a construction zone; but I firmly believe that for its price it is worth your time. The future of open world RPGs begins here.
With regard to stated drawbacks in other comments:
The addon store does exist, and prices range at around $100 for an in-game property. This is a %%$@# lot. At one time, when the game was less complete (and having an art studio to throw my money into), that was pretty crippling. However, as the game has approached completion, it has become less essential and I can vouch for a complete experience without addition investment at this point; this is especially true in offline mode.

This game is awesome so far. It is still in preAlpha state so its nowhere near done. The devs work with players and testers regularly to ensure that this game is what we want it to be. As it is still in preAlpha, there is still plenty of work to be done, and plenty of wipes as well, so don't be discouraged by this, its how a crowd funded player built game should be. I've been part of many preAlpha-Beta games, and though it is sometimes frustrating, being on the ground floor gives you a different view and insight into that game and its devs.
I highly recommend getting in to this game if you enjoy deep player progression, a great community, and devs who want your feedback to make the game what the players really want. Again, it is in preAlpha state, so it is nowhere near done, and this should be taken into account when deciding whether or not to purchase this game.

*Updated February 4, 2017*:
For the last year after writing my previous positive review, I've been playing and reviewing Shroud's development and updates. What have I seen?
Nothing of note.
The game has gotten a moderate graphical overhaul, but the core design hasn't changed. There's a ton of grinding in imbalanced, mostly-empty zones required to perform anything of note (read: anything fun) and the community, while friendly, is just as anti-social as ever. This means that while people are active in the game, it's rare that you'll find someone to group up with.
In the past year, there have been several telethons designed to acquire more funds, where the dev team has continued to be draconic with whom they award these new "stretch goals" to. I donated to a few, but it turns out I didn't donate correctly, or the right amount, or didn't buy the right thing in the add-on store, so I missed out. (Keep in mind I am not a low-level backer -- I have put hundreds into this game, and I feel like a low-class citizen).
This divide between 'whales' and actual gamers is only getting worse, and I greatly fear for this game on launch. Those high end backers are going to be the literal barons of the game world, and the majority of the economy is going to be driven by them.
We play games as an escape. Not as a means to enter a world that is merely a mirror of the real world, plagued with all of the same issues.
If you choose to spend money on this, beware. Unless you drop $300, or decide to only play offline, you're gonna have a bad time.

Previous review:
tl;dr: Not perfect. Worth playing.
Some background:
I am a huge Ultima fan, mostly of the single-player series, but UO too. I backed this game from day one, and have been playing both on- and off- Steam for a majority of the releases. I have not played nearly as much as some backers, but I have played much more than others. My Steam play time is Steam-only time for one account - my actual playtime is a bit higher.
I purposefully waited to write a review. I was actually planning on waiting until post-release, but lately, development has taken an upturn. The devs originally asked, when first being published to Steam, if backers would write positive reviews to help bump the review score. I did not feel at the time that the game was complete enough to warrant a review, and if I wrote one, it likely would not have been very positive. Lately, the devs have instead encouraged everyone to read the negative reviews before purchasing. In spite of this, I'd like to throw some positivity into the pot.
So, here we are. I believe I have seen and experienced enough of the game (as of r25) and development cycle to confidently write a positive review. Here's the breakdown:
PROS:
+Exploration. Despite slightly clunky navigation, even in an incomplete stage, the feel of wandering around, finding your way, learning terrain, and discovering well-hidden secrets is very tangible and a lot of fun.
+World map. One of the most beautiful world maps ever made in any game. Also, massive. Some people don't like dual-scale RPGs, but they are where I am most at home.
+Immersion. This is one of the things that wasn't as concrete until recent releases. NPC dialogue is getting better, the game world, now populated with player towns and many more points of interest, paint a picture of the world that is very encouraging of things to come.
+Freedom. Go where you want, level how you want, play how you want. This is the biggest part of UO, Everquest, and other "old-school" MMOs that is generally lost, but it seems that SotA is genuinely trying. Being a full-time crafter, trader, real-estate mogul, fisherman, and other non-combat professions are all viable, and the fundamental systems for all are in place (though iterative work is still being done to add depth).
+Astronomy/meteorology. The skybox, day/night/month/season/year cycles, phases of the moon, weather -- everything is there, and everything works. A huge feat.
+Social scene. The community is excellent, events happen all the time, and there are a large number of emotes and RP options available for everyone.
+Skill system. Most of the skills are fun and useful, and use-based leveling is a treat.
MIDDLE GROUND:
[These issues are things that are constantly being changed during development. However, this review is based on the most recent playable release.]
*Combat. Combat at the moment is prefaced with heavy deck-building and skill grinding, requiring you to be at least a little familiar with the systems in place before being able to become viable. When in combat, the game gives you a classic MMO hotbar presentation, combined with (optional) random elements that permit one to combine skills for greater effect, and a little action-based input. Currently, attacking can be performed either by clicking and holding left mouse or enabling auto-attack in options; and double-tapping to tumble a-la Guild Wars 2 et al. I believe the intention is to add more active input commands, such as blocking, a cover system, etc.
*Writing. As it stands, Shroud is a perfect example of "great plot, bad writing". Not all of the writing is bad, mind you, some of it is quite good, but how you get to those bits of story is extremely clunky. Navigating through NPC dialogue is still slow and at times can be unintuitive how to get an NPC to say what you want them to. Books are a fantastic addition, a good step towards filling the world with flavor. Regardless of being in an MMO environment, the plot is still enjoyable enough for you to follow its little threads wherever you can.
*Polish. Obviously this is something an early access game does not have, but for a gigantic semi-MMO, the veneer is one of the most important parts.
CONS:
-Not enough in-game encouragement to party up. The game world is huge, this is true, and in early access its hard to find regular players except on release days, but its still difficult to find a friend to quest with. Pick-up party members are extremely rare, so unless you have at least one friend who is interested in playing at the same time, and that's something that matters to you, keep that in mind. The community vis-a-vis the official forum is generally very welcoming, so friends can be found there, but generally speaking I must conclude that party play is not going to be big until the game goes live.
-Clunky input. Running around is a little sloggish, jumping still *feels* unresponsive, and sometimes you'll have to click a skill twice to get it to pop. The interface as a whole lags, probably due to lack of graphical optimization.
-Bag inventory. Just use list mode. Despite the ridiculous fun it was organizing bags in the U7, 8 and UO days, now you're bogged down with a huge amount of items and a tiny window to shove them all in. It doesn't make sense, and this is one thing that really, really needs improving, especially to grab that old UO feel for the people that want it.
-Bad combat feedback. Damage numbers don't proc sometimes, making it hard to tell if you've hit; interface/graphical lag makes it so that you have to take an extra second to be sure your target is dead; there's no real details except for damage taken and damage dealt. Most of the math is hidden and the devs don't seem super keen on sharing it (though it is likely to change).
Thanks for considering Shroud. I still believe in this game, now more than ever.
(This review will be updated upon release.)

I have only played the game's campaign missions, thus my review will not cover skirmish or multiplayer content.
Pros:
+All factions have unique base building mechanics. The ED construct their buildings like a puzzle, connecting each building to the others; the LC construct their buildings by stacking modules like towers, the UCS use droids (the former two drop their buildings from spaceships) to build their buildings and then construct add-ons onto them, while the Alien race construct their units by cloning and mutating their units themselves, instead of constructing buildings to produce the units (though they can create defensive buildings).
+The majority of the factions can customise their units - you research different weapons, armour etc. and can then design the units from those parts. Thus, the same unit can be fitted for different situations, such as anti-air support, siege, anti-armour role etc..
+The graphics of the game itself aren't half bad, considering how old the game is.
+Units don't have infinite ammo - conventional weapons need to resupply ammo, while energy weapons overheat and become less effective after repetitive use.
Cons:
-The story doesn't have a proper conclusion. It just ends on a cliffhanger.
-Unexplored areas on the map are covered in static, instead of just being blacked out. Not really a pleasant effect. Also, there's no proper fog of war - it's unclear how far it stretches, so units can suddenly appear like out of nowhere, because that area was actually covered by a fog that you can't see.
-Cutscene graffics have aged poorly.
-Some campaign dialogue between the characters locks down control of your units and builidings.... yet time doesn't stop, so your units will end up doing whatever they please until the dialogue ends... or you skip them to stop your units from getting themselves killed.
-The alien race is the only faction without customisable units, limiting strategic options with the faction. Also, the faction's mechanics aren't so well done. Units need to be close to a water source to absorb a certain amount of water before they can be cloned or morph to a different unit and, since all ground units use the same resouce, the area around a water source gets very clunky. Especially since there's no option to select where the cloning/morphing should take place - the unit just does it on the spot it was standing at when you give the order. When more than one unit is being cloned/morphed, any other units blocking the way are moved away and can even end up on innaccessible terrain.
-Most air units in the game are pretty useless. Bombers cannot be moved anywhere unless they're given a target... and then they need to fly to it all the way from your base.... and they're not all too fast, so they're unpractical for anything more than base defence. Other air units can usually be shot down in one or two shots even by anti-air troops, not to mention base defences, before they can really do anything, so their usefulness is limited.
-On the other hand, ground units move relatively slowly and most of the campaign maps are large, maze-like, and with narrow passages, so the units have to move in single file. Not the best way to launch an attack when the majority of your units are stuck in traffic.
-Lack of a decent manual or something of the sort on how things work, so quite a few things have to be figured out through trial and error. Such as, how to give a series of commands to your units, what weapons are effective against what and how ammo reloading works. Also, some campaign mission objectives are vague (e.g., in one level, it tells you that you need to free character X, but it doesn't specify that you need to bring your hero character there to do so).
All in all, at the time of writing this, the game costs 5 Euros and I got it on sale for just 1 Euro, so it's a sufficiently decent game for its price in my opinion.

I should have learned my lesson from Tabula Rasa. Fool me once, shame on you - fool me twice, shame on me.
Face the facts - Garriott already struck gold with the Ultima series, particularly Ultima Online. The primary reason for his success was a lack of competition that allowed him to remain ahead of the curve as far as innovation. Nowadays? No matter what he does, he'll be playing catch-up. He's competing with the long-running success of the other MMO's, he's competing with the unfair expectations of his loyal fans from his past successes, and the game itself shows that he's competing internally with himself as to what his vision for this game truly is.
What's worse is even if he does have a vision of where this game is headed, he's shooting himself in the foot with his marketing model. The ratio of actual content released as opposed to cash-bought store items is jarring - and shows their focus is on collecting money, not finishing a game.
What bothers me is this - Why would Garriott not simply make the game then release it to the public to stand or fall on its own merits? It's not like he's lacking economically - the dude lives in a castle and can afford to vacation in freakin' outer space. It's not like he doesn't have a pre-existing fanbase - he has enough people willing to throw money at anything with his name on it to make any other developer green with envy.
So, I ask again: Why would Garriott not simply make the game then release it to the public to stand or fall on its own merits?
The answer is simple: Because he's already done that, and it failed (despite being a success, sales-wise).
So this boils down to one thing... A cash grab. Not only that, but it's a cash grab by someone with more capital than most of us will ever see in our lives combined. A classic case of the rich getting richer, while we're left holding the bag.
Garriott's time has come... And gone. He's shown us that he's no longer worthy of our adoration, our respect, or our money.

I can't think of anything in the first two F.E.A.R games that really made no sense or wasn't explained through the collectible lore drops or the story, In F.3.A.R a lot of stuff goes unexplained. There are points in the game where normal enemy soldiers, rather than walk in, or get airlifted in or something like that, they literally walk out of walls or are formed from lightning, with no explanation apart from some crap about "but psychics".
Moreover I just found the enemies in F.3.A.R. just aren't as interesting as in the previous games,
A whole bunch of aspects in F.3.A.R. just seem to contradict the first two games' story, albeit sometime only the inferred story. in the first two games the actions of the character's are somewhat justified, whereas in F.3.A.R. the motivation is hard to see.

Horror relies on jumpscares many of which fall flat

Tom Clancy's The Division (TCTD) easily has some of the best post-launch support I've seen. Massive continue to improve and add to their open world shooter, and are extrememly in touch with their core playerbase (something surprisingly lacking with modern games). The most recent 1.8 update added a wealth of content as well as providing some welcome overhauls to core gameplay. To get an idea of the size of this update, it is easily as expansive as The Taken King was for Destiny, yet this was FREE.
If you like your shooters to have strong RPG elements and good CO-OP then this is the game for you. The atmosphere this game creates is fantastic. If you pay attention to the story then you'll find it gripping you, and you'll likely agree that Massive have some really interesting ways they can progress in future updates/sequel(s).
The game looks fantastic and is well optimised. Running it at 1440p with an I7 and GTX 1080 (and of course plenty of RAM) I get an average of 80fps on ULTRA. Also worth noting here that there's an option in the settings to turn off enhanced lighting, do it. It looks so much more atmospheric (and realistic!), just be careful when entering the PVP Dark zone areas!
To finish, throw away all your preconcieved notions of the game. Ignore everything you heard before about TCTD. I didn't buy this game for the longest time because of what I'd heard and seen, even going as far as to speak ill of it. I absolutely adore this game now. If you also played the game but got burnt by it, come back, I have a few friends that have and they love it. And the community is still very much active (and I believe has even seen growth!).

There’s not many bad things I can say about
; I have, however, said [read: screamed] many bad things
it. While no Super Meat Boy, this platformer can be brutally unforgiving and has no problem beating Ori, the small fluffy forest bunny/mouse/spirit-animal thing you play as, into a fine pulp. Repeatedly. You will rage. You will curse. You will wish painful and slow death and destruction upon every being and spiky object within the titular Blind Forest. And you won’t be able to stop playing.
The reason for this is
impeccable controls mechanics - the game just feels great to play! Not only does Ori always moves and jumps exactly how you intended in tight, visually pleasing animations, the game goes out of its way to keep you feeling calm and relaxed through its gorgeous artwork combined with a soothing soundtrack. This calm is sometimes broken by a voiceover that is about as subtle and welcome as a wakeup call via vuvuzela, but that’s my only (small) gripe with the game’s art direction.
While
does very little that’s unique for the genre, it is solidly designed, impeccably paced, and engaging throughout. New mechanics and abilities are introduced at just as you’re mastering the old ones and environments change and vary enough that you’re never left bored of the scenery. If you can overcome the occasional difficulty spike,
is definitely well worth your money and time if you are a fan of well-made platformers or looking for a fun way to spend a weekend. If you are looking for a game with a lot of replayability or a good combat system, this might not be the game for you. However, I would still recommend picking it up if you can get it cheap during a sale.

Skullgirls is a very fast, Capcom-esque 2D fighter that is most similar to Darkstalkers, both in its control scheme and its character design ethic.
Its greatest flaw is that, being a crowdfunded indie title, it comes nowhere close to the overwhelming size of Darkstalkers's playable cast, with a mere nine vanilla characters.
STORY AND AESTHETIC
Skullgirls features full hand-drawn graphics with extremely fluid animation - the only problem being the amount of attention dedicated to boobs and butts. For most characters this isn't a major problem, but some details such as Filia's tie suffer because all the effort was apparently put into her wildly bouncing boobs in the affected animations.
The game has a wonderful excuse to give all of the characters girly bits: the artifact you're fighting over is the Skull Heart, a voodoo-looking artifact which can grant the wish of any woman. This means that predominantly females will be searching for it, but as several of these characters are all-too-familiar with the Skull Heart's Soul Edge-like nature and wish to capture, research, or destroy it, there is nothing barring male characters from pursuing it for the same reasons.
The Skull Heart has a habit of turning its owners into titular Skullgirls, creatures of evil and hatred not unlike liches. These Skullgirls raise the dead and create vast armies to spread blight across the world. This has been going on long enough that international war is almost unheard of, as the Skullgirl's threat has been accepted by every nation, and every military institution featured in this game is more-or-less dedicated to fighting Skullgirls and their minions.
The majority of the characters are avatars / hosts inhabited by or wielding supernatural or sci-fi entities known derisively as parasites; removing a non-sci-fi parasite invariably results in the host's death. The Suggested-For-Newbies character Filia, for instance, is an otherwise-mundane schoolgirl whose scalp has been infested by Samson, giving her the ability to shape her hair into blades, needles, or fists like she's Kirby. Samson, however, is known to manipulate his hosts for his own selfish ends, and poor Filia is no exception.
The female characters (i.e. everyone except Big Band) are almost all voluptuous and jiggly with the exception of Painwheel and Peacock, and almost all morbid or grotesque in some way with the exception of Filia and Valentine.
BASIC GAMEPLAY
Darkstalkers. Remember that game? Three punches, three kicks, you can chain them together almost freely? Your specials are mostly done by inputting directions and pressing two punches or two kicks? It's a lot like that. The two differences are that normal attacks aren't buffed up by pressing two punches or kicks (those are done for special bar moves), and it's harder to chain punches into kicks or vice versa.
Skullgirls has had some advanced detection systems integrated that allow you not only to escape from infinite combos - you can Combo Break if your opponent repeats any attack previously used in the combo - but also protection from multi-unblockables; that is, protection from two attacks headed your way such that blocking one requires you to get hit by the other.
You have a super gauge, the ingame name of which I forget, and each character has at least 2 finisher attacks that utilize the gauge. Some of these finishers are throws, but most of them are simple quarter-circle + two punches or kicks inputs. The game has another protection: if you're using an analog stick, it will notice when you begin inputting a full-circle input and will stop your character from jumping when you press Up. If you're using a keyboard like me, however, then you're ♥♥♥♥ed and also you should really not use a keyboard to play a fighting game.
WRITING AND VOICE ACTING
Character writing is perfectly adequate, considering the wide variety of alternate stories available based on who you're playing as and the general lack of volume to the story making it difficult to flesh out characters' behaviors and relationships.
The voice acting is, thank gosh, quite good, featuring talents such as Liam o'Brien (Leviathan). In addition, characters who are not Peacock are smart enough to shut up for the majority of combat - Peacock is designed explicitly to be annoying and exploit opponents' anger, thus she... doesn't do that. Characters also have a variety of victory lines, my favorite being Squigly tickling Leviathan under the chin and musing "Whos a gud widdle dwagon monstur~?"
When using more than one character on your team, some of them have unique lines when switching out, e.g. Big Band switching to Squigly (who he knew when she was alive) may occasionally say something like "Sing it, girl!" and characters who switch out to Ms. Fortune might make cat puns.
FINAL WORDS
It's a great fighter suffering only from a small cast and about 5% more distracting boobage than is normal for the genre. Give it a try and be sure to keep up with the free DLC offers.

What would life be like if you played Baldur's Gate for the first time but instead of you being you, you had a lobotomy and Baldur's Gate had co-op mode. This is how I would summarise the hell of playing through Divinity.
First of foremost, the game itself doesn’t even believe it is a good game, as most NPCs and quest lines hit you with “le random spoon of doom” humour making my experience with any sort of plot line unbearable.
Secondly, I played on tactician mode meaning the game loved to waste your time with never ending combat sequences whereby to kill a rabbit you had to hit it ten times in ten different turns making sure you were using the right elements that it was weak against.
Thirdly, the voice acting sounds like it was all done by the same BBC actor used in the last ten seasons of Doctor Who or someone who got rejected from a King Arthur film. Like as if it was an American trying to sound British without ever meeting a British person.
Take it this way, I was playing Dark Souls III last night when my life partner walked in, found me fighting a mimic and retorted "See? That is a stupid enemy, something you would see in Divinity".  The comment run up my spine like a cold shiver, Divinity is now the measuring stick for a badly written RPG.
The bitter sweet finale to this magnum opus of a steam review is the fact that this game had an amazing co-op mode, it was fair and balanced and it’s what we need to see more of in the role-playing community. But when the game that you are spending 55 hours on with a friend is what seems to be a handicapped version of the forgotten realms franchise. You know you’re in trouble.
We need co-op RPGs, but we need them to be worth playing.

I have decided that I WOULD be willing to recommend this game as of the release of r26, and this date, 2/18/2016. But recommend WITH STRONG WARNINGS!!!
First of all, I want to point out that even my original review, I was confident that the things forcing me to give a negative review would be fixed and I must say, MOST have been.
First and foremost, the dev MOST responsible for the combat system has came through in a MAJOR way just like i said he would. So great work Chris Spears if you read this. The combat system that was messy and very opaque has been cleaned up and fined tuned A LOT. Is it perfect? Of course not. This is EARLY ACCESS. Is fun? Damn right it is. The skill system is broken in to several different trees. With recent changes, these trees now have a lot of VERY fun synergies. Remember the old days of Ultima Online and the skill mixing to create your own brand of monster slayer? Well, Chris has done it again. I cannot begin to list the number of FUN, interesting, UNEXPECTED, and just flat out strange skill tree combinations that work and work well. Are some a little better than others? Of course. Are their going to be "FotM builds (Flavor of the Month for you newbs out there!), absolutely. Will they make your build obsolete? NOPE! And as a bonus, for you folks who like dual spec options so that you can have multiple builds on the same character: SotA has that too! And they have done it WAY more interesting, clever, UNIQUE, and just flat out creative than anyone else has. So yes, Chris, kudos again.
So now that I am done ranting about how fun and open to YOUR creativity it is as of r26, let me ammend something else. The combat system itself, the background numbers and math and insanely ridiculously complex math they have going on in the combat system has recently been polished. MUCH is finally working as intended AND as expected. Is it done? How many times do I have to remind you it is still Early Access? ;) But I feel it is VERY close to a launchable state. There are still a couple things that need to be fixed/tweaked/corrected but all-in-all, combat works in a manner that is both predictable because you get results that you expect, but also unpredictable because there are still a few unknowns in the background to add an element of realistic unpredictablity in combat at the same time. It is done in a FUN and good way 90% of the time. Combat should not be 100% predictable in a game that is hoping to be very immersive. We need some unknowns. And I like it that way.
Now on to the crafting system. The actual CREATION OF FINISHED PRODUCTS is great. Going back to the good ol' days of Ultima Online again, for those of you who were with us then, if you recall the different material types of ore for example (Copper, Iron, Bronze, Verite, Valorite, etc), and the way that crafting a Plate Helm with each of the different metals delivered different results, that is a small example of what to expect here. An item in SotA will require multiple components, which can each be made of different material types, and combined to create an ENOURMOUS amount of Plate Helms, all with different stats. Now multiply that buy the number of gear slots, and you end up with thousand of possible armor combinations. Crafted to your specific needs exactly. And honestly, it is fun and engaging. It is not just mindless clicking. You get to plan it out. Fit it to your own unique character class that you have built using their extensive skill system.
Now for the Bad. HERE ARE MY STRONG WARNINGS!!!
There is still not much actual game content. There are not many real adventures. There are not a lot of quests. Their is not a real dungeon experience. Do they have these things? Absolutely. But they are holding them back as to not spoil the game for us Early Access players before launch. And because of this the game is VERY VERY VERY GRINDY. If you are not one who can have fun simply GRINDING and testing things, please just wait. I want you to have a great first experience with the game. If you need actual finished GAME CONTEN to enjoy yourself, just keep waiting. SotA is NOT ready for you.
However, if you are able to enjoy yourself grinding, experience, harvesting crafting materials (grinding harvest nodes), decorating homes, tending gardens, testing game mechanics, posting feedback for the devs to read (AND YES THEY DO READ IT...People need to stop saying they dont. They honestly do. They cannot do every single thing every single one of us asks for, but they have proven over and over again that they will make RADICAL changes to their design path to appease the testers when there is overwhelming feedback. I am not always happy with them, but i am happy often enough to keep coming back for more!). I have spoken in to devs. I have played with the devs. I have even taken one of their devs on a tour through one of their "dungeons" so that he could understand the bugs I was reporting with the place. They reply to my threads. They even watch my twitch stream. They absolutely are working with their backers and letting us help design a game with them. If THAT sounds fun to you, SotA is ready for you.
TLDR;
Combat system is mostly fixed, very innovative, unique and fun.
Crafting system is finally being implemented. First wave is fun, very well thoughtout, and allows for players to be creative.
Skill system is FINALLY starting to take on its final shape. It allows for a LOT of different playstyles and custom building. It is very fun and your imagination is the limit.
Finished game content(Storylines, dungeons, raids, bosses, etc..) is NOT available because they do not want to spoil the game for the Early Access players
Game is still VERY VERY VERY VERY GRINDY
Devs DO pay attention to players, they DO interact with players, they DO play with players, and they DO make radical shifts in direction when something gains enough momentum with players.
REVIEW POSTED ON AND BEFORE Jan 5 @ 3:38pm is now OBSOLETE due to RADICAL improvements to the game over the last couple releases. Great job Portalarium and special shout out to Chris Spears(@catnipgames). I knew you would pull it together, I just did not expect you to fix so much and radically improve that combat system in just 2 short releases. I wish I had been just a bit more patient before my previous review. Awesome work. Looking forward to next couple releases.

Played the free weekend trial several weeks ago, was okay. Played the free weekend just been, really enjoyed it.
The graphics are amazing, immersive.
The loot system is rewarding, not always, but generally you find better loot, which encourages gameplay and makes side-missions and detours worth the effort.
Finding loot that is common, but still can be used, rather than useless pick-me-ups, until you find better gear.
I enjoy playing Single player - less stress/more relaxing than multiplayer. This game you can solo, and still enjoy it. Play at your own pace. I appreciate that sort of gameplay nowadays.
Picking up items to increase health OR stumble on citizens needing such items, give it to them, receive random loot and XP. Now that is a cool concept, and makes picking up things/looking through buildings more rewarding.
I enjoy the 'pick-locking' of uncommon doors. This means you need to go back once you have a lock pick, which means you will face respawned enemies at a higher-level in the area, usually with a 'boss' present who gives a bit more of a challenge. He also drops worthy loot, and once unlocking the room you usually find something worth going back for. That is cool.
Every game has grind - but with unique and varied voice overs and side missions with different and realistic, sometimes humorous lore, is excellent. It's refreshing, not boring, and attracts my attention to keep playing.
The amazing graphics, unique street layouts - the realism, and the non-boring grind for better loot makes this game really enjoyable to play and get in to.
So, yes, I bought the game for $25 NZD and think it is an excellent piece of entertainment to enjoy.
On reading peoples reviews regarding the season pass and extras, I don't think I would get those. A few new modes? The base single player game is sufficient, and the developers have really done well with is game.
Thank you for making this game for us and I recommend other people purchase the game at the discounted price and enjoy it themselves.

The game is very good in terms of hitting the right spots. It's not a game for everyone, but for me, the combination of 3rd person shooter, loot system and gear advancement possibilities makes this a very good fit.
What is rather surprising is that after all this time this game has been out it still has numerous bugs, ranging from audio and graphical glitches to gear being lost at random.
Here's a list of glitches and bugs I've discovered only the past couple of days:
* Audio glitches, NPC's in adjacent areas still start speaking, but then are cut off about 0.1 second into their speach, which means at various parts of the map and in the underground you'll hear people constantly going "Eh...", "Il...", "Mu...", etc.
* Another audio glitch, several times during underground missions it seems that when then last NPC left (that we haven't killed) speaks the voices of all the other NPC's we've already killed are laid on top of it, which makes this sound like a cacophony of "all together now"
* Graphical and map glitches, several places in the main city there are places where the game sometimes fail to load the correct assests, leading to disappearing sidewalks, doors standing in the middle of the street, etc. If you happen to walk over such an asset you might end up falling through the map
* Sharing items must be used with caution. 2 times have I experienced sharing 1 item only to have another item being removed from my backpack. Example, I looked at the new backpack I had gotten and verified with my friend that it might be a good upgrade for him. Before sharing it I looked at the kneepads, which also were a good upgrade. I shared the kneepads, only to find the backpack gone afterwards. The second time I had 2 new items and shared one of them, the other one disappeared with it. My friend lost a G36 through similar circumstances.
* Some encounters in the main PvE world doesn't spawn enemies from time to time. To solve you have to log off and back in.
* The game still randomly hitches as you move around the map, presumably because it loads in map and graphical assests. This looks like you suddenly are running in molasses for a second only for you to get superhuman speed and sprint to make up for the lost distance afterwards.
* Delays between firing and bullets hitting. Fire your gun at an enemy, watch the enemy keep running for another 1-2 seconds before you see the damage number and the enemy falls. This doesn't happen often, but it happens. The enemy can still fire at you too so sometimes getting the jump on an enemy simply doesn't work.
* When teleporting or loading into some of the safehouses they will at random times have the exit door closed. Need to teleport away and back or relog to fix it.
* Cover system seems to break sometimes, locking you to a wall and not letting you escape for seemingly no good reason. Keep hitting Space and you might succeed exiting cover though.
For a game that has been out so long, and has even prioritized adding loot crates for real money it is surprising and quite sad that they haven't fixed these bugs and problems. Some of them, like the map and graphical glitches, the audio glitches, the hitches, have been around since day 1.
Guess earning more money is more important than fixing the game.
Mostly gripes, but the sharing function must be used with caution, so beware!
I still recommend the game though, when it works it is a *very* nice game.

This was my second playthrough. First time was in 2009.
All told I think I have about 250+ hours into FO3.
The first time through I was about 100 hours in before I finished the main story. This time I finished the main story in about 20 hours. I think it felt better this time to stay on track before going out and exploring the wastes. I mean, I needed to help my dad! Last time I was so distracted and I think I even forgot about helping him.
This time I played on hard. It was a lot of fun, and way too easy after level 18 or so..
I still ended up always looting too much and being overloaded. Games with a lot of stuff to loot and keep track of really help me see my obsessive nature.
This time I didn't use VATS so much, and I got to experience what a poor shooter the game is. The weapons suck and are always breaking. So early on I put all my skill points into repair skills. I loved having well-maintainted gear, and it made it easier to immediately make use of stuff that was loading me down.
The Pitt was the most memorable for me.
I felt so conflicted by the quest's ultimate decision. Am I wrong for choosing to side with the ex-brotherhood dude despite him enslaving people? I trusted his ultimate intentions, and his vision seemed more broad than the slave's. I supposed he could possibly have the means to carry out his intentions and that maybe the wastes would benefit. The slave seemed to be acting mostly out of anger, and he lacked information to tell me why I should help him. But.. He was a slave. I naturally wanted to help him.
Mothership Zeta was maybe 10% interesting and the rest was just mundane and boring. And why where some of those alien dudes so so so tough? That was crazy.
Operation Anchorage was nice because the simulator had blue sky.  The color was nice. The story was easy.
Would I recommend a second playthrough?
I don't know.. I had fun. But I think it was better back in the day. This time, I enjoyed more the way that I played it. The order of the quests made it much more interesting.

Skullgirls is a very fast, Capcom-esque 2D fighter that is most similar to Darkstalkers, both in its control scheme and its character design ethic.
Its greatest flaw is that, being a crowdfunded indie title, it comes nowhere close to the overwhelming size of Darkstalkers's playable cast, with a mere nine vanilla characters.
STORY AND AESTHETIC
Skullgirls features full hand-drawn graphics with extremely fluid animation - the only problem being the amount of attention dedicated to boobs and butts. For most characters this isn't a major problem, but some details such as Filia's tie suffer because all the effort was apparently put into her wildly bouncing boobs in the affected animations.
The game has a wonderful excuse to give all of the characters girly bits: the artifact you're fighting over is the Skull Heart, a voodoo-looking artifact which can grant the wish of any woman. This means that predominantly females will be searching for it, but as several of these characters are all-too-familiar with the Skull Heart's Soul Edge-like nature and wish to capture, research, or destroy it, there is nothing barring male characters from pursuing it for the same reasons.
The Skull Heart has a habit of turning its owners into titular Skullgirls, creatures of evil and hatred not unlike liches. These Skullgirls raise the dead and create vast armies to spread blight across the world. This has been going on long enough that international war is almost unheard of, as the Skullgirl's threat has been accepted by every nation, and every military institution featured in this game is more-or-less dedicated to fighting Skullgirls and their minions.
The majority of the characters are avatars / hosts inhabited by or wielding supernatural or sci-fi entities known derisively as parasites; removing a non-sci-fi parasite invariably results in the host's death. The Suggested-For-Newbies character Filia, for instance, is an otherwise-mundane schoolgirl whose scalp has been infested by Samson, giving her the ability to shape her hair into blades, needles, or fists like she's Kirby. Samson, however, is known to manipulate his hosts for his own selfish ends, and poor Filia is no exception.
The female characters (i.e. everyone except Big Band) are almost all voluptuous and jiggly with the exception of Painwheel and Peacock, and almost all morbid or grotesque in some way with the exception of Filia and Valentine.
BASIC GAMEPLAY
Darkstalkers. Remember that game? Three punches, three kicks, you can chain them together almost freely? Your specials are mostly done by inputting directions and pressing two punches or two kicks? It's a lot like that. The two differences are that normal attacks aren't buffed up by pressing two punches or kicks (those are done for special bar moves), and it's harder to chain punches into kicks or vice versa.
Skullgirls has had some advanced detection systems integrated that allow you not only to escape from infinite combos - you can Combo Break if your opponent repeats any attack previously used in the combo - but also protection from multi-unblockables; that is, protection from two attacks headed your way such that blocking one requires you to get hit by the other.
You have a super gauge, the ingame name of which I forget, and each character has at least 2 finisher attacks that utilize the gauge. Some of these finishers are throws, but most of them are simple quarter-circle + two punches or kicks inputs. The game has another protection: if you're using an analog stick, it will notice when you begin inputting a full-circle input and will stop your character from jumping when you press Up. If you're using a keyboard like me, however, then you're ♥♥♥♥ed and also you should really not use a keyboard to play a fighting game.
WRITING AND VOICE ACTING
Character writing is perfectly adequate, considering the wide variety of alternate stories available based on who you're playing as and the general lack of volume to the story making it difficult to flesh out characters' behaviors and relationships.
The voice acting is, thank gosh, quite good, featuring talents such as Liam o'Brien (Leviathan). In addition, characters who are not Peacock are smart enough to shut up for the majority of combat - Peacock is designed explicitly to be annoying and exploit opponents' anger, thus she... doesn't do that. Characters also have a variety of victory lines, my favorite being Squigly tickling Leviathan under the chin and musing "Whos a gud widdle dwagon monstur~?"
When using more than one character on your team, some of them have unique lines when switching out, e.g. Big Band switching to Squigly (who he knew when she was alive) may occasionally say something like "Sing it, girl!" and characters who switch out to Ms. Fortune might make cat puns.
FINAL WORDS
It's a great fighter suffering only from a small cast and about 5% more distracting boobage than is normal for the genre. Give it a try and be sure to keep up with the free DLC offers.

Side scrolling platformers are not my favorite genre. Ori and the Blind Forest, however keeps me interested and entertained.
What will leap out at you from the get-go, is the colors, then the level of detail extending way into the background and  the atmosphere it all conveys. A rich, natural world with all sorts of elements to it worth taking a minute to stand still and admire. It is evident this game was made by people who wanted to create an experience beyond just a game.
Ori is a nimble creature and even with the basic abilities, it's a joy to jump around, climb and fight off enemies. As you progress, you'll unlock new abilities which will allow you to jump higher, float on air currents, swim and more.
There is a some backtracking, but, as you might expect, it will simply give you the opportunity to enjoy the places you've been (and traverse them with new abilities) once more.
There are parts where you have to take a deep breath and push to get get through. But when you do (after an accpeptable amount of tries) you'll be elated you made it.
The story is not super deep, but good. The game is not long, but satisfactory and very re-playable (€20 is quite fair).
Ori is one of (if not truly) my favorite games of 2015. It would definitly make the list of all-time top 10 favorites and I'm not saying it would be at number 10 either.
A must-have. Well doone, Moon Studios.

This isn't a game.  It's an alpha.  It's not "pre-alpha."  It's alpha.
I was optimistic about this one.  Ultima was fun, UO was fun, but this one's just going to fall flat.  Here's why:
The gameplay is currently strangely satisfying for a couple of houjrs, but ultimately it's just...  Lacking.  They have a lot of work to do and not a lot of money to do it with, and I'm almost certain that the game won't be anything more than a polished turd when it's done.  It's an ambitious project for certain, but here's where it's going to fail:
Four game modes.  Really?  With 7.6 Million raised, you're going to make 4 game modes?
Major housing and the like already p2w.  Want to own a castle?  Shell out 12 grand and you'll get everything you ever wanted.
You have to pay to test the game.  Who the hell thought that would be a good idea?  Shut the damn game down, create your skills, and then open it back up when it's ready for an actual alpha/beta test.
The community is toxic.  I expected ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥gery from a large PvP crowd in Ultima but this is worse.  This is carebear, PvE, solo-player, memememememe♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥baggery.  It's an assumptive crowd that's full of butthurt all the time.  All. The. Time.  In almost every thread.  Did you know they have strict enforcement of pedantic things, like minor wording and signature requirements?  Who does that?
The current mechanics make no sense.  Buggy isn't even the word for it.  Ridiculous is.  I expect things to really lack in an alpha, but all signs are pointing to "stay away."
"We're crowd sourcing.  But only music.  Even though we were going to crowd source everything else."  I know too many modders with too much time on their hands, but apparently their work is just not good enough.  The game looks alright, if we're still in the 2010s.
I spent the past 24 hours training for combat, only to be able to kill the starter mobs slightly more efficiently.  Should tell you everything you need to know about the current state of the game mechanics.  And this is after release 23.
Hope you like playing every variety of sword and board you can think of, because that's all you really get for the first few hours until you've made enough money to buy yourself something else.
Honestly, I don't see this game ever getting released.  They're a year into full development, two years past kickstarter originally began, and still in "pre-alpha."  They're still lacking any sort of community organization and marketing, the game mechanics still look like sawdust on a shop floor, and the funds just aren't there.  I had some intention of playing the game, but honestly it's just going to be a battle of the wallet warrior kings over their hamlets while the rest of the player base grinds bandits for days on end just so they can kill tougher bandits.
3/10, rated on an alpha scale.  If this was rated towards an actual game it'd barely scratch 1/10.

You can mix and match from any glyph tree and certain glyphs can be combined with others to create more powerful abilities. As a death mage, I had an undead skeleton warrior to fight for me. Add a glyph of enlightenment and you summon a more powerful skeleton mage, who is more effective against armor.
With crafting, you do not have to grind through worthless recipes to level. You can "discover" recipes and craft only what you want.
Having said all that, does this game have bugs? Yes, of course it does. But it is WAY more playable than any game I've played in Alpha. The head dev was talking about playing his game for 8 hours straight because he was having so much fun. It's a very good sign when the head dev likes to play their own game.
The company developing this game is doing everything to stretch every dollar they raise. And Lord British put up his own money as well. When they moved offices a week ago, they didn't even hire a moving van. All of the devs moved themselves and some local fans came to help out. That is someone who respects crowd-sourced money and a good businessman.
Let me compare this to Star Citizen. I donated to SC when they had $16 million dollars. The dev team was in a cramped basement and they needed to move. They moved in to an office withn huge glass windows, a huge porch that ran the length of the building. No doubt the rent on this place is incredible. Same with the SC offices in California. Talk about high rents! To me, Chris Roberts is a horrible business man and does not respect crowd-sourced money. He's acting like he has already made an epic game. CR, if SC is an epic game that makes you rich and backer's estattic, that is when you can spend lavishly. Right now, your game is a year late and predicted for 2017.

Earth 2160 Review – Raymond KT
Summary: EARTH 2160 is the official sequel of the award winning, very popular and top selling EARTH series and continues the brand of "Earth 2140" and "Earth 2150." Only a few thousand humans managed to escape from the Earth before its collapse in 2150 A.D. They spent the next few years on the terra forming of the red planet, developing new technologies and building up new civilisations. Somehow each of the three fractions "Eurasian Dynasty", "United Civilised States" and "Lunar Corporation" did this independently and separately from each other - but in the year 2160 something strange happens in this new world. If ED, UCS and LC join forces or continue their old war against each other - is possibly now, up to the player. Beside the usual venues in the solar system, there are some strange looking locations: planets with moving and reflecting liquid surfaces. And beside the standard RTS - resource acquisition, base building and destruction of enemy bases, the year 2160 will have some adventure inspired tasks for the players. [Zuxxez]

+ Interesting concept that feels fresh due to the inclusion of decidedly novel elements
+ There are four giants to work with, all with a selection of abilitites, many of which must be unlocked during a given playthrough
+ Player can create biomes and populate them with resources and life; feels rewarding to watch life grow
+ Healthy selection of resources available to seed
+ Human populations need to be managed carefully; too many resources make them greedy, whereas too few will hinder or halt population growth
+ Close-up, visuals are detailed and aesthetically pleasing
+ User intervace is straight-forward and intuitive; information is therefore easy to find and access
+ Vast amount of unlockable projects, etc; this serves to enhance gameplay as one continutes to play, building off of earlier successes
+ Synergy is a welcome challenge to effectively manage, often requiring constant adjustments
+ Tutorial is excellent
- Soundtrack suffers from lack of variety, and will replay frequently
- No control over which projects are started
- Giants move slowly, and time cannot be advanced (only paused)
- There is a crippling lack of game-mode variety or customization

Depth is, simply put, a fantastic game. It's an asymmetrical multiplayer game pitting divers against sharks, but an offline play mode versus bots is also available. There are two game modes, Blood and Gold and Megalodon Hunt. Blood and Gold is arguably the main game mode, and at the time of writing it offers six playable shark types: Great White, Mako, Tiger, Hammerhead, Thresher, and Bull. Each has differing stats and a unique ability, leading to a completely different playstyle for each shark. From the tanky Great White, to the nimble Mako, each shark has a place. Divers can purchase a variety of weapons, but more on that later.
In Blood and Gold, four Divers escort a submersible robot known as S.T.E.V.E. to various safes throughout the level. At each safe, S.T.E.V.E. takes some time to unlock it and you have to cover him while fending off two sharks. After all safes have been cracked, the divers must escort S.T.E.V.E. back to the ship. Divers can swim around the area to pick up gold while S.T.E.V.E. works, and though doing so exposes them to sharks, it is necessary to do so to buy better weapons. Starting out with a pistol, the divers will get better weapons as the match continues, including spear guns, sentry guns, and naval mines. Each weapon has a variety of upgrades, from explosive ammunition to night vision scopes. Sharks get points as the match progresses to pick and upgrade a variety of skills. Each side also has a set number of respawn tickets. The divers win once they have made the sharks lose all of their tickets or escorted S.T.E.V.E. back to the ship. The sharks win upon making the divers lose all of their tickets.
Depth does something many other asymmetrical games fail to do: the humans are fun to play. Before each game, players can choose to queue as sharks or divers, and this cannot be changed in-match. Playing as a diver is an extremely intense experience, desperately shining your flashlight around and firing wildly into the darkness as your teammates are picked off one by one and your heart is thudding in your ears. All of the weapons are extremely satisfying to use and each has a unique identity. They all have clear pros and cons, and it's never an easy choice what to buy. Depth  also does something else other games fail at: the support items are fun to use. A small hand-held vehicle to move around the water allows easier collection of gold. A portable radar spots sharks and treasure for your team. Deployable medkits and supply packs increase your chances of survival. Choosing to support your team is its own rewarding experience.
Playing as a shark is a fantastic, unique experience as well, and when you lunge and grab a diver in your jaws you have to shake your mouse wildly to finish them off. You feel powerful swimming around the darkness, and you can't help but smile when you spot a lone diver off collecting treasure.
Depth is WELL worth the price of admission, and with free updates adding new content, it's never too late to jump into the fun.
