I rarely write review for games, but No Man's Sky pushed me across the limits that I guess I have to write something about it. I m a big fan of Sandbox survivals or exploration base games, I clocked numerous hours in games like Ark Survival, Terreria(not in my steam),Starbound and Astroneer. I love the genre to death and that what made me so furious at what No Man Sky could have been but didnt.
==============================================
Firstly, Let start with with No Man's Sky Pre-foundation Update
==============================================
1. Game was very pleasing and very fun exploring a single planet.
2. Although gameplay became a pattern, at least there is always a node / new landmark to explore.
3. The game wasnt much about Units(In-game money) and more like exploring and discovering.
4. Speaking with the lifeforms which inhabits the planet is interesting and it feel the planet is alive.
5. The game was chill, key materials like Plutonium and stuff was abundances in certain planets.
6. Very chill but can get boring due to pattern repetition.
7. Goal were simple. Expand Inventory, Ship and Multi Tool. Explore, Relax, Discover. * Find Altas *
8. Checkpoints / Landmarks / New Locations were easy to scan for.  Making good for short term goals.
The game was obviously lacking to some player in terms of things to do, but to me, it was simple and relaxing. You enjoy the sceneries and you gathering around. Hit some jackpot planet and celebrate.
During pre-foundation update, I hardly jump from suns to suns. I spend quite alot of time on one planets before shifting to another. That was probably the simple joy I had with the game. It did get boring, but the game design was solid although little.
=========================================
Post Foundation Update ( Where it went horribly wrong?)
=========================================
Post Foundation update was exciting, I was telling my friend and excitied to jump back into the game to see what cement with the old game design with the new stuff. Nowhere in the patches did they unveil to me, the horror to a certain extent the foundation update had to bring...
1. Key materials start to become sparse in every planet ( I start hoarding plutonium and fearing of losing my stuff )
2. Checkpoints / Landmarks / New Locations become super hard to locate. It came down to a chance system.
3. I cant seem to find anymore Lifeform ( Korvax or Gek ) anywhere in the planets anymore... I only see platnium caches / ruins / drop pods and locations with nothing but a save point.
4. No more signal scanner ( Non-buildable ones) means no more tranmission towers = no chance to find new ships.
5. Base-Building locked behind a very specific questline (making it a wild-goose chase).
6. Freighters and new ships cost a bomb without base building aspect.
7. Planets become more of a resource node than a planet to explore.
The new foundation update threw away alot of what i loved about the game and gave me something wholly new and may not be the best thing. This is because the game has become less of a exploration game and more of a wild goose chase for materials and base building.
I don't get excited to find new planets to land because landing cost me plutonium and plutonium has become fearfully little on planets. If I dont see a material i want from a planet in the planetary scan, i just turn away and scan another.
The landmarks have also become so little it scary. Last time, i get annoyed that there was so many landmarks left unchecked on my screen it feels so clustered and annoying. Now I want that back cause I CANT FIND A SINGLE place on the planet. There is probably 1 or 2 markers to lead to me something but usually not something I want.
the Quest line is hilarously stupid. The game tasks the player to find a very very rare and specific resource to unlock more base building. It really pushes the player to view planets more as resource nodes than planets with life to explore.
It seems easier to purchase everything with Units than to do anything else now, cause instead of being fun and relaxing, it starts being tedious and unproductive. Largely, I believe due to the amount you get from mining. It feel like you are getting very little for each rare material you harvest and harvesting an entire rock structure of material can take awhile.
Overall, You guys might feel that I m ranting, and I do feel it too but I have placed so much faith in Hello Games to make things better and right yet to only see it has fall to the ground. I stilll believe this game can get better but if the team stop believing that procedural generating and randomization can prolong this game ( it willl not).  I will still sink hours and hours into the game to complete and max out my spaceship(bag and multitool already max), clear the base building questline and find for all the Altas story. But these Hours will probably not be the same 20+ hours i sank in the pre-foundation update.
Now, I go on a wild-goose chase for Spadonium, and treat each planet like a resource node. Cause without base-building, I probably can't afford a freighter unless I found a planet which drops ultra rare items.
TL;DR version
Pre-Foundation Update ( Fun but repetitive which leads to being boring but still a chilll game)
Post Foundation Update ( Annoying > fun, Repetitive, Everything is Random, More stuff but no improvement, Planet feels more lifeless )
TO THE DEVELOPERS( IF YOU SEE THIS) :
1. Add mulltiplayer ( this would boost the game so much with base building Ref: Astroneer, Ark Survival)
2. Bring back Pre-Foundation Gameplay cause some of us may not want to spend hours completing base building to gain an income to afford new shiny stuff.
3. Please make scanning for new landmarks easier. The ? marks don't help and are usually disappointment.

Be warned, this game runs awfully on newer systems. Be prepared to patch the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of this game, or else it'll crash every time you do anything. Quicksave (F5) is your friend.
However, overlooking the technical aspects, this game is wonderful. There's tons to explore and do, and the atmosphere is great. Sometimes creepy, sometimes crazy, and sometimes downright confusing, this game hits the nail on the head. I enjoyed the plot to an extent, but I wouldn't call it the game's strong point, which I would argue is the element of choice. Want to blow up the biggest city in the game? Have at it, but you'll be known as a public menace.
There's replay value, but don't expect the questline to be much different the second, or especially the third, time around. There's pretty much only one way to win the game, and that's to be the good guy.
As far as DLC: Mothership Zeta is boring, but worth one playthrough. Broken Steel is necessary, if you want to actually finish the game (one of the game's lowest points, IMO). The Pitt is interesting, and definitely worth a playthrough. Operation Anchorage is buggy as hell and really only worth it for the kickass power armor you get, so it's your call on this one. Never got around to playing Point Lookout, but I've heard it's one of the more fun DLCs of this game.
Overall, discounting any technical hiccups the game might have (which are fairly easily fixable, if you do a bit of research), this game is well worth the money. In fact, go ahead and just get the GOTY version, since it's so cheap now.
Playability (Does the game run well?): 5/10 (can be a 8/10 if you get the Unofficial Fallout 3 patch and tweak some settings)
Story (How fun and engrossing is the plot?): 6/10
Graphics (Does the game look good for its time?): 7/10
Value (How much playtime does it offer for the price?): 9/10
Overall (without tweaks): 6.75/10
Overall (with tweaks): 7.5/10

What is there to say about Fallout 3 that hasn't been said by now? Fallout 3 is the Bethesda's followup to the original Fallout series; it's a great game, and if you haven't played it yet, you're missing out.
Action, adventure, big guns, and
, the Bloody Mess perk: awesome. The story is entertaining, the gameplay is enjoyable, and there's dozens (potentially hundreds) of hours of content to explore - especially with the addition of the DLC in the Game of the Year Edition.
Fallout 3 is open-world, allowing you to explore at your own discretion. The problem is, however, that navigation of unexplored areas (both in the world and local map) feels more like a chore than anything. A lot of the optional side quests send you running miles out of the way, often followed with more miles of hallways or tunnels - and once you've finally reached your goal, despite having killed every enemy in the area along the way, most of the time you'll find yourself backtracking just to reach an exit for fast-travel.
Don't get me wrong,
This game isn't the first (or the last) to make the player jog for hours (literally) all over the game map. The problem is there's just so much repetition along the way to points of interest (ex. same enemies, same items, same abandoned buildings) that it makes exploration a lot less interesting than it could have been.
In my case, this caused me to skip
of the optional content and streamline the main story so I could complete the game - but your mileage may vary. I wrote this after a replay and knew what I was getting into - but I think anyone heading into the game blind will have an awesome time, and absolutely get their money's worth.

This is like the indie Payday 2 of fighting games, minus the rpg elements, lag, bad ai, and horrible combat.  If you couldn't tell, I like this game.

This is a review of a pre-alpha game during Early Access.
Graphics: 1/10
The graphics look muddy and confused, not sticking with any one specific style from object to object. While this is pre-alpha, the graphics are almost _frighteningly_ bad.
Characters look cartoonish and flat, but armors are supposed to be realistically detailed. Mobs are low-polygon messes reminiscent of the playstation 2. But player housing - all of the items you can buy for real money in their store - are lovingly detailed. The whole chimera is a haphazard collection of unclear art direction.
Trees sprout up from the ground in identical pole shapes with identical leaves. No roots or rocks or leaves litter the ground; only a few strategically-placed bushes cover places where terrain meets walls. Cobblestones are not individually shaded, and the flatness of every ground texture rapidly becomes a blur of brown and grey in your peripheral vision.
Each "scene" is bad enough, with textures that inspire nothing but boredom... but the walls of each scene are even worse. You can look off into the distance in certain open scenes, but don't worry about that far-off mountain peak: You can't get there; it's not real. The zone borders are on loan from the local elementary school theater - flat, painted surfaces that do nothing to help you feel as though you're in a living world. As of a more recent update, there's a breeze, and even a scene with grass. But every environment is static. Your character walks the same through knee-deep water as it does through waist-high grass. The constant breeze blows the leaves of the copy-and-paste lollipop trees, and most scenes don't even have grass. Nothing helps you feel connected to the zone you're in. Every color is a muted brown or grey. Realistic, perhaps, but not very nice to look at hour after hour.
One point is given for the skysphere. The day / night changes aren't bad, and there's even the beginning of a weather system in place.
I get that it's pre-alpha, and there are a fair few missing textures still, but these graphics are very, very bad.
Sound: 4/10
Arrows and swords ping against your armor, and certain monsters hiss frighteningly at you as you strike them. The sound feels weak, however, lacking a solid meaty THUD as you crush bones with a mace. The level up sound is a good one. Music is unobtrusive.
Not much else to say on sound; it's not finished yet. Crocodiles bark at you like a dog, which is good for a laugh.
Combat: 2/10
This will be controversial, but, I don't think the random deck system is going to be long for this world. And I even like the idea behind it!
You get abilities - like fireball or shield bash - as you level up. These abilities, called "active glyphs" or just "glyphs" sometimes, can be built into a combat deck with the default keystroke "y". This allows you to build a deck with more than one copy of each ability, if you like. A deck can be saved with equipment alongside it. It's confusing to write about, but after poking with it for a few minutes, you'll get it. Basically you can use abilities three different ways: you can lock them, place them, or random them.
Locking abilities lets you play like a standard button-bar MMO. You pick ten abilities, lock them into your bar, and you use them. Done. However, this costs extra mana to use, and involves a cooldown on skills that otherwise doesn't exist. So, while this is possible, it hamstrings your character pretty soundly.
Placing abilities tells the system to pop up ability X in a certain numbered slot. So in this method, you draw your weapon and have to wait for the ability to come up. When it does, though, it will come up in that numbered slot. So your fingers can get used to the necessary button presses, without the added mana cost and skill cooldown.
Finally, randoming the abilities - glyphs, sorry - means that any glyph in your deck can randomly appear in that spot.
The developers have gone all-in on this system. Several skills in the fairly limited skill pool deal with the glyph system. For example, you can get a skill that lets you discard all of your current glyphs and draw a new hand.
I think the idea behind the system - letting players have a more exciting combat rather than just memorizing a "rotation" - is a very, very good one. I don't think the implementation works well, however; you spend half of your time staring down at the button bar to see what's popped up so you can use combos.
Combat is overall terrible, button bar aside. You frequently fail to autoattack for no reason. Ranged monsters run away from you after every minor hit, causing you to chase them across entire zones for a kill. You can end up surrounded by monsters with weird aggro radii, hit with fireballs from half a zone away, and unable to melee autoattack a crocodile you're standing on. For fun, try to melee a stag to death. It jumps through you, and as you run after it, you'll occasionally swing awkwardly in a random direction. Sometimes, you end up stuck in the swing animation as you turn around to chase the dratted thing again. There's no real weight to the combat system, either, which is a death knell for melee.
Shroud's weird and weightless combat makes it impossible to enjoy.
Other:
* Loot is meaningless. I'm hoping it's not implemented yet. You get the exact same loot from a massive Elder Wolf as you do from a baby crocodile.
* Durability is WAY too punishing AND crafting is WAY too resource-greedy. It takes days of play to gather enough materials for a platemail chest. After crafting it, you'll get to enjoy it for a short while until it finally becomes un-repairable. Repair scrolls to extend the life of your gear cost 100g each.
* Travel over the map starts to get old quickly. Since the random encounters aren't implemented yet, this just serves to further stretch out the time between actual video game playing. This, in turn, reinforces the idea that you're not really playing a true online game - you're basically loading the lobby.
Overall: Not Great
I'm really, really worried about this game. It doesn't look good right now. The graphics aren't just bad, or muddy, or missing textures - although all of those things exist too. Nor is combat merely uninteresting or dominated by a particular playstyle - although, again, those things are problems as well. Rather, the game is just poorly designed from the ground up. Numbers can be tweaked, loot can be fixed, and crafting can be made meaningful. I like the ideas of more randomized combat, and I'm excited to see where they take that. But overall there are enough deep-seated problems in the bones of the game that I am concerned.
I sincerely hope that the developers can turn this around, because right now it's just not looking great.

Typically, destroying any armies sent out by villages increases their awe rating; as long as you continue to perform miracles and/or kill insurgents, no one will challenge you. I know there are a ton of negative reviews of this game. A great deal of early reviewers where people who felt disappointed about what the game was in relation to what they expected before it was released. Personally, I strive to always keep my expectations of every new game I play relatively low and go into each new experience with an open mind.  With NMS, I was excited about the uniqueness of concept that this game brought to light.  In that, I was not at all disappointed. It is new and unique.  Sure, they use a proven formula that works well with many MMOs; that is to say you must gather materials and make achievements to upgrade your character and equipment.  To many people, this can be boring, but to millions, this can also be fun because it promotes exploration.
Here's what I love about the game: 1) It is beautiful 2) I love free exploration 3) I can play it how I like and make up my own story as I go 4) I can change how I play the game in a multitude of ways 5) It is unique and different 6) I can pick it up and play it for any amount of time and put it down in a moment's notice without feeling like I'm interrupting my game... it is fun to play if even for just a few minutes 7) like in Minecraft, I'm in it for the long haul and excited about what the developers are planning. Each update and new release (like with the foundation update) will only draw me back in and let me play the game just a little differently so I really don't mind waiting for them 8) finally, I love that the developers seem to embrace the modding community.  There are many mods that change the look, feel, and/or experience of the game so if you get bored or frustrated with something, you might just be able to change it with a mod.
If you like a baked-in story and want clear instruction on what you're "supposed to do" in a game, this is not for you.  If you want weekly content updates, this game is not for you. If you want action-packed multiplayer battles, this game is not (at least yet) for you. If you can't get past what you expected the game to be so you can appreciate what it actually is, this game is not for you.
Personally, this game is one of my three favorite casual games, right along with Farming Simulator and Minecraft.  I love shooters, adventure games, MMOs, and traditional RPGs also, but when it comes to relaxing, simple fun, I love this title.

I could see how the game might get old, to a player, much in the same way that Destiny does, or Borderlands; but hopefully the expanded content will provide new game modes and different styles of play.  Overall, I give it the proverbial Thumbs Up.  It's an pleasant gaming experience.

What is there to say about Fallout 3 that hasn't been said by now? Fallout 3 is the Bethesda's followup to the original Fallout series; it's a great game, and if you haven't played it yet, you're missing out.
Action, adventure, big guns, and
, the Bloody Mess perk: awesome. The story is entertaining, the gameplay is enjoyable, and there's dozens (potentially hundreds) of hours of content to explore - especially with the addition of the DLC in the Game of the Year Edition.
Fallout 3 is open-world, allowing you to explore at your own discretion. The problem is, however, that navigation of unexplored areas (both in the world and local map) feels more like a chore than anything. A lot of the optional side quests send you running miles out of the way, often followed with more miles of hallways or tunnels - and once you've finally reached your goal, despite having killed every enemy in the area along the way, most of the time you'll find yourself backtracking just to reach an exit for fast-travel.
Don't get me wrong,
This game isn't the first (or the last) to make the player jog for hours (literally) all over the game map. The problem is there's just so much repetition along the way to points of interest (ex. same enemies, same items, same abandoned buildings) that it makes exploration a lot less interesting than it could have been.
In my case, this caused me to skip
of the optional content and streamline the main story so I could complete the game - but your mileage may vary. I wrote this after a replay and knew what I was getting into - but I think anyone heading into the game blind will have an awesome time, and absolutely get their money's worth.

- The characters
- The soundtrack
- The backgrounds
- The voice acting

I honestly can't think of anything bad to say about this game. And trying to think of bad stuff to say about it brings up little annoyances but nothing that breaks the game entirely or would bother anyone to the point of a rage quit (with maybe one exception).
The little annoyances or 'the bad' if you will are very minor things that you learn to deal with eventually or can just avoid at your leissure. Maybe it'll bother you, maybe it won't, but that depends on your play style and tolerance to fighting games.
- Peacock is a keep-away  character and will spam her bombs and other cartoony antics at you until you've been his so many times by little 8-ball bombs that you get a little frustrated or own her via block buster moves. First time playing, she annoyed me at first but you get used to fighting her own time and will develop ways around her multitude of bombs and planes flying at you constantly. (and for a 90's kid like me, the fact she makes so many refferences to well-loved cartoons is also a plus. i giggle everytime she says 'Hellooooooooo Nurse!')
- Fukua, a character added through a patch as an April Fool's joke (to poke fun at SF's Decapre). Her story mode seems somewhat random compared to the rest but you fight all of the characters in your roster with Filia as the final boss. AND OMG FILIA AS A BOSS IN FUKUA'S STORY MODE WAS SO FRIGGIN DIFFICULT I RAGE QUIT MULTIPLE TIMES. I eventually figured out how to beat her or at least keep her down long enough to attack so i beat Fukua's story mode... But fighting Filia as a final boss in that storymode... you'd think the game was hacked or on Nightmare mode even when you have it on Easy difficulty. I promptly gave her the nickname 'cracklia' because she moved so fast and rapid that i didnt have time to make Fukua react... You will get your♥♥♥♥♥pummeled mutliple times over before you beat Fukua's story mode (the ending though... is fanfic worthy...)
- Some moves that require you to move the analog stick or directional buttons diagonally and in a certain pattern really confused me (could be because i never grew up playing XBOX though, so it may just be me still adjusting to the controller). These moves are a challenge to pull off in training mode, often resulting in my skipping training
- Big Band is overpowered compared to a lot of the cast, which might make you rage quit your first few times fighting him but you can find ways around it similar to fighting Peacock. I'd still prefer fighting Peacock to Big Band though
- Without the DLC characters the original roster was 8 characters. Fukua is now included through a patch so you may say there are 9 characters in the base game now?
That's all i can really say about the so called 'bad'...

I feel it's ok to have your waifus and fanservice girls in anime, manga and games. I don't say boo to a female character with a large chest, butt or anything else for that matter. Gauntlet is a series of games consist of hack n' slash dungeon crawlers.  The games have been pretty straightforward and enjoyable, and this version of Gauntlet doesn't deviate too far from the formula.  Gauntlet isn't an HD remake of the first game.  It is a modernized retelling, keeping some things but adding in a few new things to change things up---with mixed results.
Gauntlet is a decent looking game that plays pretty well.  The game's strongest point is how each character plays.  The four choices (Warrior, Valkyrie, Wizard, and Elf) have relatively unique playstyles.  You'll have to excuse my controller references coming up, but the Warrior and Valkyrie can be most closely associated with "button mashers," relying more on the face buttons to perform commands.  The Wizard and Elf, on the other hand, are "twin-stick" shooters, relying on heavy use of the right analog stick.  Each character also has special abilities to offer further variety, but the most diverse character is the Wizard.  While the other characters are easily accessible, the Wizard has a learning curve due to the number of abilities he has (in comparison to the others).
The game still stays true to its hack n' slash, dungeon crawling roots.  The game
to have some kind of story for why the characters are thrust into the Gauntlet, but it is paper-thin---almost unnecessary.  I know we're supposed to be collecting shards for a sword, but I really just wanted to kill some monsters with my friends.  Now, something that makes this game stand apart from other dungeon crawlers is the lack of a leveling system.  Your character doesn't gain levels (they do gain "masteries," but more on this shortly), and is just about fully equiped with every ability they will ever have.  I find this to be a welcome break, and it helps keep the game accessible to anyone.
Unfortunately, I found there to be more negatives than positives to this game.  The game offers up "masteries," which are basically perks that require
of investment.  Most of the revolve around killing enemies, but having to continuously play through levels to kill enemies is rather annoying.  If, perhaps, the mastery requirements were lower or if they were shared across all characters (where applicable), I wouldn't be as annoyed with the mechanic.  However, the amount of work and time needed to entirely unlock them isn't worth it, in most cases.  The rewards are so incremental that it makes me wonder why they're there.
Something that may also help is a stronger level variety.  There are 30 levels in the game.  27 of them are part of 9 "standard" levels and the other 3 are boss levels.  When selecting a non-boss level, you are committed to a three-level endurance run that, despite the aesthetic changes, all follow the same formula: 1st level is a "long, standard" level, 2nd level is a "short, environment hazard" level, and 3rd level is an "arena" fight.  Given that the levels are not procedurally generated (a "hot" item in more recent dungeon crawlers), the replayability falls short.  The bosses aren't incredibly fun to fight either, making them rather underwhelming.
Another downfall about the level structure is the "hub" area.  After completing either the series of 3 levels or a boss level, all players are transported to the hub area to select a new level or purchase items.  The game offers the players items in the form of relics---which can only be used if potions are collected, or loadouts---which are only cosmetic permutations for the characters.  The relics offer a little more variety to the potions (instead of just "clear the screen of enemies") and the permutations don't hurt the game at all, but relics can never be used on bosses and the loadouts require us to beat the bosses and specific difficulties to unlock (and even then they cost gold to purchase).
This game also harkens back to the original Gauntlet by restricting the group to one unique character per player.  We cannot all play as Wizards or Warriors in a 4-player group.  I like the idea of having team variety, but forcing it typically leads to a lot of players quitting from a game since they can't play as a character they've invested time into.  However, as with most games, playing this game with more people is always a good time, and with a recent patch text chat has been made available.  On top of the other tweaks that have happened since the game's launch in September, it is apparent that the developer's aren't just letting this game settle.  They plan to keep improving it.

Cons:
Suggestions:
Despite my lists of complaints, I am still recommending the game.  I do not think this game has earned my $20 just yet, but perhaps with additional updates down the road it will get even better.  Right now, I'd say the game is worth a $10 purchase.

A really fun, and funny game. I'm surprised by just how much I enjoyed this.
The skills are cool, and some are amusing (Like dropping a tank on top of your enemies), and I was playing simply to unlock more skills to see what they were like.
There isn't a lot of dialogue, and most of it's just random comments from the characters when you use new attacks are find something new, etc. Although not really bad in a game like this, it'd be better if there was more story to it, no matter how much seriousness said story lacks.
It's not all that difficult if you play on normal, most enemies are some kind of creature crossed with an element, and so have weaknesses, you get a scan bot that lets you see said weaknesses so honestly as long as you don't forget to keep your weapons and skills diverse you're going to be fine. Each area generally has a focus on one or two elements, so you can focus on those with your weapons as well.
The shop so far has been pretty pointless. I've not completed it yet, but I've literally only bought a few coffees from it before a boss, you don't really use items enough to use up the ones you find, and the weapons you find are generally good as well. Getting materials for crafting is simply a case of grinding as well.
Better quests would be good, it seems all the npc's just want food, even just a "kill n monsters" or something would keep it more interesting. Just going out and fighting is fun enough in itself though, so it's not really a big issue.
I feel like I've complained a bit about it, but despite everything I've said, the game is genuinly enjoyable, which is generally the biggest factor in a game.

What to say about a short, but great game. Right off the bat I felt like this was a story that started off like Final Fantasy 7 did once you met Aeris. You care about the story and the characters.
This was a great story about how no matter what life throws at you, it's still possible to not only have a dream, but still be able to achieve it, albeit in a strange way. You care about these characters. You care what happens to them. The little plot threads hint at something deeper and the story is told in pieces that unravel what is happening. Cut scenes give you back story to the character that always wanted to go to the moon. If this was a book, it would be a page turner. If it was a TV show or movie, you would want to see it. The characters all have their own personalities and the relationship between the two doctors is hilarious.
The music in this game is nothing short of brilliant. It sets the mood of each scene. Haunting, inspiring, and tear-jerking all at once. More games should have music like this. The music has such a great ability to set the mood and elicit certain reponses, such as fear, compassion, and love.
This game is not a long game, but it shows that great games do not need long stories in order to be good. More games need to have a thoughtful and poignant story like this. I hope you all enjoy it as much as I did. Do yourself a favour and play this.

After the initially strong start I became concerned that this game, while beautiful visually, musically and emotively, lacked depth in it's actual gameplay mechanics, not standing out significantly against it's other metroidvania peers (For example Dust: Elysian Tale's sword combat mechanics) even to the point of being too easy. However as the game progressed the mechanics and difficulty quickly ramped up and by the Ginso tree the game makes it painfully clear the training wheels are off, and it quickly ramps up to old-school nintendo hard and becomes a real blast to play mechanically speaking.
Going in, I also had concerns the story was a little saccharine and basic, having heard some negative words to this angle (Not least Zero Punctuation's scathing review), however after time to digest what was going on, the story was surprisingly nuanced and upon replaying for achievements I noticed a couple of very subtle details that greatly change the context of the story. In otherwords, it's only simple and saccharine if you don't try more than scratch the surface, but if you dig down it's surprisingly layered.
Visually and in terms of sound production it's simply phenominal, proof that sprites and traditional art techniques have a place in a 3D world - but, I don't need to go into depth on this it's been said a million times before and with very good reason.
The only "negative" is the length clocking in at average 9 hours for first play through. However, I don't feel dragging it out would have added to it, it tells the story it wanted to tell and does so in style and it does have some replayability value.
Overall, I overwhelmingly recommend it.

I’ve given Original Sin a decent amount of time to get me invested and it simply hasn’t. In my 9 hours of gameplay I wasn’t having any fun. There is nothing to the world that gripped me, it feels like a generic fantasy world. The story has a decent concept, there is a creature destroying time and you have to find these stones to help restore it but the presence of the story feels very minimal because the characters you create and play as don’t talk much, a few lines of dialogue here and there. You choose the dialogue options and you define your characters personalities but there just isn’t enough to work with, it feels very negligible. You don’t know anything about them, they just feel again, very generic. I didn’t really feel a connection to anything because everyone mainly just spits out exposition at you while you just sit there and listen. There isn’t any engaging conversations going on you are just listening to everyone’s life story and all their problems. The dialogue you listen to from all these characters you meet takes up a lot of the game and I just don’t have the patience for it, it gets annoying. One sided conversations are never interesting in my opinion. The turn based combat doesn’t help the slow pace the game already had outside of combat, it took me hours to explore the first town and talk to everyone there and accept all the quests available, it was very boring. I’m not a fan of turn based combat, there has been exceptions like in Knights of the Old Republic for example. This game does turn based combat just fine. There is nothing really bad to say about it, I was just very bored playing it. Because I don’t like turn based combat in general a turn based combat game has to do something really special or unique to catch my attention and the combat in this game just feel like a very traditional turn based combat system, it just did nothing for me. The progression system in the game feels very slow, it takes a bit of time for you to level up and when you do you get a point or two to put into an attribute or skill. The system doesn’t get me excited to level up because I didn’t really feel the sense of progression (speaking only for the first 5 levels). The system didn’t hook me and make me want to get my characters stronger and level up like a lot of other games are able to do.  All these things I brought up doesn’t make me want to put 50 hours into the game just for the sake of beating it so I just felt like I had to stop playing, I’m not sure if I should give the sequel a try in the future…

I am about 400 hours in so, I think it is a fair time to make a short and sweet critique of SotA at this point.
It is by far the most interesting and enjoyable fantasy genre MMO I have had the pleasure of playing in a long, long...longlonglong time. SotA has the potential to be one of teh all time greats, and I see no signs of it not living up to said potential.It hearkens back to the pre-WoW days of yore where games were not all on rails and there was occasionally some thought required. I did not play Ultima and I am not a Richard Garriot fanboy, I want to be clear on that. I am judging the game based solely on its merit, not its lineage.
SotA is a wide open sandbox full of toys to play with of all shapes and sizes. It is high fantasy (dragons and wizards and magic etc) but it also has a splash of SteamPunk (weird electrical- like devices) so it has this really awesome potential to surprise me. I haven't been surprised by a game since I can't even remember.
The combat system is going through a pretty major overhaul so, I don't want to judge that aspect as I have not played it in the new "use based" system yet. Basically, ala Skyrim, you get better by using things. Swing a 2H sword for a living? Welll...you will improve...and so on.
The world grows more refined and polished and beautiful each patch it seems like. The systems are all coming on line and starting to really hit their stride. In short: The game is starting to LOOK awesome and PLAY awesome.
This game may well be a 9.9 out of 10 when they are done...with 10/10 being impossible...
Great job to the developers of this gem!

On the plus side, it means that there's always something to look forward to, but you'll need to ask yourself how big that "something" needs to be for it to be worth it. You can potentially get hundreds of hours of entertainment out of this game, but you'll have to really, really enjoy the act of slowly, *slowly* progressing through it.
It goes on sale often enough, at a very affordable price. Buy it then, and it'll definitely be worth it.

The original version of this game was a bit lackluster. After a couple years away from the game I decided to come back and see if anyone else played a game that I didn't recommend.
What I came back to was a much improved game. The levels, the way you select which level you play, down to how you play each character greatly improved. I feel what I originally played was an early access game that was not listed as an early access.
The game now feels polished, its solid all around and there are still active players. There is even a DLC to unlock a brand new playable character.
You can play in campaign mode and go through the story and play each scripted level, earning gold and upgrading your characters gear along the way. You can go back and play any level you have played, as long as you've beaten it on that difficulty. There are three difficulties that ramp up appropriately. Easy is good for one player, any skilled player can get through a majority of the levels without needing help of others. On normal you will want at least two players, if not three. On Hard difficulty you want four players; three can be done, but four is SO much better.
There is an endless mode in which some levels you see in the campaign, along with others, are randomly loaded with enemies and events. Money you earn can be used to buy food, potions or skull coins (1-ups essentially). Some levels in endless are very easy, simple. Others are loaded with lots and lots of hard enemies in one locked room.
Between the two modes, and a coloseum mode that I have not played, I have to recommend this game. Buy it now while there are still players! Othersie you will need three other players to play with you either in  local multiplayer, online, or a mix of both.

To the moon tells a wonderful story, of life, love and loss.  It's more a piece of art than a video game.  Anyone who enjoys a good story will enjoy this game.  If you're looking for cutting edge graphics, or state of the art gameplay this won't be for you.
In fact this game is pretty devoid of gameplay outside of moving from one scene to the next.  The game has some very simplistic puzzles which can typically be solved in under 10 moves.  Although game isn't about defeating enemies, gaining experience or collecting loot.
You play as a pair of... well they are called Doctors but I think they are more or less Scientist.  Their job is to go into someone memories, unlock the meories and use them to rebuild the memories in such a way as to fulfil their dying patients wish..
This story centers around a dying man named Johnny who wished to visit the moon.. hence the games title.. To the Moon.  Along the way of recovering Johnny's memory a wonderful story of love, and loss unfolds before your eyes..
This game is very good, it tells an amazing story, which if you enjoy stories, you'll love, if you are the pew pew pew, kill enemies, collect loot, gain levels type of guy, you should stay far away from this.
The game will last about 2 hours give or take a few minutes for solving the puzzles.  The ending will bring out the feelings in even the most hardened gamer.  Although as good as the story is, it can be pretty predicatable, although that isn't really a bad thing..
I'd recommend this game highly, great story, great music, and generally enjoyable enough..

Villages will grow once they complete projects, projects are random buildings that pop up requiring X amount or resources to be finished. Resources you place can give multiple, well resources, (like some fish give both Food and Gold) They can be given buffs to give out more, placing them near certain other resources will grant a bonus to their yield, and sometimes location determines how much they produce. (For example, a fruit tree will do better if in a forest and surrounded by other trees) You wont know what works where until you just try it out, then beat the crap out of the test village you just made extremely greedy before they kill someone.
2 problems I have with resources.
1) Resources at first will confuse the crap out of you if you are anything like me. You assume a village needs food right?  WRONG!!! Unless they are building something that requires food, it is a worthless resource that only takes up very limited space. You dont need a balance of all the resources, you just need whatever it is the villagers happen to want at the time. This means that your villagers could want to build a granary one second requiring a bunch of food, and after that is done they suddenly want Gold so you have to replace all of the food squares with gold. Which can be really annoying.
2) To add more challenge I guess, villages also have a "Greed" meter. Give them to many resources at once, they will do one of two things. attack and kill another village or attack and try to kill the closest giant to them, basically forcing you to send Rocky to pummel their settlement into dust (Also forcing you to start over, do not walk off or another village will spawn almost instantly in the same place and get greedy almost instantly because of the resources that are there, destroy them) This is so irritating when something requiring completely different resources pops up. You can combat greed with danger, say put some scary animals near the boarder, they will kill them instead of going to war. But again, uses up space.

The game is about managing multiple villages at once so that they will all grow slowly around the same time and wont get to greedy. (Until one of the little S***s tries to build something that requires them to win a war, in which case give them a bunch of crap and say goodbye to another village) Give them what they need so they will give you what you want (ambassadors) so you can make bigger better towns to populate your planet before your timer runs out and your tired giants pass out ending the game. It is simple to learn, very hard to master.
It is a lot more fun than it is irritating I will say that, worth a try at least.

Divinity: Original Sin Enhanced Edition is definitely my GotY, and lands in the top-5 for my all time favourite games. It'd make 2nd place for sure (Planescape:Torment sitting in that spot for likely ever), but there's some frustratingly unintuitive quests, particularly towards the end.
So.. yeah. Damn what a great game, and it boggles my frigging mind that Larian Studios pulled it off with a tiny team.
I'd rather jump into D:OS2 right now than write a novel of a review, but here's the highlights.
The Bad:
* Unintutive quest objectives, and a reliance on pixel-hunting for switches occasionally. There's some stuff that I never would have gotten without looking it up online. It's rare, but I wouldn't play this without an internet connection ;)
* Modal states when an action is happening, stopping you from doing something else. It's weird because you can queue actions, but I can't start to heal someone with my mage, then immediately switch off and start something else on another character - I have to wait. It's a turn-based game during combat, so it's fine there, but slows down my post-combat healing and such
* That's it. Niggles here and there, but those two bits are the only things worth mentioning
The Amazing:
* Imo, best combat system ever devised in a turn-based RPG. It uses Action Points and a variety of stats, and it is absolutely fantastic.
* Lots of thinking - caveat of the Bad point above. The game doesn't hand-hold, and with a large game like this, there's a lot of content, and a lot of ways things interact. I won't spoil anything, but even the "starter quest" is way, way more impressive than most other RPGs ever manage
* Very good writing. It's a bit samey, which is slightly odd for some characters (everyone's got a great vocabulary), but overall it's really well done. The story /should/ have, by all rights, felt hackneyed and overdone, and it didn't. Lots of good twists and turns, fantastic depth to the world, pretty good depth for characters and a decent amount of RP available
* Very stable and clean - bugs were verrrrry rare, and in over 100 hours of play, I never once crashed. Again, small team, that's bloody impressive. I normally veer away from things I know are likely to break a game, and I stopped worrying about it in this.
For any RPG fans that enjoy some depth to their game, highly, highly recommend it. Would even be good with low difficulty and a walkthrough if you want some lazy fun

Reviews for Shroud have to be a little different.  Those who play the game but don't engage what's going on with the development and the community are missing what this is about. BLUF:  If you're a gamer with similar values to mine, SOTA is worth the $40 price tag.
I'm a gamer;  SOTA has gotten more play in my Steam library than any other game (besides Clicker Heroes, but that doesn't count at all).

ESO disappointed me with the Tamriel One update (whatever it's called) to scale every thing to your level.  That's not what an RPG is about to me... An RPG is about win/ lose because of your experience.
SOTA is a grindy game.  I love the grind.  It takes a que off of the single player Elder Scroll series, Rune Factory series, etc:  When you use a skill, it improves.  Love that.
Pros:
-It get's updated every month...every month gets better.
-If you like the grind, it's there.
-Great community.  Very friendly and mature.
-Very customizable housing, and if you can't get a house, the community will hook you up.
-This experience is defintely different than mainstream, and it should be supported because I think we will all be tired if games only keep throwing up the same ideas because it's safe to play by.
Neutral:
-Graphics... they pass for me, but this is definitely no Black Desert.
-Combat does what I need it to do, but it leaves some folks disappointed.
-Player base... it's low, but it's all mature gamers.  I'm glad I'm not playing with immature kids, but the crowd is niche.
Cons:
-XP Decay... this is a HUGE turnoff for MANY players.  I haven't hit the wall yet, but folks know it's inevitable to happen.  Upon death, your XP pool will decrease, which has the ability to eat at your skill level if you don't have enough points in the XP pool.   This discourages players from entering high risk situations.  A game DESTROYER.
-Not user friendly.  Quest/ story line is kinda garbage right now...  It tries to go old school with you figuring out what to do next, but the clues necessary aren't there.  I've NEEDED youtube howto vids to complete story... that shouldn't be the case.

My conclusion:
I've gotten my $40 worth, but I've put way more than that into it.  I wish a lot of gamers will give this a chance; I don't want all genres to fall into a COD type of mentality (give players the same bovine scatology without taking chances every game).  Give it a chance... if you can skip McDonald's a few times, support this.

First and foremost, this game is not pay to win. Obviously, if you do pay then you can get things quicker, but it doesn't really have any major influence on winning or not. I have been using a combination of cards that is mostly made up of the ones that I started the game with and have won more than I have lost. With regular playing and completing the challenges, you can build up a good deck and save shards and rubies to open up new characters and arenas. Obvously, if you are impatient and want to get everything immediately, then paying for the premium upgrade will help you to unlock all the main masters and some arenas. Some grinding will always be present in games where there are unlockables.
A lot of people have made the comment that the game is dependent on luck, which I don't think is entirely true - tactics can win the game. Spamming low cost cards will sometimes work, but carefully using the deck will get around this. If you don't invest time in the game, then it will feel superficial. Give it some time, try out new masters and card combinations until you find soemthng that works and then go with that.
The graphics are great, the animation is smooth and the community isn't full of people shouting obscenitites at each other. Gameplay is well paced and balanced - but it does take time to master.
An excellent game that I look forward to seeing grow. Highly recommended.

Super Scribblenauts was ok, but its visuals weren't all that good and there were limits to what you could use. It also suffered from a complete lack of story. This 3rd installment blows all of those problems away. With the ability to apply adjectives to yourself, edit objects, create custom items, and its remarkable story making this a direct upgrade.
The story has the player collect Starites in order to reverse a curse that has been set on Maxwell's (main character) sister Lily, which has turned her to stone. Finally the Starites have purpose. In order to obtain these magic items, the player must complete multiple puzzles using their notepad and God-like powers, each pretaining to whatever area you happen to be in during the game.
The only thing that really disappointed me, was that the Doppelganger (Maxwell's evil twin) has no part in the story, not even as a rival that shows up from time to time just to distract you for a bit. I think this character could use some more development.
Final verdict, the avid mind will just absorb this phenomenal game. It's the perfect way to bring your wildest dreams to life however you please. Want to have a lightsaber fight on the moon, ride a giant winged fish or shoot flames from your mouth? It's all here for you to explore. A definite must-buy!
Final Mark: 5/5

Skullgirls overall is a beautifully done game. Amazing soundtrack, fantastic animation, and fast-paced gameplay make this one of the best fighting games on the market.
Now, this game is not for everyone. Compared to games like Street Fighter, it's much faster and seemingly more random until you get the hang of it. People often say that this is one of the best games to pick up as your first fighting game, but I don't necessarily agree. Yes, it has one of the best tutorials in fighting game history. Yes, combo'ing from normal to normal (normal=punch/kick) is easy. However, the mix up and reset-heavy nature of the game can make it seem like you're just being hit until you die.
I 100% recommend this game, but I do think the barrier to competency is extremely high...but that's not a bad thing. And if you're just looking for a fighting game for you and a friend to play for fun, then Skullgirls is perfect. Just don't expect to put even 50 hours into it and expect to win very much. If want to sink some time in this game to "git gud," then it's very rewarding.
It's also updated fairly often with very reasonable balance changes (I'll miss you, Filia's j.lk j.hk overhead crossup), new characters (Beowulf hype), and game features (the new replay system will make it very easy to see just how much of a scrub we all really are.  This is MikeZ's baby and he pays attention to it.

First of all I want to say that Bloons TD 5 is a great tower defence game however this version is just too insanely easy due to a major problem in game design. Namely the double cash mode.
The first couple days of playing this were great. A little bit of a grind to unlock everything but ultimately challenging and enjoyable. The moment you unlock double cash mode though the game basically plays itself. Hard levels become a breeze and on easy you seriously don't even see any bloons appearing on screen because they are all already dead from the dozen submarines or dartling guns you built by wave twenty.
With the normal cash mode the game feels well structured and balanced but with every token spent in the extra starting cash upgrade it becomes slightly easier and gives you more options to use. Then you spend $7500 on the double cash mode and all of that careful balance and design goes out the window immediately. It hardly even feels worthwhile playing it now.
It was then that I remembered that in the flash game double cash mode was a premium upgrade bought with real cash instead of ingame currency. In other words: pay to win. Between this, the token upgrades and the new overpowered towers the game rapidly becomes hugely unbalanced and completely without challenge.
Yes, you can turn this stuff off and play without it but the game gives you no reason not to use it. Some of the levels are almost certainly impossible on the hardest setting without these things turned on.
Ultimately then what you have is a game with two options:
1. Force yourself not to use the new content you have paid for in order to make the game a challenge until you eventually just get bored or infuriated with repeating the same level over and over and quit.
or:
2. Turn on double cash mode, build an entire fleet of submarines almost immediately and watch the game stutter to 20fps as they all fire in unison and beat the game for you.
Neither of these options seems very appealing to me anymore. If I had known the game was this broken I wouldn't have bothered buying it.

This game I bought because the different art styles were all cute and interesting. What followed was a shockingly good experience that I really didn't see coming.
This game is based on RPGs like Final Fantasy and Golden Sun, but where they can be very slow (the former, particularly), this one is incredibly fast paced. I've played a fair amount of FFxiii, but I managed to catch up to my playtime for that game in a much shorter span due to how enveloping this game can be; I've wiled away more than one night by just playing the story of this.
Grinding is possible, but wholly unneeded. It seems most of the enemies have some kind of scaling, but maybe I was just at the perfect level for everything... Not being able to tell which it is is a very positive thing.
It also has a Game+ mode where you just restart the story with all your levels, skills and equipment. This is a nice feature, but I wish it had asked first as I was close to a few end game achieves that reset with the story.
The actual gameplay is, as I said, fast and flowing. A little less dependence on the mouse would have been nice (you need to click to exit combat, for example), but I still love the way this game controls. Although the interface is mind-bogglingly complicated when you first see it, everything has its place and all fits together surprisingly well for a system as detailed as this. There're skill trees, equipment collecting, weapon and armour modifications, 'flair' trinkets, stat boosters, element resistance, buffs/debuffs... You get the point. But by a few hours into the game, I understood the majority of it.
Character balancing was a bit off for me... I dunno if it was bad use of stat items and skills, but my best fighter was also my best healer and had half the max health of my others. Due to the sheer number of options, I found it hard to keep it straight in my head which character should have which (I did consider making some kind of spreadsheet, but decided against it), but I managed to complete the game on normal difficulty without too much hassle. Don't think I ever lost a fight.
Enough about gameplay, what about the story and tone? The tone is brilliant. Spot on. Phenomenal. It'd be worth playing this for the characters' interactions alone. It plays beautifully with RPG and gaming tropes, references are everywhere and as I said at the beginning, the art style is amazing. Cutscenes are done in a felt-style looping animation, battles are anime and overworld travel are chibi things. They all work surprisingly well together and give the game a very lighthearted feel that becomes all the better when the team encounter horrific atrocities.
Also there's a little easter egg that I stumbled upon entirely by accident, but could NOT stop laughing at. I won't spoil it. But damn. It just epitomises the game.
Overall, this is a fantastic light RPG that is deep enough in gameplay to be elevated beyond the flash game it is and become one of my favourites. Resolution options are terrible, mind, and it isn't integrated with steam very well. Still. Amazing game.

No voice or text chat means there is no way to strategize or interact with other players other than running around in circles. The developers said they want to make the game as close as an experience to the original arcade as possible, but are actually using that as an excuse to avoid programming more. If you are standing at an arcade machine with three of your other friends there's nothing preventing you from using your voice. The game is also unforgiving. Even on easy difficulty you should have at least three people in your party or it will be tough to proceed. Getting more people to join you should be simple, but the developers opted for the archaic "quick join" feature for multiplayer instead of giving players a list of lobbies. This means that you could click quick join and wait for minutes to join a game not knowing whether anyone is actually playing a public game at the difficulty you selected. All of this equals an unsatisfying multiplayer experience unless you know well three other people that all want to play and have the game. $80 for you and three of your friends to play a game where you can't communicate is a bad deal.

The problem I have with it is that the multiplayer aspect is so emphasized that it feels like the game was designed on the assumption that you would play it with three friends in a living room. This is bad for two reasons; one: anything at all is fun if you're playing it with your friends around a table of pizza and beer, and two: if that's how the game is intended to be played, why was it even ported to the PC, which is the worst possible platform for party gaming? Add to this a needlessly grindy system of magic upgrades and a selection of cosmetics you will never see in the game that feels like the game was made to be a vehicle for selling microtransactions, and you've got a game with a lot of problems that would still be decent casual game except that the dodging moves for the elf and the valkyrie are not only tricky to aim in the direction you want to actually go, but do not move the character a reliable distance and cause framedrops if you use them when there are a lot of enemies on screen, which is of course the situation in which you would be spamming dodge roll or spear thrust. Frankly, I would trade in the havoc physics for decapitated heads and half the polygon count for a game that could maintain a decent framerate.
That was the review I wrote when the game was new. Now, about two years later, the microtransaction gouging seems to have been removed,  the game has been optimized for better performance, an endless mode that feels even more like the original gauntlet games, with purchasable food and magic, has been added, and keyboard controls have been added, which feel very good and precise. At this point, I do recomment the game.

Reus, released May 2013, is a simulation game developed and produced by Abbey Games. In Reus, the player has control over four 'giants' (forest, water, rock and swamp) and  must use the powers of each in combination to create a world suitable for the uncontrollable people (Villagers) and support them as they grow larger and expect more from the giants.
Every so often, a village will ask the giants to help them create a special kind of building which will require certain resources based upon what type of village it is (Forest, Mountain or Swamp) and what resources the town is based around (Food, Wealth or Tec). Resources come from minerals, plants and animals, which can be upgraded to supply more resources and gain different symbiosis abilities. symbiosis is the name of the special abilities each different resource has, for example, one mineral will increase the resources it gives if next to a plant and one animal will increase resources if its next to the same kind of animal. If the player successfully supplies the village with the supplies in the required time limit, and build the special building, they will be rewarded with a village ambassador which, when given to  a giant, will either unlock or upgrade the giants ability and allow them to create better resources.
As a village gets bigger, the villagers will become less impressed with the giants and instead of giving the giants an ambassador for every building, they will only reward the play when they help create upgraded special buildings and after a while they only reward the player for every third tier building they help create.
At the same time, a player cant give a village a lot of resources too quickly, or else that village will become greedy and go to war with other villages and the only way to stop a village that has declared war is to use your giants to destroy the village, removing it from the game, but allowing another village to take its place. This dynamic stops a player from instantly creating a village with a lot of resources.
After a village gains a certain level of prosperity, it spawns a nomad, who scours the globe looking for another place to live, if the player doesn't create any other inhabitable areas, the nomad will create a village close to the already existing village, inhibiting the villages of expanding in that direction.
This is definitely one of the best indie games on the market. I liked the use of achievements to unlock better upgrades for plants, which allow for the creation of better villages. The graphics are also very well done and give the game a nice cartoon-y feel. Mechanically, the game is well thought out, with mechanics stopping a player focusing on a single are of the planet, and stopping them from upgrading a town too quickly.
It would be hard to change this game too much without changing the game completely, but one thing the game could probably do as an improvement, would be to introduce another giant, or adjust existing giant abilities that allow for the use of the sky above the villages.
In short, this game is defiantly worth picking up, and I look forward to seeing what Abbey Games does next.

Sometimes we just want to settle down and watch something grow. Reus is that kind of game, or at least would be if it wasn't for a fiendish amount of experimenation and micromanagement lurking just moments under the surface.
Deceptively simple, you control four giants with different abilities trying to shape the world around them. Each one interacts with one another allowing you to make the world of your choice and there's a huge balance going on with it all. The catch is, everything's timed. As humanity starts moving in, they'll want the help of the giants to help build projects which will require different amounts of synergy between food, wealth, and technology. And that's not all, you have anywhere from 30 to 120 minutes to make your planet as good as you can, after which humanity is on its own. If you have a couple of villages running about, it isn't too hard. But that isn't the best way to play the game. You need to have at least one of each type of village which will give you ambassadors which will give your giants additional powers. Before long there's an insane and ingenious amount of micromanagement going on and unless you're paying attention to your giants, you won't play at the best of your ability.
The game knows this though and takes it slow, giving you a few different types of animals and plants to start with, moving you up over time. The faster you adapt, the more you get to play with. There's also a free play mode too so you can figure out just what to expect from a timed run. All the while, the game remains cute, innocent, and calming, which helps.
Definately recommended, though there's a learning curve. Don't get discouraged if you don't do well for a couple runs.

I have played the F.E.A.R. trilogy on the Xbox 360, as well as the PC. (However I have yet to finish this one yet on the PC). So here is how I feel about this game.
As a shooters, is a fun game. The gun mechanics feel nice. The guns themselves feel nice. Hell, if you have a good PC running this at max settings, they look gorgeous. And I like the co-op-slash-competitive mode this game does. Whoever gets the highest score, becomes the "favorite" son to Alma. And you also level up in this game which increase stuff like ammo capacity, slo-mo, and whatever else.
However, as a F.E.A.R. game, it is terrible. And that's why I don't recommend this for F.E.A.R. fans. F.E.A.R. 3 is the weakest installment of the series, lacking everything that made the first two great. Even F.E.A.R. 2, however others feel about it, was still faithful to the first one than this. The developers have essentionally made this as Call of Duty: Psychic Warfare.
First, you are now relying on auto regen for your, now apparently low health bar. You used to be tough in previous installments, and need to find health kits to restore your health. Which was one of the things I have liked about this series. Now you can't even step out of cover without needing to GET BACK INTO cover after getting hit with a few bullets. (I'm exaggerating here, but the point is, they have basically nerfed your HP.)
(Edit: I want to add really quick that I am playing this on normal difficutly. In case you're wondering if I was playing it in hard mode.)
Secondly, the fear isn't there anymore. The game used to get you spooked with it's atmosphere. As supposed to the cheap jump scares studios typically do. (Which, there are some in previous installments, but they weren't heavily reliant.) Oh yeah, speaking of which, this one doesn't even have that. The atmosphere is gone. Now is just another generic first person shooter.
Now, in case you're thinking, "But what about the slo-mo? F.E.A.R. is known for that?" So were Max Payne and True Crime. Doesn't mean anything if the game itself is still bad, does it? Yeah, it's there, but it's not like it saved this game.
So overall, this is a disappointing installment. And this is after I said that it's a fun game. Perhaps if this was a different game, like say, a sequel to Blacklight, (Not counting Blacklight: Retribution) I could have given this a more positive review. Because it is a fun shooter. Generic or otherwise.
If you're still thinking about buying this to see for yourself, I say wait for a steam sale, or, if you still have an Xbox 360 or PS3, see if you can find a copy for cheap. They should be around $10 or less by now.

I love this game. Building your own mini empire across several settlements, setting up trade routes between them, sending out hordes of units to assault other people's castles are all fun, and getting big enough to be tipped into a faction and start politicking is also fun. People are on 24/7, building and plotting each other's demise, and it inspires an incredible sense of dedication to checking in over the course of the day and making it a part of your life. Things happen slowly, but the decisions you make are always interesting.
That said, the game has two hard currencies: time and money. The more you're on, and the more your allies are on, the more you can strategize and wage a 24/7 war against whoever. There is a way to build an efficient and collaborative war machine, and doing things besides playing this game are not it. Even if you do dedicate your waking existence to the game--and there are definitely enough people who do so that it matters--you can still be outspent by people with really deep pockets that are filled with real world currency, who spend it on things that give them free resources, production boosts, and movement boosts. I don't think it's possible for a faction that is 100% dedicated but doesn't spend a dime to overcome a faction that is 100% dedicated and has a few people spending $10. If anyone reading this knows otherwise, I'd love to hear about it.
So I'm split. The game is great fun, but only until you run into a group of players who have more time and real world money than you. Once that happens, they crush the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you and take your settlement and all of the buildings and resources you accumulated. Once you lose all settlements, it's back to square one. You're given a fresh hamlet to build up and inevitably have raided, and it becomes clear that all you're doing is producing a series of feeder farms for the upper echelons. And that's cool and all, but I get enough of this kind of♥♥♥♥♥♥in the real world.

Overall, this is a fantastic game.  The story is cute and has a few twists, and the graphics and music are consistently great the entire way through.  Don't be fooled by the cute graphics, though; this is also a difficult, challenging platformer that will scratch the itch of anybody who's looking for a hard Metroidvania.  I'd put it about in the same league as Guacamelee.  There's a large world map with a ton of secrets and little nooks and crannies to explore, and you get a few very innovative abilities over the course of the game that will make you think creatively to solve puzzles.
Still, the game has a few flaws, and they're mostly design decisions that will only really bother experienced gamers.  Most notably, there are a few areas that you cannot return to after completing.  If you miss any items or don't fill out the map there, it will haunt you forever.  After entering the last dungeon, you can't leave, and after you complete the game, it locks you out of your save game and you can't go back and try to complete things; you have to start a new game if you want to be a completionist.  There's also no way to teleport between areas, so you'll be doing a lot of running back and forth across the world map while you search for items.  Finally, there are a few timed "escape" segments that are more difficult than anything else in the game, and while they're very satisfying once you complete them, they could potentially be difficult enough to discourage people who aren't skilled at platformers.
On the up side, the developers have stated that they're working on a "Definitive Edition" of the game that is supposed to address all of the common complaints.  With that in mind, I can easily recommend Ori; even with its flaws, it's still a great game.  Buy it and play through it now so that you'll have a frame of reference when the Definitive Edition comes out and you'll want to play through it again.

Skullgirls overall is a beautifully done game. Amazing soundtrack, fantastic animation, and fast-paced gameplay make this one of the best fighting games on the market.
Now, this game is not for everyone. Compared to games like Street Fighter, it's much faster and seemingly more random until you get the hang of it. People often say that this is one of the best games to pick up as your first fighting game, but I don't necessarily agree. Yes, it has one of the best tutorials in fighting game history. Yes, combo'ing from normal to normal (normal=punch/kick) is easy. However, the mix up and reset-heavy nature of the game can make it seem like you're just being hit until you die.
I 100% recommend this game, but I do think the barrier to competency is extremely high...but that's not a bad thing. And if you're just looking for a fighting game for you and a friend to play for fun, then Skullgirls is perfect. Just don't expect to put even 50 hours into it and expect to win very much. If want to sink some time in this game to "git gud," then it's very rewarding.
It's also updated fairly often with very reasonable balance changes (I'll miss you, Filia's j.lk j.hk overhead crossup), new characters (Beowulf hype), and game features (the new replay system will make it very easy to see just how much of a scrub we all really are.  This is MikeZ's baby and he pays attention to it.
Summary: Great game. High barrier to competency, but can also be played casually with friends who aren't too familiar with the genre. 9.5/10

Fallout 3 is an open world RPG Shooter with a first and third person perspective. It takes place in an alternate timeline which diverges from ours in about the 50’s. You are a Vault Dweller from Vault 111. At risk of spoiling you are compelled to track someone down and in and around the area of a destroyed Washington DC.
The good thing about Bethesda’s Fallout is that you are allowed to explore and play the game at your own pace. You are not restricted to time limits or anything like that. You can explore many ruins and even historic landmark buildings. There are several factions in the world you can ally with, or even destroy. There are tons of side-quests and unmarked quests that can keep you playing for a long time The main quest is short, but involving and the DLC is some of the best DLC around. Add on-top of that, the modding community has made many improvements to the game, and overhauls.
The downfalls are the shooter aspects of the game, some engine instability and its aging. However if you are not concerned with graphics then the rest isn’t a terrible concern considering the rest of the game.
I would definitely recommend this game if you enjoy Post-Apocalyptic games, or even the fallout universe.

It is the Gauntlet name, theme, and characters, but it just didn't "feel" like gauntlet to me.  The static top-down view and other major differences in the game cause me not to get that nostalgic Gaunlet feel that I was looking for.  Don't get me wrong, the game itself is enjoyable.  I played one character (Wizard) through most of the game, but I honestly don't know if I would play through it again.  There are just too many differences.
1. While  the characters may be the same, their abilities are different entirely. For example: Wizard, while challening and fun, has its own skill system by combining two elements to come up with 9 different unique attacks.  That has nothing to do with the original Gauntlet game for consoles / arcade.
2. The storyline and levels are completely different.  If anything, it now feels more like a cross between old school Diablo and Magicka.
3. Character progression is awkward.  Instead of leveling up, in this game you can get mastery levels that provide certain bonuses to that character.  This is similar to an "achievement" system, where for example you kill 1,000 enemies with fire spells you get a 5% cooldown reduction on one of your fire skills.  The damage doesn't change, just the cooldown.  I miss the idea of just leveling up like the original Guantlet!  They could have had an achievement system, which is usually a great idea; but tieing it into character progression hurt the game in my opinion.
4. The Magic Potions are more or less removed from the game.  Instead of a potion you can throw out to kill everything on the screen, you now use "potions" as currency for using one of your two equippable artifacts that all have their own abilities.  While I like the artifacts, I would have enjoyed them so much more if they had their own charges and potions were still something in the game.  When you see this game's version of "Death" in some levels, you can't use a magic potion (or anything else for that matter) to get rid of him.  You just keep running away until he goes away.
All in all, the game is decently fun to play.  Not a blow-you-away-amazing kind of game, but it's a good little time sink.  Unfortunately though, I do have to caution that this really isn't "Gauntlet" in anything but name.  It isn't going to give you that nostalgic feel that you expect, so you will have to look eslewhere for that.
