When is Gauntlet not like Gauntlet?  When it's this version.
This has more in common with a multi-player version of Diablo than it does with Gauntlet.
I played Gauntlet in the arcades back in the day, when it was new, and eagerly awaited it's release for home computers, including Atari ST and zx spectrum and a few others that were around at the time.  My friends and I enjoyed the conversion and played it for many hours.
Then came Gauntlet 2 and we were excited all over again, especially  when it was released for home enjoyment, and we all spent our waking hours wandering around with different coloured versions of each of the four characters, with Red elf and yellow wizard and blue wizard and green valkyrie, it was a good time had by all without the limitations of one character type availalbe, and often we'd play as four versions of the same character to see how it played.
Now after a few other releases of gauntlet and it's clones over the years on consoles and home computers, we come to this version.
While I wouldn't say it's a bad game at all, to expect it to be like either of the first two Gauntlet games is to meet with dissapointment, and it really does have a lot more in common with diablo 1 or 2, and Diablo's spawned children than the golden Gauntlet of happiness that I still remember clearly and dearly.
There are certain things that tie this title loosely to the Gauntlet of it's title, like 4 characters named after the Gauntlet characters. Food that's fragile and can be destroyed accidentally, and the fact that it all takes place in a dungeon.  Certain sounds and phrases are very similar to the original too.  But that's it for similarity really. Anything else is from Diablo.  There aren't mazes filled with spawners of varying strengths 1-3 (though there are occassional spawners scattered here and there), and there are potions but they are needed to power artifacts which you buy with gold, outside of the levels you play through.  The speech is of course clear and everything, but it is missing the dramatic tone that the original sampled speech used to have, and doesn't fit so well.   The only characters that shoot anything off are the elf and wizard, with the rest needing to use secondary abilities to do anything beyond bashing/stabbing the monsters.  And on the subect of the wizard, I hope you like pressing combinations of buttons/keys to use an ability, out of all the ones he has hidden.
Muti-player is very hit and miss, in that you might find good players that work together, and with due caution, or more usually find completely selfish players who get the party killed and have no other care but for their own selves and getting all the money and food for themselves.  Unfortunately there are far more of the second type than the first, which makes for a less than wonderful experience in multi-player, and has made it so that I am hesitant to even consider playing multi-player when (if) I play gauntlet.  Too many people playing it as though the other gamers are just tagging along, and then blaming them for being noobs when they die because the selfish individual has taken all the money/food/potions.
All in all, I am not so willing to recommend this version as a Gauntlet game, but I am willing to recommend it as a diablo clone that's cheaper than the average game these days, and I'd not recommend it to any of my friends if they played Gauntlet and were looking for a modern version to have fun with, though hey.. it's a game to fill the quiet moments of the day with dungeons and monsters.

FIRST OFF, I DO BELIEVE THAT THIS IS A GOOD GAME, ONE THAT PEOPLE COULD ENJOY. HOWEVER, I PERSONALLY CANNOT RECOMMEND THIS TO OTHERS. IF YOU ARE LOOKING TO TRY, YOU SHOULD PROBABLY WAIT FOR A SALE.
Reus has a whole lot of interesting ideas and features to it. It has a really complex and intricate system and the mechanics of the game compliment this. I personally bought the game because I love god games, I have played Black and White (and 2), populous, dungeon keeper (and 2) and these games are all really great. Mastering control over a 2d planet and its inhabitants sounded like a really cool idea to me. Unfortunately it wasn't my thing, the idea of re-playability to me is being able to invent and control your own game every time. I understand that you are not supposed to be able to control the populous to a great extent, but I ended up playing what felt the same type every time. The achievements and unlocks I was trying to accomplish were obfusticated by these villagers. I'm sure if I stuck with it, I'd be unlocking plenty of features of the game, but I couldn't figure out how to do so. The guides and people's Q and A's did not really help. I was stumbling a lot. I felt that the unlocks should have been changed to meeting certain, more specific (and controllable) criteria. What I mean by this is that borders should have influences (people should build out for the resources they want) and projects built should be based around certain needs (so if there are tons of fish in the ocean, then they should build a harbour rather than a school, its very frustrating). This would have worked a lot better, giving the player more control for what they want to do but not give then complete power over their villages.
The main issue is that villagers build what they want to build and start essentially when they want to start. You have very little control over this besides a few environmentally-based projects and smashing down a project you don't want built. This is a nice and interesting feature, but time constraints make it feel as if I'm constantly working against the villagers. Rather than actually helping these people out and feeling that I earnt the achievement I was going for, I feel I am competing or fighting against the people. It isn't a nice feeling.

This game is marketed as a city-building god game, but ends up playing like a poorly executed puzzle game.  You have to place plants and animals near each other to create synergy, but you have to initially place things without knowing how they'll interact because the UI does an awful job of communicating what will happen.
You end up spending most of your time replacing things because it turns out you should have build it 1 space over.  Imagine doing a jigsaw puzzle with your eyes closed, your hands (the gods) moving at a snail's pace, and every time you place a puzzle piece, you have to wait a minute before you can move it.  And then, before you can even finish the puzzle, the timer runs out and deletes all your work.
The game fails to deliver satisfying, intelligent gameplay, has absolutely no depth whatsoever, and within a couple hours you'll have experienced everything it has to offer.

I enjoy this game a lot more than its tutorial led me to believe, for some reason. Mechanics that seemed convoluted in training actually add an interesting level of difficulty and strategizing during actual play.
Overall, I'd say that Reus is a very well-designed strategy game, with a good progression and a lot of variety in objectives which encourages you to explore all of the different play strategies. Depending on whether or not you use the pause option, it can be very zen or a bit more intense.
However, I really prefer the shorter game duration, as I feel like 1h+ runs can feel like they're dragging on for way too long when things are not going as you had planned. I'm not sure yet what that means for me and this game in the future - but in any case, it has already provided me with a solid 10 hours of entertainment.

Reus is one of the best chill time games I've ever played. After a long day, the beautiful art, relaxing music, and simple mechanics are really nice to sit down and immerse yourself in. The humans can become a tad frustrating to work with as village upgrades seem to be randomized to a degree, and after a while some villages will try and kill the others no matter what, but it's pretty satisfying when you've completed a high level project, your towns are flourishing, and nobody wants to go to war. The game is pretty addictive, but since most game modes have time limits you can always get to a decent milestone and have the option to stop, so if you're trying not to sit and play for 8 hours it's also pretty nice about that.
Highly recommended.

A potentially good game by a historically great Dev team throttled to death by getting lost in the numbingly cold waters of Whale hunting.
I've added a third episode of my video reviews for Shroud now, as a visual companion for this Steam review, which can be seen here;
If it's too long to watch, skip to 57m for this game in a nutshell; a game where you literally have the basic corpse looting not working consistently, or even at all, whilst people with homes worth tens of thousands of dollars dominate the skyline and economy.
A game where the programmers outright state that individually customizing Player Owned Towns, which were only ever real cash purchases and now aren't even in the add on store any more, is a higher development priority than fixing the over land map that every player shares in.
A game where the community is becoming toxic to the point of debating whether they can form groups to "hold reviewers accountable", where moderators of that community openly discuss banning critics for actions the critics apparently never even committed... but where being financially invested allows you to bend the rules and avoid the claimed consequences of your otherwise outrageous behaviour.
A game where the developers themselves will get involved in fights with their critics, saying you've not played the game recently enough to have a valid opinion... whilst ignoring the criticism you made at the time, so bugs pointed out 2 years ago are still in the game. But then, when the Whales complain they can't profit as expected, in under 24 hours they'll act to re-rig the economy and allow them to continue manipulating it. And then ignore the complaints made at this current time again, that the economy is now horrendously broken...
And yet, there are still glimpses of potential hidden behind what is now a frankenstein's monster of real money driven greed, cult like thinking and development deafness. Every now and then you'll see little quality of life issues that are somewhat charming, only for them to be abandoned because if it's not a decoration in the store, you aren't buying it. They finally added fishing for instance, which is always rather relaxing; until you realise that it only actually works to catch fish at very specific pre-set nodes, rather than in any body of water as you might expect. And then this was left behind and forgotten in favour of the need to add limited edition, $400 airships in the store again. In my original review, I said this;
"Another example: There's no sign the Dev team plan to include a player bought or even crafted steampunk Radio to listen to the in game radio stations that backers can. Constant calls to at least sketch out what systems will be accessible for basic purchasers are ignored for more decoration you can purchase in the store; #134 added real cash trees for instance, but there's no mention of whether a normal person will ever be able to purchase their own vegetation for decoration. Gardening and farming, originally mentioned as part of the Nature to Nutrition design brief hasn't even been hinted at since the early days. "
You'll see in the video review that I butted heads with Starr Long over this, and to their credit not long after a miniture music player was added as a Final Wipe reward. What is unforgivable is that my review has been the highest ranked for Helpful on Steam for years now, and despite the above quote being in it, they didn't seem to know that actual gameplay was locked off in their own game until I had to go mano-a-mano with a Dev.
Gardening is in now, in the credit column. If you guessed "But only if you own a house above a certain size, and those are only in from someone making a real cash purchase at some time", well... now you're thinking with Portalariums.
If you believe I'm being unfair though, do take the time to watch the video review above. I had to cut out huge swathes of criticism just to get the video down to anything like an hour; but the first two responses to it on Youtube raise good points that I just didn't have the time or space to further expand upon. The reason that re-hashing the questions from Ultima doesn't work is it shows no understanding that the Principles and Virtues weren't interchangeable, one was supposed to be an amalgamation of many of the others by definition. It's like the difference between eggs and cake; one is an ingredient of the other but if you start saying "Whisk your cake now", it doesn't work, because the instructions are set for the sub-part not the larger item.﻿ Most of the fans don't care, because it's literal fan-service for them; A peak up the renaissance skirt of that Ultima wench they'd always had a soft spot for. But as coherent fiction, to an outsider it just doesn't make sense.
Likewise, it's hard to describe in even an hour just how unfair the economy is by design; I put up the screenshot describing Crowns of Obsidian because I hope you'll pause each bit of evidence in the video and think about the information presented where I don't have time to fully explore. It states there that yes, Crowns (which are the F2P currency added in) can be converted not just to longer lasting buffs (and thus, are the definition of P2W currency too) but directly into both paying housing tax, and outright into in game gold at a fixed rate. So even my account starts with 1000g more than you. At the rate I was earning it trying to craft, that's about 3-4 hours of grind I don't have to do. And if I focus that free money upon getting Lottery tickets... and win the housing lot whilst you STILL can't buy one from an NPC, only other players...
And I don't have time to expand upon all the shady, indecent behaviour exhibited by the players either; if you think the clips in the video were bad, look at the sociopathic abuse in the Steam forums heaped upon any one who tries to point out those trying to sell you housing aren't telling you the truth, and are just trying to pass on their eventual financial loss when the game craters to you. I didn't have time to discuss the issue of scamming and treating the game as "economic PvP" that was always the intention of some of those backing the game;
I believe I know who one of those scammers were; and also that his permanent ban became a temporary one when he pointed out how much he invested. And that you can in turn be banned for talking about moderation which in any just world we'd rightfully be howling at the sky about the sheer gall of.
At every level, in ways that are crushing in their intensity, in detail you can't discuss without seeming obsessed because it truly is staggering to any sane mind how much of it there is, Shroud has gone from the wonderful game of a better world in a different place that we imagined at Kickstarter into a true parable of our modern world; ruined by the financial abuse of those who use money to buy power but never any sense.
And the wolves still don't even path find correctly! Unleash the Yakety Sax, folks.
Don't purchase this; Really, trust the negative reviews, please. You have no place in this world unless you're rich (or just foolish with your money) in real life. It breaks my heart to say it, especially about Lord British whose early games were such a formative experience on myself and my perceptions of virtue. But it's true. New Britannia is only a home for the same old sins and scammers and seriously cultic.
Update: As funding starts to dry up, Portalarium have resorted to some unbelievably unethical business practices. See comments below.

At the start of the game you play through wave 1-50 on easy, then maybe 1-65 and then playing through 1-85 twice. Essentially you play the waves 1-50 four times in EVERY MAP! I just can´t get behind it.
Other than that i really dislike that you can "freely" place the towers. There are no spots predetermined for them so itching you mouse a tad bit to the right might validate the placement of the tower you want to build, but i guess thats only my opinion.
When i look back to this game, the only thing i see is wasted potential of a developer that clearly has the knowlage of how TDs are supposed to work. Such a shame.

Sorry for the long review, there is just a lot I feel I need to discuss about this game.
Where to start? I am giving it a thumbs up as it has the most played time in my Steam library presently, above Skyrim and Borderlands 2, even though it is definately not as good a game, and I am not the type of person to play something for that long and then eventually give it a thumbs down. Buuuut......
This game is sooooo frustrating! This game has so much potential, and could have been the one that people talked about for years. The more you play, the more you see little things that seem so obvious to have been included, but are not. The developers, seem to be patching the game and adding content, but it is slow. Hopefully with further patches it will be worth the price.
The game is polished, in that it never once crashed on me, and I only encountered small glitches, most that benefited you, such as removing a hydroponics tray in your base after adding a plant, and having the plant still grow fine, and being able to hit the melee button followed by the jetpack and moving a lot faster than sprinting allows.
Some of the things that are the most frustrating about the game include:
- Even though animals and plants are procedurally generated, the majority of land animals are either two or four legs, with various random features. But other than this the only "alien" type creates that I have discovered are ones that look like plants, that mostly jump. Where are the six, eight or more legged creatures? Snakelike ones? Blobs? Surely alien life would be a LOT more varied than this? In regards to swimming and flying animals, they seem even less varied, and in all my time playing, I only really encountered 3 different types of flying animals, with small batlike ones, and large phallic looking ones the most common.
- Although the planets are procedurally generated, everything still looks the same. It feels like every planet is the same size, there is no change in gravity (surely this is a variable in the code, as the gravity doesn't work until you are close to the planets surface so should be easy to randomise?), and it seems like each planet is created by randimising the terrain, colouring this with a two or three different colours then adding features specific to that planet, like floating half domes, spires, craters or other rock features, and then dotting these across the landscape, interspersed with discoverable features like camps and buildings. In the end it feels like each planet you go to is just different coloured rolling hills, with features dotted in every 500m or so. Once you have first landed and looked around, you have really seen everything, as flying halfway around the world to land again, you will feel like you have landed in the same spot. I have never encountered, forests, jungles, plains, swamps, large lakes, running water, rivers, waterfalls, large cliffs in all my play time.
Worse than this though is the caves. Once you have seen one you HAVE seen them all. Where is the randomness in this? Where is the discovering that amazing spot or feature in the game?
- The combat in the game is awful, with no real purpose. they could have just left this out of the game entirely and it would be much the same. The sentinels that are your only real "enemies" besides the odd hostile creature, and they are more annoying than anything else. Space combat is okay for the first couple of times, then it is just tedious, really just being, turn, shoot, turn, shoot. The HUD doesn't accurately tell you where enemies are located, so to find them, you really just scroll the mouse around searching till you find it. Where is the hostile aliens? The big hostile creatures that are hard to kill? The hostile packs of animals?
- Even though for the first couple of hours the scanning feature gets you into scanning and looking for wildlife, after a while there is no real reason to do it beyond getting the achievements. The game is really about exploration and discovery, but most of the time you are just collecting materials to make Warp Cells, warping into systems, and then warping again. 90% of the systems I visited I was there for 10 secs, before warping again, without landing on or exploring any planets at all. Why not reduce the distance to the galactic centre, and everytime you warp into a system, you need to explore to find something that is stopping your warp drive from working. Maybe an artifiact, animal, plant, landscape item?
- There REALLY needs to be some sort of bad luck protection when getting blueprints for things. Over 230 hrs of playtime as of writing this, and still don't have the blueprints for 2 of the Warp Drive Upgrades, Photonix Core, or the Atlas Pass V2. Only got the Atlas Pass V3 after 125hrs or so. You just get the same blueprints over and over aagin, and after a while you just give up.
Some of the things I think this game just needs (which may come in future patches) include:
- Spaceship building. It is clear that there are base ships with different decorations applied from the varied ships you see land at space stations, so all these are in the game. Why not after buying a certian type of base ship you can then customise it with your own colours, decorations and accoutrements?
- Really needs to have more things that people can add through the Workshop. The basis is there for truly random stuff, but allow others to create different things for animals, plants, landscape features, spaceship items, base items, spacestation items etc.
- Why not have procedurally generated instanced caves, buildings, space stations, carriers etc, with decent combat to get rewards at the end. I know the game was meant to be massive with no loading screens (but the warp animations, black hole animations, and teleport animations ARE loading screens, they just don't say that), but instanced areas that are randomised wouldn't hurt this idea too much. This could be tied in with warping into a system and having to explore to find what is interupting your Warp Drive, with an animal or plant deep in an instanced cave doing this, requiring you to kill  or scan it to be able to warp again. Have random "stories" for each system leading to you to this end. Shouldn't be too hard to add random story to the game, so that you warp into a system, have some various quests (scan a specific animal, scan 5 plants, collect some of this, kill this, kill that, find this etc) which lead you through the planets in the system and allow you to explore more, which is what the game is about. Allowing people to make workshop content for this also, so unlike the carriers and space stations in game presently, they are actually different and random.
- Needs more randomised content, so some of the items I mentioned above will appear in game (jungles, forests, plains, cities etc.
In the end, if this game actually had a bit more randomness to the landscape, making it feel rewarding to actually explore, and more story to encourage you to explore each system you landed into it would be amazing. Learning a bit more about the races of the system, rather than just that Gek's are traders, Vykeen are warriors, and Korvax are hive entities would have been great. Being able to sit at a waterfall that you have found, explore everything in an abandoned carrier, fighting your way into a space station or city/town, piecing together lore etc......
Each system you landed in would be truly random, with you having to do truly random things to get you Warp Drive working, and exploring more, which is what it is meant to be all about.
While giving a thumbs up, I still have missgivings, mostly tied to frustration on what this game could have been.

One of the most difficult RTS games I have ever played, and still one of the most entertaining despite a somewhat buggy client and no longer supported multiplayer servers.
Each race has a different building style, and you are able to customize and build different units.  The customization adds an interesting level of change to a game because if you research heavy into laser based weaponry and your opponent recognizes a pattern they may start to develop more units with reflective shielding making your units less effective and forcing you to change to rockets or bio weapons.  Paying attention to little details like the animations of weapons fire, or looking at the type of armor units are equipped with can be really important.
To wrap up, if you are a hardcore RTS fan this game may be for you because of the difficulty and complexity.  If you're a beginner or unwilling to look past a games flaws to see how much it actually has to offer, then you should probably stay away from this one.

Easily one of the richest, deepest, best turn-based CRPG's of all time.
Like a lot of RPG's, this game can be very unforgiven to new players. The combat can be brutal in the beginning and the game doesn't hold your hand when it comes to quests. You're going to need to summon your best old-school RPG wits and stubbornness to proceed. You will die a lot. Resurrection scrolls are to be used liberally. No joke.
Character progression, like all the best RPG's, offers so many options and so much depth that gimping yourself is totally possible, and indeed, probable. You're going to want to respec one of your two main characters (if not both) at some point. It's okay: the game offers a chance about 2/3rds of the way through. You'll probably want to play through the game a second time with "perfect" builds all planned and plotted out just so you can see how your ideal builds will work. That's the kind of game this is - your character builds are going to consume a lot of time in planning.
I will repeat: The game doesn't hold your hand. A lot of quests require you to find some obscure, hidden item, scroll or key. You're going to probably spend a fair amount of time checking Google in order to progress. That's okay. It's a throwback to old-school RPG's. Be persistent. Be relentless.
Combat in this game is amazingly fun, especially once you get a few levels under your belt and have a few skills and spells to throw around. It's turn based and very tactical; it rewards people who want to think strategically and micro-manage each and every decision. Positioning matters. Playing a rogue is incredibly fun because of this. This is one of those games where a single, well-placed spell (like an Ice Wall) can turn the tide of a battle. The combat reminds me a lot of "The Temple of Elemental Evil" which was also really fun and about as good as turn-based combat gets.
Quick-save often. You're going to reload quite a bit in the early stages of the game. But eventually you'll get comfortable with everything and get into a groove and your plucky band of heros will start to show their strength.
The game is huge; bigger than you realize. There's a lot of neat areas, tons of quests (like a good RPG should have) and a lot of interesting characters. Everyone is fully voice-acted and the dialog is often quite cheeky. If you're into that sort of thing you'll find the game very funny at times.
The art is fun and fanciful and the game is loaded with great looking boss monsters. There are some epic battles.
I'm a big fan of CRPG's like "Baldur's Gate 2", "Pillars of Eternity" and "The Temple of Elemental Evil". This game easily ranks right up there with the best of them. Fun, engaging, and appeals to the character/class builder in me. Figuring out the optimum build for my characters took some time, but it was totally worth it.
This is definitely one of the great RPG's.
one of the must-play RPGs

This game was fun during the leveling phase. Leveling was fun and engaging because you were running around the map progressing through the story, completing missions. Once you finish the story campaign, the game goes downhill drastically.
The end game missions on the harder difficulties gets old really fast. Incursions are EXTREMELY boring and the Dark Zone is tiny and a complete lag fest.
The concept of the game is great. However the execution of it sucks. There aren't enough weapons. There aren't enough attachments. This game basically takes a Diablo/WoW type of item finding/grinding system but doesn't have enough items nor enough locations to grind them. There should have been special items that are extremely rare. Like walking into a main city in WoW and seeing someone with a Hand of Rag or Thunderfury back in the vanilla days, would have made those items worth grinding for.
Also the dark zone....is way way way too small. You literally find yourself running back and forth covering the whole map over and over again and you get to a point where the items you find there are all worthless, so you continue to farm the dark zone for consumable items just to have a chance to craft a weapon or piece of gear that you probably already have in the hopes of getting one with slightly better stats.
The lag in the dark zone was unbearable. Getting shot at and running behind a bus only to die 2 seconds later when you're completely behind cover is ridiculous.
The voice chat can also be dangerous. It creates a peer to peer connection with the other players and anyone with malicious intent can get the IP address of whomever they're teamed with and do any sort of malicious action they choose from there. To make matters worse, UBISOFT blocks connection to the game when you're using a VPN, disallowing you to anonymize your IP address and basically forcing you to make yourself vulnerable.
This game had incredible graphics but not enough and/or boring end game content.
Lastly dev's can screw with your gaming experience. They can monitor everything you're doing and make you sink into the floor, forcing you to teleport back to the nearest safezone so you have to run back to whatever mission you were doing.

Synopsis - The evil bloons are assaulting the monkeys again.  You must defend yourselves at all cost.
There are three base versions of this game.
1.  The original flash game on
.  It is free, with microtransactions for what are essentially cheat codes, or to save time unlocking stuff.  It also has less features than the other two versions.
2.  The mobile version available for 2.99 on its and Android.  Even though it's paid,  it still has the same micro transactions as the flash version.  However, it receives the latest updates.
3.  The Steam version you see here for $9.99.  It is more costly, but there are NO microtransactions.  You earn everything that you buy as a microtransactions in the other two games by simply playing the game, including 'cheats' that can be disabled/enabled as you please.  It also recieves the latest updates, so you don't miss out on anything.
As for the gameplay, it's a simple(ish) tower defense game.  It has tons of maps, which come in 5 different categories: Beginner, Intermediate, Advanced, Expert, and Extreme.  Each of these has 4 different difficulties:  Easy, Medium, Hard, and Impoppable, with increasing rewards with greater difficulty.  Each map has 3 other modes that are not winnable, but more of a challenge mode.
Apocalypse - The bloons never stop coming.  How long can you survive?
Deflation - You start with $50,000, but can earn no more money in the game.  All abilities that generate cash are disabled.  How long can you last?
Sandbox - A testing ground for strategy.  You have infinite cash and lives, and you choose what bloons come out as you want.
There are 21 unique towers in the game, with 8 upgrades each.  Each tower has specialty buildings that can be unlocked with the in-game currency you earn by playing.  However, you can only use one specialty at a time.
Personal opinion:  Absolutely get this game!  It's a challenging game for all ages, so even if you're 48 years old with a 4 year old child, you will both love this game.  As for hardware needed, you onmy need to asj yourself a few simple questions.  Do I have a computer?  Did I get it in the last 8 years?  Is it working?  If you answered yes to these questions, it will run on your computer without much issue.
I myself haven't been able to use my PC much lately, so I mostly use the mobile app (No cheat unlock for me ;-;).  The two versions have the exact same gameplay, with the PC having no microtransactions, so this review shouldn't be overlooked for low playtime.  I have put HOURS into this game.  Heck, I had the PC version before it was on Steam.
Note: They recently introduced something called 'masteries', however I haven't unlocked it so I can't say anything about it.  I also haven't read about it, because I want to discover it for myself.  However, I am very close, and will update this review when I unlock it.

Recommendation:
First a warning. Some of the features I will mention are still in development.  This game really is in Pre-Alpha.  No one should expect a functional, feature-complete, fun, balanced or polished experience when playing this game today.
Only purchase if you are seriously interested in watching / helping a game in development.
Those of you who are still interested, please consider joining the game forums:

to provide input and feedback that the Devs really listen to, and help make this game great!
Like:
No monthly subscription. Once I buy it, I will be able to play online, or with friends only, or by myself.
At launch I will even be able to download it and play completely offline to my heart's content.
The world is made up of zones that you enter from a world map.  The world map is interactive, I can see my character, and walk anywhere I want, and I see others walking around on it too. Soon, monsters will be seen walking around that will attack me, or I can try to avoid.
This map is a beautiful 3d scale of the world, with a hidden grid of hexes as its foundation. I can enter most any of these hexes to explore the adventure scene inside.  The beauty of this system, is that dynamic content can be added without requiring a game patch.  Say, a regular forest hex is updated to have a special encounter, like a dragon or a traveling merchant who sells special items. Or a town could suddenly be attacked by an armie of undead.  As I zone from a hex to the world map, the new content will be loaded for me, and i'll see the updated hex represented on the map.  No exiting the game and restarting required.  These types of opportunities are a part of SotA's vision for this 'old-school' mechanic in an online setting.
One of SotA's key features is interactivity with the game world.  If you see an object that looks like it should have a function, double click it! Campfires, torches and candles can be lit/unlit.  If you see a chair, you can sit in it. See a ladder, you can climb it. Have an instrument? You can play it. Radio's actually broadcast community-run radio stations that broadcast live during community events, so you can experience the event, and hear it at the same time!
Crafting. Everything in Shroud of the Avatar is craftable. From normal clothes to chairs and tables. The tools you use to craft other items, are in turn craftable.  If I make an  armor chest plate, I can choose to use copper plating or iron plating.  The recipe is the same, just switching out the desired types. Copper armor has different enhancements than iron, and when you where it, you can see that it's made of the reddish colored metal!
Magic in the game uses both reagents, to make a spell more potent, and words of power to alter the qualities of a spell.
The day/night cycle has deep in-game meaning, with entire magic skill-trees dedicated to be useful in daylight/night.  Several other satellites in the sky have their own specific orbits you can study, and as the various heavenly bodies form conjunctions, or pass through constellations in the sky, they invoke special events, like being able to craft certain items only during that time, or possibly the opening of lunar rifts (portals) in the world.
NPC's don't just stand in one spot waiting for you. They have activities they perform throughout the day, and sleep at night. (unless they are a night guard, who would do the opposite of course).
Dislike:
Add-on store: I've never been a fan of add-on stores. It always raises a flag for me.
But playing SotA doesn't require any purchases outside the game itself.  Everything else needed to play can be gained through regular gameplay. Want a house? They can be purchased with in-game gold.
Online games must be maintained.  WoW reports that after launch costs to keep the game going add up to an average of 50 million dollars per year.
Large indie games with budgets in the $1-$10 million range are awkwardly caught in the middle - they have to do MUCH better than a smaller indie team needs to thanks to the much higher development costs, but they don't have the resources to compete toe-to-toe with the larger & more experienced companies.
After watching this game develop for a while now, I'm actually really glad it has this store. Many people like to purchase cool looking items, and this allows the Dev team to continue the game without the need for a monthly subscription.  It's a win for everyone.

Shroud of the Avatar is a unique game in pre-alpha with a lot of potential.
Shroud of the Avatar is one of the very few MMO's that provolks curiousity anymore. I always find myself slowly walking through dungeons looking for hidden passages (of which there are tons in most of the scenes of the game) finding hidden treasure and being enveloped by the atmosphere of the game.
Most people I find are greatly opposed to the way Shroud of the Avatar handles combat. For the sake of buyers on the fence I'll explain how this works. In Shroud of the Avatar you build a deck of the skills you invest points into. So if you invest 3 skill points into a fireball skill you'll get three cards of fireball to put in your deck. When you engage in combat the game hands the cards out at random. Now let's say the game randomly deals out your three fireball cards well instead of casting fireball three times you can stack your cards and empower the spell while reducing the mana cost.
If this doesn't suit your fancy you can always lock your skills on your hotbar deck for the standards mmo experience however it's currently not as powerful as the original system of randomly dealt skills. You can even mix the two options I.E locking a healing spell on your bar to use when you really need it but still having your fireballs dealt at random whatever tickles your fancy.
That's really what Shroud of the Avatar is about. 'Whatever tickles your fancy.' In the future the game will probably become more streamlined with quest that lead the player through the world. However in it's current state as of Release 19 the game is 100% player driven. Which means you do whatever you want or feel like doing. The game is on a monthly update track with new area's, new monsters and more content coming online every step of the way.
My average Shroud of the Avatar experience is spent exploring the handcrafted areas and soaking in the games atmosphere. It's hard to describe in essence what I enjoy so much about the game other than it feels like and 'old school MMO' it's nostalgic in that sense but modern enough to do it right. I throughly look foward to the full release of Shroud of the Avatar and will continue playing every Release up till then.
I don't really involve myself with the community so I can't speak for the quality of that I usually just explore with a buddy of mine and we do alright.
P.S there's a Monty python reference in the deepest part of the Spectural Mine if you're a bad enough dude to get down there. Good luck and remember "thou shalt count to three no more no less, three shall the number thou shall count and the number of the counting shall be three..."

Stay away for now until it is a game that can catch your interest and draw you in (Crosses Fingers). As it stands, the company is burning through iteration after iteration, changing and back-changing things left and right, with no actual solid feel of improvement. I seriously think they're going to burn through half the cash just realizing they're making a game from last decade. Whoops!
I thought I owed the game a bit more detail to post a sort of pros and cons list of some sorts...
PROS:
Ambiance is nice
Like the classless-ness feel
You can own a house/land
The interaction system isn't a giant exclamation mark, and requires thinking
Crafting system is very in-depth
Music is absolutely beautiful and player-made/designed
Overland map is beautiful
I like single-player online (private instanced world, yet affected by others playing)
CONS:
Developers seem to be HUGE newbies...meaning they change things, then undo, then change again, then undo again, then change...they seriously are "flying by the seat of their pants" or "have no fkn clue wtf is going on." or "have no direction" or are "at the mercy of a madman running this crazy vehicle." etc...
They are horrible money-grubbers. Not just for a crowd-sourced game, I mean in general. I dislike this. Developmental resources should be allocated for core game improvement, not fluff to make a cash shop. When the game's finished...fine..but in this state? Horrible waste of resources.
Out of date graphics, textures, movement, world, environment, skills, weapons, etc...it just screams "last decade"..and this is AFTER the move to Unity 5 Engine
Boring as can be...same old "Talk to every NPC to get every quest to max every skill to get the most gold and the biggest house." Okay...
Unintuitive tutorial system. Expect a learning curve that shouldn't be there
Combat absolutely sucks. They should delete the combat system and start from scratch. Seriously.
The interaction between character > World/Environment is horrid. Get stuck on an invisible pebble, can't walk up a stair that's on the ground because it's "too-tall", then die in combat, etc.
Feels empty
Quests seem boring
Highly buggy (expected..alpha) chat/interaction
Stupid card-system for combat...tries to make it "fun" and take out the "waiting for cooldown on skill #7" by...making you wait for a cooldown on CARD # Unknown...brilliant.../sarcasm
**EDIT**
I am amazingly enough changing my stance from not recommended to recommended. The release of R26 has really made the game playable for me.
This feels like drastic improvement. There are still bugs that persist, but they are indeed minor things (like ranged character doesnt face the right way when firing an arrow, but it hits, no biggie.)
Some things that are extremely notable to me that make this game stand out from others in its' current state are:
No more levels. Your character doesn't seem to have a solid level to hold you back anymore from trying anything. You also can't max entire trees within a short period of time. The experience distribution system is much better, and you actually earn xp for using your skills, as opposed to put points into it after leveling. I really really like this way of progression, and hope it stays around for good. This allows me to play how I want, and naturally become stronger in those areas. It's also pretty sweet that the trainers can't train you in everything anymore...you actually have to travel to seek out a trainer that has the skill you need.
The class-lessness feel isn't there as MUCH anymore, but only because they help you with a beginning path (at this time ranger/fighter/mage), and you can then do whatever you want from there. This is actually nice and helps you sort of keep your skills around a certain weapon or change to a hybrid class at will.
Crafting:
Amazing improvements. The trees feel much more flushed out, and the way they have the skill trees setup, although still a bit light, makes more sense. The materials themselves affect the crafting outcome more than the crafting skills themselves. I like this, and think it helps me want to explore the crafting area more rather than feel that I'm not high enough level to make anything worthwhile.
I made my own set of armor, was able to easily find a crafting trainer that had recipes for sale. There were benches nearby that were very intuitive on how to use and some of the gear I made was even an upgrade. This is a big change from earlier, when it seemed an extreme chore. Instead, yes, there is a "gathering grind", however, it seems that the process is now worthwhile; you get crafting gather XP as you do it, and it just seems more friendly all around.
Where this game shines for me now is in how different combat and the immersive experience is from before.
Combat isn't nearly as clunky, and seems to have a much better flow to it. You also are able to, as an archer, use snares and blinds effectively to engage multiple targets and actually KITE them finally. This is exciting because beforehand you would literally get slaughtered with more than a couple monsters if you weren't a mage or a tank.
Though there are still some empty placeholder skills and issues floating around, I really have to give this company props, because they've managed to make me really flip my opinion about how they've actually progressing internally as a company, and I do believe they may know WTF they're doing. Yay for the players!

This game is a joke, being a parody of Final Fantasy,
BUT
It's not a joke.
Not only does this include a difficulty system that actually tells you everything major that changes (Besides things like the Bomb Slimes and Purple Squids entering battle with nine poison stacks on Epic) but the game is still reasonably difficult without putting it on Epic, unless you're so used to Epic that in your second playthrough on on a sequential save half of the enemies one-shotting you in the power plant due to you being two levels underleveled feels normal. My first experience with Epic was nearly getting killed on the first battle in the game, gg. What truly makes this game difficult is Epic is insanely hard, but you can adapt to it. You can get hit by the enemies and survive, and most things that the enemies can do aren't out of your power, unlike a lot of games you see today. It puts the player and the enemies on nearly equal ground, but manages to still keep the game reasonably difficult. That is a sign that the game's difficulty is well designed.
This game contains parodic references to almost every game in the book that your childhood was composed of. My favorite cluster of references is the graveyard in Graybone Cemetery, there are many tombstones on one screen, a few of them are damaged, but the ones that aren't contain jokes that are mostly references of some sort. This is only a pinch of what is included in the actual game, though.
The dialogue in this game somehow keeps a decent balance between "Absolutely hilarious and cannot be taken seriously" and "Deep storyline" despite the final boss being *SPOILER* a cat god.
I think my favorite thing about the dialogue in this game is either the fact that there is a one-liner for nearly every skill in the game, or the fact that dialogue can randomly trigger when walking around the map, and these times it's at it's funniest. There is one cluster of dialogue where Lance is staring at highschoolers and Natalie calls him a pedophile. Another is a conversation between Matt and Lance where Matt seems to be trying to explain to Lance that despite all the cameras he apparently has in his posession that he uses to stalk Natalie, it's still stalking and over the top stalking at that. The items even get some of this amazing humor, every one having a one-liner for a description. Achievements even get thrown into this bucket, there is one that nearly everyone knows about for clicking Natalie's boobs.
The only negative that comes to mind is the lack of an optimized full screen resolution and no access to STEAM features ingame, besides syncing, achievements, and cards. However this is understandable for a game ported from flash.
There isn't much to say about art style, it's not super duper flashy, and it definitely doesn't try to be edgy. It just tries to be cartoonish, cute, and funny, as it should.
I can't say much about the music, purely because music is almost never my main focus. Although I can say the music is definitely catchy and worth listening too, HFX definitely did a good job in my opinion.
This game has very nice replayability too, but the story isn't really the strong suit. I personally replay for the comedy and the challenge, and I do NG+ to get gear and etc. I didn't grab the first time around.
Overall, Matt deserves much more attention than he gets, but should never stop being a semi-solo developer. When you work with a lot of people and publishers, games like this are only dreams.

Love this game, mainly because of the great battle system.
While I do dislike how negotiating with NPCs is done through literally rock-paper-scissors, and how in order to reach the end of the game you have to complete a few specific sidequests because of the rewards they give you, these are issues that didn't really ruin my enjoyment.
The real fun is in the battles, and most battles offer different enough challenges for it not to feel like the same encounter appears many times. The terrain affects battle, and quite a lot of fun comes from affecting the terrain to harm enemies (and sometimes the most frustrating fights are those where the enemy puts you in a tough spot because they affect the terrain better).
I also love the character customization - each character is given a starting set of skills and stats, but you can choose where you allocate points gained by leveling, so you choose what your characters specialize in and what skills they will know, which can lead to some dilemmas later on with higher-tier skills.
Overall, a game I would recommend to any RPG fan.

NOTE: Although I didn't actually get this game for free, I got it in a bundle which I didn't buy for this game specifically, so it was effectively for free.
summary:
Secrets of Rætikon is a game where you fly around and grab things. This sounds overly simple, but the game makes use of the very simple mechanics in some really interesting ways. I won't go into too much detail, so as not to spoil the experience, but you'll likely discover some really interesting ways to manipulate the game world. This, really, is the primary enjoyment in the experience for me.
Unfortunately, it isn't without its frustrations: A bug caused an object to glitch out of apparent existence, so I had to access the game files to modify its position to myself. Additionally, I got lost on the task of trying to find the last macguffin, which I'm not sure whether to put down to me being bad at finding things or that object being hidden too well.
The game is fairly short, and although it supports steam workshop, there is almost no content on it. (although I haven't tried what is  there yet) Finally, the ending is not exactly a story ending (and this is not really a story game).
Pros:
-Nice feeling movement
-Simple mechanics that interact in interesting ways
Cons:
-Abstract ending that may not be satisfying for many
-Short game
Recommendation:

Beautiful autumn colours, indiosyncratic artstyle, and the freedom of flight. I had been anticipating playing Secrets of Rætikon when the leaves in my neighborhood lit up the sky with deep warm hues, computer monitor and nature mirroring each other.
The apple tree outside of my window has maybe a few yellow leaves left. It is at this time I am now comfortable just letting this game go instead of preparing for disappointment any time I thought about launching it.
Secrets of Rætikon is not a horrible game by any means. The reason I'm Not Recommending it is because it feels like it was given unnecessary game mechanics instead of allowing relaxing exploration. I was hoping to traverse these angular naturescapes with flow, but instead I was expected to avoid/reclaim objects from way-too-sharp enemies and navigate an environment with inconsistent indications of collisions (i.e., it's difficult to tell which trees you can pass through, and which branches will prevent movement). The fetch-quest nature of this game doesn't feel quite rewarding, either, as is the case with many games.
Not much is clear on what needs to happen here. Usually, I enjoy figuring out what's going on, even basking in confusion. The same was true of this game for the first half-hour or so, until I realized I needed to backtrack with objects quite a bit.  I also wouldn't have minded if damage wasn't dealt so easily, from the really mean birds to the thorns, to flying into the rocky mountains. It is quite unfortunate that Secrets of Rætikon contains so many elements that prevent a luscious experience, otherwise I probably would have loved this game.

Let me just say this first. I wanted to like this game. I REALLY wanted to like this game as I am generally a big fan of cRPGs and Pen & Paper RPGs. I have been since my dad introduced me to Divine Divinty, my first cRPG when I was nine years old.
This game, as it deals with experimental implementation, is flawed. While the core of the game (tactical combat style, real role-playing in a role-playing game which you surprisingly don't see that often, and a light-hearted and fun vibe) is very well executed, pretty much everything else (while good on a standalone level) clashes with other aspects of the game, making this game a somewhat grating experience.
Point 1: One of the main innovative aspects of the game is the true moldability of character creater, as the are no set classes. This is good. However, because of the way that the combat works, most of the default RPG builds i.e. the tank, the mage, the healer, the archer etc. are completely shattered. If you were to look online for "good starter builds" you will find dozens of posts that pretty much all have the same thing. Main 1 rouge w/ sole dex focus and craploads of damage; Madora with sole str focus, a greatsword, and leadership, doing tons of damage; Main 2 being a hydrosophist healer/ buffer with sole int focus and being able to re-cast huge healing spells every turn; and a geo/pyro murdermancer who gives Madora a damage boost and proceeds to blow everything up. Also cc. Lots and lots of cc from everyone. Without this sort of super meta-gaming, the game can be near impossibly hard on tactician or god forbid honour mode.
Point 2: Limited xp. If a cRPG is going to place a level cap that's fine. What isn't fine is making the recommened player level the highest level that they possibly be at this point. You have to do every single side-quest, find every single encounter, explore everywhere, and talk to every NPC to be on level or maybe one level above if you do literally everything.
Point 3: Do NOT use random drops AND degrading equipment in a game with only so many encounters. The three mechanics work perfectly fine alone or even with two of them in place it could make the game more challenging. But with all three of them implemented save scumming becomes an integral part of the game and blacksmthing doesn't really help cuz both it and the crafting system are usually poopy.
Point 4: For a game that is supposed to be completely free roaming, it sure is pretty linear as if you try to go anywhere except for exactly where the game is pointing you towards you immediately get into a fight and die 5 times. You know, like all good open world-esque games should be.
Point 5: Did they really need to voice act EVERYTHING? Seriously, whenever I would walk pretty much anywhere in Cyseal, I would just take my headphones off. It would be awesome if they only voiced the important characters, i.e. the PCs, the weaver of time, The Conduit etc.
Point 6: The UI in batteles can be super glitchy. When aiming for an attack, more than %20 of the time I misclick by around 5 pixels and have Bairdotr run up to the hulking whatever and die almost instantly. It's even worse if an enemy is knocked down. And because of the highly tactical and difficult nature of the game, one mess up like that and it's back to the F8 button. Again.
Final Point: In my mind there are three ways to say that a game is hard.
1. Hard: the game requires a buttload of skill and is designed around that idea (Dark Souls or Castlevania)
2. Challenging: the game requires alot of knowledge of the game, a little bit of luck, and good deal of skill (XCOM or Cuphead)
3. Difficult: the game's difficulty can be very challenging or easy on the same settings based on how much meta gaming you're willing to exploit (artificial challenge) (Civ 5 on Emperor+ or this game)
Also there's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t difficulty where a game is just broken to hell (Bubsy 3D or Sonic 06)
The latter two are problematic for the game industry as a whole.
TLDR:
- Pros:
-A fun experience with innovative, environmentally interactable comabat that encourages teamwork and character combos
-Solid writing and fantasical story (which is also kind of stupidly hilarious at the beginning because Cyseal, a fishing town, has an orc invasion, undead attacks, secret cults, demons telling people to kill themselves, Sourcerers brewing up a huge storm, a big murder mystery, the literal end of time coming from a void dragon of absolute death chaos evil destruction, and a wizard's giant lightning mech out of control all at the same exact time. How does that even happen?)
-A ton of content which almost none of seems contrived or tacked on
-Awesome soundtrack
-Actual role playing that affects who your character is
- Cons:
-Everything else
Overall I give this game a 5/10 (for my ratings 5 actually means average so yes even after all of the complaining I've done the game still has merits and is a decent game to me)
So unless you are a hardcore cRPG fan with a lot of patience and willingness to cheat the system, I would reccomend giving this game a pass.

Earth 2160... Where do I start? This game is buggy, central multiplayer server is dead (altrough direct connect still works and will most likely work forever), lots of mechanics are annoying, DRM activation works but demands your personal data...
...And despite of that, this is one of the most enjoyable, complex strategies you will ever see! I am writing this review over 10 years since the game release and it is still unbeatable when it comes to many aspects.
Let's start with factions: there are few of them and all of them are completely different - not just when it comes to most obvious things like visuals or different "game finisher" end-game units, but also the way they build the base (and not even single faction reminds typical strategy, with most familar one being UCS), recruit their units, research technologies and how their army fights. In addition (major spoiler alert)
. The biggest differences are in base building:
UCS base building look most similar to other RTS games, but all their buildings are semi-modular, meaning you can extend them with additional parts (for example, refinery can be extended with parts giving additional extractors or with storage facilities raising your population cap). Their energy network is rather crude, with power plants as separate buildings and need to build energy relays to extend the network.
ED bases are basically huge, modular buildings - complexes with multiple power generators, barracks, storage facilities, turrets etc. connected together. The only constructions that can be built disconnected from complexes are walls and turrets that can move on these walls like on rails. Energy pool of this faction is bound to single complex (but you can have more than just one).
LC philosophy is "build up, not wide": their bases tend to be relatively small compared to all other factions, you can stack most buildings on each other as long as tower is kept at sane height (if you have big towers close to each other, destruction of one will start domino effect). Their walls are made from energy walls connected with turrets, in addition attempt to fly over them will result with turret insta-killing the enemy air units with energy ray. It is the only faction with global energy pool.
Micromanagement which is very common in this game might be seen as pro or con - this is matter of preference, altrough in case of one of factions amount of micromanagement grows exponentially with game duration and quickly reaches stage in which it is very difficult to take care of everything needed.
From technical side, game have some serious flaws when it comes to pathfinding: land units have big troubles finding a path to the target, it is almost impossible to get them out of complex base, armies with different move targets will often block each other. AI don't really "know" how to play using ED faction, but can be challenging especially when playing against Morphidians, but don't really expect any surprises from it. Graphics are still relatively good for over 10 year old game, with nice looking physics and big attention to details like visual representation of damage. Music is nice, but don't expect hearing too much of it - something is wrong with music system, so it plays very rarely. Sounds are acceptable.
If you look for very good, complex RTS with base building + careful resource management and bugs/other annoyances don't scare you - then this is the game for you, especially if you have few friends to play with. If you look for something similar, but more modern and polished - trying
might be good idea (that game takes most of its gameplay elements from Earth 2160, but simplifies them and removes most of micromanagement).

This game is many things, but above all, it is delightful. The graphics aren't glorious and it doesn't have a rich story accompanied by hours of cutscenes, but it is absolutely delightful. Let me give you an idea of what I'm talking about. This game is like one of those things that I dreamed about playing when I was little. "Wouldn't it be cool if someone made a game where you could make any object appear?". I'd like to imagine the look on my 6-year-old face if I saw that, yes, someone actually made that. Granted, you can't spawn absolutely everything, but that would actually be impossible, considering that you would also need to make art for pedophiles, glockenspiels, all the members of Monty Python, rare engrams, and New York City, along with everything in the known universe. But hey! You can add adjectives!
To make things even better, this is the definitive edition of the game, in my opinion. Not only can you make your own objects by using other in-game things you can spawn and then adding scripts to them, but you can also share your creations to Steam Workshop. This is an absolute joy. Sure, you can't spawn Dragonball Z characters by default, but you can through the wonders of the Steam Community! This adds a whole new level to the game. It was enough that they let you create your own things to spawn, but the fact that they also allowed you to share and download your and other people's creations adds to the experience. I could spend hours just screwing around with this game. But of course, there is a mission mode. The missions are fun, because they force you to utilize your skill to spawn an uncountable amount of things to solve problems. This adds an element of logic to the game. Also, the music and graphics are charming, although simple.
Even though sandbox games have recently become third-person open-world games exclusively, it's still fun to partake in experiences like Scribblenauts Unlimited. Sit back and let your creativity flow.

As of this point, I am very disappointed with how this game is turning out. Yes this game is still in alpha, and they have been making pretty steady updates. But I have a feeling there will not be a lot of improvement from now until launch.
1. Graphics - The graphics are honestly not very good. Its better than something like Everquest, but its worse than Vanilla Wow, which came out 2004. The game is running on Unity 5. Unity 5 is capable of producing some nice graphics. I feel like if they weren't willing to invest in graphics, they should have kept it at an Isometric view, similar to UO. That way it wouldn't be as much of an issue. This is the part that concerns me a lot, because I doubt they are going to revamp every model and texture in the game between now and launch.
2. Sound - Sound is just ok, but that can easily be improved by launch.
3. Music - Not as good as music in the Ultima series, but its not bad either.
4. Combat - Combat is pretty bad right now. They have a unique system in where your action bar has skills randomly appear like a card game, but other than that its pretty simplistic right now. You just stand there autoattacking and hitting skills as they appear. They have plenty of time to improve this though.
Overall this does not feel like a professionally made game. It feels dated, and it hasn't even launched yet. If you are hoping for something that resembles the Ultima series or UO, don't bother with this. You won't find any of that here.

SoTA seemed promising at first, but the developers have made too may poor decisions for it to have any long term success (I'm sure the developers consider it a success since it pays their bills while they drag the alpha then beta out while continuing to create new ways to rake in funds)
:
- as a limiter of what active abilities you can have available, it feels forced and gets old very quickly.  Yes, you can turn it off and set static abilities but you are penalized.
- Immersion is completely broken when you zone in and out.   It takes very little time to explore a zone and once you've done so you feel no draw to return.    Exploration feels stymied by this.
Much of the community comes from the old UO days.   Cliques and holier-than-though attitudes are abundant.
-  Many major changes in design come about by big-dollar whale pledgers being allowed to influence priorities and direction.     Far too much designer time is spent creating custom content, cities, and fluff decor for people who have already spent and continue to spend money before the game could even be considered a game.    Half the items in the updates are usually new things you can spend money on before the game is out.   If you're not part of the big-spender in-crowd you're effectively a peasant.
-  The animations feel stiff and artificial.
Let's face it, SoTA is not a spiritual successor of UO, it's a veiled attempt by the two primary developers to monetize reminiscence and prey on the want to recapture the good old days while they attempt to stay current in a market that passed them by close to twenty years ago.

Preface:  I have 3.7 hours on the Steam version of this game, but have played the standalone more.  It likely doesn't amount to more than 8 hours total.
Bait and switch.
That about sums up how a lot of us who bought into this game feel.  There was a healthy discussion about this on the Steam forums until they were closed because of all the negativity.  When will devs learn that censorship just makes things worse for you?  Edit:
- this is exactly what I'm talking about.  The developers are begging their "loyal backers" to go out and keep conning people into buying this game and shutting down avenues of unmoderated communication (closing the forums).
This game was marketed to the Ultima Online crowd from day one.  With quotes like, "From the team who brought you Ultima Online," to all of the UO discussions, the in game property ownership, the font of the title, the crafting etc.  Slowly but surely, it fell further and further away from UO with the defense being, "no one ever said this game would be UO."  Sure, maybe no one ever said it in those words exactly, but the expectations were laid from the get go, and people heavily led to believe otherwise.
The reason this game is and will be nothing like UO is largely due to the world map feature and instancing.  Owning property in UO served as more than just a place to decorate, and location made a huge difference.  You could be out adventuring in the woods and come across someone's cabin, or heading out of Britain and come across a player made town with player owned vendors, etc.  All of this, right there in the world as you explore it.  This will not happen with Shroud of the Avatar.
Every location in Shroud is instanced.   Gone are the days of exploring around and happening across any of the things mentioned above.  Now, if you want to come across player towns, you have to zone into the areas set aside for player made towns.  The location of your property makes no difference, because you have to go to the specific instance it's in, then the location within that instanced zone.  No longer will travelers happen by your house and engage with your vendor on the fly.  This will only happen if players transition out to the world map, walk over to the player made town, enter, and look around.  As of now, the player towns serve only as a place for people to decorate and play dress up.
Speaking of playing dress up, that's the vast majority of what this game has been up to this point.  It's full grown adults playing house and dress up in game and standing around "singing" and playing pretend.  The game is a LARPers dream right now, since that's all folks seem to be doing.  Decorating houses, dressing up their characters, then standing around imagining what they're going to be doing when the game is finished, and giving tours of the player made towns (that have nothing to do other than look at people's houses).  I'm going to guess the reason this is happening is because even after 18 updates, the combat is still awful.
That's right, 18 updates, and still complete garbage combat.  The deck system is just plain bad, the combat is dull and there seems to be no reason to get into it, the story is still miles from done, and the gameplay is just not engaging whatsoever.  Granted, the devs say they are aware of this and are working to fix it, but take that for what it's worth: not much considering the game has seen so many updates and is still not fun to play.  Add to these facts that the animations are also bad, it just makes for a very bad time.  For many builds now, male characters appear to be running like an obese guy out for the first jog of his life (his arms hanging and flapping from his shoulders, looking like it's all he can do to keep from falling apart).  I would think a great adventurer, or Avatar, would be in better shape than that.
Overall, this game feels like a bait and switch.  Talk about UO, lead people to believe the next UO is coming, then push out ... whatever this is.  Shutting down the Steam forums because of negativity won't change that fact, either.  That kind of move just provokes people like me to write a review so people are aware of what's really going on here, when I likely wouldn't have otherwise.
Fool me once Richard Garriot (Tabula Rasa) shame on me, fool me twice... well, at least it won't be a third time.

Ah Fallout 3....... While my log for this game on steam doesn't speak much for it, I have played this game for well over 1000  hours on the xbox 360 version.  This was the game that got me into RPGs and one that still has a very special place in my heart and memories.  From all the different easter eggs and references to the witty dialogue, loveable characters, and vast, yet beautiful game world, this game has many awesome characteristics.  While some things haven't aged well, this game is very much like a fine wine in my opinion.
For gameplay a lot of the good things have already been listed in the paragraph above. While the shooting mechanics are nothing special the rest of the combat is rather enjoyable. You will laugh at killing your enemies with teddy bears shot from the rock-it-launcher, gaze in awe as you blast stuff with mini nukes, and hang on the edge of your seat as you fight for your life against a world full of mutants, monsters, and organizations that want nothing more than to see your bloody and mangled corpse on the ground.  The look and feel of the game is great. Dated graphics aside, its easy to get lost looking at the different scenery that this game has to offer, and the game does a good job in immersing you into the world regardless of if you are in a dark, rundown subway tunnel or walking through bombed out ruins of Washington DC.
While there are many good things about this game it does have it's flaws. For some odd reason this game doe not play well out of the box on windows 7 and up, and doesn't doe well with multithreading. This is nothing to be to concerned with as there are plenty of guides and ways to fix this. Second the main story is somewhat bland and not that long in itself. This is quite the letdown considering considering how many top quality actors Bethesda has voicing the main characters in this game. Your dad is voiced by Liam Neeson for god sake! And that talent is largely wasted as most of his presence in the game is during the beginning during your time in Vault 101. The main quest could have easily been longer and more detailed to allow talent of that caliber to really shine through and carry this game to the next level.
But the biggest problems with the game are the ones that have always been present in Bethesda games. This game is loaded with bugs, of the official patches this game had many of the bugs they tried to fix still happened. This can unfortunately be linked to this game being rushed out the door, half finished, by the urging of Bethesda's lawyer run, parent company Zenimax. Just like Morrowind, Oblivion, New Vegas, Skyrim, and Fallout 4. They have been doing to Bethesda what EA has done to Dice and Bioware(Among many others.lol) and Microsoft and Sega have done to Rare and Creative Assembly, for over a decade now. The AI is also TERRIBLE at times. I won't go into detail on this however, as it will just turn into a very long rant. Just take my word for it.
With all of the base game stuff out of the way I would like to highlight one very important aspect, and the main reason I believe pc is the only way to for Bethesda games. There are mods for basically everything you can think of for this game!   Minus the bugs with the game engine, most of the bugs have been stomped out by an unofficial patch made by the modding community. The graphics have been largely updated by more than a few mods as well. New quests have been added, new weapons have been made, and entire gameplay mechanics have been overhauled! Most of all there are still mods coming out for this game and many of the older ones are still supported and updated by their authors!
Seriously, buy this game! It won game of the year for a reason and it shows even today.  Just remember the limitations of the tech at the time this game was made compared to now.

Player population low(?), but you can play most (all?) the content solo. Re: bullet sponges - difficulty scales (read: enemy armor/hp) with each additional player in your group. A full five? Enemy hp scales into the stratosphere. Incompetent teammates make that scale feel sharper than it really is.
Playing solo, enemies aren't bullet sponges if you play smart - don't waste time blind-firing into torsos and decide early how you're going to prioritize your build. Identify and terminate enemy combatant types (CQC, snipers, and grenadiers, in order of priority) whenever you start an engagement. If you're running between locations, always watch out for random spawns and don't let yourself get flanked. Kite elite enemies after clearing their lackeys.
Regarding player build, I prioritized Firepower first, Stamina second.  I also tended to ignore the flashy DPS number in favor of weapons with high per-hit damage. Combined with utilizing cover, maintaining range, and focusing on headshots - or my LMG/assault rifle in CQC - I haven't had any problem with non-elite enemies. Efficacy of ARPG abilities depend on your build and how intentional you are about your choices - like everything else.
Content itself is repetative like any ARPG. It's been engaging enough for me running around grabbing collectibles between missions - ESPECIALLY at level 15+, because groups of armored enemies with elite leaders start showing up at random as you roam, and if you're ill prepared it becomes an ordeal. Dark zone is interesting - read some guides so you understand how it works before jumping into it. Spent my first hour there tonight, enjoyed it immensely.
As far as I can see the majority of microtransactions are for vanity items, with 3 convenience, 'minimize your grinding' benefit items. I feel no pressure to purchase those, though, because I enjoy the base game and the grind doesn't feel like much of a grind to me. Maybe I have bad taste, though.
