Basically, this game is what I wanted Clash Royale to be.
Minion Masters offers a similar "tug of war" gameplay to Clash Royale in which players summon creatures and play spells into two lanes in an attempt to push forward to take out the enemy Master (= King). However, as compared to Clash Royale, Minion Masters has both more strategic depth and a much more player-friendly business model.
There is a lot to like about this game, but I think what I like best is how well the developers have done at differentiating the various Masters. Each player has a Master who stands on a fixed base at the back of the arena and has a different basic attack to defend itself. (Some Masters have generic basic attacks, others are strong against certain types of enemies -- e.g. AOE attack vs Swarms -- but weaker against other foes.) Additionally, each Master has three special abilities that have a significant impact on both deck-building and gameplay. Basically, the goal of deck-building is to maximize the synergy that you have with your Master's abilities (while still making sure you have answers to the threats you expect to face).
With regards to the business model, the game features a model where units and spells are represented by cards. Cards have different rarities, and the game is generous with giving you the currency you need to acquire random cards. Like many games that feature cards there is a "crafting" system that allows you to destroy cards you don't want (or have extras of) in order to create the cards you want or need. The two things that really make the business model player-friendly are: (1) the generousity with regards to cards and currency; and (2) the power-level of common cards. Many games that use rarity-based systems have high-rarity cards that are strictly more useful/powerful than lower-rarity cards. In Minion Masters, the lower-rarity cards are shockingly useful in a variety of decks and don't get overshadowed by higher-rarity cards.  There are certainly opportunities to build synergy-heavy decks with an assortment of high-rarity cards, but you can also build a deck with lower-rarity cards and do very well. Essentially, high-rarity cards are more specialized and niche -- and can be useful with the right synergies -- but don't seem to have more raw power.

Reus is a puzzle game about placing objects in a line to create synergies, providing resources for towns.  It is not a strategy game, and it is not quite a god game; it is a puzzle game.  The major flaw seems to be that every action needs to be premeditated; if you don't keep track of every single item that the giants can create (and in what contexts the item can exist), you can't create enough resources for the towns to progress.  The game seems to be best played with a piece of paper detailing all the important synergies in order to be able to place the very few successful combinations that can get you to advance.  Without an incredible supply of patience and a taste for puzzle games, the game simply isn't all that enjoyable.

==========
The metroidvania subgenre has seen a lot of success in the past. Metroidvania (named for the 2 games that the term originates from: Metroid and Castlevania) games have very specific qualities and features that define it. The biggest of which is an expansive, inter-connected map. Other features includes secrets hidden everywhere, and progression being affected by new, unlockable abilities. They usually involve action-platformer elements as well. Ori and the Blind Forest perfectly fits all these criteria, and is one beautiful yet extremely challenging game.
==========
Ori and the Blind Forest features a fantastic story, and you will most likely be moved to tears within the first few minutes. A quick (spoiler-free) rundown is as follows: The voice of the Spirit Tree in the forest of Nibel serves as the narrator, and the story begins when Ori fell from the tree during a storm as a newborn and was adopted by a sasquatch-like creature named Naru, who raised Ori as her own. After a series of events, Ori later meets Sein, a being who both guides Ori on his adventure and attacks enemies. In order to restore the forest, Sein guides Ori to recover the light of three main elements supporting the balance of Nibel: Waters, Winds and Warmth.
Typical gameplay plays out like a platformer, with Ori learning new abilities as you explore and progress through the forest. Double-jumps, wall jumps, and more are all skills you will acquire and more than likely have to master if you wish to survive. There are enemies, shadow creatures, and more around every corner. And with Sein by your side, you have a way to defend yourself. At the press of a button Sein can fire off what's called Spirit Flames, which can be gradually upgraded with Skill Points. Skill points are earned when you collect a certain number of Spirit Light, which are dropped by defeated enemies or found hidden in dark corners of the forest. Skill points can be invested in 3 different skill trees, and you can spread points across all 3 trees if you wish.
Ori has a few simple stats, which are upgraded by finding collectable power-ups: Life and Energy. Life is, well, how many hits Ori can take before dying. Energy is used to fuel certain abilities, such as creating a Soul Link (used to save your game and spend skill points), Charge Flame, and more. Defeating enemies and destroying certain objects in the forest can replenish both life and energy.
==========
Ori and the Blind Forest is a stunning game. It reminded me of Child of Light a lot. The backgrounds and foregrounds are very detailed, seemless, and flow smoothly as Ori traverses different sections of the forest. Speaking of sections, each one looks a bit different. Some are green and vibrant, filled with plantlife. While others are dark and dreary, covered with briars and the like. The cutscenes and character models are extremely well animated and polished. Everything concerning the looks of the game are nearly perfect. I couldn't find any flaws it in whatsoever. It's simply gorgeous.
==========
The music is hauntingly beautiful, almost spiritual, and that is made apparent the instant the menu screen comes up. In some areas it's ambient and soothing. In others it is desperate and tense, and usually fiting the theme of each section of the forest. The sound effects are crisp and fitting. Spirit Flame destroying enemies, jumping off walls, running across lush vegetation...all sounds great. I have no complaints about the sound or music in this game. There's simply nothing to critisize here!
==========
Ori ran at a very healthy 60FPS at all times on my mid-tier custom-built rig, during cutscenes and normal gameplay. I experienced no stuttering or lag at any point. No slowdowns, and skipping, and no random crashes or freezes.
The game has full controller support, which is *almost* a must for this game. Sometimes it requires precise button presses and platforming, which is made a lot easier with a controller. I didn't even try any other control schemes, as my controller worked so well.
==========
Ori and the Blind Forest is one of the most beautiful and challenging games I have ever played. It shines in nearly all aspects, and is what I consider a near-perfect game. Lots of platforming, puzzles, and enemies to overcome make this a fulfilling Metroidvania title, and one that everyone should at least give a try. If anything, at least experience the opening story segments. If that hooks you, you are in for a wonderful ride.

Fallout 3: Game of the Year Edition is my 200th game review, it is also the first in a trilogy of Fallout games released since 2005, which are a continuation of the original Fallout series for the PC. Fallout 3 takes us to Vault 101, where you play as a male/female character of your choice who leaves the vault to search for their father. Along the way you encounter struggling towns, various NPC's, complete quests, explore, and dungeon delve buildings, ruins, and other vaults as you progress through the story.
Fallout 3 is a First Person RPG where you interact with your environment and engage in FPS-style combat with enemies. It has an impressive list of voice actors and an immersive story that pulls you into the world of the Post-Apocalyptic Capital Wasteland, essentially the ruins of what was once Washington, DC. Fallout 3 was a blast to play on the PS3, as well as the PC and spawned 2 sequels which take place after the events of 3. If you enjoy post-apocalyptic games as well as FPS combat and RPG's, I recommend picking this game up and giving it a try. The Game of the year edition comes with all 5 DLC's included, so make sure you pick up this particular edition to get the full Fallout experience. Don't forget to tune into Galaxy News Radio, and everyone's favorite disk jockey, Three Dog, for some memorable dialogue and music.

Be warned that the game is short, so depending on how much you value 3 or 4 hours of gameplay, that should dictate how much you want to pay or wait for a sale. I completed this game in one sitting, and that was probably best, to enable me to really get into the story and keep going (and once you’ve started you want to finish – be warned before you start!).  There’s not much to actually do in the game apart from point and click around a pre-defined route, collecting objects, analysing a bit of scenery, and talking with various characters.  There are a few mini games built into the story, for example, fairly simple puzzles you can complete in a few clicks, horse riding, a scrolling platform where you can walk against ‘zombies’ and fire some plants at them!
BUT – The positives are a fairly well-designed storyline, and a decent sound track.  The story had me questioning my life and philosophy – why do some people achieve ambitions while others live to have regrets near death? Does getting to your goal matter, or is it the precessional life events via getting to the goal that happen that really matter?  If I took just one simple decision differently, would that have a dramatic impact on life? Why do people cling to ‘momentos’, and does a link of momentos go to make a life story? It’s interesting that the patient can’t see forward in life to see the ‘mistakes’ in the actions he’s taking, but the scientists can view his life backwards, going to his nearest memories first and working back.  They can start to piece together how he ended up where he did and why he wants to go to the moon (and the reason will keep you guessing throughout).
The twist in the middle of the story is heart wrenching.  It’s just something you don’t want to see in a game and anyone playing it would be cold hearted not to cry.  How many games can give that emotional reaction?
While this is based on sci-fi technology, some of the end story does not make sense to me – I thought the scientists would grant a real life wish? But the wish appears to be granted only in thoughts, like a dream?  No matter what the scientists do to change his life direction, you know the man’s reality was very different, and what he had to endure was pretty sad.
The graphics are fairly basic, reminds me of games made decades ago.  But the game does fit within a few hundred MB so is a relatively quick download.  The game also has only one achievement – to complete the story.  Perhaps a few achievements could have been added around the mini games (complete the games in the minimum number of moves?).  To counter though, steam trading cards are available.
Worth a try if you like emotionally driven linear stories where you have to reflect on life, without freedom to deviate from the story.  If you don't like this, you may get bored.

To the Moon is great if you want to spend 4 hours or so crying. And giggling, sometimes. But mostly crying.

It comes with 2 DLC minisodes, but that's approximately 30-40 minutes of extra content and both of them are teasers. Neither of them are very profound. They just hint at big questions that--I assume--are going to be revealed in the sequel.
I got it on sale for $2.49, which is *perfect* for this amount of content. $10 seems a little steep for 3 hours of game + 2 teasers, but you might find it worthwhile if you're looking for a good, tearful story about life.

About the only criticisms that can be made are that the game can be a bit anime-fanboy-crude, with emphasis on fan service with breasts and scantily-clad females, but the actual characterizations of the female characters are well-done, so if you can look past the lewdness, it's really not bad in that regard. The other thing is some battles can get a bit long and repetitive. Most of the time, combat can be over quickly if you're paying attention to your elemental damage, but then sometimes you'll be up against an enemy that has a ton of health, and while the enemy doesn't pose a huge threat to you, it takes a long time to kill. Still, a few battles turning into a bit of a slog isn't that big an issue, either.
Overall, it's funny and well-written and the gameplay is just an absolute charm. There are a lot of elements between the equips and elements and consumables and upgrading of items, but none of these elements are overly complex to the point where thye become annoying. It's easy to find almost any piece of information you want, and the gane doesn't penalize you too heavily for forgetting to attend to any of the ongoing tasks.
A solid installment in a solid series, heartily recommended to anyone who enjoys RPGs, anime style, humor, or casual gaming experiences. Not that the game is overly casual, but it's so easy to learn, it's a great gateway into RPGs for the casual gamer.

I will probably date myself in this review, but I've been an avid fan of the Ultima games, including those from the NES and SNES and even starting back at Ultima 1. The Ultima series is what really got me to get into PC gaming. Up until now there has only been Ultima Online, which while old, is still going strong. When news of SotA being developed I was extremely excited. A world like UO, but in 3D? Sold!
Reading over many of the reviews, the good and bad, I'm not quite sure what people were expecting or assumed they were getting, but I'm not displeased at all with what the game is now and what it will become in the future. Currently on R18, I have been playing it on and off since it was first made available for players to join (before any Steam release) and the game has come a long way. Are there issues? Of course! Is something broken or not working right? Yup! Its an EA title for a reason. The game is in development and is not a finished product.
Another aspect is, this isn't your standard MMORPG type game. It doesn't give you pretty path markers or detailed directions on where to go. It doesn't give you a carriage to ride along in to your destination so you can complete that quest. You are told to go speak to this person at this town and give them this or do that. You talk to other NPCs or even ask another player on where to find the person and you head out on your way.
Recalling some users mentioning there was a lack of class system or similar, from what I can tell, that is correct because you develop your skills as you see fit to make your character yours, not some typical mage or warrior. There is a skill tree that you spend your points into that you get as you level. Each branch has its own perks and abilities.
So many other things about this game are appealing, from its interesting and complex crafting system all the way to housing that isn't hidden away in some instance, it is definitely a game that can keep you interested whether is be by crafting, fighting, PvP or just wandering and collecting items and trinkets for your home.
The game style may not appeal to everyone, and in my opinion its still got a long ways to be completed, but the promise is there and the features are coming if they haven't already.

Okay, wow.  The ending to this game is the most egregious bullcrap I've seen in years.  Never mind the thing everyone complains about -- to get there you're forced to be deliberately evil in a way that goes entirely against the gameplay it's been enouraging the whole time (what with returning bird-eggs to their nests and such).  And then, once the game's finished kicking your face, it rubs it in by emphasizing how unfun and petty your reward for your actions is.  So whatever point the dev was trying to make gets crushed under the weight of "Congratulations, you're an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥!"
This is a statement that works for, say, the ending of the genocide run of Undertale — and the reason "Congratulations, you're an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥!" works there is that it's a reflection of deliberate gameplay choices the player made over the course of their game experience, and it's possible to make other choices which don't reach that point.  It is NOT a statement that works here, because the game is 100% linear.  Aside from a single hidden-objects sidequest which gets you a powerup, everything you're doing from the time you start playing is building up to that reversal.  It only took me a couple of hours to finish, but if I'd known in advance that the game was going to call me an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ for my investment of time, I wouldn't have bothered.
It's certainly gorgeous, which is the nicest thing I can say about it.  The gameplay is generally fun, but with its own share of frustrations.  A required gameplay element -- being able to reassemble shattered statues -- is never explained nor even hinted.  There's a lot of trial and error in your interactions with hostile fauna.  The lack of a map was annoying, and the runes you pick up merely serving as a "key" means that I was decoding the story tablets at the start of the game (figuring them out from context) and the end of the game (comparing them to the key) with equal slowness; would it have killed them to sub in discovered letters on the tablet for easier reading?
So, yeah.  An ambitious game with some good points, which left a very sour taste in my mouth relative to time spent.  Ugh.

Released in 2014, Secrets of Raetikon is a 2D adventure puzzle game created by Austrian developer Broken Rules. Set in an uncharted area of the Alpine mountain range, players assume the role of a native bird who uncovers the remains of an ancient civilisation.
Secrets of Raetikon uses an open world environment with a heavy emphasis on exploration, item collection and puzzle solving. The primary objective is to retrieve seven mysterious shard fragments and return them to a central location. Each piece is protected by a combination of hostile wildlife, hazardous surroundings and environmental based puzzles.
In theory the game world is open plan, allowing the player to free roam and collect shard fragments in any order they like. However in practice, the routes you take often require you to complete a puzzle before you can proceed further, which ultimately results in a much more linear gameplay experience. There is no in-game map so players must keep track of their route themselves.
Secrets of Raetikon uses a simple control scheme and your bird protagonist handles responsively enough. It does a particularly good job at conveying a sense of flying by utilising wide open aerial spaces and wind currents to help propel you faster through the sky. There are hostile animals which present some light combat elements, but there is more of a focus on evasion and retaliation through indirect means.
There is a decent amount of interactivity built into the game world. The puzzles revolve around physics based gameplay, usually requiring you to manipulate a mechanism or assemble a statue in a jigsaw piece fashion. These concepts initially feel quite novel and satisfying to solve, however they really are quite simplistic and do become a bit repetitive by the end.
Graphically is where Secrets of Raetikon truly shines. It uses a 2D polygonal art style which has a paper craft / origami look to it. It combines bold shapes with strikingly vivid colours to create a genuinely unique and appealing aesthetic. The game also conveys a good sense of scale by occasionally panning the camera angle back to reveal large background canvases set against your tiny protagonist. The soundtrack also deserves an honourable mention as it provides some nice instrumental tracks which help provide a theme to each territory.
With regards to storyline, there is no real overarching plot. The only slight hints at lore are presented in the form of rune stones which are written in a coded language. Runic letters are hidden throughout the game which will enable you to transcribe the cyphers. However, these rune stones reveal so little in the way of story that it becomes a large investment for such a small return. The ending scene is also an enormous disappointment, the tone of which feels counter intuitive to everything else portrayed in the game.
Overall, Secrets of Raetikon is an entertaining enough game with highlights in its art style and soundtrack. It is a short diversion which should only take a few hours to complete. It does have some definite flaws and weaknesses which are hard to overlook but I personally feel that there is still enough enjoyable content here to warrant a positive recommendation.

I like the game, I like the concept, I like the gameplay, and I like the price. I would buy this game in a heartbeat if it weren't for a couple of little things. It seems really unbalanced for the sharks and here's why:
Divers can just camp in small rooms and guard the entrances. There needs to be a longer period where the bot is vulnerable outside of rooms because even though you can break certain sections of wall or doors or windows as the shark any experienced diver will know which segments can be broken and they will just corner camp with guns.
The Shark is very hard to aim at Divers. Coupled with the fact that most divers will corner camp or sit right around doors or behind alcoves this makes it very difficult to actually score hits on divers, made even worse by the fact that the divers are always together and will simply focus you down with high level weapons. You are basically a sitting duck if you enter a room at all.
The Shark/Diver ratio is unbalanced considering how fragile the Sharks are. You can kill a Shark with just a few shots from different guns and since there are only 2 Sharks and 4 Divers it's very hard and takes a lot of skill on the Shark's part to actually win games.
All in all I love this game and it's a lot of fun playing as the Shark, but the game's mechanics could use some work. I expected a fast pace predator-esque experience as the Shark and a horror-esque experience as the Diver, but what I ended up with is a campy experience as the Diver and really irritating controls as the Shark.
I'm glad I got it on the free demo because I'd definitely be refunding it.

"How the mighty have fallen", said Pius Augustus to Mantorok. I think the same applies here. The first FEAR was a "visceral" FPS, offering an honest challenge and a great atmosphere. FEAR2 was much less horror, more streamlined, but still OK.
Alas, a common plague in the video game industry is the need to make trilogies, when it's uncalled for or there is not enough substance for it- or both.
F3AR falls in this category. Sure, the fate of Alma was still hanging after the end of the previous game, but this one has nothing to tell. Story has not to be the strong point of a FPS, but when it's that shallow, it impacts the game itself.
F3AR is very short (5 to six hours) with only 8 levels, two of wich are fillers (the store after the first crash, the bridge after the second crash) and the last is an dream-like stage, glorified string of mini-cutscenes culminating with the destruction of Harlan Wade (wich, of course, is a giant abomination with a glowing weak point).
So the only goal is to rejoin Alma whose psychic contractions are bringing doom to Fairport and its surroundings. F3AR fails what I like to call the Teleportation Test : when a story can be resolved with just the protagonist(s) being teleported to a certain location.
And it's exactly the case with F3AR. There is no need for character development, nothing to seek or activate, nothing to accomplish really, just go see Mother. Jin (who, because Plot, is now dear to Pointman's heart ?) is just needed to pinpoint a certain location and is discaded afterwards.
Now, of course, all this could be forgiven with brilliant gameplay. No such luck here. Using Pointman's slow-mo power is still fun, but kinda loses its edge after two games. Weaponry doesn't have anything outstanding, apart maybe for the impaler thingie, and even using mechas is not as fun as it could be.
The level-design is dull and makes for a very, very linear progression. Of course you gather ammo, otherwise, the only things to seek are corpses to "consume"... For points. Doing certain feats (headshots...) also grant you points, and every now and then you will "level-up" to gain new skills (that you can't choose, of course).
If you play in co-op, points also determine who will be the favorite son, hence deciding the ending. The first player is Pointman, the other one is Fettel, who can blast psychic rays and possess people, giving a bit more fun. This co-op option is a good thing, because I sincerely think it's the only way to get some real enjoyment from the game.
As far as I tried, multiplayer is dead and the campaign has little to no replay value.
My advice ? If you want a few laughs, wait for a -75% discount, find a friend to play it with during a rainy afternoon and call it a day.

Stronghold Kingdoms is a passable game if you like building villages and castles, along with some strategic warfare.
It is a multiplayer game which you play online against other people in real time.
It is based upon a map of the world, which is divided up into kingdoms and provinces. You can choose an area for your base, and then build a castle. You can remain as an independent player, or join an alliance.
However, you will discover that - if you really want to play the game properly (and not have your castle taken over or destroyed by enemies) - you have to play the game pretty much every day, which is a big ask.
I enjoyed the building up aspects of Stronghold Kingdoms; the military aspects were OKish; but once I realised that the game is based upon the notion that you are committed to play the game every day, then I started to get over it pretty fast.
By the way, the game has achievements, although they are not linked to Steam.
Apparently, the game can be pay-to-win (you can buy extra abilities for short periods); however, I haven't noticed that aspect being too obvious (although it may not be too apparent, as you can win extra abilities, so you wouldn't know if your castle was being beseiged by someone who had paid for extras or not).
Whilst I have logged a lot of hours on this game, the actual number of hours playing the game were a lot less than actually logged - as Stronghold Kingdoms is a small programme which can run in the background whilst you are doing other things on your computer (as buildings can take hours to construct, increasing each time you finish another building, I would swap to Stronghold Kingdoms every hour or two, click on a couple of items, and then swap back to whatever else I was doing on the computer).
So, if there are wider statistics available on how many hours people have been playing Stronghold Kingdoms, those statistics may be a vast over-estimation of actual hours of game play.
I can recommend this game for people who like strategy games, but only if they want to commit to playing almost every day for months on end.
If you don't want that sort of commitment, then I recommend you don't play it.
However, it's a free game, so no big loss if you play it for a few weeks, and then walk away from it.

Reus is an casual and original god-game. You use four giants to terraform the earth, which will then be populated by villages. Those villages in turn give you quests, which on completion grant you acces to more terraform capability, wildlife and plants after you complete achievements and finish playtroughs. You need this increasing diversity to meet the late-game quest demands, which are quite steep. This is also perhaps my main problem with the game. Early on it is quite casual, but once you progress towards higher-tier quests, the synergies you need to plan get so complicated that you almost need spreadsheets. And if that's your thing, then obviously go for it. However, if you let the game lie for a couple of weeks, remembering and reworking trough all the complex synergies against the clock late-game can become quite frustrating. So after let's say 10 or 15 games there is a discrepency between the audience the game targets, and the math involved to succesfully complete an era.
Super addicting if you are into games that let you creat wolrds and govern over them, like minecrat and civilization.

Having never written a game review on steam, while having over four thousand hours in tf2, csgo, and similar games, Let it be a point that I almost never feel the need to review a game. However I felt it was necessary to make an exception for skullgirls, I havnt played many fighter games aside from the soul calibur series, a little mortal kombat, and the many games at local arcades. But Skullgirls had a feel none of the others did, every fighter has its flaws, most feel too floaty, and weightless, some are too easily won with button mashing, some just lack depth, Skullgirls on the other hand felt "bouncy" which is in no way a flaw, You feel the snap back of someone hitting the floor after a combo, the models dont spin through the air after every kick, and the hit animations are detailed almost to compliment this trait, certain details show how serious they are about making quality over quantity.
The best example of this artwork wise are two of the playable characters, Peacock and Double. Watching them frame by frame shows detail after detail, and the hitboxes after recent beta updates have been tighter than ever, Effort was put into this, The creators arent just hungry for cash, Theyre strapping in to make some real deal business here.
the combo system is intricate and balanced, with far and few kinks, that are being tweaked and tweaked in the beta,
If you dont intend to play the storyline, and just want to fight with your friends, Always try the beta first, It may have new content compared to the final version.

Skullgirls is a 2D fighter that takes a lot of excellent elements from several classic Capcom games and creates a comfortable-feeling fighting game, where if you have played fighting games before, you probably know how to play this game. It will immediately enchant you with it's beautiful art and well-detailed characters and animation, or may immediately turn you off because it's a fighting game with a bunch of anime girls.
It has a quick (but not zany) pace, and each character not only feels unique from each other, but some ideas and styles are explored in this game that just aren't present in any other fighting game. For instance, one fighter (Ms. Fortune) can throw her head off, and you can attack with it, while still retaining control of your body to attack from two places at once. Also, this game has a very forgiving combo system that makes you able to pull off lots of varied strings of multi-move combos to make you really feel like you are giving your opponent a beat down.
All-in-all, a worthy fighting game to own, and it exemplifies the concept of easy to learn, hard to master.

This is a fun game and I would recommend it, but there are 3 things you should know before you buy.
1) You're in for a Super-Slow Start
The first few hours of the game are poorly explained (fighting, leveling, etc) and you're stuck in a giant town of bland quests. Expect a restart or two. If you're not down for that kind of early game shlog, then don't buy this.
2) There Are Many Chores
Laborious inventory management, a boring crafting mechanic and the endless struggle to pick up dropped loot. This game is very polished in some ways, but has plenty of procedural hang ups that could have easily been ironed out.
3) It's Pretty Goofy
The trailer doesn't give you any sense of the game's actual tone. It is not a serious fantasy story. It's much more akin to Fable with cartoonish accents, wacky characters and many moments that break the medieval fantasy 4th-wall. If that's your thing, then you'll love it, but I just spam through the silly dialogue.

"Are you sure", he asked.
I took a deep breath and started typing.
"Yes, I am. I know, I know, I have a huge backlog and I want you to buy me Game of The Year edition that will probably swallow hundreds of my hours that I don't have if I don't give up."
Soon enough, Fallout 3 GOTY landed in my library.
I consider myself to be a completionist, however, my work and habits prove I've become more of a collector. I was happy to get Fallout 1, Fallout 2 and Fallout Tactics on GOG for free when they were removing them from their library back in 2013. Then I've replayed Fallout 1 and started playing Fallout 2, creating character named after my daughter. I've stopped middle game and decided to return later (never did, but I will probably at some point). Same friend that got me Fallout 3 GOTY gifted me Fallout: New Vegas that I also didn't complete, but I've used to justify my laziness as 'my own plan to play the series in chronological order'. So of course, when I got GOTY, I was stuck and needed to deliver - at least to myself.
Fallout 3 GOTY stands independent of the other titles in the series. It was Bethesda's revolutionary change of perspective. Instead of old isometric view, Bethesda went with first person, immersing playerbase even deeper in 50's inspired postapocalyptic nuclear wasteland. We went upclose and personal with mankind's ♥♥♥♥ed up end.
To make a long story short and to avoid any spoilers, your main mission in F3 is to find your dad who left Vault 101. That requires exiting the Vault yourself for the first time in your life. Your first encounter with other humans and their pitiful destinies will probably happen in the city of Megatron from where your adventure will explode in every single direction possible. It is hard to describe Fallout 3 properly in short form. However, if we say we're having an unbeliveable, mature, choice-and-consequence heavy RPG title that sometimes intentionally goes silly and offers almost unlimited freedom along sidequests more complex and interesting than the main questline, we wouldn't go wrong.
F3 GOTY comes packed with base game and additional DLC materials that will make you chase ghouls, mutants and raiders for tens and hundreds of hours, even in military virtual reality program. Its rich lore, interesting characters and unexpected plot twists here and there, along with the possibility to drive the game your way based on your choices is what makes it so appealing. It's hard not to enjoy sounds of rustling wind in the outskirt of devastated Washington DC. Letting go and losing yourself in loneliness of human misery never felt this good.
Game fails a bit short in the shooting section. Hit detection is appearantly offset to simulate RPG system of risk and chance, luckily for us, F3 integrated V.A.T.S. queuing system that lets you hack the enemies to pieces, cripple their limbs and create some dramatic fighting scenes, all based on some sophisticated dice rolling.
But, here comes the big but(t). It's silly to recommend Steam's version of Fallout 3 GOTY. Simply, it doesn't work.
I was informed of several issues that Windows 7, 8 and 10 users were complaining about before I've decided to play the game. But how severe these problems are, I had no idea. My hours in the game were characterized by random crashes, sound and graphic problems and unbeliveable glitches. I've tried it all - vanilla play, unofficial and official patches, different and recommended high rated Nexus mods, uninstalls and reinstalls, LOOT launcher installation. Latest problem occured literally out of nowhere. After 3 hours of installing and reinstalling drivers from different sources and ultimately completely messing up my display settings without being able to run the game, I've decided to quit.
I feel sad and angry. Fallout 3 is, in the end and as much as I've managed to play, a great, great, loveable game. However, Bethesda's ultimate and insolent refusal to patch this gem is the reason why you shouldn't get it. Chances you will end up with good game badly broken are pretty high and that's something not worth risking. There are no excuses for not fixing what can be fixed, especially when almost 20 years old original and sequel are running flawlessly on modern systems.

Ultima was the first game series that really got me into PC gaming. And since then, was one of the last that I have played that gave the player the opportunity to really feel part of the world they are playing in. From decisions impacting your virtues, the story being so well written and involving, to almost everything you see being intractable, and so many ways to progress through the story, the Ultima games always quickly became a way to lose track of time and enjoy every moment.
So far, the potential to relive my Ultima experiences are showing with SotA. Like any Alpha/early release game, much is still coming, being tweaked, and being added. But I can already see so much potential. It had been fun completing the monthly tour quests, and following the updates from the development teams. Even though I might only play a day or two a month (it's still young,) I am always fascinated and intrigued by the upgrades and improvements added to the game with every update!
I am excited to see where the combat system goes. I have played so many online games (SotA can be Multi or Single player) that I am relieved to see a new way to master combat being handled. I have enjoyed testing the deck system, and like the ability to combine abilities together for a stronger or variation of either attack alone.
I wouldn't put too much weight into it yet, but the conversation system is also a breath of fresh air (again, we are in Alpha - meat is still being put on the bone, but the mechanics are working.) This mechanic is a lost tradition that I fear we will not see in many games in the future. The fact that you get to choose exactly what you say to NPC's opposed to picking from "canned responses" is fun and more involving. It also makes the story much richer. I like how it ties into progression of "quests" you can receive as well - as the story is something you are wise to get involved in, ask more questions to NPC's to learn more, etc. There are no "floating !'s and ?'s (thank god.) Instead, you have a journal that records short notes about conversations to remind you (the player) about what is going on. The use of these notes and personal memories from conversations / actions / other quests to further the story and explore the world make you feel more involved, and makes the world feel more alive!
(Not into the story side? No worries. You can click through conversations so far as well. However, while you may be able to progress a main story, you may have different outcomes, or miss many other opportunities when you choose not to lose yourself in the details!)
Keep up the great work Portalarium! I am looking forward to this quality game! (I am long overdue for a quality experience!)

Bugs abound. But since its Early Access, thats to be expected.
UI needs more work.
Need more tooltips.
Character animation is somewhat choppy, but serviceable.
Tutorial seems outdated.
If the overworld map could show which areas contained which plants/ores/vegetables available to harvest, that would be great. Currently just relying on writing down which area has what raw materials.
Summary: Basic features are there, but needs a great deal of polish. Portalarium claims Beta will be mid-2015 and that is possible, just difficult for a non-employee to see how. I recommend waiting for their Beta release or full release before deciding whether or not to buy in.

I played for a bit on Free weekend, so take my review with a grain of salt. This game is good fun if you like bullet sponge rpg's, so consider this a 'recomended' review if you are looking for that.
Pros:
The open world is very large, and puts Destiny to shame with it's four tiny planet themed maps. There's no loading screens between going from the open world, to being in a social space, or a pvp area.
It's pretty, and has a good options menu
The world has a high level of visual detail, with nice snow effects, and cubemapped interiors for the various towers around the city.
The matchmaking is fast, and you can jump into any mission you have unlocked/completed using the map.
Cons:
I experienced some big stuttering issues when walking around the city sometimes, I don't know if it was caused by network problems, or loading problems.
U-play account needed, and U-play installed to play this game.
The game is always online, even if you just want to play through the story just by yourself. My internet service went down on my first session just after I finished the tutorial area, and the game disconnected during a cutscene. It was frozen, so I had to alt-tab and force the game to close.
There are no options for changing the field of view either, as far as I could tell. I would have prefered it wider, but it wasn't too narrow like MGS:V.
The story and cutscenes are terrible, and you wont care about any of the characters in the game. It is a very impersonal story experience, the typical "you are special" but "you are just 1 of a million other characterless, voiceless online players" that these always online shooter games go for.
The level design just isn't interesting to me. Because this game is a ground-based cover shooter, every encounter feels decidedly two dimensional, which is fine if the gameplay is fast and hectic, but here you are putting ten+ pistol shots into an enemies face until he finally drops dead.
The game is basically just you running around, doing missions and shooting enemies with your weapons, in order to get new guns with slightly better stats to keep doing it over and over again.
For me the game just wasn't satisfying to play, mostly due to the way the game punishes strategy and tactics, but rewards mindless grinding for better weapons. So then people who waste their time grinding away will get bored because of how easy it is and how long they have had to play, and people who want a challenge that makes them think on their feet will get annoyed at how impossible the game is.
This game is garbage and a waste of time. I was lied to and denied a refund even though they lied about half the features in the game. 0/10 would never reccomend.

I don't leave reviews very often, but I felt that I needed to for this game.
At the moment, I'm 4 hours into it. Impossibly, until today I not only had not played No Man's Sky, but I had also managed to avoid any spoilers or gameplay videos. Like everyone else, I was hyped for its release, and I didn't want anything to possibly risk my pristine experience of this game. Of course, I couldn't avoid hearing about the massive disappointments, but that's it. Though I preordered it, I was stuck having to wait until I got a computer that could handle it, and that finally happened today. In a sense, I'm glad I waited, because it's no longer at the center of so much media attention, and I feel I can be a bit more objective as I go into it. Also, my first experience will be with whatever updates they've released for it, so at least I'll get to experience a later version.
Though I'm not at all far in the game at all, I just want to share what my first 4 hours have been like. In summary, they've consisted of dying, dying, and some more dying. I started on survival mode and the game dropped me smack dab in the middle of a frozen planet. As I figured out the controls and the way the different parts of the game worked, both my hazard suit and life-support system depleted pretty quickly, and I died and had no resources with which to get back on my feet. I had no idea what to do, and I didn't want to search for help online, or restart my game to hope for a better planet. I wanted to survive here, and I wanted to succeed.
The next 4 hours after that consisted of little tiny attempts to run in each direction, to plot out as much of the area as I could before dying. Little by litle I learned, and got better. I figured out what sparse materials I needed to prioritize to recharge and repair my equipment, and managed to survive a little bit longer each time. Just now, I finally finished the longest of these excursions - the one that finally got me to my ship - and let me tell you, my heart is still beating. Never before has a game given me such an experience. I feel like I just came out on top of some major life challenge, that I would tell friends and family about for years.
Very few games have ever managed to give me an experience like this, and that's why I needed to come straight here and give it some credit. True, I haven't even touched space travel and apparently that's where people's criticisms really come into play - but such an incredible experience over the course of 4 hours? I've bought and played indie games that run about the same length, so if this was the entire game I would be cool. BUT IT'S NOT THE ENTIRE GAME, AND THERE'S MORE.
No matter how disappointing the rest is, the fact that it was already amazing, and still has more to offer, at the very least puts it towards the top of the most memorable games I've ever played. I look forward to continuing, and playing resource management/survival in real life as I balance my NMS levels and my grad school grades.

So this review is about a game i havent played for long yet but i can only say that it already is very good.
Now about the game i can say that i had to turn down some of my settings for a good fps but after i did that it was solid. My PC is decent but not a high end gaming PC and most of the games on my Library were played on this PC without problems so you can see that it isnt that bad of a PC after all. Back to the point. The game runs good on my settings and i have no fps drops so far.
The main controlls, those were an issue for me in blockland, are easy as in every other Lego Game that we know. You use WASD to move around. F to interact with things. Q and E to change the size of your brush and space and controll to ascend or descend.
The Controlls about going up and down and resizing mainly play a role when you fly with a helicopter or when you build something. While flying in a helicopter you use mainly WASD to move around but you use space and controll to move up and down. While in buildmode though you also use Q and E to resize your brush so you can use it on a bigger or tinier area.
As of for the main game there is currently not much to do. The reason for that is that the game is currently in early acces and having the game itself and the engine done is for me good enough. The game is still in development and updates can come whenever. But since there is not much to do at the moment it might be boring for some people what is understandable.

My Final Score is

♥ Diverse levels.
I'm not one to mind repeating levels/maps in games however it's clear that they put effort into the design of Fear's world. I quite liked how each chapter was a change from the last...you explore a variety of buildings and are put into a number of situations, instead of facing the same boss over and over again, or being forced into a series of mazes.
Diversity in its design is a strong virtue of Fear 3.
♥ Made me jump.
Though Fear 3 isn't nearly as scary as the past titles, it did have several spooky moments in it. Granted I'm a total scaredy cat yet who wouldn't jump at an angry little girl leaping at them while they're climbing up a ladder? ; _ ;
♥ Enjoyable co-op.
Whenever someone has wanted to play a co-op game with me, I used to always suggest playing Fear 3 together. Why? For one the co-op is balanced, a fact that I appreciate. Unlike other games it has both players doing equal amount of work and requires teamwork without going overboard.
For another, I liked how the average time to beat the game, at least for my friends and I, was around 8 to 12 hours. I liked having a game to invest time into without having to play it week after week with someone. I understand others have found the main story lacking time wise yet this was never a problem for me.
In case you're bored or finish the main storyline, there are four, multiplayer, mini games to play. Very fun!
✘ The story IS lacking.
I can understand people who value games by looking at all aspects - the sound, the story, the graphics, etc. I can also understand people who have the view of looking for one thing, excellent graphics, beautiful music, and the like above all else. For me what matters most is the story of a game.
Compared to the other Fear titles, I agree that Fear 3 is lacking in its story. They could have taken it so much farther than they did - I found the relationship between the two main characters was filled with possibility that they seemed to purposely shove aside. I don't believe we need to be pirvy to every aspect of a character, however they made them seem like cardboard cut outs, instead of real...Humans, ghosts, aliens, there was no difference for they all acted flat and emotionally frigid.
Not once when I've replayed Fear 3 have I ever felt a connection to any of them nor have I felt pulled in by the story. As scary as I found the first Fear to be, it DID pull me into the story and the world of Alma. The dev team had so much they could have worked with backstory wise, relationships between characters, etc. and used none of it. I'll stick to fanfiction to get an emotional high... ' - '
✘ Very hard to play with motion sickness.
As my motion sickness has gotten worse, I've had to give up playing many games, Fear 3 among them. Despite its flaws, I have always enjoyed the game, and would replay it every few months. If anyone suffering from motion sickness is thinking about buying it, I would strongly advice you to think twice, for the game isn't kind to those who suffer from it!
✘ I think the main reason people are let down with Fear 3 is when they buy it thinking it's going to be a horror game. Does it have jump scares? Yes. Is it spooky? To me it is. However unlike the others in the series, I consider Fear 3 a shooter/survival game more than anything. It's wonderful if you're looking for a co-op game, no fault there, but as a horror game? Not so much. Still it might give you a spook or two!
Overall if you're looking for a co-op game, Fear 3 would make a wonderful choice. If you're considering it from the aspect of loving the Fear series, I'd skip it.

This game is excelent, but not quite perfect.

Second, the musical score. Its great. Deffently one of best game soundtracks in a long time.
Now how it controls... keyboard controls are doabel. And what i mean by that is it works, but this was clearly meant to be
played with a controler (Note: if you are not using a controler use keyboard and mouse. Thank me later)
The combat isn't that special ether. When there is combat, you just spam one button and that is it. Luckily, most of the enemyes are infequent and quite easy, especialy with the right upgrades.
The save system is... wierd. Why? Because you have to manualy place most of the save points in the game. And its bad for both the fequent saver and the one who doesn't. If you save fequently with your own savepoints, you're going to lose all of your energy, and when you get to a energy door or a breakabel wall, you cant go trough. And if you don't save enough you are gonna lose a LOT of progress most of time. Which makes me wonder why didn't use a autosave system, after it does so at vital times, thankfuly.
But before you think '' Welp this game sucks'' it does still have some more redeming features than just art and music.
Platforming is solid with many more moves being tacked on as you progress, kepping the game somewhat fresh.
And some of the chalenges you face are also pretty good and keeps the game fresh fx. changes in gravilty, changes in the area and being starked by a one-hit kill enemy and having to go to safety before it kills you.
So it is the worst game ever? No, not at all. Is it the best? Close but not quite.

I did not like the ending, but I still feel this game is worth recommending because I felt the remainder of the experience was enjoyable.
The rest of the game was well done. Decent length. The player movement mechanics, and how you interacted with the environment was refreshing and enjoyable. Growing up, I was one of those kids who would make up fake languages instead of doodling in class, so I really enjoyed how exploration rewarded you with new information and stories. Reminded me of some of the Pokemon games where you could read the letterforms shaped like Unowns.
But I really did not like the ending. It felt dissonant with what you were doing the rest of the game, and came as a real surprise that personally left me with a bad feeling. Sure, plenty of exploration games out there have abstract endings, but the good ones will give you hints about it if you explore far enough. With SoR, I scoured these maps hard (originally looking for the entrance to the last shard zone, which I missed at first) and read every single runestone. None of it really provided clarification for me on what the ending meant or why it happened.

If you can remember this game the first time around you're probably like me; couple of kids (in thier bed right now), a penchant for all things mystically nostalcic and incredibly thinning hair. Not 40 yet though ...
In short the original was awesome. I remember it taking an age to load (on the speccy) and then spending HOURS with my best mate killing ghosts, skeletons etc. etc.
The reboot definitely lives up to the playability of the original, though times have changed. I'm running it on a machine that makes my 128k speccy look like the first wheel and my partner in rendering 'bum kicking destruction' is my good lady wife.
To be honest, we're not that far in to the game, having only completed the first two scenarios but we've experienced, in no particular order; edge of the seat tension (thanks Death!), tactical analysis, acute tactical deficiencies, where the hell is the next chicken dinner?, smoke breaks, dying (a lot), spamming the B button to do Thor's whirly thing, shouting, heatedly debating, the children, halfway through play, spilling juice all over their bedroom and an EPIC amount of GOLD. This is what a game should be all about :)
Being a Diablo III player I thought that this would be the usual kinda romp through a dungeon with no particular level of difficulty, however, I was totally wrong. This game is hard - playing it solo on normal with Thor will get you killed fairly quickly. Like other games of yesteryear you had to learn them especially when soloing, so I was pretty chuffed when the missus stopped on WoW and decided to have a bash. Better. Much Better.
You really get the benefit of the differing abilities of the characers when you play as a team. We were playing as Thor & Questor (Tank & Damage respectively) and were pretty effective at knocking out the generators/portals or whatever you want to call them.
Hard on two player, No. Challenging, Yes. but that doesn't mean it's not FUN. I've thorougly enoyed the last 3 hours of play and if it wasn't for my eyes about to dry out, I'd probably be on it for a few more tonight.
By comparison Diablo is a bit of a cake walk, if you really want something to get your teeth into, then give this a go, I double dares ya!!!
P.S. I bought the 4 pack which I think is really good value for money. If you're gifting, you'll have a lot of fun with whomsoever you send it to.
P.P.S The kids bedroom carpet is ok ;)

"Stronghold Kingdoms" is an answer to strategy fans who want to play in an online living and breathing world.
I wanted to wait a few monthes till I review it to give a better review as the game is massive and the amount of layers it has is enourmous.
Some words about the game:
- Takes place on a real map, one can choose to start in many maps such as : World, Europe, Germany, UK, USA, Poland, Turkey, France, Italy, Russia etc.
- You play as a lord with a fuedal titel starting from  a "village idiot" up until "crown prince", those in essence are equivalent to "levels" in MMORPGs and provide you with more possibilities. You rank up by gaining "Honor" which is in essence "Experience" in MMORPGs. Honor can be collected in noumerous ways: Be it warefare, economy or pollitics.
- The core of the game is building and developing yours villages castles, of course as being built villages can also be conquered.
Economy:
-Resources are gathered from natural deposits and are used to build buildings or craft weapons (wood, stone, pitch and iron).
-Food is used to feed your population (apples, cheese, meat, bread, vegetables, fish and ale)
-Goods are used to hold banquets increasing your honor (meat, clothes, metalwork, furniture, wine, spices, silk and salt)
-Weapons are used to arm your people (Bows, Pikes, Swords, Catapults)
- Every resource can be created, traded or foraged.
- Everything is wraped under a large research tree.
Warefare:
- Scouts are used to gather reports about enemy castles.
- Armies are used to both defend your villages and attack your enemies villages.
Politics:
- There is a beautiful fuedal system in place, lower ranks answer to their lieges in the following system: Village < Perish < County < Province < Country. The higher position you hold the more glory you bring to your house. Political positions are acquired through voting but of course can be pressured using warefare or religeon influence.
- Lords fight under a banner of a faction (equivalent to guild in MMORPGs), and factions fight under a banner of a house.
- At end game houses struggle over the map domination.
Costs:
- How much does this cost?
Sadly a freemium bussiness model is in place which means that you can invest as much as you want.
In my opinion in order to stay competitive an investment of a few euros per month will be necessary.
- Will a player that invests more money that you have certain advantages? Yes, he will develop and progress faster. Is this a deal breaker? Absolutly not, some people play longer and some people pay longer... Up to each one.
N.B:
- Some people are unhappy about being razed, conquered and loosing all their hard worked on villages. I would like to say a few words about that:
It is true that "Stronghold Kingdoms" is not for the weak hearted... Yes you may loose all your villages in a war but you will get a new village and will still keep your fuedal rank, your research, your gold, faith and honor. So rebuilding is not a big deal and it is faster every time, like in real life... Sometimes we fall, but the whole point is to raise up again, this time even stronger.
To summerize:
A brilliant massive online strategy game that allows one to play as he wants. You may concentrate on warefare, farming, pollitics, religeon or whatever suits your intrests best.

I was really reluctant to give this game a recommendation. It depends highly on what you like in a game - I like the extensive crafting possibilities and also the slow and interesting fighting system. The community around the game seems top notch as well (if a bit elitist, seeing how many of them already bought houses and castles for hundreds if not thousands of $$).
A big downside: graphics - they look sooo last century in many ways:
- cities like Ardoris have a mixture of European and Chinese styles, which looks really weird. Some tiles are overly bright, so lighting needs some work there. Bright red directional signposts don't fit at all.
- player houses are even worse - a viking house next to a medieval castle (which has electricity ...) looks quite out of place
- other players slide instead of run/walk (though I hope this will change by release time).
- chars seem to float above ground, but get stuck at the slightest raise in ground  - a board can be an insurmountable obstacle (they can go up stairs though ...)
- (affordable) houses have very small rooms, so there's not much you can decorate.
- speaking of decoration: most of the items also look out of place, not belonging to the world/house around them.
- villages and fighting areas look very restricted since there's half-transparent grey walls all around that you can see from far away
- I set the graphics quality to "fantastic" @ 2560x1440 - but it's not. E.g. shadows on the walls are pixelated, even with AA on.
So I think the game is in dire need of a good graphics team and a common coloring, lighting and style scheme. Reminds somewhat of good old Horizons. 12 year old EQ2 looks better in many ways. Not to speak of newer titles like ESO ...
Sound: forget about it for now, some cheap and cheesy MIDI music, crocodiles that bark and no NPC speech, not even short greetings.
My biggest fear: it wont be possible to get a lot for your house if you have a job and don't have time to play 24/7 to get the gold for it fast - it's already difficult to find a decent place for a house now in pre-release.
I guess release wont happen before 2016 if they don't want it to flop - there's still lots of work and bug fixing to do.
To not make this review sound too negative: it's lots of fun for me and it didn't crash once yet on my iMac (2014). It's a game that has high potential to keep you interested and occupied for a long time.

I kinda am losing hope on this title, and in its current state, I simply can not recommend it anymore. I did start playing it a few months ago, and at first I appreciated the atmosphere and the lack of handholding - you have to figure out things for sure. Can you handle that mob? Well, there is no level # to show you, you attack it and see how you do. When you talk to NPCs, there are keywords you can click or retype to unlock more conversation and get assignments/quests.
There is that Lord British-touch all over the game, and so there is a tiny bit of Ultima/LB-magic, even though this game wasn't meant to be UO2 or whatever people expected.
However - slowly but surely I lose hope, because:
- development seems to take forever, and I really don't think it is moving forward at a pace that makes it realistic this game will be "live" sometime soon.
- I understand the need for funding, but a LOT of focus seems to be on the cash shop, while at the same time, a lot of the items you get for your pledges aren't even in game yet.
- The "deck-fighting-system" (with your abilities in like a deck of card that pop up on your action bar randomly was fun at first... it was a bit different, and with some good will, you could consider it realistic, as in "Hey, this is a sword fight, and my opponent just didn't cover himself well enough so I have a chance to hit him with this attack right now.
At the same time, movement and battle feel kinda slow and clunky. I havent dabbled with the magic abilities, as they seem to require mats to cast, and I am not sure that that still is a valid system nowadays... I always disliked that about UO, even if it may be more "realistic" (as realistic as casting spells can be)
- There still are a lot of broken or undeveloped things, and some rooms or areas give me SERIOUS lag especially after they changed the engine the game runs on. My PC can easily handle AC Black Flag, TESO or even  GTA V at normal to high settings. I stepped into a basement in SOTA which had lots of tables with candles on it and had severe lag, to the point where I had to leave.
- I am aware this is in alpha or beta or whatever, but so far, the story seems totally underdeveloped. This is nothing new actually, because even though some of the Ultima-games had quite a bit of story, I realized eventually that LB, in many games, doesnt care as much about the story and lore... UO sucked in that aspect, and reading the book on LB and Ultima, he talks about how he never read much fantasy but instead watched movies that inspired his stories. While this might have worked back then, I just don't feel enticed at all by the lack of story or lore in this game. It just feels like a random place with hardly any background or feel of mystery that might motivate you to actually find out the story... and the mixture of medieval and magic with Steampunk elements and mohawk hairdos kinda kills immersion for me.
Is this trying to be fresh for the sake of being different, or does this odd mixture make sense?
On one hand, you have this really nice feeling of medieval/fantasy forests and stuff, and then you see guys in steampunk-cliche tophats, generators etc.
- Crafting can be fun, even though parts of it are kinda broken. You can experiment, mix stuff to get better results, and I hear crafted stuff is supposed to be better than looted stuff. But gathering mats is silliness, and an immersion killer. You are in a forest full of trees and you have to find this one tree you can chop a tiny bit. Why not increase amount of mats required, or chance of getting useable logs, but allow more trees to be chopped? I mean, I am standing with an axe in the middle of a forest and have to search for several minutes to find a tree or two I can chop? Same for prospecting.
- The AI is really not looking like it will be any challenge. Ranged mobs? Move into some corner, wait until they walk around it, fight them as melee. Unless they shoot an arrow or two, move 10 ft, shoot another arrow, move 10 ft... annoying and really old-fashioned, but not in a good way.
- There are weekly emails with news and stuff, plus updates often. However, in the last 5 or 6 days, the game has downloaded about 350 MB of data over night. Not a problem, but it's just weird that it keeps downloading on a daily base, with no explanation. Not a big point, it just is odd to open steam every morning and seeing that SOTA downloaded another file for some reason
- The overland map is pretty anachronistic and another immersion killer.
- I took a bit of a break from the game, and when I tried to log in 2 days ago, I was disconnected 5 times in about 15 minutes of playtime, causing me to give up. This seems to be a new thing, and it kills the fun even more, especially since the game takes a LONG time to load the different instances on a fast computer with a very fast internet connection
- I dont know whether the prizes have changed, but they were pretty unbalanced when I played this a lot. The repair kits you often need to repair your armour and weapon (both have low durability, or lets say the durability goes down rather quickly) are pretty expensive, and it's kind of annoying to have armor and weps fall apart that quickly especially in a game that has quite a bit of grinding.
- Now, let me say this: Yes, I am aware this game is in alpha. Does this mean I can't list the things I dislike or that made me wanna stop playing. The devs made the decision to put the game on Steam, where you can review even early releases - its part of the system at Steam. They even posted at the SOTA-forums, saying that the average rating doesnt reflect nicely enough on the game, asking for more positive reviews by players.
My point is - the game is up on Steam, you can review it, you pay quite a bit of money to be in this alpha, and so far, it doesnt look good. The development is very slow, and I don't know where they are headed here. SOme things are VERY promising, like the crafting, the old school-vibe of certain aspects of the game (the silly AI is really old-fashioned, same as the heavy instancing, the load times, the gathering - but not in a good way. However, I did like that the game doesnt hold your hand too much, I dont mind the grindiness of leveling (killing wolves and skeletons in different areas for hours).
I was excited about the game when I first tried it, but at this point, I just don't know how much longer this game will be in development, and instead of improving, some things seem to get much worse, for example regarding connection issues, lag, loading times.
I really wanted to like this, give it a chance, was even into it for a while. But this alpha seems to take forever, and it shouldnt be used as an excuse for all the problems the game has right now when you charge like 40 Euros for it, have pledge rewards that you can spend thousands of dollars on (you dont have to, of course, and after seeing the slowness and weirdness that this development phase is, I stopped pledging), and put it on Steam where people can review, then ask players to write more positive reviews when many things get WORSE (how can a game so small have such loading times, how can there be THAT many disconnects now?!?), don't be surprised that people get discouraged.
I might go back to this, now that I have an account and have pledged some, when it's done, whenever that is (I seriously doubt that at this pace, this will be done before 2017), but until then, I lost all interest to follow the development. Go ahead, call me out and tell me that this game on Steam for fourty bucks is only alpha, so I can't review it negatively. You charge for it, you have an ever-growing store with "limited time offers", you published it in an online store that always has reviews, and all I did was write down that totally killed my interest or enthusiasm for this game.
Obviously it's not Ultima Online 2, but there a lot of UO elements here.

Instantly tried playing Arcade on "Normal" and I was used to wipe the floor (sometimes literally). If you're somewhat new to fighting games like I was, do the Training levels more than once. Even on "Easy", a poor player will get nearly or completely destroyed. (Damn you Big Band) Since I'm only a few hours in, I've still got much to learn. But damn, this game is really addictive. Recently, the game hasn't left my mind. Getting a chain higher than 3 gives this sense of achievement. I really love and enjoy the art style; it has its own uniqueness to it.
Some criticism: The campaigns could be more related to each other as well as a bit longer. Other than that, I've been having fun.

Coming from a brand new player: Skullgirls is a fantastic fighting game. It is not, however, a particularly FRIENDLY fighting game. The tutorials are incredibly detailed and can easily overwhelm you, demanding mastery of precise controls when all you want to do is just punch the other character until they fall down. Don't let it intimidate you, though, there's a terrific game just waiting for you to catch up to it.
My advice to fellow beginners: select "Single Player Mode", set the difficulty to "Sleepwalk" (the easiest possible), and go nuts. Story or Arcade, just grab a girl and dive in headfirst. Then swap to another. And another. See who you like and who you don't. Then start studying the move lists, poking through the tutorials, and digging into the details. If you're like me, this first taste of actual (though super easy mode) gameplay won't make you an expert, but it will make you hungry for more.

Depth is sharks vs. divers with 2 game modes. One mode has the divers gather treasure which can be used to purchase weapons, attachments, and eguipment to combat 2 shark players. The sharks have different species you can play as, each have their own unique abilities and you can upgrade them by killing the divers to get evolution points. You may realize that this game seems similar to how Evolve is and honestly this is a much better game than Evovle. When you play as divers you have a very small draw distance so its really hard to see the enemy sharks. Therefore it adds a lot of tension since you don't know when the sharks will pop out of nowhere which makes this a very unique mult. game.
The 2nd mode involves 6 players trying to kill the Megalodon to become that shark and kill the other divers to win the game. It may not be as much depth than the other mode but its still a lot of fun to play.
The developers have been very active with the community by adding maps, skins, and more sharks which tells you this game gets more support than other mult. only games.
Conclusion: This is a really fun and unique mult. game that I wish a lot of people would be playing it. Ya its only 2 game modes (really everybody plays 1 until there is a sale for this game more people are playing) but they are really good game modes that you get a lot of replay value out of this game. Pretty fun and surprisingly deep for the price. Also harder than it looks, even on easy difficulty. Suffers a little from unforgiving RNG which can sometimes feel unfair.
The game mechanics are pretty straightforward and turn based, there are two separate parts to the game, the strategic part where you collect resources which you spend on upgrades to your kingdom or recruiting and upgrading new units. Random events pop up which allow you to go questing or seach for resources or treasure items that you can equip to your soldiers, or you can focus on healing your units or researching new technology. Or you can choose to fight tactical battles against the enemies, which you have to fight before your kingdom gets overrun.
The tactical battles are played on a relatively small grid filled with terrain obstructions. Placement of units seems fairly random and there doesn't seem to be any way to set a formation for your units to stay in. You can get badly screwed by initial placement pretty easily especially if you're going with a team of glass cannons like rogues and mages. I've only played about an hour but so far I found these battles pretty tough. The enemies are equivalent if not superior to all the units available to you at the start, so you'll need to team up and at least plan to use 2 units of your own for every 1 enemy, and even then it can be a close thing if the RNG goes their way.
Anyway, it's a challenging but fun game with a surprising amount of depth, and it's cheap. Give it a shot!

I had the honor of being one of the testers  for this game. Not because I'm any good at testing stuff, but because I genuinely enjoyed playing it.
Blades of the Righteous is a turn-based strategy with two main aspects - managing your fantasy kingdom and fighting battles with the vile spawns. As the wise ruler that you are you get to recruit an army, choose individual skills and equipment for each unit and participate in random events that occur on the map - gather resources, deal with merchants, necromancers and other wanderers. And then there are battles - these can get rather challenging as the game progresses and will require careful tactical approach and planning.
The main campaign of the game can be completed in 3-5 hours depending on the chosen difficulty level and your skill. One way to prolong the experience is to delve into side-missions - these are pretty straightforward and there is a repetitive element to them, but as the events of the game and spawning enemies are random, each mission plays out differently.
For me personally the game has a fair amount of replayability - after completing it twice I am still eager to start a new playthrough, try various team setups, develop units in a different way and maybe finally beat it on the hardest difficulty.
The video and audio of the game are simple, but pleasant to eyes and ears. The battle theme is quite cool, and the graphical models for units are awesome. My favorite are the peasants - they just look so well animated.
To sum it up - I have no hesitation recommending this game, especially if you enjoy games like Heroes of Might and Magic or X-Com and are down to play something similar, if a bit more simple in design.

The graphics alone possess an artistic talent on the same level as Bastion, Transistor, Dust, and Braid, with musical direction to match. I write this review with mixed emotions. Raetikon is a beautiful game with a slightly tedious but vibrant world. The art, sound and music are top notch and the game mechanics are simple in a fun way. After flying back and forth completing your fetch quest, you are rewarded with... the ending... which I'm so conflicted about.
Reading the forums, the devs basically want you to think about the impact of humanity on nature and question your own morality on whether killing in one context any more justified than another. The problem though is that there is no context what-so-ever to the overall goal of the game and the runes which you can translate don't explain any lore reasoning. There is also a pacifist achievement which flies in the face of that message. The execution was done extremely poorly and the credits sequence is a slap to the face on top of a kick to the balls.
I can only recommend this game for the art and would avoid any future games by this developer if they think this is the way to write a story.
