Sorry. It had to be done. But seriously, get this game. If you ever enjoyed the old arcade version of Gauntlet, or if you ever spent a week locked in your next-door neighbor's basement trying to get to the next board, you will LOVE Gauntlet.
If you ever played the N64 or Playstation editions of Gauntlet, this is nothing like them.
Several words to the wise:
1. Get a gamepad. Don't play this with mouse and keyboard, it is nowhere near as fun. There were a couple things I found more convenient with the M&K controls, but the fun factor greatly increased with an easy-to-hold gamepad. Try it both ways, but srsly: TRY IT BOTH WAYS. Don't buy this if you don't have a gamepad.
2. Get x360ce (Google it) to make sure your gamepad works with Gauntlet. Put it in the "binaries" directory, not the game's root directory.
3. Don't even bother with single player. You'll have trouble getting past the first monster spawner on normal difficulty.
4. Start with the Valkyrie. Your natural inclination may very well be (as mine was) to start with the warrior (generally the simplest class to play in any game), but I found it much easier to play the Valkyrie. Consider the Wizard an "advanced" class. You need to stay on your toes and you need to remember the button combos for all your spells.
The graphics are... whatever. Who cares? They're good, but they don't need to be. The sound effects are modern, but they very effectively hearken back to days of yore. Controls are... preeeeetty good. I'd prefer if the Valkyrie's dash ability (for example) allowed me to rotate while it's "charging" after I push the button.
The difficulty is good, the multiplayer works smashingly with only the hintiest hint of lag and the level design is enough to keep me interested.
The one big issue I have with this game is that there basically is no single player mode. You can play by yourself, but on normal difficulty the enemies are already scaled up to the point that you can't really do well. On the face of it, that doesn't bug me THAT much. This is a fairly new game, and there are always people on. But in a few years when it's not the latest and greatest anymore, I basically won't be able to play it outside the context of a LAN party.
If you were EVER a fan of the Gauntlet genre back in the day, you will love this game.
EDIT: Don't buy this game if you don't have someone to play with over a LAN. The community is absolutely dead. Due to a completely inattentive developer and a couple much-lamented gamebreakers, you're going to sit in the matchmaking lobby for ten minutes or so before you get hooked up with ONE other player (this owing to the fact that you can't join a game in progress). And then pray whomever's hosting the game has a steady connection, because if they dump out the game ends. The one time I got in a game with two other people, it lasted about three minutes, then the host dumped out and we waited five minutes for him to get back.
It sad, really. This game is a lot of fun, but because of the absolute ridiculous design choices of static game hosting and lack of jump-in/jump-out games, it's essentially dead after a month and a half.

Stronghold Kingdoms is a massively multiplayer online city builder, where the player has to manage the construction of a village and the adherent castle. The castles with defensive structures and soldiers are responsible for protecting your village from other players, who can - amongst other things - take it over (permanently). By doing tasks you earn experience (honour, as the game calls it) and by reaching new levels (ranks), you can research new village buildings, technologies, castle defense, increase in production, etc. and even the possibility to establish new settlements or conquer existing ones.
The game draws heavily on a game from 2001, Stronghold (its HD edition is available on Steam):
It's a nice little city builder - castle simulator set in a stylized version of medieval England. The graphics is almost entirely the same, moody and detailed.
So what's the difference between the two? Well, this is multiplayer only and set in the globe (you can start in Australia for example, which has little to no effect on the gameplay). The player community is mixed, just like in other games: there are helpful ones and there are sociopaths. This has nothing to do with the game itself.
What has to do is that it's a dumbed-down version of the original game. The best things (castle sieges, large scale battles, resource management) have been simplified here, making it a poor alternative to the original (did I mention that its HD edition is availabe on Steam? :))
There are many new ideas in Stronghold Kingdoms, the important role of scouts for example, who can not only spy upon your enemies, but can also discover resource packs and hidden AI castles on the map (earning you both valuable materials and honour, making them the first unit to research as soon as you start the game) religion and the fief system, but there are just too many good things the game has lost to value these improvements.
The game is playable and enjoyable enough without investing money in it, bonus cards (which you'll receive occasionally anyway) and premium tickets aren't necessary. Be prepared however that this game requires you to be online and check on your settlements quite frequently. It uses an external client so playing it through Steam isn't really justified.
Do I recommend it? Well, yes it's fun, and a good city builder mmo in its category, but if I were you, I'd buy the original Stronghold for only 3,99€ (mentioned above), that surpasses this game in almost every aspect.
PROS
+ balanced city builder with customizable defense
+ lots of things to research
+ it's free
CONS
- the problem with all mmos: no story, no ending
- dumbed-down version of the original game
- requires too frequent online presence
RATING
5/10

I must say... I LOVED this game, that’s why I’m upvoting it, BUT it is very PAY to WIN. Not pay to play. You can enjoy your time, and even do WELL, even great without paying, but you will most likely never WIN, unless you are willing to devote a TON of time to it.
Now, about my time on game. I have approximately 2000 hours of game time, but on the site version. I got this again to mess around when I needed it. The game is great if you find a cool group to hang out with (Find Jezdeb, or Maria Sine, on any world tell them Lord Dark sent ya, then be loyal and you’ll have a blast, best gang ever)
The politics are great, combat is fun, and the whole world feels SO alive... Honestly when I started it was like the stratgist dream... The pay to win was not as big. You could buy cards, but none did THAT much, and they would be quickly drained. To really get an edge you had to KNOW how the game worked, and that took time, skill and thought. The game STILL NEEDS that. Yes EVEN if you put 2K into this you will FAIL MISERABLY if you do not understand how the game works VERY well.
I guess the biggest problem here is that, there are a few hundred players, who actively play on almost every world who LITERALLY devote their lives to this game, play nothing else, and spend tens of thousands of dollars on this game, a few to many people take it WAY to seriously.
Now if you don’t want to be the next greatest faction to rule the realm, and your okay with playing hide under interdiction then burn, and if your okay with trying VERY hard to fight, you will LOVE this game, EVEN STILL. It gets harder and harder though. Each “Card Release” adds more and more ways for those who pay to pay more, but do SO much more. There is nothing they get, so special units, nothing like that, just speed increase. That’s what this game focuses on strategy and time management.  If you want to get into this game, message my steam profile, I’ll try and get you in with some of the good people, I had connections everywhere.
If you play this game you will understand what I mean when I say, the community CAN save the game, if you find the right group, or it can kill it in the wrong one. I mean who doesn’t love to join a BRAND NEW server and have people be like “Hey dude, I remember you, you destroyed my faction last game, you guys are so cool!” Or have loads of hatemail after burning a whole group of players.
TLDR: I stopped this game cause it took up way to much of my time not the P2W, it is P2W, but its’ STILL VERY FUN! Try it out, send me a message if you do and I’ll drop ya some tips. The games fun, really fun, just you have to learn the tricks, and trust me, there are millions, a good player CAN outdo one who pays to play. You just gotta try hard.

Divinity: Original Sin delivers what the enthusiastic critical reception highlighs: the magic / skills / combat mechanics are excellent and bring some most-needed new and fresh ideas to this old genre. If anything, this game has given a big contribution to the development of a genre I love.
Yet my review is negative because of some major issues I must highligh. My biggest complain is about the screenplay. The plot is poor and predictable, the characters are insipid and dull, the quests pointless and above all the humor is cheesy and not funny. I tried but there was nothing apart the fights to compel me playing the game (and if I was looking for a hack and slash game, I had plenty of better options).
Something else I feel wrong with DOS (although forgivable in comparison with the storytelling lacks) are the character creation and the looting system. Every rpg player loves the first 30 minutes of these games: generating the protagonist you will take care of and bring to the endgame. Well DOS gives you no race (ok, no problem with that) and eleven classes to choose among. With very little other characterization option if not the aesthetic ones. Digging further in the sheet (I could not believe it was it), it gets confusing. Until you press Alt + Tab and go googling what the hell changes from a class tot he other, since they all seem to have the same skills etc. Nothing changes except the starting equipment, and they are no real classes with different progressions, but instead only premade sets. Sets that you can fully customize at will, but then again why making it so tricky? The set description only gives a background to the character, background that will have no influence whatsoever on the story. I can only think the developers were afraid that a detailed and deep character generation would have bored the new players, without realizing that it is one of the most wanted part of the game.
Last note: the money / loot system. As many other games in the genre, you can steal (err, collect?) item here and there in you wanderings and the sell them over to merchants. Differently from the majority of other games, though, you will never make enough money this way. Instead, your pgs‘ economy should work like this: collect and buy stuff, combine items together and sell the outcomes for good money. DISCLAIMER: This is literally the first review I've ever done for a game. I am doing it because I felt it was necessary to help put an end to all the negative reviews. Instead, I will break up the pro's and con's into "Experiences" and "Expectations".
EXPERIENCES:
EDIT: This game does have a cash shop for COSMETIC items only. There is absolutely NO pay to win archetecture here despite the overwhelming ignorance below this detailed review. NOTE: All cash items can, and will be bought with in game gold, including the Tax Free land plots and house deeds. Do not let the negative reviews try to sway you from this excellent title. Thank you.
Alright! So where to begin? Well, I got into the game roughly a week ago now. I have been working really close with the sommunity managers to get all the information I could for this review. I was there during the end of R16. I was present for all the social events that were hosted by the diehard community. From the PaxLair One Year Anniversary, to the final BMC Grid Iron PvP event, and then some. For those of you who don't know what either are, PaxLair is a completely player-owned town within SotA (At the time, PaxLair was settled unofficially within the town of Valemark but now is it's own official town made possible by the Devs). BMC Grid Iron is hosted by a dominate guild (Britannia Mining Company). It is a fully customized, underground fight club where players place bets on fighters and can walk out with large sums of gold. Both events were extremely interesting to be a part of, and even moreso considering how warm and welcoming the community is to strangers.
Now we are in R17. Many more events are planned and I've even had the chance to attend some thus far. Including the first ever, exclusive walkthrough of the Metropolis of PaxLair with Winfield, the owner of the city. Which at the end of the tour, the Dev's jumped in game and danced around with the players, all while adding everyone they could see to thier friend's list. Something I haven't ever seen occur in a game to date.
The combat in the game is considerably solid at it's current state. I, and many people who have put considerable time into SotA picked up the mechanics relatively fast. Though, it currently is a bunch of hotkey spamming, there is a method to it. Especially when stacking status effects and using such effects to boost the damage, buffs, or healing of the other abilities, or when creating what the game calls "Combos". Fighting a group of cultists has never been so tactical.
The classes in SotA are the best I've ever seen in a game. Because there are no classes. Much like how Bethesda sold everyone on Skyrim with the slogan "You are what you play", this title boasts it louder. There are seperate skill trees for many different skills. Each with their own perks and "Castable" hotkey's. There are two catigories to choose from when allocating skillpoints: Combat and Magic. You are free to take out skills, and put in skills whenever you wish to completely change your build of your character with absolutely no hassle. So if you are a heavy armor wearing, two handed axe wielding tank, and you feel it's time to be a light armor wearing, dual wand wielding, magic glass cannon, then go for it.
Granted, there are a few instances where the game can be a pain. Though, you must all realize, and plant into your heads that this is a Pre-Alpha. So here's some expectations for all you new players.
Expect some animations to be buggy.
Expect some frame rate drops in bigger cities.
Expect the combat to be glitched at times.
Expect many quests to not be fully integrated yet.
Expect some confusion when talking to NPC's until you get the hang of keywords.
Expect to run around blindly until you get a guide to help show you the ropes.
Expect to spend quite a bit of gold on repair kits until you learn the crafting trade.
Expect to die and be a ghost.
Expect to die by a ghost.
Expect to have your characters wiped with many new releases.
Expect to be blown away when you discover there is an actual radio station hosted by the players in game and they take requests. (Amber Raine and others)
Expect to actually be accepted into a thriving community of dedicated players who have been around for nearly 30 years due to the work of Richard Garriott and Starr Long. Do not be afraid to contact someone and ask for help.
Whew. Okay, so that essentially covers just about everything.
Listen, we know the game isn't 100% completed. The Overworld map itself is only about 10% done and it's still extremely massive. There are bugs, and it's okay to embrace them for the time being. Just be open-minded, experiment with the mechanics, RP with the community at times, and have a blast doing it.
TLDR;
Richard Garriott fought Star Long in front of the whole town - 32/10, would choose sides again.

Shroud of the Avatar is currently i  "PRE-ALPHA" release (emphasising the pre alpha there). So bugs, graphics, incomplete items and skills etc is bound to be noticed. However, the development team quickly act on the forum bug reports and produce updates and patches within the first few hours and days of release.
It's important to remember that it's still a game that needs to be nurtured to good health and the community provides fantastic support in filling in the gaps. From player run events like PvP, to maze runs and even decoration contests. All these contests i've been honoured to see and take part in. Most not if all are very rewarding from the community themselves as well as developers giving out cash coupons. They do hangouts at periods of time talking about the new releases and giving away awesome products from gaming headsets, sound systems and keyboards.
The forum community is one of the best I've seen and it's so supportive. If you've got questions or comments, you almost immediately get a reply. Developers pop on and check whats happening, commenting on threads and being more hands on. Even in game I had the opportunity to tour Lord British around my home.
The game itself is very immersive if you allow it to be. If you simply look at it as an unfinished product, then that's all it'll be until it's completed. Because it is unfinished and it does need time. So give it a chance. To be part of a game thats developing into what I believe will be a masterpiece, is exciting. It doesn't get boring especially with the amount of events taking place each week.
There have been issues with graphics and frame rates at times but they have fixed that and slowly working on making it better. The transition from unity 4 to 5 is very time consuming yet they are producing beautiful work. The flexibility available in this game is endless and you are given so much freedom to do what you wish.
I have made amazing friends during the past couple of months playing this game and it's been really exciting to go on teamspeak, roleplay, take part in contests and have laughs with a wonderful diverse community.
Over all the good points are:
*Immersive gameplay even for prealpha stage
*endless hours of gaming time
*many events (avatars circle)
*many rewards ingame and out of game
*Community support!
*Monthly releases and exclusives
*Roleplay is fantastic
*Decorating, being in guilds and parties!
*The community make the game!
*The developers feel like part of the community
Negatives:
*Bugs, glitches and computer performance (but that's expected in pre-alpha)
*Graphics may put people off but every month its continuously being revamped
*Little story progression and lore
*Quite pricey add on store, hope they bring it down a bit
Overall I love this game. I've enjoyed every moment and even with the faults/ bugs etc, it's a great experience to know I'm helping a pre alpha game.

Coming from a brand new player: Skullgirls is a fantastic fighting game. It is not, however, a particularly FRIENDLY fighting game. The tutorials are incredibly detailed and can easily overwhelm you, demanding mastery of precise controls when all you want to do is just punch the other character until they fall down. Don't let it intimidate you, though, there's a terrific game just waiting for you to catch up to it.
My advice to fellow beginners: select "Single Player Mode", set the difficulty to "Sleepwalk" (the easiest possible), and go nuts. Story or Arcade, just grab a girl and dive in headfirst. Then swap to another. And another. See who you like and who you don't. Then start studying the move lists, poking through the tutorials, and digging into the details. If you're like me, this first taste of actual (though super easy mode) gameplay won't make you an expert, but it will make you hungry for more.

TL;DR: A well done JRPG styled game, with a focus on adjusting your gear and tactics for each group and boss to hit weaknesses and exploit status effects. Requires a bit of strategy for optional things, but no too deep if you just want to enjoy it.
I've actually played all the EBF's so far, and you don't need to play the others to play this one. Technically, you can play it for free on the website, minus some features, but the creator has done some amazing work on this title, so he deserves the money if you want to purchase it.
Epic Battle Fantasy has always been about adjusting your tactics to your current enemies, and 4 is no different. The game boils down classic turn based combat into a purely fun formula. Each battle, even bosses, you can run from at will, so if you find new enemies you can scan them, then flee to adjust your gear if you like, or just hammer on through if you can. Most enemies can be beaten by using gear with no downsides and the proper elements, but obviously you will get much better results, especially against bosses and larger enemies, if you adjust your gear to hit their weaknesses. Unlike most JRPGs, status effects actually matter alot in the game, and alot of them work well in conjunction. One of the best combos is the darkness status effect decreases stats over time, and increases weakness to holy...and the holy status effect reduces the other stats over time, and increases weakness to dark. This leads to combos, such as having an accessory that gives the darkness-only debuff to your weapons, and using that against dark enemies so they receive even more holy damage. The game is all about finding those neat combos and useful effects, and using them well.
The story is bare bones, but it doesn't need to be too epic (Despite the name), the summary from 3 to 4 as told in the intro is 'the heroes saved the world, so they thought they were entitled to everyones stuff, so they took it...that made people mad, insert new heroine'. The game makes light of typical JRPG tropes, without being too caustic. It also introduces new elements as you run into them, so it avoids any sort of tutorial. Sidequests are nothing more than gather materials, give to NPC.
The game has many things you can do to improve your characters besides levelling, optional skills that you can only give to one character, upgrading weapons/armor (of which there are plenty), accessories, permanent stat boosting items that can be hoarded through numerous NG+s, etc. While you can go through it on easy, the game does reserve the boss achievements only for beating them on the highest difficulty, which is an effort no matter when you do it. The optional area, Battle Mountain, is even tougher for it, as the enemies level up with you, so you have to rely on strategy (and maybe some stat boosting items) to win. Still, every group of enemies is unique in structure, and the difficulty ramps up well, a very well designed curve for the game. There is some backtracking as you gain new items, to collect old stuff, but you don't feel too put upon to do so.
Overall, I highly reccomend this game if you like a good turn based RPG that requires you to think about how to handle each encounter, without getting into a mindless slog through weak enemies.

This game had incredibly beautiful landscapes and interesting mechanics and was up to a point, inviting to play, even relaxing for a short period. Sadly that is where the few good points about this game end.
The seizure warning/flashes warning is incredibly easy to miss, so please be careful if that is an issue for you. Without a controller, it would be extremely difficult to play, and it had no colour blind options which made it almost impossible to find all the "runes" which then need you translate things manually.
I am not sure what the creators of this game were aiming for regarding the story, but the outcome is incredibly bleak and not well executed. After spending hours playing through its beautiful landscapes, I deliberately delayed the end so I could decode the runes in an attempt to understand the actions of my bird. It felt like there was supposed to be a meaning behind it all. However I was left feeling incredibly cheated, there is no grand explanation or even a simple message to this game, and the ending felt thrown together. It was like watching Neon Genisis Evangelion or Donnie Darko as a grown up and realising that it isn't at all profound.
While I think the designers were attempting to make something meaningful, they have sadly produced something pretty, depressing and not very enjoyable. If you want to play something attractive and don't mind gruesome and morbid endings, go for it. However playing this game is like putting Fern Gully in a blender fair warning!

Secrets of Raetikon is a beautiful game, with great art design and a peaceful soundtrack, makes for a really nice atmosphere. But sadly, even if the gameplay isn't awful, it starts getting really frustrating, and quite frankly, boring towards the end. The level design is convoluted, there's no map, and the game forces you to backtrack through most of the game, all of that while dodging the extremely annoying enemies trying to hurt you and stealing the object you have to carry through most of the levels, and you have to do all of that like five times, each one of them with more levels to backtrack through and more enemies than the one before it.
And all of this culminates in a rather dissappointing ending, which is just an epilepsy inducing light show and a game of Pong. Not a minigame with the same mechanics as Pong, instead the screen turns black, and the arcade game just starts playing. When you win, it says "Game Over", shows you your score and the credits start rolling. I have no idea if that's supposed to mean something.
It's not the worst game I've ever played, not even close. I'd even recommend checking it out if you got it for free or in a bundle as I did, but what I can not recommend is paying 10€ for a 2 hour game that ends up being frustrating and doesn't even manage to make sense.

Back when this game released months ago, I was pumped and hyped. And the E3 trailer really helped to give an impression as to what Hello Games wanted when they were making this. So I jumped on the train and waited, and preordered.
What we got was an exciting first world, with promise, as you slowly rebuild your ship so you can leave, and you can really feel it as you leave the atmosphere of that first planet, to be suddenly introduced to just how massive everything really is. That in itself isn't really a problem. The problem, was that the entire universe was procedurally generated.
Normally procedural generation in games like Minecraft can be pretty neat, because when you are on one planet, you kind of expect most of it to look the same with a few different biomes here and there. And when you finally find that one incredibly awesome mountain or something, it really feels rare.
When you take that and explode it, and turn it into a freaking massive universe, you run into problems.
The larger the target region of procedural generation, the more assets you need in order to make everything feel new and exciting.
In No Man's Sky, there are incredibly limited assets. I'm talking the same colors, the same creatures with different eyes, the same flora and fauna, and the same God damn planets. The only true difference between Planet 1 and Planet 2910382837 is you
find a new creature or plant, and the sky and ground will be different colors. Oh, and it may be colder or hotter or something lame like that. That's it. No really. All of the planets are redundant with textures. The team over at Hello Games went WAY OVER THEIR HEADS with this title. Given a LOT more time and A TON more assets and people working on it, and MAYBE just MAYBE they can find a way to give us a promised title.
What I hate more is that I was expecting a AAA quality game, whatever that means anymore. No Man's Sky had me really hyped up, and the 60$ price tag made it seem like the game would be even better than average. You'd figure that right?
Nope. This game is probably worth at the best 15$. I paid 4 times what it was worth, and got ripped off in the end with poor gameplay, design, and poor execution of a game in general. Sad really.
Unfortunately, Steam refuses to give me a refund no matter how many times I try to file a refund to them, and I wish I had never purchased this game. The only thing this game taught me is to 1. Never preorder again unless the press releases and review copies show positive results. 2. Never preorder a 60$ game from some underground developers who try hyping their game up far too much. The worst part is that because of Steam and other digital copies, Hello Games is likely to not suffer as much damage as punishment for how horrible they left us. At least give me a partial refund damn it!
Games like this really ruin the fun of being a gamer, but it's a good thing not all games are like this. Take it as an example third parties! THIS GAME is what happens when you go too far with limited resources. It's like trying to play a survival game without food and water. You. Will. Not. Survive.

In the current state, the game fits perfectly into the actual definition of pre-alpha. Features are still being implemented in a regular, monthly update cycle.
Even in this state, the game oozes that "classic" Ultima feel. This is an important distinction here: It is a sucessor to all Ultima games, not only Ultima Online. While UO obviously also took a lot of Ultimas climate, this is not a pure UO expirience, but rather tons of variouls ideas taken from RG's games across the years, smooshed together with other, new or old ideas and put together extremely well.
SOTA is a fairly classic RPG at heart mixed nwith some persistant MMO features. The game is based heavilly on conversation, exporation and combat. All the systems are put together fairly well at this point. but final judgement will have to wait until a more finished state.
I still recomennd the game - it is a worthwile investment if you ever liked a RG game or like promising "classic" RPGs brought into modern systems.

I noticed that someone else complained of the toxic nature of the forums for SotA, and I have to, unfortunately, backup that claim.  I also experienced this early on, getting harassed by forum admins 2x over a year period and I think I posted a total of 4x on the forums.  What else do I need to say?  The atmosphere IS "cult-like" as others have noted and the game itself is not what I was expecting when I put down my $200+ on the Kickstarter and an item or two afterwards.
I was naive to think that the glory days of early UO could be born again.  SotA will not resemble UO in anything more than a shadow.
UPDATE:  So, I finally began playing in 2016.  As you can see I've put in almost 100 hours at the time of this update.  I think it's worth saying that the combat elements do have some merit that I wasn't expecting if you take them from a strategic/card game point of view.
However, the biggest failing of the game is the Unity engine itself.  The towns are oversaturated in items and my machine has yet to run any large map without hiccups on a steady basis.  This isn't my machine failing though, believe me.  This is the game servers themselves that can't keep up with the morass of loot and buildings and player creations, combined with a serious lack of optimization on the part of the dev team.
Overall there is a clunky feeling to the game that really shouldn't be acceptable.  I would have preferred a different approach to be honest, if it would have meant the gameplay would be more like the original Ultima Online, but just with updated graphics, sounds and added quest lines.  And with smoother, fluid gameplay.
Perhaps SotA will improve its engine enough at some point to shock me, but I will not be holding my breath.
I still cannot recommend this game in its current condition (Feb 2017), except to the most diehard of Ultima fans that will be willing to deal with shortcomings.

This game is a culmination of a genius game designers lifes work, a masterpiece.
This game is carefully crafted together using game design systems that have been perfected over time across multiple genres. For example, the skills system enables you to pick glyphs based on how much experience you've gained. Those glyphs are then used to create a deck ( like in magic the gathering ) and that deck is affected by another skill called Focus which will help you draw,discard and use your deck more efficiently. During battle, the glyphs are served to you much like drawing cards from a deck and can be used, combined together or even combined with itself to create more powerful maneuvers during battle.
One of the biggest things this game focuses on is utilizing the community to build the game, many players contribute to the game and become part of the games canon. Community members have coded frameworks for things like electricity and an in game radio that plays a community driven radio station.
There is so much going on with this game it can't be covered here.
Let's also remember that this game is currently in a pre-alpha state at the time of this writing. The game is awesome right now, and will only get more awesome.

Ori and the Blind Forest is one of the most beautiful games I have ever played, seen, or heard.
The soundtrack is a vast, colorful realization of its source material and is to Ori what John Willians and Howard Shore are to Star Wars and Lord of the rings. It is perfect, poignant, and petrifying. Gareth Coker deserves a grammy for this magnum opus; this relentless orchestra of soaring and sinking feelings. I am in love with the music in this game. It will fill your soul and leave it aching.
The visuals are bright, playful, and evocative. Every bounitful section of this Metroid-like adventure is a masterful experiment in color and style. The blues are like the brightest LEDs you have ever seen and the reds are like lava flowing from your monitor. It is jaw dropping every step of the way and always motion. Ori and the Blind Forest is a work of animated art that should be experienced by any gaming enthusiast or skeptic.
The gameplay is fun and concise. The controls will never let you down. If you fail it will be your own fault and you will welcome the challenge with determination. The skill tree and leveling system will feel familiar to anyone familiar with side-scrolling adventures like Super Metroid. New abilities will give you access to new areas and secrets while a skill tree gives you multiple options on how to build your character and explore the world. The pace is addictive and it never feels tiring or over-complicated.
What can I say about the story that wouldn't give away what makes it so amazing? All I can say is that I love Ori and the Blind Forest. It was my favorite game of 2015 and one of my favorite games of all time. More than any other game I have reviewed on Steam I implore you to give Moon Studio's first project a try. You will not regret it.

Ten out of ten.
Story: Simple, but well-written and beautiful. Minimal text. Character voices are cute and mild, not annoying at all. The voiceovers are in another language (maybe a made-up one? I dunno) a la Shadow of the Colossus. Cutscenes are as short as they need to be to tell the story - they never feel too long or boring.
Graphics/Art: Gorgeous. Many many layers in the background and foreground, things moving all the time, pretty glows. Each area has its own distinctive feel, making every area seem fresh.
Mechanics: Some of the later skills take some getting used to, but once you've mastered them they feel effortless. You really can zoom around. Movement feels really smooth. I felt like a parkour badass the whole time.
Level design: Great! The harder puzzles have clever solutions. Lots of variety. Not stupidly hard. I consider myself a gamer of average skill, and this game was challenging enough to be interesting, but never frustrating or tiring.
Music: Great. Beautiful, haunting, bittersweet. The main menu tune might get stuck in your head. Buy the soundtrack. DO IT
TL;DR: Great game. Never gets boring. Every new skill is exciting, secret areas are really fun to hunt down, platforming is smooth and really fun. Beautiful art, music, and general atmosphere. A+ experience throughout.

I'll say right off the bat that I am indeed a fan of the original F.E.A.R. game, I do not like the second one very much, and I think this third game is a complete atrocity. I promise I tried to make this review short, but there's just so much to say... Sorry. Let us begin.
I shall also mention that, at the time of writing this review, I have completed the game twice - once as Fettel, once as the Pointman. I have not yet played the coop, although I'm sure it'll be a grand old time.
Right off the bat, it is glaringly obvious that this game is intended to be cooperative. Is that a bad thing? Well, not inherently, coop shooters have been around for a very long time and there are a couple examples of cooperative horror done right. That is to say, it is still very scary indeed in spite the fact that you are not alone. However, given the fact that F.E.A.R. 3 doesn't deserve to be called a horror game - I'll get to that later - that's a rather moot point. So, you play as either the Point Man from the first game, or his brother Fettel. The Pointman obviously has bullet time, and Fettel the ability to possess enemies for a given time. I will say that the Pointman plays how you expect him to, no problems there, and Fettel is quite fun to play as well with what seems - to me, anyway - to be a rather well fleshed-out special ability. However, at the same time, it seems well balanced to the Pointman's and the enemies around. Although it would not surprise me if it is commonplace to fight to get Fettel over the Pointman.
Getting back on topic, coop in itself is not an issue really, but I do believe that it was one of the big downfalls of this game. I shall elaborate at the end of this review.
The second glaringly obvious addition which made me very upset when I first saw it was the inclusion of a per-level point system, complete with goals to earn you additional points which are snarkily or punnily named. Well, that's not very F.E.A.R.-like at all, now is it? Or horror-game like in general, really. Why, you ask? Well, in terms of U.I. and game mechanics, having a score system - let alone one with a little status menu you can look at in-game (by pressing F1) - kinda breaks the player's immersion. Maybe a post-mission stats screen would be okay, but having nothing at all - like in the last two F.E.A.R. games - would be a lot better. Hell, in the first game, immersion was one of the biggest things they were striving for! Hence the inclusion of such details like a full shadow for the player, good arm models, and the ability to look down and actually see your legs and feet. Same with the stigma the first game had about never taking control away from the player when possible. There were probably two cutscenes in the first game, and most of the times control is taken away from you is a few seconds after something whacked you on your butt and your person gets up, and even then it's almost nice as a breather between the action. This game, on the other hand, of course has that point-system, and cutscenes galore; the things bookending every single level.
Although to be honest, immersion is a bit of a moot point with the lack of actual scares in the game...
Let's get onto the horror elements, now. Or rather the lack-there-of. This game is not a horror game at all, it is a first-person shooter through and through. What makes me say that? Well, there are only four or five times in the entire game where it even tries to scare you or creep you out - and those times a very shortlived and ineffective. Going in fully blind, I didn't even get that sense of dread and not wanting to keep moving forward like I did in the first game. It did make me jump once in fear, although that was when I was walking through a seemingly empty house and an enemy - unintentionally - snuck up behind me and started yelling while clawing at me. T'was unexpected, but I don't think most people would even get scared by that - assuming they were playing it like one should an FPS; keeping their head on a swivel. There really just seemed like a lack of effort with the scares, to be honest. While I am sure they did try their best with the scary moments that
present, keep in mind there's literally
.
Alright, so because this game is an FPS now, let's cover that next.
The short version? It's your standard console shooter. What do I mean by that? Well, we now have regenerating health, a full cover system, a two-weapon carry limit, a very standard assortment of weapons outside of two which are even then not too interesting. You read that right, regenerating health in a F.E.A.R. game. A cover system, too, which I thought at first was kinda nice and was a change I'd be indifferent too. However, about midway through the game on my first run, I had a realization; the cover system was killing the pace of the combat. Hell, there's practically no need for the Pointman's bullet time given this. Just play it like you would Gears of War or similar and you're good to go. There's no panic or amazing action like in the first game, where there was no cover, and you had to be quick and clever to take out a whole squad. Though this was helped by a normal - or nowadays 'old school' - health system which, of course, gave you one-hundred points of health, and up to ten medkits which healed you a certain amount at the press of a button. Here, even if you try and replicate the amazing shootouts you remember from the original F.E.A.R. - and even the second game to a lesser extent - you're going to die, because the very nature of the regenerating health system doesn't allow such things. Even if you pull it off, you're just handicapping yourself really.
However, then I had a thought. I stopped thinking about it as a F.E.A.R. game. Suddenly things got a lot better. This isn't a lazy, poorly made cash-in in my eyes, it was just made with the wrong license. If this game didn't have the F.E.A.R. title attatched to it, I would like it a hellofalot more. There was effort put in, and it is certainly fun to play at points, and at it's worst it's just like any other standard MMS (Modern Military Shooter), and I'm sure it'll be a blast when I get around to coop. It just shouldn't have been a F.E.A.R. game.
While this is byfar the worst game in the F.E.A.R. franchise, but it's not a bad game on its own. Unless you count modern shooters bad, and I don't disagree with you if you do.

I've been excited for this game since I saw the trailer (which is the prologue for the game) for the first time. I remember tearing up and getting goosebumbs from watching the trailer so I was very excited for what was in store for me.
As I played this game, I fell more and more in love with it and it exceeded all my expectations for the game, which were very high to begin with. Not only is it a piece of art visually speaking, the story was very engaging and emotional, with the soundtrack being on par the whole time, delivering everything from songs that made you tear up, to songs that make you want to try over and over again, urging you to never give up.
I would lie if I said I didn’t become frustrated while playing this game, but the frustration was never towards the game or anything, it was directed towards myself. See, this game doesn’t hold your hand. They introduce you to your new skills when you get them but in stressful situations, it’s your own memory of how those skills can be used and your own skill as a player that’s important.
Making a game like this would not have been possible if the game didn’t have the extremly precise, tight and responsive controls that it has and that’s why you’re never angry at the game when playing, because it’s always your own skill and ability to make the best of a situation that matters.
I love this game, if you haven’t noticed. If I would have one complaint about the game it’d be the lack of replayability. Sure, I can replay the game to get some of the achievements (some which require you to finish the game in 3 hours or beating the game without dying) but other than those achievements there’s nothing making me wanna replay the game right away.
Still, I HIGHLY recommend this game as it's, in my opinion, one of the greatest gaming experiences this last decade.

You play as a fluffy little creature, that got me to buy this game.
The art and music is amazing, that got me to pay attention to this game.
The platforming is fun, and the combat is very simple but satisfying! That got me to have fun with this game.
The difficulty ramps up, that got me to stay interested in this game.
The story is breathtaking... that got me to get emotionally attached to this game.
This game is one of the best story-driven games I've played,  if not THE best.
When you beat this game, or go far enough and get bored. Play it over from the beginning. You catch some things that you would have otherwise missed.
Much like Metroid games, and some other open-world platformers. There are some secret ways to "cheat" the system and get somewhere before you're normally able to, you are usually rewarded with an extra life cell (heart container) or energy cell (mana upgrade). I earned several pickups like this, and felt proud getting them, then I progressed a bit further and got a new ability that made the area easier to get to.
Before you even get to the gameplay, you see a ton of story, through an interactive prologue (takes about 5-10 minutes). When tragedy strikes, you wander off and start your real adventure. Nothing is explained to you, except that you see something that you need to get to, and you have nothing left to stay home for..
If the prologue gets you to cry, watch out for the rest of the story.. especially when you get to your second playthrough. Understanding the situation makes the emotions even stronger, could even flip your entire view of the story upside down.
Onto the gameplay, it's a simple platformer. Run, jump, avoid hazards, etc. Until you find some stuff you can't pass through, which hurts you when you touch it. Then you find your "weapon" and now you can get past that barrier, but enemies also appear and you need to fight them off.
As you progress, you earn new skills, such as a double jump and the ability to climb walls. And much like Metroid, you often get these skills after being thrown into a point-of-no-return, where the only way out is with the new skill, giving you time to learn it.
You earn experience from defeated enemies and other tasks. When you fill your experience guage, you gain an ability point. You can spend this point on new abilities, these range from new attacks, pickups being dragged towards you like a magnet, more defense, more damage, even seeing certain rare powerups on the map.
At any time (when not in immediate danger) you can hold a button to save the game, when you die you immediately return to that save point, with all progress lost since the save. The game lets you save often, so do it.
Whenever you die, it is almost always your fault. There are some events that may surprise you and cause you to lose, but during these it will automatically save at the beginning, and not allow you to save in the middle to prevent getting stuck. These escape sequences can be a bit frustrating at times, but never too much.
The combat is simple, based around where your player is. The attacks are homing, so there is no need to aim (until a certain skill later in the game, which is used for much, much more than just attacking), just stand in range of the enemy and press buttons in various patterns while avoiding the enemy's attacks.
The story is something that simply must be experienced personally, it is amazing and deserves all of your attention.
This game is simply beautiful. The art, the music, the characters, the story, everything is beautiful! It really succeeds at capturing the player in the world. If you've got $20 to spare, and enjoy platformers, give it a try. If you rage easily, this may not be for you because the difficulty really ramps up towards the middle of the game.

I was expecting Ori and the Blind Forest to be good.  That illusion was quickly shattered.  Five minutes in, I had a huge grin on my face and realized I underestimated this game.  About ten minutes later, I knew this game would be something special.
Before I continue, there is one matter I must touch upon.  A few days ago, it was announced Ori is getting a Definitive Edition this fall (same year standard version released).  For most games, I'd cry cashgrab. But with Ori, I'm glad.  More Ori for me, and a well-deserved second wind for GotY awards while exposing Ori to a larger audience.
PRESENTATION
Anyways back to the review.  The presentation is simply phenomenal in all regards. Foregrounds, backgrounds, and animation ALL look amazing.  At times mistakable for something from Miyazaki/Ghibli or classic Disney.  Very rarely, effects and lighting will make it to hard to see yourself, but it's worth it to keep the gorgeous art.
The music and sound are wonderful, and features several recurring themes.  Whether it be the incredibly upbeat piece during Naru and Ori's adorable fruit gathering adventure in the prologue, or the calming yet thrilling music of the difficult end segment of the Ginso Tree that keeps you going "one more time" for 20 more times.
The story has a great blend of show AND tell which keeps it exceptionally effective, despite being simpler and getting far less screentime than something like Dust (let alone a major RPG). Usually events are handled extremely quickly, typically within either 5-20 seconds of in-engine events or 1-3 text boxes, then you're playing again.  There are about six exceptions that go on over a minute: the amazing playable prologue, the ending, and about 4 scenes that occur midgame.
GAMEPLAY
The gameplay can be described as a 2D Metroidvania, but squarely focused on platforming with some light puzzle solving over combat.  Controls are fast and highly responsive, you press jump and you jump right away. Combat exists, but giving your main attack omnidirectional auto-homing was an intentional choice made to keeps the main focus on little Ori's movement.
Most of the game can be played anywhere from fast and risky to slow and methodical.  However, there are some challenging setpieces, and the first is of those is a forced "rush it or die" situation.  Nothing ever achieves Super Meat Boy insanity, but Ori occasionally dips into the lower end of Rayman's treasure chases.  Luckily, death is minor as you respawn very quickly and an early skill let's you set down your own checkpoints.
NITPICKS-Nothing unforgivable, but worth mentioning.
1]Certain areas become permenantly locked off.  Meaning an extra playthru to 100%
2]There is no ingame option to change what buttons do.
3]The amazing setpiece moments can be brutal on a first playthru.
4]The voices are not in English and sometimes one voiced word comes out to a full text box.
5]I'd love seeing Ori in Smash Bros, but as Microsoft published Ori, chances are poor.
CONCLUSION
.  When I first cleared the game and the end credts began, I got out of my chair and gave a standing ovation.
RATING
9/10, VERY HIGHLY RECOMMENDED, and the current frontrunner for my GotY.

I will not recommend this game because of the following:
First of all, I must say that this one of the most beautiful games I have played in my life in terms of artistic visuals. The story is also beautiful and you may drop a few tears with its emotional plot. The soundtracks are exquisite and fit well within the story.
But, don't be lured by the smooth-looking cover and the beautiful soundtrack. You may shed of few drops of tears of emotion but most of your tears will be out of rage. This game is SADISTICALLY hard. It will squeeze the s**t out of you. It will make you want to smash your computer. I don't know what kind of pleasure the devs have in making us strain like hell while making us believe it is a nice and lovely game. This game is as hard as Mario Forever and you need to be precise to the nearest millimetre and millisecond. You keep dying over and over again and you need to keep trying. You even need to use things that kill you to advance in the game. You have no options. You cannot even go back to certain areas once you finish them and even if you saved before that, you still cannot.

New to fighting games? You could go play Street Fighter IV and get thrown in the deep end with just a list of character chains to perform, but you won't learn anything that way.
You wont know anything about Mix-ups, hit confirmation, overheads, cross ups and how to block them. This is why I recommend anyone new to fighting games to play Skullgirls. It actually teaches you important game mechanics with an excellent tutorial, which is something Street Fighter IV fails at completely.
The game is heavily influenced by Marvel vs Capcom 2 from what I can tell .. because I played that game to death back in the early 2000s ... it plays exactly the same, with team assists, snapback attacks, ground recovery, super jumps, air dashes and hyper combos ... errr I mean Blockbuster Attacks .. :)
Combos are clean and feel great to perform and its not hard to rack up hits with just some basic chains.
The art style is great and the music and sounds are very fitting. Character art is very "anime", while it might not appeal to some I like it a lot.
Highly recommended.

I'm not surprised that reviews are mixed. Like many games, if your expectations are right, you won't be disappointed. For patient lovers of politics and building up an "empire" - this game is a winner. But, expectations...
1) This is a wargame. In wars, sometimes you lose. Pick the wrong friends..♥♥♥♥♥♥off the wrong people - and you will get crushed. Plan carefully, you'll do the crushing. BUT if you are the victim, rebuilding is not that hard. Just about all players face some losses from time to time.
2) This is a perpetual world game. It is always running. You can't go away and come back a few days later and expect to find everything as you left it. You need to spend a little time each day. If you are around 1+ years, that time can climb to 1-2 hours/day pretty easily.
3) "Free to play" - hmmm - yes, it is possible, but you probably will not be as satisfied. You can do quite well on $10-$15/month
4) "Pay to win" - the worlds are so big with so many players that, while a person spending a LOT of money will  have some advantages which can be large, they aren't big enough that they can dominate the game. They can control a piece of the world. Overall, I think the game mechanics make it difficult  to pay to win - and sustain it for a long time.
5) Its a social game. Like all social games, if you find a good bunch of folks, you'll be happy. If you end up with a bunch of trolls around you - you won't. If that happens, abandon your villages and go elsewhere...or to another world.
Between industry, army, and politics, the games has something for everybody. But if you are playing the game for fancy graphics, elaborate story-telling, great music - nope, not here.  The game mechanics are simple, and gameplay can seem to be redundant - but that's really where strategy and politics make the game interesting.

This 'Gauntlet' is an action RPG shooter with large open spaces and hordes of monsters running at you, while the original Gauntlet games were more maze games where you had to find the exit and outsmart the monsters doing it (yes there were hordes of monsters back then as well).

The nostalgia is strong with this one, I was ten years old in 1985 & my favourite game at the local Arcades was Gauntlet. I played this to death with my friends and this remake does the original justice. Another game from the same era was Smash TV, it involved kiting yourself around avoiding waves of incoming enemy's. There are many similarities between the two games, both involved avoiding zerging waves of enemies which created a high thrill "seat of your pants" gameplay. Gauntlet can be compared to many games including Diablo and other action RPG's though it is still very unique in its style. This was a genre defining game that has never been equalled and without doubt is a must play for all Action RPG fans. I give this remake a 9/10, it is very true to the original and that's what makes it great.
WARNING: This is not a game for those who need Epic L00t as there is none. The gear you unlock by completing certain stages at different difficulty levels is purely cosmetic. Relics and Mastery levels add some abilities and increased power to your characters but these are the only none cosmetic customisations available.

This is actually a surprisingly fun and addictive game. I really was not expecting too much from this game as I have already heard that its purposes from the devs were to be the surpasser of the original 1985 Gauntlet and not Dark Legacy or Legends, but I am silenced by its gameplay and mechanics. The masteries, relics, and loadout armors definitely keep you hooked, regardless of soloing or group play! I would most certainly recommend using an Xbox 360 controller with this game as it is much easier than mouse/keyboard.

When I first saw previews of The Division I was simply blown away. The wait for the game became simply excruciating. At the time I couldn't imagine a game that I wanted to play more. Then time passed, slowly my excitement waned, and it released. I forgot about it. It wasn't until a good while after it launched that I realized it was already out. So I read reviews to see how great it was (it must be...right?)
They didn't have nice things to say. And so, bummed out, I passed on it. Fast forward to a few years later, I took some medicine that I will not disclose the name of but just tell you that it can severely impair your judgement and woke up the next day with no memory of the night before and got on my computer to find The Division (and several other games) in my library. Great... I zombie-bought all these games. I figured I should at least try The Division up to two hours before refunding it so that I can at least see for myself what is wrong with it. The short answer; nothing at all. It's superb.
The long answer; from what I've gathered, Massive/Ubisoft have updated and polished the game so well having had enough time that it easily the best game of it's kind. (Looking at you Destiny) There is a plethora of extremely diverse and engaging end-game content thanks partly to all the amazing additions added with the DLC, a particular standout being the Survival game mode. But the base game without the DLC has a great amount/variety of end-game content too. Plus, everything leading up to end game is fantastic as well, some would even argue it's the best part of the game but I disagree as I enjoy the end-game loot quest more.
I highly suggest buying the game and the DLC if you are a fan of the genre as it perfects the formula and most critically, in comparison to other genre leader Destiny, it actually has a tangible end-game that isn't some short, shallow pathetic excuse of an end-game for casuals. I rate it a 9/10

I love the combat system in this game. It's freeform/organic, has surprising depth and every ability has it's uses. There's a ton of enemy variety on display here and they all have some kind of weakness to exploit. Not all of which are the obvious use fire on ice enemy, etc.. The story doesn't take itself seriously in the slightest. Lots of 4th wall breaking and self referential humor. There's a crap ton of hidden items/loot to collect. And for the most part every single new piece of equipment is unique. With it's own stats, element, procs, counters, etc.. The game is pretty linear with a few optional areas to spice things up. And finally, if you crank the difficulty up the game can get pretty challenging. Especially the boss fights. It's easily the best tradition RPG I've come across on steam. Well worth your time.

Combining CBFPS and a progression Grinding works, your gear gets better and your number gets bigger with the randomized loot that drops, or bought from NPCs. Map progression through a very lifelike dead city, with interactive enviorment of missions, collectables, and encounters, each with its own little intro and storyline information, helping you understand the story behind The Division. Collectible phone conversations, laptops, and cool 3D "echoes" also help out giving great backstory and filling the meat on The Divisions bones!
The Story is not lacking or bad, but.. unimportant? You never get the feel that the world is in peril, even though the many phone conversations and lore objects like files and laptops are sometimes very dramatic. Youre there to shoot stuff, not save the world from some virus. But if you dont run around for hours looking for all of them, you might not understand why or what you doing.
Gameplay is great! The shooting is fast paced, but not ridiculus. Usage of cover and flanking manouvers really help you out, as if you simply sit and spray from one place the enemies will flank you. Enemie AI seems to range alittle, sometimes they run up to your face and let you shoot it off, othertimes they are smart with good usage of grenades and flanking. You can play solo, but having a buddy or two really helps the fun, and the game has built in a great matchmaking system letting you team up with other players to tackle the hardest missions.
Unused or old gear can be sold or dissmantled, which will grant you crafting materials to craft new gear, with blueprints gotten from mission rewards. Also vendors do sell decent gear if you are unlucky with drops, or get loaded with cash. Good ways of making sure you will be able to get better gear.
All in all, i recomend this game if you do like what I have described. I reached level 23 out of 30 on the free weekend, so the game is not at all slow to level up and progress, by the time you are feeling done with an area, you are ready to procceed to the next.
So get out there and save this city, soldier!!

Secrets of Rætikon is a flight-based puzzle platformer with a gorgeous low-poly aesthetic, nimble controls, and some excellent and imaginative setpieces. It's hampered a bit by technical issues, punishing item-collection requirements, and -- depending on your point of view -- how the final section of the game works. I'll talk more on that later with a spoiler warning.
You control a bird-like creature trying to activate a large machine with an unknown purpose. You explore several large forest and cave environments to collect the energy you need. Along the way, you'll encounter by a variety of flora and fauna, some peaceful, some hostile, and find runes that expand the lore of the world once you translate them. The translation element was really impressive to me, and seemed to embody the philosophy of the game: a high level of trust for the player to intuit and understand what was necessary without explicit hints or hand-holding.
This sort of thing is a high-wire act in puzzle-platformers or adventure games, rarely tried since the early 90s. Done wrong, it's baffling and arbitrary, and leads to players getting lost and failing to understand quirks of the game's mechanics that aren't explained. Done well, it gives an immense satisfaction that you had a creative idea and it actually worked. I had several of these moments playing Rætikon.
Translating the runes isn't automatic even as you pick up the letters, and your bird character has to cling to the rune stone while you're trying to decipher what it says, still able to be attacked (or drown if the rune is underwater). Similarly, some machines and environmental challenges are presented with no clues about what they're for or how to interact with and navigate them. I was careful to keep track of artifacts I found, where I had left them, and where they might be necessary, and the game rewarded me for it in a way I wasn't expecting. Trusting the player to bring their A-game and be patient and resourceful enough to figure it out is a huge risk, likely to alienate a lot of players, but the rewards are similarly big in a way that's hard to quantify.
The game unfortunately has some the technical issues common in indie development, like objects getting lost behind foreground elements (most indicate the presence with an outline, but not all), or the player character getting stuck under heavy objects or inside level geometry (uncommon, but it can happen). There's only one auto-save and no manual save system. Every single sliver is required to finish the game, although you have a button that will indicate where nearby ones are. Hostile animals are difficult to actually fight off as you don't have an attack button, but you can grab them or use the environment to damage and kill them (I actually like how the ability to attack is almost accidental, an indirect result of the grabbing mechanic). The environments are almost too large, some taking a long time to traverse empty space or backtrack many screens carrying different objects when you're not sure where they go.
Overall, I appreciated the approach of this game and had a lot of fun playing it. There's one caveat, which is hard to explain without spoiling anything, so avoid this if you don't want to risk it.

If you are looking for a shoot 'em up type game - this isn't it.  If you want an RPG, open-world, MMO - this isn't it.
This game is something rather new, and while it's hardly perfect, it is very enjoyable, relatively peaceful (a word another reviewer used that I think is well suited to the game) game, and it has a fair amount of content.
Sometimes it can feel empty - certainly you can feel alone.  But there are some good challenges in the game, some good progression in updating your equipment, learning languages, learning how to craft, and where to find the stuff you need to make the next thing you want.  And there are some central goals in the game - but the bottom line?  This is a game of exploration - of wandering around on a planet generated especially for you, that no one else has ever seen, and discovering the things that are unique about it - and the things that aren't so unique.
If you can't imagine yourself wandering around on a planet for several hours, cataloging new alien species and plant-life, finding upgrades and new technology, meeting aliens and learning how to speak with them, finding alien artifacts, etc. - this isn't the game for you.  But I've really enjoyed it, and I hope they keep adding more content, and more complexity to the game so I can continue to enjoy it for a long time to come.

It's a peaceful game, it's also pretty, sure I could complain about the fact it didn't give me what I was looking for like everyone else but for what it's worth, they did make something unique. If you are looking for something to relax to and listen to good music, this game is for you, I'd say it's a Work in Progress but it's a good one.

Everytime I give up, I take a break for a few months, then try to get back to it but the journal and quests are so bad I never remember what I'm supposed to do and where I'm supposed to go.
The story, quests and dialogues are so BORING it kills all the fun of the excellent combat system. Basically the main story is a retake of the Pandora Box, and almost every quest goes like this :
- talk to an NPC and go through 10 pages of USELESS filler dialogue to get the quest
- an entry is added to your journal telling you NOTHING about what you're supposed to do
- just keep doing the main quest or explore the world randomly until you get to the area where you'll find what you're looking for after 10 hours of play
- get back to the NPC to get your reward
In other words the quests just solve themselves when you get to a certain point and I hate that, I don't feel like I'm actively doing the quests, I just wait for stuff to happen. A good example is the quest with Sam's collar that you get really early. You can explore the whole world, you'll never find it until you get to that optional cave and beat the big "sea spider" thing under the pirate cove with the orcs, but only after you've defeated the undead pirate captain to get the key to the big black door. You just randomly stumble on the collar there, and the ghost of a woman to solve the lighthouse quest at the same time, because why the f*** not ?
Sometimes you'll just get to an area to see 3 or 4 quests being solved at the same time and you don't even know what you did to solve them.
Another problem is that the game is waaaaaay too long. After 60 hours I felt like I was barely halfway through, and it probably lasts for 100+ hours. It reminds me of another RPG I could never finish : Kingdom of Amalur. Like D:OS, this game had fun combat and gameplay, but the story, quests, dialogues and characters were all uninteresting, and it was way too long.
The companions are also really uninteresting, almost worse than Pillars of eterenity and DA:Inquisition combined. I used Madora and Jahan on my first playthrough but didn't care one bit about their story, same with Bairdotr later. Wolgraff seemed to be more interesting but my main character was already a scoundrel, having two of them would have been a waste.
And then there is the UI and inventory. OMG that inventory always full of useless stuff, and you always have to transfer this or that to your character with the identify skill, then identify all the loot one by one, they give each item to each character to compare if it's better or not than what they have, then give all the useless stuff to the character able to carry all that stuff because it weighs a ton, then you have to give all that stuff to the character with the best bartering skill and reputation to sell everything to a vendor...

I really wanted to like this game.  It has several features that helped pull me in.  Some of which are the single player and friends only multiplayer because I am tired of games that end up focusing more on PVP content and end up having people just farming kills on lower level less geared players.  Another nice feature is the open class system where you can choose how to play your character by selecting skills from a number of skill trees.  I also enjoy the crafting aspect of mmo's and this game has a very robust crafting system, to the extent where crafting at this time is more tedious then it is rewarding.  The crafting system has a long way to go and the game is still in pre-alpha so there will be a lot of improvement.
The combat system in this game was at first glance good.  The way it works is you pick the abilities you want your character to have available and the game will randomly place those abilities out on your action bar.  Using your mouse to drag and drop the random abilities you could stack like abilities to make them stronger or combine two abilities to create a unique combo.  This was something new and I had not seen it done until now.  And at first I liked it. After using the system I found myself  watching for abilities to stack or combos to create and not watching the action.  I would much rather be able to see what my character is doing or the effects it is having on my opponent.  The standard defense you will hear is that you can lock your abilities and not have to worry about watching the bar.  If you do that you will find your character severely handicapped and the game becomes just another insert your favorite mmorpg here  clone.

Bloons TD5 is a full release of a popular browser game, Bloons Tower Defense. I hadn't heard of it, but the positive reviews and bright screenshots caught my eye when the price dropped to 75% off in a sale. When I installed the game and started it up, I got a message from no less than three friends stating their love of Bloons. I was also accused of living under a rock since I hadn't heard of it.
So, being a simple rock dweller who has not played the browser/flash versions of BTD, I can only give my opinion as a fan of tower defense games.
The premise, like most TD games, is simple, something is attacking, and you must defend! In this case, balloons are attacking. Their motives are unknown. Probably they wish to pillage our villages and take advantage of our women. If one slips by you, you lose a life and get that much closer to failing the level.
The balloons start out simple - regular red balloons you can pop with one hit. They quickly advance to multi-layered balloons, lead balloons that can only be popped by explosions, camouflaged balloons which must be detected, ceramic balloons, or even balloon blimps that explode into a myriad of other balloons when popped.
As you can guess, your defenses must advance as well! Starting from the simple dart thrower, you will advance to bomb towers, ninja monkeys who can see invisible enemies, minigun monkeys, mortar towers, glue guns to slow the horde of incoming balloons, or ships that can pull a whole blimp out of the sky. Every tower can be upgraded as well, and there are two upgrade paths you can choose to pursue. When you take all this into consideration with the fact there are 21 individual tower types, there are a TON of options and strategies.
There are also over 40 tracks, 4 difficulties, and the option to play each track in reverse. You can also use the currency you get for beating each track to unlock permanent upgrades to attributes such as attack speed, starting money, popping power, etc. or other bonuses such as Double Cash Mode, and one that increases the range of the Monkey Village (a tower that gives an aura increasing the power of your other towers).
My one qualm with the game is, it seems to get a bit too easy once you unlock Double Cash Mode and the Monkey Village range increase. It takes the game from a respectable challenge on normal difficulty, to very easy even on the harder difficulties. But there is still plenty of replay value, and I am still challenged on Impoppable (the hardest difficulty).
I also love the visual style, and it runs smoothly even when there are thousands of balloons on my screen. It will start to lag a bit if you get to the higher levels in freeplay mode. I also really appreciate some of the quality of life additions, like the option to automatically run through the levels (ie. skip the pause time in between levels) for experienced players. It's also handy for quick replays of easy missions.
I've got 30 hours on Bloons and I'm nowhere near done yet! One of the best $2.50 impulse buys I have made.

This is a really fun tower defense game for about 20 - 30 hours, at which point you should have reached level 49 and have all the different tower upgrades. At that point there is still a lot to do in the game. In fact, way too much to do in the game. There are so many levels and power ups and achievements and whatnot that either you'll buckle down and decide to put the extra 50 - 100 hours playing all the levels, getting all the medals and everything else or you'll force yourself to write a review and delete the game.
Probably one of biggest pushes in the second direction was realizing that the strategies for each regular level don't need to vary so much for success. Special missions and daily challenges force you to get more creative but don't add a whole lot to making the game fun again. It's like continuing to play Mario 64 after you get the special triple jump - there's nothing really left to do except mess around, and there are just too many other games or things to do at this point to make a 30 hour game a 100 hour game.
Still, those were 30 good TD hours. Had the developers made me think it would have only taken 60 to get everything, I probably would have tricked myself into doing it.

Naturally once people realized that the game was not an independent shooter and was actually published by a big name corporation they pretended that they didn't like it as much as they really did.
When the sequel came out it recieved pretty much nothing but praise because all of the nerds that want to look cool and pretend they don't like something popular couldn't deny the fact that they all fired off a couple broken arrows to the thought of Alma slamming them against the wall and taking their virginity with her haunted hot pocket.
As for the third game, it recieved a relatively "eh" reception. At this point I would have to agree, but only if you take the story into account. I prefer to ignore the story completely. Anyone who is a huge fan of the previous Gauntlet for the N64 is in for a real let down. When they said, "The classic Gauntlet ... returns in a completely new experience!" They weren't kidding...

Warrior- Next to useless, DPS, Good timed-based attacks.
Valkyrie- Infinite defence against everything besides AOE, next to useless.
Ranger- Dodge skill, ranged base attacks.
Wizard- Magicka-esque controlls. Combination of 3 skills for various effects. Completely steals majority of loot.
Level design have zero regards for the previous Gauntlet since they're short, very boring and leave no impressions like, "Oh, remember that one time at the sand level..."

I was pleasantly suprised by this game when I discovered it was a significant improvment on its predecessors. I enjoyed playing both the original arcade version of Gauntlet Legends and the PS 2 Gauntlet Dark Legacy.

Each character actually has unique abilities/skills (for once) which make them better in different combat situations.
Can be challenging at times, instead of everyone blowing up everything instantly.
Fair voice acting and dialogue
Moody atmosphere as opposed to really cheesy music blaring constantly.
Secret areas require some thought and perception instead of firing weapons randomly and hoping to hit something.
Boss fights more innovative and less hit-until-dead.
Cons:
Sometimes a bit laggy, even with computers that have good specs.
Fairly short compared to Dark Legacy, but not a terribly short game overall.
All in all, I would give this game a 9.5/10 for its significant gameplay and graphical improvements while still holding true to the feeling of the original games. A solid and well-rounded game with a hint of the childhood classic we remember.
