Secrets of Rætikon is a somewhat visually interesting game without much lore or depth of gameplay to it.  Or rather, it might be better to say that the lore is hard to keep in mind when it is there (and is confusing anyway) and the gameplay is just a tad bit wonky enough to be offputting.
The gameplay loop is more or less: As a bird, explore > find shards > use shards to get crystal > carry crystal back to the start of the game.  This can be a little frustrating due to a lack of map, and the game often has aircurrents and 'invisible' ceilings (just max elevation for your bird to fly) so you cant always expect to be able to take straightforward paths.  Exploration can reward you with an anagram cypher so you can read various runes around the game world on obelisks, but its not really easy to do so because its not automatically translated for you, hence why I said the lore is hard to keep in mind.  Its a lot of mental effort to try to guess out letters without the whole codex.
Finding shards is more or less easy, but the crystal carrying can be a different matter.  The other animals in the world will attack you or steal the crystal from you as you try to carry it back and make you have to chase them down to get it back.  This just feels frustrating and like your time is being wasted, it isn't fun.  The controls are passable, but I never felt like they were amazing and executing the needed moves to chase down elusive enemies or avoid attacks can be a pain.  Gameplay just never felt good.  I only kept playing because I had started playing and presumably was progressing towards finishing.
Lore wise?  Was hard to keep in mind when I played the game, but I really can't say I remembered any of it.  I got all but one or two of the needed crystals to roll the credits then just gave up on the game.  I looked up the ending on youtube and it feels like a bit of a rediculous jab by the way of the developer.  Sure it can be interesting to have a joke on the expense of the player but if the other party can't figure out the joke and you dont explain it to them then its not funny or 'deep.'  I just sort of shrug my shoulders at this part, there wasn't enough of a story to be meaningful.
I wouldn't recommend it.

Honestly one of the best fallouts to this day. Fallout 3 is one of the most expansive open world games I have played in a very long time and is one of the best games developed by bethesda by far!

-Excellent plotline
-Wide variety of playstyles
-Fun character customization and levelup processes
-Huge open world to play in
-Liam Neeson voices your father
-Massive amount of content for the price
-Massive replayability
-Buggy
-Compatibility issues with newer systems is common
-VATS is basically required in order to use guns effectively
-Some stats are decidedly more useful than others
Fallout 3 was Bethesda's first foray into the Fallout universe, and it was also Fallout's first three dimensional game.  The graphics are about on par with Elder Scrolls: Oblivion, and the open world has the same feel to it.  The game is amazing and fun and a huge time sink if you take the time to explore everything.  NPCs range from deeply well developed, to entertaining, to annoying, and everything in between.  Leveling up oftentimes can open up entire new ways of playing the game, and exploration is always rewarded.  Bethesda is known for their open world games, and they did a great job here as well.  It's worth the buy if you like... well, anything Bethesda has done in the past decade.  It's likely you won't encountered everything in one playthrough, and any serious encounter will have multiple solutions, making the replay value of this game through the roof.
The DLC is all included in the GOTY edition, but the vanilla brand Fallout 3 is available on Steam as well if you want to save a few bucks.  You'll have to pay to buy the DLC for that version however, which makes this version more cost efficient.
The game crashes frequently, and has compatibility issues with newer systems, particularly Windows 8 and up.  But if you can't get it to play consistently, you can always refund it within the first 2 hours of gameplay, so there's no harm in buying just to see if you can play it on your computer.  Additionally, because this is Bethesda's first attempt, they hadn't quite figured out gunfights.  Hip-shooting is comically inaccurate, and VATS is required in order to have any real shot at hitting things beyond melee range.  This is resolved in New Vegas and Fallout 4, but in Fallout 3, Perception and Agility are both must-haves if you plan on using ranged weapons of any variety.
Still, these are very minor issues.  The game is easy to become immersed in, and I often found myself in game for several hours longer than I intended just finishing that "one last thing" before quitting.  I played the whole game once before getting it on steam in a sale, and replaying it years later, it's as good as I remember it being.  Pick it up if you're itching for more Fallout and haven't experienced this one yet.
Definitely worth the money

Wonderful art set in a 1940's era, smooth animations that lead to bombastic attacks and a varied cast, both in appearance and gameplay, allow this game to stand heads and shoulders above others in its genre.
Because of its fairly modest cast (which is constantly growing) each character is an archetype for their playstyle: Cerebella is
definitive grappler, Peacock is
definitive zoner.  Because of this, each character is polarized and all play very different from one another.
Unlike almost every other fighting game, Skullgirls is constantly being balanced and patched instead of releasing an "Ultimate" or "Second Impact" version of the game for full retail price, meaning you will always have the most updated version.
In regards to DLC, Lab Zero kindly gives out their downloadable characters for free for the first three months after they've been released.
In addition, Skullgirls offers the best tutorial and training modes of any fighting game, making it a great introduction for newcomers wanting to learn.
That said, the game is not without flaws; its biggest is, perhaps, merely its genre.  Fighting games are not easy to get into: it takes practice to simply perform basic motions for special moves consistently and even more to use those moves effectively during an actual fight.  Timing and distance are also difficult factors in fighting games and while Skullgirls is more lenient than others, they are still very inflexible.   Even with its excellent tutorial, you are told to use "MK" or "HP" rather than the keys you've assigned to medium kick or hard punch and even then the input scroll along the bottom shows your inputs as if you're using a fighting stick instead of a keyboard or controller, meaning you have to do some conversion in your head to find what you've done and what the game wants you to do.  If this is your introduction to fighting games, you will need to put some dedication into learning the game.
On a personal note, I'm not a fan of the default button layout: A,S,D are the three punches, Z,X,C are kicks, the arrow keys are movement and right Enter and F are start and select respectively.  It feels more comfortable having movement on the left side and attack buttons on the right and even then some motions like performing a quick 360 on a keyboard are difficult.  I'd very much recommend using a controller or fight stick if they're PC compatible.
Skullgirls is an excellent fighter.  It's a good starting point for anyone interested in the genre but will take some time for new players to get the ropes.  Once mastered however the game is a blast, chock full of a myriad of special moves, glamorous blockbusters and "Holy Crap" moments that'll keep you playing for ages.

"Ask and it will be given; seek and you will find; knock and the door will be opened."
SOTA is an older-school MMORPG sandbox.  Similar what is alluded to in the quote above, the game has to be explored with an open mind to be found.  SOTA can seem small and short on reward at first.  But its size and rewards become apparent for those willing to spend the time to go see them.  Exploration reveals many scenes richly decorated.  Within these scenes can be found hidden features including dungeon entrances.  While each of these dungeons provides an adventure of their own, many also connect as a nework to form a broader underworld. Finally a game that uses dungeons again as open transit and adventure space for random players to find themselves together in instead of group-only instancing.
Similarly, SOTA's lore is often in view but also has to be found.  With no NPCs with exclamation points above their heads, one has to engage NPCs in towns and learn their stories, which may give side quests or intertwine with the game's main story lines, within which the Avatar's journey to understand their virtous (or not) destiny is enshrouded.  Here the virtues are at play, you choices and deeds subtley influencing how you are judged (for some later grand purpose).  This feature, with its chat-text-driven quest dialog about the virtues is, perhaps, the greatest throwback to old Ultimas that SOTA presently has.
SOTA really attempts to innovate with its combat system.  The game offers what may be an unprecendent level of flexibility in how skills are accessed.  One can choose to use a fully locked deck of skills like many common MMOs, totally randomize the draw of all of the skills available to the player using a deck system, or customize the skill bar with a combination of both.  Moreover, the system allows auto-attacking or charged attack options too.  On the skills front, with a number of armor, melee, magic and tactical skill trees that a player can choose to train, untrain, and retrain without a defined class system,  the game offers a maximum level of character skill selection freedom that negates the need to reroll characters or have required alts.  Lastly, advancement is skill, not character level, based.  The more one uses a skill, the more it levels.  In practice this means that a player will find themselves tracking the leveling of 40+ skills instead of watching one character level, providing for more obvious signs of character development progress while gaming.
The game's player-owned town and player-housing are also significant features.  Built with sand box flexibility in mind, even in a pre-release state the game already allows superior player owned town and house game play.  I've literally lost days configuring and reconfiguring a player keep, there are just so many choices for decoration and improvements keep coming to allow more all the time.  All of this is fueled by a strong player crafting system which delivers much of the game's itemized content.  I think SOTA falls short on adventure loot drops, but what it drops in resources more than makes up for what players are able to craft from those resources to fuel the economy.
Overall SOTA is a great, if still developing game, for those looking for a smaller, tighter-knit sandbox MMO experience that allows some impact on the game world.  I've played many AAA MMOs that allowed for almost no real world interaction.  SOTA is much different.  On the other hand, those looking for a totally seemless world with an utterly vast map might feel that this is not their game on first look.  Just keep in mind that games with smaller surficial worlds (DDO is another example) are sometimes deceiving in their true adventure size.

If you do have enormous faith in the venerable Lord British, despite games like Tabula Rasa under his belt, the first thing you’ll notice are constant load screens and the lack of an interactive, open world.  You may have not known, or forgotten, how games of 15-20 years ago were like this.  You might be thinking this this game is surely an evolution over the 10 year old World of Warcraft, or atlest better than the orignal Ultimate On-line.  Think again.  Load screens.  LOTS OF LOAD SCREENS. Run in a straight line for 60 seconds in any direction, and chances are you'll either hit some kind of invisible wall, impassable terrain object, or a load screen. These unity scenes/zones are similar to the original Everquest, although I feel the Original EverQuest had larger zones.
I should also point out, that graphics in these zones, and your character models, are terrible, and the animations laughable.  The combat mechanics are also tab targeted, sloppy, and have little of the innovations of recent, modern MMOs.  There are no telegraphed hit boxes or twitch skill based combat of more modern MMOs, but there ARE fireballs that track you through objects and hit you no matter how move, and ugly, muddy mobs that skate through the terrain and hit you with massive reach.
Well it's Early Access, right?  Well, 7 Days to Die is also Early Access and also uses Unity (the same engine) but has none of these issues of SotA and remains an exciting, open deformable world on a much smaller budget.  So what is happening with SotA to make it go so far afield?  Was the 6+ million it gathered so far not enough? Lack of design talent? Lack of programmer skill? Lack of time?  I'm sure there will be many excuses, but the end result is the same.  Wait to buy.

What to say about this game? It's beautiful.
Motion around the game is crisp, and overall gameplay centers more around using the different movement skills you acquire during the course of the game to figure out how to get you from where you are to where you need to be, with a small amount of puzzling, rather than on taking out all the enemies (which aren't terribly numerous) in your path.
The game can potentially get frustrating at times though, especially where certain areas require you to execute a sequence of motions with near flawlessness because you are racing against a clock, and a missed jump will send you all the way back to the very beginning to try again. This may not be the game for you if you are not somebody who is willing to keep on trying the same challenge over and over again until you get it just right; some of the more difficult ones took me several dozen attempts to nail down. At the end of the game I was averaging a bit under one death for every minute of playtime.
The soundtrack is amazing, a good blend of both the atmospheric and melodic, and well integrated into each environment or scene. Sound design is pretty decent overall, and I have to point out the absolutely cute gasp Ori makes when he surfaces to breathe after swimming underwater.
The artwork and visuals are completely gorgeous. Everything felt like a seamless painting. About the only complaint here is that glowy item pickups sometimes look too similar to glowy projectiles which you don't want to hit.
Add to that a great story that sets everything up nicely at the beginning, intervenes here and there as you progress through the map to direct you onwards, giving tidbits along the way about why everything is happening, and then culminates in a finale that left me sniffling through the credits sequence.
Perhaps not a game that you might play through a second time, unless you're looking to find the areas you missed, or to challenge yourself to the more difficult achievements (under 3 hours? without spending any ability points? without dying?!? O_o). That said, look forward to a treat should you decide to venture through the game at least once.

The game looks gorgeous, and there is plenty of voice-acting, but I just can't seem to get myself over the early-game blues. It's missing that special something; it's failed to awaken that magic spark of interest in me.
To be honest, I find the game over-tuned and unnecessarily difficult, even on the easiest setting. Everything moves so slowly, and I don't just mean combat. I don't mind turn-based combat, but I feel like the characters are constantly walking through mud. It took me nearly 3 hours of play time just to get to the first real combat zone, and once I've gotten there, I've found the combat is stacked against me and incredibly unfun. Too many enemies that seem to get too many attacks and have too many abilities. I'm fighting simple skeletons and they're all constantly healing each other and casting resurrection on themselves (lol what kind of skeleton archers are able to cast healing and resurrection???)
I've been reading tips online on how to do better, and it's a mix of impolite "git guds" and "you need to have your party built in this specific way." I guess I don't wholly have a problem with that, except that the game gives you way too many ineffective options at the beginning. Why are there all these classes to choose from if most of them are the "wrong" class? I feel like I'm being pigeon-holed into a very specific role and I do not enjoy that at all.
I guess I just don't get this game. I was expecting something more along the lines of Baldur's Gate from my childhood (of which I've recently finished again both the first and second enhanced editions on Normal difficulty).
I don't know. I must be missing something.
There are a lot of other negative reviews about the pacing of the game and the storywriting, and I also have to agree with their assessments as well. The plot is very, very rushed in the beginning, and there's hardly any time to even get to know my own character before I'm suddenly - and I must say, rather randomly - whisked away into some kind of space fortress and appointed as the Savior of the Universe. It was a really blunt and uninspired plot device which became even laughable when I was then cast back down to the real world only to then get slaughted by a bunch of level 4 skeletons.
I don't get this game. Playing it bothers me on some deep level, like rubbing two pieces of tinfoil together.

<My first hour:>
Customized two characters for my party.  Appreciated the graphics and turn based combat, which has substantial depth.  Had to restart and lower it to "normal" difficulty.  Did the tutorial dungeon, some nice physics (you can burn out poison clouds with fire, throw covers on gas grates).  Made it to the first town.  I have a letter of introduction, but the two gate guards are illiterate and won't let us in. AI Player #2 Mors Gotha (the antagonist of Ultima Underworld 2 and a name that I've used for years) is set to "rascal" personality and insists we attack the guards for insulting us.  I caution against it, and lose a few rounds of scissor rock paper.  She wins and attacks the guards.  We defeat them and enter town.  Suddenly orcs attack.... during the battle, I hear townspeople yelling for the missing guards by name.  After the battle, I return to the scene of the crime and notice another legionairre examining their bodies and asking what happened to them.  I say nothing.
Currently talking to a couple guards, one who has a love-potion-charmed-feral-orc as a girlfriend, I'm voting we let love take it's course, Mors is saying it's not permanent she tried a potion on me without any luck.  Despite putting a point into Charm to make me better at scissor, rock, paper -- Mors Gotha wins again.  And we bash the orc's head in and she dies.  The guard runs away crying.  I'd say it's off to a good start.
<Halfway or so thru: The continuing misadventures of Mors Gotha, the Good Idea Fairy:>
I'm now hooked.  Bottom line is it may very reminiscent of the feel of the Ultima series, which was my favorite growing up (I did play the 2002 Divinity and liked it and thought it was well written, but this is far better).  I liked this game enough that I bought part 2 during the Christmas sale and plan on playing it next.  I like the combat -- although I tell myself I like "turn based," I find most games far too inferior to X-Com 2 to be fun.  Not here.  This combat here is pretty tactical, there are alot of options and possible outcomes and I like the fights.  The AI seems pretty good, I've seen a lone unit run to another squad and I've seen them use environmental effects against me. But they also aren't omniscient enough to know I'm immune to Frost and try freezing me (which is fine).  The game looks good on big screen and is optimized for controller (the only negative is to  hide helmets you have to log in once as keyboard, took me half the game to find that out).  I'll skip plot points but I like the story so far, and you effectively have your own base you can build up.  I also like that although it's a D&D variant system, it's not so alien I feel like I have to learn a new language just to play.  There is some nuance to it and making the builds you want, but I got the hang of it.  Also, it may be the best videogame voice acting I've ever heard -- I rarely skip through the speech.
And about that Mors Gotha, although I have +Charm items and statpoints to make it easier to win at scissor rock paper (currently 6 to her 2 points), she occassionally wins.  She is almost always the Bad Idea Fairy.  Like the original murder of the city guards, when she wins I just let her win and see where the game takes me.  She insisted on guessing the obviously wrong answer to a riddle, and we had to kill the mushroom ring riddlekeepers.  She turned down the "thieves guild" type missions in Silverglen.  Just now she insisted on beating a talking chicken to death, for basically no good reason.  The ones I overrule her are funny too, no Mors lets not beat the crying Orc to death and take his dead brother's burial armor.  It probably sucks anyway, Mors.  She occassionally agrees without argument, so it's not that she's always deliberately contrarian -- but it's a neat game element that I've never quite seen like this.
A+, all around.  Why haven't I played this sooner?

The environment is almost NEVER an issue, presumably because sub zero temperatures mean nothing when you have a parka and a scarf. Oh, and that irradiated building? TLDR: Just wander around until your numbers are high enough to wander around somewhere else.

I've had nothing but a good time playing this game.
It's a JRPG style turn based combat game, with an overworld map exploration aspect to it (secrets to be found, items that open up new areas and paths usually to treasure in old areas).
There are no random encounters, and only optional enemies respawn; once you clear a 'path-blocking' encounter it remains cleared.  Turn-based combat with a focus on using skills/spells that the enemies are weak to, with a party-wide 'summon meter', lots of items and equipment to be had all with varying effects to them such as "randomly summons a wooly mammoth to fall from the sky onto an enemy each round", "randomly blesses the character", "counters attacks with xxxxx skill" things like that.
The humor in the character/NPC dialogs is light hearted if a bit geared towards a younger crowd (not kids though).
Fans of turn based RPGs should give this one a shot, it's very easy to play in short bursts when you feel that RPG itch, or you can get 30+ hours out of it like I have so far!

Well here's the 4th game or this amazing serie.
EBF4 is a classic-styled RPG : Turn by turn combats, Équipments, Magics, Element system, ALL the Items, Aventure!!!
The game's tags already spoil it all, nothing new.
There are only 2 things you find less often in that one game tho' :
- Grinding.... ooooooh the grinding... very glad you didn't corrupt this game.
- Random battles. Yes yes! YOU decide when the action scenes starts!
The musics are amazing, so much i'm currently listening to them from the in-game gallery. Amazing idea to have more than one battle theme too, it prevents them to get repetitive too much.
The game is funny and you might need a second playthough to spot and/or get all the references mentionned in the short but frequent character's lines.
The game difficulty can be changed at will in the game's settings, so it's hard for me to give a negative point by saying that the Epic difficulty mode really can make you remember to save after every fight. Of course you could flee the battle and come back later if they are too strong for you... but really sometime you simply don't see the insta-death attack coming.
Except for the bosses, the first 10 levels gives you short and enjoyable battles with basic tutorial windows that pop-up so new players aren't too lost. After you get to level 20-22 tho', battles can sometime get long and repetitive, especially with a high difficulty setting. Because the enemy monsters usually matches the current place you are in, it can happen that you just want to see some differant landscape in hope to see the foes also change accordingly... as you will stay in some specific 'biomes' for quite a few battles.
The generous amount of ready-to-be-opened-gold-trimmed chests usually help you to not get too tired of these long 4-waves battles.
The playable characters slightly lack some personality and backstory, yes, but i guess it's the perfect occasion for the 5th title to be even better that this one. Those who already played ( and loved ) the 3rd game should not see any problems with that tho'.
The price is fair, and the game deserves every single of the 9 points I can give out of 10.

Bloons TD 5 is a very fun and addicting game. As Ninja Kiwi's most popular and rapidly-expanding game, Bloons TD 5 has found its way to Steam. It's not very unreasonably priced, nor is it identical to the flash version. This version of Bloons TD 5 is similar to the one released for iOS and mobile, as it includes way more maps as well as three new towers - the monkey engineer, the bloonchipper, and the submarine. The game is interactive, as you can play with friends cooperatively, and there are a vast amount of settings for each of the levels to keep the player busy. The harder, faster modes offer a more challenging take on the game, though easy/medium mode is fairly simple for anyone to play. The game is really straightforward. Basically you start off with a designated amount of money, which is used to fund towers (usually monkeys). The towers attack the balloons (or bloons) that zip through the track every round. As the amount of bloons and their variations increase, the towers must be upgraded for more concise gameplay. The more medals you win, the more levels you unlock and the more achievements you earn. You also get monkey money that can be used to purchase extras or "special agents" to be used in-game. It runs smoothly so there's no problems there. The game doesn't take up much space on a computer (unlike other games). Personally, I greatly enjoy this game. I played the original version a lot before, so I was excited to venture into this broader form of the game. Leveling up the towers while battling the huge bloons is thrilling and challenging. This is also a much better option than getting Bloons TD 5 Deluxe, as all of the content from that game is available in this one. I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys tower defense games or has played any games within the Bloons franchise before.

Im a mid 40's old school CRPG player who played countless hours of Ultima 7, Ultima 4 and even Ultima 8. Im an Ultima Online vet as well so I jumped at the chance to back this during Kickstarter.
I'm honestly scratching my head over this new game by Richard Garriot, its not at all what I've come to expect from him. He used to be very cutting edge with technology, or at least give it his best shot to be cutting edge. Playing this game really makes me reflect back at some of his failures: Ultima 9 which was released in a partially undeveloped state, Ultima X which was partially developed but never released, Ultima Online 2 which was actually advertised on the back of the U9 Jewel case that never came out, and finally Tabula Rasa's back and forth development and eventual closure.
All of these games Garriot pointed fingers and really accepted none of the blame for what happened to them. Listening to his interviews, Im afraid he suffers from hubris and is honestly out of touch with the gamers who loved his games in the 80's. In playing Shroud of the Avatar, the ideas are solid but the delivery is not. Currently there is nothing engaging about the game. The cash shop and the prices for in game items currently should be a red flag. Im used to cash shops but the amounts being charged are hardly worth it, especially for what is being currently delivered.
The graphics and animations of the game are incredibly poor. The character models themselves have a clay like appearance and the hair, especially the facial hair, look terrible. In some cases the facial hair actually floats like a turd on the upper lip of your character which is suppose to be a mustache. Think Everquest 2 style but not quite as good with obvious texture placement issues.
I hate to say it, but I truly believe that all of his past failures are just that.. his failures. He deserves credit for creating some of the most revolutionary CRPG's and being a true pioneer of game development, but hes definitely not as technical savvy as he was in the 80's.  Ultima Online was brilliant, but as soon as PC's started really pushing the envelope on CPU and GPU technology, is when Richard Garriot failed to keep up.
I still have hopes that this game gets cleaned up, but as it sits now I would definitely not recommend it to anyone.

I didn't think it was possible to turn a slow-paced, freeform game like a god simulator into a compulsive skinner box, yet here we are.
Once you get past the tutorial, you realize the game proper ends after a set time, during which you have to clear challenges to unlock new upgrades and technologies. So you have to keep playing one short morsel of a game after another to progress. There's a freeplay mode, but it's limited to what you managed to unlock.
And yet, you can't go *too* fast either, because of the greed mechanic. Villages that acquire resources too fast get greedy, and start waging war on other villages and will even try to kill you, ending the game prematurely. There are ways to prevent this, but they're only vaguely covered in the tutorial.
And by the the time you managed to unlock everything, the game's practically over because in the end there really isn't much to do. It's both rigid and shallow, and it ultimately comes down to memorizing synergies to bolster resource acquirement. So the truth of the matter is that all the limitations are there to squeeze as much game time as possible out of what little game there actually is.
In short: stay away from this game if you still have some self-respect.

Lot's of fun.  There's a steady progression through the achievements, and the achievements unlock things in-game to allow you to play longer, builder higher level buildings, etc.  Each round is quick, lasting up to 2 hours.
The gameplay is pretty simple and straight forward.  However, as others have mentioned, there is a certain level of effort required to 'remember' which buildings go with what powers, etc.  I see that as a positive thing, because it means you either use someone's build from the wiki(which I'm not a fan of) or you actually use your own brain and think ahead about what you want to accomplish.
Games are short, lasting 30, 60, or 120 minutes.  To progress you have to do achievements, so the pattern is pretty simple.  Pick achievements you want to try to get in the next game you play, then build cities that are aimed at those achievements.  Utilize buildings and powers that help you reach those achievements.  Game ends; get achievements; rinse and repeat.
I find it to be a lot of fun doing this.  There's a certain level of replayability in Reus as-is, but the achievements are basically there to force you to think about different ways to advance a city,  different ways to get people to wage war on each other, etc.  This is opposed to a lot of strategy games where it's always the same build order, always the same strategy, and steamroll until the end-game condition - all off of a 'strategy' you find on a wiki.

Wonderful art set in a 1940's era, smooth animations that lead to bombastic attacks and a varied cast, both in appearance and gameplay, allow this game to stand heads and shoulders above others in its genre.
Because of its fairly modest cast (which is constantly growing) each character is an archetype for their playstyle: Cerebella is
definitive grappler, Peacock is
definitive zoner.  Because of this, each character is polarized and all play very different from one another.
Unlike almost every other fighting game, Skullgirls is constantly being balanced and patched instead of releasing an "Ultimate" or "Second Impact" version of the game for full retail price, meaning you will always have the most updated version.
In regards to DLC, Lab Zero kindly gives out their downloadable characters for free for the first three months after they've been released.
In addition, Skullgirls offers the best tutorial and training modes of any fighting game, making it a great introduction for newcomers wanting to learn.
That said, the game is not without flaws; its biggest is, perhaps, merely its genre.  Fighting games are not easy to get into: it takes practice to simply perform basic motions for special moves consistently and even more to use those moves effectively during an actual fight.  Timing and distance are also difficult factors in fighting games and while Skullgirls is more lenient than others, they are still very inflexible.   Even with its excellent tutorial, you are told to use "MK" or "HP" rather than the keys you've assigned to medium kick or hard punch and even then the input scroll along the bottom shows your inputs as if you're using a fighting stick instead of a keyboard or controller, meaning you have to do some conversion in your head to find what you've done and what the game wants you to do.  If this is your introduction to fighting games, you will need to put some dedication into learning the game.
On a personal note, I'm not a fan of the default button layout: A,S,D are the three punches, Z,X,C are kicks, the arrow keys are movement and right Enter and F are start and select respectively.  It feels more comfortable having movement on the left side and attack buttons on the right and even then some motions like performing a quick 360 on a keyboard are difficult.  I'd very much recommend using a controller or fight stick if they're PC compatible.
Skullgirls is an excellent fighter.  It's a good starting point for anyone interested in the genre but will take some time for new players to get the ropes.  Once mastered however the game is a blast, chock full of a myriad of special moves, glamorous blockbusters and "Holy Crap" moments that'll keep you playing for ages.

1) New to Fear ? If so, then start here. If you've played any F.E.A.R game before go on to section (2).
Fear is a combination of "Bullet Time" shooter and walking simulator. So there will be sections of each level that are arenas for gunfights, and then there will be areas that are you walking around while "spoooky" things happen. A few sections combine the two, but they are mostly segregated experiences.
I would reccomend you don't start with this game. Instead you should play FEAR 2 (which does everything this game does but better) or F.E.A.R (The original) because its has the best enemy A.I that you will EVER find in a fps game. This game was mainly built for Co-Op play. The problem is that these Co-OP systems are only semi-optional. They are very intrusive in the single-player experience.
If you're looking for a co-op fps , this isn't bad, (though it is a bit buggy, but nothing too horrible).
2) I avoided this game for a long time because of the common wisdom that it just wasn't good compared ot the previous 2 games.
That is true...but
The campaign is about *half* ish as long as the second game. You're meant to replay the game as Fettel (the ghost brother) . But his gameplay experience isn't so much different that you'd want to replay the game over again.
The co-op and multiplayer systems are not bad,  but they aren't really anything special either.
The game does have some very nice "scary" sections in some places. It also does *try* to provide a satisfying conclusion to the *story*
Everything is in service to the multiplayer systems however, including the story.
I could only see this being reccomended if you can get it for a very low price or if you want a decent 3-8 hour multiplayer experience.

Ori and the Blind Forest is a very solid game in the "metroidvania" genre.
Gameplay mechanics are well thoughtout and implemented. I never found myself frustrated by them, and generally had fun, particularly with the bash skill. One could argue that this skill makes the other ones rather pointless, but it didn't bother me.
The game is typically all about exploring an area to find the next skill, while killing ennemies and navigating around traps set in the map. While there are some puzzles to solve, they're all simple enough that you won't get stuck because you can't figure out what to do. The beginning might be a little frustrating because there are few designated save points and you need to create the others, but you get past this "hurdle" pretty quickly. There are also a couple of instances of fast-paced platforming action, fitting a "die and retry" style. These sections are challenging enough to warrant a few fails, but clearly not so hard as to♥♥♥♥♥♥you off.
Controls are tight and work as intended.
The soundtrack is excellent and fits with the game very well. I did had to drop the bass levels on my sound system because there are too many explosion sounds when dealing with ennemies. I recommend you either do this or turn down sound effects, the default balance isn't the best.
Ori and the other characters are cute as ♥♥♥♥. Some of the cutscenes genuinely made me smile or sad. I can't even remember another game that had that effect
While this is an excellent game, it does have its flaws.
There's a particular game design flaw that I find very annoying: some collectibles were put in areas you can't return to. While I have nothing against the use of one time areas/puzzles, I don't find it's a good decision to force a player who wants 100% to restart because he missed one energy cell in the first third of the game, even if it's a short one.
I also didn't like that you can't go back to your save file after you've completed it, but I honestly can't remember if the game warns you about it. You can find a powershell script on the forums that allows you to go back to your game and even one time areas if you want to go for missing collectibles, but there's one you can't get if you missed it the first time.
The game is short. It took me around 6h to beat (5h34 in game time). While this encourages additional playthroughs, I did wish for a little more.
Some achievements seem glitched. While this isn't relevant to the in-game experience, I somehow don't feel like trying for the speedrunning, ironman and minimalist runs if I'm not sure I'll get my "reward" at the end. I do like to have something to show for my efforts
In spite of this, Ori and the Blind Forest remains a very good game. The characters, music and overall universe will make it excellent for you if you're open to it.

This is a through explanation on the gameplay:
It's like clash royale but more simple. You have no archer tower, you only have one king(master) tower. You can choose your king(master) from a variety of kings(masters) and each of them have their own different skills. Also your lane and the opponents lane are connected by bridges. You will have control over a bridge if your minion is the last one there(standing or passing over the bridge) and vice versa. Controlling the bridge will make you level up faster. Yes your king(master) have level. Everybody start on level 0 and will start gaining xp to level up with the max being level 3. ## Bemusing in game story aside from my first few hours in Richard Garriott's world... I am hooked.
In all seriousness, many of the Greenlight reviews are written by cretins that shouldn't be granted the privledge of following a game from ALPHA to GOLD. Are there lemons here? Yes, but this is not one of them.
I remember fondly the 'alpha" and "beta" of Ultima Online. That odd penninsula I started off on, with no clue what to do next. How barren the world was and lastly how slowly it came together. I was there when Lord British was assassinated. The shock and awe that act rippled across the community and became the stuff of legend. Oh, and the community - role players and dreamers that grew up on a diet of Ultima and were looking once again not only to leave our world and become the Avatar, but to share those experiences with others. UO was special.
I also remember Tabula Rasa - an ingenious, woefully underrated MMO that died far sooner than it deserved to. Tabula Rasa was special.
That is the pedigree I see once again unfolding with not only Uncle Richard G back at the helm, but the infamous Starr "Lord Blackthorn" Long (whom, if I might add, gained a wealth of experience post-Origin at Disney Interactive.)
While still very early in Alpha, you can see this world taking shape and it has much more potential than the short sighted are seeing with the negative reviews.
* Quality of talent behind the game (BLACKTHORN VS BRITISH II: Electric Steampunk Magical Boogaloo)
* The text based interactivity - invoking SCUMM LucasArts, early Sierra and of course Infocom games (or to get really technical the MUDs, MOOS and MUSHEs of telnet yesteryear.) Say hello to engage with an NPC; goodbye, farewell or fare thee well to disengage.
* Level of fidelity - at first I thought the titles serving as NPC names were place holders... how wrong was I. On a hunch I asked an NPC her name, and suddenly her floating name tag changed to reflect her name, not Barmaid anymore. Want to know who an NPC is? Just ask. Knowing the level of interaction in old Ultima and Ultima Underworld games, I wouldn't be surprised to encounter in the future an NPC that lies or refuses to even tell you their name. Love it. Little things like your signature appearing when making a transaction on the "bill of sale."
* Thriving community - already many plots that player houses can occupy are filled. Homes are already established, decorated with crafted and found goods. Entire guilds building crafting areas to teach newcomers. I see here the foundations of what made the Ultima Online community special coming together here. Nay, there is already an awesome community.
* Interesting combat system - I am really, really digging the glyph and deck building system for moves. Adds an interesting dynamic to the traditional static toolbar of abilities. Looking forward to seeing it progress.
* The Overhead Map <TM>: Soon with new and improved roaming monsters! ** FLASHBACKS ** Love it.
That is just some of the things that jumped out to me. I finally realized I was entitled to a steam key so decided to stop using the windows version and go for the ease of having it part of the Steam library, so hours played don't reflect how much I've been sucked in since release 14.  Is the world still barren? Yes, of course it is. Are single player content and storyline (Episode 1) in the game yet? Nope. Are animations still early and need much fine tuning? Yes. But for an early alpha, with so many systems starting to fall into place from crafting to combat, to what is already there and the talent behind this I will be watching and checking in ravenously with each new release, gladly accepting wipes and starting fresh. Also weekly updates - I wonder how many upvotes some other titles receive by some of the negative reviewers here - titles where devs go silent for months? Food for thought when reading the negative reviews. Like with Chris Robert's Star Citizen, there is something new from the devs every week. The Origin veterans are doing it so right (can't wait to see what the vets behind Underworld Ascension come up with - they too are dropping weekly content nuggets and not even out of Kickstarter yet. Do some of the younger gamers here even realize the legacy of the Origin vets?)
This is the apology letter for the Ultima IX collectors edition I got on release day that was buggy to all hell. I loved it once it was patched, but it wasn't as "Ultima" as it should have been. The return of Lord British with Shroud is something every gamer worth his weight in water should be supporting. They are taking feedback; they are asking for bug reports. This is already a special title  and can be more. If you know your gaming roots, and know what Ultima titles can provide when Lord British is on top of his game, then rather than bashing an incomplete very early build (which is asinine - sorry), it would be more productive to help make what could become one of the top 5 RPGs of the next decade.

Scribblenauts Unlimited is a game where you play as Max, a cartoon characer in a side scrolling world consisting of many different themed places. The goal is to use your creativity to summon creatures and objects the solve the problems of the people through out the world using a magic pencil.
The game excels at being a basic, sandbox where the player can summon a variety of different objects to change the world they are in. The games strongest point is that it is extremely flexible in what you are allowed to create. For children and young teenagers, the game has lots to offer as being a fun sandbox to mess around in.
As an adult though, while the game is extremely flexible compared to other games, there game suffers from having a limited selection of items that should be in the game. It is recommended you try to take the simplest approach to the tasks in the game if you are trying for completion.
The game also suffers from having very specific requirements to complete quests, especially as the game progresses. Some quests require knowledge of a specific aspect of culture or a joke in order to complete, and can be confusing for adults and children alike. Many of the optional in game challenges can be frustrating because of this.
Overall, this is a game designed for younger people and will probably have a limited amount of enjoyment for adults. It's worth the money if you enjoy playing all the way though it, but it does tend to get dull. Recommended for children, not recommended for adults.

NOTE: If you end up not purchasing this title, I encourage you to read the last spoilered-out part of this review, which deals with the, in my opinion, worthy and relevant message of the game.
The game begins with your bird-character falling from the sky into a gorgeusly rendered forest. Apart from a few tutorial messages explaining the controls, you aren't told anything about what you're expected to do. You will soon find out that you are supposed to collect slivers, which you can turn into crystals at shrines, and then bring the crystals back to your base. During your journey you can collect runes that will help you translate ancient tablets (although it is quite easy to translate them even without getting the runes).  It looks like everything is in place to make this an enjoyable exploration-based experience.
And then you start encountering enemies, who promptly show you who is the boss in this forest. Unlike you they have reliable attacks and can move around much more gracefully. Your character has no reliable way of fighting (you can try dropping stuff on your enemies or luring/dragging them into thorns). Evasion won't work 100% of time either, since you seem to have a much clumsier "flight model" than your adversaries, who will often be coming at you from several angles and are about as fast as you (not to mention that you will often be carrying objects, which slow you down considerably). The biggest problems by far are the magpies, who will try to snatch away the crystals you're carrying. It's a nightmare to get the crystal back from them, and to get out of their range before they steal it again truly requires the stars to align. The developer recommends using a controller for this game, but even while using one, I was fuming with anger and frustration. I can't imagine playing this game on a keyboard. The levels seem to be designed with maximum frustration in mind as well, with wind and other obstacles getting into your way just when you need every bit of speed you can muster. It doesn't help that you will have to deal with the same challenges everytime you're backtracking home with a crystal, which makes the game extremely tedious.
About halfway through the game I've started thinking about what snarky review I was going to write. I came up with: "Pros: Will make you go out into the woods; Cons: in order to horribly maim and murder woodland creatures and burn it all down." Then came the ending,
Fortunately, I wasn't furious enough with the woodland creatures to miss the message of the game. The people complaining about the brutality and "senselessness" of the ending  have actually missed it in the most ironically hilarious of ways. See,

This game ranks as one of the biggest disappoints of my life and disturbed four people that represent three generations of gamers. Good job Broken Rules!  We all need therapy now!
As you can see from the screenshots, Raetikon is visually stunning, with gorgeous graphical design and an engrossing world.  It plays like a simple Metroidvania type game that relies on puzzle elements.  Areas are gated off behind a "collect the bits" mechanic, but everything is so pretty, you don't even mind.  The creature designs are origami given life.  You play as a weird bird with shoes, that controls very much like the arcade game Joust, which works very well and seems fluid.  The game dumps you right into the action, leaving you to figure things out, which is refreshing with all the hand holding these days.  The story is pieced together by collecting runes to decipher ancient tablets, a gimmick that my kids and mother both enjoyed as they worked together to crack the code.  It's not a necessary thing to accomplish to beat the game, but a nice side diversion.  The music is also suitably haunting.
Sounds good so far, and it is.  We enjoyed the laid back pacing that I would liken to the exploration of Proteus or Journey.  Some have complained of the difficulty, but I had no issues, and only died once, in the bramble maze while being reckless.  And there's two major issues with this short little game.
BUG.  I have seen on forums where the developer promised to fix this over a year ago and guess what?  They didn't.  It's still there.  If you open the areas in an order that the developers did not intend, the game becomes impossible to complete the traditional way.  You get to a point where you are short three gold slivers to progress, and they simply do NOT exist if you mistakenly tackled the areas in the wrong order.  This happened to me and the only way past it is through ANOTHER BUG that allows you to access the end areas by an obscure method.  We wandered around for almost two hours backtracking, thinking that we were just missing a few slivers.  It was triple checked, so I hit the internet and found mention of this bug on a forum.  None of this was repaired as promised, so do NOT leave the area above the evil tree for last or you will have problems.
FINALLY... it's the ending.  It IS memorable, you can't take that away from it, but does it ever kill a bit of your soul and leave a bad taste in your mouth.  You go from heroic hope to stupid and evil.
SPOILERS!!!
....
....
...it seems through the whole adventure of Secrets of Raetikon that you are trying to save animals in cages.  Yet at the end, you find out that you kill them and use their blood/essence to power a primitive game of Pong.  After the credits, it dumps you into free roaming mode.  The real horror is here, for not only did you murder the caged animals, but EVERY SINGLE animal on the planet.  Everything is dead.  Everything.  So your stupid bird could play Pong.  It's depressing and senseless.
We had talked about how fun it would be to just go back and replay it but that's not happening now.  Your journey seems pointless, tainted and corrupted.  Raetikon leaves a black splotch on your heart and a dead feeling in your soul.  My kids were disturbed, and my mother was so messed up she watched several Let's Plays on youtube just to see other rections and if there's another ending.... the answer is NO.  No other endings.  You can't change it.
Therefore, I have a hard time recommending it, even though it's this lovely, wonderful game up until the end.
If you don't mind absurdly bad endings and would like a game that combines Castlevania:SOTN, Journey, Proteus and Joust together, then give this a shot.  Personally, I doubt we will ever play it again.  We discovered the Secrets of Raetikon afterall...
The secret was... the ending sucks.
Fly around and solve puzzles while trying to not get murdered by other birds. It's kinda short, but has some neat puzzle designs and an interesting message to the whole thing.

Originally, I was unable to play Secrets of Raetikon because my old computer was ridiculously slow. After upgrading and moving all my games over, it played fine.
The first thing is the art. Secrets of Raetikon is a gorgeously different game, with elements that bring you back to the "good days" of gaming. I personally had no trouble with the game mechanics. I rarely found it difficult or frustrating to move around in the game. Others have complained that the birds stealing cores from you made the game unplayable; I disagree. I thought it was a fun challenge that was not overly difficult. And yes; the ending is messed up.
I enjoyed this game. I found it entertaining and a good way to spend a day.

Secrets of Rætikon is almost a good game.  The art style is absolutely gorgeous.  It really gives a good sense of some hidden fallen world that has been overrun by nature.  Additionally the core feeling of flight was nailed down perfectly.  Just being able to fly around and pick things up is actually quite a joy.  Being able to fly around the areas and explore the little nooks and crannies that have little secrets hidden in them is really fun.
Then there is the rest of the game.  The core gameplay loop is that you go around and collect little gems.  You then find a machine that you put the gems in.  When you’ve put enough gems in the machine it then gives you a bigger gem that you need to drag back to the central hub and put it into a great machine.  While doing this, every single animal tries to steal the item away from you and prevent you from putting it into the machine.  This would probably be somewhat tolerable, except that there is really only one path connecting all of these machines so instead of the big machine acting as say a hub that then links you to different areas, you end up going through the same areas over and over in excessive backtracking that wears on you and becomes monotonous after a while.
There is a backstory written on little rune stones that are located throughout the world, but the runes are somewhat obnoxious to read.  They are just written in a strange font and so you have to go around and collect items that tell you which character is which English character.  When you read the rune stones though all it does is put up the font conversions on the side of the screen so you still have to manually go through and look up the letters to figure out what was written.  It becomes very annoying after a while especially because most of the rune stones don’t have anything very interesting to say.
Lastly there is the ending.  Without spoiling it, I will say that the game ends on a pretty forced message that makes you question why the developers even decided to make this game in the first place if that was their point, because obviously they don’t respect you playing it.  Though even then that might just be what I think that they are trying to say because the execution is pretty poor.
Which I guess is the best way to describe Secrets of Rætikon.  Some good ideas.  A few executed very well, but the majority executed quite poorly into a wholly unsatisfying experience.

While there are a couple downsides(and only a couple,) Epic Battle Fantasy 4 features many positive aspects of classic RPG gameplay, while also lightheartedly poking fun at RPG, anime, and video game tropes. It's cheap, too, so you should definitely pick up a copy!
+ RPG: It's oldschool!
+ Options: All there
+ Graphics: Cute, colorful, and with nice animations.
+ UI: Remembering the last used spells is sooo convenient!
+ Humor: Very much present.
+ Price: Low, especially for playtime.
+ References: EVERYWHERE.
+ Variety: ALSO EVERYWHERE.
+ Combat: It will keep you doing different things.
- Not higher resolution!
- KB Mode still requires mouse
+/- You'll have to fight alot of waves of monsters.
+/- You'll also have to backtrack quite a few times.
Epic Battle Fantasy Four...now that's a name! Like its name, EBF4 seems to be a parody of all things RPG. It sports fairly good writing, self-aware humor, a wealth of items to find, and the equipment all has unique art assets. We're off to a good start! So what's the story like?
It's a bit like this. You're a girl from a small woodland village. Three protagonists from the previous titles in the series have ransacked your village, and its prized jewel is gone! You track them down and force them to join up with you, after realizing they didn't steal the jewel, as repayment for their pillaging. You then go on to the next village to find their jewel is also gone. Okay, you should grab some popcorn for this: The jewels are meant to be seperated, and when brought together could spell doom for humankind. This is because of Catgod. Yes. Catgod. Catgod created the world, and all its creatures. It created cats in its image, but became jealous of their relationship with humans, and decided to take the cats' arm and legs, and destroy their greatest works in the world. Now someone, maybe these cats, wants to even out the punishment! You must take your lovable band of misfits and stop them!
So, we're already in for an interesting ride. What else is there you ask? Read on!
This is the kind of game where the more I play, the more I appreciate it. There is humor in spades, which sometimes falls flat for me, but it's very self-aware, so I still appreciate it. Something also everywhere is references, and I LOVE references! Other things are also everywhere, such as: skills, summons, equipment, upgrades, monsters, quests, hidden treasure, and barriers blocking your path.
The graphics are cute, with much of the stuff in the game sporting decent and equally cute animations. There are plenty of options in the settings menu. There are overworld monsters, so when you feel like skipping battles, you can. The blockades barring your way actually keep things interesting, since your equipment will all remain useful depending on what enemies you are fighting, and everything in this game can be upgraded or scales with your level. This sets a great pace for exploration, and encourages you to find all the hidden unblocked treasures you can get your grubby hands on.
Progression has a good curve. You'll level up, find items, get new weapons, and clear areas at a steady pace. There's also a lot of content to this game, for only 12$ off sale, so you'll get your money's worth, too. The game likes to parody cliches found in anime, games, movies, you name it. The humor will keep you going even if the gameplay gets old, and if it does, a quick break is all it ever took for me to fix that.
For example, I once started a battle with a woolly mammoth to then inadvertantly drop a woolly mammoth on top of it right after my party commented about how tough the fight would be. I was close to taking a break, but instead laughed plentifully and wanted to keep going. There are plenty of other nice things that will keep the game convenient and easy to play like the ability to scan monsters and instantly see their strengths and weaknesses, the ability to leave a battle without having to play a minigame or roll dice, zone teleports, instant healing slimecats, recently used spells list, and more!
Getting around in Epic Battle Fantasy 4 is easy. The UI is simple enough, although slightly clunky. There are keyboard and mouse movement options, but keyboard mode still requires the mouse for battles, unfortunately, and there's no controller support. The game also maxes out at 720p, which is quite low for modern displays. There is also, on the negative end, ocassional lag and stuttering. There are plenty of settings to mess with so you can likely find a setting that fixes that for you.
All in all you'll want to experience this game for the story, humor, characters, references, varied battles, and sheer number of items, equipment, and potential upgrades.

EBF 4 is a turn-based RPG inspired by games like Final Fantasy and Golden Sun. It's the first of the series to be on steam, as the others were browser games on websites like Kongregate and Armor Games. I  remember playing one of the EBF games, although I don't remember which one. I don't remember much, so I wasn't sure what to expect.
There are quite a few unique mechanics in EBF 4. First, the backup mechanic requires one of your four people to be in "backup", and therefore not fighing, who can be switched in without using a turn. At first I hated the mechanic, but I grew attached to it and it does make for some interesting situations. Second, when you win a battle, you get AP. This is how you obtain and upgrade skills, as not a single skill is learned through leveling. Skills in the "special" catagory can be learned by two or more different party members, but only one can actually learn it. For example, Anna and Natalie can both learn heal, but if Natalie knows it, then Anna can't. Which, I recommend you do just that, but that's just what I do.
There is also "waves" system where if a battle has three waves, you have to clear out three screens worth of enemies. This is backed by the fact that all enemies are on the map, and you can engage them at any time and flee at any time, with the only punishment for flee being that the hurt or killed enemies reset.
One of the things I love about this game is that both hardcore RPG fans and newcomers to RPG's can both enjoy the game. There are ten elements and twelve status effects, every enemy has unique resistances and weaknesses to elements, statuses, and debuffs, your party's weapons give them elemental normal attacks and armor give elements and status resists and weaknesses, a complex upgrading system with a large array of crafting materials, and the HUGE amount of skills is insane! We've got buff spells, debuff spells, elemental spells, partially elemental and partially physical, spells that damage and may caused status effects, spells that damage and may debuff enemies, spells that take away enemy buffs, take away your team's debuffs, limit breaks, spells that element changes depending on the weapon you use, spells that power up in certain conditions, spells with lots of power but debuff your character, HOLY CRAP, I'm geeking out! At the same time though, the first time you use a certain spell, or get hit by a certain attack one of your characters says some, whether it be funny (most of the time because the spell speaks for itself and doesn't require explanation), or it be important information like saying the Barrier and Heal More spells are really important (which they are probably the game's two most important spells.)
Graphically, the overworld looks much different than the battle graphics, but both serve their part well. The story isn't impressive, but it certainly gets the job done, especially considering the game is lighthearted and never takes itself too seriously. Until the final boss. That's some dark crap right there. Also, I feel the need to say this. I won't spoil anything, but I had Anna and Natalie at 31, Lance and Matt at 32, and didn't even use Lance. I changed my armor sets according to the different forms for maximum effieciency. The fight took me an hour, no joke. Speaking of the final boss, the music in the game is great. Not Shovel knight is Mega man levels of great, but pretty close in my opinion. Oh yea. The final boss theme is great. The game's lighthearted theme and humor is one of the things that kept me engaged. I loved laughing the hilarious and silly dialogue, as it just added a unique spice to the battles.
If I had to find some complaints I had, they would be few, but the one big issue I had that there is a bunch of optional content, and I wanted to do as much as possible, but it just wasn't as interesting as the main quest. There is a whole bonus area with upgraded versions of the bosses in the main story, but fighting the same enemy with better numbers and a few more tricks just... isn't engaging as fighting them for the first time. But the big kicker that killed my motivation for the bonus area was that you don't get any EXP, AP, or gold from the fight. If I got even a little, I might have gone a bit farther, but I didn't even feel up to getting past the second boss.
Overall though, it's amazing. Definetly in my Top 20 or maybe 15 favorite games I've played. Top 10 would be a bit of a stretch, but it's possible. Get it if you are a hardcore RPG fan or want to start getting into RPG's. I mean, I've played RPGs ever since I was 6, I know a good RPG when I see one. And this is a good RPG.

Took me 9 hours, did some side exploration, found most of the goodies. Probably contains another two or three hours worth of metroidvania if you want to do absolutely everything and are not more competent than me.
I died about 350 times before I saw the end credits. It was at times very challenging, but didn't feel unfair. Sometimes I couldn't instantly see how a jumping puzzle was to be solved, but often that was just me being stupid (or under time pressure). You regularly get into an amazing flow, and even if you die in one of the "run for your life" passages you respawn instantly so the flow is not broken too much. The ability to create respawn points at your desire is a nice addition as well. Just don't forget doing so.
Story wise it is absolutely lovely. It's a fairytale with only few characters, but all of them are likeable or even loveable.
I found the soundtrack to be pretty amazing, with a very strong and memorable main motif that carries you through the game and plays in different variations at different times.
The art style is just beautiful and very cleanly executed, animations are fluid enough. Sometimes, however, I could lose sight of where Ori actually was, as her small shape was obscured by enemies or effects.
The only thing that bothered me slightly is the rather lengthy final area, especially since it's a fire level - long fire levels are uncomfortable for me, I don't enjoy staring at red for extended periods very much.
Still, it was a very worthwhile experience and I can wholeheartedly recommend it.
Exceptions:
- "cute isn't your thing"
- "fairytales are for kids"
- "yeah, that bit of jumping must be easy as pie"
- "I have no heart"

Due to the fact that almost one hundred percent emphasis on PVP battles in real time, all aspects of the game motivate you to take part in matches as often as possible, not to create queues waiting in the lobby.
That is why the battle lasted a few minutes. And for those few minutes you get to a sea of emotions, trying to overcome the enemy. After one fight, I want another one. What is logical is screwed ranking system to gradually climb the ladder of professionalism. Every month rank resets and plus a certain portion of the experience to start from scratch. In parallel with the grades there is a system of levels. For obtaining the new give us all sorts of useful loot.
Minion Masters the whole battle system is built on passive management. You choose a card from the deck, put on the field unit and see how it goes Rashit opponent using your skills and characteristics. Cards quite a lot and have relative counterparts of each other with only minor differences, and there are very unusual, unique card. Accordingly, there is a gradation of values cards. You can get them in the process of leveling hero, and buy at the store for the local currency, and Donat. I was not hard to score a pack of different cards and brute force in the battle to find the perfect composition that I hardly will soon change. Although sometimes I enter a new map for testing.
Another advantage of Minion Masters is its simplicity. Simplicity is evident in all aspects. Intuitive interface, a minimum of superfluous information. Even the graphics, pleasing to the eye, looks rustic. Why I attribute it to the pros because the person who wants to play half an hour in such a game would be enough to spend no more than five minutes in the lobby and the same time in the battle to master all the mechanics of the game and get pleasure from it.
For a $5 Early Acess Game this is a solid fun game.

It's been a long time since I wrote this review. However, I want to reiterate that my views have not changed at all. If anything, my opinion of this game is worse now that it's in effective release stage, though they don't call it that, we all know it's what it is. A "work in progress" meaning it will always be. A good many people who were once positive about the game have since moved on for good reasons. And here I am again, updating my review with no changes in my opinion about the game.
Look at the positive reviews. Nearly all of them agree the game is "rough." This has never changed, and it's far, far beyond the original promised release date of 2014. Don't hold your breath.
There is nothing innovative about the game design. Most of it is from the 1980s, and that's why the game appeals to an older crowd that want to relive that time period and the early Ultima games. Those folks usually have the funds to invest also, and are stuck in their ways of what they believe a game should be like. Many of them have stated this publicly on the Shroud forums.
Add to that the Unity 5 game engine, technically ok with a lot of potential that has not, up to the point of this writing, being utilized adequately by the development team.
I pledged back when this was a Kickstarter campaign in March 2013. I had very high hopes and anticipation since I had played Ultima Online for 10 solid years. But as time went on, I began discovering all the systems they were creating that were not even close to what UO used to be. Maybe that's good news for some people. But for me, not so much.
Their funding/investment system is obscene. I hugely dislike the combat system, the ridiculous crafting system, and mining resources is tedious at best. But to me, the worse offense came when they created Player Owned Towns, right after the ridiculously expensive housing system. The land barons want to keep everything limited so they can keep their property values and sell them at a premium. Some have openly admitted in the forums to buying multiple POTs and houses to sell and rent. I do not like the purposeful division of the "haves" and the "have nots." It created a rift from the beginning and will only get worse.
There are too many arrogant entitled investors in that game, and Portalarium created the problem with a poor business model. It's not only "House of the Avatar," it's far worse. Resources spent to continually keep the land barons happy and investing more money. If that appeals to you, go for it. If not, then please use your money on something that's genuinely fun.

I tend to get really excited about MMORPG's and then once I play them, l lose interest real quickly because I romanticize the idea of an MMO moreso than the actual product I purchase. That being said, I am loving this game so far. Im a total noob and it feels great. Im exploring and since its in alpha, completely unconcerned with leveling up or making my character top notch. Instead I am wandering around, finding out where NPCs are located, discovering caverns and other neat areas that are being added at a frequent pace, and generally being a part of this game's growth. Hell, Richard Garriott himself will log on and talk to players gathered at Owls Head, its amazing.
Pros:
-The community is fantastic (within an hour I had a guild and a couple pals who hooked me up with gear)
-I like the idea of typing text to an NPC to get more information instead of following a glowing trail and ignoring the virtual world the devs have spent days building. Not sure where the tavern is? Ask a guard and he will say something like "Behind the defense tower in the center of town" instead of a flag on a map.
-Exploration is rewarded
Cons:
-Still in Alpha, lots of work to be done especially on the PvP side
-Can certainly be intimidating to newcomers and those used to more theme-park MMOs
-Price is a bit steep at the time of this posting
Loving it so far

I wouldn't call this a Gauntlet game.
Perhaps that's because my understanding of Gauntlet came from Gauntlet Legends and Gauntlet: Dark Legacy. Both excellent games with hours and hours of gameplay and tons of playable characters with alternate costumes (so you and a friend could both be warriors but look entirely different) and discoverable characters, leveling up, familiars, and a vast array of locations with interesting themes for each.
Maybe it was too much to hope this game would return to styles of those forementioned, but instead fell just as flat as Gauntlet: Seven Sorrows. I even had to Google that title up because I had forgotten what it was called.
Anyway, if you're wanting a game like Legends or Dark Legacy, this is not the game for you.

It's alright, maybe worth getting on the cheap, but I think my friends and I were a little underwhelmed and lost interest quickly.
We'd all played Gauntlet back in the 80's, and while this does generally stay true to the basics (characters, keys, potions etc), the level design just seems lazy and linear. Linear's not a bad thing in games, but in this instance it takes an already simple game and points you forward. With limited character attacks that soon become repetitive, and only the illusion of character skill trees/progression, it all adds up to you thinking you could spend your time better elsewhere.
The levels are split into 3 sets of 4, with each of those 3 sets having it's own theme. One of those themes is mostly dark caves where the only light source is a slight glow around your character, which doesn't really add to the atmosphere, it just makes it annoying to navigate. Each themed set is also very samey.. I think they've been a bit lazy and could have not only put ALOT more levels in, but also more variety. Kinda feels like a tablet game in that respect.
On the plus side, it's a bit of fun with friends, especially with the difficulty up when in rooms where you get swarmed, but unfortunately it mostly lacks any real frantic play.
If you like working on Achievements, you'll find a third of the achievements are for playing very badly, another third for progress, and the last third for playing way more than you really want to.
I'd give the game a neutral rating if I could, but in honesty I don't think it has enough to recommend it.. seems like development was a bit lazy, although it's not buggy or anything.. just design choices really.

Reus is an entertaining game designed for the min/maxxer in you.  You'll frequently find yourself trying to work out how to squeeze another five food and three science out of a village's limited space, preferably without having to redo a lot of the work you've already done.
The unlock system of both resources and space/time means that the game has a very natural tutorial and progression system.  At the beginning of the game, you only have a few resources available, but you need to experiment a lot to use them efficiently.  As you gain new resources, you'll work with the old ones more efficiently, but will have to meet higher targets in the same timeframe.  Unlock a new tiimeframe, and you'll have more time to meet those higher targets and to experiment more with the newer resources.  And so it cycles, to a point.  By the time you've unlocked the largest planet and the longest timeframe however, you'll probably be champing at the bit to have access to the highest tiers of resources.  Which will instead require quite a number more games, each trying to meet a few more of the remaining unlock requirements.  Meeting these specific requirements does present interesting challenges, and the game's UI makes it easy enough to keep track of what achievements are still locked, but by the time you've unlocked all, or nearly all of the available resources, you'll probably have little interest left in continuing to play as it does get somewhat repetitive in the longer run.  The journey there is quite engaging, nevertheless.
While it's longevity is in doubt, there's no question that the game poses an entertaining and reasonably challenging proposition that's well worth the price.
