Let me start off by mentioning this is a fantastic co-op game for two. I initially came across this while trawling for games to play with my girlfriend, and while I was skeptical of it at first I'm glad we picked it up. Plenty of turn-based RPGs have done the old "split the party between two players" trick, but trust me when I say Divinity makes it work. The world is filled to the brim with memorable quests and characters that make it feel less like a watered down version of the game and more like an adventure to share with someone dear. Playing co-op also doesn't rob any kind of agency from either player: party members are free to wander from one side of an area to the other without pesky loading zones limitting your exploration. With so many quests requiring a combination of investigation and problem solving, an extra brain can certainly help. Not to mention your characters will have their own unique choices of dialogue that will sway their personality and broaden your bond beyond "two people that enjoy beating up randoms monster by the wayside."
Even if you're not looking for something to enjoy with your player 2, Divinity: Original Sin is one of the most solid RPG experiences I've had. Characters are fully customisable in terms of stats and abilities without being shoehorned into classes. That said, most characters will inevitably fall into a typical fantasy role without the need for classes. Strength boosts one's ability to fight with large weapon and heavy armour, finesse boosts the use of light armour and either daggers or ranged weapons and intellects affords the user access to all 5 spell schools but limits them to robes. It's both possible and reasonable to combine these stats to create the kind of character you'd prefer, but the more thinly you spread their abilities the worse they're likely to perform at each. This makes it feel natural to have your typical knight, rogue, ranger and wizard set-up that harkens back to old-style DnD type RPGs while still allowing the player to experiment as they so choose. I personally ended up sticking to the single stat set-up for most of the game, but eventually splashed some intelligence onto my knight to get some extra tricks up my sleeve.
The combat feels consistently threatening even on the classic difficulty. This encourages the use of ambushes, terrain and positioning to gain as much of an advantage as possible in order to succeed. While many RPG players have a tendency to hoard items, Divinity has a way of coaxing them out of even the most prudent hoarder. Potions cost only two action points, a fraction of any other healing in the game. Scrolls provide players not only a selection of magic to those not able to cast it, but also a way to defy some of the wizard's hefty cooldown. Arrows and grenades also serve as a cheaper alternative to spells. When resurrection is tied to a limitted supply of resurrection scrolls it's important to use whatever tools you can to stay alive.
Rivellon, the game's world, has an uncanny ability to feel both relatable yet magical. It eases you in with a simple murder mystery then quickly introduces you to the many oddities of the world. At every turn it instills a sense of wonder, compelling you to explore every nook and cranny. It's becomes more than just a slog for loot and experience (which do you get plenty of anyway) and transforms into a real adventure that will keep you coming back for more. I'd be quite happy to sit down and go through it all again if not for the fact that I'd doubtless be glued to it for another 80 hours and I haven't even started on the sequel.
If I have to say one bad thing though it's the bugs. Some quests either don't resolve properly or are impossible to complete for one reason or another. I could count on one hand how many times this has been a real problem and considering how big of a game it is coming out of a small company I'm surprised there aren't more. Just a fair word of warning to those whose immersion may be completely broken by enemies taking 15 seconds to think about their turn every now and again or having an incomplete quest from the beginning town all the way to the end boss.

I've loved the Divinity saga for a long time now. They're chock full of side quests, quirky characters and deep lore. They're what I'd call proper old style RPGs. Overall the game is quite solid but can be a bit confusing for newbies. I think the combat tutorial could have been improved. I personally have yet to really get to grips with the combat elements but I love everything else. The characters you meet are great, I find the story interesting and I just love the weird humour in this game. It makes me happy, genuinely happy...
That said it is sometimes too easy to get lost or to feel unsure about how to actually complete a quest chain. There is a quest log but it can be a bit vague at times. For example, in the first main quest you get (solving a murder! As fun as it sounds), it wasn't always obvious where you should look for clues, who you should speak for next or even how to resolve the case once you thought you'd found all the answers. So this isn't a hand-holding sort of game by any standards.
Another criticism however - again regarding combat - is that it is very easy to come across enemies you're not prepared to fight or fall foul of hidden traps. I guess this, again, goes under the heading of 'not holding your frickin hand'. The UI is a bit clunky and could have been a lot more sexy and helpful - but hey, it's functional, just a little hard to navigate at times. I guess those are my main criticisms because I think basically the game is very well designed but there are some basic elements (UI,signposting  difficulty scaling) that could have been improved. Just my opinion of course.
That said, if you're willing to look past a bit of a rough aspect and don't mind dying to skeletal archers or goblins now and then, then I recommend this game. It's for people who love old RPGs and quests that are very involved. And for those with a sense of humour.... that's vital, since you'll be spending some time talking to disembodied heads and dogs.

TL;DR:  Just buy the game. It's awesome.
Ori and the Blind Forest is, in a word, captivating. It manages to capture airtight platforming, gorgeous vistas, clever level design, and a beautiful story in one inspiring package. The heartfelt tale of two inseperable companions torn apart by death could tug at the hearstrings of even the most stoic of us. Anyway, the forest becomes "blind" due to the death of a great tree, and it's up to Ori the tree spirit to return the forest to life.
At it's best, Ori and the Blind Forest has you performing a nuanced aerial ballet, with each perfectly timed jump or bash propelling Ori to the next in a series of dazzling aerobatic maneuvers. The frequency of these blissful platforming sections is just one in a group of reasons why this game is great.
Platforming wouldn't be nearly as fun if controlling Ori wasn't silky smooth like it is; That's just as well, because OatBF is challenging and demands a lot from the player. But, with the exception of some parts of the escape sequences, it's never cheap. Death is handled well, with each one immediately sending Ori back to the most recent checkpoint, and saving is easy: just hold down B and one orb of energy is consumed to save the game. These savepoints also allow access to Ori's ability trees. There are three in all: one for combat, one for exploration, and one for platforming/survivability. No one tree breaks the game.
I'll briefly touch on the weaknesses of the game. There's a lack of enemy diversity, as you'll see the same frog-stompers and spike-slugs throughout all of the zones. Also, the same mini-boss encounter is used several times throughout the game as a block to the next area. Combat breaks up the jumping around nicely, but I feel like it's there just for the sake of it. I'm not saying it's not enjoyable, but platforming is way more fun here. Additionally, the ending dungeon sequence drags just a little bit.
Finally, I'll give a quick shoutout to the soundtrack, and what a soundtrack it is. The musical themes range from touching to haunting to triumphant and the synergy between the storytelling and the music really packs an emotional punch. It works in harmony with the action on screen to a level I haven't seen in any game since Journey.
Well there's nothing written here that couldn't be better expressed by the game. Stop reading and buy it so you can experience one of the absolute best games of 2015.

is a very unique looking exploration/(light)metroid-vania game in which you control a bird, and have a bigger mission to accomplish, and a cryptic backstory to uncover.
It's an interesting game, and I enjoyed a whole lot of it. However, it has a few bugs. That would not be a problem -- except for the fact that these are
bugs. I haven't been able to finish the game because of it.
These bugs are more common than you would think, and many of the threads in the Community Hub are actually asking for help to solve them. As far as I can see, too many people need to tweak the game files in order to finish the game, if at all...
Tith this whole preface, expect this to be a biased review. I spent probably 30% of my time with this game very frustrating, and trying to overcome bugs. It's ultimately why I don't recommend this game.
The game looks amazing!
The main attraction, for me, is how they've done
. The game is very geometrical, mostly full of triangle, with each one of them having a different shade.
I can't explain it very well, but look at the screenshots! The bigger animals are really well done, considering they're a bunch of triangles.
The smaller animals are a bit weaker, and the birds' flying animations can be a bit awkward. Still, nothing
!
However, there's a big problem that comes from this.
When you see a wall, it's a lie. The real wall is probably inside the rock, somewhere. It feels wrong to fly through part of the walls. Not sure why they didn't limit the levels properly (maybe to give it a sense of 3D?), but it didn't work for me, at all.
They cover up your vision and it's annoying.
Alright, moving on to the
and
. One quick problem is that it doesn't save your volume options when you exit the game. So, if you need to balance the audio, feel free to do it every single time...
Now, on to the actual topic. The music is a strange aspect of this game. The game is very nature and life inspired, so I was expecting some more folk-y music. Instead, it's a strange, more modern ambient music. I don't know. It doesn't really seem to fit, most of the time -- although, it certainly does fit when you meet the more complex structures. It makes the world feel a bit more alien, and the music certainly helps with that.
The sound-effects, were almost spot-on! There's a
contribution of the wild-life present in the game to the atmosphere. You'll be constantly listening to birds chirping, chittering from the rabbits, foxes, etc.
When you're flying, the wind also intensifies. Overall, it all comes together and creates a very immersive atmosphere! It's impressive.
This game is openworld and almost maze-like, at this. A cool thing that it does, though, is that the world is circular -- if you go right as much as you can, you'll eventually find yourself where you started. The downside is that it doesn't really serve as a handy shortcut, except in very specific circumstances. Still, it's a nice addition.
Other than that, you have an hub area where there are several missing shards. Your main motivation is to find those shards, and see what happens.
When I said it's a
metroid-vania, was because you need to open up some areas and find your way around. Unfortunately, there isn't much in terms of power-progression. There
one power-up, but it's optional, and revealed itself incredibly useless -- its main possible advantages were actually disabled. What it ended up being was a very fun way of causing chaos. Fun for a few minutes, then it becomes just a mess.
Anyway... The game has several gates, that require
to open. The shards just the same. These slivers are simply spread around to world, and you'll collect them by normally exploring -- in the best case scenario. The worst-case scenarios are game-breaking and I'll mention them later.
Then, you can also collect other kinds of slivers -- blue ones. These work almost like Demon Souls' souls, in a very superficial way. If you collect X of them, you'll get a life. When you die, you'll lose a life, but respawn where you died. Otherwise, you'll drop the blue slivers you have, and go back to the Hub area. You can get those back.
Their whole purpose is as lives, but the whole lives-system seems a bit directionless.
The interesting thing, though, is
you collect these. There are eggs and nests spread around the world. If you drop an egg into a nest (without breaking it), a bird will be born, and drop a few of these blue slivers.
Otherwise, you can also get it by reading runes spread throughout. These runes are written in english, but the characters are highly stylized, almost in code.
You can collect these symbols (which are often well hidden) to be able to decode these messages easier. It's NOT needed, however. With a little effort, you can decode them yourself!
I think this covers the basics.
The best aspect of this game, to me, is how
it feels. Animals interact with each other, and also with you! Some are aggressive, some a more passive, but there's always some kind of interaction. You can also bait them into attacking into other, and even kill them, if they're making your life too difficult.
Especially when you're carrying the shards, everything becomes attracted to you, and every animals steals your shard! You then have to run after them and get it back. I can imagine it being frustrating, but I found it really cool!
Now, a mixed bag - the backstory. It's presented simply through the rune-stones. And these are strange and hard to read. They also have different writters. So, in a way, you get invested and interested in the world it presents. In another way, it's all done through such incoherent methods that it's very hard to follow. Maybe if you replay it, but otherwise... You're unlikely to retain most of it, which is really unfortunate.
Also, you can't simply "collect" these runestones to read them later. If you want, you'll need to re-run through the whole areas separately. It's... too inconvenient, honestly.
In regards to this, I think it's a very cool idea. However, it's too disjointed for me to enjoy it.
Now, for the huge problems -
.
These feel so out of place. A lot of it is carrying or moving stones. Couple this with unclear hitboxes and what you get is yourself trapped between rocks and the wall. Off you go, then, altering the game's files to reset your position (the game could easily account for this with a reset button, but there isn't even that! It's a known issue, with half of the gamepad unused...).
Then, you can carry
items between zones. In the beginning of the game, it's easy to see one and try to bring it to the hub area -- didn't work, drop it somewhere. Later, you realize what it was for! Eureka! ... Well, where is it, now? Go around and around looking for it, praying that it's not behind foreground! It's very annoying, when you start.
Then, the biggest problem. Slivers are exactly counted for you to finish the game. Not one too many.
However:
1. They can spawn inside walls and be impossible to get without tweaking the files;
2. Some gates consume more than they're supposed to;
3. You can drop them easily (and lose them);
4. Deaths can somehow lower your number -- this was my problem. It's a bug. One that had supposedly been fixed. Well, tough♥♥♥♥♥♥ I was 1 sliver short. One tiny shard of 100+.
If all of these are KNOWN issues why couldn't they just add a few more for safety purposes? It's such an easy solutions...
I'm out of characters. BEWARE -- buy at your own risk!

F.E.A.R. 3 is a game with a serious identity crisis. Developed by Day 1 Studios instead Monolith (although they were apparently creatively involved), this is a seriously weak conclusion to a promising trilogy, with much of the signature creepiness and atmosphere plucked out in favour of imitating modern day shooters. Does it want to be a horror game, or does it want to be your standard points-based shooter with generic enemies?
I recently played through F.E.A.R. 2 for the first time and enjoyed it, feeling that its shooting mechanics were great fun. It just felt smooth and easy to play through, with a couple of unsettling moments along the way that helped to make up for its less-than-stellar story. I guess I've always had an issue with the way this series tells its story, never quite fleshing out Alma Wade as a truly menacing presence, and being too cryptic about how the whole thing comes together. This wasn't really a major problem with the first two games though, as the frantic shooting and solid slo-mo mechanics more than made up for it.
Perhaps the biggest issue with F.E.A.R. 3 is that most of the horror elements have been sucked out in favour of copying Call of Duty. This is a co-op shooter now, with a points system based on certain actions within the game. Co-op in horror games almost always dilutes the impact of the experience, and while I didn't get to try out the game with another person, I can't help but feel that these elements have affected what's here. Many of the scenarios within involve simply moving from one area to another, clearing out a bunch of soldiers along the way and maybe a few monsters later on. It isn't that there aren't some creepy moments (one early sequence wading through a warehouse with a bunch of flickering TV's is actually pretty effective) but they're thrown into a generic shell. The shooting is quite well done, with decent guns, and the tried-and-tested slo-mo effect helping you to take out enemies effectively, but it's just all very... "meh".
By the end of F.E.A.R. 3 I felt like I'd sort of slogged my way through it just to see how the story concludes. I never felt truly invested due to how different the game feels from its predecessors, and the attempt to copy COD and modern shooters has drained much of the personality that previously existed. This is just a generic shooter now; a slightly painful limp to the conclusion of a story that was never brilliantly told from the beginning. You'll be playing this purely to finish out the trilogy, not because it's a good game. It doesn't stand out, it's not unique and it'll make you appreciate Monolith's two strong efforts all the more.

Cute art. Relaxing, but fairly repetitive game. Trying to unlock everything can be challenging. If you're not a completionist, you'll probably get bored after the first few games.
You control four elemental gods: rock, forest, ocean, and swamp. They can create three inhabitable biomes upon the planet: swamp, forest, or desert. Additionally, they can each create and improve different versions of the three resources: food, gold, and tech. As you create resources, villages settle around them. As the villages improve, they will pick specialties and demand more of some of the resources. If you give them too much too fast, they will become greedy and attack each other. If you don't satisfy their needs in time, their specialty will disappear. If you do satisfy their needs, they will gift you with an ambassador. Ambassadors are used to increase the power of your gods. Each god will get different powers from the ambassador depending on the village's biome.
On its face, the game is quite simple. When you aim for some of the more advanced achievements, you are forced to strategize a lot more. On which biomes should I allow villages to settle so I can get the best ambassadors? Which giant should pick up that ambassador? How do I grow this village without it becoming too greedy? If you enjoy micromanaging, this game might be right up your alley.

There are several reasons why I really enjoy
and believe it to be a well-made and fun game.  I can certainly see why it may not appeal to absolutely everyone, but I think it does what it does well and does so in a charming little way that remains unique to its own identity.
It is a casual game, and a very much toned-down “civilization-management” style game compared to others in that genre.  It is actually a “god-sim” style game where you influence but do not control the civilizations in your world.  Furthermore, it is round based, each round starting from scratch and lasting 1 to 2 hours; however unlocks and certain progressions are saved across all rounds.
The main thing that I like about
is that it satisfies the desire to play a civilization-management / god-sim style game without overloading the player with piles upon piles of data to keep track of.  The tutorial is great, and slowly introduces the mechanics to the game.  Even after the tutorial ends, things in the game are unlocked relatively slowly as the player completes rounds of gameplay.  All this prevents you from feeling overwhelmed when you start playing.  And you can really understand how the game works piece by piece instead of it all just being tossed in your face immediately after clicking “New Game.”  It is a bit of a double-edged blade, however, as some players may inevitably find
to be lacking, as it is truly far less complex than many other games involving civilization-management.
The game is quite simplistic and it is way more god-sim than it is civilization-management; and it shows in the gameplay.  Control is limited and simple, and much of the development is automated while the player just makes sure everything is going smoothly by managing resources, and occasionally divinely-intervening in affairs of the NPC civilizations.
The art style, music, and even the game mechanics all add to the simple charm of the game that gives
its positive identity.  The game isn’t very innovative but it does have a unique feel that will satisfy.  Once you get into the swing of things, you will find
to be quite addictive.
In summary, I would say that hardcore fans of the civilization-management genre will probably find
way too casual.  In truth it is much more so a casual god-sim than it is anything else.   But for people who are interested in getting a small taste of civilization-management without the overwhelming feeling and tedious gameplay, they may be pleasantly surprised at what
has to offer.

I can no longer in good conscience recommend this game. The developers seem to be making the game more frustrating and less enjoyable with every change. The focus on the game is now entirely on grinding XP.
The overall world is interesting and the graphics are good. It's a long way from release, so I'm hopeful they'll get better. The audio needs a ton of work still.
World design: A
Graphics: A
Travel around the world is very boring. Your character runs very slowly, and there are virtually no fast-travel features.
Overall world travel: D
The combat system is a mixed bag. The "deck" system, with randomly drawn glyphs looks interesting on paper, but plays very poorly. Since you have no way to know what skills will be drawn in a a fight, you spend all your time staring at the hotbar. Basically, you are completley removed from the game around your avatar and your enemies. This combat system would have worked well in a turn based combat game, but it doesn't work in this one.  Add to that a very frustrating UI for combat, and it becomes very frustrating.
Combat System: B
Combat Mechanics: F
Combat UI: F
The crafting system is really just a lot of grinding combat. Every combatant can be a crafter, so there's no avenue for a dedicated crafter to make a living. Crafting is also an intentional gold sink. If a crafter takes a lot of time to produce something of value, the game will never pay more than the inputs cost. The wide array of things to make, with lots of crafting outputs being crafting inputs in differing skills is done quite well.
My original motivation for the game was the dedicated crafter play-style. The developers will no longer even discuss that as a possibility, and many of the statements they have made regarding crafting show a direction for crafting that is more-and-more focused on combat.
Crafting system: F
Crafting mechanics: B
The skill system is interesting, but with a few fatal flaws. The fact that the game is not a level grind is great. It's much more interesting having everyone that has a decent amount of experience to all be around the same level. However, the lack of a hard skill cap means the game is essentially owned by a few very hardcore people.
Skill trees: A+
Skill system design: F

I was a big fan of all the old Ultima games, and this made me back Shroud of the Avatar quite a while ago. I really think it is quite a different approach to first person fantasy role playing. Lots of ideas I missed in games of this type seem to be happening in Shroud of the Avatar - at least that is what I am hoping for. The crafting system sees neat - though I am not the crafting guy.
What I like is that there is a whole world to explore that really feels alive. Sure, we do not know what the final game will be like, but I like how different the regions of the world feel and that many cities already have a unique look.
This makes exploring so much more fun.
Also, I expect that by putting the game on steam, it will have quite a large player base. And that is important to me, because AI NPCs are not what makes a game like this a unique experience.
I am looking forward to the final game!
By the way, the play time shown here is only the steam play time. I played much more before SotA was on steam.
And now, test on, alpha testers!

Game Dev Tycoon is one of those games where you're put in the shoes of a game developer and given the freedom of creating video games by assigning time, personnel and resources to each aspect of your game. The game rewards you with more research and experience points for innovating with new game ideas and later on for good management.
The flaw with this system is that you're often punished for releasing sequels, or for choosing to train your staff. There are also some very big flaws in the design of this game, i.e. any new technological innovation you've made has to be incorporated into an entirely new game engine, you can't even properly make a sequel without researching it first when you get the option to in the midgame, and you will randomly get punished with bad or mediocre review scores for really stupid reasons, even if you sink a lot of design and technology points into your release.
Mods only go so far as to fix some of the game's glaring flaws. Overall, I'd avoid the game because it gets repetitive and unrewarding very quickly.

This truly is a beautiful game, with a very unique style and lighting.  The gameplay is quite different too - although I wouldn't say I've played many games in the "metroidvania" genre.  Actually, hearing it described as "metroidvania" would have put me off, prior to playing, as I might have assumed it was going to be impossibly difficult with little to no storyline.
Now, it doesn't really have a massively developed storyline - there is one, but it's not particularly complex.  Oh and whilst at time there were some touching moments, I didn't find this as tear-inducing as I had expected given previous reviews.  However, none of this detracts from the fact that this is a very enjoyable game to play!  The mechanics are incredibly well tuned, it's challenging but not impossible, and there is a sense of real achievement.  The lack of frustration in this game stems largely down to the portable save game system - you can save wherever you want, but it uses energy to do this so you do have to make wise choices.  Saves are instant, so the flow of the game is not interrupted, but you're not compelled to save every 3 seconds because of the energy requirements - a very good idea.
The fact that this game is one giant level with no load screens makes for a very fluid experience.  All in all, it's polished and interesting platforming, with some fun abilities and challenging set-pieces.
I would definitely recommend giving it a go if any of that appeals to you!

To the Moon....certainly took me to the stars! 4.5 of them anyway. So let's get down to reviewing.
To the Moon is a story driven 2d RPG/Puzzel game. What I mean by this is that the game includes momentos (hah...see what I did there.) to the common mechanics in the genre's but really is nothing more then an Role Playing game. The role which you play is of two Sigmund Corp. scientists, Dr.Neil Watts and Dr Eva Rosalene, who are sent to asssist a man named Johnny who is on his death bed. Their job is simple, use a large machine in order to edit his memories to allow him to die with his final wish, to go to the moon. Over the course of perusing around his memories to collect momentos the dynamic duo learn Johnny's entire tragic life as well as about River his late wife whom place a major role in making you cry. The story of the game is exceptional, one of the best and most memorable experiences in indie games. It will make you cry, laugh, cry and laugh, feel unsure of how much you should be laughing or crying, etc. It's a tear jerker and a memorable experiece for sure. And there's something that will forever be rewarding in the final sunset of the game. The characters are well developed and beautifully dynamic (Neil is also my spirit animal). River and Johnny's interactions will make you smile like a child and cry like your wife died. So if you love a good story, head To the Moon. However you have to be into this game for the story because when it comes to game mechanics and game play there is very little. To the Moon is meant to be detail based in it's gameplay. It asks the player to searh it's 2d environments for objects and conversations of significance to Johnny to progress. After the environment his been explored you have to take the memory links you've gained and used them to unlock the momento. The momento can then be used to travel through to anouther memory by solving a puzzel. And these puzzels are easy. it doesn't matter how many moves you solve it in you will still progress. Other then these "fetch quests" and puzzels, there is one hallway fight involving throwing trees and it's a fun change of gameplay however breif. So in short, the gameplay is a fine change of pace and the fetch quests let you absorb alot of the envirnment and story you would otherwise miss, but honestly there just isn't alot of game. The graphics are also heavily stylized. Kan Gao made this game in RPG maker, so I understand that the engine has it's limitations and the game doesn't look bad. Areas are well modeled for the most part and diverse. And while I personally didn't care for the NASA HQ, it certainly doesn't mean that the designer did a poor job. Ontop of that, the diversity of the characters looks to the NPCS is very refreshing, as there is always clarity on who to talk to. Not to mention each of the chosen Momentos are symbols, and these symbols are designed with great litterary purpose. The only thing that I would say detracts from the game's look are the cut scenes which look like they were made in GIMP. But even then, these computer drawn images have alot of charm to them, so as much as they are bad, they are good. The OST is breif yet beautiful and mostly is composed of piano. And while I wouldn't say to go out and buy it, as the OST is very related to the game itself, I would say it's meshed perfectly into the story. Each song builds up emotion perfectly and never feels out of place in a scene. Honestly, after you finish the game then by the OST as the soundtrack will remind you of every heatfelt moment.
So to sumarize:
- PROS
- Memorable, emnotional narrative
- Heartfelt and memorable OST
- Beautiful character design
- Extreme Detail and interactability
- "Charming" graphical design
- Forces you to explore the environments your in.
- Emotional replay value
- CONS
- OST tracks are brief and repetitive if not for what they are related to.
- One area modled strangly
- Cut Scenes look cheap.
So what if you're a completionist? Well fear not, this game will be the easiest you've ever completed. While it has no completion bonus beyond closure to a beautiful story, you only have to do one thing to complete it. Get Johnny to the moon! Just sit back, and enjoy this five hour story and as long as you don't keal over from heartache or smiling so hard your face gets stuck, you'll have completed the game. As for the DLC minisodes, they just add 40 minutes of story and a cool new gameplay mechanic and are completely worth playing. They expand the universe nicely without making the game any harder to complete. So in short, just finish the game and congrats, your a completionist, no struggle at all.
So finally my rating for this game is 9/10 , Complete it!

To the Moon is not so much a game as a story driven interactive narrative. The gameplay is minimal and it mainly consists of moving around, but once you get into the story, believe me, you won't give a s#!t. This is an absolutely AMAZING game that will make you both laugh and cry. Words cannot describe my experience with it. Just... Just play it.
Amazing Story - I will not spoil any details about the story, but I will vouch for it's quality. You play as a pair of scientists who work for a sort of "Make a Wish" foundation, but which use an Animus-like machine to enter peoples memories and alter them in order to grant the dying person's wish. The story is divided into three acts, and takes about 4 hours to naturally progress through. Some may argue the story elements are a bit cliche, but frankly it was so well executed and related that I cannot say that bothered me. Also, great piece of advice from me: Pay close attention to everything. Even something that might not seem relevant will prove to be a foreshadowing of a greater truth. It's worth it to pay close attention to surroundings, dialogues, scenery, anything and everything.
Great Characters - The characters' personality is well defined, and you will grow to like them, especially Dr. Neil Watts, one of the controllable characters, who is the comic relief of the story and does a great job. But in all seriousness, everything is so amazing about this story.
Amazing Music - If anyone says music in gaming doesn't impact on experience they have obviously not played this game. The music is absolutely amazing and only hearing different tracks can put you in a different mood. You can go from happy to sad to worried to sad in a few minutes.
Beautiful Pixel Art - The game's retro RPG style graphics is a strong point in my opinion. It makes you concentrate more on the story. Anyways, the environment is beautiful, lighting is superb and I've never admired a pixel graphics game with such attention thus far.
Free DLC! - So far there were two mini episodes released which you can download and play for free! Also, the OST, which is paid, apart from being beautiful, offers 50% of the profits to charity. This is DLC done right.
Resolution - This isn't about graphics, and you won't even notice, as the game really sucks you in like a good book, but I was having problems opening up the game, and instead of upscaling to full HD, the game resorts to a very tiny resolution that might cause issues to some. Also, it's 4:3, and you'll see black bars. This is most likely because of the game engine they used.
It ends. - At some points i couldn't wait for the story to go on so I can see what happens, and at the end I wish it didn't because I was just sobbing at the ending. Amazing.
This game is an excellent visual narration, and I recommend it to anyone wanting to read a great story in a great manner. The Overwhelmingly Positive reviews are truly deserved. Also gift this to people who play tough, and see if they cry at the end. I was surprised I did.

Plummeting down at sonic speeds towards the ground and saving myself from becoming a splattering heap of blood, my first moments of this new and strange world were quite horrifying. It  was strange that despite my near death experience I couldn’t help but feel that these lands felt promising in being a tranquil place to live the rest of my life. Unsure of what was to become of me…
The world looked incredibly strange, full of triangle shaped forms, from the trees,caves and sculptures down to the animals themselves. Unsure of my surroundings I had to familiarize myself with what would be useful. Finding red triangles I noticed made me healthier while the blue triangles when gathered enough saved my life.  Funny how these items were of similar shape and resemblance to my environment. Forming together a sort of harmony.
Further traversing the lands I noticed that inserting the triangles I found, into the towers would make them activate. I noticed how they would shine - like they were calling for me to pull the levers. What I found interesting the most was the golden triangles that seemed important though I was somewhat awestruck and confused of their purpose of being held within these contraptions. I realized later that I could insert these gold triangles into a machine that revealed a prison of animals. I was determined to free them from their cages once I have found the rest.
Before I knew it I was altering the land by lifting rocks out of passages and solving puzzles to unlock paths. The place became more and more dynamic the more time I spent on interacting with the environment, shaping the terrain to a degree sort of speak though albeit a small degree.
The journey seemed difficult but I learned some new tricks as I explored, though there were some issues in actually using these tricks…Calling out to find objects hidden within the world elluded me If i was carrying anything of significant importance.
One time for example the black triangle I was carrying around was being indicated when I called out to objects, I didn’t notice this at first and was wondering why my senses seemed to freak out and rotate so much. Making me somewhat - dumbfounded at my own foolishness. I had to abandon the object in order to properly search around for the treasures of the world.
Going around and around was pretty tiring, having to see the same environments several times again since the point of interest was in the middle of the forest. Especially when enemies got in the way and stole my triangles it was rather annoying having to fight them for it - I tried my best not to kill them though. I progressed slowly closer and closer to my goal of collecting all the gold triangles to activate whatever the giant machine did until there was only one left.
Finding the last gold triangle - quite frankly has given me far more trouble than I bargained for. I looked around the world several times backtracking here and there, in order to find whatever I missed that could lead me to it. Constantly trying to avoid danger while looking for news ones I couldn’t help feel that what I was doing was a fruitless labor.
The statues I rebuilt to their former glory might have helped me navigate through the forests - however being able to find that last piece was still a pipe dream. I was simply losing my mind at this point and picking fights with the local birds that have long annoyed me since the beginning, slaughtering them left and right to never see them again.
Eventually what would happen is a land of lifelessness and void of any creatures, my madness for created by the lust of the last gold triangle got the better of me. Now barren in this world where I live I looked up at the sun and attempted to suicide, being thrown down by the strong winds I decided to take a dive into the water latched onto a rock and allow myself to suffocate - until my very being was taken from this world.
The world looked pleasing, unique and interesting to explore. Outside of the eye candy though laid a series of bad game design choices concerning navigation. The restrictions put on you from really ascending to great heights - to the frustration of having to backtrack constantly back to the hub. There is a lot of potential this game had if it were to erase the backtracking by making the activation of the mechanisms trigger the cages instead of the triangles but the over-focus on this element lead to the game’s downfall of making it into a tedious chore.

text: Artistic garbage.

It is entertaining, but will not deliver any
sense of accomplishment, even upon completion. I think although maybe a hair off in execution, that is wonderful, but know that your reward will be a series of thoughts and feelings rather than a shot of dopamine and a pat on the back for rescuing the princess or stopping the communists.
It's similar to Fez in the sense that you're dropped into a world and hinted into completing a quest of collecting things to unlock other things in order to collect more things, all the while exploring and wondering what exactly you're doing, why, and to what end.
You're a bird(man?) and in essence all you can really do is traverse the environment and manipulate it the way a bird would. You flap and fly and dive, and you can grab things to pull or lift or turn them. If you encounter an unfriendly bird, there's no special power with which to thwart it, no aiming and hitting A to attack. If you'd like that bird dead, you'll need to manage to grab it, hold onto it, and fly in a fashion that manages to hurl it into the ground or some hazardous object. Again and again. Plus, animals you kill stay dead, there is no respawning (except for you.) There's something about the difficulty and lack of abstraction of the combat system that really adds to the game's point and feel. Beyond bird on bird crime, you might manipulate the populations of the different areas by returning eggs to their nest to hatch or bringing a pairs of rabbits together, providing additional targets and an advantage for yourself.
The art is quite cool, the system of animals interacting is fun to observe (and/or disrupt,) plus plenty of fun nooks and hidden passages to find, though none overly difficult. There is no map in the game, but not having one to refer to does a good job of forcing you to focus on your surroundings. The world is also small enough that you'll be able to sort it out in your head with time.
A good romp through the world, ending before the mechanics get stale. The game isn’t particularly difficult, though there are a couple tricky segments. It's probably good for a second playthrough, given some of the things you might discover towards the end of your first, but there is no 'new game+' in the strict sense.

It dawned on me that the title of this game isn’t just a fun play on words—if you’ve ever wondered how hordes of zombies would fare inside a blender, then you’re in for a treat!
Zombie Grinder plays exactly as it reads—and it’s
. Moments after starting any game mode, the ground is painted green, and littered with chunks of flesh, goo, and an assortment of other gross odds and ends.
No holds barred, there’s an extensive assortment of weaponry at your disposal, all of which offer a satisfying means drop tonnes of zombie chunks. New players are equipped with a pistol and additional weapon pickups are strewn throughout levels, although it’s a lucky dip-esque scenario, which can raise the stakes in stressful situations. Zombie mobs will occasionally drop weapons in the same fashion, too. Otherwise, character level milestones will unlock weapons that become purchasable in a shop accessed via the main menu; these can be equipped for immediate use at the start of any game.
As well as weapons, cosmetic items are available for purchase in the shop. The range includes: hairstyles, accessories, and colours to dye the aforementioned. These are fun additions, though be weary of durability; nothing lasts forever!
The number of character customisation and playstyle options may seem overwhelming, but they provide a welcome sense of autonomy. Players can alter their character’s dexterity and abilities via a vast skill tree, accruing skill points to invest upon levelling up. Opting for certain skill pathways will lock you out of others, to prompt roles or specialties (support/damage/and so on); this is especially important for multiplayer sessions, where survivability is reliant on teamwork. Re-rolling your skill points is available at a small cost, thankfully, which offers an incredible level of flexibility (or the means to fix any mistakes from trigger-finger clicking).
Zombie Grinder stands out in a market saturated with pixel art titles; a lot of care and time has gone into crafting assets that are very easy on the eyes. It’s especially impressive that nothing seems entirely flat, or flush to a set plane, as can be the case with this art-style. Instead, props, characters, and settings possess a satisfying level of depth with respect to one another.
A friend recommended buying Zombie Grinder on a whim, as we’ve been searching for multiplayer games worthy of our time and money. Still being in development, I was initially hesitant, but upon purchase and our first play session, I was taken aback by the polish and playability it offered. Surprising still, the game isn’t complete, and yet the standard has been set so high! Ultimately, that’s what compelled me to write this review, as I have nothing but praise for this work-in-development.

Reus is a beautiful looking game with a cool, unobtrusive soundtrack. At the lower levels, this is quite a calming game, it's the sort of game that's really good to play occasionally to take a break from more involved gaming.  As you gain achievements and advance to the final era, things become a lot more involved and challenging, but you can always go back to playing shorter games if you like.

Reus should be a therapeutic game about cultivating a planet with animals, plant life and minerals in order to sustain the human inhabitants. Essentially the game punishes you for speedy success, so each level becomes a delicate balancing act... With a 30-90min time limit.
To change the world, you don't exert god-like power over the land and seas (aka: good bits of Black & White), you instead have to command four different titans to do it for you (aka: ban bits of Black & White). Don't get me wrong... The game is pretty and kinda fun and apparently I sunk 23hrs into it without reaising, but it can't quite make it's mind up over simulation, sandbox or RTS...

I love this game, I have backed it since alpha release 7 (only because that's when I heard about it - had I heard about it earlier, I would have been in earlier!)

One of my favorite things about it harkens back to the Ultima series, when you actually get to talk to NPCs, ask them keywords (like name, or job, etc) and they'll respond.  You're not force-fed quests and only get certain dialog.  I also like that if you ask them their name, instead of seeing them in the game as "Guard", once you learn their name they become named (like Guard Joran).  If they have quests, then they'll engage you that way in the way of dialog, not exclamation points over their head.

This is pre-release, so there are kinks to be worked out, but I have absolute confidence in the developers.  I would recommend this to anyone who enjoys RPGs, and anyone who enjoyed the Ultima series starting back in the late 80s. :)

Overall, I believe this game has a lot of promise. The land of Novia is beautiful, detailed and full of mysteries to explore. Crafting is extremely robust, even at this early development stage. Housing is almost a mini-game unto itself. And the option to play solo, with friends or with no restrictions at all  provides an excellent firewall against griefers.
But to be fair and frank, there are issues that have yet to be resolved and need some attention. Combat is currently unbalanced, and the "deck system" feels clunky, random and fussy. Playing anything other than a sword-and-board fighter results in a frustrating combat experience. There are also PvE quests which route players through PvP zones, which can be extremely aggravating if you're not a PvPer (I'm not).
However, I don't think these limitations diminish the overall promise of the game -- assuming they're addressed. The big question is how they will be addressed prior to the title's launch this year.
ADDENDUM:
The game is now two months away from its final wipe, and the deck-based combat situation proved to be just the tip of the iceberg. The standard leveling system was replaced with a skills-based one, and the point-and-click controls were converted into a reticle-based targeting system. I've been hanging in with this game since Kickstarter, but I feel rather worn out with the direction things have taken. I can't really recommend it anymore based on the host of spotwelded, immutable features Portalarium has implemented.
CLOSING NOTE:
I sold my stake in game through the SotA forums, and recovered about $4,000 of my investment. (Irony: I sold my online house, and put the money toward a real one.) This game has strayed completely into pay-to-win territory. All items -- including pledge rewards -- degrade over time to the point where they perma-break... unless you're willing to obtain ultra-rare "Obsidian Coins" to repair them. These coins, unsurprisingly, are sold in packs on the add-on store.
Prepare to bleed money eternally if you want to play this game. As for me, I'm out. I would also like to add that the comments regarding SotA's toxic community are not entirely wrong. Some members are wonderful. Many more are not. Some members of Portalarium's staff are fantastic (FireLotus and Rustic Dragon in particular deserve medals), while others are quite belligerent and dismissive.
We're past the point where Portalarium can rationally hide behind the "it's still a work in progress" argument. They've had more than enough time to flesh out chapter one of their product, and there are four chapters still left to complete as well (per their Kickstarter goals). The constant fundraisers, telethons, publicity stunts, nickel-and-dime microtransactions, etc. are all extremely worrying. When and if this product crosses the finish line, I have grave concerns over whether it will survive. And if it doesn't? Kiss all that money you sank into this game goodbye.

I never thought a game could be perfect, but this game is as close to perfection as a game could ever get. I played through the entire game trying to find one mistake that the developer made. Needless to say I found absolutely nothing wrong with this game at all. Ori and the blind forest was clearly created with love by the developers and every feature was considered and researched properly before being put into the game.
A very intriging story. Theres not much I can say about the story without spoiling it. What I will say is it is follows a family love between characters and is filled with moments that could make you cry or smile with delight. It is a rare game that can bring out these feelings in you and it is a truly beatiful story.
Anyone who is a fan of platforming games will love this. What really suprised me though and I didn't expect it is that as well being focused on platforming it also has a large focus on combat. A great combat system at that. Very fun combat which leaves you having to run and jump about while fighting to avoid being hit. Also a large enemy variety that make you have to adapt to situations to fight different enemies. The combination of this combat system and hard platforming make Ori a very difficult game that could lead to raging moments. But boy is it satisfying when you finally kill that enemy or reach that platform you've been trying to get to for ages.
Now to keep the longevity of enjoyment of a game throughout playing there has to be a good upgrade system that evolves as you play. Ori does exactly that. What is unique though is that platforming elements that are usually in a game from the start are unlocked as you play. This includes abilities such as double jump and wall jump. It means that the game gets even more fun and difficult as you play. It is a strange choice to do this but I think it works very well in the circumstances of the game. What it means is that certain areas can't be accessed until you get these abilities. It makes for some artificial linearity to the game. These are abilities are unlocked as you play through the story.
There is also another upgrade system that you can control. As you play the game you get experience through killing enemies and finding hidden secrets. These earn you ability points that can be used to unlock upgrade in one of three different upgrade trees. These include things like upgrading your other earned abilities or giving your character new abilities to use. It is very flexible and all of the upgrades seem to make a noticeable difference to gameplay and aren't useless.
One of the best soundtracks I have heard in a game. Beatiful music artisticly crafted can manipulate your feelings. All of the music fits in perfectly with the situation. So sad scenes and high energy combat scenes all have the most appropriate music. The main menu soundtrack is absolutely incredible as well and is definitely something I wouldn't mind listening to again. There are so many unique tracks as well so you definitely won't get bored of listening to the same songs over and over. This soundtrack was definitely crafted with love and it definitely shows.
Man are these great. I thought trines graphics were something that couldn't be beaten and then I saw ori. This is something else. The whole game is beatiful and nothing seems out of place. They even put effort into the smallest of details like plants to make for a more complete and flawless experience. Never have I seen a game with such a consistent art style that is such a pleasure to look at.
This was something of a suprise. Usually games neglect animations and go for pretty basic ones that do the job just well enough to work. Ori didn't follow this trend. The animations flow so well. Everthing that is needed to is animated on the game and everything is flawlessly great. This includes the main character (ori), plants and enemies. The fact that they put so much effort into making even the animations perfect really shows how lovingly this game was crafted. All animations are unique and fantastic.
I can't recommend this game enough to anyone. if you are a fan of platformers then you will "LOVE" this game. It is definitely one of the greatest games I have ever played!

This game is really fun at the start when everyone has the same cards but then the real problems start to show. Fireball a basic spell you get costs 4 mana to use and does 150 dmg, It kills some 4 mana cards and even a couple 5 which is good. The problem is healing fireball and the healing spells, buildings, units in general. Healing fireball costs 2 half as much mana and heals for 400 over double what the 4 mana one does. Preistess is a 4 mana card that heals a unit near it, pretty normal for a game like this. The card however can attack while healing and can attack air units as well, meaning that the only counter to is using a spell like fireball right? nope. The game right now so far is someone saving for a large minion with a lot of health then puppy guarding it with cards that increase its health total as well as heal it like preistess or healing fireball. The spell that does the most damage is a 6 mana spell called Beam of Doom which generally kills most things besides the 7-9 mana costing cards. This means that you do not have a spell that can reliably kill their strategy. You might kill the preistess with this and damage the minion they are guarding but then they will only spend 2 mana and quickly heal it right up. Ive been trying to find a way to stop this and there is a 4 mana card called Lighting Bolt that kills a random enemy minion witch is the only way around this. If you hit the lighting bolt you tend to win but if you miss its a guranteed loss. The past couple days every game has been this way. I mainly play doubles but I have seen this problem in singles as well. Another problem with the game is shards. It costs 2000 shards to create a legendary card but if you somehow manage to get 2 of the same you can get rid of one for 500. The proportion is crazy bad. Getting a legendary from a pack seems damn near impossible too. I have played for 27 hours and I have only gotten one legendary and it wasnt from a pack, It was from doing achievements. I have only gotten 4 of the supreme rarity cards as well. This game can be fun, the expeditions are a really cool idea that I like a lot but so far the way to win is to play a deck that makes me want to tear my hair out. I tried to make a deck to get around this colossous play and you just cant. If they are playing Mordar no matter what you do you are going to lose. Lazer turret wont work beam of doom wont work absoloutly nothing will work. I really hope they fix this problem becuase if you want to try a fun or creative deck you will get your♥♥♥♥♥kicked time and time again

A bit early to tell what this will shape out to be, but as everyone says there's a lot of potential. I'm gonna skip the pros and cons, as everyone states its early access nature and lack of longevity as its current pitfalls, which is absolutely true. Instead, I'd like to have a more constructive conversation about what the game could use added to it.
Things I'd LOVE to see:
-Options for first person camera. This is a tad odd considering the current control style, but the 3rd person view camera mucks up now and again and is simply dreadful indoors. First person would add A. more immersion to some extent, and B. a secondary playstyle for one's preferences. Some people like 3rd person (especially young kids) and some people like first person, it's simple as that.
-A more complex resource system and division between exploration (survival?) and creative building. Currently adventure is very low-risk and low-intensity, like many lego games, but if there's anything minecraft has taught us, it's that the yungins prefer creative gameplay more than survival gameplay, due to its simplicity and sandbox nature. Meanwhile, it's readily becoming apparant that Lego has once again pitched to a larger age group than they may have intended. I'm 21 and I am STOKED for this game's future simply because I grew up with Lego Creator, Rock Raiders, Racers 2, and so forth. For longevity, more progression, and generally deeper adventure (especially for their older age group), finite resources and a bit more risk would definitely be a nice feature.
-The ability to reconfigure controls in the options menu. This is kind of a big deal, really. I assume it's inevitable at some point, but thought i'd bring it up anyways.
-Movable and interactive bricks. Once again, when we stumble into the procedural open world with adventure and building options, minecraft is what we look to for setting and more or less inventing the industry standard. One of the COOLEST things in minecraft for inventors for both fashion and function is pistons, movable doors, and so forth. I would love to see blocks with hinges, usable door blocks, and so forth to create a more readily interactive and modular environment. That is asking a bit much vs the current and oh-so-static terrain system, but it's also something the game currently lacks vs IRL legos, which this game is a fierce competitor to.
-Perhaps the ability to customize or build custom vehicles. It seems, with some exceptions, that vehicles rely largely on a somewhat standard brick building base and some animated/moving parts to add the OOMPH we look for in driving them. If nothing else, why not add a car or plane template brick, that you can later add parts on top of to modify the collision and operation of some. Think lego racers 2 car design, really. Maybe add part categories for drills, seats, doors, and so forth later, but even without those being able to build cars and maybe planes like lego racers 2's system would be amazing.
-More enemy variety, as far as abilities. All enemies currently seem to just fist fight, but maybe I missed an example. It'd be cool is skellies threw bones at you, wizards summoned minions, outlaws shot at you, and vampires had superior speed or something of the such. Currently combat is rather flat, and though finding bazookas and swords does spice things up,  adding more intelligent enemy design would go a long ways.
-Bring back some retro lego references. We have a couple, maybe, I know the skellies are a classic and the wizards are like the one I used to own as a kid, as well as having the ol' broad sword, hunting rifle, revolver, and so forth as weapons brings back some of the fan favorites as far as nostalgia is concerned. Why not insert some guys from rock raiders? Lego mars? Anything you can get to fit into the environment and add variety, really I know I had a blast being a caped skelly cowboy fighting zombies with a sword and traveling by bike- absurd but so unique and hilarious it carves a path of legitimacy by pure awesomeness. LEGO already preys upon nostalgia in the most rightous of ways, and they're looking to expand their contents, I'm sure, so why not hit 2 birds with one stone?
-More complex combat system. 4 hearts isn't BAD per say as a base for players and enemies, but it means weapons and items have to scale to very large landmarks to define their effectiveness. Most things at this point only differ in attack speed or whether or not they can damage geometry. If you inflated the states to 8 hearts, 10, or even a healthbar system for a very dynamic sense of combat. With this,you could do more fine adjustments than "4 shot kill vs 2 shot kill" and more like 5 vs 7 or any real combination inbetween.
-Character stats. Possibly tie it into a levelup system, but an even better idea (in my opinion) may be tying certain stats to certain character pieces. Let's say zombie pieces are slow but powerful, and cowboy clothes are fast, but weak in defense. You could tie in a lot of mini stats with a sort of balance, adding some tactic and planning to one's character, possibly a way to build unique and flawed (challenging) characters, and even tie in the stat relevance to the price of certain characters. This would really go a long ways in my opinion, but it's a rather far fetched concept, being more or less intertwined to inflated/scaleable stats.
This game has an amazing amount of potential and some OK starting concepts to begin with. If LEGO realizes the blockbuster of a goldmine they're sitting on, this could become one of the hardest hitting games of the next couple years, for a large multitude of reasons none-the-less.

I joined a game and was playing with one of the devs which was cool, by the end we had a team of 6 and it was very fun. We ran through the story mode in roughly a half hour. After that i continued to play with this group of guys in some of the other, more random modes. This was the best experince i had playing the game and i would deffinetly recomend it considering its fairly cheap. My biggest issue of the game is just a lack of players overall. Im not sure how many regular players there are now, but this game is much more fun with other people. That being said the game is also local which is a bonus.
Now with all that out of the way i can talk about the gameplay. This game feels very much like zombies ate my neighbors on the snes. It is a game based around surviving through a wave (survival mode) completing objectives and getting to the end (story), or running through a randomly generated dungeon. In the game you can unlock various kinds of new ammo, new weapons, and some cosmetic changes like: Hair, Glasses, Hats, and other things. The weapons are the most important because it can change how the you play. There are a good variety of weapons to chose from. You can have a melee weapon, or a ranged. There is only 3 melee at the moment, being a baseball bat, lightsaber thing, and a sword. The ranged weapons range from suppourt guns, to heal, Normal boring weapons, Grenades, Turrets, and lots of cool things to kill zombies. Currency is very important becuase your weapons have a durability meter, so you may have to rebuy weapons when old ones break. The store is seprate from the game and is acessed through the main menu, so always join a match prepaired. You can only bring one weapon into a game but have various slots and find weapons as you go.  The zombie killing feels very fun and even though you can only aim in 8 directions, opposed to full twinstick movement, it feels very fluid and smooth. Killing zombies is very satisfying as it sends their body parts flying and leaves a mess on the battlefield.
A few extra things i feel that need to be mentioned are the graphics and the music. God damn is the title screen music catchy and it may be somthing i will never forget and havent since i purchased this game way back when on Desura. The art style is very distinct and looks great. When i first saw this game show up on steam i instantly knew i had played it before, despite not even touching the game for like a year and a half, but seeing the art and hearing the music in the video made me instantly remember i had played this game on Desura.

I loved the first two games in the F.E.A.R. franchise. I loved the insane action, slow-motion roundhouse kicks and bodies exploding into Jell-O(tm) when you pumped a shell into them. I loved the freaky-deaky story, the mysterious protagonist(s) and the occasional flirt with enigmatic storytelling, the screeching, violin-falling-down-the-stairs soundtrack that worked in all its beautiful discordance and hair-raising abruptness. The scripted scares wove ladders, hallways, doors and windows into shockingly intricate little spookouts that contrasted with the bombastic shootouts that framed them, and it all just worked out so WELL. Hell, even the ending of the second game was pretty good in my eyes.
And then this game. Oh boy.
I hardly know what to say about it, and I hardly have the energy- even now- to summon a full-blown rant on this marvelous marvelous deconstruction of a once-great shooter franchise. The scares? Gone. The lonesome eeriness? Gone. Hope you like playing co-operatively with your psychic *** brother who has lost all of his charm now that you can see how he works and he's always trotting along beside you like a goddamn doberman. The Half-Life-esque presentation that kept you in the protagonist's perspective constantly and almost never thrust you into immersion-punching cutscenes? Hope you didn't like them, because apparently neither did WB. Did I mention that this game isn't scary?
It gets most of the action from previous titles right, but it's more than just lacking in the horror department. The game called... CALLED... 'Fear'? It doesn't even try to be scary. At all.

Strangely the game feels a lot more like COD than F.E.A.R.
As such I cannot recommend it.

It feels good to be back and reviewing Reus. Let’s begin.
I – Story [7/10]
Reus is a simulation, god game from Abbey Games. Story-wise there’s not much to Reus. The player takes control of four elemental giants and uses their powers to indirectly influence humanity developments and expansions. It is very much a choose your own adventure style of game and it worked rather well with this one.
II – UI [10/10]
The user interface in Reus can be pretty intimidating if you rush in before you get a decent handle on what you’re doing. Not to worry, as the game provides you with an excellent tutorial to walk you through it. Once you’ve played through said tutorial, the world will be your oyster as far as Reus is concerned. Everything you need to see is plainly displayed on the screen. If you’re not sure what something is just from the icon, hovering over it with the pointer for a few seconds will tell you all that you need to know.
III – Gameplay [9/10]
Getting things to happen that you actually want to happen in Reus can be challenging at times. As I stated above, you cannot control any humans directly. You are left to influence any advances through using your god-like powers and shaping the world around them. In order to get things done, you’ll have to experiment around and see exactly what things will do in what locations. It’s all very much trial and error.
Additionally, a balance must be kept between the giants and humanity. If you give too many resources to the humans, the can grow greedy. A high level of greed can lead to villages warring with each other or even with the giants themselves. There are several methods you can employ to keep the greed level in check. Certain combinations of symbioses with animals and minerals/plants can raise the village’s danger level. This makes the humans wary and keeps them too busy to get very greedy. Alternatively, you can sync up certain animals/minerals/plants to generate awe. This also keeps the humans in check and humble. Attacking the villages with the giants can cause the humans to become humble once more, but, on occasion, you may be left with no choice but to lay waste to their village in it’s entirety.
Ultimately, it is your call on how you want things to take shape, but you’ll have to lead it carefully in that direction.
IV – Content [8/10]
There is a seriously large amount of content in Reus and it will take you quite some time to discover/unlock all of it. There are five types of biomes for humanity to settle and explore. There are a great many varieties of animals, minerals, and vegetation alike. The giants all have their fair share of powers, but I feel like there could have been a little bit more content in that department. Cultivating a world is hard work with a limited tool box, but it still gets the job done in an enjoyable manner.
V – Visual [10/10]
The artwork in Reus is hand-drawn and beautiful. The giants are all very detailed and unique. All the animal and plant life you’ll encounter throughout the game is likewise intricately detailed the more you zoom in on it. Reus is eye candy for sure and it makes the game that much better.
VI – Audio [10/10]
Music appears intermittently throughout Reus, but when it does, it’s fantastic. It’s very lighthearted, even during combat sequences, and often incorporates overtones of victory and accomplishment. The sound effects are, likewise, good. Whether your using your powers to help humanity or put it back in it’s place, the sounds are wonderful. They are also relative to how closely zoomed in you are on the map.
VII – Overall [9/10]
Overall, Reus is a great game with deep gameplay and balanced learning curve. I picked this one up during the Steam Holiday Sale (what a bargain), but I wouldn’t have felt bad for paying full price on this one. If you’re looking for a weekend activity, Reus is a good choice.

I finished the longest era and thought I'd pretty much seen it by then, stopped playing it for about a year.
Well last month I came back to the game and I'm enjoying it so much more now. Instead of wanting to mess around I noticed how many of the things I never unlocked in this game and decided to really complete it. It's a lot more challenging than I thought and I really love it. In the end I'm playing it far less like a god game and much more like a city building kind of game, which makes a lot more sense because it involves a lot more 'building' planning than being all powerful, it's just that the buildings are animals and plants brought to life.
Anyway it's kind of hard to play this game in the background because at times you will need to spend quite some time looking up things on the wiki and thinking out a strategy to reach your next goal. However there are also some times where you just need to wait around for a while, because you've finished setting everything in place. This is where the gorgeous graphics and little details help a lot to still enjoy the time where you're doing nothing. I was quite surprised how far you can zoom in, much further than really necessary, and it'ce nice to see what's going on with this world you've created. Even though not much happens, everything is just so pretty to look at. And this really makes me want to unlock more things too, not just for the helpful effects but I really wonder what it will look like.
I'm not sure what else to say about the game, I just wanted to make sure it gtes my recommendation.

As a long term Ultima fan (not UO though) I enjoy the new game of Lord British.
Still in pre alpha stage the game shows a huge potential - and  I already have lots of fun to play.
Most positive aspect is the huge community with lots of ingame events like partys, maze runs and tournaments.
Not to forget the monthy great tour events where you can collect rare hats.
Outstanding is the feedback from the developers; they have monthly pre alpha releases with input from the players + regular hangouts with Q&A sessions. They also provide quite many patches for the most annyoing bugs (or ajust balancing).
Note about the higher pledge tiers and add-ons: you can spend quite some money on a higher pledge tier (which I did). This is not a P2W but mainly for a bigger house (the items are mainly decorative or have starter level, so may accelarate your start, but after some hours game play you can get equivalent gear). Housing will be limited and especially bigger lots be rare. You still can get a lot and house with ingame gold, but if you want to ensure to start with a nice lot you should think about pledgeing and supporting the development with a higher tier.

Please disregard all the negative feedback on this game, I have quite a few early access titles in my library and most of them I have given them negative reviews. Most of those were not the fact they were bad games. They were mostly given because of the lack of updates or updates on future updates. This game has one of the best development teams in the gaming industry and also the community is one of the best. All people are eager and willing to help when you first start. This is not a game you are going to just be able to pick up and go for the first npc you come across with an enormous star over there head, like in most mmos in the genre. You must talk to people by typing text or clicking keywords to the different npcs to get stuff added to your journal. After that you must explore the towns to find these other people you are looking for to finish your quest or adventure. So this is not Skyrim or even TESO, its more complex and in my opinion more fun. The game is no where near being finished but so far I still enjoy being a part of this fine community. This  is one you should never turn your back on because its going to be great
Note about this game before you buy dont think that you are going to be getting a head start with a player because right now its hard to build a character up because of frequent wipes. So just note that you are really buying the game to test and try to have fun doing so

This unconventional free-flying 2D action/puzzle/exploration indie game has quite a few good things going for it with the occasional flaw but overall a worthwhile experience.
The good:
1. Astoundingly beautiful, both still and in motion. Both the visuals and sound effects are excellent, the music was very fitting but did not particularly strike me as being memorable.
2. Smooth flying and generally peaceful exploratory gameplay with the occasional bit of stress when there's a fight you need to waggle out of (you cannot directly attack opponents but need to time grabbing them and/or environment objects to disable them) - there's a caveat mentioned in the bad below.
3. Interesting puzzles and setting, the story is not explained in depth but enough is said to build your own interpretation
The bad:
1. There are some rare bugs involving getting stuck in the environment. You can literally fly almost anywhere there is even a small crack so sometimes you can get stuck but thankfully there is a simple workaround described in the community guides here. This also works for a case I encountered where I had insufficient shards and could not progress as there were no more available in the areas accessible to me (the game was expecting a different completion order) but I got around the problem with said fix.
2. The ending is both shocking and lackluster, this was supposed to be a trilogy but insufficient sales killed off the sequels so the end here was rushed to a closure. Ignoring this, the mystery of the rest of the game is worth experiencing.
This is a game for people loving nature, exploration and a good (if somewhat vague) mystery. Sure, it may seem short but at the price it's worth going for.

You know those Hollywood comedy movie trailers? All the good jokes  end up in the trailer, very often making the movie seem interesting. Then you go about watching it and realize there's not much meat on those bones. The whole movie can fit in those 5 minutes of trailer footage and nothing would be lost. Secrets of Rætikon is like that - screenshots and videos oversell it. It's a visually charming game, yes, in which you get to fly through a forest filled with wildlife and mysteries. And that's pretty much it.
Downsides list is a bit more extensive than that. Let's start with the name - "æ", seriously? How do I even type that, let alone read it? Nevermind, let's go further. In SoR, you'll learn that forest animals are quite the racist scumbags. Nothing would unite a falcon, a crow and a lynx better than a killing campaign against an orange bird (= the player). And they're quite persistent about it, to the point where trying to move an object from screen to screen often becomes a Sisyphus's task.
The exploration part of the game is somewhat hindered by a lack of map or any other kind of orientation tool. This becomes most obvious near the end of the game - if you lack one item to finish the game, it may take you quite a while to find it. SoR is on the short site - it provides around two hours of gameplay, unless of course, you miss that one item, in which case the time might easily double.
Endgame sequence is one of the most wtf moments you'll ever witness by finishing a game, and not in a good way. After a gruesome scene that makes all your effort either seem in vain or just plain disturbing,  you get to play a dull dull dull match of pong and see a "game over" screen even if you win it. What?
Whoever is the visual artist of the game, please run to another studio while you can.
