I thought that name would have some deeper meaning behind it and it somewhat does. It's based on the Roman province of Raetia, which used to be located right where I live and in fact the name is still widely used and synonymous with our people. And the game is in fact set in the alps, so there's little confusion as to what is meant. However I'm not sure what the secret that lies here should be because as far as I can tell there isn't one.
I'd like to say that Secrets Of Raetikon is basically a cousin to FEZ, a highly stylized game with beautiful scenery and a gorgeous aesthetic built around collecting small pieces to either advance to the next area or form larger pieces that you need to collect as well to make the ending happen. But the reason I say it's only a cousin and not brother to FEZ is because it's nowhere near as good as FEZ. It's not a bad game per se, all the elements are there and work perfectly fine but what made FEZ interesting to me was the immense creativity put into building this world that seemed so utterly, soul-crushingly lonely in spite of the fact that the whole game looks absolutely awe-inspiring.
Secrets Of Raetikon tries to do similar things with the what I title "alien alphabet", though in this case they're just variations on runes, but it just seems like less effort went into building this world as opposed to FEZ. The game lets you collect runes throughout the game in order to decrypt a variety of messages in the game but A) I never needed to collect the runes because I for one can actually read a couple of variants of Futhark (runic alphabet) and even if you can't, most letters are made similar enough to the modern Latin alphabet that you shouldn't have much trouble deciphering the messages (I had all the letters of the first message decrypted instantly and only needed to wait for other messages to see how the other runes looked to deduce what they stood for) and B) the messages are entirely pointless. They try to paint this ethereal picture of what is happening in the game but unfortunately, there's no story or plot to be found in this game. Again if I may return to FEZ, yes if you just play the game, collect all the cubes and get to the end, you're none the wiser, but that game is chock full of clues as to what this world is about, even though the first messages of that game delivered by the golden cube were a silly joke form Phil Fish, but you had to actually decrypt an entire alien language with no hints given, as well as a numeric system that isn't easily translatable to arabic numbers. Not to mention all the other secrets and absolutely insane puzzles that game features. Secrets Of Raetikon by comparison basically has one puzzle you have to solve about 4 times in the whole game, which is collecting pieces of broken statues and putting them back together in order to unlock something.
And it just occurred to me that I haven't even talked about the gameplay yet. You play as a bird and fly around the levels and explore every last corner of the map because there are a variety of hidden sections masked as rock where you can actually fly through, so yeah, the secrets in this game are basically just hidden in plain sight with no thought required. However unlike FEZ, this game actually has other creatures, meaning different animals and not all of them are friendly. To defend yourself from them, you can pick up basically anything, including enemies, so you have ways of dispatching them by picking them up and throwing them into spikes or picking up thorny plants and smacking enemies with them. It's not that easy and it can get annoying at times because whenever you pick up one of the shards you need to bring back to the machine at the hub, all of the animals suddenly go berserk and want to take the shard away from you.
Another problem is the fact that this game makes you backtrack an enormous amount because the machine isn't located at the center of the world so every time you unlock a new area you can't go there directly from the hub, no the world is basically laid out in linear order from left to right like any regular side-scroller, so to get back from one part, you have to traverse all the previous levels to get back and the lack of a map-screen makes it hard at times to remember where you've already been and if you forgot to do something in one place it can take a while to remember where you have to go to get back to a certain place. Of the 3 hours it took me to beat this game, at least a quarter of that went into running back and forth and looking for level exits.
Another problem I have is with the ending so spoiler alert:
There are also two optional shards you can collect but one of them can only be found at the very end when you already almost beat the game, so I'm not sure why they included it. Maybe there's another secret hidden somewhere but once you collect those two you get a special power whereby you can suck everything in the world towards you. Don't know why and I'm not inclined to go back and investigate any more because in the end, I had limited fun with this game.
Like I said, the overall aesthetic of the game is magnificent, but the final execution simply leaves a lot to be desired. I'm usually the guy who likes these artsy pretentious games because they offer something different but in this case I'm really not satisfied with the result. And of course, and I know I sound like a broken record, but $10 for a 3 hour game where you really don't get to do much is simply too expensive. I bought the game somewhere else and paid less than that but I simply cannot recommend this game at full price for what it offers. Which is a shame because I was really looking forward to playing this when I saw gameplay trailers and screenshots.

For now, this is a first impression review. I will update this if I am able to finish the game or new and relevant info presents itself.
First off, this game is beautiful. For what it is, I cant think of a more artisitic presentation. Really, really pleasing to look at.
So, what is the game? hehehe...that is actually a good question. You are a bird, flying around, finding translations to the symbols that are seemingly used to present the story that defines the world. I have found ten so far I believe, so 16 to go (although I doubt I will need all 16 to translate the story). You are also unlocking aspects of the world, wich so far have been represented by releasing new animals into the environment. I have unlocked four of these so far, with another 6 or so to go. Each is a cage on a very large structure which you pick up pyramid pieces for and return to it to unlock said animal cages. The pyramid pieces are found by repairing other structures around the map, which you do by collecting and assembling the broken pieces of statues (so far) or by collecting other smaller pyramid pieces which you can, when you have collected enough, unlock the other buildings which then open up new map sections that hold the main pyramid pieces.
While you are doing all this, other birds and as you progress, other predatory creatures such as the lynx that you have released back into the wild, will attack you and each other, steal the pyramid pieces, and generally mess with you. You can fight back, which takes the form of dive bombing them, picking them up and dropping them from heights, causing the environment to hurt them (such as causing rock slides), and so on. You also have to contend with the winds, thorns, and other natural obstacles. You can regain health by uprooting small trees, saplings, and also by killing other critters.
anyway, so far, I have found all this to be quite interesting and yet marginally confusing all at once. You are pretty much left on your own to figure all this out, which is fine. The one real impediment however is a lack of an actual map so as to figure out where you are and how to get back to where you possibly might need to be. No map equals a lot of unnecessary flying around at times, trying to find your way back to the big building to unlock the next cage, and presumably later, even more wandering around tring to read all the statues that hold the runes you need to translate in order to actually read the storyline, lol. I really would have liked to have seen a map or mini map included with this game. That said, I am still enjoying the game and intend to continue on, but man....please ALWAYS put maps in games that require a lot of travel back and forth through a lot of different sections!!!
Oh...btw...this is a 2D metroidvania style scroller (the gameplay isnt metroidvania however, lol).

In the end I find that it is mostly a game of skill, of learning how to move around, dodging attacks and striking back whilst exploring the world. Therefor I strongly recommend using a controller and not going for the keyboard, as I did lol.
I think the vision was better than the actual result which was rather messy boxed up in beautiful graphics. So, if you understand their vision, I'm pretty sure you'll like it!

NO. GRINDING.

A bit early to tell what this will shape out to be, but as everyone says there's a lot of potential. I'm gonna skip the pros and cons, as everyone states its early access nature and lack of longevity as its current pitfalls, which is absolutely true. Instead, I'd like to have a more constructive conversation about what the game could use added to it.
Things I'd LOVE to see:
-Options for first person camera. This is a tad odd considering the current control style, but the 3rd person view camera mucks up now and again and is simply dreadful indoors. First person would add A. more immersion to some extent, and B. a secondary playstyle for one's preferences. Some people like 3rd person (especially young kids) and some people like first person, it's simple as that.
-A more complex resource system and division between exploration (survival?) and creative building. Currently adventure is very low-risk and low-intensity, like many lego games, but if there's anything minecraft has taught us, it's that the yungins prefer creative gameplay more than survival gameplay, due to its simplicity and sandbox nature. Meanwhile, it's readily becoming apparant that Lego has once again pitched to a larger age group than they may have intended. I'm 21 and I am STOKED for this game's future simply because I grew up with Lego Creator, Rock Raiders, Racers 2, and so forth. For longevity, more progression, and generally deeper adventure (especially for their older age group), finite resources and a bit more risk would definitely be a nice feature.
-The ability to reconfigure controls in the options menu. This is kind of a big deal, really. I assume it's inevitable at some point, but thought i'd bring it up anyways.
-Movable and interactive bricks. Once again, when we stumble into the procedural open world with adventure and building options, minecraft is what we look to for setting and more or less inventing the industry standard. One of the COOLEST things in minecraft for inventors for both fashion and function is pistons, movable doors, and so forth. I would love to see blocks with hinges, usable door blocks, and so forth to create a more readily interactive and modular environment. That is asking a bit much vs the current and oh-so-static terrain system, but it's also something the game currently lacks vs IRL legos, which this game is a fierce competitor to.
-Perhaps the ability to customize or build custom vehicles. It seems, with some exceptions, that vehicles rely largely on a somewhat standard brick building base and some animated/moving parts to add the OOMPH we look for in driving them. If nothing else, why not add a car or plane template brick, that you can later add parts on top of to modify the collision and operation of some. Think lego racers 2 car design, really. Maybe add part categories for drills, seats, doors, and so forth later, but even without those being able to build cars and maybe planes like lego racers 2's system would be amazing.
-More enemy variety, as far as abilities. All enemies currently seem to just fist fight, but maybe I missed an example. It'd be cool is skellies threw bones at you, wizards summoned minions, outlaws shot at you, and vampires had superior speed or something of the such. Currently combat is rather flat, and though finding bazookas and swords does spice things up,  adding more intelligent enemy design would go a long ways.
-Bring back some retro lego references. We have a couple, maybe, I know the skellies are a classic and the wizards are like the one I used to own as a kid, as well as having the ol' broad sword, hunting rifle, revolver, and so forth as weapons brings back some of the fan favorites as far as nostalgia is concerned. Why not insert some guys from rock raiders? Lego mars? Anything you can get to fit into the environment and add variety, really I know I had a blast being a caped skelly cowboy fighting zombies with a sword and traveling by bike- absurd but so unique and hilarious it carves a path of legitimacy by pure awesomeness. LEGO already preys upon nostalgia in the most rightous of ways, and they're looking to expand their contents, I'm sure, so why not hit 2 birds with one stone?
-More complex combat system. 4 hearts isn't BAD per say as a base for players and enemies, but it means weapons and items have to scale to very large landmarks to define their effectiveness. Most things at this point only differ in attack speed or whether or not they can damage geometry. If you inflated the states to 8 hearts, 10, or even a healthbar system for a very dynamic sense of combat. With this,you could do more fine adjustments than "4 shot kill vs 2 shot kill" and more like 5 vs 7 or any real combination inbetween.
-Character stats. Possibly tie it into a levelup system, but an even better idea (in my opinion) may be tying certain stats to certain character pieces. Let's say zombie pieces are slow but powerful, and cowboy clothes are fast, but weak in defense. You could tie in a lot of mini stats with a sort of balance, adding some tactic and planning to one's character, possibly a way to build unique and flawed (challenging) characters, and even tie in the stat relevance to the price of certain characters. This would really go a long ways in my opinion, but it's a rather far fetched concept, being more or less intertwined to inflated/scaleable stats.
This game has an amazing amount of potential and some OK starting concepts to begin with. If LEGO realizes the blockbuster of a goldmine they're sitting on, this could become one of the hardest hitting games of the next couple years, for a large multitude of reasons none-the-less.

As an animation enthusiast and active gamer, I was excited to find this game in development, back when it was only on Xbox 360 and Playstation 3. My favorite part was that nearly everything in this game, from the background to the character animations themselves, was hand-drawn. I respect any group of animators who put themselves through hand-drawn animation. Anyways, Skullgirls is a 2D fighting game about various girls with wacked-out themes fighting over an artifact dubbed "the Skull Heart," giving the winner absolute power and near-immortality. But, who cares about the prize? Fighting games have rarely given good endings.
Skullgirls features a very oddball cast of fighters. There's a schoolgirl with a hairy parasite, a circus freak who loves her pro wrestling, an adolscent girl who loves her cartoons, a literal cat burglar, a general who fights with her umbrella, a sexy ninja nurse, a demonic nun, a cybernetic cop that loves his jazz, a zombie girl with an undead dragon serpent, and, coming soon, an Egyptian goddess. A veru colorful cast, indeed.
This game is great for tournament players and I'm glad the love for this game has increased tenfold. Casual gamers may want to stay away from multiplayer and online functions, but I recommend this game for being visually dynamic and beautiful while maintaining the fast-paced style of old-school fighting games.

I love this game!  My first online game was Ultima Online.  I pledged early on for Shroud of the Avatar knowing that this was not going to be Ultima Online, but a game created by Lord British. The developers care about the community and listen to what we say and suggest.   The overall direction of Shroud of the Avatar leaves me to believe this will be one of the best MMO's out there, and perhaps replace Ultima Online as my favourite MMO of all time. Overall this is an excellent game, amazing community, with a strong development team.  I have 0 regrets in my pledges!  Keep up the great work!

This is the single most absorbing, engaging and addictive game I have played - and it is only pre-alpha!
There are pluses and minuses:
Plus:
A rich, wonderfully textured and graphic sandbox environment, where the player is free to explore and quest at will.
A deep, engaging underlying quest (this is not released at this stage of development)
Many mini quests given by NPCs for varied rewards
Classless character development - be the kind of person you want to be
Continual challenges - either PvE or PvP, according to preference
Ability to beautify and decorate homes "from the ground up" - using only materials harvested from the environment
An amazing, cooperative and supportive community, which is already giving rise to in-game events (tournaments, exploration quests. welcome quests, in game radio, plays, fan fiction stories, parties, hangouts)
The "tease" of having to figure things out by serious questing and talking to NPCs - there is no exclamation mark to poke you along a quest.
Minus:
It is pre-alpha. As clearly stated on the login screen, it is a work in progress. Many elements are under construction, some things do not yet work. Full optimization is yet to happen, loading times can be slow. Unless this is understood it can cause frustration.
Because the game is changing so rapidly (monthly releases with new content each time) a detailed player handbook is not possible. New players can be bewildered. An in-game player guide provides elementary advice, also I recommend two things:   Asking advice in game is usually worthwhile. The players are mostly helpful, courteous and will freely give advice and help. Also if you post a question at the forum at
it will be answered in no time.
Overall, watching this game develop is like watching the growth of an architectural masterpiece. Even with bare walls and a skeleton the scale and grandeur can be appreciated. I truly believe it will be a game to surpass all others.

This game started out so good. I was getting ready to have a nice relaxing atmospheric run like Dear Esther but more proactive. It showed some really pretty art and I dropped to the ground and messed around with the controls collecting stuff and poking at the wildlife and enjoying the sights.
Then it all went to♥♥♥♥♥♥ Not only is there no map or fast travel - something which immediately becomes obvious and a big problem when you make your first shard since you have to make a return trip every time you make it and they get longer as the game goes on - but there is also no reliable way to defend yourself. I understand the whole thing about being a non-predatorial bird creature but come on. In nature any bird that can lift animals can pretty efficiently dive bomb them to the ground. Here it sometimes works and sometimes doesn't. Much like the "weapons" and dropping heavy objects on things.
Enemies are not similarly handicapped by any means, they will relentlessly and brutally attack you. Some of them will outright grab you and stop you from moving while mauling you with no means of escape. Apparently the enemies I experienced were the nerfed ones. One can only imagine how they were on initial release.
Now one could easily say "meh, I can handle that." and be absolutely correct. However the biggest issue is that (at least in my playthrough) there is a bug in the positioning of slivers - the things that you build shards with - that make one in particular get placed behind a background object. Making it unreachable without editing your save files. Which is what I did as detailed
so that I could complete the game.
Wasn't really worth it in the end though. I normally have a policy of not spoiling in reviews even using spoiler tags, but here it's so pointless I might as well say it.
I don't know if either of those things were an attempt to be "edgy" or philosophical but they failed in both respects. Making it just seem silly.

The premise for a good game, trapped in a mediocre one. Rather disappointed in this game, all things considered. The entire design of the game is just... flawed. You have to find things in the game world with no indication of where they are and no map to look at when you're not sure where else is left to check, so you can end up running around in circles because you have no clue where you need to be. When you find the relics you need, you have to bring each. and. every. one. back to one room. This involves carrying them across multiple decent-sized screens, with other wild animals chasing you and trying to steal the relic from you, at which point they toss it between each other in an attempt to♥♥♥♥♥♥you off, err, I mean, keep it away from you. What does this tedious slog accomplish? It's not more than a frustration builder. Not even "hard", just frustrating. There's also instances where you have to attempt to solve a puzzle with an animal attacking you (and no effective way to fend it off) which usually results in tanking damage to get what needs to be done, done. The game's save system is bare-bones, to the point where it can only hold one fixed state, so everything you do is permanent and it's possible to glitch in the terrain or otherwise make the game nigh-unwinnable in various ways. Fortunately, the game is short (a few hours, max, and only some 6-7 major screens, with a few subscreens). Which is for the better, since any bigger and it'd be impossibly frustrating.
I like the premise though. The main character controls well, the environment is pretty, the music relaxing. The language, not so much, I would've preferred an auto-translate for any runes you'd found, I couldn't be bothered to translate myself. The ending's also not great. To spoil it, spec ops: the line, bird edition. That's not really an explicit spoiler, but ehh. The game's story isn't exactly the focus here, as far as I can tell.
Overall, I wanted to enjoy this game, but there's just... not a lot to enjoy.

You play a girl from a village that had their idol statue stolen. 3 Heroes from the prior games (Not on PC all tablet) figured since they saved the world they are entitled to everything so they are on a mass pilfering spree. The villager finds them and beats them up only to find out that they did not steal the statue. The surrounding villages have also had their statues stolen. For its simplistic look it is really a very good looking game. You can tell that this is a port from a tablet. The music is outstanding and is even available as a soundtrack. There is no voice dialog but the storyline and text dialog a great. The game makes fun of the whole RPG and Anime environment.  The characters are often making fun of each other and making jokes. Each character has a specialty and can learn most the others.
You have the main girl who does Earth damage, the second girl (the "pretty one") who uses advanced magic and anime style heals, a techno guy who uses guns and has a tank, and the last guy who does mostly direct damage "meat shield".
The game looks simplistic and will quickly ramp up in difficulty. Definitely a great turn based RPG game to have with lots of comedy!

Reus has a cute, endearing art style that really works and brings the game together into a cohesive whole. The problem is that that cohesive whole is more of a morsel than a full meal. Gameplay purely comes down to optimizing a very small set of tiles while managing a similarly small set of values, and that truly boils down to a lot of tedious testing which feels more like work than fun. Or you could just go search the wiki for optimal builds, because ultimately, memorizing what building goes with what other building is your end goal. Once you know that, the game is over, and that just isn't enough depth to persuade me to choose it over the myriad of other strategy titles.
Abbey Games was really onto something with Reus. I see the potential, but somewhere along the way, they took a wrong turn. I really wanted to like this game -- and I did enjoy the art style -- but the gameplay truly fell short. And what is a game without good gameplay?

To sum Reus up in a few lines:
1 - You start off with a clean world, create habitats and life. Nice!
2 - People start settling, you grant those people what they need. Noone is complaining!
3 - Everyone is happy and loves you. This should be easy now...
4 - Different peoples start to have different objectives. Tough, but doable.
5 - Villages start to attack each other. Hey, stop that!
6 - A massive avalanche of goals and deadlines start to overcome you and
7 - OH GOD WHY THE HELL DO YOU GUYS KEEP ATTACKING THOSE HALF-WITTED FISHERMEN WHO THE HECK TAUGHT YOU THIS BULLSH*T AND WHY IS THAT GUY NOT RESPONDING TO
8 - You start off with a clean world...

Very good expansion to the F.E.A.R. series. I just wish that metacritic didn't belittle it so much. Thanks to Metacritic, we're probably not getting another game. F.E.A.R. 2 was the best for story, F.E.A.R. 3 is the best gameplay, and F.E.A.R. 1 was AMAZING when it came out. Just a good series all around.

Altough I recommend, be warned. This almost feels like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ cousin of Farcry, the Farcry that was hidden under the sofa from the neighbours. I would only suggest this for big fans of the series.
Graphics:
- Good, rich environments and very varying techniques. I thoroughly enjoyed the visual quality of this game. But it clearly looks like a console game. The performance is good, but I did have to drop my Antisotropic Filtering slightly which baffles me?
Sounds:
- Good, realistic and believable but suffers from the same problem as Fear 2 in that the music is cued and sometimes kicks off in strange intervals during a fire-fight.
Gameplay:
- This game is not scary. It is deviod of scares and just doesn't have the same element of fright as 1 & 2.
- The environments are varied, and are done justice. Altough I do not like the fact that the game starts in Brazil, it was believeable.
- Not all of the guns are useful, I hated the Combat Shotgun and only used the pistol when I was forced to. SOme weapons were absolutely useless.
- The AI sucks, it seems to have gotten worse as the series has progressed.
- The game is riddled with FMVs. FMVs? Is this the 90s? Is this Final Fantasy? I don't want FMVs in my action-shooters, I want action.
Story:
- Load of crap. It feels like multiple people had their opinions and ideas added and removed as the story progressed and the full view was just hard to follow and uninteresting.
- I do like that they included The Point Man, Paxton Fettel & Becket, but the weaving of the characters together is so forced it feels like it's being helf together by super-glue and band-aids.
- The protagonist (The Point Man) is so unlikeable it's ridiculous. He looks like a serial-killer and acts like someone who would NEVER have been accepted into the F.E.A.R. operatives in the first place.
- The game starts in Brazil. Brazil? of all places, why Brazil? It's so far removed and misplaced. Guantanamo Bay, I could still believe, but a random slum in Brazil? WTF?

I just finished this game after having it in my backlog for quite a long time and honestly part of me wished I didn't play this game at all because of how much I love F.E.A.R and F.E.A.R. 2. Don't play this if you loved the previous F.E.A.R. games, which sucks to say, but this is not the experience you'd want for a sequel.
Performance/graphics:
Performance is ok in the sense that I was able to play at 120fps most of the time, but did have dips on occasion, There aren't as many graphics options compared to the first two games, but there are still some. What really bothered me was the forced Motion Blur the game had and the only way to turn it off is via an options.cfg in the game's local folders. Not too big of an inconvenience, but definitely something they should have added in the game's options menus especially when it was toggable  in the previous two games. Graphics themselves are ok, still good looking, but honestly F.E.A.R. 2 looks way better, at leas to me.
Combat:
F.E.A.R. 3's combat is 100% different compared to the first two. Obviously they're all FPS games, but the actual weapon combat(aiming, weapon firing/response, etc.) is completely different and I don't think it was for the better. You're limited to only two weapons at a time, no medkits/armor pickups(regenerative health), but there is still slow-mo and vehicles in the game. Also there are still around the same amount of weapon variation in the game compared to the first two, but you're just limited to only two at a time which I think is a huge negative, but might be because of the co-op mode the game has, so to balance it out.
Atmosphere:
Still "scary", but compared to the first two games F.E.A.R. 3 is more action than horror and that's bad. I'm not sure if it was because of the co-op addition so they couldn't account for player positioning for jumpscares or scene build ups correctly, but the games are suppose to be scary, but this game probably only scared me once out of the four hours I played it.
Story:
I appreciate the closure the game has given me for wanting more after completely F.E.A.R. 2, but I wish I didn't experience this closure exactly. The game has two endings, one considered "Good" and one "Bad", but I'd say both are pretty bad. I won't post spoilers, but if you love F.E.A.R and F.E.A.R. 2, don't play this.
Price:
This game is not worth $19.99, not even close to that. I got it for $4.99 a while back and that's honestly all I would feel comfortable paying.

The final entry in the F.E.A.R. franchise as of this writing, F.E.A.R. 3 provides a much better story than that of F.E.A.R. 2 (which could fit on a post-it and was generally non-existant and boring), better visuals, better performance and much better gameplay. Is it better than F.E.A.R. 1? No, but it's a lot of fun in single player (I don't play co-op) and offers a campaign both as Point Man and Fettel, with the Point Man being the protagnist of the first game and Fettel being a ghost, offering interesting dynamics. The shooting is fast and fluid and the bullet-time mechanics the franchise is known far work beautifully in a series of shootouts involving soldiers and mechs providing a varied challenge. The addition of stick to cover mechanics isn't distracting. Although the shooting takes place mostly in tightly scripted sequences of areas with the occasional signposting problem where you need to look around to figure out where to go next, the steady clip of the action punctuated by good cutscenes maintains a solid pace throughout. A satisfying conclusion to the series that redeems the pathetic F.E.A.R. 2 and although I'd have liked more of the super intelligent AI of F.E.A.R. 1, this'll do.
